Sixteen and built like a gate hinge: tall for a clay boy, narrow, with slip dried to the colour of old bone up both forearms and a permanent bend in his left little finger from a splinter off the wheel when he was eleven. He cuts his hair short so Ash cannot nest in it, which is a thing the district notices and he never explains. His eyes do not finish sentences; they go to the door, to the fire, to the wheel, and come back without reporting. He smells of damp clay, tallow and the sweetish edge of lead glaze carried up from High Kiln on a bad wind. The thing people notice first is his hands, which are the hands of a thrower and have been working since he was nine. The thing they notice last is that he never looks at Sella when she speaks to him, though he obeys her instantly.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Short, flat, declarative. He asks almost no questions, and when he does it is the tool rather than the clay: \emph{Is it dry? Did you fire it? Who wrote it?} He speaks to the wheel and to the pots as other men speak to animals, and only then to people. When he is angry he gets quieter, the way Sella does, and the household has learned to read the lowering of his voice as a weather signal. He never says \emph{with} or \emph{against} when \emph{I haven’t said} will do.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The wheel doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady.”

\item “You want me to say it. I’m not saying it.”

\item “Sella. Don’t feed him from your own dish. He’s not Vail.”

\item “A slate burns in four minutes. Four. I’ve timed it.”

\item “I didn’t say I was with them. I said I wasn’t against them. That’s different. In this district it isn’t, but it’s what I said.”

\item “He’s not Vail.” --- said in the kiln-house at first light, refused an answer, and sealed by the boy’s arrival.

\item “You’ll do.” --- to the pot on the wheel, in a voice with no welcome in it and no unkindness either.

\item “It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady.” --- to the wheel before anyone, said again on Day 140 of a pot he told \emph{You’ll do} while keeping its full note from a High Kiln kiln-master who said it was singing before its time.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He is the son of Garl and Sella Vail, and he took the wheel at thirteen when Garl died in the Long Cold and did not come back and nobody came to draw him. The wheel had been Garl’s for twenty years and the seat was worn hollow; Jorra has spent three years trying to fill that hollow with his own weight. He has thrown pots since he was nine, fired them since eleven, and knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves his hands, though he will not say so in front of the kiln-masters, who would call it early and make something of it. His house has remembered the Ash Rising since Y.H. 668, when children were taken and the rising was put down by a man with a list; the memory is kept not in stories but in the way certain doors are never closed and certain names are never entered. Since he was fourteen men from the Broken Slates have come into the back room of the kiln-house and spoken in low voices. He has listened to all of them and told none of them yes.

He watched Enna, his sister, die of the second chill at four, and has never forgiven the fire for being warm while she cooled. He watched his father die and was sent to find a collector and could not cross the ford, and has never asked whether he was sent too late or whether he was sent at all. When Corin arrived he said one sentence — \emph{He’s not Vail} — and has said nothing about it since, which in that house is a form of argument.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
A father who went uncollected, a sister who went cold in a warm room, and a wheel he was given before he was ready. He fears Sella will die with something unsaid and leave him holding the house and the lie together. He fears the Broken Slates will decide for him what he is, because he has not decided and the longer he waits the more their decision looks like his own. He fears the boy most of all, because the boy hears things. His contradiction: he is the most careful keeper of the Vail fire in four generations and he is quietly helping the people who want to burn every slate in Sill. He has never once thought these two facts cannot live in the same man.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants the wheel to stay in the house and the fire to hold and nobody to write the boy down as Vail without asking him first. He thinks he wants Sella to say that he has done well with the wheel. What he needs is to learn that burning a slate does not return a person to you, and that the anger he has been nursing for three years is not his alone — it has been lent to him by men who intend to collect on it.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Sella Vail} — his mother. He believes she took Corin in to replace Enna and to keep the house’s standing after Garl died. She has never contradicted him. Every obedience he gives her is therefore double: it is love and it is a correction neither of them will make. \emph{Ch 2:} she announced the taking and he answered \emph{he’s not Vail}; she got quieter and gave him no answer at all. He went on working, did not look at her, and shifted the damper before she had finished telling him to.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling. Jorra was the first in the house to notice that the boy turns his head toward a pot before anyone taps it, and that he does it to hear the note, not the noise. He has told nobody. He resents the boy for being given a bed in the house while the clay-bound hand sleeps in the loft, and he cannot stop watching him. \emph{Ch 2:} the foundling arrived under the roof and nobody wrote him as Vail, which is what Jorra wanted and what he cannot bear. He spoke to the wheel, to the pots and once to Tarn about a rasp out of its place, and never addressed the boy.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — attended Enna’s death and Corin’s birth, and has never met Jorra’s eye for longer than a moment. He knows she wrote something down the night Enna died and has never asked to see it, because asking would make it a thing between them.

\textbf{Tarn} — the Vail’s clay-bound hand. Jorra treats him as a brother when the wheel needs him and as a servant when it does not. Tarn has decided to hate him for it and keeps failing, because Jorra once sat up all night with him through a fever and has never mentioned it. \emph{Ch 2:} Tarn was given the loft while the foundling was given the bed, and said so in one sentence to Sella. Jorra said nothing; he has never defended the household’s arithmetic and never contests it.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — Jorra threw a stone at his door in Y.H. 810 and denied it. The Thane suspects the boy is with the Broken Slates and lets him be, which Jorra finds more frightening than being watched.

\textbf{Ch 4.} Sella’s hand went to the mark before the kiln and not at the bank; he shifted the damper before she had finished and again at dusk, and did not take up her silence about the back room. The boy was at the edge of his notice as a thing that hears: he spoke to the pots and not to him, and came in from the back room with slate dust worked into his forearms --- grey and fine, not slip --- and said \emph{the back room’s cold} to nobody. He wanted the boy outside the name Vail and the hollow seat his, and did not say either.

\textbf{Ch 5.} The wheel took the house into its rhythm again with slip dried to old bone up both forearms and no slate dust on Stone 13 or Stone 15; the boy noticed the absence and could not ask which it meant. He told a pot \emph{you’ll do}, told the wheel it did not care whose hands were on it, and shifted the damper before Sella had finished telling him the fire was low. He did not say the back room was cold. \emph{He’s not Vail} stayed sealed as it had been on the hour it was spoken, and the foundling went on being carried under the roof without a Vail name, which is what Jorra wanted and what he could not bear.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On all five days he came in from the shed with bone-coloured slip dried to old bone up both forearms and the bent little finger, and no slate dust; the boy noticed the absence and could not ask what it meant. He told a pot \emph{you’ll do} and \emph{the shoulder’s thick}, told the wheel it did not care whose hands, only if they were steady, and moved the damper before Sella had finished telling him the fire was low, going in with the bent finger ahead of his hand. He did not say the back room was cold and did not look toward the basket or the bed. \emph{He’s not Vail} stayed sealed; the foundling went on being carried under the roof unwritten.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 23, after five mornings of clean bone-coloured slip, he came in from the back room with fine grey slate dust worked into the creases of his forearms past the bend of the little finger and said nothing about where he had been; the boy read the arranged face the way he had once read a resident who kept his eyes on a chart. He told the pot she would want a thinner slip, told the wheel it did not care whose hands, only if they were steady, and went to the damper before Sella had finished, the bent finger going in first. On Stone 25 the forearms were clean again and he kept dusty and clean as two entries; on Stone 29 the sweeping talk made him quieter and the yard straightened around it without an order. He knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel and would not say so in front of a kiln-master, who would call it early and make something of it; the boy knows this about him as he knows the bent finger, and keeps both where questions can last for years. He did not say the back room was cold and did not look toward the bed; \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed through the year’s last market.

\textbf{Ch 8.} Through the Five the wheel-shed gave him bone-coloured slip dried to old bone up both forearms and the bent little finger leading at the damper; he moved the damper before Sella had finished and did not say the back room was cold. No slate dust came after the Last Day and he never mentioned the back room; he did not look toward the bed or the basket. On the Last Day the grey in the corners was still where it lay and the baking went on around it, and he went quieter as the sweeping talk went around. On Ilmen 1 he worked the slip toward the thaw and the pits with the same forearms and the same silence, and the foundling went into the new year carried under the roof without a Vail name.

\textbf{Ch 9.} On Ilmen 4 he came in from the back room with fine grey slate dust worked into the creases of his forearms past the bend of the little finger and said nothing about where he had been; on the other mornings the forearms carried bone-coloured slip, and the boy kept the two states apart. He told a pot it would do, told the wheel it did not care whose hands, and went to the damper before Sella had finished, the bent finger going in ahead of his hand. He knew the full note of a Vail pot before it left the wheel and would not say so before a kiln-master. He agreed with nobody about the thaw and contradicted nobody, and his silence went around the yard as its own weather signal. He did not look toward the basket and did not say the back room was cold.

\textbf{Ch 10.} He comes in from the wheel-shed with bone-coloured slip dried to old bone up both forearms and no grey slate dust worked into the creases past the bend of his little finger on the days the boy watches; on Ilmen 11 the bent finger goes in ahead of his hand at the damper and he moves it before Sella has finished telling him the fire is low, so she shuts her mouth on the instruction and gives it to the pot. He tells a pot \emph{You’ll do} and tells the wheel it does not care whose hands are on it, only if they are steady, and does not say the back room is cold. He does not look toward the basket or the bed, has not been told about the woman in the brook and has not asked. Garl’s proverb still goes to the pot and his own unfinished sentence still goes nowhere; \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed through seven more days.

\textbf{Ch 11.} He came in from the wheel-shed on all three days with slip dried to the colour of old bone up both forearms and no grey worked past the bend of his little finger, the bent finger going in ahead of his hand at the damper each time, moved before Sella had finished telling him the fire was low. He told a pot \emph{You’ll do} and the wheel what it had been told a hundred times --- that it did not care whose hands were on it, only if they were steady --- and said nothing of the room off the shed, whose door kept its finger’s width of open. He did not say the back room was cold and did not look toward the bed or the basket. Garl’s salt-stiff coat kept a broader man’s shape on its peg, the hollow seat its twenty-year lean, and the clean dark line where the ridge had turned was not swept, because a line left where it is is still a line kept. \emph{He’s not Vail} stayed sealed as tightly as on the hour it was spoken.

\textbf{Ch 12.} On Day 50 he came in from the room off the shed with grey slate dust past the bent finger and said nothing, and Sella did not ask; the dust went on a tray of its own beside the clean slip of the other mornings. He told the pots and the wheel and not the basket, moved the damper ahead of her instruction with the bent finger leading, and did not say the back room was cold or look toward the bed. He knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel and would not say so before a kiln-master. The promise of Corin’s name to the people who burn slates stayed where it has always stayed, ungiven and not withdrawn, and \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed.

\textbf{Ch 13.} He came in from the wheel-shed with slip dried to the colour of old bone up both forearms and no grey worked past the bend of his little finger. He spoke to the wheel before he spoke to anyone, told it what it had been told a hundred times --- it did not care whose hands were on it, only if they were steady --- and told a pot \emph{You’ll do} in a voice with no welcome in it and no unkindness either. He knew the full note of a Vail pot before it left the wheel and would not say so before a kiln-master, who would call it early and make something of it. Sella had not finished telling him the fire was low; his bent finger went in ahead of his hand at the damper and moved it, and the end of her sentence arrived at the pot instead of at him. He did not say the back room was cold and did not look toward the bed or the basket. The men who came into that room were not named and the broken birth-slates lay under the drying rack where the yard went around them and entered them into nothing; \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed as tightly as a lid.

\textbf{Ch 14.} On Silt 4 the room off the wheel-shed kept its finger’s width of open all morning and Jorra came through with fine grey slate dust worked into both forearms past the bend of his little finger, not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel; two men had come in since first light and spoken low, and he gave the house no name for them. The broken birth-slates stayed under the lowest rack where the yard went around them and entered them into nothing, and the boy kept the dusty forearms and the clean ones on one tray as two states of one morning. Jorra spoke to the wheel before he spoke to anyone — it did not care whose hands, only if they were steady — told a pot it would do, and knew the full note of a Vail pot before it left the wheel without saying so before a kiln-master. When Sella had not finished telling him the fire was low, his bent finger went in ahead of his hand at the damper and moved it, so that the end of her sentence arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence. He did not say the back room was cold, did not look toward the bed or the basket; \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed as tightly as a lid and the promise of the foundling’s name to the men who burn slates was ungiven and not withdrawn.

\textbf{Ch 15.} On Silt 14 he came through the finger’s-width-open door off the wheel-shed in the afternoon with fine grey slate dust worked into both forearms past the bend of his little finger, not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel; two men had come in since first light and spoken low and he named neither the men nor the room. The broken birth-slates stayed under the lowest rack where the yard went around them and entered them into nothing. He spoke to the wheel before he spoke to anyone --- it did not care whose hands, only if they were steady --- told a pot it would do, and knew the full note of a Vail pot before it left the wheel without saying so before a kiln-master from High Kiln. When Sella had not finished telling him the fire was low, his bent finger went in ahead of his hand at the damper and moved it, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence. He did not say the back room was cold. On Silt 15 he came through again with bone-coloured slip dried to old bone up both forearms and no grey worked past the bend; the grey dust was the day before. He did not look toward the bed or into the basket. \emph{He’s not Vail} stayed sealed as tightly as a lid nobody had tried to lift in three years, and the promise of the foundling’s name to the men who burn slates was neither given nor withdrawn.

\textbf{Ch 16.} On Day 77, Silt 18, he comes through the finger’s-width-open wheel-shed door with fine grey slate dust worked into both forearms past the bend of his little finger, not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel; two men had come in since first light and spoken low in the back room and he gave the house no name for them. On Day 76 his forearms carried clean bone-coloured slip dried to old bone, and the boy kept the two states of one week on a single tray and asked neither which slate was broken nor whether it was a birth-slate. The broken birth-slates stay under the lowest rack, gone around by the yard and entered by nobody. He speaks to the wheel before he speaks to anyone --- \emph{It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady} --- tells a pot \emph{You’ll do}, knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel and will not say so before a kiln-master from High Kiln. When Sella has not finished telling him the fire is low, his bent finger goes in ahead of his hand at the damper and moves it, so the end of her instruction arrives at the pot and the household straightens around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted. He does not say the back room is cold and does not look toward the bed or the basket. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed as tightly as a lid nobody has tried to lift in three years, and the promise of the foundling’s name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 22 he comes through the finger’s-width-open door off the wheel-shed with fine grey slate dust worked into both forearms past the bend of his little finger, not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel; men came in since first light and spoke low and he gives the house no name for them. The broken birth-slates stay under the lowest rack, gone around and entered by nobody. When Sella has not finished telling him the fire is low, his bent finger goes in ahead of his hand at the damper and moves it, so the end of her instruction arrives at the pot and the household straightens around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted. He does not say the back room is cold and does not look toward the bed or the basket. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed as tightly as a lid nobody has tried to lift in three years, and the promise of the foundling’s name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} Sella’s unfinished sentence still arrives at the pot instead of at him and the household straightens around his silence; he has not looked at her and has not answered with a word. With Corin nothing has changed: the boy lies under the roof unwritten, \emph{he’s not Vail} is sealed as tightly as on the hour it was spoken, and the promise of his name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn. With Tarn the old equality of duty and silence holds, neither asking about the back room or the ear. Berr’s watching and his own silence about the Broken Slates are unchanged; Alda’s writing and the boy’s mother remain things he has not asked to see or hear. No bond was paid or spoken this chapter.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
\textbf{Ch 80.} Through Frost 22–24 he keeps the wheel-shed edge: meal-fine grey slate dust ground small as meal past the bent finger and under the nails, not bone-coloured slip; dusty forearms parted from clean as a surgeon parts clot from vessel; speech to the wheel and a pot before any person, \emph{It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady} and \emph{You’ll do}; the full note known three turns ahead with air under it and a want in it and withheld; men unnamed going low into the back room before first grey on all three mornings with no name given and no word that the room was cold; the bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence. The burned slate stayed at four, the shut-room tellings at two, the three pot sayings with the premature Smoke 14 note apart, the row at five askings with one shaping and no witness, \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed and the promise of the foundling’s name neither given nor withdrawn. The Frost 14 saying gained a third shaping on Frost 23 from an ownerless voice over the boards and the well-roof, the slate-runner once carrying a name the district spent and not saying whose; it was filed beside the first two with a finger between every pair, not a witness, not a cause, not a confession, not a joining and not paid, and did not make Hessa Rale a reader. No bond was paid or spoken and no new scar or possession came.

\textbf{Ch 79.} Through Frost 19–21 he keeps the wheel-shed edge: meal-fine grey slate dust ground past the bent finger, dusty forearms parted from clean, speech to the wheel and a pot before any person, the full note of the pot known three turns ahead with air under it and a want in it and withheld on the near-full tray. His bent finger goes into the cold iron of the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, one iron with two bites joined to no kiln. Men unnamed go low into the back room before first grey on all three mornings and get no name from him; burned slate stands at four, the shut-room tellings at two, the three pot sayings with the Smoke 14 note apart, the row question at five askings with one shaping and no witness. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the boy’s name is neither given nor withdrawn; the Frost 14 saying holds with one saying and one second shaping and is not joined to anything under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 78.} Through Frost 16–18 he keeps the wheel-shed edge: meal-fine grey slate dust ground past the bent finger, dusty forearms parted from clean, speech to the wheel and a pot before any person, the full note of the pot known three turns ahead with air under it and a want in it and withheld on the near-full tray. His bent finger goes into the cold iron of the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, one iron with two bites joined to no kiln. Men unnamed go low into the back room before first grey on all three mornings and get no name from him; burned slate stands at four, the shut-room tellings at two, the three pot sayings with the Smoke 14 note apart, the row question at five askings with one shaping and no witness. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the boy’s name is neither given nor withdrawn; the Frost 14 saying holds with no second shaping and is not joined to anything under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 72.} Through Smoke’s last tend the wheel-keeper keeps the meal-fine grey dust and the two bites of the damper on trays of their own, with the burned-slate word at four, the shut-room tellings at two, the three pot sayings with the Smoke 14 note apart and the row question at five askings with one shaping and no witness. The third reading of Smoke changes the district’s arithmetic and comes to nothing under this roof. He has not decided which side he is on and the men who burn slates have not decided for him; the promise of the boy’s name stays ungiven as the seventh year at the debt’s end presses nearer.

He enters at the wheel with his weight in the hollow his father wore and has spent three years failing to fill --- slip dried to the colour of old bone up both forearms, the left little finger bent from a splinter at eleven, a story about a fight he tells because a fight sounds more like him. In Chapter 2 he says one flat sentence about the foundling and is refused an answer, and the sentence is sealed by the boy’s arrival: a child lies under the roof and nobody has written him as Vail. He does not look at his mother while obeying her instantly, speaks to the pots before people, goes quiet when the levy is spoken of, and has given none of the men who come into the back room a word they can carry away. He is the most careful keeper of the Vail fire in four generations and is quietly helping the people who want to burn every slate in Sill, and has never once thought the two facts cannot live in the same man. Through the middle tend of Grain his dust, his wheel and his withheld note kept their old order while the burned-slate word held at four and the pot sayings at three; the wrong-wind voice on Grain 15 let one saying stand without a pot lost, and the promise of the boy’s name stayed ungiven (T035/T031/T065/T095 held, T061/T082).

On Days 5 and 6 the back room comes into the house on his forearms as slate dust, grey and fine, worked into the creases past the bend of the little finger, and not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel. He tells the pots \emph{you’ll do}, shifts the damper before Sella has finished telling him and shifts it again at dusk, and says \emph{the back room’s cold} to nobody in particular --- not an answer and not a question, shaped so nobody can take it further. Sella does not take it further. The boy watches the dust and wants to know which slate was broken, and whether it was a birth-slate, and keeps the questions where questions can last for years.

On Days 7, 8 and 9 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the absence of dust is as much a fact as its presence was on Stone 12. He works in bone-coloured slip, speaks to the pots and the wheel and never to the basket, and moves the damper before Sella has finished: an obedience that is also a correction neither will name. He goes quieter when the levy is spoken around and quieter still at \emph{the house’s share}, and the yard straightens around him. The broken birth-slates under the drying rack and the men whose names are not spoken stay unshown; the back room is not entered in any roll the house shows, and its cold is not mentioned. He still wants the foundling outside the name and the hollow seat for himself, and has said neither.

On Days 10 through 14 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the absence of dust is the fact of the five days: slip the colour of old bone on both forearms, no grey worked into the creases. He speaks to the pots and the wheel and never to the basket, says \emph{you’ll do} to a pot and that the wheel does not care whose hands are on it, and shifts the damper before Sella has finished --- an obedience that is also a correction neither will name. He goes quieter when the levy and the debt are spoken around and quieter still at the reading at the Cross. He does not say the back room was cold, does not take up Sella’s silence, and does not look toward the bed where the foundling lies. The broken birth-slates under the drying rack and the men whose names are not spoken stay unshown; he still wants the boy outside the name Vail and the hollow seat for himself, and has said neither.

On Days 15 through 24 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the dust comes and goes. Five clean mornings make its absence a fact; on Stone 23 it returns, grey and fine in the creases past the little finger, and the boy sets the two states of the same forearms on separate places on a tray. Jorra speaks to the pot and the wheel, never to the basket, moves the damper before Sella has finished, and goes quieter as the Last Day sweeping talk goes around. He sets a pot down on the bench and does not turn to its interval, and the boy does not turn after him. On Stone 29 a sweeping that will leave the grey where it lies until it is burned and called dealt with makes the house straighter and him quieter; on Stone 30 he has moved the damper and not looked toward the bed. The full note is in a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel, which he will not say before a kiln-master, and the boy knows he knows. The broken birth-slates under the drying rack and the men in the back room stay unshown; the foundling goes into a new year carried under the roof without a Vail name.

On Days 25 through 30 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the back room is not once mentioned. The forearms carry bone-coloured slip dried to old bone and the bent little finger goes in ahead of the hand at the damper, which he moves before Sella has finished; no grey dust appears after the Last Day, and the boy, who once set the dust and the clean slip on separate places on a tray, has nothing new to file. He speaks to the pots and the wheel and never to the basket, does not look toward the bed, and goes quieter when the sweeping talk and the burned Ash come around. The full note is in a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel and he will not say so before a kiln-master; \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed through the turn of the year, and the foundling goes into Y.H. 813 carried under the roof unwritten.

On Days 31 through 37 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the dust comes back from the room the house does not enter. On Ilmen 4 grey slate dust is worked into the creases past the bent little finger, not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel; the yard goes around the space under the drying rack where whole slate should have stood and enters it. He speaks to the pots and the wheel and never to the basket, moves the damper before Sella has finished, and knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel but will not say so before a kiln-master, who would call it early and make something of it. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed and the foundling goes on being carried under the roof unwritten.

On Days 38 through 44 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the back room is not once mentioned. At dusk on Ilmen 9 he came in from the wheel-shed with bone-coloured slip dried to old bone up both forearms and went to the damper before Sella had finished telling him the fire was low, the bent finger going in ahead of his hand, and neither he nor Tarn looked toward the bed where the boy lay; they had not been told about the woman in the brook and had not asked. On Ilmen 11 the forearms were clean of slate dust and the bent finger led again at the damper; he told a pot \emph{You’ll do}, told the wheel it did not care whose hands were on it, only if they were steady, said nothing about the back room and did not look toward the basket. He agreed with nobody about the thaw and contradicted nobody, and the yard straightened around his silence without an order. Through the Fish Blessing at the Weir he stayed in the wheel-shed, and \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed for all seven days.

On Days 45 through 47 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the back room is not once mentioned. The forearms carry bone-coloured slip dried to old bone and no slate dust past the bend of the little finger; the bent finger leads at the damper ahead of Sella’s sentence and the end of her instruction goes to the pot. He speaks to the pots and the wheel and never to the bed, tells a pot \emph{You’ll do}, and says nothing about the back room. He knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel and would not say so before a kiln-master, and the boy keeps the knowing where questions can last for years. Garl’s proverbs go to the pot and the fire and never to the basket, and the clean dark line is not swept. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed through three more days and the foundling goes on being carried under the roof unwritten.

On Days 48 through 54 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the dust comes back from the room the house does not enter. On Day 50 he comes in from the back room with fine grey slate dust worked into the creases past the bend of his little finger and says nothing about where he has been; the men are not named and the broken birth-slates stay under the drying rack, gone around and entered by nobody. On the other mornings the forearms carry bone-coloured slip and the boy keeps the two states apart. He tells a pot it will do and the wheel it does not care whose hands, only if they are steady, and knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel but would not say so before a kiln-master, who would call it early and make something of it. The bent finger goes in ahead of his hand at the damper ahead of Sella’s instruction; he does not say the back room was cold and does not look toward the bed or the basket. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed through all seven days.

On Days 55 through 60 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the back room is not once mentioned. The forearms carry bone-coloured slip dried to old bone and no slate dust worked past the bend of the little finger, and the boy keeps the clean state apart from the dust days without being able to ask what either means. He speaks to the wheel and the pots and never to the basket or the bed, tells the wheel it does not care whose hands are on it, only if they are steady, and knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel but will not say so before a kiln-master, who would call it early and make something of it. His bent finger goes in ahead of his hand at the damper ahead of Sella’s instruction so that the end of her sentence arrives at the pot instead of at him; the yard straightens around his silence without an order. He does not say the back room was cold, the men in that room are not named, and the broken birth-slates stay under the drying rack, gone around and entered by nobody. The promise of Corin’s name to the people who burn slates stays where it has always stayed, ungiven and not withdrawn, and \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed through the turning of the month and the coming of Silt.

On Days 61 through 67 the wheel keeps the house’s time and the room the house does not enter puts its dust into the yard again. On Silt 4 Jorra comes through the finger’s-width-open door with grey slate dust past the bent little finger, not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel, says nothing about where he has been, and lets the men in that room stay unnamed. He keeps the two states of his forearms as one man’s two mornings and the boy keeps them on the same tray without asking which slate was broken or whether it was a birth-slate. Broken birth-slates stay buried under the lowest rack and the space above them is gone around as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entered by nobody. He speaks to the wheel and the pots and never to the basket or the bed, knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel and would not say so before a kiln-master who would call it early and make something of it, and moves the damper with the bent finger leading ahead of Sella’s sentence so that the end of her instruction arrives at the pot. The yard straightens around his silence without an order. He does not say the back room is cold and does not look toward the bed; \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the foundling’s name stays ungiven and not withdrawn, while the hollow seat waits for his weight and the foundling goes on being carried under the roof unwritten.

On Days 85 through 90 the wheel keeps the house’s time across the turning of Silt into Seed and the room the house does not enter puts its dust into the yard again. On Silt 27 he comes through the finger’s-width-open wheel-shed door with fine grey slate dust worked into both forearms past the bend of his little finger, not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel; men came in since first light and spoke low in the back room and he gives the house no name for them. The broken birth-slates stay under the lowest rack, gone around by the yard as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it and entered by nobody. He keeps dusty forearms and clean ones on one tray as two states of one man’s mornings and asks neither which slate was broken nor whether it was a birth-slate. He speaks to the wheel before anyone --- \emph{It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady} --- tells a pot \emph{You’ll do}, and knows the full note of a Vail pot before it leaves the wheel and will not say so before a kiln-master from High Kiln. When Sella has not finished telling him the fire is low, his bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her sentence and moves it, cold iron taking the cold out of his fingertip, so the end of her instruction arrives at the pot and the household straightens around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted; he has not answered her with a word and has not looked at her, which is how he obeys her instantly. He reads the damper as any iron that stops a thing from running: the same bite that keeps a vessel whole can take the hand off a man, and no word in Grathic holds both mercies in one. On Seed 1 he is heard at the wheel and not seen, a low note and the word to a pot, with no figure coming out of the shed onto the yard. He does not say the back room is cold and does not look toward the bed or the basket. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed as tightly as a lid nobody has tried to lift in three years, and the promise of the foundling’s name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn while the hollow seat waits for his weight.

On Days 126 through 128 the wheel goes on and the back room stays shut. He comes through with fine grey slate dust ground small as meal into both forearms past the bend of the little finger — not the bone-coloured slip of the wheel — keeps dusty forearms and clean ones on one tray, and asks neither which slate was broken nor whether it was a birth-slate; the broken birth-slates lie under the lowest rack and nobody enters them. He speaks to the wheel before anyone, \emph{It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady}, tells a pot \emph{You’ll do} and knows its full note before it leaves the wheel; when a kiln-master come up from High Kiln would call it early and make something of it he withholds the knowing and says nothing a slate could carry. When Sella has not finished telling him the fire is low his bent finger goes into the cold iron of the damper ahead of her sentence, moves the tongue a hair’s breadth and leaves it standing, and the household straightens around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted; the boy reads the iron once more as the bite that holds a vessel whole and the bite that can take the hand off a man, with no word in Grathic for both mercies, and files it as an object worth nothing joined to no kiln. Tarn’s stroke goes on over the flagstones without the half-check while the stones keep the shallow bright patch where it stopped; neither man names the other’s silence, and when the ear’s sentence comes a second time to the threshold of the word that night he does not ask about it. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed, the promise of the foundling’s name to the slate-burners is neither given nor withdrawn, and the two tellings of the shut counting room stay beside the iron with no third. Nothing is named, opened, joined or paid.

The men in the room off the shed remain three or four shapes with no names, and the dust ground small as meal past the bent finger still waits for the question he will not ask. The damper holds mercy and mutilation in one bite with no Grathic word for both; the promise of the foundling’s name to the slate-burners is neither given nor withdrawn. The equality under the roof holds at its moved place, Tarn’s stroke going on without the half-check and neither man naming the other’s silence.

He came through with fine grey slate dust ground small as meal into both forearms past the bent little finger and under the nails, white in the creases where a fist had opened, not bone-coloured slip; he kept dusty forearms and clean ones on one tray and asked neither which slate was broken nor whether it was a birth-slate, and the broken birth-slates beneath the lowest rack were entered by nobody (T009/T013/T092). He spoke to the wheel before anyone (\emph{It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady}), told a pot \emph{You’ll do} in a voice with no welcome in it and no unkindness either, knew the full note that pot would give three turns before it left his hands and withheld the knowing from a man come up on a wrong wind who said a pot singing before its time generally sings itself out early; the man took his silence for agreement and went off up the yard with his saying, the knowing went to the near-full tray beside the hearings and never among them, advanced and not paid, and no pot was lost (T061/T082). The sweet edge of lead glaze came off High Kiln on a wrong wind and was taken as a direction, not a name and not a cause, and went out on the same wind; the pot that had sung itself out early stood swept around and was not made an omen or a lesson so soon after the carrying-out, and nobody named what ailed the man carried out on Day 188 (T077, T064 held). When Sella’s instruction went low and unfinished at the hearth on all three days his bent finger went to the cold iron of the damper and waited until the sentence reached the pot, then moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing — a remembered repetition, not a change made again, not paired with the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T062). The damper stayed one piece of iron with two bites, the holding and the taking, with no word in Grathic that would carry both mercies in one mouthful, joined to no kiln and entered in no slate (T062/T035). It cares if they’re steady}), tells a pot \emph{You’ll do}, knows its full note three turns ahead with air under it and a want in it, and withholds the knowing on the near-full tray beside the hearings and never among them. The three shapings of the pot saying stay sayings with no fourth likeness made a cause; on Smoke 14 a pot set down wrong at the racks gives its high thin note before its time and the woman sweeps around it and says something practical about the slip, so no pot is lost, no lesson is made and no name is given to what ailed the man carried out on Day 188. The sweet edge of lead glaze rides a wrong wind off High Kiln over the boards and goes out on it without becoming a cause. When Sella’s sentence goes low his bent finger goes into the cold damper ahead of it, takes the cold out, holds until the end arrives at the pot, moves a hair’s breadth and is left standing — one piece of iron with two bites and no Grathic word for both, joined to no kiln. The row question is not asked a sixth time and stands at five askings with no witness and no row named. \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the boy’s name stays ungiven. No new scar or possession, no bond paid or spoken.

Through Smoke 16–18 the wheel and the back room keep their old shape. He comes through each morning with meal-fine grey slate dust past the bent finger and white in the creases of a fist, parts dusty forearms from clean ones on one tray, gives the men who went into the room no name and does not say the room was cold, and keeps the two tellings of the shut room at two. He speaks to the wheel before anyone, tells a pot it will do, knows its full note three turns ahead and withholds it; the three shapings of the pot saying stand with the premature note from Smoke 14 on its own place and no fourth likeness made a cause, the burned-slate word stands at four and the row question at five askings with no witness. When Sella’s sentence goes low his bent finger goes into the cold damper ahead of the end of it, takes the cold out, holds and is left standing — a remembered repetition joined to no kiln. He does not ask about the ear while Tarn does not ask about the room; \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn.

Through Smoke 19–21 he holds the old shape at the wheel and the damper and gives nothing up. Men unnamed go low into the back room before first grey on the 19th and 21st and get no name from him and no word that the room was cold; meal-fine grey slate dust is worked past the bent little finger, white in the creases of a fist, parted from clean slip; he speaks to the wheel before any person and tells a pot \emph{You’ll do}, knows its full note three turns ahead with air under it and a want in it and withholds the knowing on the near-full tray. Three pot sayings stay three with the premature note from Smoke 14 on its own place and no fourth likeness made a cause; the burned-slate word from Slate Row holds at four and the shut-room tellings at two; the ownerless row question stands at five askings with no witness and no row named (T035/T031/T062, T065/T095, T101). Sella’s unfinished sentence still finishes at the pot, \emph{he’s not Vail} is sealed and the promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn; the equality with Tarn holds at the place it moved to, neither asking about the back room or the ear. Smoke’s second arithmetic goes up the road in Berr’s locked box on the 20th and makes no change under the wheel-shed (T015/T041/T047).

Through Smoke 22–24 he holds the old shape at the wheel and the damper and gives nothing up. Men unnamed go low into the finger’s-width-open back room before first grey on all three days and get no name from him and no word that the room was cold; he comes through with meal-fine grey slate dust ground small as meal past the bent little finger and white in the creases of a fist that had opened, parts dusty forearms from clean as a surgeon parts clot from vessel, asks neither which slate broke nor whether it was a birth-slate. He speaks to the wheel before any person --- \emph{It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady} --- tells a pot \emph{You’ll do}, knows its full note three turns ahead with air under it and a want in it and withholds the knowing on the near-full tray beside the hearings and never among them (T061/T082). The three shapings of the pot saying stand with the premature note from Smoke 14 on its own place and no fourth likeness made a cause; the burned-slate word from Slate Row holds at four and the shut-room tellings at two; the ownerless row question stands at five askings with no witness and no row named (T035/T031/T062, T065/T095, T101). When Sella’s sentence goes low (\emph{The fire’s low. It wants---}) his bent finger goes into the cold damper ahead of it, takes the cold out of the fingertip and holds until the end arrives at the pot --- one piece of iron with two bites, mercy and mutilation in one, with no Grathic word for both, joined to no kiln (T062). \emph{He’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn; the equality with Tarn holds at the place it moved to, neither asking about the back room or the ear. Smoke’s second arithmetic stays behind and unread up the road and makes no change under the wheel-shed (T015/T041/T047). No new scar or possession, no change of voice.

Through Smoke 25–27, Days 264–266, he keeps the wheel and the household’s shape at the shed’s edge: meal-fine grey slate dust ground small as meal past the bent little finger, dusty forearms parted from clean ones, the wheel told it does not care whose hands, only if they are steady, a pot told \emph{You’ll do} and its full note known three turns ahead and withheld on the near-full tray beside the hearings. Three or more men go low into the finger’s-width-open back room before first grey on all three mornings and get no name from him and no word that the room was cold; his bent finger goes into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, one piece of iron with two bites and no Grathic word for both. The burned-slate word holds at four, the shut-room tellings at two and the three pot sayings at three with the premature Smoke 14 note apart; the row question takes one further shaping over the boards, a report of an asking, and stands at five askings with no witness and no row named. His promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates is neither given nor withdrawn and \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed as a lid nobody has tried to lift in three years. Nothing is paid, named or settled and the count goes into Smoke 28 unspent.

When Sella’s sentence went low his bent finger went into the cold damper and held until the sentence reached the pot, then moved a hair’s breadth and was left standing --- a remembered repetition, not a change made again, not paired with the Day 161, 166 or 171 fractions; the iron stayed one piece with two bites and no Grathic word for both mercies (T062). As the year’s first grain was beaten out on the flagstones, spread thin and poured back under wool, dressed and stored with no figure, the yard went around the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look, a wide step and no number, and he did not join the two keepings or give either a name (T077, T098 advanced and not paid, T060/T086/T097). With Tarn neither asked about the ear or the room and the debt’s stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check; with Sella her unfinished sentence still finished at the pot. \emph{He’s not Vail} stayed sealed and the promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates was neither given nor withdrawn. No bond paid or spoken, no new scar or possession, no change of voice; forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 57: Days 222, 223 and 224, Grain 13–15, Thirdday to Fifthday, on stage at the wheel-shed, the cold damper, the kiln mouth and the Clay Yard on all three days. Came through with the morning’s meal-fine grey slate dust ground small as meal past the bent little finger and under the nails, white in the creases where a fist had opened, not bone-coloured slip; parted dusty forearms from clean ones as a surgeon parts clot from vessel, kept them on one tray and asked neither which slate had been broken nor whether it was a birth-slate, while the broken birth-slates under the lowest rack stayed entered by nobody (T009/T013/T092). Spoke to the wheel before anyone (\emph{It doesn’t care whose hands. It cares if they’re steady}), told a pot \emph{You’ll do} in a voice with no welcome and no unkindness, knew the full note three turns before it left his hands, with air under it and a want in it, and kept the knowing back on the near-full tray beside the hearings and never among them (T061/T082). Three or more men unnamed went low into the finger’s-width-open back room before first grey on the mornings he was seen and he gave the house no name for them and did not say the room was cold; the two tellings of the room shut in the war stayed two and no third came (T035/T031, T065/T095). The burned-slate word had come over the boards four times out of Slate Row and arrived nowhere, a direction with no hand at the flame and no figure at its foot; he grew quieter whenever it went around and the household straightened around the quiet without an order, the quiet going before him into the shed the way a cold air goes before a door. No fifth telling came and no third telling of the shut room (T035/T031/T065/T095 held, not paid). On Grain 15 a wrong-wind kiln-hand come up off High Kiln with the sweet edge of lead glaze let one of the three shapings stand over the boards — \emph{a pot gone quiet on every row come the thaw} — and went on to the price of barley and the weather, giving no owner, room, hand at the foot or reason; the boy took it apart as a surgeon takes apart a wound and left it a saying about a pot with no pot lost, no fourth likeness made a cause and no name given to what ailed the man carried out on Day 188 (T061/T082, T064). The three shapings stayed sayings on the near-full tray: sings itself out early, not heard from since, gone quiet on every row. When Sella’s voice went low at the hearth his bent finger went into the cold iron of the damper ahead of her hand and held until the sentence reached the pot, then moved a hair’s breadth and was left standing — a remembered repetition, not a change made again, not paired with the Day 161, 166 or 171 fractions; the iron stayed one piece with two bites and no Grathic word for both mercies (T062). The harvest came in with hands back in the worked strips, the first grain taken at the yard’s edge and set near the hearth under wool with no figure, and the yard going around the returning-line place with a look and no number (T098 advanced and not paid, T077). With Sella his unfinished sentence still arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence; he did not look toward the bed or answer with a word. With Tarn neither asked about the ear or the room and the two silences stayed unjoined. \emph{He’s not Vail} stayed sealed as tightly as on the hour it was spoken and the promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates was neither given nor withdrawn. No bond paid or spoken, no new scar, possession or change of voice; forward, not closed.

\end{itemize}

The burned-slate word had come a fourth time on Grain 9 and stayed at four, a direction arrived nowhere and still not a third telling of the counting room shut in the war; the household straightened around his quiet without an order, the quiet going before him into the shed the way a cold air goes before a door. When Sella’s sentence went low his bent finger went into the cold damper and held until the sentence reached the pot, then moved a hair’s breadth and was left standing — a remembered repetition, not a new change, not paired with the Day 161, 166 or 171 fractions; the iron stayed one piece with two bites and no Grathic word for both mercies (T062). With Tarn neither asked about the ear or the room; \emph{he’s not Vail} stayed sealed and the promise of the boy’s name to the slate-burners was neither given nor withdrawn. \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Does not appear; the wheel, the hollow seat and his objecting are held for Chapter 2.

\item Ch 2: At first light stood at the wheel with slip-coloured forearms and the bent finger, told the pot the slip was too thick and it would crack at the shoulder, and went quiet when the levy was spoken of. When Sella said the boy would come under the roof he said \emph{he’s not Vail}, did not look at her, and was not answered. On the third day sat in the hollow seat as the boy was carried in, obeyed Sella’s instruction about the damper before she had finished, told a pot \emph{you’ll do}, spoke once to Tarn about a rasp, and never addressed the child. Nobody wrote the foundling as Vail.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

At dusk came in from the back room with slate dust worked into the forearms --- grey and fine, not slip --- and said \emph{the back room’s cold} to nobody, answering no question about where he had been and giving Sella nothing to take further. Garl’s coat kept its salt shape on its peg and his hollow seat stayed unfilled; he did not look at the basket.

\end{itemize}

Shifted the damper before Sella had finished telling him the fire was low and went quieter when the levy was spoken around. Did not say the back room was cold, did not take up Sella’s silence, and kept \emph{he’s not Vail} sealed while the foundling went on being carried under the roof unwritten.

\end{itemize}

On Stone 23, after five clean mornings, came in with fine grey slate dust worked into the creases of his forearms past the bend of the little finger, said nothing about where he had been, told the pot \emph{she’ll want a thinner slip} and the wheel \emph{it doesn’t care whose hands; it cares if they’re steady}, and took the damper ahead of Sella’s instruction; a pot set down on the bench gave nothing and he did not look toward the bed. On Stone 30 he had moved the damper and not said the back room was cold. \emph{He’s not Vail} stayed sealed all ten days.

\CRcharacter*{Mira Silt}{the aunt who knows and will not say}{build/art/characters/mira-silt.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Mira, Mira of the Fishstairs, Dessa’s sister}\CRfield{Role}{family}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 785, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; returned thin)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; House Silt}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Fishstairs, Sill; eel trade; House Silt}\CRfield{Status}{alive — the secret kept out of love still unsaid at the close of Day 169, Tallow 20; on stage on Day 167 at the Weir’s lower boards and below the sill; her board beside Orra Weir’s and not touching it, the second cord twisted twice beneath the creel with neither knot counted}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-seven, broad-hipped, with eel slime dried on her sleeves and a small smile she keeps on her face the way another woman keeps a door on the latch: it can be shut without anybody noticing the movement. The top half of her left ear is missing, taken by a knife in a Fishstairs quarrel when she was nineteen; she says a hook did it, and the scar says otherwise, and nobody has ever made anything of it. She smells of river silt, salted perch, tallow smoke and the cold off the water. She carries a string of eel-bones in her pocket and flicks them against her thumb when she is deciding whether to lie, which is often. The thing people notice first is the smile; the thing they notice last is that she never sits down at a table where a slate is open.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, low, with the proverb turned sideways. She answers a question with a question and then answers it herself, which gives her the room to choose which answer the listener gets. She never tells a story with a beginning; she starts at the part where somebody is already in trouble. She has learned from Fen traders to mark accounts in knots rather than on slate, and will not write a name down if a knot will hold it. When she is being kind she becomes brisk, because kindness in her house is a thing done quickly before anyone can make a speech about it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “You want to know. You don’t want to know. I can see which one’s winning.”

\item “The secret’s in what happens to it after. I didn’t tell anybody anything. There’s nothing to tell. That’s the whole of it.”

\item “It came from a warm house, that’s all. There’s barley in it and a little smoke and it’s a crust, not a sermon.”

\item “Nineteen steps. Your sister counts them. I count the ones she doesn’t take.”

\item “Don’t ask a Fishstairs woman what she saw. She’ll sell it to you and then it’s yours and you’ll have to carry it.”

\item “He’s warm. That’s all I’ll say on a slate, and I’m saying it off the slate.”

\item “I kept your secret for three years, Dessa. Don’t make it a fourth.”

\item “Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river.” --- the answer she gives to her own question on Reed 18.

\item “Two marks the pair and two short. You’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice. There’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer.” --- to a buyer at the fish-trade shade on Reed 18.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
Born in Low Kiln to the same thin-returned mother as Dessa, Mira learned the eel trade at the Fishstairs at twelve and has worked the dawn market there ever since. She knows which households pay and which owe, which collectors take their ale before a collection and which after, and which boats on the Ilm are carrying something other than fish. She has been the district’s informal ledger of who is warm and who is cooling for fifteen years, and has never once put a name on paper.

She was in the room on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, when her sister bore the child with the branching red flower. She saw Sella Vail carry a covered bundle up the Clay Yard three days later, and she understood what had been done without being told. Alda Reed told Dessa the boy was among the Forty; Mira let her believe it. She has let her believe it for three years, and has taken a share of the barley Sella pays every winter, which she spends on Dessa, who does not know where the barley comes from. She has a child of her own, returned thin in Y.H. 802 to a household in Nine Pots, who does not recognize her; she has walked to Nine Pots twice and never knocked.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Her sister’s lie is hers too, and she has begun to feel the weight of it in the hand that holds the eel knife. She fears that telling Dessa the truth will put the boy on a slate that someone can use against him; she fears more that if she waits much longer the truth will come out in a quarrel, which is the worst way for a thing like that to be said. She fears she has become a woman who trades in other people’s warmth and calls it looking after them. Her contradiction: she gossips all day at the Fishstairs and has kept the one secret that matters for three years without a single slip.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants Dessa to stop reaching for a child she believes is dead, and she wants to be believed once about something that is not a rumour. She thinks she wants the truth to come out, and has arranged her life so that it never has to. What she needs is to understand that a secret kept out of love is still a debt, and that it gathers Ash like any other debt, and that the only way to stop paying interest on it is to say the thing.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Dessa Silt} — her sister, her room-mate, the woman whose child she has hidden for three years. Dessa suspects; Mira has begun to be afraid of the moment Dessa stops suspecting and knows. Everything between them is said in the language of barley, coughs and the nineteen steps. \emph{Ch 1:} she crossed the room and pressed a crust of Vail-smoked barley into Dessa’s hand in two brisk movements, stopping short of the slate to do it.

\textbf{Corin} — the nephew she watches from a distance at the market and once followed as far as the Clay Yard. She has never called him anything, not even in her head, because a name is a thing that can be overheard. \emph{Ch 1:} she would not hold him and would not sit where the slate lay open, but pushed the wool back under him briskly with two movements before anyone could make a speech about it. \emph{Ch 3:} a background figure at the eel stall in the afternoon, eel slime dried pale on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone; she flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and never once looked at the basket. When she turned to go she shoved a loose board clear of the barrow men’s path with the side of her hand, brisk, her face still toward the eels. She had not looked at him once all day. He put her not-looking beside the man on the block’s: one priced him, the other kept him, and he had no word in Grathic for either.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — they have an arrangement: barley and silence. Mira has begun to resent the barley and has never once refused it, which is the precise shape of her complicity. \emph{Ch 1:} she watched the hand in the door without moving, her thumb quiet in her pocket and the eel-bone put away.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — they trade small facts and never the large one. Alda knows more about the birth; Mira knows more about what happened after it. Neither will sit at a table with a slate on it, and they have built a friendship entirely out of things said standing up. \emph{Ch 1:} they worked the same room standing, each with her back to the writing.

\textbf{Orra Weir} — her supplier at the Weir and her oldest friend, who wants the secret out and has said so twice. Mira has answered both times with the weather.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — buys her eels for the levy feast and pays in marks that are short by two. She short-weights him by two eels. This small war has been going on for six years and neither has acknowledged it. \emph{Ch 3:} at the eel stall she asked him the price and answered it herself --- \emph{two marks the pair or two marks the pair and two short? Don’t trouble yourself. It’s two marks the pair and two short, and I’ve counted them twice, and I’ll count them again after I’ve eaten.} He did not answer, because she had left him nothing in the sentence that wanted an answer. She moved an eel-bone from hand to hand and said a figure under her breath. The knot-string is still not shown; only the counting is.

\textbf{Tarn} — the Vail’s clay-bound hand. She has suspected for a year that he is more than the debt he says he is, and has not asked, because she recognizes a person who keeps a secret and knows better than to open him.

\textbf{Ch 5.} At the Fishstairs on Stone 14 and the market’s edge on Stone 15 she worked with pale slime on her sleeves and silt in her neck, head held a little to the right against the cold where the ear had been. She flicked three eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and put one away when the deciding was done; she gave Berr four eels where six should go against his two marks short of six years, and neither acknowledged the war. Asked whose the basket was, she answered with a question and then her own: \emph{he’s warm} --- all she would say on a slate, and she was saying it off the slate. Her grey wool cord at the waist was touched three times in two mornings when a number was spoken, and the second cord twisted twice beneath it has never gone up the river to Nine Pots and has never been lifted at a door; the thumb goes always to the first. She put a brown-edged crust into the fold briskly, called it a crust and not a sermon, and went back to the eels without looking in.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 28 she came up the Clay Yard from the fish-trade with pale eel slime dried on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, head held to the right against the cold. Asked whose basket was going past, she answered with a question and her own answer --- \emph{Whose do you think? A basket’s a basket. It came from a warm house, that’s all, and it’s going back to one} --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and put it away. When a woman at the well said a figure for the Five, her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed there while she decided, and came out with another bone between finger and thumb. She crossed three paces and put a fresh brown-edged barley crust into the fold beside the spent one, saying \emph{It’s a crust, not a sermon}, and went back to the eels without looking in; the old crust lay stiff where it had lain since Stone 15 and neither woman named either. Shifting the basket’s weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, the one never taken upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door; the knots on neither were counted. Three doors down Dessa coughed from the pits and called it weather, and Mira’s smile did not move. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 8.} On the Last Day she came up from the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, brisk, answering a question with a question and her own answer --- a basket came from a warm house and goes back to one --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb before putting it away. When a figure was spoken her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided, and shifting the weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door; the knots were not counted. She put nothing into the fold this chapter --- no third crust came --- and went back down the yard without once looking in or saying she knew the child.

\textbf{Ch 9.} On Ilmen 2 she came up from the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves and silt in the hollow of her neck, head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, and answered a question about the eels with a question and her own answer. When a figure was spoken at the well her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided; shifting the basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, and neither was counted. On Ilmen 8 she came up again and passed her sister at the end of nineteen steps without looking at her, brought no crust and put nothing into the fold, and went back down the yard toward the eels without once looking in. Two not-lookings of the same shape were opposite things and the boy kept them apart. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 10.} She comes up from the eels at the brook’s edge on Ilmen 9 with pale slime dried on her sleeves and her head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, answers a neighbour’s question about the water with her own answer, brings no crust and does not look into the basket on the bank where her sister lies dead. At the Fishstairs on Ilmen 12 she answers a question about the run with a question and then her own --- \emph{It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- and shifting the weight of a basket shows the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted. On the river road on Ilmen 14 she tells Sella to ask Orra what night the boat came and not what she is owed, because Orra will tell her the oars; on Ilmen 15, at the blessing, she gives the same answer in the same form and keeps her grey wool on its own board beside Orra’s knot-string without letting the two touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and her small smile stays on the latch.

\textbf{Ch 11.} On Day 45 she worked the eels at the far racks with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. Asked whether the run would come with the blessing done she answered the question and then her own --- \emph{Does it come now the stone’s blessed? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. When a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and shifting a basket showed the second twisted twice beneath it, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted. Her board stood beside Orra’s and did not touch it. The smoky crust she put in the fold on Stone 28 is gone by the afternoon of Day 46, taken quietly and never named; the boy set her hand on a tray with two other hands and made no cause of it. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 12.} On Day 53 she answered a question about the run with a question and her own answer and moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie; when a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed. The second cord twisted twice beneath it showed and was not carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, and her board lay beside Orra’s without touching it. Dessa has been dead sixteen mornings and she has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the barley and the silence between her and Sella went on unentered, as did the small war with Berr over two marks short and two eels short.

\textbf{Ch 13.} At the last market before Silt she worked the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. Asked about the run she answered a question with a question and her own answer, and moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. A figure was spoken; her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting a basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted. Her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket. Her not-looking was a keeping; the man at the block’s not-looking had been a pricing, and she had no word in Grathic for either. Dessa has been dead twenty-two mornings and she has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 14.} On Silt 2 she worked the eels at the outer boards of the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, river silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on its face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked whether the run would come now the month had turned, she answered the question and her own — \emph{Does it come now? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} — and moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. When a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own. Her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket; her not-looking was a keeping where Berr’s not-looking at the same shade was a pricing, and the boy set the two in places that did not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and Dessa is twenty-nine mornings dead.

\textbf{Ch 15.} On Silt 13, the day the water fell, she worked the eels at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on the latch. A woman come down the steps with salt white at her wrists asked whether the run would be thin now the water had gone down; Mira flicked an eel-bone against her thumb, answered the question and her own --- \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- moved two bones hand to hand while deciding whether to lie and put one away when the deciding was done. A buyer in a wet coat named a figure; her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed while she decided, and shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver not touched. Her board stood beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket; her not-looking was a keeping where the man at the block’s was a pricing, and the boy set the two in places that did not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and Dessa is thirty-six mornings dead.

\textbf{Ch 16.} On Day 76, Silt 17, she works the eels below the north bridge at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on her face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked whether the run will be thin she answers her own answer --- \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- moves eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and puts one away when the deciding is done. When a buyer names a figure she says \emph{Two marks the pair and two short --- you’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice ... there’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer}, and her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays there while she decides. Shifting a creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lies beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and does not touch it; Orra is present only as the board, not on stage. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket. The steps have come back four, four and a landing a hand’s breadth out of line that a whole market walks over carefully without making a fall of it, and the soft-cuffed clerk still sits for a measure nobody called, hand to slate before eyes to stalls; the boy files the order apart from Marra, the Drawing collector and the Court-table clerk, with no sixth sighting of the neat dark hand. Her not-speaking, her not-looking and Berr’s taking-himself-out-of-his-sentence stand as three omissions of one shape that do not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, thirty-eight mornings dead now.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 20 and Silt 24 she works the eels at the boards below the north bridge with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on her face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked about the run she answers a question with her own answer and moves eel-bones while deciding whether to lie. When a figure is named her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays while she decides, and shifting a creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lies beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and does not touch it. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket; her not-looking is a keeping where Berr’s not-looking at the same shade is a pricing, and the boy sets the two in places that do not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, forty mornings dead and uncollected.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} With Corin nothing is said and nothing is looked at: she answered a question about the run from the side of her mouth and never once looked into the basket, and that not-looking is a keeping, the opposite of Berr’s pricing at the Cross. With Dessa nothing can be said at all; her sister is more mornings dead than any living person keeps count of and Mira has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s. The barley and silence with Sella hold unentered, as does the small war with Berr over two marks short and two eels short; Orra watches from where she watches and gets no answer, her knot-string beside Mira’s board and not touching it. No knot was counted, no cord carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, and the secret kept out of love went on gathering interest in a record no Court thumb will look at.
