At each going of the light she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her and river wind behind, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread unwiped and went to her own bed; the two rooms did not touch. The private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is.

Through Days 183–185 (Ember 4–6) the keeping takes the measure of a week that settles into the kiln month’s ordinary arithmetic and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and eighty-three, then one hundred and eighty-four, then one hundred and eighty-five days old and nobody says so. She gives every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom and running water and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, goes wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the bare dark trough whose water is called weather, the pan’s gone place and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15, with a look and a wide step and no number or explanation of the turns to the basket. The fire under the broken pot answers four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-three, four and five days; the carried fire keeps its one opening behind the household, the mark touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk since, because a morning and a shelf are not openings and the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. On Day 184 she sends a neighbour with a wet pot to the pot and the weather with no figure, the question carried away level with nothing slopped. On Days 184 and 185, when her instruction goes low and unfinished at the hearth, Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper until the sentence reaches the pot; the fraction is held and unspoken, a remembered holding and not a new change, not paired with the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf or the Day 171 flagstone half-check. Men unnamed go low into the back room before first grey on the last two mornings and she gives them no name and does not say the room is cold, and no third telling comes. She tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, and does not look toward the bed. Her finger does not go beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal stays unread. At each going of the light she carries him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her and river wind behind, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, leaves the thread unwiped and goes to her own bed; the two rooms do not touch. She has said nothing about the stone in the loft, whose taking above her house she cannot have heard as anything but the scrape of a pot’s foot. The private roll stays unshown and she has not said whose child he is.

Through Days 186–188 (Ember 7–9) the keeping takes the measure of three ordinary days in the middle of the kiln month and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and eighty-six, then one hundred and eighty-seven, then one hundred and eighty-eight days old and nobody says so; the widow’s mark hangs where it hung, untouched at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour. Every instruction goes to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shuts her hand half over nothing without touching it, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, counts under her breath toward no opening, and does not look toward the bed. The fire answers four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-six, seven and eight days, and she goes around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the bare dark trough, the pan’s gone place and the field’s empty place with a look and a wide step and no number (T088, T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). On Day 187 a neighbour come up from the tubs with a wet pot asked what the firing cost now the kiln month’s middle days were on; she glanced once at the clay jar, shut her hand half over nothing and sent the question to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried it away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, paid small and non-fatally:} on Day 188, after a rack-worker’s pot gave its note before its time and sang itself out early with the woman going on with her hands and making no lesson of it, two men carried a glaze-room hand out of the kiln and across the yard toward the clay road, one with a thumb hooked under his arm to keep the head from lopping. She set the basket down at the yard’s edge, turned the boy’s face as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it, went wide around the place the carriers crossed, and gave the yard no name for what ailed him; nobody called a collector, gave a figure or opened a slate, and the cost stayed entered nowhere (T077 advanced, not paid). At the going of the light each day she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her in long low bars and river wind behind, and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, base first and the weight settled as a woman sets a vessel that must not rock, the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, the thread left frozen and unwiped. Her finger did not go beneath the front edge of the loaf shelf on any of the three days; the charcoal tally stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100 carried). Her end of the instruction waited at the hearth on all three days while Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper and the sentence reached the pot, the fraction a remembered holding and not a new change, not paired with the Day 166 shelf beat or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T062). The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the pale line at the gum, the sweet breath on the wrong wind, the cost carried up the road unentered, the two men’s passage across the yard and the number nobody says, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 189 through 191 she carries him at the half-pace from every open slate, gives the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and leaves the widow’s mark where it hangs, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1. On the first Account-day of Ember she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off through the reading and the bell, giving no reason to the basket; on the two mornings after she sends women’s cost-questions to the pot and the weather and goes wide around the unswept places and the place the carriers crossed with a look and a wide step and no number. Her finger stays from beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal stays unread. The fire’s payer goes unnamed for a hundred and eighty-nine, ninety and ninety-one days, and the cost of the man carried out on Day 188 is entered nowhere.

Through Days 192 through 194, Ember 13–15, Thirdday to Fifthday, the keeping takes the measure of three quiet days after the reading and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and ninety-two, then ninety-three, then ninety-four days old and nobody says so; the district keeps calling Tallow the firing month and Ember the kiln month and neither usage is corrected. Every instruction goes to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, feeds him barley gruel from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, wipes the spoon on her sleeve and does not wipe his mouth, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, stands with the back of the pot in her hand counting under her breath toward no opening — the small intake, the hold, the letting go — pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, and does not look toward the bed. The fire under the broken pot answers four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and ninety-two, ninety-three and ninety-four days. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, untouched at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, afternoon and dusk, because a quiet morning after a reading is not an opening and there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1; nobody praised what it mended and nobody saw it broken. On all three days a cost-question goes to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and goes away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077). She goes wide around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone round ring, the bare dark trough whose water is called weather, the field’s empty place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and the place the carriers crossed, each with a look and a wide step and no number (T009/T013/T092/T098). When her instruction goes low and unfinished at the hearth, Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper until the sentence reaches the pot, then moves the tongue a hair’s breadth and is left standing — a remembered repetition and not a change made again (T062). Men unnamed go low into the back room before first grey and she gives them no name and does not say the room is cold, and the two shut-room tellings stay two with no third (T035/T031/T065/T095). Her finger stays from beneath the front edge of the loaf shelf on all three days, so the charcoal tally stays unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100), and the stone in its pot in the loft stays cold and unreconciled without her speaking of it (T006). At the going of each light she carries him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her in long low bars and river wind behind with the taste of water over water, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, base first and the weight settled the way a woman sets a vessel that must not rock, puts the fold right at his ear and under his chin without once looking at his face, leaves the thread frozen and unwiped, tells the fire it was the thaw, banks the coals with the back of a broken pot and does not touch the mark, because a dusk is not an opening; the two rooms do not touch — hers holds a pot, a fire and a woman counting toward nothing entered, and his holds a crust two inches from an ear and an empty place beside it with no name. The counting under her breath at the fire, held as she sets down the pot and as she banks the coals, becomes the measure by which the boy holds his own inch in the small hours, though no word passes between the rooms and she is asleep when he does it. The private roll stays unshown and she has still not said whose child he is. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no opening and no bond paid.

Through Days 195–197 (Ember 16–18) the keeping takes the measure of three more days of the kiln month’s second working week and adds no explanation. She gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale off the coals, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, feeds him gruel from the house’s own dish with the spoon on her sleeve and his mouth not wiped, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, stands a moment counting under her breath toward no opening — small intake, hold, letting go — and does not look toward the bed. Cost-questions go to the pot and the weather on all three days and arrive level with nothing priced, refused or entered. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, untouched at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, because there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1; nobody praises what it mended and nobody sees it broken. Her finger stays from beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal remains unread; at the hearth her unfinished sentence is allowed to finish at the pot behind Jorra’s standing finger as a remembered repetition, not a new change. She carries him home up the clay road at each going of the light, going wide around the unswept places and the carriers’ place, sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen; the fire’s payer is unnamed for a hundred and ninety-five, ninety-six and ninety-seven days.

Through Days 198–203 (Ember 19–24) the keeping takes the measure of the second reading and the kiln month’s last tend and adds no explanation. On Day 199 she carried him to the Cross at the half-pace, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through Berr’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving no instruction or reason to the basket and keeping her hand off the mark because a reading is not an opening; the box went up the locked road with the true subtraction inside and the printed figure standing. Through Days 201–203 she gave every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never the basket, said \emph{the house}, kept her half-pace, glanced once at the clay jar without a touch, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, set the pot handle two inches beyond his hand with the half-beat at setting, fed him from the house’s own dish with the spoon on her sleeve and his mouth unwiped, moved her lips along a row with two unnamed gaps and gave nobody a figure, kept her finger from beneath the charcoal, told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, and counted under her breath toward no opening — small intake, hold, letting go. Cost-questions went to the pot and the weather on all three days and went away level. The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no other hour, because no morning, shelf, market, road, yard, basket, afternoon or dusk was an opening. She carried him home around the pan’s gone ring with a wide step and no number, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face, left the thread frozen and went to her own bed. The fire’s payer was unnamed for two hundred and one, two and three days; at the hearth her unfinished sentence was allowed to finish at the pot behind Jorra’s remembered finger and she asked nothing of the men who went low into the back room.

Through Days 204–206 (Ember 25–27) the keeping takes the measure of the kiln month’s last working week and turns nothing into a story. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings and gives the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, shuts her hand half over nothing without a touch, feeds him from the house’s own dish with the spoon on her sleeve and his mouth unwiped, moves her lips along a row standing with two unnamed gaps and gives nobody a figure, keeps her finger from beneath the loaf shelf so the charcoal stays unread, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, stands counting under her breath toward no opening — small intake, hold, letting go — pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat at the setting and does not look toward the bed. The fire answers four low pulls with the fifth missing under the floor, its payer unnamed for two hundred and four, five and six days; the river keeps its note through the finger’s-width door and the boards keep four nails, four and a knot, three counts in three places that do not become one. Cost-questions go to the pot and the weather and away level, nothing priced, refused or entered. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no hour since, because no morning, shelf, yard or dusk is an opening and there has been no opening in twenty-six days. She hears the burned-slate word go around the boards and makes nothing of it; her unfinished sentence still finishes at the pot behind Jorra’s remembered finger. She carries him home around the absences with a wide step and no number, sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, leaves the thread frozen and goes to her own bed before the last small hours. The house keeps Garl in objects, not in a story, and no collector is called. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 52.} Through Days 207–209, the last working week of the kiln month, the house is kept in the same grammar: instruction to the fire, the wool, the pot, the broom and the river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the pot handle set two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, her lips moving along a row with two unnamed gaps and nobody given a figure, her finger kept on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, and the widow’s mark hanging where it hung since the opening before the kiln on Ember 1 — no opening in twenty-nine days, at a shelf, a well, a market, a road, a basket, an afternoon or a dusk. She tells the fire the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sends cost-questions to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered, and goes wide around the pan’s gone ring, the bare dark trough, the rack space, the field’s empty place and the place the carriers crossed with a look and no number. Garl is kept to the very last day in objects and not in a story — salt coat holding a broader man’s shape, hollow seat with its leftward lean, clean dark line and finer grey unswept, proverb gone to the pot, debt against the tiles uncalled and worse for being uncalled — no lesson made, no collector called, his name unspoken for two hundred and nine days. On Day 209 she carries him down to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stands half a pace off through Berr’s third reading and the bell’s four, four and a gap, gives no instruction or reason to the basket and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what was read over him. The fire answers four low pulls with the fifth missing and its payer unnamed for two hundred and seven, eight and nine days while the river keeps its note through the door and the boards keep their knot — three counts in three places that do not become one. Her unfinished sentence at the hearth is allowed to finish at the pot behind Jorra’s bent finger as a remembered repetition; the two silences stay unjoined and Ember goes out without a boundary drawn.

\textbf{Ch 53.} Through Days 210–212, Grain 1–3, the house keeps the turning of the month the way it keeps the fire: without a boundary drawn, without a figure spoken and without correcting either of the district’s two names for the months. Ember thins into the ordinary tending of a year begun and the yard goes around its left places — the clean dark line and the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space under the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone round ring, the bare trough whose water is called weather, the field’s empty place and the place the carriers crossed — with a look and a wide step and no number. Garl is kept in objects and not in a story: the salt coat holds a broader man’s shape, the seat its hollow and leftward lean, the proverb has gone to the pot and the debt against the tiles is circled without a name, worse for being uncalled, with no lesson made and no collector called and his name unspoken for two hundred and twelve days. Sella gives the instruction to everything but the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps the half-pace and the two inches, moves her lips along a row standing with two unnamed gaps and gives nobody a figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, glances once at the cold clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing without a touch, tells the fire it is the thaw and says \emph{The house will keep it}, and does not look toward the bed at the setting. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung at a shelf, a well, a yard, a basket and a dusk, because none is an opening and there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1. Cost-questions go to the pot and the weather and arrive nowhere; a number in a fist goes back into a coat with nothing paid. The fire answers four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and ten, eleven and twelve days. Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 54.} Through Days 213–215, Grain 4–6, the house keeps the first working week of Grain the way it keeps the fire: without an entry, without correcting either of the district’s two month-names, and with no market and no Account-day until Grain 10 (Day 219). She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shuts her hand half over nothing without a touch, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, moves her lips along a row standing with two gaps and gives nobody a figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, tells the fire it is the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot and stands counting under her breath toward no opening (small intake, hold, letting go). The pot rim goes out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand and her hand rests a half-beat longer at the setting; on the last day she does not look toward the bed. The fire answers four low pulls with the fifth missing under the floor, its payer unnamed for two hundred and thirteen, fourteen and fifteen days, while the river’s note comes through the finger’s-width door and the boards keep their knot: three counts in three places that do not become one. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no hour since — no opening in thirty-five days — and the private roll stays unshown while Dessa’s cost stays unentered. Cost-questions at the door and the well go to the pot and the weather and away level, nothing priced, refused or entered; a number in a fist goes nowhere and pays nothing. Garl is kept to every day in objects and not in a story: the salt-stiff coat with its crease at the left shoulder, the seat’s twenty-year hollow and leftward lean, the clean dark line and the finer grey called the thaw unswept, the proverb gone to a pot with no crack, and the debt against the tiles neither paid, settled nor named, worse for being uncalled, with no lesson made and no collector. When the burned-slate word goes around the boards a third time she makes nothing of it; when Jorra grows quieter the household straightens around the quiet without an order from her, and her unfinished sentence at the hearth still finishes at the pot behind his remembered finger (T058/T079, T100, T077, T009/T013/T092/T098, T035/T031/T062, T065/T095, T088). Forward, not closed.

\textbf{Ch 55.} Through Days 216–218, Grain 7–9, the house keeps the second working week the way it keeps the fire: without an entry, with no market until Grain 10, and with the same grammar of instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket. She comes to the fire before the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her half-pace and her two inches, holds her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, and leaves the widow’s mark untouched for thirty-six, thirty-seven and thirty-eight days. The fire misses its fifth with its payer unnamed for two hundred and sixteen, seventeen and eighteen days; the river’s note and the boards’ knot keep three counts in three places that do not become one. A pot saying takes a third shaping and the burned-slate word a fourth telling, both directions arrived nowhere, and she joins neither to the house. Jorra’s quiet goes before him into the shed and the household straightens around it without an order; her unfinished sentence still finishes at the pot behind his remembered finger. Tarn’s ninth stopping stands with no tenth and no collector; Garl stays in objects with the tile debt uncalled. The boy is carried home at the half-pace each dusk, set on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, with the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen; the two rooms do not touch. Forward, not closed.

Through Grain 10–12 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: the boy carried up and down the clay road at the half-pace, set in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay at Grain’s first market, and set on his bed and not in the Debt Loft each night with the fold put right without a look at his face and the thread left frozen. She gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, moves her lips along the two-gapped row without a figure, and leaves the widow’s mark hanging where it hung through thirty-nine, forty and forty-one days without an opening. The seventh green and the seventh shape come and go across the square without reaching under her roof; nothing is explained, entered, paid or named.

Through Grain 13–18 she brings the year’s harvest under the roof in two steps and keeps both by covering: the first cut grain comes in off the strips and is set near the hearth under wool, then across Grain 16–18 it is taken out, beaten with a flail on the flagstones, winnowed on the river wind, spread thin to finish drying and poured back under the fold --- dressed and stored, counted in glances and handfuls and by the carrying arm’s weight, with no slate opened and no figure given. Every cost-question goes to the pot and the weather and arrives nowhere; a number comes up out of a fist and goes back into its sleeve. She goes around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the bare trough, the field’s empty place and the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, each with a look and a wide step and no number. Her pot handle stands two inches beyond the reaching hand, her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting and never looking toward the bed; her finger lies on top of the shelf’s front edge while her lips move along a row with two gaps, and the charcoal is not read. The widow’s mark is untouched since before the kiln on Ember 1, no opening in forty-two through forty-seven days; her private roll stays unshown, Dessa’s cost unentered, and Garl kept in objects with the tile debt uncalled. She carries him home at each going of the light without looking at his face, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and leaves the thread frozen. Forward into Grain 19, not closed.

Through Grain 19–21 she keeps the house in the same grammar with one more tend behind her and Grain’s second Account-day read over the basket on Day 229: she changes nothing under the roof in answer to the figure, sends cost-questions to the pot and the weather, goes wide around the yard’s places with a look and no number, and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what was read over him. The dressed grain stays dressed and covered with no figure, and the returning-line place stays gone around with a look and no number; T098 advances and is not paid. The widow’s mark has now gone fifty days untouched since the opening before the kiln on Ember 1, and the rule still holds that the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. On Grain 21 she goes to her own bed before the small hours and leaves the coals to keep themselves; in the room that does not touch his her breaths go small intake, hold, letting go — a count kept toward no opening and never offered to any ear under this roof — and the wall stands between that count and his ear. She has taken in a foundling, kept a fire, held a wheel in the house through a son’s silence and a husband’s uncollected debt, and has never once said what any of it cost or asked where the boy’s memory came from. Nothing joined, named, opened, spent or ended.

Through Grain 22–24 (Days 231–233) she keeps the last tend of the harvest the way she keeps the fire: by instruction given to the tool and never to the basket, by a figure sent to the pot and the weather, and by a wide step around every place the yard has left where it lies. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, tells it the thaw, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, moves her lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, and does not touch the widow’s mark — now fifty-one, fifty-two and fifty-three days since the opening before the kiln on Ember 1. She turns the dressed grain for damp, spreads it thin and gathers it back under the fold, counted in glances, handfuls and the carrying arm’s weight, entered on no slate and given no figure. The second ownerless asking goes over the boards in the afternoon of Day 232 and is answered with the pot and the weather as the first was, the weather first and the price of barley after it, and the row stands where it stood. She goes around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the bare trough, the field’s empty place and the returning-line place, each with a look and a wide step and no number. She sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, goes to her own bed before the small hours and leaves the coals to keep themselves; in the room that does not touch his her breaths go small intake, hold, letting go, a count kept toward no opening and never offered to any ear under this roof. She has taken in a foundling, kept a fire, held a wheel in the house through a son’s silence and a husband’s uncollected debt, and has never once said what any of it cost or asked where the boy’s memory came from. Nothing joined, named, opened, spent or ended.

Through Grain 25–27 (Days 234–236) she keeps the last tend of the harvest the way she keeps the fire: by instruction given to the tool and never to the basket, by a figure sent to the pot and the weather, and by a wide step around every place the yard has left where it lies. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, tells it the thaw, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, moves her lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, and does not touch the widow’s mark — now fifty-four, fifty-five and fifty-six days since the opening before the kiln on Ember 1. She turns the dressed grain under wool for damp, spreads it thin and gathers it back by the handful, counted in glances and the carrying arm’s weight, entered on no slate and given no figure. The third ownerless asking goes over the boards on the afternoon of Day 235 and is answered with the pot and the weather as the first two were, the weather first and the price of barley after it, and the voice goes off up the terrace with the row standing where it stood and nobody leaning in to take the answer down. She goes around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, goes to her own bed before the small hours of Day 236 and leaves the coals to keep themselves; in the room that does not touch his her breaths go small intake, hold, letting go, a count kept toward no opening and never offered to any ear under this roof. She has taken in a foundling, kept a fire, held a wheel in the house through a son’s silence and a husband’s uncollected debt, and has never once said what any of it cost or asked where the boy’s memory came from. Nothing joined, named, opened, spent or ended.

Through Smoke 1–3 (Days 240–242) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance without a touch, the hand shut half over nothing, the burn-wrist pushing coal-black hair back so the grey streak shows pale, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, cost-questions to the pot and the weather. \textbf{The one change in these days was hers:} before the first firing of Smoke she went to the kiln mouth, put her hand to the widow’s mark, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot; the fire took with its fifth still missing and no payer named, nobody praised what it mended and nobody saw it, and she put it behind the household without a word. She did not touch the mark again at any shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk in three days, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour, as on Tallow 1 and Ember 1. The dressed grain was turned under wool for damp, spread thin and gathered back by the handful, changed in state and given no figure, entered on no slate and laid across none of the absences. A wrong wind off High Kiln on Smoke 3 brought the sweet edge of glaze over the boards, touched the fold and went out on it, and she let one of the three sayings stand as a saying with no fourth likeness made a cause. She carried him home each evening around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, set him on his bed under the roof, left the thread frozen and went to her own bed before the small hours. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, and the private roll stayed unshown.

Through Smoke 4–6 (Days 243–245) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the tool and never to the basket, \emph{the house}, the half-pace, the jar-glance, the hand shut half over nothing, the unread charcoal under the shelf’s front edge, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour. The dressed grain is turned under wool and given no figure; the fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth whose payer is unnamed for two hundred and forty-five days. On Smoke 6 a wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards and takes it out again. She goes wide around the walked-around places, sets him on his bed under the roof, leaves the thread frozen and goes to her own bed before the small hours. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands.

Through Smoke 7–9 (Days 246–248) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the tool and never to the basket, \emph{the house}, the half-pace, the jar-glance, the hand shut half over nothing, the unread charcoal under the shelf’s front edge, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather. She goes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, and sets him on his bed under the roof at the going of each light, leaving the thread frozen and going to her own bed before the small hours. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour, and a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk are not openings. The dressed grain is turned under wool, spread thin and gathered back by the handful on all three mornings, changed in state and given no figure. On the afternoon of Smoke 8 the ownerless question comes over the boards a fifth time and she answers it with the weather first and the price of barley after it; the row stands where it stood, nobody leans in to take the answer down and no witness stands. A wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards, touches the fold and goes out on it, and she makes no lesson of it. The fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth whose payer is unnamed for two hundred and forty-six, forty-seven and forty-eight days. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no opening made after the first.

Through Smoke 10–12 (Days 249–251) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance without a touch, the hand shut half over nothing, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather with nothing priced. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, lips along the two-gapped row without a figure, and sets him on his bed under the roof at the going of each light with the thread frozen and unwiped, going to her own bed before the small hours. The dressed grain is turned under wool, spread thin and gathered by the handful on all three mornings, changed in state and given no figure. On Smoke 10 she carries him down to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off through Berr’s twice-read figure and the bell, giving no instruction and no reason to the basket, and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what was read over him and going wide around the walked-around places with a look and no number. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour, and no lesson is made of the one opening behind the household. The fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth, its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty-nine, fifty and fifty-one days. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no opening made after the first.

Through Smoke 13–15 (Days 252–254) she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance with the hand shut half over nothing, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, and cost-questions sent to the pot and the weather with nothing priced. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, lips along the two-gapped row without a figure, and sets him on his bed under the roof at the going of each light with the thread frozen and unwiped, going to her own bed before the small hours. The dressed grain is turned under wool, spread, gathered by the handful and laid flat on all three mornings, changed in state and given no figure. The widow’s mark has not been touched since the opening before Smoke 1; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour, and no lesson is made of the one opening behind the household. On Smoke 14 a pot set down wrong at the racks gives its high thin note before its time and a woman sweeps around it with a practical word about the slip, making no cause of the sound; a wrong wind off High Kiln brings the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards and takes it out again. The fire answers four low pulls with a missing fifth, its payer unnamed for two hundred and fifty-two, fifty-three and fifty-four days. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no opening made after the first.

Through Smoke 16–18, Days 255–257, the keeping goes on in the same grammar and makes one small domestic change she does not name. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, gives every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom, running water and river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} and \emph{The house will keep it}, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, counts under her breath toward no opening, and keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread. On Smoke 17 she gathers the dressed grain in by the handful for the last time before Smoke’s second reading, draws the wool over it and sets it away from the hearth on the cool stone at the rack end, giving the heap no figure and saying nothing that the work has ended; the arithmetic that will be read over it on Smoke 20 will not know what it cost. On Smoke 18 she gives the instruction to the bucket and the fire and never the basket, goes around the trough with a look and a wide step, and lets the yard call the white frost on the well lip weather, because a well is not an opening. The widow’s mark hangs where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no hour since; the one opening stays behind the household with no lesson and no payer, and the next real opening is the first firing of Frost, far off and unbrought. At the going of the light on Smoke 18 she sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face, leaves the thread frozen and goes to her own bed. The wall has acquired no door.

Through Smoke 19–21 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom and river wind and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate, the jar-glance with the hand shut half over nothing, coal-black hair pushed back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. The dressed grain is lifted for damp and laid back on the 19th, turned under wool and laid back on the 21st, and given no figure on either day; on the 20th the district’s arithmetic changes a second time up the road and nothing under this roof is settled by it. On Smoke 20 she sets the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off through Berr’s twice-read figure and the bell, carrying him home at the going of the light and saying nothing of what was read over him. At each dusk she sets him on the bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, market, morning, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on these three days, because a market and a reading are not openings (T058/T079, T077, T100).

Through Smoke 22–24, Days 261–263, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the keeping is made as much of what she leaves undone as of what she does. She comes to the fire before the basket on all three mornings, tells the coals it is the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stays unread, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without giving either gap a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She lifts a corner of the wool over the dressed grain for damp on the 22nd and 23rd and turns it under the wool on the 24th, each with no figure, so the arithmetic on Smoke 30 will not know what it cost. She carries him about the yard and up at the going of the light at the half-pace from every open slate, goes wide around the seven walked-around places, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, afternoon, dusk or going of the light in these three days, because none is an opening; the one opening stays behind the household with no lesson, sign, mending or payer, and the next real opening is the first firing of Frost, far off and unbrought (T058/T079, T077, T100). Nothing is priced, named or entered, and the wall has acquired no door.

Through Smoke 25–27, Days 264–266, she keeps the house through the third working week’s going out: fire before basket, the thaw told to the coals, the back of a broken pot, \emph{The house will keep it}, the count under her breath toward no opening, the finger on top of the shelf’s front edge with the charcoal unread, the two-gapped row without a figure, the glance at the clay jar and the hand shut half over nothing, the pot handle two inches out with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. On Smoke 26 she draws the wool wholly back from the dressed grain and turns it piece by piece in her flat hand for damp and rot, setting each piece where it lay, then covers it and carries the dish from the hearth; on Smoke 27 she turns it once with a lighter touch. No figure on any day, so the arithmetic on Smoke 30 will not know what it cost. She carries him at the half-pace, goes wide around the seven places, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Smoke 1 and at no hour in these three days, because none is an opening; the one opening before Smoke 1 stays behind the household with no lesson, mending, sign or payer. Nothing is settled by the week’s going out and the count goes into Smoke 28 unspent.

Through Frost 1–3, Days 270–272, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and in the first light of Frost 2 she performs the month’s one real opening. She comes to the kiln mouth before the basket and before any word, holds the widow’s mark one breath, lets go, lifts the clay lid with the back of a hand and tips the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire takes, still answering four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have stood, its payer unnamed two hundred and seventy-one days. Nobody praises the opening and nobody names what it mended; no slate is entered, no lesson made, no bond changed hands, no payer named and no sign made. She does not touch the mark again at a shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 1, 2 or 3, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour; four openings in four months are four and not a rule, and the next opening stands in a later month’s first firing, far off. On the other mornings she tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, keeps her finger above the charcoal, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, turns the dressed grain beneath the wool for damp with a progressively lighter touch and gives it no figure, carries him at the half-pace, goes wide around the seven places and sets him on his bed under the roof with the thread frozen. Nothing is settled by the firing and the count goes into Frost 4 unspent.

Through Frost 4–6, Days 273–275, she keeps the house through the week of going around, and in the middle of it makes the chapter’s one change without a word. She comes to the fire before the basket each morning, tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without giving either gap a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, a half-beat at the setting and no look toward the bed. On Frost 5 her finger goes beneath the shelf’s front edge and stays for two counted breaths where on Day 166 it stayed for one, and comes away without a look, a word or a going back — a change a house can make and say nothing about (T100 advanced, not paid). She turns the dressed grain under wool for damp on all three mornings with a progressively lighter touch and gives it no figure; she goes wide around the seven walked-around places and sets him on his bed under the roof with the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Frost 2 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 4, 5 or 6; the first firing of Frost stays behind the household with no lesson or payer and four openings remain four. Nothing is settled by the week’s going out and the count goes into Frost 7 unspent.

Through Frost 7–9, Days 276–278, she keeps the house through the week’s going out, and on the last morning makes the chapter’s one change as maintenance and gives nobody a figure. She comes to the fire before the basket each morning, tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counts under her breath toward no opening, keeps her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge with the charcoal unread, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without giving either gap a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. The white the frost wrote on the well lip on Frost 8 does not go with the sun as it went on Frost 4, and stays past noon, past the going of the light and onto Frost 9; the rope stiffens, the trough takes a skin and she banks the coals an hour earlier at the going of the light, and the yard calls all of it weather. On Frost 9 she goes to the trough with the back of the broken pot, presses the skin until it gives with a thin dry sound, lifts a plate of ice clouded with silt, sets it on a flat stone out of the path of feet and draws what the yard calls weather, telling the weather where to stand and giving nobody a figure (T083/T085 advanced, not paid). She turns the dressed grain a second time that morning because the stone has gone cold, lifts the wool with a lighter touch and gives no figure, so the arithmetic that will read over it tomorrow will not know what it cost (T077). She goes wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, sets him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs, touched once before the kiln on Frost 2 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 7, 8 or 9, because none is an opening; the first firing of Frost stays behind the household with no lesson or payer and four openings remain four. Nothing is settled by the week’s going out and the count goes into Frost 10 unspent.

Through Frost 10–12, Days 279–281, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the month’s first reading passes the roof without leaving a figure behind. On Frost 10 she carries him to the Cross, sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stands half a pace off through the reading and the bell, giving no instruction or reason to the basket, and carries him home at the going of the light saying nothing. The arithmetic changed for the month up the road in Berr’s locked box and cannot be changed back, while the printed one in twelve stands unchallenged and the figure read is still not the figure paid; nothing of it comes back under the roof as a lesson, a mending, a figure or a payment. On Frost 11 and 12 she turns the dressed grain under wool for damp with a lighter touch and gives it no figure, so the number that read over it does not know what it cost, and the space between figure and price stays unsigned (T077). The grammar holds exactly — fire before basket, instruction to the tools and never the basket, \emph{the house}, \emph{The house will keep it}, half-pace, pot rim two inches out, fold righted without a look, finger above the charcoal, lips along a two-gapped row, one glance at the clay jar and the hand shut half over nothing, the widow’s mark untouched because no hour among these days is an opening. The stayed frost, the plate of ice and the week’s small goings-around are called weather and entered nowhere (T083/T085 held), the fire’s fifth stays unsupplied with its payer unnamed for three more days (T088), and Frost 20 stands eight mornings ahead and unbrought. Nothing is opened, named, called, paid or ended.

Through Frost 13–15, Days 282–284, she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire, and the second working week settles nothing. She comes to the hearth before the basket each morning, tells the coals it was the thaw, turns them with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps her finger above the charcoal so the tally beneath stays unread, moves her lips along a two-gapped row without a figure, glances once at the clay jar and shuts her hand half over nothing, and sets the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. She goes wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, turns the dressed grain under wool for damp and gives it no figure, carries him at the half-pace and sets him on his bed under the roof with the fold righted and the thread frozen. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs at every morning, afternoon and going of the light, because none is an opening; the first firing of Frost stays behind the household with no lesson or payer and four openings remain four. The stayed frost, the skinned trough and the plate of ice are called weather and entered nowhere, and the fire’s fifth stays unsupplied with its payer unnamed for two hundred and eighty-four days. Frost 20 stands five mornings ahead and unbrought, and nothing is opened, named, called, paid or ended.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 80: Days 291, 292 and 293, Frost 22–24, Secondday to Fourthday, keeper of the Vail fire, on stage under the roof and in the Clay Yard on all three days. Went to the fire before the basket at every morning and going of the light, told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, turned them with the back of a broken pot, kept her finger above the charcoal so the tally stayed unread, moved her lips along the two-gapped row with no figure, turned the dressed grain beneath the wool with a progressively lighter touch and gave it no figure, set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed, carried him down and up at the half-pace from every open slate and went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number, and left the thread frozen and the widow’s mark untouched because no morning and no going of the light is an opening; on Frost 24 she glanced once at the clay jar cold under its lead glaze and shut her hand half over nothing. On Frost 23 she heard the ownerless voice over the boards and the well-roof give the Frost 14 saying a third shaping and went on with the house, bringing nothing under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment. Gave the house no name for the men in the back room, asked Jorra nothing about his dust and Tarn nothing about his ear, and gave no instruction at any hour to the basket. The fire’s fifth stayed unpaid two hundred and ninety-three days, the grain unfigured, the frost, trough and plate of ice weather, Frost’s two arithmetics locked up the road, and Frost 30 six mornings ahead and unbrought. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond changed hands.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 78: Days 285, 286 and 287, Frost 16–18, Sixthday to Eighthday, keeper of the Vail fire, on stage under the roof and in the Clay Yard on all three days. Came to the fire before the basket each morning, told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{You’ll go when you go}, turned them with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, kept her finger on top of the loaf shelf’s front edge so the charcoal beneath stayed unread, moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps without giving either gap a figure, glanced once at the clay jar standing cold under its lead glaze and shut her hand half over nothing, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed (T058/T079, T100). Every instruction went to the fire, the wool, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; she carried him at the half-pace from every open slate, went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number — the two unswept lines called thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the skinned trough, the field’s empty place and the returning-line place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out — and set him on his bed under the roof, never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread frozen where it lay (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). The dressed grain lay covered and unfigured under wool at the rack end, turned for damp on the three mornings with a progressively lighter touch and given no figure, so the arithmetic that had read over it on the tenth still did not know what it cost (T077). The stayed frost lay white on the well lip past the going of the light, the trough kept its skin and the plate of ice stood clouded with silt on the flat stone out of the path of feet; she told the fire it was the thaw and gave nobody a figure (T083/T085 held, not paid). The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Frost 2 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 16, 17 or 18, because none of these was an opening; four openings in four months stayed four and not a rule, and nothing of the Frost 14 saying came under the roof as lesson, figure, mending, cause or payment (T058/T079). She heard Tarn bring the ear-sentence to the calling word and stop there on all three mornings and gave the end of her instruction to the pot, asking nothing; she did not ask Jorra about the men or his dust, and neither man named the other’s silence. Frost’s first arithmetic stayed locked in Berr’s box up the clay road with the printed one in twelve unchallenged and the figure read still not the figure paid; Frost 20 (Day 289), the second Account-day, stood two mornings beyond the close and was not brought into a day that had not earned it. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no change of voice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 77: Days 282, 283 and 284, Frost 13–15, Thirdday to Fifthday, keeper of the Vail fire, on stage under the roof and in the Clay Yard on all three days. Came to the hearth before the basket every morning, told the coals it was the thaw and \emph{You’ll go when you go}, turned them with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, kept her finger on top of the loaf shelf’s front edge so the charcoal beneath stayed unread, moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps without giving either gap a figure, glanced once at the clay jar standing cold under its lead glaze and shut her hand half over nothing, and set the pot rim two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed (T058/T079, T100). Instruction went to the fire, the wool, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; she carried him at the half-pace from every open slate, went wide around the seven walked-around places with a look and a wide step and no number — the two unswept lines called thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the skinned trough, the field’s empty place and the returning-line place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out — set him on his bed under the roof and never in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread frozen where it lay (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). The dressed grain lay covered and unfigured under wool at the rack end and she turned it for damp on the three mornings with a lighter touch and gave it no figure, so the arithmetic that had read over it on the tenth still did not know what it cost (T077). The widow’s mark hung where it hung, touched once before the kiln on Frost 2 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, morning, hearth, afternoon, dusk or going of the light on Frost 13, 14 or 15, because none was an opening; the first firing of Frost stood behind the household with its face turned away and no lesson, sign, mending or payer made of it, and four openings remained four (T058/T079). The stayed frost on the well’s north lip, the skinned trough and the plate of ice standing on its flat stone out of the path of feet were called weather and entered nowhere, and no figure, sign, cause or payer was taken off any of them (T083/T085 held, not paid). The fire’s fifth went unsupplied for two hundred and eighty-two, eighty-three and eighty-four days with its payer unnamed (T088), and Frost’s first arithmetic stayed locked in Berr’s box up the clay road with the printed one in twelve unchallenged and the figure read still not the figure paid (T015/T041/T047). On the afternoon of Frost 14 she carried him down at the half-pace and up again at the going of the light while the yard well went about its small commerce; she heard nothing that made an opening and gave no instruction at any hour to the basket, and the saying that passed between two women at the well was not brought under the roof as a lesson, a joining, a cause or a figure (T080 advanced, not paid). No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond changed hands, no opening made and nothing paid.

\end{itemize}

On Frost 9 she went to the trough with the back of the broken pot she turns the coals with, set the flat of it against the edge and pressed; the skin gave with a thin dry sound and a hairline ran out from under the pot, and she lifted a plate of ice clear at the rim and clouded where silt had risen into it, held it a moment with the water draining back in strings, and set it on a flat stone beside the well where no foot went, standing it where it would not be trodden. She drew what the yard calls weather with the pail against her knee, told the weather where to stand, gave nobody a figure and said nothing to the basket.
