\textbf{Ch 80.} Through Frost 22–24 the exact account holds at the kindling: six checkable in the worn thumb-mark, the seventh at the lip where the house cannot check, Garl’s unforged sentence beside it, \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late while wanting the late because it puts off the paying, the Seed 16 breath unspent, the ear-sentence to the calling word and stopped on all three days as a remembered \textbf{ninth} stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven, and the loan uncalled with no collector up or down the clay road. Ash stays worked into his knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring holds what light there is, his stroke goes over the shallow bright patch without the half-check, and the warm stone lies cold and unreconciled in its unmarked loft pot, which is not forgiveness. He did not ask about the room and Jorra did not ask about the ear. The boy’s hundred and sixty-second answer was filed as an object and not a hearing joined to his own held breath; the ownerless third shaping of the Frost 14 saying on Frost 23 was not brought under the roof as a cause or payment.

\textbf{Ch 79.} Through Frost 19–21 the exact account holds at the kindling: six checkable in the worn thumb-mark, the seventh at the lip where the house cannot check, Garl’s unforged sentence beside it, \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, \emph{Yes, house} to those who want the thaw early and those who want it late with the late still kept because it puts off the paying. The ear-sentence comes to the word that would call the loan on all three mornings and stops there — a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven — the Seed 16 breath drawn and not spent, chest tight, Ash in the knuckles, pale clip-ring at the wrist, stroke over the bright patch without the half-check, the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its loft pot by not trying, which is not forgiveness. The next I don’t count}, \emph{Yes, house} to those who want the thaw early and those who want it late with the late still kept because it puts off the paying. \textbf{Ch 72.} His seventh year stands at its very end through the last tend of Smoke and has still not given; the sentence that would call the loan that can hear comes to the word and stops on all three days, a remembered ninth stopping with no tenth stood up to join it. He keeps the exact account of what he owes that the house cannot check, the warm stone cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, and the equality with the boy and with Jorra unbroken. Smoke’s third arithmetic goes up the road in Berr’s box and changes nothing at the kindling.

He enters already sweeping, before anyone wakes, a bent man of twenty-two with grey Ash in the creases of his knuckles and a pale ring round his left wrist where the clip sat in Y.H. 806. Six years of a seven-year term lie behind him and he has counted every one and will not count the next. In Chapter 2 he pockets the small bench knife and then says of his own accord that he took it and put it back and they can check; he stops his broom for two strokes when a pot is set down and gives its flat note, turns his head a degree and says nothing; he banks the coals without looking at the fire. When the foundling is given a bed and he is given the loft he makes one short sentence of it and goes back to sweeping. His deference has a nail in it, and the nail is the one possession the house cannot check. Through the middle tend of Grain his account held unchanged — six counted and the seventh at the lip, the breath unspent, nine stoppings with no tenth, the loan uncalled and the stone cold — while the yard went around the returning-line place and he agreed the early thaw and the late, wanting the late still (T036/T076, T006, T098 carried).

On Days 5 and 6 he sweeps twice and says nothing. The small knife goes into his pocket and back onto the sill where it can be checked, announced unasked both times; the broom stops for two strokes when a Vail pot gives its flat note through the wall, and he does not turn his head or name the sound. The reader sees the second ear in the house; nobody under the roof does. Six years of seven are behind him and he will not count the seventh, which is the one entry in the house the house cannot check. He keeps his head down over the broom and the one thing he owns out of the house’s reach.

On Days 7, 8 and 9 the ear is no longer only the reader’s. He sees the boy expect a note from a pot that has not yet been set down, and stops his own broom at the set-down that gives nothing, and the two of them go on under one roof without a word between them --- a loan that can hear now knowing he is not the only one, which makes the thing he owns both more valuable and more dangerous. The small knife goes back to its sill and is announced unasked; six of seven years are counted and the seventh is held back, the one entry in the house the house cannot check. He stops for two breaths when Sella says he has done well and then goes on sweeping, because an argument has nowhere to put its foot when a man agrees with everything.

On Days 10 through 14 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. He measures the kindling as a debt and finds a fifth place empty; the knife goes to its sill and is announced twice more; when Sella tells him he has done well the broom stops for two breaths, the nearest thing this house allows to being struck by a kindness he cannot enter. A pot turned toward on the bench gives nothing and his broom checks half a stroke at the empty set-down, a second silent keeping beside the boy’s. He holds the pale clip-ring to the light and says the breath takes a man in his sleep and that Mud End called such a death merciful, and wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off what is payable. The ear is worth more than the debt that holds him, which makes it dangerous, and he has said nothing of it to anyone.

On Days 15 through 24 the seventh year stays held back and the ear is exercised twice without being spoken. He goes for a collector for a neighbour and brings back a man with grey fingertips, and on the way a carried vessel gives its flat note past the door; his head turns a degree, his hand goes back to the broom, and only the boy under the roof sees the turn. A pot cracks in the yard two paces from the basket and his broom checks at the place where it stood and goes on. The knife goes to its sill and is announced to the empty yard on Stone 22, 23 and 30; on Stone 29 he offers to check the Ash ridge by thumb, the nearest a clay-bound hand comes to touching what the house keeps out of its accounts. He still wants his exact account and grudges the house the loan of a bed; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 25 through 30 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The knife goes to its sill and is announced unasked to the empty yard, six of seven years are counted every day and the seventh is never named; the Ash in his knuckles is the colour of the ridge nobody will sweep and no scrubbing lifts it. In the Long Night he says the six and holds the seventh back in the dark, and sets the knife where it can be checked; the boy hears the told bell beside the heard bell and he says nothing about either. He still wants the thaw late because it puts off the paying, and on Ilmen 1, with the Ash burned and called dealt with and the district’s slates opened elsewhere, he sweeps toward the slip pits with the count unchanged. The loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 31 through 37 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife goes to its sill and is announced unasked; six of seven years are counted every day and the seventh is never named; the Ash in his knuckles is the colour of the burned ridge’s old place, which is now a clean dark line. He wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off the paying, and the thaw is coming on anyway. On Ilmen 6 his head turns a degree at the nearly-full note in open light and he says nothing, and the boy hears it and says nothing, so two not-sayings stand in the same place. The loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 38 through 44 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife is on its sill before light on the first morning and back on it at dusk, announced to the empty yard, six years counted and the seventh held back; Ash is worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts. He swept the place by the bench where no note had come, swept around the corner where the clay-heavy water had come up behind the racks, and swept the road toward the Fishstairs over and over without turning, the road a man goes down when a house wants a collector; no collector came for the woman in the brook and he did not go for one. On Ilmen 11 he set the knife on its sill, told the yard \emph{It’s back. You can check}, held the seventh year back and wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying. He agreed with both sides about the water and said nothing about the omission or the sound the yard had not heard. On Ilmen 15 the knife was back on its sill and the count unchanged, and he did not look toward the bed where the boy lay with both crusts in the fold.

On Days 45 through 47 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife is on its sill before the light goes, announced to the empty yard on the first two mornings and to nobody on the third, because the yard has already been told; Ash is worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. His broom goes over the road to the Fishstairs without once looking along it, and no collector comes down it for the woman the brook took nine mornings ago, and he does not say that the thing which has not happened has a name. He agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. When Sella tells him he has done well he stops for two breaths and then goes on. The boy keeps Tarn’s silence beside his own and does not let the two touch; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 48 through 54 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife lies on its sill with six counted and the seventh never named; Ash is worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. His eye goes a degree toward the slack oiled paper before the light does and he says nothing. A vessel gives its note past the yard door on Day 50 and another pot answers nearly full on Day 52, and his head does not turn at either and he does not call either a seventh hearing or name the sound in Grathic. He agrees with the ones who want the thaw early and the ones who want it late and keeps wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying; his broom goes over the collector’s road on Days 50 and 53 without once turning along it and no collector goes down it for the woman the brook took. He does not look toward the bed or the basket. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 55 through 60 the seventh year stays held back and the ear stays kept from the other side of the same silence. The small knife is on its sill the whole time with six counted and the seventh never named, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; Ash is worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. At the well and in the yard he agrees with the early thaw and the late, saying \emph{Yes, house} to each, and keeps wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. His broom goes over the road to the Fishstairs over and over without once turning along it, and no collector comes down it for the woman the brook took; the omission has no word and has not made a doctrine of itself. On Ilmen 28 a vessel gives its flat note past the yard door and his head does not turn and he does not name the sound; two ears keep their equality under one roof and the loan that can hear stays uncalled. When Sella tells him he has done well he stops altogether for two breaths, then sets the knife where it can be checked and goes back to the broom. On Silt 1 he keeps sweeping toward the thaw while the month turns and the brook runs higher; the count is unchanged. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and the sentence has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 61 through 67 the seventh year presses against the rising water and is still held back. The small knife lies on its sill and is announced to the empty yard, six counted and the seventh nearly gone but never named; Ash is worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring holds the light and gives it back. He agrees with the early thaw and the late so thoroughly that there is nowhere for an argument to put its foot, and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the brook is higher and the paying comes with the water. His broom checks half a stroke at the cracked-pot place and goes on, and his head does not turn at a vessel’s note past the door; on Silt 6 it goes a degree toward a nearly-full pot and back to the broom. He does not name either sound or look toward the basket. Jorra’s dust out of the back room goes unremarked by him, and he does not look at the dusty forearms. Two ears keep their equality under one roof and the loan that can hear stays uncalled; the sentence that would call it lies under the days as it has lain for six years. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and it has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 68 through 74 the seventh year presses against the flood and is still held back. The knife goes to its sill and is announced to the empty yard, six counted and the seventh nearly gone and never named; Ash is worked into the knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring holds what light there is and gives it back. He agrees with the early thaw and the late so entirely that no argument can find a foot and keeps wanting the late one because it puts off the paying, though the paying has come up the road and stands in the hollows of the bank. His broom goes over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, and when a vessel gives its note past the door in the afternoon of Silt 15 his head does not turn and he does not name the sound. Two ears keep their equality under one roof and the loan that can hear stays uncalled; the sentence that would call it lies under the days as it has for six years. A loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and it has still never been said in the house where it is truest.

On Days 75 through 77 the seventh year stands at the edge of the sill and is held. The knife is where it can be checked and the seventh is where it cannot; the broom goes over the collector’s road without turning and a whole vessel gives its note past the door without a turn of the head. The boy has brought a new shape into the yard --- a head that turns a half-beat after the knock, a loaf that passes without a slate --- and Tarn does not turn toward that either, and the boy does not put the two turnings together. The equality under the roof is unchanged: two ears, two silences, an ear worth more than a debt, and a loan that can hear and has never been called. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and the end was not written here.

On Days 78 through 84 the seventh year stands at the edge of the sill and is held. The lean week goes around the mud the flood left and Tarn goes around it with the same broom and the same account: six years standing in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat, the seventh nearly gone and still held back, announced to the empty yard before the light and not named to the kindling except as the one he does not count. Ash in his knuckles is the colour of the clean dark line the yard will not sweep and no scrubbing lifts it; the clip-ring at his wrist holds the little light. He agrees so completely with the early thaw and the late that an argument has nowhere to put its foot, and wants the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying stands in the ruts. His broom goes over the collector’s road over and over without a turn. When a vessel gives its note past the door he does not turn and does not name it, and the boy does not call it a seventh hearing; two ears and two silences keep their equality under one roof. The head that turns half a beat late at the well is not his and he does not join it to anything. Something must give at the end of the seventh year, and the end was not written here; the loan that can hear stays uncalled.

On Days 85 through 90 the seventh year stands at the edge of the sill through the turn of Silt into Seed and is still held. The small bench knife is on its sill before the light on Silt 26, 27 and Seed 1; he tells the sill first and the yard after where it is, six years standing in a mark his thumb has worn almost flat and the seventh never cut, nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house cannot check. To the kindling he says \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifts it; the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holds what light there is and gives it back. He says \emph{Yes, house} to both sides of the thaw argument, agrees so entirely that no argument can find a foot, and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts all week and goes over the boundary into Seed unchanged. Three stoppings now stand on the interval tray and none of them is a payment. \textbf{Four stoppings now stand on the interval tray and none of them is a payment.} The seventh year is pressed past the middle tend of Reed, the knife back on its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh held where it cannot, the unforged collector sentence beside it and the breath from Seed 16 still unspent. \textbf{Ch 37.} The firing month finds his seventh year still one tend from its end and held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check, the seventh at the lip of the sill where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge with the unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath unspent with its small interval at the top of each reach, his chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into his knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist holding what light there is. He takes the broom only after it has been instructed and says \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late, wanting the late because it puts off the paying. On all three days his stroke goes on over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without even the half-check; he does not turn along the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, and no collector comes. The equality with the boy has stood a hundred and fifty-two days: his ear for a pot before a knuckle touches it, the boy’s turn toward the note before anybody makes it, two silences of one shape and a loan that can hear never called. At the going of the light on Day 152, with the coals banked, he tells the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}; the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it comes up as it had come up nine times before, but on this day it is \textbf{not} brought to the word that would call the loan --- it stops short of the threshold, no tenth stopping stands up to join the nine, and he draws the breath that should have gone in and does not spend it, says \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and goes back to the broom. Sella, within hearing, gives the end of her instruction to the pot and asks nothing; Jorra does not ask about the ear and he does not ask about the room. The nine stoppings stay nine objects with no payer named to any, a tenth before the seventh year is earned would be a debt invented to make the nine into a bill, and the absence of a tenth is a keeping and not a payment. No new scar or possession, no change of voice; the loan uncalled and something still to give at the end of the seventh year.

The sentence about an ear worth more than the debt that holds it does not come up in these seven days: no tenth stopping stands up to join the nine, and the boy files no new interval, for a tenth before the seventh year is earned would be a debt invented to make the nine into a bill. Sella gives the end of her instruction to the pot and asks nothing; Jorra does not ask about the ear and he does not ask about the room, and the two silences stay unjoined. The seventh year stands at its very end and has not given; the small knife stays at the very edge of its sill with six counted where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it and the Seed 16 breath still unspent. The sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it still comes to the word that would call the loan and stops there, nine stoppings with no tenth, a remembered interval and not a payment; no collector comes on Grain 10, 11 or 12. Offstage at the market, he keeps the bright patch and the collector’s road unturned and lets the day’s new colours and shapes stay outside the house.

Through Grain 13–18 the exact account under the Vail roof goes on without a tenth standing up. Forward into Grain 19, not closed.

Through Grain 19–21 his seventh year stands at its very end and has still not given: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn and not spent, nine stoppings with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled with no collector up or down the clay road on any of the three mornings. He brings the ear-sentence all the way to the word that would call the loan three more times and stops each time with no figure and no name, a remembered stopping and not a new one, and he wants the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went. The warm stone lies cold and unreconciled in its loft pot, a keeping taken out and looked at once on Ember 4 and put back, which is not forgiving. His stroke goes past the bright patch without the half-check, so the Day 171 movement stays a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction and the Day 166 beat. He is a debt with a body, one year from the end of his term, valuable because he can hear and therefore unsafe, and the sentence that would call the loan that can hear has still never been said. Nothing paid, called, spent or forgiven.

No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond paid or spoken; the loan that can hear was still uncalled, the count crossed into Smoke 1 exact and unspent, and something must give at the end of the seventh year.

No bond paid, sold or spoken, no new scar, possession or change of voice; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

The next I don’t count}; agreed with the woman who wanted the thaw early and the man who wanted it late on Grain 15, agreeing so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went (T036/T076). His seventh year stood at its very end and was still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings — Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 — nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan uncalled; chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifted it, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back. On all three days he brought the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name; the stopping was a remembered stopping and not a new one, no tenth stood up to join the nine, and no collector came up the clay road on Grain 13, 14 or 15 (T036/T076, T061/T082). His stroke went over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without once turning along it, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf, not repeated and not paired into a rule (T062, T100). Above the shed the warm stone Sella gave him in the winter Garl died lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled with the debt by not trying, which was not forgiving (T006). The harvest came in with hands back in the worked strips and the first grain carried under the roof; with the returning hands the yard went around the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number, and the boy kept the bundle and the absence on separate trays, T098 advanced and not paid (T009/T013/T092, T098). The burned-slate word held at four and the three shapings of the pot saying stayed sayings, a wrong-wind voice on Grain 15 letting one stand without a pot lost (T061/T082, T064). The next I don’t count}, and kept the knife at the very edge of its sill with six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot; Garl’s unforged collector sentence lay beside it and the breath from Seed 16 stayed unspent, with its small interval at the top of each reach (T036/T076). The ear-sentence came to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, the stopping a remembered stopping and not a new one; the nine stoppings stood as nine objects and not a rule, no tenth came before the seventh year at its very end, and the loan stayed uncalled (T061/T082). His stroke went past the shallow bright patch without the half-check and over the collector’s road without a turn, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf; no collector came on Grain 10, 11 or 12. Ash stayed worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and the pale clip-ring held what light there was; he agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Does not appear; the broom, the knife and the loft are held for Chapter 2.

\item Ch 2: Swept the kiln-house before anyone woke and stopped for two strokes at a pot’s flat note without turning his head or naming the sound. Put the small bench knife in his pocket, then took it out and put it back where it could be checked and said so unasked. Told Sella \emph{Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.} Carried up from the Debt Loft with a broom on the third day, banked the coals, and said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} when the boy was given a bed. Heard the second flat note of the three days from a pot set down on the bench and did not say what it was.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. Swept before light on Stone 11 and again at dusk on Stone 12, with Ash in his knuckles and the pale ring at his left wrist. Took the small bench knife out and put it back where it could be checked, saying so unasked both times. His broom stopped for two strokes at the flat note of a pot through the shed wall and he did not turn his head, name the sound or say that it was a sound at all --- the second ear in the house, witnessed only by the reader. Said \emph{yes, house; I’ll sweep it; I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again} to the ground and kept his head down over the broom. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not counted. He said nothing about the note all day, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 7--9. On Stone 13 came up the yard with the small knife already back on its sill, checked it with his eyes only, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot before Jorra set it down; his broom stopped half a stroke at the set-down that gave nothing and he said nothing about either. Counted six years of seven and held the seventh back, and stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then swept again. At dusk put the knife back where it could be checked and announced it unasked, and kept his head down over the broom while Sella counted loaves and bits. Said nothing all three days about the note that did not come, and nobody asked him to.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Days 10--14. On Stone 16 measured the kindling stack with his eyes, four, four and a space at the end, and said to the stack \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count.} On Stone 17 set the small knife on its sill and told the yard to check, stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} and said \emph{Yes, house} before going on; his broom checked half a stroke when a pot turned toward on the bench gave nothing. Scraped Ash from his knuckles with the knife, held the pale ring at his left wrist up to the light and put the knife back without announcing it this time. Named the kiln’s breath as the danger and said a man in Mud End who slept before a kiln with the damper shut was called a merciful death; said he would take the late thaw, a longer week before the paying. On Stone 18 said he had swept and would sweep again; on Stone 19 agreed a late thaw was a longer week before the paying and offered to check the ridge; on Stone 20, Account-day, told the yard again the knife was back on its sill and let his broom stop half a stroke at the place where no note had come. Six of seven years counted all five days, the seventh held back and never named.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Days 15--24. On Stone 22 set the small bench knife on its sill, told the empty yard \emph{I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check}, and said to the kindling \emph{Six counted; the next I don’t count}; was sent for a collector for a neighbour two doors down and returned with a man whose cuff was soft from washing and fingertips the colour of skimmed milk gone off, who said \emph{the measure is taken and the account stands as entered} to a slate. On the way back his head turned a degree at a vessel’s flat note carried past the door and he did not name it or look at the basket. On Stone 23 swept around the place where a pot had given nothing and said \emph{I swept it this morning; I’ll sweep it again}; Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked by him. On Stone 25 and 26 his broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked in the yard with the flat knock and he said nothing about either; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. On Stone 29 held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light, said \emph{I can check the width, house. I’ve a thumb as good as any}, and took his eyes off the ridge. On Stone 30 the knife was back on its sill and announced once more, unasked. Six of the seven years counted every day, the seventh held back and never named; the ear kept silent and the loan uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 25--30. Through the Five set the small bench knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was, and said to the kindling that six were counted and the next he did not count; the seventh year was held back on every day. Scrubbed at the Ash in his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts, and kept the silence about the flat note all five days and about the boy’s ear as before. On the Long Night said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark. Wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying; on Ilmen 1 swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife back on its sill and the seventh still held back, and did not touch the ridge or the mark.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Days 31–37. On Ilmen 2 noticed the oiled paper had stopped lifting hard before he noticed the light, and swept toward the slip pits with Ash in his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted; six years of the seven counted, the seventh held back and not said to the paper or the boards or anybody. Agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 3 set the small bench knife on its sill and announced it to the empty yard --- \emph{I put it back. You can check} --- and scraped at the Ash in his knuckles. On Ilmen 5 swept near the bench and did not say what the pot gave or look toward the basket. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound. On Ilmen 7 stood with the yard as the Singing Sill gave its low note early and the argument ended in weather, and said nothing about either. Through the seven days kept the silence about the flat note and about the boy’s ear, and carried the count into Ilmen 8 with the knife back on its sill and the seventh year held back.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Days 38–44. Set the small bench knife on its sill before light on Ilmen 9 and again on Ilmen 11, told the empty yard \emph{It’s back. You can check}, counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back; Ash worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted, the pale clip-ring at his left wrist catching the light. Swept around the place where the clay-heavy water had come up behind the drying racks and swept the road toward the Fishstairs over and over without looking along it, the road a man goes down to fetch a collector; no collector came for the woman in the brook and he did not go for one. Agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. Said nothing about the sixth hearing the boy had heard out of a person on the bank, and did not look at the basket on the way back up the yard.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Days 45–47. Put the small bench knife on its sill and told the empty yard \emph{It’s on the sill. You can check} on Days 45 and 46; on Day 47 put it back and told nobody, because the yard had already been told. Counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back every morning, Ash worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifts, the pale clip-ring catching the light. Swept the road down toward the Fishstairs over and over without once turning to look along it; no collector went down it and he did not go, and he did not say the omission had a name. Stopped altogether for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then said \emph{Yes, house} and went on. Agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one because it puts off the paying. At the well on Day 47 went once over the collector’s road and again without turning. Said nothing about the boy’s ear or his own, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 12: Days 48–54. The small knife lay on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back; Ash was worked into his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring caught what light there was. His eye went a degree to the slack oiled paper at the window before the light did and he said nothing. A vessel gave its note past the yard door on Day 50 and another pot answered nearly full on Day 52 and his head did not turn at either; he did not call either a seventh hearing or name the sound. He agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying; his broom went over the collector’s road on Days 50 and 53 without once turning along it and no collector came. He did not look toward the bed or the basket, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 13: Days 55--60. The small knife stayed on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back, the one entry in the house the house cannot check; Ash worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, the pale clip-ring at his left wrist catching what light there was. At the well and in the yard he said \emph{Yes, house} to the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and to the one who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying (T036). His broom went over the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector went down it for the woman in the brook (T009, T090). On Ilmen 28 a vessel gave its note past the yard door and his head did not turn; he did not name the sound or supply the Grathic word for it and did not call it a seventh hearing (T061, T076). When Sella told him he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths, then set the knife where it could be checked and went back to the broom. On Silt 1 he kept sweeping toward the thaw with the count unchanged; the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 14: Days 61–67. Set the small knife on its sill and told the empty yard \emph{It’s back. You can check}, with six years counted and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry the house cannot check; held the pale clip-ring to the light and kept Ash in his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line. Said \emph{Yes, house} to both the early and the late thaw and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. His broom checked half a stroke at the cracked-pot place and went on without turning or naming the sound; a vessel gave its note past the yard door and he did not turn. On Silt 6 his head went a degree toward the nearly-full pot and went back to the broom; he said nothing and did not look at the basket. Jorra’s dust went unremarked and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 15: Days 68–74, Silt 9–15. Set the small knife on its sill before light and told the empty yard where it was, six years standing in a mark worn almost flat by his thumb and the seventh nearly gone and still held, the one entry the house could not check; Ash in his knuckles the colour of the clean dark line, pale clip-ring held to the light. A third movement of the equality under the roof, the Seed 22 half-check returned changed, held and unspoken — not a reconciliation, a hearing, a stopping, a payment or a mercy, no payer named, no slate entered and the loan uncalled; the boy filed it on a place of its own beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 held beat beneath the loaf shelf, three held changes on three places and not a pair, a doctrine or a rule (T036/T076, T062, T061/T082, T100). \item Ch 67: Days 252, 253 and 254, Smoke 13–15, Thirdday to Fifthday, on stage at the kindling, the hearth, the flagstones, the loaf shelf’s low angle, the Clay Yard and the collector’s road on all three days. Took the broom only after it had been instructed, told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} in the tone of a man stating the weather, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire, agreed with the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, swept the collector’s road without once turning along it, and no collector came up or went down the clay road on Smoke 13, 14 or 15 (T036/T076). His seventh year stood at its very end and was still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings — Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 — nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven, and the loan uncalled (T036/T076, T061/T082). On all three days he brought the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it all the way to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, the stopping a remembered stopping and not a new one, the small interval showing where the breath should have gone in and was not spent; the loan that can hear was worth more and more unsafe, and no tenth stood up to join the nine. Chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifting it, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back; the warm stone lay cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft, a keeping taken out and looked at once on Ember 4 and put back, which is not forgiving (T006 held). His stroke went over the shallow bright patch and past the road a house sends a man down when it wants a collector without the half-check and without turning along it, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 fraction and the Day 166 shelf beat. With Jorra the old shape held under one roof, the bent finger standing in the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence while the debt’s silence kept its own place, neither man asking about the back room or the ear. No bond was paid, sold or spoken, no new scar or possession; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 68: Days 255, 256 and 257, Smoke 16–18, on stage at the kindling, the hearth, the flagstones, the loaf shelf’s low angle, the Clay Yard and the collector’s road on all three days. Took the broom only after it had been instructed, told the wood \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count} in the tone of a man stating the weather, said \emph{Yes, house} to the fire and to an early thaw and a late, agreeing with both and keeping the late because it puts off the paying though the paying had stood in the ruts since the water went, and swept the collector’s road without once turning along it; no collector came up or went down the clay road on Smoke 16, 17 or 18 (T036/T076). His seventh year stood at its very end and was still held: six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the small knife at the very edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath drawn at the top of each reach and not spent, nine stoppings — Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26 and 29 — nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year at its very end and still ungiven, and the loan uncalled (T036/T076, T061/T082). On all three days he brought the sentence about an ear under this roof being worth more than the debt that holds it to the word that would call the loan and stopped there, a remembered stopping and not a new one, with no figure and no name, the small interval showing where the breath should have gone in and was not spent; the loan that can hear was worth more and more unsafe, and no tenth stood up to join the nine. Chest tight since the dark, Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line and no scrubbing lifting it, the pale clip-ring at the left wrist holding what light there was and giving it back; the warm stone lay cold and unreconciled in its unmarked pot in the Debt Loft, a keeping taken out and looked at once on Ember 4 and put back, which is not forgiving (T006 held). His stroke went over the shallow bright patch and the collector’s road without the half-check or a turn, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 damper fraction and the Day 166 shelf beat, not repeated and not paired into a rule (T062, T100). He did not ask Jorra about the men, the dust or the damper while Jorra’s finger stood in the cold iron, and Jorra did not ask about the ear; the two silences stayed unjoined. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no bond paid or spoken; something must give at the end of the seventh year and it did not give here.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter{Veno Brine}{the factor who can turn a damp document into a fortune}{build/portraits/veno-brine.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Veno Brine, the factor, Veno of Greybank, the man who never signs anything}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 766, Vhal, the Sallow coast}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Vhaleni)}\CRfield{Origin}{Vhal, the Sallow coast; a house with no boat-share and an excellent memory for wet paper}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Greybank counting house; agent of Sere interests in the north; Council of Tides by correspondence}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 130}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Forty-six and carefully dressed in a lowland cut that he has never quite got right, which he does not care about because the clothes are for the people he deals with and not for himself. He is a narrow Vhaleni man with a client’s smile that he can hold for an entire negotiation and drop the instant the door closes, which the clerks of Greybank have learned to read as the true end of the meeting. His hands are soft, with salt-paper stains at the fingertips, and he never carries a pen, because a factor who is seen writing is a factor whose word can be checked. He has a gold crown mounted in a ring which he wears on his little finger and which he has never earned in Grath, a detail he considers the only beautiful thing about the place. He smells of tar, wet rope, expensive soap and — when a Sere matter is in hand — myrrh, which is the smell of the empire and of a room where a person has been entered. The thing people notice first is the smile; the thing they notice last is that he never touches a slate, not even to move it, which in a counting house is a form of armour.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Vhaleni sibilance flattened for lowland ears, with long pauses and questions that contain their own answers. He says \emph{the document}, \emph{the weather}, \emph{the understanding}, and never \emph{the contract}, because a contract is a thing that can be read and he has built his life on things that cannot. He speaks of people as positions — \emph{the widow, thane, the collector} — and has a way of offering kindness with a figure attached, so that the recipient must decide which part was the gift, which is the whole art of his trade. When he is genuinely angered he becomes courteous to a degree that makes the room cold, because everyone has seen what precedes it. He has two laughs: one for clients, warm and brief, and one for himself, which is a single breath through the nose and means he has just been found out and does not intend to admit it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The paper is damp. It’s a bad season for documents. In Vhalen we consider that a virtue. A law that lasts too long stops earning, doesn’t it?”

\item “I have not paid you. I have advanced you. You’ll see the difference when the grain comes.”

\item “Forty measures for one return. Ask me why forty and I’ll tell you the figure is the figure. Ask me again in private and I’ll still tell you the figure is the figure.”

\item “I don’t buy people. I buy the shape of them. A beautiful return must remember enough to be exhibited. There’s a difference, and the Council calls it civility.”

\item “You want the girl. I want the share. We’ll write it down in the rain and see which of us has a document in the morning.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in Vhal to a family with no boat-share and an unusual talent for reading documents that had been left in the rain, which in the salt republic is the most marketable gift a man can have. He worked the counting house, learned that a contract on salt-paper in damp weather is no contract at all, and spent twelve years turning that fact into a fortune and two enemies, one of whom he later bought out with a damp document and a warm smile. He came up the Salt Road to Greybank in Y.H. 796 as a factor for Vhaleni glass and stayed, because the north buys measures and a factor who can buy a debt before it is due is a factor who never needs to buy the person. He has represented Sere interests in the north since Y.H. 803 without ever admitting to the Sun-Emperor’s Council that he works for them, and has sold grain, glass, quiet ash and whole returns to people who believe they are dealing with a Vhaleni and not an empire.

In the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812, he carried the slate for a private whole return from the Greybank factor to the collector in Sill, and could not spell the purchaser’s name, which he has never told anyone and has never forgotten. He has spent the years since trying to work out who bought forty children’s warmth for a foundling with a flower, because a man who cannot identify a buyer is a man who cannot charge him again, which in his profession is a form of insult. He has begun to suspect the Unbanked, then the Court, then a third thing that looks like both, and has kept each suspicion in a different document, all of them damp.

He has kept Solene Ember in a room with good light since Y.H. 810, which he describes to visitors as protection and to himself as an investment that has not yet matured. He has twice offered to buy Pia of the Quay’s mother’s boat-share and been refused twice, which he has entered as a debt owed to him by a girl who does not know she owes it.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no house and no share, which in Vhalen makes him a man whose account is always current and never his own. His wound is that he can turn any document into nothing and therefore cannot make anything that lasts, which is a strange hunger in a man who deals in permanent arrangements. He fears wet paper in the wrong hands, which is the only thing that can undo him, and fears more than that a person who reads a contract as a person rather than a shape, which is what the foundling from Low Kiln does when he looks at a vessel. His contradiction: the man whose whole trade is the convenient disappearance of evidence has kept three damp documents dry in a private drawer for ten years, because a factor who keeps nothing can never be blackmailed and a factor who keeps everything can, and he has chosen to be the second kind in secret and the first kind in public.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a boat-share, which would make him a Vhaleni instead of a man who deals with them, and he wants to know who bought the whole return in Y.H. 812, because an unspelled name is the only account in his life he cannot close. He thinks he wants the north to remain a place where a damp document is a fortune. What he needs is to understand that a person with no account is cheaper than a person with one, which is the Council’s doctrine and his own, and that he has spent his life making people cheaper in order to call himself civility. When he finally learns the purchaser’s name, he will not say it aloud; he will write it on salt-paper in the rain and watch it disappear, which is the only honest thing he has ever done with a document.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Solene Ember} — the beautiful return he keeps in a room with good light. He is kind to her in the exact way a creditor is kind, and she has never mistaken it, which is why he keeps her and why he distrusts her. He has begun to fear that she will refuse a fourth return, which would be a loss and a precedent, in that order.

\textbf{Pia of the Quay} — the salt girl who refused his offer for her mother’s share twice. He has entered the refusal as a debt and has never collected, which in his vocabulary is the beginning of an interest he cannot name.

\textbf{Marra} — the collector whose slate passed through his hands in Y.H. 812 and whose name appeared on a document he was not supposed to read. He has not told anyone and has used the knowledge once, gently, in a negotiation, which is how he tests what a thing is worth.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — who signed the levy he carried and forgot the purchaser’s name deliberately. Veno has never pressed him, because a Thane who has forgotten a thing on purpose is a Thane who can be made to remember it at the right moment, which is a kind of leverage he has kept warm for ten years like a coal under ash.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling whose name was written before a face. Veno has tried three times to buy his ear for the College or the Sere factors and has been refused three times, and has begun to suspect that the boy is not an account at all but a creditor, which is a category he has no word for.

\textbf{Avis Wake} — a Council member who votes against taxing the glass boats and whom Veno pays to do so, which is an arrangement the Council calls representation and Veno calls the cheapest insurance in Vhalen.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
No chapters are written yet. He enters in the Greybank counting house, smiling at a widow while declining to touch a slate, and the reader will take him for a merchant until the first damp document turns a household’s debt into nothing.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No chapters written yet; first appearance planned for Ch 130 (the Greybank counting house, the offer for the boat-share).

\end{itemize}
}

\chapter*{The Atlas}
\markboth{The Atlas}{The Atlas}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Atlas}
\CRmap*{The Bone Orchard — outside the north gate of Sill}{build/atlas/bone-orchard.jpg}{The burial ground a league north of the Cross, drawn at walking scale along the north gate road: the rough-staked ground of the thin-return children’s shallow graves, the east ground where pots are broken for the dead and left where they fell, the barrow of grey Ash that goes out through the north gate on every market-day and comes back empty, and the road running on through the gate to Cold Acre on the ridge with its six houses, its barley and turnips and its well that never freezes. The north bridge, the Ilm and Sill are drawn faint at the foot for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the barrow, the unslated graves, the pots broken for the house and the road that is clay to the ankle in Silt. An engraved broken pot in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Cold Acre — on the ridge two leagues north of Sill}{build/atlas/cold-acre.jpg}{The farm hamlet two leagues north of Sill, one league beyond the Bone Orchard by the north gate road, drawn at walking scale: six houses and a byre in their drift-stone wall, the barley strips and turnip ground, the bare ring of ground about the well where frost will not hold and the children leave the untaken turn standing, and the well itself with its stone lip, clay dish, well-rope, eleven links to the water and the twelfth that hangs dry in the hand. The well-shrine and the children’s stone stand beside the curb; a red nought marks the place where the thirteenth would stand. The road runs south to the north gate, Sill and the Bone Orchard drawn faint below, and east to the Tallow Works two leagues off; the frozen Ilm and the Singing Sill lie at the foot. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the ninety-four days of ice, the bell that comes up the ridge four, four and a gap with the gap not ours to fill, the assessor’s column that has never held a figure, the barrow of grey Ash that goes past on market-days, and no Last Day on a ridge. An engraved clay dish set on a stone sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Cross and the Fishstairs — Sill’s market and the steps below the north bridge}{build/atlas/cross-and-fishstairs.jpg}{The ground the boy is carried over on every Account-day, drawn at the scale of the market: the market square with its stalls, the reading block under the moot-post and its finger’s width of shade, the eight pigs on the weighing rail and the turnips left standing with figures beside them, the Court’s table at the Slate Row fringe; below the north bridge the Fishstairs counting four steps, four, and the out-of-line landing, the edge of the fish-trade in the bridge’s shadow, Rusk’s room, the hard sill and the Singing Sill under the water, the dotted line of the Breaking, and the south bridge on the way to Low Kiln. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the reed month.}

\CRmap{Greybank, the Court’s gate}{build/atlas/greybank.jpg}{The Court’s granary town eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, drawn as its own surveyors would draw it: the Ilm and its quay, the factor’s house where the tally for Sill is kept, the Vhaleni Counting House with Veno Brine’s private drawer of dry documents, the Court’s granaries and banking hall, the winter ford, the burial grounds, and the ends of the Clay Road and the beginnings of the Salt and Hearth Roads. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{High Kiln — the glaze terrace above Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/high-kiln.jpg}{The other half of Sill, drawn at the scale a potter walks: the terrace two hundred paces above the low yard with its barley strip, House Clay and the folded red cord and locked box, the Glaze Room where lead is mixed and tasted, the master potters’ houses and their breathing kilns, the broken terrace lip, the steep street climbing from the north bridge and the Cross, the Ilm with its four-foot sill and Singing Sill, and Low Kiln below drawn faint for neighbourhood only. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{Sill and the Lower Ilm — the country of the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-region.jpg}{The clay country about Sill, drawn out a few days’ walking: the Ilm from Nine Pots and the Ferr to Greybank, the weir, the Old Kiln, Cold Acre, Mud End and the Reedholt marsh. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap{Sill and the Two Kilns — the birth-town}{build/atlas/home-settlement.jpg}{A detailed plan of Sill on the Ilm, drawn to the ground a child can walk: the four-foot fall and the Singing Sill, the two bridges, the Fishstairs and the Cross, Slate Row, Low Kiln with the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, High Kiln and the Glaze Room, the family houses, the smithy, the meal mill, the wells and fields, the Bone Orchard and the edge of the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{House Silt and the Birth Room — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/house-silt.jpg}{The house three doors down the Clay Yard from the Vail house, drawn at the scale at which a basket set just inside the door sees it: the front birth room with its bench by the door, hearth and slip pot, board-bed of grey wool with the hollow where the pale river stone lay, the round pewter tin above the bed with its pale fold and thumb-bright rub, the shelf’s chipped cup, the birth-slate and the six narrow pages turned face-down toward a floorboard, and the grey Ash ridge left where it lies along the skirting into the back room. There a neighbour scrubs at a board with lye water and a low song comes up through the floor. Around it, drawn faint: the Vail kiln-house, the smithy, the Drawing house, the drying racks, the slip pits, House Reed and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook where Dessa Silt was taken, and the nineteen counted steps. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.}

\CRmap{Keld Keep and the First Seam}{build/atlas/keld.jpg}{The Warden’s fortress city against the Rim and the deep survey cut into the stone beneath it, drawn cold and mineral as the Keep’s own survey-clerks would draw it: the walled Keep with the Warden’s hall and the mine-reeve’s room; the Rim Road coming up from Sill and going on ten leagues to the Cold Pass and its survey post; the Listening Stones five leagues higher in the Rim; and below, the timbered shaft of the First Seam with its galleries, the Descent, the Duelling Floor cut into the stone with nine clamps to the floor and the tenth behind the board, the survey room holding the crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 and its branching red mark, the Ninth Gallery with the tin lined with warm-stone, a seam-serpent’s passing entered only as a change in the numbers, and the hot-lead warning of the Sweating. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with a compass, a league scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the measure before the name, the Warden’s claim, the once-a-year reading of the paper, and the insistence that no map is honest past the last pass.}

\CRmap*{Mud End — the peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill}{build/atlas/mud-end.jpg}{The peat hamlet three leagues downriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale on the dry shelf above the marsh: nine houses and their peat stacks, the byre where the moot meets and its moot-post, sods set out to dry, the peat cuttings in the southern banks, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The Clay Road runs west to Sill and east the fifteen leagues on to Greybank, both drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only; the marsh drain comes down into the river, and Reedholt stands faint among the reeds to the south. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the winter peat that decides who stays warm, the man taken quiet in his sleep and called merciful, and the wolves of Reedholt. An engraved peat spade sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Nine Pots — the rival kiln hamlet west of Sill}{build/atlas/nine-pots.jpg}{The pottery hamlet eight leagues west of Sill, drawn at walking scale along the road of the old feud: four kilns and one shared clay pit, the potters’ houses and worked strips, the moot-post, and the road east forded over the Ferr toward Sill. Stonemouth stands three leagues east where the Ferr meets the Ilm, with its lime kilns and coarse sandstone workings; the blue-grey Lead Run comes in from the west, and the Rim Road passes north on its way to Keld Keep. Sill and Greybank are drawn faint at the east edge for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Ember, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the feud, the lime and sandstone trade, the Lead Run that makes a man thin, and a cord from the Fishstairs never carried upriver. An engraved pot counted out at Nine Pots sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Reedholt — the reed-cutters’ hamlet in the east marsh}{build/atlas/reedholt.jpg}{The marsh hamlet four leagues east of Sill, drawn at walking scale: reed-cutters’ huts on posts on the dry hummock, the mud-wife’s hut with its grey-wool knot, the peat-dry with its drying sods and lifted tally board, peat stacks, the boardwalk over a cut with one plank gone, the peat-hut, the Reed Cut and its cut bundles, and a landing and punt on the Ilm. The river road runs above the marsh toward Sill and Greybank; the marsh road comes down from Mud End, passes the hamlet and goes off toward the Quiet Acre and the Standing Post, both drawn faint or set down in notes. The black peat and the bog-cow are written in the surveyor’s margin and drawn nowhere, for a figure would make a thing stand that does not stand. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Frost, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on going into the marsh in pairs, the reed-wolf’s five clicks and the man with two fingers gone, borrowed ground and standing reeves, peat and grey weighed under an apron and sealed under a Court name, and the child cutting a first bundle in the dark. An engraved reed-wolf and an engraved count-stick sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{Slate Row — the Court’s quarter in Sill}{build/atlas/slate-row.jpg}{The Court’s quarter, a quarter league east of the Cross, drawn at walking scale: the Clay Road passing through the Row to Greybank, the steep street climbing to High Kiln, the Ilm and its reedbeds along the south edge. The Court’s room with its bench by the door, pot, draught felt at the ankles and a place in the figures where a line should stand; the assessor’s narrow house of Y.H. 776; the collector’s table with its slate and cold-iron tube; the barred Waiting Room where the Forty of Low Kiln were held in Y.H. 812; the Court’s table at the market fringe and the printed one in twelve. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Tallow.}

\CRmap*{Stonemouth — where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm}{build/atlas/stonemouth.jpg}{The quarry village five leagues upriver of Sill, drawn at walking scale where the Ferr comes down to the Ilm: the sandstone workings and the lime yard on the rising bank, the lime kilns with their smoke, the ale-room beside the kiln, the village houses, and the weigh-clerk’s bench by the landing with punts on the river. The river road runs east to Sill and west over the ford to Nine Pots three leagues away; the Lead Run comes in from the west stained blue-grey from an old working, and the Rim Road passes north-west toward Keld Keep. Sill and Nine Pots are drawn faint at the edges for neighbourhood only. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Grain, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the lime, sandstone and reed-wolf tooth that go out by water, the Ferr that makes a man thin with no figure set against it, the thirty-year habit of stopping at the end of the part when a clean coat comes up from Greybank, and the name kept in a room against the name kept on a slate. An engraved reed-wolf tooth sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Clay Yard and the Vail House — Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-clay-yard.jpg}{The close ground of Low Kiln drawn at the scale a clay child walks: the Clay Yard with its slip pits and ruts, the Vail kiln-house with its hearth, loaf shelf and bed, the wheel-shed with the Debt Loft and the finger’s-width-open back room, the drying racks with the space beneath the lowest, the row of houses to House Silt, the smithy, the well and the birth-flower shrine, the Slip Brook behind and the Ilm at the reedbeds. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Drawing House — the death-house two doors down the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-drawing-house.jpg}{The unnamed neighbour’s house two doors down the yard from Vail, drawn close at the scale of a basket set at the edge of the light: the bench by the door with its pot, the draught going along the floor before the cold is felt, four nails, four and a thumb’s-width knot overhead, the grey Ash ridge a finger’s width thicker than Vail’s and turning the corner by the door without a break. Inside, the drawing pallet against the far wall with the pale round place on the arm, the collector with the cold iron tube wrapped in wool and the slate face downward, a hearth, the folded quilt on the other side with the warmed stone at the belly and the pot set between child and door. The Vail kiln-house, wheel-shed, smithy, drying racks, House Silt, the birth-flower shrine, the yard well and the slip pits are drawn faint for neighbourhood; the Clay Yard and Clay Road run below, west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the room that bears no name, the knuckle set before the iron and the note before the figure, and the child who grew worse before the day was out. An engraved cold-iron tube in its wool sleeve sits in the margin.}

\CRmap{The Hearthseat on the Keel}{build/atlas/the-hearthseat.jpg}{The Court’s city, built over the Hearth a hundred and fifty leagues south-east of Sill, drawn cool and clean as its own surveyors would file it: the Weighing Hall with the grating of cold iron over the never-out fire and the Hearth shown in cut beneath the floor; Slate Row with the College of Assessors and its second file; the Steward’s room, the sealed files, the bank where measures are pressed into newborn vessels, the rooms of fewer than twenty Kept, the back rooms, the printed notice, the Hearth Road from Greybank and the way out to the Nine Wells. Surveyed and filed in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Old Kiln and the Ash Throat — one league south of Sill}{build/atlas/the-old-kiln.jpg}{The collapsed kiln in the grey clay a league south of Sill, drawn as its surveyor would draw it: the fallen crown and its broken brickwork, the fire mouth on the south-east flank, the flue broken at the top, the concentric throat where the ash runs deeper than a man, the hollow in its wall from which a slate was carried north to Low Kiln, the grey banks that will not take a glaze, the surveyor’s stakes and his cord, the track from Sill and the marsh way to Reedholt. A slow coil copied from the back of a slate is inked into the margin and left unread. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Tallow Works — the rendering house two leagues north-east of Sill}{build/atlas/the-tallow-works.jpg}{The sheep-fat works known in Sill only by the smell on a north wind, drawn at walking scale: the rendering house or fat-house with its three vats, the hot flue and the thumb-wide warm crack where the wall meets it with grey paper nests hung behind, the lamp-room with its trimmed lamps and the leaf kept under a cracked saucer, the byre where the men sit at the turning of the year, the nest-fire at the shed door with the burnt paper beside it, the sheep-folds on the rise, and the sluice run carrying ash and wash-water away south-east. The ridge road comes in from the north gate past Cold Acre, both drawn faint, and the sweet smoke goes down on a north wind toward Sill. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Bone, with compass, a league scale in paces, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the fourth cup poured under the bench and the clerk who set it on the floor, the wasp that comes to the warmth and not the fat with twelve nests burnt and no value arising, fever first and the cold after with no figure asked for, the coal that comes up in clay on Kindling and the Long Night’s cost, the nought written where a name should stand, and the second warm crack in the cold north wall that has never held a nest and is set down in words but not marked on the wall. An engraved tallow lamp and an engraved tallow-wasp sit in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Weir and the Eel Traps — one league upriver of Sill}{build/atlas/the-weir.jpg}{The eel weir on the Ilm a league upriver of Sill, drawn at the ground the trap-keepers walk: the V of stakes and its traps, the plank walk, Orra Weir’s hut and salting-racks, the hearth-maids’ blessing stone, the shoals and reeds, and the river road. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year.}

\CRmap*{The Worked Strips — the barley fields east of Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/the-worked-strips.jpg}{The ground east of Low Kiln drawn at walking scale, the chart the lived days have fallen on from the planting of Seed through the cutting and dressing of Grain to the wool-covered grain of Smoke: five long rutted plots with their furrows and a flood stone a woman swept around, the clay-heavy Slip Brook coming down behind the drying racks, the reedbeds standing grey in the ruts where the barley stood, the Ilm along the head of the chart with its landing and punt, and the river road above the strips. Low Kiln, the Vail roof and its smoke, the drying racks and the Cross are drawn faint at the western edge for neighbourhood only; the Weir lies a league upriver, Mud End and Greybank downriver, Reedholt away through the marsh. Cartouche dated Y.H. 813, the month of Smoke, with compass, a hundred-pace scale, a convention of signs and surveyor’s notes on the arm that knows a bundle’s weight and no slate its price, the clay-heavy rise that took a woman from the end of nineteen steps and was called weather, and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out — described in the margin and marked nowhere, for a mark would be a figure and no figure stands. An engraved ear of barley with its top grain gone sits in the margin.}

\CRmap*{The Vail Kiln-house — the roof over the boy, Low Kiln, Sill}{build/atlas/vail-house.jpg}{The house known by its objects before its people, drawn at the scale of a basket set just inside the door: the boy’s room with its bed, one crust in the fold and four nails, four and a knot overhead; the other room with the carried fire under ash at four and a gap, the loaf shelf with two unnamed gaps and the charcoal beneath unread, the clay jar, the charred slate and the clean dark line beside the finer grey called the thaw. Beyond it the kiln at its mouth, the wheel-shed with the cold damper of two bites, the Debt Loft and the finger’s-width-open back room, the drying racks, the flagstones with the bright patch, the yard well with its bare trough and the Clay Road going west to the Cross and east to Greybank. Surveyed and inked in Y.H. 813, the month of Ember.}

\CRmap*{Vhal and the Sallow coast}{build/atlas/vhal.jpg}{A salt-chart of the principal Vhaleni port and the five leagues of shore east of it, drawn in the tar-and-wet-rope manner of the Council’s own surveyors: the Quay with its piers, crane, moored salt boats and the pulled benches; the Council room that smells of tar and wet rope, the tide-tally house and the glass furnaces within the town; the Salt Pans outside it with their dippers at dawn and their drying salt-paper; the blue-green Glaze Cliffs stained by old lead workings, and the glass-sand pits behind them; the silt-mouthed Ilm entering from the west and the Salt Road coming up from Greybank by the coast pass. In the sea the Sallow draw runs seaward against the wind, with a brine-gull, a salt boat and a salt-thing by report, and a surveyor’s notes on boat-shares passing through mothers, contracts that rot in the damp, and children warned not to lick the cliffs. Cartouche dated Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, with compass, league scale and a convention of signs.}

\CRmap*{Sarn — the bowl between Hearth and Waste}{build/atlas/world.jpg}{The known world as its own surveyors would draw it: the Rim and the cold beyond, the Sallow Sea, the Keel and the Hearth, and the nations between. Surveyed in Y.H. 812.}

\chapter*{The Codex of Sarn}
\markboth{The Codex of Sarn}{The Codex of Sarn}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Codex of Sarn}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\small\color{faded} Documents of the world, gathered from its ledgers, shrines, roads and kitchens.\par}\bigskip
\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A Bowl Not Poured, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Harn of Nine Pots at Greybank in Y.H. 813}
\CRsheetheading{A Bowl Not Poured, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere, Set Down by Harn of Nine Pots at Greybank in Y.H. 813}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A journeyman potter’s travel account, begun on the backs of dry grain-sacks and copied forward on the back of a Court tally-roll; part itinerary, part price-list, part complaint, with the figures of a Sere counting-house clerk entered in the margin and one line added in Greybank by a hand nobody will own · Written at the factor’s counting house in Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by Harn of Nine Pots, a thrower’s son who went down the Peat Line in Y.H. 812 with a cart of coarse ware, two bales of wool and nine bars of Keldish iron, and came back in Ash with a purse of gold crowns that no man in the Clay Yard would change. Set down first on three dry grain-sacks and copied onto the back of a discarded Court tally-roll, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a clay tube stoppered with wool. It survives with the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a thumb of olive oil at the head, a wine-ring at the foot, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, one crown pressed flat between the third and fourth leaf, four corrections in the leaning hand of a Sere clerk who borrowed the leaves at the market, and a line at the back in a narrow upright hand added after the copy reached Greybank.\par}\medskip
I went south with pots. That is the whole of my reason and I will not dress it as a pilgrimage. Nine Pots has four kilns, a shared clay pit and a quarrel with Sill about a road neither town has mended. A journeyman who can throw a jar in four beats hears that a house in the south will pay for a coarse jar to hold oil, and he hears it the way a man hears water in a dry well. He goes.

I left in Seed of Y.H. 812 with a cart, two bales of wool off the Tallow side and nine bars of Keldish iron got honest at Stonemouth, and came back in Ash with a purse of gold crowns that no man at the Cross could change and a figure in my head that would not leave. This is the figure. I have set down what happened and what did not. A man who writes only what happened writes a ledger, and I have read enough ledgers.

\subsection*{The road down}

The Clay Road ends at Greybank and the south begins somewhere past it, though not all at once. The Empty Cantons come first: wells with the rope still on the windlass, doorways with the thumb-polish worn into the lintel, and nobody. A Fen man told me the people were taken in the first Returns and paid for by a line of figures. I asked him where the line went.
