He said a line goes where it is written and a figure stays where it is put, and went back to his eels.

At the Peat Line the wet begins. A reeve took a mark off me for standing on a board he had not pointed to, which was within his right. The Fenfolk say a dry man is a dangerous man, put us up on the Standing Post and did not tell us which boards would bear us. We learned. Sere’s northern advance stopped here in Y.H. 634 and the Fenmarch has paid tribute in eels ever since, which tells a man more about the south than any temple tells him about the Hearth.

Past the Line the dust comes up off the roads and lies on the pots like grey slip. The burning winds take the skin off a man’s lips. I had been told the south was warm; it is warm the way a kiln is warm, with the door open and the breath coming out, and a man goes thirstier there than he does in a Grathic winter.

\subsection*{The bowl at the third hour}

The Bowl of Sere is three hundred leagues from Sill and has no wall worth the name. Its courts are open and each has a fire in the middle. Men sit in the heat of them with their coats on the ground beside them, and the dust settles in their hair, and nobody brushes it off.

At the third hour of the day a public bowl of wine is emptied, and that is how the Sun-Emperor’s acts are announced. I stood in a court and watched a man in a pale coat tip the bowl out onto the stones. The crowd leaned in. I asked the man beside me whether a debt had been forgiven or a province ruined.

He said, “Yes.”

“Which?”

He looked at me as though I had asked a pot which side was the bottom. “Measure for measure,” he said, and went back to his wine.

I have since learned that the phrase means whatever the speaker has already decided. It is a fine phrase for an empire. At home a man says \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, and the notice and the man between them keep a whole district warm for a season. Here they empty a bowl and call it the same thing as a number.

They sing this at the wine-presses. I have set the Grathic words under the southern tune, which loses something, as Grathic always does when it is made to carry a tune.

\begin{quote}\itshape Fill to the lip and let it go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot was made to pour;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cup that keeps is the cup that sours\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cracks along the floor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the house and one for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the slate we burn by lot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one stands full and is not poured ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask not whose debt. Ask it not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The burning of slates}

Valen Openhand, whom they call the Bowl-Priest, preached in the court while I was there. He teaches the Spending: that a vessel was made to be emptied and a life hoarded is a life wasted. He is not a thin man, and neither are the priests who say it after him, which a traveller notices after standing in a court all morning.

At the end of a feast they burn one household’s debt-slates, chosen by lot, and then make new ones. I saw it done. A woman whose slate went into the fire wept, and the crowd was kind to her, and then the new slate was brought out and the crowd applauded that too. I have not got used to the second applause.

The warmest funerals in Sarn are in Sere. A house will burn a year’s grain under a dead man to keep him warm, and the Court taxes the ash, and the house is ruined by degrees and called generous. A poor funeral is a small fire in an open court. A great funeral can empty a province, and the province is then bought cheap, which is the sort of arithmetic the south has made its own.

A girl of sixteen emptied the bowl at her Bowl feast and named a debt she intended to carry. The applause was for the debt, not for her. She had seven names by then and would keep whichever her household liked. I asked a bowl-surgeon beside me how a person becomes one person out of seven. He said a vessel keeps the shape it is poured into, and sold me a nest of tallow-wasp resin for four marks. He held the nest up to the light and listened to it the way a potter listens to a pot, and asked whether it had been taken in a frost. In the Clay Yard we burn the stuff. Here it goes into a graft.

\subsection*{People with no measure}

Slavery is open here and legally simple. A slave’s warmth is the owner’s holding, and a slave has no measure in law. This is not an oversight. It is the whole of the law. A beautiful house-slave is given a whole return and exhibited at feasts as proof of the owner’s generosity; a slave who runs is returned thin and set to the grain mills. I heard the mills grinding at night, a low sound under the wind, and was told that the people in them had once been someone.

At a feast I saw a northerner exhibited for small coins. He was thin-returned and could not say where he came from. He looked at me the way a man looks at a wall he half remembers, and said a word that might have been \emph{slip}, or might have been a bit of the Ferr water coming up in him. I did not go to him. In a southern court the man who buys a curiosity and the man who claims a countryman are the same man until he has paid.

I have written this plainly because it was plain. I have not written what I think of it, which is a thing a traveller keeps to himself if he wants to travel back.

\subsection*{What I fetched}

Twelve bits to a silver mark. Twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and does not stay in Grath. The Court books in embers and will tell you an ember is worth five marks; no man has ever exchanged one for the other, and I left them off.

I carried south — Sold for — I carried north — Cost me\par

Nine bars of Keldish iron, Stonemouth — 2 crowns and a half — One green glazed bowl — 3 marks\par

Two bales of wool, Tallow side — 1 crown, 9 marks — A skin of southern wine — 6 marks\par

A score of coarse jars, Nine Pots — 11 marks — A phial of oil for a lamp — 4 marks\par

One nest of tallow-wasp resin — 4 marks — Four crowns, changed at the quay — would not change at the Cross\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Written across the wool row in the leaning hand of the Sere clerk who borrowed the leaves at the market:} Wool entered at the crown rate. The figure is current.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} It was current until he went home. In the morning the same buyer wanted two marks less for the same bale, and the clerk was not there to enter the difference.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the last row, in the same leaning hand:} Coins entered as four. The bowl not entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And below, in mine:} He entered the coins and left the bowl, which is the whole art of that country in one line of writing.\end{quote}

The green bowl cracked on the third morning after I got home. It gave a small flat knock when I set it down and went from lip to foot without anything falling out that I could see. A southern glaze will not take a northern frost. In Sere they would have told me what it meant. In Nine Pots we swept around it and called it a bowl gone wrong.

\subsection*{The bowl that stands}

At every feast a fourth bowl is set down full and not emptied. It stands through the feasting and is carried away still full. Nobody pours it and nobody says whose debt it holds. I asked three times and got three different silences, the last of which was the kindest.

This is the figure I brought back. There is a place in every Sere account where a bowl should be emptied and is not, and the clerks go around it the way our yard goes around the space under the drying rack. I have set it down because I saw it and not because I understand it. A hearth-maid would cover it with a date. A Court clerk would give it a number and the number would be nothing entered in the wrong column.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the foot of this section, in a narrow upright hand added at Greybank, the verbs left out as though a verb were a thing a man could hide in a cuff:} No fourth bowl. Not carried forward.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine, underneath:} I have left his line standing. If it is not carried forward then it stands where it is, which is what I said before he wrote it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Coming back}

I came back in Ash with the dust still in the seams of my coat and a crown pressed flat between the third leaf and the fourth. The year before I went down had been the Long Cold. The barley was thin, the fuel dear, and a potter with nine bars of iron was a man with a reason to leave. I found the reason had followed me home: the same levy, the same printed figure, the same men going around a place where a line should stand and does not.

The crown buys nothing at the Cross. In Sere a coin is a thing a man can empty into a bowl and call it generosity. Here it is a thing I keep because I cannot spend it. I have not spent it and I have not entered it. The fourth bowl stands where I left it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A Tide Not Yet Seen, Being a Letter Written in the Rain and Answered in the Margin}
\CRsheetheading{A Tide Not Yet Seen, Being a Letter Written in the Rain and Answered in the Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on salt-paper, from the Salt Pans to the Quay at Vhal, carried out in Ilmen and returned in Silt, with the answers of the woman addressed, one correction from a Council clerk, and a word of an older law stuck fast to the leaf · Written at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in the second tend of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by Enna Salt, a salt-worker of the pans, to Vea Net of the Quay, who holds a twelfth of a boat through her mother; carried along the Salt Road by a glass carrier, rained on in Silt, and returned with answers in Vea’s hand and one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides. Kept since in a dry tin among what the house calls nothing. The leaf survives soft at the fold, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a nick from a fish-hook, and one word of an old Council decree that will not come off the paper.\par}\medskip
To Vea of the Quay, who holds a twelfth through her mother and will not say it before company. From Enna at the pans, where the wind has been in the east nine days and the paper will not take ink.

I have written this in the rain. The factor come up from Greybank does it and gets a fortune by it, so there must be something in the practice. If the Council reads what is left of this there will be nothing in it to read, and a letter that cannot be read is the only kind I have ever wanted to send you.

The seventh lot is short. I raked at the fourth hour and the crust came up as thin as the skim on the Sallow on a still morning, and when I told the pan-master he said the weather and went on with his counting, which is what a pan-master does when a woman has told him the truth. A brine-gull took a coal off the brazier while my back was turned. I threw a chip of cliff-glass at him and missed, and he went off with the coal warm under his crop, as though he had been invited.

The dippers came at dawn and trailed the nets and said the draw ran against the wind again, which it always does and which the Council is always surprised by. The clerk entered the figure that would be profitable and left the other standing in the wet where he could not see it. My mother used to say a law that lasts too long stops earning; the Council has made a virtue of it and then hired men to write things down. It is the funniest thing I know and I have never once laughed at it.

Old Iven went out on the ebb in the second tend, sealed in a salted boat, and we stood on the Quay and watched until it was out of sight, which is held to be enough. I thought of you the whole while and have not entered it. If I entered it I would have to charge you for it, and you would pay, and then there would be an end of it.

A man in a clean coat come along the Salt Road from Greybank asked after your mother’s twelfth on the third day of the tend. I told him the document had been left in the rain. He said that in Vhal that was a virtue, and laughed as though he had invented it. He asked after quiet ash as well, though a salt-master has none to sell; I told him so and watched his smile go out like a lamp in a draught. He has not been back. I have not told your mother. If he comes again she will hear it from him, which is the proper order of things and costs me nothing.

I go up the Salt Road with the glass at the turn of the month. The carrier says two tendays and the pan-master says a season, and the pan-master is generally right about the length of other people’s absences. I will be gone when the ebb comes that I said I would be back for. Do not hold it against me. Hold it against the road, which has been in a bad way since Silt; a thing said in Ilmen does not travel well once the mud takes it.

When we were fourteen you walked the pans barefoot at the Salt Walk and named a tide nobody had seen, and the dippers wrote it in the salt and it was gone by noon. I have tried all winter to get the word back. I have the shape of it and not the word. It went up at the end, or it went down, and I cannot bear to choose between the two, because I have chosen wrong every other time there was a thing to choose.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, small and sibilant, the letters leaning}

Iri. It went up at the end. You have put your stop in the wrong place and always did.

Do not tell me the seventh lot is short. Tell me you are going up the road. I am not a pan-master, and I can bear a thing said straight if it is said once.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning in Silt, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He struck out the word \emph{short} and set \emph{current} above it. Against the tide-name he wrote \emph{tide not entered}, in the narrow upright hand they teach at the counting house, with the verbs left out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff. He put a figure in the margin where I had put none: \emph{one mark and a binding promise}, which is what a salt-worker is paid, and which I suppose he thought he was being kind to enter. I have left all of it standing. He has entered the promise and not the tide, which is exactly what the Council does with both.

\subsection*{In the margin again, lower down, the same hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rake at the fourth, rake at the turn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the crust comes up where the wind has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes the coal, the clerk takes the mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pan keeps what the rain cannot reach.\end{quote}

I have never written a rhyme in my life and I would not begin now if I had a slate to write it on. You have written it in the rain, so there is no letter, and I have answered nothing. Ask me again in the dry and I will charge you.

There is a tide that has not come. I have named it for the day you come back down the Salt Road. Do not ask me what it is like. I have not seen it, and if I had seen it, it would not be the one.

\subsection*{At the foot, in the first hand, written on the return}

It came back wetter than it went. Most of the words are gone. The ones that went deepest are the ones that stayed, which is the whole history of salt and a fair part of mine. The tide-name is still here because I pressed it with the point of a nail instead of a pen, and the rain had nothing to take. A thing written deep enough is a thing the rain cannot call a contract.

I have kept the leaf six tendays in a dry tin. I would not line the tin with glass; glass sweats in this weather and would have it away in a month. There is no word in Vhaleni for a person you write to without wanting something. There is a word for a person whose account is current, and I have used it of you in my head for nine years, and never once charged you.

\subsection*{Stuck to the leaf}

A scrap of an older Council decree has stuck fast to the back of the sheet, older than the tin and older than the woman who gave it to me. Only one word of it survives: \emph{earning}. The rest has gone the way the Council’s laws go, quietly and in good time and with everybody paid.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand that is nobody’s}

The ebb takes and does not keep. I have tried to learn that from the water and have not managed it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Before the Name, Being an Account of the Cold Kingdom of Keld Written on the Road Down, with the Prices of Iron and Warm-Stone, the Tally of Eleven Months, the Road-Song of the Carters, and the Correction Set Over It at Greybank}
\CRsheetheading{Before the Name, Being an Account of the Cold Kingdom of Keld Written on the Road Down, with the Prices of Iron and Warm-Stone, the Tally of Eleven Months, the Road-Song of the Carters, and the Correction Set Over It at Greybank}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A factor’s clerk’s travel account in the open courtesy of Sere, set down in gold ink on prepared paper and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled Court grain-warrant; the itinerary in the long-vowelled southern hand, the prices in a tally-clerk’s figures, the Keldish sayings rendered into Grathic with the hard words left hard, a mine-reeve’s correction written number-first in the margin, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk, and a line at the foot that answers to no name · Written in the last tend of Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on the road down from Keld Keep by the Rim Road, by Joren Brightbowl, a junior tally-clerk in the service of the Ten Bowls of Sere, who went north in Seed with a letter of credit and forty gold crowns to buy iron, lead and warm-stone, and came back in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with three bars of iron, a pig of lead, a fist of warm-stone, and the name of nobody who had warmed it; copied at Greybank onto the back of a grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold and carried on to Sill. It survives with gold ink worked into the grain of the first leaf, the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, grey stone dust from the First Seam along the lower margin, a ring of warm wine near the song, a hard crumb of Keldish barley bread in the gutter, a bump pressed into the third leaf where a warm-stone lay under it for a night, the mine-reeve’s blunt correction in the margin, the Court clerk’s correction laid over the text, and a line at the foot in a hand that answers to no name\par}\medskip
I went north with a letter of credit and forty gold crowns, and came back with iron, lead, and a stone that was warm in the morning and would not say who had warmed it. This is the whole of my errand and I will not dress it as a pilgrimage. The Ten Bowls buy iron and warm-stone from the mountain, and wool and grain go north to pay for them, and a clerk who can count is a clerk who gets sent. In Sere we call a debt carried gracefully an ornament of a house. In Keld a debt is a number cut into the forearm, and a man gives it before he gives his name. I set that difference down first because it cost me more than the iron did.

I write in the courtesy of my country, which is elaborate, and I have left the hard words hard. A favour done to a reader is a debt the reader did not ask for; I have done none. Where I could not learn a thing I have set down the shape of the not-learning, which is a thing a clerk can carry home and a priest cannot.

\subsection*{The road up}

The Clay Road ends at Greybank and the north begins somewhere past it, though not all at once. At Greybank a factor sold me a fist of warm-stone in a fold of wool for three marks and would not say whose fire it had come from. This was the first honest answer I had in that country. The road says: only fools and factors go up without a stone. I was a factor’s clerk, which in the high country is a fool with better boots.

From Greybank the Rim Road runs a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather. There are inns at the first three stages and after that a man lodges with whoever will have him, and pays in a figure or a promise, and finds out in the morning which one was current. On the fourth day the water in the bucket had a skin of ice before I had carried it ten paces. On the sixth I could see the Rim, which is not a mountain but a wall of cold with a sky leaning on it.

At Keld Keep a man asked my measure before my name. I gave him the courtesy of Sere: Joren Brightbowl, of the Ten Bowls, in the service of the house, most honoured to be received. He waited. When I had finished he asked again. I told him I had no number cut in my arm, being a lowlander and uncut, and he wrote me down as a lowland figure and told me it would not carry me ten leagues beyond the pass. He was right. It did not.

I asked him why the figure went first. He said a name was a thing said in a doorway and a number a thing said in a mine, and that the mine had the longer memory. I have set that as he said it. It is a hard saying and I have not softened it with any of our words.

\subsection*{What they count}

In Keld a man’s number is cut into the forearm at thirteen, on the day they call the Descent, and when a man comes back thin the old numbers are cut out and new ones put in, so that a smooth place on the arm is not a blank but a thing that happened. I saw three such places in the tally-room and asked a man with one of them what number he gave now. He gave the old one.

“But the skin has been corrected,” I said.

“The number was not,” he said, and went back to his counts.

The deep mines are worked by men bought for a term, whom the Grathic buyers call under-vessed. Their lives are reckoned at eleven months. I asked the mine-reeve what became of a man at the end of the eleven and he said the term was expiring, which is a phrase that lets a man go on writing. In the Bowl we empty a bowl at the feast and call a debt forgiven. Here they cut a number and call it a man. Both are figures in a clean hand, and neither hand washes.

What I carried north — Entered at — What I fetched — It cost — Who paid\par

A letter of credit, forty crowns — at the factor’s house, Greybank — three bars of iron — eleven marks — the house, which will carry it at the feast\par

Six ells of southern wool — two crowns and a half — a pig of soft lead — four marks — the gallery, which gives back nothing\par

One olive-oil lamp, not new — not entered — a fist of warm-stone — three marks — unnamed; I have not found the name\par

A promise of grain at the Peat Line — current until the rain — eleven months’ labour, entered as a term — not a price — the man whose forearm carries it\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the blunt number-first hand of the mine-reeve, in the margin against the last row:} Eleven. Not a price. A term. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left his correction standing above my row, as a repaired vessel keeps the old break showing. A term is the only figure in that country that I have seen a man refuse to call a number.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The stone, the iron and the hand}

On the third morning the mountain sweated. There was no cry and no bell. A man came up from the Ninth Gallery with the smell of hot lead on his coat and said only that the gallery was giving back more than it took. The mine-reeve sent the men up before he wrote anything down, which is the first time in that country that I saw a figure wait for a man. I had been told the smell was the whole warning and had not believed it until I smelled it. It is a sweetish smell, like a glaze room in High Kiln, and a man from the south might think it a kindness. It is not.

I did not go down to the Duelling Floor, but I heard a clamp set across a way. It is a small sound, a staple going into green wood, and then a boy’s breath let go in two pieces. A clamp-master told me that the first man to open a way usually wins, because the other is busy bleeding, and he said it as another man might say the price of an axe. He had a hand that would not close and held the clamp with the other.

A Keldish man told me the true Hearth lies under his mountain and that the Court’s fire in the south is a candle lit from it. I said nothing, being a guest. A Court clerk standing near said nothing either and did not argue, which is the whole of the Court’s answer in that country.

The warm-stone has kept a little heat for eleven days under my coat. Every morning I have asked whose fire it came from, and every morning I have had the same count of words: none at mine. A stone from the Ninth is a kindness bought by somebody whose name is not written where a traveller can read it, which is a generosity of the same order as ours in the Bowl and perhaps a more honest one, because it does not ask to be applauded.

\subsection*{The people who sit against stone}

I climbed five leagues higher into the Rim to the Listening Stones, where the Vorr sit against the stone for days and come away with numbers. One of them, a tall grey man with the last joint of his fingers doubled, let me stand beside him through a morning and would not let me look at the stone he kept. I asked him what the oldest marks meant. He said the numbers would be found correct when the season had turned, which is the answer they give and is not a translation. I have set it down because a courteous man owes his reader the exact shape of a refusal.

He told me, which was more than I expected, that the Vorr do not undergo the Return and are never collected. When I asked why, he said they had never been owed. He said it without pride, the way a man says that a door is locked, and I have not added to it.

\subsection*{The road-song}

\emph{Taken down in Grathic letters from a carter going up, not down, on the sixth day out. He sang the middle verse twice, the second time for a man with a smooth place on his forearm. The Keldish vowels are long where ours are short; I have put them back as I heard them and left the hard consonants standing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road goes up and the name goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number goes on the arm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the axe and two for the lead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the stone that keeps a fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven months at the seam, they say,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a warm-stone sewn in the coat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain keeps what the mountain took,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the carter carries what it wrote.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Give me the count, I’ll give you the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure stays where the man went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name in the mouth is a door in the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but a number is cut in the bone.\end{quote}

He would not sing going down. He said a song sung coming down was a debt with no date, and a man who had carried a load up the Rim Road had paid enough for the one he had carried up.

\subsection*{What the clerk did at Greybank}

A clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He set his hand on the top sheet before he looked at me, and said it was entered as it stood. He writes in the narrow upright hand with the verbs taken out, as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{a man gives his number before his name} he wrote \emph{the vessel is identified by measure}.

\item Against \emph{a life reckoned at eleven months} he set \emph{term: eleven; value retained}.

\item Against \emph{the mountain sweated} he wrote \emph{an increase in the seam-draw was recorded}.

\item Where I had left the place where the warm-stone’s payer should stand, he drew a small circle and wrote \emph{unaccounted} beneath it.

\item Against the Vorr man’s saying that they had never been owed, he wrote \emph{no charge lies against this party}, which is true in the same way that an empty cup is clean.

\end{itemize}

I have left every line of his standing above mine. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a clerk writing home wants to know who did what to whom, and the answer is in the sentence if there is someone in it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold at the head is mine; gold ink creeps into the grain of the paper and leaves a yellow edge that no washing takes out. The dust of the burning winds came north with me in the seams of my coat and has ground into the fold, a southern thing in an account of the north. The grey along the lower margin is stone dust from the First Seam; I set the leaf down on a bench where a surveyor had laid his slate and did not brush it off. The small round mark by the song is where I set a cup of wine on the first night back at Greybank and went to find the word I wanted; the wine went cold and has left a ring the colour of old lead. The bump in the third leaf is where the warm-stone lay under the quire for a night and kept the paper faintly warm until morning. The hard crumb in the gutter is Keldish barley bread, given to me on the road by a man who would take neither a coin nor a promise, and I have kept it because I could not enter it.

\begin{quote}\itshape At the foot, in a hand that answers to no name:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes on the arm and the name goes home;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone keeps the fire and the fire keeps no date.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask who paid for the warmth in a stranger’s pocket ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mountain does, and the mountain does not say.\end{quote}

I asked the mine-reeve, the Court clerk and the man with the smooth forearm, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The quire goes back into the factor’s tin at Greybank. Tomorrow the grain goes north and the iron goes south, and the number in my own arm --- which is none, for I am a lowlander and uncut --- is still the only thing about me that nobody in Keld found worth entering.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Eight and the Flat, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Clay Yard Children at the Drying Racks, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Listening, and What a Clerk Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{Eight and the Flat, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Clay Yard Children at the Drying Racks, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Listening, and What a Clerk Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A rack-woman’s gathering of a children’s counting game, set down in Grathic on the back of a spoiled pot-tally; the counting-out and the tapping verse in the children’s own half-sung speech, the manner of the play in the writer’s small hand, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by a woman who has fired a kiln for thirty years, and a line at the foot in grey slip in a hand that has not come forward · Written in Tallow of Y.H. 813 in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in Sill, by a woman who sets the coarse pots to the drying racks and has learned her letters off a broken tally; set down in charcoal and slip on the back of a pot-tally spoiled by a wet thumb at the third rack, carried to Greybank in the satchel of a woman come to have a widow’s mark confirmed and copied onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. Kept folded in the rack-woman’s apron among the slips of birch she uses to mark the wet ones. It survives with slip worked into the grain at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze in the fold, a pale thumb at the second corner where a woman with the sweet sickness leaned over to read, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a tideline where the tally went damp, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, the kiln-woman’s gloss in charcoal beside the flat one, and a line at the foot in grey slip in a hand that has not come forward\par}\medskip
I set the coarse pots to the drying racks, and I have written this because a man with a slate stood in the yard in the dry week and asked what the children counted when they put their knuckles to the pots. I told him a sound and not a figure, which is the truth of it, and he went away and sent me a clerk, which is what happens to a sound in this country. What is below is what the children said before the clerk came and what they said again after he had gone back over the north bridge with the verbs taken out of it. I have set his hand above mine where he put it, and theirs underneath where they stand, as a rack keeps the wet mark under the dry one.

The slip at the head is my own thumb. I set the tally on the lowest rack before I had done with the wet ones, and slip goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why we use it to mark a place. The grey came off a cuff that had no business lying in a yard, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a Clay Yard and nothing here gets burnt in the morning.

\subsection*{The row and the knuckles, as the children keep it}

\emph{Played in Tallow and Ember, when the pots stand rim-up on the lower rack and the slip has gone firm enough to take a tap. Not in the Five, when the children are made to stand and listen and there is no rack for it; not in rain, because a wet pot answers flat whatever ails it, and a child who counts a wet pot learns the wrong count. In Stone they tap the pots on the shelf by the banked fire, which is the same game with the cold taken off it.}

The row is as long as the day’s drying gives. Pots stand in it rim-up, belly out, with their feet on the slat where the wheel left them. One child is \textbf{the ear}, because she puts her head down to hear what the knuckle brings up; the rest are \textbf{the row}. They are called the ear and the row and never their own names, for a name said in this yard travels up the clay road in a cuff and comes back entered.

The ear taps each pot once on the belly with the middle knuckle, not on the rim. A tap on the rim gives a high thin note before the pot has earned one, and the yard calls that a pot saying a thing too soon. One line of the verse is one tap, and the verse is said to the pots and the rack, never to a face; said to a child it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.

When a tap comes back flat the ear does not stop and does not say the pot’s number. She sets that pot at the far end of the rack where the crooked ones stand, and taps the next. Which pot answers flat is the day’s business and changes with the day; no child keeps a list of them, and the rack keeps no list either. When the eight lines are done the hands come down together and the pots are left standing as they stood. There is no winning and no last tap. The flat one is not thrown out and is not counted in, which is the whole of the game and the thing the clerk could not hear.

\subsection*{The counting-out, said over the rims}

\emph{Right fists held out, knuckles up, the child who says it touching each fist in turn and not looking at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word is the ear, which is not a prize: the ear has to kneel and listen and the rest only stand in the row. The children accept this as a punishment and the rack-women accept it as practice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lip and two for the foot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the thumb and four for the soot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the rack where the wet ones lean —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one it lights on taps the first note in.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The listening verse, as it is tapped}

\emph{One line, one tap, on the belly of the next pot in the row. The eighth line is tapped like the others; the flat one is set aside when it comes, without a word and without a figure, and the verse goes on over it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the foot that came off the wheel,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the belly that keeps its meal;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the lip where the slip ran thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the ear that was never put in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the ridge where the thumb went round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the sound that comes up from the ground;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the seam that the kiln shut fast,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the one that the yard calls whole.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The flat one goes to the crooked rack.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It keeps its sound. We do not count it back.\end{quote}

The last two lines are said low, to the rack, while the ear sets the pot down. The children will not be told which pot is the flat one before they tap. Ask them and they say the pot tells you; ask what it tells and they ask you why a man wants to know what a pot tells.

\subsection*{What is said at the flat one}

\emph{Said to the pot as it is set at the end of the rack, with the head down and the knuckle resting on the belly. All the row says the last two lines together.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The note’s gone out. The pot’s still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The yard says listen and the rack says wait.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the clay and not to me —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a flat’s a body standing, not a debt.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not tap while a man in a soft cuff is in the yard}

I have this from the child who was ear, with the space left before it, which is the space the children leave when the flat pot comes. She said it to the rack with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my verbs in it. A verse tapped to a pot wants nothing added, and a verse tapped to a man wants everything taken away.

\begin{quote}\itshape Eight go round and eight come back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one sits flat on the crooked rack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it went up the road with a whole note in it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and came back answering flat to the knuckle.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate says sound and the slate says eight;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the yard says listen and the yard says wait.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The flat one keeps what the ring forgot —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name said at home and never entered.\end{quote}

The child who said this had a brother who went up the clay road in the spring and came back with a note gone flat, and would not say whether the house had known him before he went, which is a child’s way of keeping two things apart without putting a word between them. I have put no word between them either.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the tally at Greybank, being a man who cannot let paper lie, with his cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sitting in two fingers of it and will not come out. He set the row down as \emph{a batch of vessels submitted for inspection}. Against the eight lines he wrote \emph{eight sound vessels, passed}. At the flat one he struck the children’s words through and set above them, \emph{one vessel defective, rejected and entered nil; replacement issued}. At the foot, where the pots are left standing and nothing is said, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{no balance outstanding}.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He writes of a thing always true and so has no need of a child kneeling in it. I write for a child with her ear to a pot who wants to know which hand to lift next and whether the pot she set aside will still be there tomorrow. He has put a figure where a pot was standing, and a figure travels up the clay road in a cuff and a pot does not. A nought is a number. The flat one is a place at the end of a rack, and it is not the same pot twice. He has written one pot where there are as many as the day gives, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the listening and the setting aside, and he said that was an account of pot gone wrong taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes into the yard. They take it up again when he is past the gate with his satchel under his arm, and they never once count the flat one.

\subsection*{The gloss in charcoal, by the woman at the kiln}

The woman who fires the Vail kiln pressed one line into the margin beside the sixth tap. She has kept that fire thirty years and does not write often, and when she does she writes small, the way a person writes where somebody is sleeping.

\begin{quote}\itshape A flat pot is a pot that tells you where it broke. The dangerous one is the one that rings and is hollow behind the glaze. I have mended the loud ones and thrown out nothing in thirty years.\end{quote}

I have left it where her thumb put it. She said a pot that keeps its break where you can see it is a pot you can carry, and that the yard’s way of setting the flat one at the end of the rack is the only honest repair she has ever seen in clay, and she would not say whether she meant pots.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is mine and has worked into the grain, which is why this leaf takes a mark and never gives one back. The green bead came off a coarse pot broken at the third rack and rolled as far as the fold before anybody saw it; do not touch the edge, the sweetness is in it and the sweetness is not a kindness. The pale thumb at the second corner is from a girl of the glaze room with the pale line at her gum, who leaned over to read and touched the tally and went back up the terrace. The grey in the gutter came off the cuff that had no business lying there, and I have not swept it. The tideline took two words off the back of the tally and I have not written them in again, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The twist of grey wool through the hole is mine, tied for the word I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey slip, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I like the flat one. It’s the only one that tells you where it broke.\end{quote}

No hand will own it. The letters are set down as they were made, hard at the \emph{th} and one of them backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a tally and not off a book. I asked whose it was and had three answers and no hand, as I did with the grey print. I have left it where it was written.

The leaf goes back into my apron and the pots go back to the rack. Tomorrow the row will stand as long as the day’s drying gives, and eight will ring and one will not, and which one will not is a thing nobody will enter and nobody will keep, and the children will set it at the end where the crooked ones stand and tap on. If the clerk comes again with his pen I shall put the verbs back. He may keep the nil; the pot comes back to the rack at the end of every count, and no tally in this yard has ever had a place for it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Mud Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Fenfolk, Gathered at the Standing Post and Glossed for a Man from the South}
\CRsheetheading{The Mud Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Fenfolk, Gathered at the Standing Post and Glossed for a Man from the South}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A reeve’s gathering of the proverbs, board-maxims, counting-words and curses of the Fenmarch, set down in Grathic letters though Fen Cant is not written; the sayings in a thick half-sung English, the glosses in the reeve’s own hand, with a factor’s clerk’s corrections in Ledgerhand and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Standing Post in Reed and Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Nib Peat, a reeve of the Post who learned his Grathic letters off an eel-trader out of Reedholt; carried down the marsh road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, so that the two barks and the slip lie sewn with eel-sinew in a folded reed wrapper under the Post’s loose board. It survives with a brown peat thumb at the head, wet reed pressed across the second leaf, a bog-water tideline along the gutter, a fish-hook nick, eel slime where a trader set his hand, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie. Two corrections are in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk who borrowed the leaves at Greybank; one line at the back is in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I am a reeve of the Standing Post and I have set my people’s sayings down in the south’s letters, which my mother could not read. Fen Cant is not written. It is carried in the mouth, cut on sticks and tied in knots; a notch is still there when the stick is wet, which is more than can be said for the paper they use at Greybank. A man from the factor’s house stood on the Post one Silt morning and asked what we say when there is nothing to say. I told him we say it to the ground. He paid me two marks and a question and went off with his cuff wet to the elbow. A saying written down for a man who has never stood on a board wants its ground with it.

The manner of them first, because a saying said wrongly is a different saying. Say it through the nose, slow, and let the last word fall into the mud instead of finishing it. Do not look at the man you say it to. Say it to the pot, the board, the water, the ground under the water; said looking at a man, it becomes an argument. Some words here cannot be written at all; they are made at the back of the throat with the nose shut. Where one falls I have tied a knot in the margin, which is how we write what cannot be written. The factor’s clerk has been at the leaves since I copied them. I have left his hand standing and my words under it, as a board keeps both the man’s weight and the water’s mark.

\subsection*{Of standing, and the ground that is lent}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The bog keeps the man who stands longest.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Reeves are chosen by standing in a bog until the others have had enough. It is not strength. A strong man goes in hot and comes out early; a reeve stands until the mud has taken his measure and found it enough. About half our reeves are women and the saying does not change for it. We say it of a feud as well: the side that can stand longest is the side the mud calls right.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Stand where you stood, and the board will mind you.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said to a man newly come up on to the Post, before he steps on a board nobody has pointed to. The boards have borne ten thousand feet and will bear his if he puts his foot where the others went. It is a promise about boards and not about anything else.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Dry ground is borrowed.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Every dry place among us is a loan from the water, and the water calls it in when it pleases. Our houses stand on posts so the loan can be called without taking the house with it. A man who builds on dry ground in the Fen has mistaken a loan for a gift, which is a mistake the south makes in a larger way.}

\subsection*{Of warmth, and what the mud does with it}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The Marsh Mother keeps it warm and hands it back.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The peat holds the warmth of a whole country under a skin of water. We do not dig it out; we ask. A priest come up from Greybank told me this was the Hearth under a Fen name. It is not the Hearth: ours has no keys, no slate and no figure, and needs no man in a clean coat to open it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} The measure is retained in the peat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has taken the verbs out, because a thing always true has no need of them. I have put \emph{keeps} and \emph{hands back} under his because a man standing in water to his calf wants to know who is doing the keeping, and whether he will get it back.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “What goes into the mud is kept.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — On death a Fen body goes out on a peat raft into the reedbed and we do not fetch it back. The mud keeps what it wants, which is not always the whole of a person, and we have never asked for the rest. In Grath they lay their dead with their feet toward the river and break a pot at the door. We let the water keep the account.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A thin return is a return. Ask for more and you get a colder one.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What a reeve says at the Post when the Court’s man has read his figure in a clean voice and gone. Our children come back as ours often enough and strangers often enough, and the house keeps both. We do not say what a whole return costs; a man who buys one has paid somebody, and in the Fenmarch we know who, because he paid here.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} The return is whole as entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} It is whole in his figure. It is thin in the house that got the child. Both stand.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Cold iron takes. The mud takes. One of them writes it down.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A draw leaves a pale round place on the arm that shows through the winter; the mud leaves nothing an officer can enter. Ask a Fen woman which is the kinder and she will ask you why a man wants a kind way to be emptied. This is not a saying for a feast.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “If they come before the name is given, give them the number and keep the word.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A Fen mother names her child before a collector reaches the hut, which is the closest thing we have to a declaration. If she is too late, the officer has his figure and the child has a name besides; we say the name at home and do not enter it. A name said at home is a door. A number is a hole in the wall.}

\subsection*{Of names, slates and knots}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Do not sit where a slate lies open.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A slate is a stone with another man’s hand on it. We will not put our mouths near one and say things we would not have carried away. Reeves settle feuds standing up on the Post; a man from the Court who wants a statement may have it after we have left the table.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A knot remembers what a name forgets.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We tie grey wool when a thing is owed and untie it when it is paid; a knot does not care whose hand tied it and it keeps longer than a name. The eel-women upriver keep theirs in cords and will not say where they learned it. A factor’s clerk entered our knots as nil, because a knot is not a figure. He was right. That is why we keep them.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Say the name three times and the mud will know it. Write it once and it belongs to the clerk.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A reed-name is said, not cut. The third saying is for the child who cannot yet say it, so the mother says it into the ground beside the hut. A written name travels where the person does not.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A stick has no ear.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Cut your meaning in a stick and it cannot argue with you, which is the only honest witness in the Fenmarch. A man who will not believe a notch will not believe his mother, and no reeve can make him.}

\subsection*{Of the Line and the south}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The Line stops warm and starts wet.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Sere’s northern advance stopped at the Peat Line in Y.H. 634 and we have paid tribute in eels ever since. North of it a man is a neighbour, which costs less and holds more; south of it he is a bowl, and the bowl belongs to whoever filled it. We trade with the south and do not move there.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A bought breath has a hook in it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Bought breath is common among us and we do not dress it. The hook is in the mouth, so a man cannot say the word he would need in order to complain of it. Do not say this to a buyer. He will hear it as an insult, which it is.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Take the eels. Leave the crown.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Gold crowns come north and will not change at Greybank. In the south a coin is a thing a house can empty into a bowl and call generosity; here it is a thing you cannot spend, and a thing you cannot spend is a thing somebody has already paid for.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The Quiet Acre has no smoke and it has doorways.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The ground between Grath and us, which the Court calls the Empty Cantons, we call the Quiet Acre and leave it alone. A doorway is built for coming back through. We do not say who went, and we do not say what hung in the square of bare clay above the lintel, because a thing you can put a name to is a thing the Court can put a figure to.}

\subsection*{What the young are taught}

\emph{Sung crossing the Post at dusk going in, not coming back, by children who have cut their first bundle in the dark for the Reed Cut. If the bundle comes back wet, the child is not yet of the bog and goes again.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the boards and one for the slack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reed says wet and the reeve says wait;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mud takes a name and the eel takes a mark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was lent goes back to the water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners and four for the post,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not score it and we do not step,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the count comes back as it came to us.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The fifth is not a board and not a name. Children ask and are told to ask the water, which is an answer given by people who asked the same thing at their own Reed Cut. The factor’s clerk put a nought in the fifth place and wrote vacancy beside it. A nought is a number. The fifth is a place.}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hand did}

The factor’s clerk struck out three verbs and numbered the fifth place. I have set my words under his. A sentence with its verbs taken out travels well and arrives empty, which is what the Court wants of a sentence; a knot arrives as it was tied. I asked what he wanted with our sayings; he said the factor wanted to know what the Fenfolk owed. A man who asks what you owe has already written the answer, and the only work left is to watch where he puts his stop.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat thumb at the head is mine. I held the bark down on the Post in a wind off the bog and did not know I had marked it; peat goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why I use it to sign. The wet reed across the second leaf came from the morning the Post stood under water and the sayings were said to the boards instead of to a man. The tideline in the gutter is bog-water and has taken the ink off two words, and I have not written them in again, because a saying with two words gone is a saying said slowly, which is how all of ours are said. The fish-hook nick and the slime at the foot came off an eel-trader who set his hook in the edge while he was paying me and did not apologize. The grey print nobody will own came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it. The knot of grey wool through the hole in the first leaf is mine, tied for the word I could not write. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man is a board laid across water. The water does not owe the board anything.\end{quote}

I asked the reeves, the eel-traders and a man from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back under the loose board at the Post; next Reed the young will cut their bundles in the dark and come back wet or dry, and I shall not say which. The sayings will go on being said to the ground as before, and if the clerk comes again with his pen I shall put the verbs back, and tie another knot for the word he cannot hear.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Four and Four and a Slack, Being the Hauling Song of the Ilm Barges, Set Down Between Greybank Quay and the Sill}
\CRsheetheading{Four and Four and a Slack, Being the Hauling Song of the Ilm Barges, Set Down Between Greybank Quay and the Sill}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A barge-crew’s hauling song in the low-country speech, shouted in call and response on the towpath of the lower Ilm and never sung coming down with the current; written in a steersman’s hand with a burnt stick on the back of a Vhaleni tide-tally, with the count as the crew keep it, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk, a line in the leaning hand of a Council tally-man, and a verse at the back in a hand nobody will own · Taken down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 from the mouths of the men who hauled a salt barge up from Greybank to the Sill, by the steersman of that barge, who learned his letters off a glass carrier out of Vhal and has no ink on a boat; carried folded into a coil of tow-rope and copied forward at the Fishstairs. It survives with grey silt in the gutter and pressed into the rope-fibre at the fold, a tar thumb at the head, a dark streak of eel slime along the foot, a white salt bloom on one corner, a nick from a boat-hook, a green bead of lead-glaze from a pot broken on the quay, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one correction in the hand of the Court’s factor’s clerk, and one line at the back in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I steer the salt barge that ties up below the north bridge when the water is high and at the Fishstairs when it is low. I set this down with a burnt stick on the back of a tide-tally that a Vhaleni tally-man left on our gunwale and did not come back for. There is no slate on a barge. A slate on a barge goes overboard in the first reach, and a man who writes with ink on a boat writes with water. The burnt stick is the only hand that stays.

This is not a song for a fire. It is hauled, not sung. Coming up from Greybank against the current, four of us on the rope and the bow-man calling, every line is a pull and the last line of each part is the rest. You do not say the last line loud. A man who pulls when he should hold goes into the silt to his thigh and comes up with a boot and no dignity. Coming down with the pots and the tile and the peat, we do not sing at all; the river does the work, and a man who sings going down has not yet learned which way his living lies. What follows is the up-song, which is the only one that wants words.

The call is said to the rope and not to the men. Say it to a man and it becomes an argument; say it to the rope and the rope tells your hands when to lean. The bow-man says the first line of each pair, and the four on the rope say the second. Nobody says the last line of the last part until the rope is made fast. I have set the words as they were called, with the rests left in.

\subsection*{The song, as it is hauled}

\subsection*{The cast-off}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cast off where the Clay Road ends,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hand over hand and mind the hands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope is stiff with yesterday’s salt\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a cart pays twice to travel one road.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four on the near bank and four on the far,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a slack where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope keeps the count and the river the rest,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place goes down with the load.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The long reach}

\begin{quote}\itshape The silt is deep and the pole is dumb;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape push where the other man put his thumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A loaded barge answers dull\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape when the mud has got into her.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The gull goes off with a coal not cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the eel goes in where it cannot get out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river takes what the potter made\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and gives back salt, and a doubt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four, and a slack, and again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the near bank holds and the far bank waits.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who pulls when he should hold\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape comes up with the silt on his hands.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Under the stone}

\begin{quote}\itshape Below the bridge the ledge gives one note,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape low as a man’s throat under water;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the town sets its clock by it and says nothing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we say nothing, and haul.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four and a place where the fifth should be,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Sill keeps the note and the bank keeps the mark;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up the road in a clean hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the barge goes up the river in the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ninety-four days the ice held, they tell us,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no collector crossed from the quay;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we were warmer for it, and thinner,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and paid for both in the spring.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The bank}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt in the sack and iron in the hold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one mark for a skin and two for a bar;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve bits to the mark, and the crown goes south\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where a man is a bowl and is counted by the mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four, and a slack, and made fast;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope is let go and the hands let go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The account stands where the water stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth is a place, and we do not pull it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not sing before the factor’s clerk}

There is one more part. They take it up when the man from the counting house has gone back over the north bridge with his satchel under his arm, and break off if he turns. I have it from the bow-man below the bridge, with the space left before it, which is the space they leave in the singing:

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, one in twelve,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read twice so the late ones may hear it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the barrow goes out of the north gate\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nothing is weighed and nobody enters it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Orra up at the Weir keeps hers in wool —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tie once for owed and untie for paid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we keep ours in rope-burn and river-silt,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court keeps its own in a clean dark hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four and the place where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the barrow goes out and the slate stays in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope keeps what the slate will not,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and hands it back in the spring.\end{quote}

I asked the bow-man what the last three lines were worth, and he said a song was not obliged to be worth a figure just because a clerk had written it down. Then he put his tar thumb on the corner of the tally to keep it from the wind, as the women do at the yard.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on the morning we unloaded, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{the place goes down with the load} and set above it, \emph{the vacancy is carried forward}. Against \emph{the rope keeps the count and the river the rest} he wrote \emph{the measure is recorded and the residue unentered}. At the count he wrote \emph{eight, fifth nil}, which is a true figure and a false place.

I have put the words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them; I put them back because a man up to his thigh in the silt does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to put on the rope. A nought is a number. The fifth is a place where a man rests. He has put a figure where a rest should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

\subsection*{The tally-man’s line}

The Vhaleni who left the tally wrote one line in the leaning hand they use at the Council, above the part about the stone:

\begin{quote}\itshape The tide follows the Warm, not the moon; the water goes where it is told.\end{quote}

He wrote it of the Sallow, which is his river, and it is true there, the dippers say. I have left it where he set it. Of the Ilm I will say only that it runs downhill, which is more than can be said for the money, and that it does not need a man in a clean coat to tell it where to go. He came back for the tally after all, but did not ask for the writing on the back of it, and I did not offer it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tar thumb at the head is the bow-man’s; he mends the ropes and does not wash before he sings. The silt is in the gutter and in the fold and worked into the rope-fibre where the leaf lay coiled; I have not knocked it out, because a tally that has never gone up the river with a barge is not the sort of tally a bargeman keeps. The eel slime at the foot came off a basket set down on the leaf while a man counted six eels and was paid five marks for them, or five eels and six marks, which is a thing he will not settle and I have not entered. The salt bloom is on the corner that lay under the sack. The boat-hook nick is mine. The green bead came off a coarse pot broken on the quay while we unloaded; it rolled under the beam and I put it in the fold. The grey print nobody will own came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a boat. I have left it. There is no Last Day on the river.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fifth is the stroke you do not pull. It is the stroke that brings her up.\end{quote}

I asked the bow-man, the tally-man and a carter waiting on the quay, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the coil of rope, and tomorrow we go down again with pots and tile and peat, and sing nothing, and come back up with salt and iron, and haul the four and leave the fifth where we found it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sayings of Grath, Being the Maxims of the Clay Country, Gathered in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln and Glossed for a Child Come Back from the Bank}
\CRsheetheading{The Sayings of Grath, Being the Maxims of the Clay Country, Gathered in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln and Glossed for a Child Come Back from the Bank}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A slip-treader’s gathering of the proverbs, pot-bench maxims, firing-counts and household threats of the Grathic, set down in the common tongue; the sayings spoken low and said to the ground, the pot or the fire, the glosses in the treader’s own charcoal hand, with a kiln-master’s correction in broad charcoal and a Court clerk’s figures in a narrow upright hand, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Gathered in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln in Sill through Ash of Y.H. 813 and written on birch bark in the Five Cold Days at the turn of the year by Hesta Tallow, a widow who has trodden slip for one and thirty years and holds a small kiln by the widow’s mark. She set it down because she had begun to forget one of the sayings and because a child returned thin to the yard would want to know what the house used to say; bark is used because a saying that travels must go where the speaker does not, and slate is for figures that stay put. It survives folded twice and tied with a strip of grey wool, sewn at the fold with eel-sinew got from the Fishstairs, with wet clay ground into the first leaf, a chalk thumb at the head, a scorch along the lower edge where the bark lay too near the kiln mouth, a small-ale ring, a pressed sherd between the third and fourth leaf, grey Ash in the gutter, and the sweet green of lead glaze at one corner where a woman from High Kiln set her hand\par}\medskip
I have trodden slip in this yard for one and thirty years, and this winter I found I could not bring up one of our sayings when I wanted it. It was gone the way a name goes from a person banked too often: I knew the shape of it and not the word. So I have put them here, in the tongue we speak, on bark, because bark will go where a body is not going.

A child came back to us this year who had been paid for out of the bank and knew nothing but a liking for the smell of wet clay and a hand that went toward a cup before he had seen it. He is ours and he is not ours, and what the house can give him is the old sentences. A saying said at the fire stays at the fire. A saying written on bark goes on with him.

These are not sung. Say them low, to the pot, the clay, the floor, the fire, in that order, and to a person last. Said looking at a person they become an argument, and there is enough arguing at the Cross without carrying it home. A Grathic sentence is short and has a hard edge to it; if you say it soft and long you have made a Vhaleni sentence, which is a thing with no ground under it.

\subsection*{Of the pot and the note it gives}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Knock it. A whole pot tells you what it is; a cracked one tells you what it was.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The first thing taught in a yard and the last thing a potter does before he lets a jar go. A sound vessel answers full under the knuckle. A vessel gone through gives a small flat knock and no amount of looking at it will put the note back. We do not ask the pot why. We set it by the door or we break it, according to whether it held anything worth keeping.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Never praise a pot before the firing.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Green clay will stand up straight all day and slump in the night. There is a firing between the thing you made and the thing you have, and until it has come through the fire it is only an intention with a wet edge.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The pot remembers the hand. The clay forgets it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Thumb marks go into the slip and stay there; that is the clay doing what it is told. What the pot keeps is the shape the hand meant, which is a different thing. A kid asks which one is the real pot. Feed it and stop asking.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A patch honestly set is a patch. A patch set to hide a crack is a crack with a lie over it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — There is a cupworm that bores from the inside, so a pot looks sound and goes at the first pouring. A false repair is the same trick done by a person. Both answer flat, but one of them wanted to be found out and the other did not. Only one of those is a sin in this yard, and it is not the one with the visible seam.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Set a wet thing down and it will tell you in the morning what it would not tell you tonight.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said of pots, and of wages, and of a promise made with a hand still wet from the bucket. You will pay for it in the thaw, whatever it was.}

\subsection*{Of the fire and the iron}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Don’t set that near the fire. You’ll pay for it in the thaw.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The whole of Grathic household wisdom in eight words, and it is said to the thing before it is said to the person who set it there. The pot, the coat, the bread, the child: all of them learn it from the same sentence.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “One iron holds the heat in and takes the heat out. Say which mercy you mean.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The damper. We have no word in Grathic that holds both bites of it, so we make the speaker choose. A man with his finger in it will hold his tongue instead, which is the answer most of us give.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A banked fire is a fire with its mouth shut. Ask it in the morning what it kept.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The carried coal comes up the yard under ash at the turn of the year, and each hearth touches its own flame from it and passes on what is left. Nobody says where the first flame was lit or who paid for it. A child who asks is told to ask the fire, which is an answer given by people who asked the same thing at their own first firing.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The kiln’s breath is a merciful death to a man who has not had to carry the body out.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — It kills in sleep and leaves no mark worth speaking of. The people who call it merciful are the people who have not had to go in after breakfast. Do not say this at a death-house; say it at the pot.}

\subsection*{Of the slate and the figure}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “One in twelve, as the notice says.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Printed on the Weighing notices and read twice over the basket on Account-day. The notice is not a lie. It is not the whole truth either. In this district the figure that goes into the slate and the figure that comes out of the house are two figures, and the difference is not called a tax, because a tax has a name and this has none.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, written against this saying:} Deduction one in twelve. Printed. Current.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has put a figure where I put a sentence. A figure travels well and arrives empty. A sentence stays where it was said and knows who said it.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A number goes into a slate, not into a well.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said to a man who brings a figure up out of his fist and wants it spent on something he can see. If the house wants it counted, there will be a slate at the watch. Until then it is a man’s own trouble and he may carry it back down the road with him.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A debt left lying is not a debt forgiven.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — This was said over Garl’s tile debt through seven days of high water and it was true then. The debt lay where it lay. It did not rot. Nothing in Grath rots as slowly as a debt nobody has picked up.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The collector comes with a slate, not a threat. The threat is in the slate.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — He does not raise his voice. He writes. A house can shout at a man and be done with it; a house cannot shout at a figure that has already been entered. A cold iron tube and a clean hand are the whole of the law as it arrives at a door.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Rent is eight marks and the frost is free.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — This is the dry joke of the district and it is not funny in Stone. Fuel is four marks and food is twelve, and a man who misses three days of work has begun to owe. The frost asks nothing and gives less.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A thin return comes back liking a country it cannot name.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Many measures pooled and divided make a stranger with a taste for a house that was never his. We feed them. We do not ask them to remember us, and we do not say what a whole return costs, because a person who buys one has paid somebody, and here we know who.}

\subsection*{Of the grey in the corner}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The grey in the corner is not dirt.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — It gathers where a promise was not kept and shows plain by tallow-light. In the daytime it is not there. On the Last Day it is left where it lies and burned the next morning, and the clean line where it stood is not the same as gone. This is not a saying for a feast.}

\subsection*{Of children and the yard}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]
