\item “Knuckle the pot. If it sings, the house eats. If it lies flat, the yard takes another year.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The First Firing at twelve. A clear note and there is a feast; a flat note and the child serves a year in the yard and tries again. It is the same test every pot must pass, and it excuses the child from nothing.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A foundling is named by whoever writes first.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The hearth-maid or the collector, whichever reaches the bench before anyone looks at the face. The name is what the slate can hold, not what the child is. It has no house-name until a hearth claims it, which is the way of keeping a person from inheriting a debt he did not make.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Good axe, two marks. Cow, twenty-four. A boy sweeping the yard, six bits a day.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Not a proverb. A list. It is kept here because a returning child will ask what he was worth and a grandmother ought to be able to tell him the price of an axe without pretending it was love that set it.}

\subsection*{Of the river}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Ask the river what the water cost. The river will tell you the weather.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — An answer given with the weather in it and no figure anywhere. It comes down from the Fishstairs and up the Weir and is the same sentence in every mouth along the Ilm. A person who wants to know what the flood took had better have a slate, because the river has none.}

\subsection*{Of the south and the Court}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A man without a kiln-mark is a man without a debt, and we do not trust him.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Travellers are lodged at the Cross and watched. Sere traders are disliked because they buy poor measures and pay in crowns that will not change at the Cross, and are sold to anyway. A Wasteling is not disliked so much as pitied in a way that closes the door.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Measure for measure means what the man who said it has already decided.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A southern phrase, brought back by men who went down the Peat Line with wool and came back with a figure in their heads. At home we say one in twelve, as the notice says, and the notice and the man between them keep a whole district warm for a season. The south empties a bowl and calls it the same thing as a number.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The Court owns no slaves and calls that civility. Its Kept belong to their accounts and calls that kindness.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Fewer than twenty in the world. They sit in rooms with good fires they cannot feel. Say this at the pot and not at the Court table, where there is a clerk who will write it down as an opinion and send it up with the figures.}

\subsection*{The tread-song}

\emph{Sung going round the slip pit in the first warm days of Seed, feet bare, one hand on the rail and the other at the small of the back. It is not a work-song exactly; the work gets done whether it is sung or not.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tread it round, tread it slow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clay knows more than the hands will know;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape fire it stiff, knock it light ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot sings and a cracked one lies flat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the pit and one for the rack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the firing that will not come back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the last goes round without a name ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the yard keeps it. The slate does not.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — Children ask what the last one is. They are told to ask the clay, which is what their mothers were told, and their mothers before them. It is not a board and it is not a pot. It is the count that goes round the yard and never stands still long enough to be entered.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the broad charcoal of the kiln-master who borrowed the bark at the firing:} A pot that sings before its time is green and will slump. There is no note to argue with.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left his correction standing. He is right about the pot and wrong about the song, which was never about the pot alone. He has read every line of this bark with one eye on the kiln.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The chalk at the head is my thumb; I held the bark down on the bench in a draught from the yard door and did not know I had marked it. The scorch along the lower edge is where I laid the fold too near the kiln mouth one evening, and it took the corner off three sayings; I have not written them in again, because a saying with its corner gone is a saying the yard has half forgotten, which is how most of them reach us. The sherd between the third and fourth leaf is a piece of a jar that answered flat and was set here to remind me what flat sounds like. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that lay where no cuff had business lying, and I have not swept it. The green at the corner came from a woman who stood at the pot board with glaze in the crease beside her mouth and put her hand down here while she was deciding whether to buy. She did not buy. The strip of grey wool is mine and holds the fold; there is a knot in it for the one saying I could not bring up, and I have not untied it to see whether the word has come back.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot remembers the hand. The hand forgets the pot. The slate remembers neither.\end{quote}

I have asked the kiln-master, the hearth-maid and a man come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. The bark goes back under the loose board beside the wheel. If the child who came back from the bank asks what the house used to say, let him be told: tread it round, knock it light, and do not put a wet thing near the fire. That is the whole of it, and the rest he can learn by staying.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Half a Word, Being the Rope Game of the Quay at Vhal, with the Ten Counts, the Held Turn, and What a Clerk of the Council Made of the Half}
\CRsheetheading{Half a Word, Being the Rope Game of the Quay at Vhal, with the Ten Counts, the Held Turn, and What a Clerk of the Council Made of the Half}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A net-mender’s setting-down of a children’s rope-skipping game in the low Vhaleni speech, written on the back of a dipper’s tide-tally spoiled by wet; the words in the children’s own half-sung chant, the manner of the turning in the writer’s hand, a correction in the narrow upright counting-hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides, a line in the leaning tallies hand of a boat’s clerk, and one line at the foot in grey chalk in a child’s hand · Written in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the Quay in Vhal, by a woman who mends nets there and holds no share in anything that floats; set down with a tarred needle-point on the back of a tide-tally gone soft on the face, the figures washed off it, and kept in the coil of a mooring rope under the net-bench, where tar and salt between them kept it out of the rain. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a rope-burn along the outer edge, one corner softened by wet where a tide-name went and did not come back, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the Council clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, the boat-clerk’s line in the margin, and the grey chalk at the foot in a hand that will not be claimed\par}\medskip
I mend nets on the Quay and hold no share in anything that floats. I set this down because a man come up from the counting house stood at the net-bench one Ember morning and asked what the children chanted when they turned the rope. I told him they counted a boat. He asked whose boat. I told him it was every boat and no boat, and that the count had a half in it which was not the half of anything he could enter. He went away and sent a clerk, which is what a man does when he has been given an answer he cannot use.

They play it on the open boards between the net-racks and the tar-shed, where the planks keep a little warmth after the sun and the salt has eaten the splinters off. In Ember the boards are too hot by noon, so they play in the early hours or after the boats have gone out on the draw. They do not play in rain, and they do not play when a boat is casting off on the ebb, because a rope stretched across the Quay is a rope that has to be stepped over, and somebody will lose a finger to it. Two turn the rope and one goes in. The one who goes in is the boat.

There is no slate on the Quay that a gull will not carry off, and no paper that will last a morning in the salt except the paper the Council writes its contracts on, which is made to go soft at the right moment. I have written with a tarred needle-point on the back of a tide-tally gone soft on the face. Tar is the only ink here that the weather cannot read and cannot take.

\subsection*{The counting-out, before the rope is taken up}

\emph{The children stand in a row and hold out their right fists, knuckles up. The one who says the words touches each fist in turn with the untarred end of the rope and does not look at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word takes the coil: she will turn, not skip. She is the one who has to keep the half true, which the children accept as a punishment and the Quay accepts as practice. Say it to the rope. Said looking at a child, it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Mother and mother and share and share,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat goes out on the draw;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape touch the knuckle, not the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one it lights on holds the coil.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The rhyme, as it is skipped}

\emph{One line, one jump. The tenth line is the half. At the half the rope is held still at the skipper’s hip and she stands on one foot without hopping. The half is not jumped. It is stood in. The refrain is said together while the rope is held.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the mother that kept the share,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the aunt that the share passed through,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the mast and the rope it bore,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the pan where the crust came to;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the glass that sweats in the tin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the rain the captain keeps in a barrel,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the coal that the gull went off with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the eel-bone laid on the board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine for the mark and the binding word,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a half for the man they let aboard.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the half and set no foot down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the share goes down the mother’s line, the word goes round;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape name me a tide and I’ll come back in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape on the turn of the water and not the wind.\end{quote}

\emph{Said to the rope. Said to a person, it becomes a bargain, and there is always a person who will take it as one.}

\subsection*{The held turn, and the going aboard}

If a child hops at the half, or sets her foot down while the rope is held, she is aboard wrong. She goes to stand with her back to the game, facing the Sallow, until somebody names a tide that nobody has seen. The children have a hundred names for tides that have not come and not one of them is written anywhere; a name said on this quay is like a name written in salt up at the pans, which the sun takes by noon and the Council has never found a way to tax. If she cannot name one she stands until the rope turns again, which the children call the ebb, and the ebb takes a while.

No one explains why the naming brings her back. Ask a child and it will tell you to ask the water, which is the answer its mother gave it. I have known a child go aboard wrong on purpose, on a morning when there was no fire at home and the boards held what the house did not. I have set that down and have not mended the sense of it.

\subsection*{The verse they do not skip when a man from the Council is on the quay}

\emph{I have it from the child who holds the coil, with her back to the counting house. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it within sight of his turned cuff. She said it to the rope.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the mother and one for the boat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the man they let aboard;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape his word’s half a word and his debt’s a whole,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and his name goes on no mother’s line.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The share goes out and the share comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was kept is called a lack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council writes the half as nil\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water goes where no clerk has been.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name me a tide and I’ll come back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape not to the chapel but to the coil.\end{quote}

I asked her what the half was. She said a child who had never been given a share would not know where to stand, and went back to the rope. That is the answer the Quay gives to everything it does not want entered, and I have set it down as she gave it, with nothing added.

\subsection*{What the Council clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a morning when the tally-man had his figures out to dry, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes with the cuff turned back twice and the ink on the first joint of two fingers, the way a man writes who is paid by the line. He struck out \emph{and a half for the man they let aboard} and set above it, \emph{one half-share acquired by marriage; opinion weighted at one half; no vote entered}. Against \emph{hold the half and set no foot down} he wrote \emph{rest nil}. At the foot, where the children name a tide, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{tide not entered}.

I have put the children’s words back underneath and left his standing above, as the rope keeps the tar on one side and the salt on the other. He has made a share of a stance and a figure of a coming-back. A half in the mouth is a place to stand; a half on a slate is a debt. He has set the debt where the standing was, which is the whole art of that hand. The children stop when the turned cuff comes along the boards. They take it up when he is back over the quay, and they never once change the half.

\subsection*{In the margin, in the leaning hand of a boat’s clerk}

\begin{quote}\itshape We count a boat by who bails. The Council counts it by who signed. Both are true, and only one of them floats.\end{quote}

He wrote it in the sloped letters of tallies, never of decrees, and did not put his name to it. I have left it where he set it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom at the head has eaten two letters of \emph{share}, which I have not written in again; a word the salt has half taken is the only honest spelling of a half-share. The tar thumb is mine: I turn the leaf with the hand I mend nets with. The green bead came off a coarse pot carried down from the pans, and it is sweet and it is lead, and I have not put it in my mouth, whatever the children say of the sweetness. The fish-hook nick is from a man mending a line beside the bench who did not apologize. The rope-burn went along the outer edge where the leaf lay coiled. The soft corner is the wet: the tide-name in it went with the wet and did not come back, which is the condition I have described in the game itself and have now been given in my own paper. The grey print came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a Quay; I have not swept it. There is no Last Day here, and the salt does the sweeping for us.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey chalk, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I held the half. They went on without me.\end{quote}

No hand will own it. The letters are set down hard at the \emph{th} and one of them backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a slate and not off a book. I have asked whose it was and had three answers and no hand, as I did with the grey print. I have left it where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the coil under the bench. Tomorrow the boats go out on the draw and the children will stretch the rope across the boards and count a boat that is every boat and no boat, and the tenth line will be held where it is held now, and the ones who go aboard wrong will be brought back with a name, which is more than can be said for the district that has a figure for everything else. I have kept their words and I have not joined them to anything.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Hold the Next One, Being a Letter from a Physician of Low Kiln in Sill to a Physician of the Quay at Vhal, Concerning a Girl Come Down from the Glaze Room, a Child in the Second Chill, the Fever That Cooks, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Council Clerk’s Correction on the Outer Fold, and a Warming Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Hold the Next One, Being a Letter from a Physician of Low Kiln in Sill to a Physician of the Quay at Vhal, Concerning a Girl Come Down from the Glaze Room, a Child in the Second Chill, the Fever That Cooks, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Council Clerk’s Correction on the Outer Fold, and a Warming Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter in iron-gall thinned with barley-water and charcoal, written in Grathic on the back of a physician’s charge-sheet spoiled by a wet thumb, folded thrice and sewn with a twist of grey wool; carried from Sill up the Clay Road to Greybank and from there up the Salt Road in a salt-factor’s saddlebag to the Quay at Vhal, answered along the margin in the lean salt-coast hand, corrected on the outer fold at the tide-tally house, and kept since in a physician’s tin among the grey rags and the tasting-spoons · Written at Low Kiln in Sill in the last tend of Smoke, Y.H. 813, by Vess, a physician who learned her trade in the clay yards and not at the College of Assessors, to Orrel, a physician of the Quay at Vhal who keeps the salt-wives’ book and reads the Sallow draw at dawn; carried eighteen leagues up the Clay Road and sixty-two more by the Salt Road, answered at the Quay in the first tend of Frost, Y.H. 813, and borrowed at the tide-tally house, where a Council clerk set a correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand on the outer fold. It survives sewn and salt-stiff with a thumb of tallow at the head, clay slip worked into the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a pale line at the margin where a finger went to a gum and stopped, salt bloom along the fold, grey Ash in the creases, one word struck through with a chisel-point and written above, a column left standing under a clerk’s \emph{No such column}, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
To Orrel at the Quay, who reads the Sallow draw before he opens a door. From Vess at Low Kiln, who has never seen the sea and has mended what the sea’s country sends back.

I write on the back of a charge-sheet a wet thumb spoiled. The entered figure shows through every line of it: \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}. I did not choose the paper. A physician who writes on a slate writes what a clerk will read later; a physician who writes on what was thrown away may write what she saw. The charcoal is thinned with barley-water and takes badly on paper that has been sized. Do not rub the fold. The salt will have it if you do, and then there will be no letter to correct.

You asked, in the matter of the girl come down from the glaze room, what we set to a pale line at the gum. I will tell you what I do and then what the Hall does, and you must keep the two apart as I have had to, or you will end by believing the second.

\subsection*{What I do, and what the Hall does}

The Hall says sweetness answers sweetness. They give sour wine for the sweet sickness and send the glaze hands back to the mix with a clean bill and a line at the gum the size of a thread. I have watched the line go off a girl who left that room for three weeks and come back on a girl who stayed. I have never seen the lead, which is a thing a man may believe in without seeing; I have seen the going and the coming, which is a thing a physician may enter if she has a column for it. There is no column. I have set it on a table instead, where the clerk cannot carry it out in his cuff.

For the fever that cooks they put cold iron to the temple and bleed at the elbow, and say the vessel is overfilled and must be emptied or it will cook its own contents. I bled four in the Thin Year. Two were quiet after it and did not wake. The measure went out of them and the fever stayed, and quiet is not better; I have known a man go quiet who was gone. I keep my knife in its fold now. When a household asks why I did nothing, I tell them I did the thing that lets the person stay in the room, which is not the same as saving them and is the only thing I can answer for.

The beautiful return is the hardest. They come back calm, want nothing, take the cup when given and do not ask whose child she is. The Hall writes \emph{a beautiful return} at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures, and on the third day the hand shakes and the family is given a phial of quiet ash at sixty marks, and nobody asks what the first pouring took. My mother crossed two fingers and called it the quiet. A woman who does not know her own child is not quiet. She is gone. I have entered the calm because the rolls will take nothing else, and I have not crossed out the sentence, because a sentence is not a figure and can be left where a clerk will not look for it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in Orrel’s hand, written at the Quay with the pen still wet from the tide-tally:} The girl came down our road with the green still at her mouth. I set her three weeks at the pans away from the furnaces and the line went pale; then a week at the glass and it came back brown at the edge. So the lead is yours after all, and the sour wine is a kindness sold at sixty marks. I will not argue with you in a margin. I have put this on the back of a spoiled tide-tally where your clerk can read it if he wants.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The cases set down here and not on any slate}

What was brought — What was set to it — What was entered — What I saw and did not enter\par

A girl of the glaze room, High Kiln, green at one mouth-corner — Sour wine; the hands sent back to the mix — The sweetness answered with sweetness — The line went off her when she left and came back on one who stayed\par

A child three days out of a thin return, grey at the fingertips — Barley water, a watch, walking to the fourth day — Entered as a birth, not a worsening — I held two and walked eleven and did not write which fared worse\par

A man of the Weir with the fever that cooks — Cold iron to the temple; bleed at the elbow — The quiet entered as a mercy — Bleeding let the measure out and not the fever; two of four were quiet and did not wake\par

A returned woman gone thin after a third pouring — Nothing; I tapped her once to hear her — The flat was not in her, which is true — A body is not a banked cup. I have not tapped a person since\par

A collector, fingers grey at the tube — Rest near the Hearth — Entered as age — A hand greyed in one winter and it was not age\par

A woman who did not know her own child — A phial of quiet ash at sixty marks — The calm entered as the sign of a beautiful return — She was not quiet. She was gone\par

The bankers tap a cup before a pouring and know by the note whether it will hold. Sound answers full; cracked answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. I borrowed the trick and tried it once on a returned woman gone thin, and there was nothing there for the knuckle to find. I wrote that the flat was not in her, which is true, and have not written what else might have been. A person is not a vessel of the Court’s kind, and a Kept vessel is not a person, though both hold without leaking. The examination room has no word for the difference and the College has eleven words for a deduction.

\subsection*{The second chill}

This is the one I am writing to you about. It comes after the warming, not before. A child three days out of a thin return begins to fail at the very moment everybody has begun to hope; the fingers grey, the warmth goes, and the household says the graft is settling. The Hall walks them. A warmed body spends faster, I say, and walking faster still, and a child who is walked through a fourth night spends what she had. I say hold her and count with her, and I have said it so often that it has the sound of a proverb in my mouth, which is how a thing becomes a saying and stops being an instruction.

I held two and walked eleven and did not write which fared worse. That is a sentence I would like to be able to cross out and cannot. The physician at the Hall wrote in the margin of my book: \emph{Hold the next one and see if you can write what you saw.} It is the only advice given to me in this trade that cost the giver nothing and might cost the child something, which is why I have kept it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Second margin, in Orrel’s hand:} I held the next one. A child out of a thin return, grey at both hands, on the third night. I did not walk her. I sat with her and counted with her breathing and put a stone off the pan-wall at her feet. She was warmer at the end and died on the fourth morning quietly. I have written what I saw, which is that she was warm and not better, and that holding does not buy a day. It is the only day I can account for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Third margin, in the same hand:} On your bleeding. I have bled two and not bled two. The bled ones were quiet sooner. Quiet is not better; I have known a man go quiet who was gone. Keep your cold iron for the temple and your knife in its fold. The Sallow draws against the wind and a man who argues with it gets wet.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The warming verse}

\emph{Said low to the child and never to the account. There is a place after the fourth stroke where the fifth should stand, and no singer has put a finger in it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire gives four and keeps one back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the well says over and under;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a child comes back in someone else’s shape\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house calls it a mercy.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the hand. Count it through.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a place where the fifth should stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have put no finger in it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire has not asked me to.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes in slow comes out slow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the warm goes where it’s told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a woman comes back and does not know\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the child that she came back to.\end{quote}

The clerk at the tide-tally house struck nothing out of the verse. He could not find a verb in it to take away, which was the first thing about it that pleased me.

\subsection*{What the clerk did to the letter}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Outer fold, in the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk:} \emph{took} struck through and \emph{drawn} set above. Against \emph{the lead}: \emph{the sweetness of the trade}. Over the column headed \emph{Who held the hand}: \emph{No such column}. At the foot of the fold: \emph{The Council does not enter hands. It enters what was drawn.}\end{quote}

He sent the leaf back with the correction uppermost, as though the top of a page were the truth and the bottom something a woman had muttered. I have left my words under his and his words over mine, which is the only honest way a corrected paper can be kept. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way; the slate is the difference, and the slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it. He has eleven words for a deduction and no word for the small intake and the hold and the letting-go of a breath that a person keeps beside a child through a night nobody will enter.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head came off a woman’s thumb when she held her child to me across the counter and would not give me her name. The slip in the gutter is mine; I did not wash it, and I am not sorry. The green bead in the corner came off the girl from the glaze room when she leaned to see the writing with the sweetness still at her mouth. The pale line in the margin is where I put my finger to my own gum and stopped, because a physician who writes about a thing may still be afraid to look at it. The grey in the creases came off the skirting of a room where a Kept vessel sat and felt nothing; it entered itself and I have not burnt it on the morning after the Last Day, for there is no Last Day for a letter.

The bell at the Cross goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself. I have kept the told bell beside what I heard with my own ears and have not made them one. At the Weighing they read one in twelve in a clean voice and the figure goes out warmer than the room it was read in. Here the figure shows through every remedy on the back of the sheet, and nobody has asked me to check it against what it cost.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own:}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The book keeps what was drawn; the room keeps what was held.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The child went between them and neither entered the hand.\end{quote}

I asked Orrel whether he had seen the lead, and he sent me back a brown edge and a child warm and not better, and the clerk sent back \emph{No such column}. Three answers and no hand. Tomorrow I shall go to a house where a child is worse at the moment everybody says she is better, and I shall put the stone under her feet and count with her, and write down what I saw in a place the clerk cannot carry out, because a child is not an account and a woman at a bedside wants a hand more than she wants a correction.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Four Sayings, Being the Order of the Return as It Is Kept at the Collector’s Table}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Four Sayings, Being the Order of the Return as It Is Kept at the Collector’s Table}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} The Keeping’s own order of service, in seven stations, said over the dying at the draw and again at the pressing; copied from a Weighing Hall order and kept at the collector’s table in Slate Row, Sill, with the rubrics of the room, the four sayings of the Court, the answers of the house, the correction of a visiting clerk and the contrary notes of a woman who used it at bedsides · Copied in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the collector’s table in Slate Row, Sill, by the clerk who keeps the order there, from an order of service brought down from the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat; set down on the back of a spoiled district tally, sewn with wire into a board cover, and used at the draw and at the pressing. It survives with a press of cold-iron filings at the head, a lamp-black thumb, a tallow print from a draught under a door, a spot of barley, a grey Ash print along the gutter, a ring of small ale and a hair caught in the fold, with two hands of correction upon it, the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College of Assessors who borrowed the leaf on an Account-day and the thick charcoal hand of a woman who used it at bedsides. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the space left the length it is and the struck line left struck.\par}\medskip
I keep the order at the collector’s table in Slate Row. That is a fine name for holding a leaf while an officer sets a cold tube to a man’s arm and I write down what the house gives him. The leaf came down from the Weighing Hall in a clean hand with no thumb on it. I have kept it eleven years, and the clean has gone off the corners, which is the only part of it the Hearthseat would not recognise.

What follows is the Keeping’s own litany. It is said over the dying, at the draw, and again at the pressing when the measure goes into the new vessel. I have set the rubrics underneath as the room actually does them, because a rubric written in the Hearthseat is a rubric for a room with no draught under the door. The house has a hand in this leaf as well. I have not washed it out, and the clerk who borrowed it on an Account-day has not been able to wash his out either.

The filings at the head came off the tube-case when the officer set it down hard. The grey along the gutter came off his cuff when he knelt to look at the ridge in a corner and said it was old ash from the firing. He went on with his counting. The tallow print belongs to a woman who held the leaf in a draught while her sister was being lifted out of water, and I have left it where she put it.

\subsection*{How it is said}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The leaf lies face down until the officer is ready. It has heard enough from the waiting.

\item The saying is not sung. It is read in the clean voice, the one that takes the reader neatly out of his own sentence.

\item The answer is said by whoever is in the room, including the child, who cannot say it and says it anyway.

\item When the bell goes at the Cross, stop. It is counting a different thing. Begin again after.

\item At the pressing the leaf is turned face up. The dead do not mind. The new vessel cannot yet read.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{The officer says. The house answers. The rubrics are mine.}

\subsection*{I. Of the walls}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot came up from the rack and answered full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Set down on the bench again, it answered flat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wall was not malicious. It was old.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Warm went out of it the way water goes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape out of a cracked cup into trodden ash,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the ash is the floor of the world,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which holds what nobody found a place to hold.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the officer waits with the tube laid by. Nobody touches the dead before the saying is done.}

\textbf{The house answers:} The measure is banked.

\subsection*{II. Of the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron is cold before the hand that takes it up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It does not take. It opens the way.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate takes. The slate is a piece of stone\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a clean hand on it; the hand does not shake\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure does not sweat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Take what is owed and leave the shape behind.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the tube goes to the arm and I write while the officer draws. The house looks at the floor. There is no ceremony in it, only iron, a small hiss, and the time it takes.}

\textbf{The house answers:} The account stands.

\subsection*{III. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers into the cup, not years.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A labourer books forty. A child books twenty.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dead book what the living can pay to have back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it small. The slate does not care\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape how large a thing looks when it is written down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Read it twice: once for the moot, once for those who came late.\end{quote}

\emph{Here I read the figure twice, as the notice requires. The second reading is for the people at the door, who have not yet been told they are late.}

\textbf{The house answers:} Your return is recorded.

\subsection*{IV. Of the share}

\begin{quote}\itshape One part in twelve is kept for the fire, as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the notice is not a lie. The fire wants nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What a thing wants nothing, that is kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who gives to a thing that wants nothing\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape has paid the only debt that cannot be owed back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve. Printed. Unchallenged.\end{quote}

\emph{Here I touch the printed figure. In this district I do not read the other one aloud. Nobody has ever asked me to.}

\textbf{The house answers:} Nothing is lost that we have kept.

\subsection*{V. Of the pooling}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: he comes back as himself,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the price of bread and the name of the pot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many measures into many: they come back as they can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a taste for a country they cannot name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a hand that goes out to a cup already broken.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both are booked the same.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the leaf leaves a space the length of a name. I do not say whose name. The officer does not ask.}

\textbf{The house answers:} The measure is banked.

\subsection*{VI. Of the new vessel}

\begin{quote}\itshape The measure is pressed into a vessel that has not held a cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes the shape of the walls it is given,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way slip takes the mould and keeps the thumbprint.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The name is written into it before it can refuse one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape On the third day it will grow worse before it grows better.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep it. Keep it anyway.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the hearth-maid warms a stone in her hand and tries it on her own wrist. This is not part of the litany. It is the part before.}

\textbf{The house answers:} Your return is recorded.

\subsection*{VII. Of the Kept}

\begin{quote}\itshape Blessed are they that are Kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape No want can reach them. They no longer feel the cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is nothing left in them for the Hearth to take,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and so they are past the need of any return.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There are fewer than twenty in the world.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Speak of them with pity. Do not ask one whether he is warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he will say no, and you will have no other question.\end{quote}

\emph{Here I close the leaf. The dead are already in Slate Row and the new vessel is under a roof I shall not enter.}

\textbf{The house answers:} Nothing is lost that we have kept. The account stands.

\subsection*{The four sayings}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item \emph{The measure is banked} — written at the draw, in the officer’s hand, before I set the figure down.

\item \emph{The account stands} — read at the Cross, twice, over the pigs.

\item \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept} — printed on the Weighing notices and at the foot of every slate.

\item \emph{Your return is recorded} — said in the Remembering, in a clean voice, to the room and not to the person.

\end{itemize}

There is no fifth saying. The house keeps a place where a fifth would stand, and I have left the place the length of it.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the College came down on an Account-day with a cuff gone soft from washing, and ink in two fingers that would not come out. He borrowed the leaf and gave it back with my verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the wall was not malicious, it was old}, he wrote, \emph{The vessel failed, having reached its term.} Mine stands beneath.

\item At \emph{take what is owed and leave the shape}, he set \emph{the measure is drawn and the residue entered}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{one in twelve, printed, unchallenged}, he put a small stop in the figure and wrote the figure again above it, larger. It is the figure they like to see.

\item At \emph{they come back as they can}, he wrote \emph{a thin return is entered}, which is a true thing in a language nobody in this room speaks.

\item In the space where the fifth saying would stand he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man at the draw does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold out.

\subsection*{What the other hand put back}

The house has written in the margins at the bedsides. The charcoal is thicker than mine and it leans. I have copied it as it stands.

At I: \emph{It was a good pot. It split at the lip. We set it by the door and went around it.}

At II: \emph{Take it and go. It is not ours to watch.}

At VI: \emph{She was warm when I wrote it. She was cold by the fourth day. Both are in the house roll and only one is read.}

At the four sayings, against \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept}, the same hand has written: \emph{The grey in the corner is not dirt.} Then, struck through and written again underneath, very small: \emph{We leave it. We burn it in the morning. The clean line where it stood is not the same as gone.}

At the foot, where the answer should be, a line is struck through twice. Under it:

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you were.\end{quote}

And under that, in letters pressed hard into the bark:

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

I have left the struck line standing. A thing said over a child is a thing a house has to use.

\subsection*{In Ilmen}

In Ilmen a woman was taken by the brook below the nineteen steps and no officer was called. There is a space on the leaf where her measure should stand. The clerk has not put a nought in it. I have not filled it, and nobody from Slate Row has asked why it is empty. The house says she was gone before anybody could reach her. That is true, and it is not the whole of it, and I have written both sentences down because the space is the right length for both.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lamp-black thumb is mine; I held the leaf with the same hand I write with and did not know I had marked it. The barley is from a crust laid down on the leaf and not eaten. The ring is small ale. A hair is caught in the fold and I have left it, because the fold is where the leaf opens and somebody was always leaning over to see what was written. The tallow is the woman’s, and the grey is the officer’s, and neither of them will own either mark.

\subsection*{At the foot}

\begin{quote}\itshape The measure is banked. The account stands. Nothing is lost that we have kept. Your return is recorded.\end{quote}

That is the clean voice, which is the Hearthseat’s own. Under it, in a hand that is nobody’s, struck once and written again:

\begin{quote}\itshape Four sayings and a place where the fifth would stand. We say the four. We keep the place.\end{quote}

The leaf goes back under the slate on the collector’s table. A slate is a thing that gets carried into the square and read in a clean voice; this is a thing that gets read by the light of one lamp after the house is in bed. If an officer ever finds it, let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, as I did, and will warm the stone first.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Measure for Measure, Being the Sayings of the Bowls, Gathered at the Ember House and Glossed for a Boy from the North}
\CRsheetheading{Measure for Measure, Being the Sayings of the Bowls, Gathered at the Ember House and Glossed for a Boy from the North}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An under-steward’s gathering of the proverbs, courtesy-maxims, press-songs and curses of Sere, written in thin gold on prepared paper in the open courtesy hand; the sayings in the long-vowelled southern speech with the ends thrown into the fire, the glosses in the same hand with less gold in it, with the leaning corrections of a bowl-house tally-clerk, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Gathered in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 811 at the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere by Dalia Ember, an under-steward who keeps the fourth bowl, for a boy come down from Greybank who sat at the lower table and did not know when to applaud; written on seven leaves of prepared paper in gold ink, the sayings in the thick gold and the glosses in the thin; carried north in a glass consignment in Ash of Y.H. 812 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor’s clerk corrected it and put a nought in the margin; carried on to Sill and copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813. It survives with gold worked into the grain of the first leaf, the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a small wine-ring at the third hour, a thumb of olive oil at the head, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a green-glazed shard from a northern bowl pressed into the fold, one corner scorched where the leaf lay too near a court fire, a gold crown pressed flat between the fifth and sixth leaves, the leaning corrections of the house clerk standing above the glosses, the narrow upright correction added at Greybank above both, and a line at the back in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the fourth bowl at the Ember house. That is my whole office: to set a bowl down full at the third hour, and carry it away full when the feasting is done, and answer no questions about it. A boy come down from Greybank sits at the lower table and watches my hands to learn when to applaud. Last Grain he clapped at the new slate and the man beside him told him to clap at the old one too, which he did, and he has not been right since. I have set these sayings down for him in the thinner gold. The thick gold is kept for contracts, and a contract is a thing said to a man who is not in the room. A saying is said to the bowl. If the bowl answers, that is between them.

The manner of them first, because a saying said wrongly is a different saying. Say them with the vowels open and the ends thrown into the fire, so that the listener supplies the last of the thought. Said looking at a man, a saying becomes a lawsuit; said to the bowl, or to the fire under the bowl, it stays a saying. There are words here that are only spoken at the third hour, when the wine is up and an act of state is being announced. Write them at another hour and they look like anything. A northern clerk copied one into a slate once and was polite about it for a week, which is the longest politeness I have ever seen a northern man sustain.

\subsection*{Of the bowl and the pouring}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The pot was made to pour. The cup that keeps is the cup that sours.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Valen Openhand says it at the third hour, and the priests who say it after him are among the fullest vessels in the empire. A visitor notices this; a child of the house is taught not to. A vessel was made to be emptied gloriously and a life hoarded is a life wasted. Say it over the wine, never over the accounts, where it would be a very different sentence and might cost somebody a province.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A debt carried gracefully is an ornament of a house.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What is carried gracefully is still carried. At sixteen a girl emptied the bowl at her feast and named a debt she intended to carry, and the applause was for the debt and not for her. Three houses asked for her in the same hour. They were not asking for the debt. I have put that in because the boy will see the applause and want to know who is being honoured, and the answer is not the person.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Burn the slate by lot. Write it again before the wine is cold.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the end of a feast one household’s debt-slates go into the fire and new ones are made. A woman whose slate burned wept, and the crowd was kind to her, and then applauded the new slate. I have set both sentences here. The boy will want one of them to be the true one; both of them are true, and the second one is the one that is copied.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A year’s grain under the dead is a warm send-off. Buy the ash back at the price they ask.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The warmest funerals in the world are ours. The Court taxes the ash and the house buys it back as quiet ash, and a great funeral can empty a province, which is then bought cheap. We call the house generous. I have not written what I think of this, because an under-steward who writes what he thinks is an under-steward looking for another house.}

\subsection*{Of courtesy and the face}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “There is no rudeness in Sere. There is only a person who has not yet been told.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Our courtesy is long and open, and a man who does not know it is never refused; he is confirmed in being a stranger. The boy has one name and is ashamed of it. A child here has seven by adolescence and keeps whichever the household prefers. He asked me why one name is not enough. I told him a bowl holds one pouring and a house holds seven, and let him make what he could of it, which is how courtesy is taught.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Say yes. If they ask which, say measure for measure.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the third hour a public bowl of wine is emptied and an act of the Sun-Emperor is announced. A potter from the north stood beside me and asked whether a debt had been forgiven or a province ruined. The man beside him said yes. When the potter asked which, he said measure for measure and went back to his wine. I have learned that the phrase means just what the speaker decided before he opened his mouth. It is a fine phrase for an empire. It is not a fine phrase for a contract, which is why it is never written in gold.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A woman may own the bowls and the slaves and a husband’s debt. She may not enter the room where her numbers are read.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Inheritance goes to the eldest surviving child regardless of sex, and a woman of a great house may hold a great deal. The room where her measure is counted has a door in it, and her numbers are read to her by a man. This is a courtesy with a door in it. The boy asked why a woman who owns a house may not count it. I told him a door is not an argument and will not fight him, and he let it go, which is a courtesy he has learned from us already.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Concubinage is a public measure. Do not call it a kindness.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Returned slaves are kept openly and are counted as part of a household’s standing, the way a good fire or a row of bowls is counted. A kindness that can be seen and admired is not a kindness but a receipt. This is said in the court and not in the counting room. The slaves know it before the boy does; he will learn it from them, which is the ordinary order of learning in this country.}

\subsection*{Of dust and the open court}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The courts have no walls. The dust settles in the hair and nobody brushes it off.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Men sit in the heat of the court fires with their coats on the ground beside them and let the dust lie where it falls. A northern man brushes himself and is noticed. We say a man who brushes the dust off has decided he is only passing through, and a man only passing through may be charged for the hour.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The south is warm the way a kiln is warm, with the door open. A man goes thirstier here than in a northern winter.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The potter who asked about the bowl said it first and got it right. I have kept his words because our own say the warmth and leave out the thirst, which is the whole art of a southern saying. He had been told the south was warm and found it no comfort.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The burning winds take the skin off a man’s lips and leave the grain standing.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The winds come yellow off the east and a traveller’s lips go first. The grain stands through them, which is why the empire has grain and the traveller has a skin he does not recognise. We say the wind takes what is loose. It is a saying about lips and about households, and neither of them is safe in it.}

\subsection*{Of the fourth bowl}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Three go round and are poured. One stands and is carried away full.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At every feast a fourth bowl is set down full and not emptied. It stands through the feasting and is carried away still full. Nobody pours it and nobody says whose debt it holds. I asked three times and got three silences, the last of which was the kindest. The boy asked once and I told him to ask the bowl. He did. The bowl did not answer, which is the answer they gave me in finer words.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “There is a place in every account where a bowl should be emptied and is not. Go around it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The clerks go around that place the way our yard goes around a thing set down where a child might knock it. I have set the bowl in the margin where a figure should stand, because the bowl will not lie in a column. The tally-clerk has tried twice to give it a figure. Both times the figure has stood and the bowl has stood beside it, and the two have not touched.}

Bowl — Poured for — What is said over it\par

The first — the house — the debt named at the Bowl feast\par

The second — the fire — the act announced from the third hour\par

The third — the slate — the burning by lot and the new writing\par

The fourth — nobody — nothing\par

\subsection*{What they sing at the wine-presses}

\emph{Sung at the tread, not at the feast. The third verse is said to the bowl and not to the company. He has learned to keep his hands off the fourth bowl, which is more than I managed at his age.}

\begin{quote}\itshape At the press we tread and the wine comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a neck for the house and a neck for the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the third goes down on a slate burned by lot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth goes back to the shelf.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We clap for the debt and we clap for the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we buy back the ash at the price of the grain;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the year that we burned under one we loved\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape was the year we had meant to spend anyway.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names on a girl and the house keeps one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the others go into the fire with the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three go round and they all go dry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth stands full and is carried away.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

A clerk of the house borrowed the leaves after the third hour, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the leaning counting-hand, with the gold gone thin and the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could spill out of a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the cup that keeps is the cup that sours}, he wrote \emph{vessels are made for use}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{a debt carried gracefully}, he set \emph{obligation acknowledged, current}, which leaves the ornament out and the obligation in.

\item At \emph{measure for measure} he wrote \emph{equivalence recorded}, and underlined the equivalence.

\item At \emph{buy the ash back at the price they ask}, he set \emph{quiet ash, market rate}, and put a figure in the margin where I had put the price.

\item Against the fourth bowl he wrote \emph{a reserve retained, no charge against it}, which is a true thing in the language of a counting room and has the bowl standing in it still.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing above my words. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because the boy wants to know whose hand poured, and there is always a hand.

\subsection*{What the northern hand did}

A factor’s clerk at Greybank corrected the copy on the back of the voided warrant in the narrow upright hand. He has never been south and has strong views about dust.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the courts have no walls}, he wrote \emph{the premises are unenclosed}.

\item At \emph{the dust settles in the hair}, he wrote \emph{atmospheric deposit, not entered}, which is a description of a room after everybody has left it.

\item In the margin beside the fourth bowl he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} underneath.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand standing over mine, the way a new slate is laid over the burned one. A nought is a number. The bowl was not a number, and nobody has poured it to find out.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold at the head has worked into the grain and will not come out, which is why we write contracts in it and sayings in the thinner mixture: a contract is meant to last and a saying is meant to be carried. The dust in the fold came off the court bench and I have not shaken it, because the boy will one day ask what the yellow is and I should rather he asked than knew. The wine-ring is small and belongs to the third hour. The olive thumb is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I carry the bowl with. The husk of grain stuck in the gutter came from a loaf sent north and returned uneaten, which is a journey I could enter if I chose and have not. The green shard in the fold came off a bowl the house bought from a northern potter and cracked in the first frost; the tally-clerk has asked for it twice and has not had it. The scorched corner is where the leaf lay too close to a court fire. The crown pressed flat between the fifth and sixth leaves is one the boy was paid in and cannot spend here, which makes it the only coin in the house nobody has tried to enter. In Sere the ash is bought back and burnt in a bowl; that is another way of saying nothing is left where it lay.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three are poured and the fourth stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house does not know whose debt it holds\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and would pour it if it knew.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is the only thing in Sere nobody has spent.\end{quote}

I asked the bowl-keeper, the tally-clerk and a factor come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the oiled wrap under the fourth bowl; tomorrow the third hour will come, and I shall set the bowl down full and carry it away full, and the boy will watch my hands to learn when to clap.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Nine to the Floor, Being a Drinking Song of the Duelling Floor in Keld Keep}
\CRsheetheading{Nine to the Floor, Being a Drinking Song of the Duelling Floor in Keld Keep}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A Keldish floor-song in three parts, taken down by the clerk who keeps the numbers at the Duelling Floor; the verses in the hard Rim speech, the corrections in the verbless hand of a Court survey-clerk, one answer from the Listening Stones, and a lowlander’s verse at the foot · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep, on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by wet slate, the figures on the face of it gone soft; carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road with a survey party in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank. Kept in the floor-clerk’s board box among the spoil slips. It survives with coal dust at the head, a press of wet reed across the first leaf, a smear of hot lead at the fold, an ale ring, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print along the gutter, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the Court, one line in a hand that writes very large and very slowly, and a verse added in Grathic by a clay-man who had been levied to the Cold Pass.\par}\medskip
I keep the numbers at the floor. A man comes down from the shift or off the stone and states his measure before he states his name, and I set the two down in that order, because that is the order the Keep uses and I have never known a man to complain of it until he has had a clamp across his arm. What follows is not part of the account. It is what they sing after, in the room off the floor, with the cups out and the irons put away. No one sings it on the stone. A man with a clamp in his hand has no breath to spare for a refrain, and a man who has just opened a way in his forearm is not in a singing mood.

I have put the words down as they came. The coal dust at the head came off the sleeve of the man who dictated the third part to me; he would not wash before he had finished, and said a song that had never been in a mine was not worth the paper. The lead at the fold is not mine. I have left it where it lies, and I have not swept the grey out of the gutter either. There is no Last Day in a board box.

\subsection*{The song, as it is sung}

\emph{Sung standing. The cup in the right hand, the left palm flat on the table stone: the hand that has held a clamp does not hold a cup at the same time. The room says the refrain together. A man who has just come off the floor says the lines of his own part, and nobody says his name.}

\subsection*{The first part: the floor}

Nine to the floor and one to the stone, state your measure, then your name; the cup goes round and the cold goes round, and the number is not the same.

The iron bites and does not let go, the arm below goes the colour of rope; a man says his measure, a man says his name, and the third thing he says is a hope.

They put hot iron to the palm and ask if you owe, and the honest come back with a hand gone dead; I have known eleven honest men and not one of them lied, and nine cannot lift a cup.

Nine to the floor and one to the stone, state your measure, then your name; the cup goes round and the cold goes round, and the number is not the same.

\subsection*{The second part: the Descent}

At thirteen he goes down for a single day and comes up with a number changed; his mother asks what he saw in the dark and he tells her the dark, and his hands tell her the rest.

There is a mark on the inside of the arm where the way was cut and kept open while it scarred; it aches before the thaw and aches after, and he answers to whichever number the room has given him.

Some come up with the same number and some do not, and the clerk writes the second down without a mark beside it, which is the only honest thing a clerk can do.

Nine to the floor and one to the stone, state your measure, then your name; the cup goes round and the cold goes round, and the number is not the same.

\subsection*{The third part: what comes up through the stone}

When the lead smells hot in the lower drift, stop singing. The warm comes up through the stone like a river loosed in a room; the grub in the warm-stone knew it a tend before any man did, eating from the inside and leaving the stone standing hollow.

We go down in pairs and come up in pairs, and where there were two at the mouth there is sometimes one. The number stands. The number stands. That is what we say, and we do not say it twice.

Five leagues up where the bare stones sit, a Vorr sits still and comes down with a figure; ask him what it means and he will tell you once, \emph{the numbers are correct}, and he will tell you twice.

Karric shut the Pass in seven hundred forty-one, and the border was fixed in forty-seven by men who had never walked it; we drink to the Warden and we drink to the road, and the road has no name and the Warden has two.

\subsection*{The cup at the end}

There is a cup set at the end of the floor that nobody takes. It stands for the one whose number was changed twice. We set it out. We do not drink from it. The clerk leaves the place the length of a name.

The last cup goes to the man just off the stone, not to the one that won but to the one still standing; he drinks with the left hand, for the right has gone cold, and he states his measure, and after that his name.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf when the survey table sat at the Keep in Ilmen. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{the cup goes round and the cold goes round} in both places and set above it, \emph{the measure is circulated and the chill is entered}. Against \emph{the number is not the same} he wrote \emph{the vessel was re-entered}, which is a true thing said in a language nobody at this floor speaks. At the end, where the cup stands that nobody takes, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it.

I have put the words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man who has just come off the stone does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to drink with. A nought is a number and a place is not. He has put a number where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

\subsection*{From the Listening Stones}

The leaf went up to the stones with a surveyor who had a question to ask and was in no hurry to hear the answer. It came back with one line in a hand that writes very large and very slowly, a hand like a man learning to use a tool he has no use for:

\begin{quote}\itshape The numbers are correct.\end{quote}

I asked the surveyor whether that was an answer to the song. He said it was an answer to the numbers, which is not the same thing, and that a man who wanted a Vorr to translate a thing had chosen the wrong sort of man. I have set the line where it was written and have not glossed it. In this country a sentence that can be carried away and still mean nothing is not a small thing; it is the only kind of sentence that survives the winter.

\subsection*{The verse at the foot, in Grathic}

A clay-man from the low road was at the Pass in the year the snow lay long, and he wrote this in the bottom margin in a small careful hand, with the \emph{th} hard and the vowels short as they speak them down the Ilm. He had been levied and had not chosen to come.

\begin{quote}\itshape I do not state my measure. It was stated for me\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by a man with a clean cuff and a number already written.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Where I come from a pot split lip to foot is a pot gone wrong\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the yard goes around the place where it stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Here they clamp it and call it a repair,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the repair gets carried all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners and four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should be --- even up here.\end{quote}

I have not struck it out. He asked me what the fifth was, and I told him I had never known a man who could say, and he said that was the answer his mother would have given and went back to the wall.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal dust is the Shift-man’s, who dictated the third part standing and would not sit. The press of wet reed came from the board walk at the Weir, where the survey party put the leaf down while a barge unloaded and it took the weather. The ale ring is not a mark anybody owns; three men put a cup in it over one evening and no man will say which. The tallow thumb is mine: I held the sheet down in the draught that comes up the shaft and did not know I had marked it. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff I had no business putting into a corner in the room where the cups were, and I have not washed it off and have no wish to.

The board box goes back under the survey table with the spoil slips. The figures on the face of the sheet are gone soft on the wet side, and the song on the dry side is plain enough to read. A man will state his measure and then his name tomorrow as he did today, and the number of some of them will be changed by the end of the tend, and the clerk will set the second down without a mark beside it, which is the only thing he is allowed to do honestly.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Nineteen Out, Nineteen Back}
\CRsheetheading{Nineteen Out, Nineteen Back}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A work song of the slip pits and the drying racks, Low Kiln · Taken down on a market morning in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, from the mouths of women treading slip in the Clay Yard of Sill, by a clerk in the factor’s house at Greybank whose name has been rubbed from the corner of the sheet; the copy stands on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, folded into an apron pocket, and survives with slip-stains, a green bead of lead glaze, a thumb in tallow, and the clerk’s own square hand striking out one line. The song is held to be older than the Clay Road.\par}\medskip
I set this down because I was told to copy what the women sang and not what I thought they ought to have sung, which is a harder thing than it sounds. I am a clerk. My hand wants a verb where there is no verb, and a line where the line breaks off and goes around the pot instead of through it. What is written below is as near as I could come, with the knocked-out parts left standing so that a man reading it in Greybank may know what he is looking at. The slip at the top right is not mine. Nor the green. The tallow thumb is the woman’s who sang it loudest; she put her hand on the sheet to keep it from the draught and did not know she had marked it.

\subsection*{The song, as it goes round the yard}

The pit is cold before the sun, the slip is old bone under the heel; tread it, girl, and tread it again, it will mind your weight and keep it.

Tread, tread, the clay says more than the potter will say before company; a fist in the belly, a thumb at the rim, and the crack shows where you left it.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, a pot on the hip and the broom at the track; four and four and a want in the Count, and the rack keeps the dry and the pit keeps the wet.

The wheel does not care whose hands, only that they come steady and come soon; bone-pale slip to the bend of the finger, and the hollow seat keeps the shape of a man.

Set it down. Let the pot speak first. A whole one answers full under the knuckle; a cracked one gives a little flat knock and will not be told what it should have said.

Leave the crack showing. Let the glaze go over the good part and the bad part alike; a repair is a scar with a pot around it, and the pot is the one that gets carried.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, and a place at the end of the rack where nothing stands; the yard goes around it, the broom goes around it, and nobody puts a pot there, and nobody says why.

Up the terrace the glaze room breathes sweet, sweet enough to make a body careless; a pale line at the gum is the first of it, and a woman with green at her mouth still sings.

One in twelve as the notice says, three loaves to the levy and one to the dish; the bell at the Cross goes longer than a church bell, and nobody crosses himself at it, and the pigs go over the boards.

When the river comes up and takes the low steps, the steps come back a hand’s breadth out of line; the yard calls it weather and goes on using them, as a woman calls a cough weather and goes on.

Nineteen out and nineteen back, the fire keeps the breath it will not give; bank it with the back of a broken pot, and leave the grey where it lies till the Last Day.

\subsection*{The fourth line, and what I did to it}

The women sang, \emph{the pit is cold before the sun}. I struck this out, being used to a verb in its place, and wrote above it, \emph{the cold is in the pit before the sun is}. Missy Clay, who sang loudest and keeps her hand on my sheet, looked at what I had written and asked me which of us had been standing in the pit, because the cold was not in it before the sun and never had been; it came up out of it when you trod, which is a different thing and not the thing on my notice. I have left my line standing above hers so that the correction can be seen. It is the only place in this copy where the Court’s grammar has got the better of me, and I am not proud of it.

\subsection*{A note on the counting, in the same hand}

The nineteen is not a number I have ever been able to make agree with anything. It is the steps from the slip pit to the drying rack, out and back, and a woman of House Silt has walked it every day since Y.H. 806, which is six years, and will not vary it by one. I asked her why nineteen and she asked me why a tend has ten days in it, and when I told her the Court had not made the tend and could not unmake it, she said that was the answer, and went back to her tread. There is a twentieth place at the rack’s end where a pot once stood. I put it in the song because they put it in the song. I cannot tell you what pot it was, and no one I asked would tell me either, so I have entered it as a place and not as a loss.

The \emph{four and four and a want in the Count} is the kiln’s breathing, or the stack’s, or the bell’s; they use the same count for all three and keep the three counts in separate places in their heads. I put down what I heard. I would not join them for a crown.

\subsection*{The verse they would not sing before a man from Slate Row}

There is one more verse. The women broke off at it when a collector crossed the north bridge with his satchel under his arm, and took it up again when he was past the Fishstairs, and would not let me write it while he was in the square. I have it now from Missy Clay after the market, and set it here with the proper space left before it, which is the space they left in the singing:

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron comes cold and the slate comes clean,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that writes is not the hand that’s seen;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes in the pot is not what comes out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account stands, and the bowl’s about.\end{quote}

I asked her what the last line meant. She said it was a song, and a song was not obliged to mean a thing just because a clerk had written it down. Then she put her tallow thumb on the corner of the sheet again.

\subsection*{At the foot of the leaf}

A grey ridge runs along the skirting in the room where they sang, near two thumbs wide, turning the corner without a break. It is not swept until the Last Day and is burnt the morning after, and called dealt with. I touched it with the edge of my notice and it came off on the paper, which is how the grey at the bottom of this leaf got there. If the sheet is ever read in the Hearthseat, let that be entered against me and not against the women: I moved it, and they would have left it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Number Before the Name, Being the Sayings of the Keldish, Gathered Above the Shaft Mouth at Keld Keep and Glossed for a Man Come Up the Rim Road}
\CRsheetheading{The Number Before the Name, Being the Sayings of the Keldish, Gathered Above the Shaft Mouth at Keld Keep and Glossed for a Man Come Up the Rim Road}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A key-woman’s gathering of the proverbs, tally-maxims, iron-sayings and stone-curses of Keld, set in Grathic letters on the back of a shift-tally because Keldish is cut in bone and does not travel; the sayings in the hard Rim speech with the endings struck off, the glosses in the writer’s own hand, with a Court survey-clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a notch cut in the edge where a word would not come, a carter’s sloping addition, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered in Bone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands called the Thin Year, by a woman who holds the mine-reeve’s keys above ground at Keld Keep, from men waiting their turn at the weigh and from the old women who count at the mouth; written in charcoal on the back of a shift-tally gone soft at the fold, cut once at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, carried down the Rim Road with a cart of lead in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, where a survey-clerk of the Court borrowed it and set his hand above hers.
