\begin{quote}\itshape with the cold of the pit and the print in the mud.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the wheel}

\emph{Not sung at the wheel itself. Said under the breath by the thrower while the pot goes up, with the thumb kept steady and the knuckle kept for afterwards.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wheel goes round and the seat is worn\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape on the left where a man leaned, and the lean stays on;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put the pot where his thumb was put\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and listen to what the pot has got.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wall goes up and the thumb goes in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape at the one place where the wall is thin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it once with the knuckle bone ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape full is a note that a house may own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tap it once and it answers flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sweep it around where the potter sat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A crack once made is a crack kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave the crack showing and the yard goes through.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the kiln}

\begin{quote}\itshape The kiln draws breath and the kiln lets go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the breath and a place in the row;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire takes what the fire will take\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leaves a brown edge on the loaf we bake.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glaze runs sweet where the lead has been\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a girl at the cup has a pale at the gum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape she sets the cup down on the bench and goes\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape out to the racks where the dry slip shows.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the fire takes out of the clay\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house finds in the corner at dawn;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we leave it there and we leave the pot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the crack showing, and carry on.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the seventh held in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flaw goes shallow and the note comes back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six under the heel and the foot comes up free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes out of the clay comes home to me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they do not tread when a man from Slate Row is in the yard}

I have it from the caller, with the space left before it, which is the space the treaders leave in the singing. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it within sight of his cuff. She said it to the pot I had set by the wall, with her back to the road.

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the years that the slate will name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the year that the household keeps;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes in and the man goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey in the corner goes up a thumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the pot and one for the hand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that put the thumb in and could not command\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the place where it failed. The yard says weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The legs say nothing. The slate says never.\end{quote}

I asked her what the seventh was and she said a man who had never trodden would not know where the foot comes up, and went back to the pit. This is the answer the yard gives to everything it does not want entered, and I have set it down as she gave it, without mending the sense.

\subsection*{The old woman’s correction in the margin}

Against \emph{two for the bubble that breaks and is not}, a woman who has kept the racks thirty years wrote in a small hard hand: \emph{Not air. Water. My mother trod this pit forty years and it is water that comes up between the toes, not air, and water will not burst a pot in the firing. The pot that went flat in our kiln had been dried too fast against the east wall.}

Under it, in mine: \emph{Both stand. I have felt the bubble break and I have known the east wall. A song that has been corrected in the margin is a song that has been used, and a song nobody has argued with is a song nobody has trodden to.}

\subsection*{What the clerk wrote above the seventh round}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank, being a man who cannot leave paper lying. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{the seventh held in} and wrote above it, \emph{one part in twelve withheld from the tread; the deduction is entered.} Against \emph{what goes out of the clay comes home to me} he set \emph{labour retained in the vessel; no residue arises.} At the foot of the last round he wrote \emph{six turns performed, rest nil,} and drew a line under it that went a finger’s breadth past the margin.

I have put the women’s words back underneath and left his standing above, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it. He has made a rest into a deduction and a deduction into a year. A rest is when the foot comes up; a year is what a clay-bound man does not get back. He has set one where the other stood, which is the whole art of that hand. The treaders stop when they see the soft cuff come into the yard. They take it up when he is past the bridge, and they never once sing the seventh.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The bone-pale slip at the head is off the hand that drew the line in the pit; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard uses it to mark a place and not to write a name. The wet-clay thumb at the second corner is mine. I signed in slip because I have no slate-name and the pot was mine before it was a leaf. The green bead came off a pot broken by the Glaze Room and rolled to the gutter while a woman held the tally down in the draught; I did not taste it and have not put it in my mouth, whatever the children say of that sweetness. The brown crust is a barley one with the edge burnt, given to a child who would not eat it and laid down here instead. The tallow print came off a lamp set too near the leaf at the Long Night. The tideline took two words off the back of the tally and I have not written them in again, because a song with two words gone is a song said slowly and all of ours are said slowly. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a yard; I have not swept it. The Last Day is for corners, and a folded leaf has none.

The tally goes back into its fold of oiled paper and into the pocket, and tomorrow the pit will be cold again and the four of us will be there or the two, according to the water. The caller will say six and the feet will answer six, and the seventh will stand at the lip where it stood this morning, and the clay will close over the instep the way it always does, and whatever goes out of it will come home to somebody.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The flaw is where the thumb was. The thumb was somebody’s.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six go into the pot. The seventh goes home in the leg.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the yard what it counts and it will tell you the weather.\end{quote}

I asked the caller, the old woman of the racks and a carter waiting on the road, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Ten at the Racks, Being the Palm-Count of the Low Kiln Girls, with the Manner of the Clapping, the Still Hands, and What a Clerk Put in the Eleventh Place}
\CRsheetheading{Ten at the Racks, Being the Palm-Count of the Low Kiln Girls, with the Manner of the Clapping, the Still Hands, and What a Clerk Put in the Eleventh Place}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A rack-woman’s gathering of a children’s hand-clapping game, set down in charcoal on the back of a spoiled rack-tally; the count in the children’s own half-sung speech, the manner of it in the writer’s small hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk borrowed at Greybank, a gloss pressed in charcoal by the woman who keeps the birth-slates at the shrine, and one line at the foot in grey chalk in a hand that has learned its letters off a slate · Written at the drying racks in the Clay Yard at Low Kiln of Sill in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, of an evening when the racks stood half full and the girls clapped over a tally of wet pots; carried to Greybank in the pocket of a potter gone to have a kiln-mark renewed and copied onto the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at one corner. Kept folded in the rack-shed under the loose board beside the wheel. It survives with slip dried pale in the creases at the head, a tallow thumb, a chalk score along the fore-edge where a line was drawn and rubbed out, a small-ale ring, a green bead of lead glaze in the fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, a gloss pressed in charcoal beside the ninth line, and a line at the foot in grey chalk nobody will claim\par}\medskip
I keep the drying racks in the Clay Yard, and I have set this down because the youngest girl who used to clap here went up the clay road in the spring and came back with a number where her name had been. She stands now at the end of the racks and watches the hands go round and does not put hers in. I am not writing it for her. A leaf of charcoal cannot teach back what has been taken out of a person. I write it for the ones who come after, who will want to know why the hands stop together on the tenth, why nobody claps in the gap, and why the ninth line is said to the rack and never to a face.

The tally this is written on counted forty pots and lost the figure in the damp before I wanted it. That is how I came by the back of it. A thing spoiled for the Court is the proper stuff for a children’s game; the factor’s man was going to throw it out and I asked him for it, and he gave it without looking, which is the only generosity I have ever had from that house.

\subsection*{How it is played}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Two girls sit facing at the end of a rack, with the pots standing dry behind them. They clap their own hands on the odd lines and strike palms on the even, so that the pattern is \emph{own, together, own, together} all the way to the tenth. It is played while the racks are turned in the last of the light and not at any other time, because the racks want both hands and the game wants them too.

\item The count is said to the rack, not to the girl across from you. Said to a face it becomes an argument, and there is always a girl who will argue. The rack has no ears and will not carry the count up the road.

\item One line, one clap. On the tenth line the two palms meet and stay met, without pressing, while the words \emph{Read the count} are said. This is the reading. A girl who claps the tenth instead of holding it has read aloud where she should have kept quiet, and sits with her hands in her lap until the other turns her palm upward and says, \emph{The count begins again.} That is the whole of the bringing back. Nobody’s name is said in it.

\item After the tenth there is the gap. The hands part and lie flat on the knees for one breath and nobody claps. A girl who claps in the gap has banked it, and sits out as above. The gap is not a day and has no clap in it; they will not be told what it is, and if you ask they ask you why a man wants to put a number on a breath.

\item When ten has been held and the gap kept, the hands go back to Firstday and the whole count turns again. There is no last round and nothing is won. The girl who has kept her hands still through the most gaps gets to say the ninth line, which is the one about the name. She does not get to say it to anybody.

\item The game is not played in the Five, when the children are made to stand and listen, nor on a day a collector has been seen on the Clay Road. It is played in the thaw on the dry boards and in Stone on the trodden ash inside the kiln-house, and the words are the same in both places.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The count, as it is clapped}

\emph{Own hands on the odd lines, palms together on the even. On the tenth the palms meet and do not move. Say it to the rack.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Firstday, and the fire is turned with a pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Secondday, and the grey goes around the cot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Thirdday, and the pot answers full,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fourthday, and the eel comes up through silt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Fifthday, and the loaf shows a browned edge,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sixthday, and the bit goes into the house;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seventhday, the wheel that will not stand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eighthday, the broom that goes around;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ninthday, the name we say at home,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tenthday, the hands meet. Read the count.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What is said in the gap}

\emph{Hands flat on the knees. One breath, no more. The words are said low, to the floor, and not across the space between the two girls.}

\begin{quote}\itshape No clap in the gap. The gap is not a day.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The hands lie down. The hands come back.\end{quote}

They keep both hands in their laps through this, and a girl who lets one hand go up an inch to begin the next count early is banked, though nobody calls it that but me. I have watched them do it for nineteen springs and never once seen a girl correct herself before the breath was out.

\subsection*{The verse they do not clap while a man from the factor’s house is in the yard}

I have this from the girl who says the ninth line, with the proper space left before it, which is the space the hands leave in the clapping. She would not say it while the clerk had his pen out and would not say it to him at all. She said it to the rack with her back turned and made me set it down with none of my words in it.

\begin{quote}\itshape They gave her a figure and sent her home,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and she stands at the end where the racks run out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we clap to the rack and not to her,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the count goes round with a place kept warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six bits a day and the crust is free;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey in the corner is not for the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine in the hands and the tenth in the house,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eleventh is not a day of the tend.\end{quote}

I asked her what the eleventh was. She said the factor’s man would know, and that he had put it in his book while she was still saying the tenth, and that she had let him because a child who argues with a man in a soft cuff gets no crust at the end of the row. I have set it down as she said it, with the letting left in.

\subsection*{What the woman at the shrine put in the margin}

The charcoal here is hers, pressed hard and small, the way a woman writes who has kept birth-slates for nineteen years and does not want the words read over a cradle.

At \emph{the fire is turned with a pot}: \textbf{She says pot. It is the back of a broken pot. A girl who has never turned coals should not say this line, and will say it all the same.}

At \emph{the grey goes around the cot}: \textbf{The broom goes around it. The house goes around it. It is the same sentence said kindly. Do not let them make it a proverb before they have swept.}

At \emph{Ninthday, the name we say at home}: \textbf{There is a name for the house and a name for the slate. Keep them on two places of the tongue, and do not let the second one travel.}

At \emph{the gap is not a day}: \textbf{We sat with a covered pot through a Long Night and did not clap. That is the only gap I have kept, and it was longer than a breath.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk borrowed the tally at Greybank on the morning the pots went down, being a man who cannot let paper lie still. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He numbered the ten lines in the margin and wrote against the tenth, \emph{the account is read and the parties are identified}. Against \emph{no clap in the gap} he wrote \emph{five days outside the tend; no observance; no charge to the district}. Against \emph{the name we say at home} he wrote \emph{the name is entered where the house requires}. At the foot, where the two hands lie on the knees and nothing at all is counted, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{eleven} beside it, and under that, \emph{vacancy}.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the hands out of it because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a girl up to her wrists in slip does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know when to clap. A nought is a number. The Five have names and no number. He has put a figure where a breath should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned by the game. I told him the count and the stopping and the bringing back, and he said that was an account of the Return taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The girls stop when a man with a soft cuff comes into the yard. They take it up when he is past the wheel-shed. They have never once changed the tenth.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is dried pale in the creases and came off the hand that held the tally down on the rack rail; it goes into the grain and no damp takes it out, which is why a rack-woman uses charcoal and not ink. The tallow thumb is mine, from the lamp I held low while the girl said the verse with her back turned and I did not want her to see me writing. The chalk score along the fore-edge is a line one of them drew to count on and rubbed out with her sleeve before she was told to, which is the way lines go in this yard. The small-ale ring is from a cup set down by nobody in particular and claimed by three girls and denied by one. The green bead in the fold came off a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, who leaned over to see the writing, touched the leaf and went back up the terrace without asking. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying among the racks; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day in a rack-shed.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey chalk, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I kept my hands still and she did not come back.\end{quote}

The letters are hard at the \emph{th} and one of them is set backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a slate and not off a book. No hand will own it. I asked the girl who says the ninth line, the woman who keeps the shrine, and a potter going down with a barrow of wet ware, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left it where it was written.

The tally goes back under the loose board. Tomorrow the racks will be turned in the last of the light and the girls will sit at the end of them and clap ten and keep the gap, and the one who came back will stand where she stands and watch the hands go round without putting hers in, and I shall not call her over. I have kept their words and I have not joined them to anything.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Apprentice Beam, Being the Standing Rules of the Kiln-Masters of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices, Read at the Cross and Nailed Beside the Moot-Post}
\CRsheetheading{The Apprentice Beam, Being the Standing Rules of the Kiln-Masters of Sill for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices, Read at the Cross and Nailed Beside the Moot-Post}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bench-copy of the guild’s standing rules in the hand of the clerk who keeps the kiln-masters’ bench at the Cross; the terms set in tables, the yard’s wheel-song pasted to the back, two corrections in the Thane’s narrow hand, one clause crossed in a potter’s charcoal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered at Sill in Y.H. 418, the year the Clay Road was made a Court road by the treaty of the Blue Cliff, and copied forward each generation from the bench rather than from a book; this leaf written at the Cross and in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives folded and soft at the nail-hole, with a thumb-worn centre where a hundred men have wiped their hands before reading, a green bead of lead glaze at the head off the Thane’s thumb, slip dried the colour of old bone down the gutter, a tallow spot at the wheel clause, a press of wet reed across the song from a day the bench stood in the rain, a grey print along the foot that is not mine and is not the Thane’s, two small corrections in his narrow upright hand, one line struck hard in charcoal by a potter who would not put his name to it, and one line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the guild’s bench at the Cross on market-days, between the pig beam and the Court table set at the Slate Row fringe. A house comes to take a child, or a child is brought to be tried, and I read what is below so that what is read in High Kiln is the same as what is read in the yard. The bench is worn smooth in the middle where thumbs have wiped it longer than any man can date, and this leaf has a nail-hole at the head and a green bead of glaze in the lower corner that came off the Thane’s thumb in the Thin Year and has not been swept since. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid in a corner where no cuff has business lying, and there is no Last Day for a bench-copy. I have set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

They are not new rules. They were gathered in the year the Clay Road was made a Court road, when a man from the Cross could first reach Greybank in five days and the guild found it had neighbours it had not chosen. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. What follows has been used.

\subsection*{The standing rules, as read at the Cross}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A house takes an apprentice, not the guild. The house answers for the child’s food, his bed, his tools and the debt he makes; the guild answers only for the note. A man who takes a child and will not answer for him has taken nothing, and the child is sent back to the moot.

\item A child may be taken from his ninth year, and not before he can carry a board of wet pots the length of the yard without setting it down. A child bound by debt goes where the debt sends him, and his years count from the day the debt is entered, not from the day he could lift a board.

\item The taking is written in the house’s own roll, in a careful hand, and the roll is kept in the house. It is not taken to Slate Row and it is not shown to a man who comes down with a slate. A slate is for the measure; the roll is for the hand. The two are not the same book and must not be set side by side.

\item A foundling is named by whoever writes the slate, and has no house-name until a hearth claims him. Until then he is a coat any house may wear. See that the coat is mended where it tears, not worn till it thins.

\item A widow may hold her husband’s fire by the mark confirmed at the Cross and by the factor at Greybank. She touches the mark before she opens the kiln and at no other hour. A dusk is not an opening, and a bank is not an opening.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the first year}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The apprentice sweeps, carries, mixes slip and sets pots to dry. He does not touch the wheel, and he does not cut the glaze. A child set to the wheel too soon learns to humour the clay instead of hearing it, and a pot humoured is a pot that will not say what it is.

\item The apprentice is kept, not hired. He eats from the house’s dish and sleeps under the house’s roof. What he earns in the yard goes into the yard, and what the yard gives back comes back as bread, not as a figure in a man’s hand.

\item No child tastes glaze. Glaze is tasted by the master, with the side of the thumb and the back of the tongue, and spit out. A pale line at the gum is the glaze’s mark and not a mark of industry; a master who calls it a good sign is selling the child short by the ounce.

\item A wet pot is not set in the sun and a wet pot is not set near the door. You will pay for both in the thaw. Fire does not know a child is sorry; feed it and say nothing.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the wheel and the ear}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Knock with the knuckle, never the nail and never the flat of the hand. The hand says what it wants from the pot; the knuckle says what the pot has. This rule is the whole trade and the rest are its corners.

\item A sound pot under the knuckle gives its full note. A cracked pot answers flat, small and dead, and the sound stops at the surface and will not go through. A pot that answers flat is a pot gone wrong. It is broken at the door, not mended and sold, and the yard goes around the place where it stood.

\item A mended pot gives a note nearly full and never quite, and the yard calls it a pot that’ll do. Leave the crack showing. A repair that will not sing is a lie in clay, and a lie in clay is the only lie a kiln cannot burn clean.

\item The cupworm hides a flaw no knuckle will find. If a hand says a pot is wrong and the knuckle says it is right, set the pot aside another year. The yard has been wrong about pots and has never once been wrong about a hand that would not let a thing go.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Crossed hard in charcoal across rule 13 in the Thin Year, in a potter’s hand that did not sign:} Strike \emph{the knuckle says it is right}. Set above: \emph{the ear hears it before the hand gets there, and the hand gets there before the knuckle}. I have not swept the charcoal. I have not put the struck words back. Both readings stand, because the bench has held both and the bench is older than either of us.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the kiln and the breath}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No child sleeps in a closed kiln house. The kiln’s breath kills in sleep and is called a merciful death by those who have not had to carry the body out. A damper is a thing to be moved, not argued with.

\item Coals are banked under ash at dusk with the back of a broken pot, not with a shovel. Iron on iron wakes what should lie. The fire is left as it was found, so that the morning’s hand knows the night’s hand was there.

\item The master opens the kiln. The apprentice stands back from the lid, because a face over an open kiln learns nothing and loses its eyebrows. The kiln takes its breath in fours and a gap; a man who counts the gap aloud will be told to count the pots instead.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the term and the debt}

Condition — Term — What gathers\par

House child, taken at nine — seven years — The note of the pot; nothing written against the boy\par

Child bound by debt — seven years, or as entered — Grey Ash in the household account, by the year and by the loaf\par

Debt left uncalled — as long as the house holds it — The debt is not forgiven. It lies where it was put, and a man goes around it as around Ash in a corner\par

Kept hand — until returned thin — No measure in the house’s roll; the house keeps the body and not the name\par

Foundling with a slate-name only — until a hearth claims him — A coat anybody can wear, and a debt nobody has entered yet\par

Widow holding a fire — by the mark, confirmed — The fire must not go out; the mark is touched before openings only\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Seven years is the common term and not a short one. Interest gathers as grey Ash in the household accounts, which is why the house keeps its roll dry and why a debt left uncalled is worse than a debt called: a called debt has an end, and an uncalled one has only a place.

\item A clay-bound child sleeps in the loft and a taken child sleeps under the roof. This is a poor household’s sorting of its own members, and it is called kindness, and it is not entered anywhere. Ask the pot. The pot is more use.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Thane’s narrow upright hand, above rule 7:} The apprentice is kept. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the apprentice is paid. He is not paid. He is fed, and the feeding goes into no figure, which is why it can be done. I have left my word standing under his, since a man should be able to see the thing he was told to change.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the levy and the First Firing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Two levies are called at the Cross, and the moot shouts at both. The levy of clay is worked out in barrow-loads and the levy of warmth in figures. The second is the heavier, and the notice says one in twelve. A household that has heard otherwise has heard wrong. The notice is what a man can be seen reading.

\item The levy is called; it is not called by the Thane, or by the bench, or by the house that pays it. The figure stands as read, and there will be a slate at the watch if the house wants it again. The red wool cord is folded into its drawer before the Thane goes home, and the bench does not follow him.

\item At twelve the child makes a pot, fires it and knocks it with a knuckle. A clear note means a feast; a flat note means another year in the yard. A foundling with no kiln of his own is judged on a pot made in the yard of the house that took him. The feast is bread and a pig’s trotter and nothing that needs entering.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The wheel-song, pasted to the back}

\emph{Sung at the second firing, standing, with the slip still on the forearms. The yard says the refrain together. Nobody sings it at the First Firing, and nobody says why.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A dish of slip and a dish of water,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a knuckle for the thing that matters;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wheel goes round and the yard goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot says what the pot has found.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the crack showing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape feed the fire, ask the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners, four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place where the fifth should be.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I made a pot and the pot said no;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I knocked it twice and it told me so.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sun’s no friend and the fire’s no friend\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to a pot that’s cracked before the end.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the crack showing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape feed the fire, ask the pot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the hand and one for the debt,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate stands in for the lot.\end{quote}

The press of wet reed across the second verse came from the bench standing in the rain at the Weir, where it went with a survey party that wanted a rule read in the open air. I have flattened it as well as I could. The words are plain enough under it.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The Thane’s clerk struck \emph{the apprentice is paid} and set \emph{kept} above. He left my figure for the term standing, saying a number is a number and a word is a word and the one has no business correcting the other. A potter struck the knuckle in rule 12 and put the ear in its place, and would not sign. The charcoal has come off on the fold and I have not brushed it away. A rule that two men have argued over is a rule that has been used.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is not entered. The hand is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape That is the whole of the trade.\end{quote}

I have asked the potters, the Thane’s clerk and a man who came up from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the two lines where they were written. The leaf goes back under the moot-post nail and the bench onto the Cross; tomorrow a house will come to take a child, and I shall read what stands here, and by afternoon the charcoal will have come off on another sleeve.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Arm and the Cord, Being the Standing Rules of the Reed-Cutters of the Weir for the Taking, Walking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices in the Beds Below Sill, with the Table of Walkings, the Bundle-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Arm and the Cord, Being the Standing Rules of the Reed-Cutters of the Weir for the Taking, Walking, Cutting and Trying of Apprentices in the Beds Below Sill, with the Table of Walkings, the Bundle-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A cutter’s leaf of rules carried in the lining of a coat against the leading rope; the rules set down in short sayings and half-sentences, the walkings and the faults in tables, the bundle-song pasted inside the cover, a knot set down in reed-ash in the margin and gone by noon, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of borrowed clerks, one line struck in charcoal by a woman who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Weir one league upriver of Sill in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813; written by Nall of the Weir, a cutter who has kept the leading rope for nineteen years, on the back of a district tally spoiled when the river came up over it, and kept dry in the oiled lining of the coat that holds the rope. It survives with grey reed-ash at the head off the flat blessing stone, silt worked into the gutter and into the grain of the fold, the press of a wet bundle across the song, a thumb of tar off the leading rope at the head, a smear of eel slime along the second leaf, salt gone white at a wrist-print, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the last verse, a ring of small ale at the foot left by a boatman who would not drink with cutters, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that is not mine and that I have not swept, two corrections in borrowed Ledgerhand standing above my words, one charcoal line struck and written again underneath, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the leading rope at the Weir, and this leaf goes in the coat lining against it. A child comes down the plank walk at twelve with nothing in the hands and asks what a cutter is for, and I tell him: to carry what the arm says is there, and to come back by the same road. Then I set him to lifting a bundle and setting it down again on the flat stone. There is no lesson before that one.

These rules were gathered in the year the river came up twice and the reed stood too long, and they are carried forward in a coat and not from a book. A rule nobody has had to use is a rule nobody can carry. These have been carried. I set them down in the words we say, short words and often directions, and where a clerk has put a figure in the place of a direction I have left both standing. A man at first light wants to know which way to walk, not what the walk is worth.

\subsection*{The rules as they stand in the coat}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Weir takes a child at twelve, by the rope and not by a house. A house may ask for the child and may not keep him. The child gives up a day and comes back by dusk with a bundle he did not have in the morning.

\item A child out of the bog comes with a reed-name, and the reed-name is enough. A child out of Sill comes with a house-name and leaves it below the bridge. We do not write either. We do not sit at a table where a slate is open, and no slate has ever been set at the Weir for a taking.

\item What is kept is the day the child first carried a bundle the length of the boards without setting it down, tied low in the cord with the teeth. A day tied in the cord is a day a man can find again by the feel of the knot, which is all a day is owed.

\item A child is taken by the arm and not by the eye. A child who judges a bundle by the weight settling into the forearm is taken. A child who counts the stalks is set to stacking and sent home at dusk, and may come again when the reed has stood.

\item A cutter’s child is not asked whether he wants the beds. He is asked whether he knows what is bought: silt to the knee, a rope that takes the wet, and hands that learn the weight before the price. The cutter cuts. The wanting comes after, or it does not.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the factor at Greybank, against rule 3:} The taking is entered; one day, one bundle. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the day is tied low with the teeth. He has entered the teeth as a figure and the bundle as a unit. A unit is a thing that can be carried up the road in a cuff. I have left both, because a man should see what was done to the day.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the arm}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A bundle is counted in the arm that carries it. The hands that cut it are counted in nothing at all. Say this to a woman at the racks who asks what the bundle holds, and go on with the next armful. Do not say it a second time; the second time becomes an answer and an answer can be entered.

\item The arm tells what was carried and never what it cost. A cost asked as a direction is answered with a direction: downriver at first light, back over the boards at dusk, and the river in between. If the woman asks again, give her the weather. The weather has never yet been entered.

\item A wet bundle is lighter to lift and harder to learn. If a child brings back his first bundle wet, he is not yet of the bog; send him again when the reed has stood and the water is off it. Do not tell him he failed. He will know it in the forearm, which is where the knowing belongs.

\item A bundle is set on the stone and never in the silt. Silt gathers in a bundle laid down and becomes a weight nobody carried and everybody pays. Lift it off; leave the silt where it fell; say nothing to the pot or the slate about it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the going-downriver and the coming-back}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A day’s work is a going-downriver and a coming-back. It is not a figure. A man who has walked it knows how far it was by where the arm begins to shake, and no slate in Sill has a column that will hold the shake.

\item The plank walk has a board that gives under a boot. Walk across it as across the rest of the boards. A woman with a creel takes the landing sideways, one hand out to the rail, and goes on selling; nobody makes a fall of it and nobody mends the board before the thaw.

\item The traps stand with their mouths upriver, so an eel goes in and cannot find the way out. The eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. On the fifteenth of Ilmen the hearth-maids bless the weir and the traps from the flat stone; stand where you are and do not look at the stone while the words are said. The blessing is the women’s. The run is the river’s.

\item At the turn of the day, straighten the cord on the flat stone. The stone lies flat and has a crossed mark in it older than any cutter’s name. Do not ask the stone what it signifies. Give the date of the blessing if a man asks twice, and give the same date a third way if he asks a third.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the cord}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The tally is a length of grey wool or reed-fibre with knots set at the lengths a man’s arm can judge, and one tied low with the teeth and a pull of the thumb. It is carried inside the coat. It would burn if put to a flame, and no clerk can take a figure from it. This is not a virtue in the cord; it is a use a man has found for a piece of wool.

\item Turn it once so the knots stand. Look at it yourself. Tie what must be tied, bite the end off, and put it back inside the coat with the flat of the hand. Do not count it aloud. A cord counted aloud is a cord with a figure in it, and a figure goes up the road.

\item To a woman who says she cannot read a cord, say \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. Say nothing after. The cord knows what the mouth will not say; the mouth knows what the cord will not count. Keep the two apart. Laying them together is a trade no honest house makes.

\item Do not lay the cord beside the knots a woman keeps at the lower boards or the eel-seller’s two twists at the Fishstairs. Three keepings laid together make a tally, and a tally wants a reader, and no reader stood at the Weir.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The walkings}

\emph{Kept in the corner of the coat lining where the days leave off. A day is tied, not written; an entered cutter could be called back to a road he has walked.}

Condition — What is kept — What is done — Discharged\par

Child taken at twelve — the day first carried, tied low — bundle lifted and set on the stone — when the arm judges without the eye\par

First bundle brought back wet — nothing tied — child sent again when the reed has stood — when the bundle comes back dry\par

Woman with a creel at the landing — nothing — she takes the boards sideways — not entered by us\par

One who does not come back at dusk — a knot low in the cord — his place gone around with a look — never\par

Knots at the lower boards — by the woman who tied them — looked at by her and nobody else — not ours to discharge\par

The leading rope — the rope itself — straightened at the turn of the day — kept by whoever holds it\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item There is no term in years. A cutter stays while the rope is in his hand and goes with nothing written down. The knot for one who does not come back at dusk is not taken out to make the cord come even; a cord kept even has forgot who tied it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the Weir\par

Stalks counted instead of carried — Bundle set down; child set to stacking until the arm learns\par

Bundle laid in the silt — Lifted; silt left where it fell; nothing entered\par

Wet bundle taken for a dry — Child sent again after the reed has stood\par

Cord counted aloud — The count stopped; the knot tied low with teeth, in silence\par

A figure set where a going-downriver stood — Figure struck; \emph{downriver and back} set underneath\par

Cord laid beside another keeping — Put back inside the coat; a hand’s breadth kept between\par

A verb struck out of a rule — Put back underneath, where the clerk can see it\par

A charcoal line swept from the stone — Not swept; the line written again below\par

\subsection*{The bundle-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung low going downriver at first light and again coming back over the boards, with the bundle on the shoulder and the cord inside the coat. Never at the Fish Blessing, and never twice in one house. The refrain is said with the whole crew; the last line belongs to whoever carried the most that day, and is not claimed.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Down at first light and back by the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bundle on the shoulder and a cord in the coat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the arm knows the weight and the arm knows the bend,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate knows nothing the river won’t take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the arm. Ask the cord.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What it carried, not what it cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four to the bundle and one gone green,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the eels go in where the mouths have been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone lies flat and the traps lie still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the run comes up whether we bless or not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the arm. Ask the cord.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What it carried, not what it cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A knot for the going and a knot for the back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one tied low where the thumb can track;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no figure on the boards, no name in the tin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court may ask the cord if it can.\end{quote}

The press of the wet bundle across the middle verse came from a morning the song was sung under a load that had not stood long enough. I have flattened the leaf as I could. The brine-gull took the last word of the last line; I have not written it back in. A verse with a word gone is a verse said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The Greybank clerk wrote \emph{one day, one bundle} above rule 3 and set \emph{transport} over \emph{carried} wherever I had put the word. Both stand. His \emph{transport} is true of a cart and a barge and a man with a load on his shoulder, which is why it is true of nobody. I have put \emph{carried} back underneath.

A clerk come down from Slate Row wrote \emph{the cost is not entered} above \emph{give her the weather} and put a round nought where the low knot is, with \emph{vacancy} beside it. The place was a knot before he numbered it. I have left his nought above and my knot underneath, because a figure and a piece of wool have never agreed at the Weir and are not going to begin here.

A woman at the lower boards wrote in charcoal, struck it, and wrote it again below:

\begin{quote}\itshape A knot is not a figure. Ask the wool.\end{quote}

She would not put her name to it. I have not swept the charcoal or put the struck line back.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is reed-ash off the flat stone, where a fire was made of the stalks that would not stand; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The silt in the gutter came up the river on the day the tally was spoiled and is still in the second leaf. The press across the song is wet reed, and goes soft when the weather goes soft. The tar is off the leading rope, from the hand that holds it while the other writes. The eel slime came off a trap set down while its owner counted the boats going up; he did not wipe it and I have not. The white at the wrist-print is salt from a woman who asked what the bundle held and went away with the answer she was given. The ale ring is a boatman’s; he would not drink with cutters and set his cup on the corner all the same. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a Weir.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cord keeps the going. The arm keeps the weight. The river keeps the man who goes down and does not come back.\end{quote}

I asked a woman at the lower boards, the eel-seller below the bridge, and a man come up from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the lining and the rope goes back into the hand. Tomorrow a child will come down at twelve with nothing in the hands, and I shall set him to lifting a bundle before I tell him what a cutter is for, and by dusk the cord will have one more knot tied low with teeth, and the Court may ask the cord if it can.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Three Years, Being the Standing Rules of the College of Assessors in Slate Row for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices in Ledgerhand, with the Weighing Rubrick and the Provost’s Corrections}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Three Years, Being the Standing Rules of the College of Assessors in Slate Row for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices in Ledgerhand, with the Weighing Rubrick and the Provost’s Corrections}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A copyist’s fair copy of the College’s standing articles, kept by the under-clerk who holds the second file; the three years set out in a table, the faults and their corrections in a second, the copying-song pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the Provost’s narrow upright hand, one struck verb in a clerk’s hand, and a line at the foot nobody will own · First gathered in the Hearthseat in Y.H. 776, the year the College built its house in Sill’s own Slate Row, and copied forward from the tin at each Opening of the Slates; this leaf written by the under-clerk of the second file and carried through Y.H. 813. It survives folded inside the second file’s tin, soft at the fold, with slate dust worked into the gutter, a grey collector’s thumb at the head, iron-gall ink in the creases of the copyist’s two fingers, a damp tide-line from the sealed-file room along the foot, a green bead of lead-glaze from a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln, one verb struck in a hand that is not the Provost’s, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the second file. It holds the names taken off the rolls, and I copy them in the same hand as the names that stayed, because a hand that changes between one name and the next is a hand that can be accused of feeling something. The College takes a boy with a name and teaches him to write a life with nobody in it. These are the rules by which that is done. I have set them down as they stand, and where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

The assessors are a guild of a sort, though the word is a clay-country one and is not used in Slate Row. These articles are not new. They were gathered in Y.H. 776, when it was found that a method could be kept longer than any man who used it. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used.

\subsection*{The articles, as they stand in Slate Row}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The College takes an apprentice, not a house. A house may bring a child, or a collector, or the Temple’s poor may be sent, but from the day of entering the child belongs to the College and to no house. He is given no kin. Graduates are given none either, which is the same rule said at the other end.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A child is taken at twelve, or in the year after, and entered for three years. A child taken later is entered for the same three. This is a kindness the College does not advertise and does not enter.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The birth-name is written once on the roll, in a careful hand, and then turned face under. A slate-name is entered in its place. The birth-name is not spoken in the teaching room. A boy who is called by it there writes his slate-name fifty times, and the fifty sheets are burned before he is let back to the copying.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item An apprentice is kept, not hired. He eats from the College’s dish, sleeps in the College’s room, and what he earns goes to the College. The College does not pay him, and does not call him paid. What comes back comes back as bread and a bed, and neither is entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A boy who cannot learn the hand is taken off the rolls and entered in the second file. The file lies in its tin beside the sealed-file room and is not read at the Weighing. His entry is made in the same neat hand as an entry in the rolls, so that no man can tell, by looking at the writing alone, which boy stayed.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a narrow upright hand, the verb struck from rule 4:} The apprentice is kept. \emph{Underneath, in the copyist’s hand:} I had written that he is fed. The Provost’s clerk strikes a verb wherever he finds one, even in a rule about food. I have left \emph{fed} standing under \emph{kept}; a boy can be kept and hungry in the same sentence, and the passive voice has room for both.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the hand}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ledgerhand is Grathic with the verbs removed, written upright and neat, all in the passive voice. The first exercise is to write a true sentence about a man and then take the man out of it. What is left is always true and can be read at the Weighing.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The passive voice is the College’s own. \emph{The measure was drawn} is true of every man who ever drew a measure, and a sentence true of everybody can be argued with by nobody. An apprentice who writes \emph{I drew} is told to write again. An apprentice who writes \emph{he drew} is told twice.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item There are eleven words for a deduction. They are spoken in the teaching room in the second year, by the Provost or the officer he sends, and are not written in these articles. A boy who writes them on a slate copies the page again without them, and the slate is scraped clean in front of him. The words are not a secret. They are a trade.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No apprentice adds a column alone. Addition is done in the Weighing Hall, where figures are read aloud and not inspected. A column added alone will not agree with the notice, and what will not agree with the notice is copied again. An apprentice who needs to add is told that a man who can add is a man who can accuse, and is sent back to the copying.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Provost’s narrow hand, above rule 7:} The passive voice is used. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that it is chosen. A rule with nobody in it is a rule nobody can be thanked for and nobody blamed. I have left my word where he put his above it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The three years}

Year — The exercise — What is taken\par

First — The upright hand; copying notices from the moot-post at the Cross — The boy’s own hand\par

Second — The passive voice; the eleven words, spoken only — The boy’s own name in a sentence\par

Third — The Weighing; the reading of a figure in a clean voice — The boy’s own voice, which he gets back only as the College’s\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the end of the third year the apprentice reads a figure aloud in the Weighing Hall, in a clean voice, with the Hearth-fire behind the grating and no priest or boy allowed to touch it. A reader who puts himself into the sentence is set back. The figure is the one the notice prints: one in twelve, as the notice says. There is no other figure in the room.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A whole return may be announced at the Weighing for a person who is not in the room. The apprentice does not ask where the person is. The College keeps a second file for the answers to questions of that kind, and the second file is not read aloud.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the end of the three years the officer is given no house and no kin and is sent where the College sends him. His slate-name goes on the rolls in the same hand as his betters’. He does not take his birth-name with him, and the College does not take it from him; it is already face down.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — Correction\par

A verb in the roll — The page copied again, in the same hand\par

A column added alone — The slate taken up for a tend\par

A birth-name spoken in the teaching room — Fifty sheets, burned before the boy\par

A figure read with feeling — The reader set back one year\par

A sealed file carried out of the room — The carrier’s own name entered in the second file\par

A slate lost — Paid in kind; a slate is a piece of stone and a name is not\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The College keeps its rolls, its Weighing notices, its sealed files and the only right to write a lawful deduction. It keeps them in the Hearthseat. An apprentice who carries a sealed file beyond the room has his own name carried into the second file instead.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The Vorr sit at the survey table and are not asked to translate. The Deep Hand is copied and not read. These are the College’s enemies, set down here so that an apprentice may know which questions to leave alone.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The copying-song}

\emph{Sung at the benches in the first year, under the breath, while the hand learns the upright stroke. Nobody sings it at the Weighing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ink in the crease of the thumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape slate dust along the sleeve;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape write the man, then take him out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the part believed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the roll and one for the file\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the name turned down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the words go out, the figures stay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house keeps its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven words and none said aloud,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a clean voice for the sum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boy who copies all night long\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is the boy it comes from.\end{quote}

The grey at the head of this leaf came off a collector’s thumb laid there while the song was being copied; he had the colour at his fingers and did not know he had marked it. I have not rubbed it out. The tin is not swept on the Last Day, and the dust stays where it fell.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The Provost’s clerk struck the verb out of rule 7, as he strikes every verb he can find, and set \emph{is used} above my \emph{is chosen}. I have left both. Another hand, narrow and not the Provost’s, struck \emph{the birth-name is turned face under} in rule 3 and set \emph{the writing is turned} above it, as if a name were a piece of writing and not a boy. I have put the name back underneath. A name turned face down is still a name, and a clerk who forgets that is a clerk who will one day find his own in the tin.

The damp along the foot came from the sealed-file room, which is colder than the rest of Slate Row and always has been. The green bead in the fold came off a glaze-mixer come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth; she leaned to see the eleven words and did not ask to read them. I have kept the bead where it fell.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A hand that can write a life without a person in it will write one for anybody.\end{quote}

I have asked the copyists, the Provost’s clerk and a man come down from the Weighing Hall, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the tin beside the names that were taken off the rolls. Tomorrow a boy will be entered at twelve and will learn to take himself out of his own sentences, and by the third year he will read a figure in a voice that nobody can thank and nobody can blame. The figure will stand as read.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Back Place, Being the Setting-Song of the Kiln Throat at Low Kiln, Sung as the Green Pots Go In, with the Rows as They Are Set, the Space at the Back That Is Gone Around with a Look, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss in Green Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Back Place, Being the Setting-Song of the Kiln Throat at Low Kiln, Sung as the Green Pots Go In, with the Rows as They Are Set, the Space at the Back That Is Gone Around with a Look, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss in Green Charcoal, and One Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A setter’s work song of the clay yard in the low half-sung Grathic of Low Kiln, counted in rows of three and the turning of the wrist, said down into the throat and not up into the yard; the rubrics in the setter’s charcoal hand, the clerk’s figures above in Ledgerhand, a glaze-girl’s green gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot nobody has claimed · Set down in Frost of Y.H. 813 by Senna, a woman who sets the pots into the throat of a kiln two doors below the Vail in Low Kiln of Sill and has set them through seventeen firings; written in charcoal thinned with wet slip on the back of a firing-tally spoiled by a thumb through the count, folded into four and tied with grey wool to a nail beside the damper; copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided weigh-slip. It survives with a wet-slip thumb at the head, brick dust in the fold, a wad of clay pressed flat between the second and third leaf, a scorch along the lower edge, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a sherd from the throat, a grey Ash smear along the gutter nobody will own, the clerk’s figures above, the green gloss in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I set the pots into the throat of a kiln two doors below the Vail and have done it through seventeen firings. A man come off the north bridge with a soft cuff and a slate asked a girl at the tubs what was said while the green ware went in, and wrote her answer down before she had finished giving it. What he took away had the doing out of it and a figure standing where a place should be. So I have set the words down as we say them at the mouth and put the verbs back.

A setting-song is not a tune. A tune wants a voice with nothing in its hands, and at the throat every hand is full. We say the words down into the clay, not up into the yard. Said up they grow a melody, and a man in a clean coat can carry the melody away and leave the pots behind him, which has happened twice in my time and both times in the same week.

The wet-slip thumb at the head is mine. I held the tally down on the flagstone with the hand I set with and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How it is set}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Carry the green pots from the racks with the palm under the belly, never by the rim. Green rim comes away in the hand and leaves a cup with no top.

\item One wad of clay under every pot, no bigger than a thumb. The wad is the only promise in this yard that goes all the way through the fire with the thing it was made for.

\item Three to a row and a thumb’s width between. The width is the heat’s road. Too close and the heat cannot pass; too wide and it runs through and the pot comes out with its green note still in it.

\item At the back of the throat there is a place where two go and three would go. Go around it with a look and a wide step. Do not set a third there to make the row come straight, and do not say whose place it is.

\item Say the refrain into the throat. Said to the girl beside you it becomes instruction, and instruction at this kiln is instruction she will unlearn at somebody else’s.

\item Do not set on a morning when the wind comes off High Kiln with the sweet edge on it. A girl who has tasted glaze cannot smell what is in her own mouth, and leans too far over the throat.

\item The count is in the rows and the turning of the wrist. A pot counted is a pot sold, and a pot sold is entered elsewhere, which is not a thing to do while it is still wet.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The last hand to come away from the throat keeps the refrain back until the wad is under the next pot. One line of the refrain to one row set.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Up from the racks with the green pots on the forearm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape palm to the belly, not the rim, or the rim goes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wet clay is a thing that trusts the hand that holds it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes apart in the hand that has only just learned.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A wad of clay under every pot, no bigger than a thumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot sits on it and the wad sits on the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the only promise in this yard that burns,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot either keeps its seat or goes over.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thumb’s width between and no more and no less;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape too close and the heat can’t get by to the far side,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape too wide and it goes through without stopping\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot comes out with its green note still in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At the back there’s a place where two go and three would go,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we go around it with the look and the wide step;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t set a third there to make the row come straight ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a straight row is a thing a clerk can carry away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what we set we don’t count, and what we don’t set we don’t name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A girl come down from the Glaze Room with the sweet at her mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leans over the throat to see the rows standing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t let her lean. The pale line at the gum is the first of it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that sets is the hand that will answer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The last pot in is the one you never see again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clay lid goes on and the mouth is shut with a wad;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what you had in your hands at the bell you have not got now,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire has it, and gives back what it chose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Set it. Leave the space. Let the heat come round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Three to a row, and the back place left as found.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fire takes both and answers to neither.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain, the length of a hand coming away from the last pot. The clerk put a nought in it, which is a thing you can hold up; a hand coming away is not.

\subsection*{The part they do not set while a man from Greybank stands in the yard}

\emph{Said low to the throat and not across the yard. Taken up when the cuff has gone back over the bridge.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three to a row and the back place gone around;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not say whose place it is and the yard does not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, twice over the basket;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire was carried here under a broken pot and answered four pulls\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the fifth missing, and nobody has named whose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The grey goes out of the north gate heaped above the sides\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody in the square looks at it twice, which is the afternoon’s work;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a brine-gull took a coal not yet cold and went upriver with it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no slate in Sill stood one mark the poorer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river keeps a note under the sill and the town sets its clock by it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the kiln keeps a count under the floor, and they were never one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three to a row. The back place stays where it was found.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk may have his nought. It will not keep a pot warm.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the tally on a morning when the weigh-slips were out drying, ink on two fingers that would not come out. He took the verbs out and set his words above mine. I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath, as the throat keeps the pot and the flagstone keeps the wad.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the only promise in this yard that burns}, he wrote \emph{clay seating, consumable; no residue arises}. True in the figure and false at the mouth, where the wad goes all the way.

\item At \emph{three to a row}, he wrote \emph{capacity, three per shelf}, and at the back place, \emph{shortfall, one position}. He has made the place into something owed by somebody; there is no owing in a look.

\item At \emph{the back place left as found}, he wrote \emph{nil}, and drew his line a finger’s breadth past the margin.

\item At \emph{the fire takes both and answers to neither}, he wrote \emph{thermal transfer, unrecorded}. He thinks a transfer entered is a transfer known.

\item At \emph{the count is in the arm that carried}, he wrote \emph{labour, one mark the day; no deduction for injury}. He has put a figure where an arm was.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the glaze-girl put in the margin}

The green belongs to a girl who comes down from the Glaze Room and has the pale line at her gum and will not say when it came. I have copied it as it stands.

At \emph{don’t let her lean}: \emph{I have leaned at nine throats and been told at each of them. The sweet is not in the mouth, it is in the habit. I have never told the next girl.}

At \emph{the pale line at the gum}: \emph{It shows white if you put a lamp to it. We do not put lamps to one another here. We put the tongue to the glaze and go on tasting.}

At \emph{what we don’t set we don’t name}: \emph{There is a name for the back place on this terrace and we do not use it. Words said up there come down on the wind and go over the bridge with a figure on them.}

At the kept-back part: \emph{I asked who the back place belonged to. She said it belonged to the firing, which is an answer you can carry to Greybank and still have in your mouth when you arrive.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wet-slip thumb at the head is mine and has gone into the grain, which is why I sign with it. The brick dust in the fold came off the flagstone and is the only thing here put there by the trade and not by a person. The wad between the second and third leaf was pressed there by a girl to hold the paper in the draught; it has gone hard as a pot that never saw the throat, and is lighter in the hand than one that did. The scorch took two words off the first verse, which I have not written in again, because a song with two words gone is said slowly, and ours are all said slowly. The green bead came off the girl who leaned over with sweetness still at her tongue; she touched the leaf, said nothing and went back up the terrace. I have kept my tongue off it. The sherd between the third and fourth leaf broke at this throat and answers flat when I knock it on the nail, the only thing in the leaf that has been through the fire and come back to tell of it. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a kiln bench; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind a nail. The grey wool ties the leaf to the nail, with a knot for the one line I could not bring up.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wad keeps the seat. The throat keeps the row.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The back place keeps itself, and the slate is read all the same.\end{quote}

I asked the girl at the tubs, the watcher at the damper and a carter under the sill, and had a proverb, a rest and a direction, and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The tally goes back on the nail. There will be firings enough, and I shall set three to a row and go around the back place with a look. If the clerk borrows the leaf he may have his figures. The pots will be where I put them, and the count under the floor will not be made to agree with the note under the stone.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Articles of the Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls at the Birth-Slates, with the Years Set in a Table, the Form of a Birth-Entry, Faults and their Correcting, the Warming-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Articles of the Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Hearth-Maids of Grath for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Girls at the Birth-Slates, with the Years Set in a Table, the Form of a Birth-Entry, Faults and their Correcting, the Warming-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bench-copy of the order’s standing rules in the hand of the maid who keeps the birth-flower shrine’s slate-box in Low Kiln; the articles in the short half-sentences the trade speaks, the years and the faults in tables, the form of a birth-entry left blank, the warming-song pasted to the inside of the cover, two corrections in borrowed hands, a page copied again with two words left out, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · First gathered in Y.H. 782, the year every birth in Grath was made a slate-entry and the Court began to pay the maids who had kept the slates for nothing since any woman could date, and copied forward from the bench and the slate-box rather than from a book; this leaf written at the shrine beside House Reed in Low Kiln in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, carried through the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813, and read to a girl brought up from the tubs with her hands already red. It survives folded in a grey wool birth-cloth among the answered slates; beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the head, fine grey slip from the upper pit at the fold, birth-water gone brown where the leaf was doubled, grey Ash along the gutter off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie, a tallow thumb, a tideline of well-water along the foot, a green bead of lead glaze pressed in by a girl with sweetness still at her mouth, two words eaten clean away and not written in again, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that is nobody’s\par}\medskip
I keep the slate-box at the shrine. A girl is brought to me with red hands from the tubs, and I read her what is below before I let her touch a stone. The trade is learned at the bench and not out of a book. There is no Last Day at a bench; the grey stays where it fell and goes into the next year under a birth-cloth. I have set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

They were first gathered in Y.H. 782, the year a birth in Grath became a slate-entry and the Court began to pay the maids who had kept the slates for nothing since anyone could date. A rule with no thumb on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the bench}
