{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A wet-nurse’s lullaby taken down from her own mouth in the women’s quarter of a great house of the Ten Bowls; the verses in the long-vowelled courtesy speech of Sere, the manner of saying them in the writer’s own charcoal, a bowl-house tally-clerk’s correction set above in his leaning hand, a northern bond-woman’s charcoal pressed underneath, a gloss in myrrh from a woman who has given suck in three houses, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Sung in the third watch of the night in the women’s quarter of a great house in the Bowl of Sere, after the household bowl had gone round at the third hour of the day and the court fires were banked, and set down in Y.H. 812 by a woman of the house who gives suck and had once kept a tally before she was bought; written in charcoal and the dregs of a myrrh phial on the back of a bowl-house linen tally spoiled at one corner, sewn with a thread of grey wool into a fold of oiled silk and kept under the cradle mat. A factor’s clerk carried it north at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied it at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where the lowland name for that year, the Thin Year, was added below the southern one. It survives with a ring of warm wine at the head, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a smear of myrrh across the second leaf, a milky thumb in the gutter that nobody will own, a green bead of lead glaze chipped from a bowl at the third hour, a curl of grey wool from a northern sleeve shut in the sewing, the tally-clerk’s correction standing above, the two charcoal hands standing below, and the line at the foot which has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I give suck in a house that is not mine, to a child whose name I am not permitted to say until the household has chosen it. I have done this for four years. I know the weight of the child on my arm the way a potter knows the weight of a pot before the glaze goes on, and I know the sound the house makes when the bowl goes round at the third hour, which is a sound with a debt in it.

A clerk come up from the factor’s house at Greybank stood in the portico and asked the women what we sang over the cradles. He wrote down the names, because names are what a clerk can carry away. I have set the song down as we say it, with the verbs left where we put them and the space left where the space is.

The ring at the head is wine. I held the leaf down in the draught under the portico and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How it is said}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item In the third watch, after the household bowl has gone round and the fires in the open court are banked for the night. Not at the Bowl feast and not on a name-day; on those days every name in the house is already in the air, and a song said then is a song with a name in it, which is a different thing.

\item Hold the child with its ear to your collar and not to the wall. Said toward a wall, the song becomes an instruction to the house, and there is no room in a great house that has not already been told what it is to do.

\item Set a cup down at the cradle’s head and do not drink from it. It is not the child’s cup and it is not yours. It stands for the one that was poured out in the court and cannot be carried back up the steps.

\item Say the refrain to the bowl and not to the child. Said looking into a face, the second line becomes a question, and there is nobody in this house, including me, who may answer it in the child’s hearing.

\item If a phial of quiet ash stands on the shelf, leave it corked. A voice that cannot arrive is not the same as a voice that has stopped wanting to.

\item Say the last line once. The space before the last refrain is the length of a name and is kept empty. I do not fill it and neither does the child.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low, with the ends of the words let fall the way a drop falls from a dipped cup. The refrain is said to the bowl.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl came down from the open court warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the colour of skimmed milk gone blue at the rim;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the household drank and the act was announced,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody asked who had carried it in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names stand ready above your bed\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house will keep the one it likes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have one name of my own and it is not mine ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I say it to the bowl and not to you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They teach in the court that a vessel was made\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to be emptied in public and praised for the emptying;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have held a cup through the whole of the third hour\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and learned which hand pours and which hand pays.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I had a child with a brown edge to his crust\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a way of turning his head at a cup;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he went to the mills when the term was called,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the voice that called it was clean.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mistress sets a phial of quiet ash by the bed\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape so no voice from a former life will arrive;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have uncorked one and smelled it and set it down ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a voice is a thing a woman can bear to hear.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Sleep, little bowl. The wine keeps warm.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape So sleep. I will not say the seventh name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is not chosen and has no weight in it yet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cup stands full where the hand set it down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the wine keeps warm for the one who will pay.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain. I have left it on the leaf. It is the right length for a name and for nothing else, and the child who cannot yet ask what it is will one day ask and will be told that names are chosen above stairs.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

A bowl-house tally-clerk came into the women’s quarter with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink sitting in two fingers of it that would not come out. He writes in the leaning hand that keeps the glaze-tallies, and he took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a woman could hide in her sleeve and carry past a door.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the wine keeps warm} he wrote \emph{the measure is in circulation; temperature not entered}, and underlined the figure twice.

\item At \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one} he wrote \emph{issue: not entered; relation: contractual}, which leaves the room standing and takes both women out of it.

\item At \emph{the house will keep the one it likes} he set \emph{name assigned by household; no deduction arises}, which is true in the figure and false in the room where I said it.

\item At \emph{a voice is a thing a woman can bear to hear} he wrote \emph{no efficacy recorded} and put a small round nought beside the phial.

\item Where the space stands before the last refrain, he put a nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a number where a name should stand, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child at the third watch does not know it is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand will hold it and which hand will be paid.

\subsection*{What the northern woman wrote underneath}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman bought out of the clay country who keeps her words on the backs of linen tallies and will not let a clerk see them. I have copied them underneath as she set them.

At \emph{I bore a child and it is not this one}: \emph{She has not seen that child in six years. She asked me whether I had, and I said no, and she put the cup down and did not take it up again.}

At \emph{seven names stand ready}: \emph{Where I come from a child has one name and a pot has a crack you can see. Here they give seven and glaze over the crack. I have set both down and joined neither.}

At \emph{the voice that called it was clean}: \emph{A clean voice is a voice with nobody in it. I have heard one. I was on my knees at the time, and I have never been able to say what the words were.}

At \emph{a voice from a former life}: \emph{She says this of the ash, but she has never asked what is in the phial. I have asked, and was told that the poor here dream in other people’s voices and the rich buy not to.}

At the space before the last refrain: \emph{The saying is not for the child. I asked whose it was and she gave me a date, which is an answer with nothing in it to argue with.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine at the head came up out of the paper itself and is the only thing here that entered without a hand. The yellow dust is off the burning winds and has worked into the fold, a southern thing in a book that has been north. The myrrh across the second leaf came from a phial set down while I was telling the child to sleep and it would not; I left the mark where it fell. The milky thumb in the gutter is mine and nobody will own it, which is right, since nobody in this house owns the milk either. The green bead came off a bowl chipped at the third hour when a woman leaned over to see the writing and put her cup down too hard on the rim; it rolled as far as the fold and I have not picked it out. The grey wool in the sewing is off the sleeve of the northern woman, caught when she reached to turn the leaf; she did not see it go and I have not told her. There is no ash left in the corners of a bowl-house to sweep up on a Last Day. They burn the slates instead, and then write new ones before the wine is cold.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl keeps the wine. The house keeps the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mills keep the child. Nobody keeps the account.\end{quote}

I asked the tally-clerk, the northern woman and the woman who carries the bowl down from the court, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back under the cradle mat. Tomorrow the bowl will go round at the third hour and the act will be announced and the women will carry it in and nobody will ask who paid, and at the third watch I shall say the same words into the same space, and a child who cannot yet say them will hear them for the fourth time. If an officer finds the leaf, let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, and will hold the child with its ear to its collar, and will not look into its face while it says the second line.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Bowl Goes Round, Being the Drinking Song of the Women of the Washing-Bench in the House of the Ten Bowls at the Bowl of Sere, with the Order of the Bowls, the Word Under the Glaze, and the Corrections Set Over It}
\CRsheetheading{The Bowl Goes Round, Being the Drinking Song of the Women of the Washing-Bench in the House of the Ten Bowls at the Bowl of Sere, with the Order of the Bowls, the Word Under the Glaze, and the Corrections Set Over It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A washing-woman’s drinking song, taken down from her own mouth at the basin after the court had gone; the verses in the long-vowelled courtesy of the south set down in charcoal, with the ends let fall as they are sung, the order of the bowls in the writer’s own hand, the house tally-clerk’s thin gold standing above, a factor’s clerk’s ruling in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a northern woman’s charcoal in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Grain of Y.H. 812, in the scullery of the House of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, by a woman of the washing-bench whose clay-name is Bowl and whose former name is under the glaze of a bowl she has never been permitted to look into; set down in charcoal on the back of a glaze-tally spoiled by a wet thumb at the third furnace, carried north with a consignment of glass and oil in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant gone soft at one corner. It survives folded in oiled silk in the fold of the washing-cloth, with a ring of warm wine at the head gone the colour of the glaze, a smear of press-oil at the second leaf, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner, a fleck of the tally-clerk’s gold, a grey bead of slate-ash from the feast fire shut into the fold, a pale thumb-print where a woman with the sweet sickness leaned over to read, a thread of wool from a kitchen sleeve, one correction in thin gold, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, a gloss in the charcoal of a bought woman come down from the north, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I am called Bowl. It is the name the house gave me when it bought me, and the name I had before that is written on the inside of a bowl on the lower shelf of the court cupboard, under the lead glaze, where I am not permitted to look. I wash the bowls of the Ten Bowls. That is the whole of my office: to take what the court has emptied, to scour it, and to set it back with the rim turned outward so that nobody sitting at the table can see what is kept under the glaze. There are nine bowls in that rack and I am the tenth, which is a jest the kitchen made once and has never made again.

A woman came south from Greybank with a consignment of glass and asked us at the basin what we sang when the court had gone. She wrote down the first line and went away believing she had learned Sere. I have set down the whole of it, with the ends put back where the court lets them fall, the clerk’s gold left standing above, and my charcoal put back underneath where it belongs. A repaired bowl keeps the old break under the glaze; a corrected leaf keeps the woman under the verb.

The ring at the head is wine. It was warm when I set the tally down and is the colour of the glaze now. I have not washed it out. A bowl that has stood a whole feast and been set down twice is entitled to one stain it did not ask for.

\subsection*{The manner of it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sung at the basin after the court has gone and before the bowls are stacked. Never in the court: a song with no debt in it is a song somebody will try to enter.

\item The bowls are washed in the reverse of the order in which they were emptied, and the song follows the bowls. The first bowl washed is the last that was handed. There is no reason for this and nobody has asked for one.

\item A sip is taken from what the bowl still holds before it goes into the water. This is not a perquisite and is not entered. The woman who drinks is not the woman who washed the bowl, so that no woman drinks her own leavings.

\item Said to the bowl, with the face turned toward the basin. Said looking at another woman it becomes a question, and there is always a woman who will answer it, and then the kitchen has two griefs instead of one.

\item Do not turn a bowl to the light. The word was cut under the glaze before the firing and the fire shut it in, and the glaze has kept it better than this house has kept anything else. A name that is read is a name the court can enter.

\item If a bowl comes up from the court still warm, hold it a moment before the water. That is the only warmth in this house that nobody has bought for us and nobody will enter against us.

\item When the tally-clerk crosses the yard, stop in the middle of a verse and begin again at the same place when he has gone. A song with a figure in it travels; this one does not.

\item The last place is kept the length of a name. Do not put a nought in it. A nought is a number. A name is a vessel.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low, from bowl to bowl, with the ends of the lines let fall into the basin. The refrain is said to the rim after every part.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl went down the length of the court,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape from the high seat to the last stone bench;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape each man named the debt he meant to carry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire applauded when he said it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wine was warm at the first of them\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and had gone the colour of the rim at the last.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It came to us with a finger of wine in it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the smell of a fire we were not asked to smell;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we drink what the court let fall\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the basin keeps what we let fall.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The basin has no column and asks for none.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a word on the inside of the third bowl,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut under the lead before it went to the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire shut it in and the glaze has kept it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape better than this house has kept a promise.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I know the shape of it under my thumb\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and have never once been told the sound of it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A child of this house is given seven names\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and keeps whichever the household likes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bought woman is given one name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one she brought is forbidden.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowls are the only vessels in this court\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape permitted to have kept two.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They burned the slate by lot when the eating was done\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and made a new one out of the same fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the debt went up in the smoke and came down in a clean hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house stood where it had stood before.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody clapped for the bowl that held the wine.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What it held is poured out. What it keeps is under the glaze.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glaze is sweet at the rim and the gum goes pale\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand forgets the cup at the end of it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody asks who paid for the wine,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody asks who paid for the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bowl stands full for the next of the house,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the next of the house is not named.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the bowl. The bowl goes round.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The word on the inside is not read aloud.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The bowl keeps it. The bowl gives none back.}\end{quote}

There is a space between the second line of the last refrain and the third. I have left it on the tally. It is the length of a name and of nothing else, and the women leave it when they sing, though none of them has ever said what stands in it.

\subsection*{What the glaze keeps}

A bowl for the court is glazed inside and out. Before the glaze goes on, a word is cut into the clay with a point fine as a needle, and the glaze runs over it and shuts it in, so that the word is there for the life of the bowl and can be come at only by the thumb or by breaking the bowl. This is done to some of the people the house buys and not to others, and I do not know why it was done to me. The kitchen says it is done to those who were once somebody and might be tempted to remember it. I asked whether the house was afraid of a word and was told the house is not afraid of anything, which is how a house answers a question it does not want entered.

The rule is that a bought woman is never to look into the bowl that carries her former name. It is not written anywhere. It is said at the basin the way a pot is said to be hot, which is information and not an order. The bowls go into the rack with the rims outward, and there is a woman at the end of the bench whose whole work is the turning of them, and who has been at it longer than I have been alive. She has never once turned one the other way. When I scour the inside I keep my eyes on the water and my thumb goes where it goes, and that is the whole of the arrangement.

A girl who washed here before me turned a bowl to the lamp and read the word on the inside. She was not beaten and nothing was entered against her. She was given a new clay-name in the morning, and the old word was scraped out of the bowl with a knife and the place filled again with glaze, so that there is a smooth green patch on the inside where the letters had been. She is at the grain mills now. I have not asked which name she answers to. That bowl is fourth from the left on the middle shelf, and I have washed it every tend since and have never turned it to the light.

I have tried to say the word once, to see whether the sound of it would still be mine. I could not get it out. This is not the same as forgetting. A thing under glaze is not lost to the woman who cannot see it; it is lost to the house that thinks it has covered it over.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk set above}

The tally-clerk of the Ten Bowls came into the scullery with his gold pen and set his hand on my leaf while I was still finding the end of a line. He writes very small, in thin gold, and took the verbs out of four lines, leaving the women standing outside them.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{we drink what the court let fall}, he wrote \emph{the residue of the public bowl is not a discharge of any obligation}. It is true of the wine and does not mention the throat it went down. I have left it.

\item At \emph{the basin has no column and asks for none}, he set \emph{all premises appear in the house inventory}. The basin is not in the inventory. I have put my line back underneath and have not crossed his out.

\item At \emph{I know the shape of it under my thumb}, he wrote \emph{unauthorised handling of house ware is a fault}, and underlined it twice. I was set to wash the bowl. A woman cannot scour the inside of a bowl with her nails.

\item At \emph{the debt went up in the smoke and came down in a clean hand}, he wrote \emph{measure for measure}, which is what a man says in this country when he has already decided what the two measures are.

\item Where I left the space in the last refrain, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{one bowl, current} beside it. A nought is a figure and a bowl is a vessel. The two have never touched, and now they stand on the same line.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back beneath his everywhere, as the word under the glaze lies under the glaze. He strikes the doer out because a thing always true can be carried into a counting room. I put the doer back because a woman at the basin wants to know whose hand let the wine fall, and the answer is in the sentence if there is somebody in it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in charcoal, a northern woman’s hand}

The charcoal belongs to a woman bought down from the low country, who came here with a skill at the press and has never learned to say the south properly. She writes on the backs of spoiled tallies and presses hard at the ends of words.

\begin{quote}\itshape In the low country they break a pot at the door of a death-house so that the heat may get out. Here they wash the bowl and the heat goes down the drain with the wine. Somebody paid in both countries. Nobody asks in either.\end{quote}

And below, in the same hand:

\begin{quote}\itshape I have washed eleven years here and can still count in marks. They gave me a clay-name the first week and I have not said my own since, but I know the number of it, which is a thing no clerk has thought to take.\end{quote}

I have set both where she wrote them. She would not sign them.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine-ring at the head is mine and I have not washed it. The oil at the second leaf is press-oil off the sleeve of the woman who wrote in the margin; it has gone into the grain and will come out with nothing. The green bead in the lower corner is lead glaze, broken off a bowl that went to the rack with a star in it; do not touch the edge, the sweetness is in it and the sweetness is not a kindness. The fleck of gold came off the tally-clerk’s pen when he leaned over me. The grey bead in the fold is ash off the burnt slate of the feast; they burn the debt and then buy the ash back, which is a way of keeping a thing and calling it gone. The pale print is from a girl of the glaze room with the pale line at her gum, who leaned over to read and touched the tally and went back to her work. The thread is grey wool off a kitchen sleeve. There is no Last Day in a scullery and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The court empties the bowl. The basin keeps the dregs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate burns. The name stays under the glaze.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the tenth bowl what debt it intends to carry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and listen to the answer before you applaud.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who turns the rims, the northern woman at the press, and a tally-clerk, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the oiled silk and the silk into the fold of the cloth. Tomorrow the court will empty the bowls in the same order and we shall wash them in the reverse of it, and the third bowl will go back on the lower shelf with its rim turned outward, and the new slate is already in the counting room with a debt in it that nobody at the basin will be asked to carry.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Bowl-Leech’s Book, Being Remedies for the Third-Day Tremor, the Sweet, the Fever That Cooks, the Guest That Wants Another House, the Graft That Will Not Take and the Northern Cold, Set Down in the Bowl of Sere with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Bowl-Leech’s Book, Being Remedies for the Third-Day Tremor, the Sweet, the Fever That Cooks, the Guest That Wants Another House, the Graft That Will Not Take and the Northern Cold, Set Down in the Bowl of Sere with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bowl-leech’s book of remedies in the long-vowelled courtesy of Sere, written in gold ink on the back of a spoiled glaze-tally and folded into oiled silk; the cures in a bowl-leech’s hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed cold into the margin, the corrections of a factor’s clerk in narrow Ledgerhand, a song for the third day with a place left where the seventh name stood, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the Bowl of Sere between Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the year the northern measures came south cheap, by Ilyra Vey, a leech attached to the house of Vey who held the third-day hand through nineteen returns; begun on the back of a glaze-tally spoiled in the pressing of a public bowl, written in gold ink on four leaves of glazed paper gummed into a fold of oiled silk, carried north with the glass in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a discarded rent-roll gone soft. It survives in a dry tin in a room with good light in the Greybank counting house, with gold worked into the creases of the first leaf, a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh rubbed into the grain, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner, a grey bead of public-bowl ash caught in the gutter, a pale crescent of tallow-wasp resin at the foot of the remedies, a line that runs out toward the gutter and stops, a small square where a word was cut away with a knife and not written back, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, corrections in the upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
A woman of this house asked me to set down what I do, and I have set it down in the courtesy we use to people we would not disagree with, which is the same courtesy we use to the returned. I have left the errors standing. A physician come down from Greybank pressed his objections into the margin with a hand that writes cold, and I have put my words beneath his where the two disagree, as a bowl is set under a shelf to catch what the shelf will not hold.

The gold at the head is leaf off the tally. It gets into the creases and stays, so that after a year the Court’s figures and my cures look alike. The ring is warm wine from the public bowl, set down while I told a girl to drink and she would not. The myrrh came off the fold the tablets slept in. I have washed none of it away.

\subsection*{The order of the sick-court}

\emph{Written small in the first leaf, with the word for the guest gone over in wine.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the sick one’s face toward the fire in the middle of the court, not toward the door. A person who faces the fire can be seen by everybody, which is how we know whether they are going.

\item Ask what debt they intend to carry before you ask what ails them. A person who has named a debt will tell you where it hurts. This is not kindness. It is the order of the room.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to a child. I learned it from a northern bought breath who put her hand on a slate, turned it, and would say nothing more. I have done it at forty births and never asked her again.

\item Give the guest a place by the door and no bowl of their own. A guest who is given a bowl will ask when the debt falls due.

\item Do not look into a bowl that has a name written inside it. The house puts a name there that the bowl’s owner may never read, and a leech who looks has taken what the household has not spent.

\end{itemize}

Against the first line the physician wrote, in the cold hand: \emph{A vessel overheated in a cold room loses faster when turned to the fire.} I have set my line above his. Both stand.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is emptied\par

The third-day tremor — A second bowl emptied in the returned one’s name, and applause — It comes on the third day after a beautiful return, when the hand will not hold the cup. We say beauty must be paid for, and pour again. The physician says it is the head rising after too much was poured, and that wine adds to it. I have poured and watched the hand steady for an hour and worse by evening. Both stand. — The household, in wine; the returned one, in another measure.\par

The sweet (the pale line at the gum) — Scrape the green off a bowl into wine; a sweet answers a sweet — The green comes north from the Glaze Cliffs in bowls, and the women here taste the mix for colour. The physician says it is lead in the glaze and that scraping a bowl into wine takes more of it. I have seen the line go off a girl who left the furnaces and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The furnace, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

The fever that cooks from within — Bleed at the elbow, to let the heat out — The Spending says a vessel emptied is a vessel saved. The physician says bleeding lets the measure out and not the fever. I bled four; two were quiet by evening and did not wake. Quiet is not better. I have written it and gone on bleeding. — The patient, in the arm.\par

The guest that wants another house — Seven names spoken at the door; a bowl set where the old bowl stood — She calls a name not given in this house and reaches for a door that is not in the room. We say a returned one has brought a guest, and give the guest the name until it goes. The physician says a spoken name puts no shape back, and he is right as a man who has never held one of these. One went off by the seventh naming; one kept it a year. — Nobody. The house, in a year it cannot spend.\par

A graft that will not take — Tallow-wasp resin at four marks a nest; a donor out of the same house if one can be found — The resin holds the wall until the vessel takes; a nest is four marks in the south and is burnt in Grath. The physician says resin holds a wall but not a want, and a wall from a donor shaped otherwise takes anyway and wants. I have seen it take and want, and never a donor who did not go thin. — The donor, in a head wine will not bring back.\par

The northern cold that stays — A bowl-fire at the belly, warm wine, and work carrying bowls — The bought breath comes south with a foot gone dark inside three turns of wool, is shown at a feast and given small coins, and is then brought to me. The extremity goes first and the heart holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming. The physician says a cold vessel cannot clot and that a foot set to the fire is a road to losing it. I set them to work and have watched toes go, and gone on. — The bought breath, who cannot stop. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

A cut from the public bowl — Wine and myrrh, then a clean fold; never the grey out of the bowl — The priests put cremation ash from the public bowl on a cut, believing a vessel spent is a vessel cleansed. I have found grey under the skin in three such cuts and could not get it out. A family buys its ash back at the price of quiet ash, and a feast can ruin a house. — The cut, in a white line it keeps.\par

The name that will not come — Seven names on a glazed tablet in gold ink, read at the door — After a return the name comes late and then wrong. Gold ink outlasts the name on the tablet, not in the head. The last of the seven goes first; I have left the space where it stood the length a name of that kind wants. — Nobody. The tablet, which keeps what the head cannot.\par

In this house nothing is given. It is emptied out of one vessel into another and called generosity. I will stand behind that sentence and behind no other in the book.

\subsection*{The note under the knuckle}

The bowl-surgeons tap green ware before they set a graft, and a bowl that answers full will take a wall where a flat one will not. The priests tap the public bowl at a feast and say the emptier it is the truer it rings. I have tapped a bowl before wine and after wine, and the note was the same: a sound bowl answers full and a cracked one answers flat. I have not put this to the priests. A leech who corrects a priest at a feast is a leech who will be tending nobody by the next one.

I tapped a returned woman once, gone thin after a third pouring, and put my ear to the little flat I thought I heard. The flat was not in her. I have written it here, where a woman with a slate may read it; saying it in a room with a slate in it is another matter.

\subsection*{On the beautiful return}

They come back calm. The returned one sits in the good light, wants nothing, takes the cup when given and applauds the debt when the bowl is emptied. On the third day the hand begins to shake. The priests call it the price of beauty, and I have called it that for nineteen years. It is a name that lets a household pour the second bowl without asking what the first one took.

I asked the physician what he called it. He said the head rises when too much has been poured, that memory goes before appetite and appetite before the walls, and that calm of that kind is a burn. He wrote it in the margin and went off with a purse, which is the way physicians go. I have set his sentence above mine and left the second bowl standing underneath. A woman at three in the morning does not want a true sentence. She wants a hand to hold the cup, and I have held it.

\subsection*{The song for the third day}

\emph{Sung low, to the returned one and not to the guest. The room says the last line with her. There is a place after it the length of a seventh name, and no singer has yet filled it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven for the names and one for the guest,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gold keeps the word that the head forgets;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the green bowl is sweeter than the wine,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the third-day hand will not hold mine.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Empty the bowl and the debt is named,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house applauds and the fire is the same;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the northern foot goes dark in the wool,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the leech sets the bought breath to work.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the ash and two for the resin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the hand that carries the glass;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the guest comes in by the door uncalled,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name goes out where the gold ink was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sing to the fire, sing to the flat bowl,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the woman the guest would know;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as it can ---\end{quote}

A factor’s clerk put a nought in the place after the last line and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a figure and can be carried out of the room in a cuff. A seventh name is a place and stays where it is.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came down from Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 811 with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the seven names he set \emph{no efficacy}. Against the guest he set \emph{a disorder of the memory, not a visitor}. Against the Spending he wrote, \emph{the measure goes out and the head does not}, which is a true thing in a cold language and of no use whatever to a woman whose sister has come back calm and will not say whose child she is.

He was right about the lead and wrong about the guest. I have left his three sentences above mine, so the next reader can tell which is which.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did}

A clerk of the factor borrowed the leaves at Greybank when the glass was being counted. His ink sits in two fingers of his cuff and the cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He took the verbs out of \emph{we empty the bowl and call a debt forgiven} and wrote \emph{the debt is discharged} above it, as though a thing always true had no need of anybody doing it. Against my column headed \emph{Who is emptied} he wrote \emph{No cost entered}, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Where I had set the donor going thin, he wrote \emph{the account is retained in the nest}, which is the most beautiful sentence I have ever read in a hand that has never held a donor’s arm.

I have put my verbs back underneath his. A clerk can speak without verbs because he is never in the room. A woman on the third day wants to know which hand to hold, and a woman whose term is not out wants to know who paid for the wine.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold at the head is mine, off the tally. The ring of wine is mine, set down while I told a girl to drink and she would not. The myrrh is off the fold the tablets slept in and has gone into the grain, so the second leaf smells of a feast in the middle of a sickness. The green bead in the lower corner was pressed in by a girl of the furnaces with sweetness at one mouth-corner; she would not say which bowl it came from, and I did not ask, for a bowl with a name written inside it is not a bowl a leech looks into. The grey bead in the gutter is public-bowl ash, caught when a woman crossed the court with a cut on her thumb. The pale crescent at the foot of the remedies is tallow-wasp resin off my thumb, setting a wall in the house of Vey; it keeps a little warmth of the nest, warm at dawn and cold by dusk, entered in no account. The line that runs out toward the gutter and stops is mine. The square cut out with a knife is not mine, and I have not written the word back. There is no Last Day in this book: the grey is swept into the public bowl at a feast and called generosity.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl keeps what is poured into it. The slate keeps what is taken out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The guest between them is kept in no house.\end{quote}

I asked the physician, the factor’s clerk and a bought breath who would not look into her own bowl, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tablets go back into the silk and the silk into the tin, and tomorrow a woman will come into the court with a hand that will not hold a cup, and I shall pour the wine and turn the slate face down before I look at the child, because a child is not an account.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Theft of Warmth, the Cold-Iron Brand and the Unclosed Account, Being Title the Sixth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Court’s Room at Slate Row in Sill with the Brand-Clerk’s Margin, the Marks Entered in the Hands of Those Who Wore Them, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Theft of Warmth, the Cold-Iron Brand and the Unclosed Account, Being Title the Sixth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Court’s Room at Slate Row in Sill with the Brand-Clerk’s Margin, the Marks Entered in the Hands of Those Who Wore Them, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the counter of the Court’s room in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the brand-book and hands the irons to the officer; the articles in Ledgerhand, the marks set down beneath them in the hands of the persons who wore them, a table of offences, a form of entry left blank, the ring-song as it is said at the counter, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Sill in the Court’s room in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Sixth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418 and added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year. It survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept in the drawer under the counter where the brand and the clip lie together in a cloth; an Ash thumb at the head, iron filings worked into the gutter, a pale ring of skin-grease at the foot where a branded wrist was laid on the leaf, a tallow thumb beside it, a green bead of lead glaze in the corner, a bare square where a word was scraped away with the point of the clip-key, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the irons.

They lie in the drawer under this counter, the brand and the clip together in a cloth gone grey where the iron touches it. An officer comes in from the yard, I give him whichever the ordinance asks for, and when he has used it I enter the figure. There is a woman will come with a cup in her apron and a neighbour’s warmth in it, or say there is, and a man who will not consent. I set down the ordinance’s figure, and in the margin, in whatever hand the person has, the mark that was left. A brand entered without a man is a brand nobody wore, and that is the kind of entry the Keeping likes best.

The ordinance is Law, and Law is the slate: what is written stands; what is not written did not happen. By that rule a brand has no pain in it and a theft is a figure like any other. I have kept this book eleven years and have never been able to add a mark. I can add the figure.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head, in mine, written very small:} Copied for the counter and from the drawer. The marks are in the hands of those who wore them; I asked nobody to write a word they did not choose. If this is read in the Hearthseat, let it be seen that the ordinance was copied by one hand and the consequences by several.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Sixth, as it stands in the Court’s room}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Sixth: Of the Theft of Warmth, the Cold-Iron Brand and the Unclosed Account. Confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418; added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782, and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the theft}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Theft of warmth is a draw made without a slate. Warm taken from another vessel by tube, by cup, by hand or by standing close, where no slate stands, is a theft. The figure entered is the embers taken, and not the marks the taking left.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a sloping hand I do not know, the letters pressed hard:} I took four embers out of a cup on the bench; the girl was at the tubs. \emph{In mine:} Written by the man before the iron came out; he held the slate while I read it back.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A cup has no standing to complain. Where warmth is taken from a vessel that cannot speak, the house in which it stood is complainant, and the entry is made to the house. The cup is not asked.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A pot cracked through gives a small flat knock when it is set down, and that is the only testimony a vessel here may give. I have not entered the knock. The cup cannot speak, which is convenient for the house and for the Court.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where the warmth taken has been spent, the figure stands against the thief’s own measure and is carried forward. An account is never closed. What is taken is taken; what is owed is owed; what is carried forward is carried forward, and the three are written in the same hand.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item One part in twelve of every measure banked is kept back for the Hearth, as the notice says. The same figure is kept back from a measure entered as a theft, so that the wrong done to a household is booked at the same rate as the right done to the Court.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have no second figure to enter. I heard a figure in the yard that would not agree with the notice; a clerk who enters a figure he cannot show on a slate is looking for another trade. I have not put it beneath this one.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the brand}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Theft punished by a cold iron brand upon the wrist and a deduction from the thief’s own measure. The brand is set by the officer appointed thereunto and in the presence of a slate. The hand that sets is not the hand that holds the book.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a small careful hand:} He set it on the left. Cold: it took the warmth out and gave none back. A pale place the width of my thumb, come up in the crease where my cuff had been. \emph{In mine:} He wrote this before he put his cuff down. I have kept his word and the cuff’s.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The brand is pale and not red. It shows through the winter. It is spoken of as nothing and is not entered as a wound.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have seen a man hold his wrist to the light under the door and rub his cuff down over it while the figure was read, and say it would go in the thaw. That is what my mother said about everything. It is not in the ordinance.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where a second brand is set over a first, the later mark stands and the earlier is not struck out. The figure is carried forward on the same rule.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a hand that shakes at the ends of the lines:} Twice now. The second over the first, the first showing at the edge. They entered the second. I have kept both where they can be seen.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the unclosed account}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Refusal of a lawful collection is the offence called an unclosed account. The vessel is clip-held by the wrist until consent is entered. The clip is cold iron and gives nothing back. The pale ring it leaves is spoken of as nothing and is not entered as a wound.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a woman’s hand, the thumb of the other steadying the slate:} I said no three times. The ring came up where the iron had been. \emph{In mine:} She consented, and the consent was entered by the officer in his own hand, as the ordinance provides. Her three words have no column. I have put them in hers.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Refusal changes no figure. The measure drawn is the measure that stood before the refusal; the account opened is the same account. What refusal adds is a mark.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman asks what her no cost her; I show her the figure, which has not moved, and she looks at the wrist, which has. There is no column for the difference. I have made one here and drawn no figure in it.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where the vessel has no house to consent for it, consent is entered by the hand of the officer. The foundling and the clay-bound are so entered. The hearth-maid lays the birth-slate on the bench before she goes to the child; this house does not say so, and the ordinance does not say so, and it is so.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{IV. Of what the articles leave outside}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The articles reach the wrist and no further. There is no entry for warmth given at a house door, nor for a pot broken at a death-house to let the heat out, nor for a measure left in a body where no officer was called.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Three things I have entered nowhere: a bowl of gruel given at a door; a pot broken at the Bone Orchard; a room I was not called to on the last night of the Long Cold, where somebody lay warm and nobody came. I have no slate for any and will not invent one. Beyond the wrist is kept here, in a hand with no standing at any Weighing.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item An officer of the Keeping has no house and no kin. The account is her family. The brand she sets is not set in anger and is not set in mercy; it is entered.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I asked the officer who came in the Thin Year whether he had a house. He said the account was his family, as the ordinance says, and asked for a string to tie his cuff, the clip having taken the feeling out of two fingers. I gave him one and did not enter it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The table of offences}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Sixth. The middle column is the figure. The last column is mine and has no standing in any court in Sarn.}

Offence — As entered — What the wrist kept — Not entered\par

Theft of warmth from a cup — Embers taken; one in twelve kept back — A pale brand, the width of a thumb — The woman at the tubs\par

Theft of warmth from a person — Figure of the measure; carried forward — A second brand over a first — Whether the person missed it\par

Refusal of a lawful collection — Unclosed account; consent entered — A pale ring showing through the winter — The three words said before consent\par

Quiet ash sold without a licence (as Title Fifth provides) — Figure entered; phial broken — The hand greyed, by the Court’s own iron — The price the seller was paid\par

Warmth given at a house door — Nothing — Nothing — The giving\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The greyed hand and the pale brand come off the same iron and go into the book by different Titles. I have not joined the rows. A clerk who joins them has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The form of entry}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Sixth. Copied with the blanks as they stand. In eleven years I have never had a name for the last line that a household wanted spoken in this room.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the theft of ------- embers of warmth from the vessel of ----------------------, the same taken without a slate; the cold iron brand set upon the wrist by ----------------------, in the presence of a slate; the deduction carried forward to the account of ----------------------; the mark entered in the margin in the hand of ----------------------, who is the hand that wore it and not the hand that took. Entered by ----------------------, who was not there when the warmth went out.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The ring-song}

\emph{Said low at the counter while the cuff comes down, never while the iron is out of the drawer. Never in the yard, never at a Weighing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup keeps a crack and the wrist keeps a ring,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the iron keeps neither, and that is the art;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a figure goes up for the warmth that went out\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a mark goes down for the part.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cold in the morning and pale at the cuff,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the thumb marks the place where the thumb was set;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a no is a word and a ring is a place,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate has a column for neither of those.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They read the figure twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cup cannot answer, the house cannot choose;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I hold the slate while the man writes his row\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and put no figure to what he must lose.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a narrow upright hand, against the last line of the first verse:} One figure entered. \emph{In mine:} Two columns here and he has numbered one. A man who numbers the other has looked at the wrist, which is how I know the College has been reading my margin.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from the Hearthseat with ink in two fingers. He struck \emph{took} out of the first article and set \emph{was taken} above, as though a theft were a thing that happened to nobody, in a room with nobody in it. I have not rubbed him out. I have written \emph{took} underneath in the margin, in the hand of the man who wrote it there himself, where the next person at this counter can see which hand had a wrist in it.

The other hand is a factor’s, leaning and brown at the edges, come up from Greybank with the treaty in its pocket. Against article five it wrote \emph{correction entered} above my \emph{brand set}, the word the ordinance uses when it wants a room to go quiet. I have left both. A correction is done to an account; a brand is done to a man.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash off my own thumb, turning the leaf toward the lamp while the officer read a figure over it; the colour of a corner swept too late, and it will not come out of the creases. The filings in the gutter are iron off the cloth the irons lie in; some comes away whenever the drawer is opened, and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the only mercy this drawer holds. The pale round ring at the foot is skin-grease where a branded wrist was laid while I read the figure back; it is not a figure and cannot be added, and I have not washed it out. The tallow thumb beside it is mine. The green bead is lead glaze from a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, who leaned to see the form of entry and set her hand down instead of asking. The bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with the point of the clip-key and put none in its place; I have not written it back. The tide-line came from the Waiting Room, where the collected are kept overnight before banking. There is no Last Day at this counter, and nothing here is swept up and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape They can add the ember. They cannot add the ring.\end{quote}

I asked the officer, a man come down from the College, and a woman who stood here about her wrist, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back into the drawer and the irons into their cloth. Tomorrow a woman will come with a cup in her apron, or say there is, and a man who will not consent, and I shall hand out the iron the ordinance asks for and enter the figure, and ask the person whose wrist it was to write the mark in whatever hand they have. They can add the figure. They cannot add the other thing. That is why I keep a second column, and why nobody has asked to see it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Browned Crust, Being the Prayer of the Return as the Bread-Women of Low Kiln Keep It on the Last Day}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Browned Crust, Being the Prayer of the Return as the Bread-Women of Low Kiln Keep It on the Last Day}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bread-woman’s litany of the Return, said over the Last Day loaves before the bread is cut and while the grey is still lying in the corners; the rubrics in the hand that mixed the dough, the stations in the words they are spoken in, the answer given by the room, a clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand set above the verbs, a woman’s note written in charcoal and flour, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written on the Last Day of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a bakehouse in Low Kiln below the sill of Sill, on the back of a flour-tally spoiled by a wet thumb; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the inside leaf of the meal-box in which the bread is kept warm in Stone. It survives folded in oiled sacking under the loaf shelf, with a bone-pale flour thumb at the head, a browned crumb pressed into the fold, a scorch where the oven mouth took the upper corner, a ridge of grey Ash along the gutter from a corner that was not swept, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl come down from the Cross, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, a thread of grey wool from a cradle blanket, a damp from the dough bench, a bare square where a word was scraped away, one correction in a borrowed hand, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I bake the Last Day bread in a bakehouse below the sill. There is no grate between me and the oven and no priest between me and the dough, and if I singe the hair off my hand it is my hand and not the house’s account. I mix before light, four loaves to the four corners of the hearth and a fifth that is set nowhere, and the women come in from the yards with wet cuffs and stand where there is room.

They asked me for a saying they could keep with flour on their hands. A woman who has lost a person here does not want a figure and does not want an argument; both can stand a sentence said to a loaf. We have said it on the Last Day since the Long Cold, when three went into the measure in this street and one came back to a table, and that one would eat nothing but the crust.

What follows is the leaf, including the parts a clerk would take out. I have set his hand above mine and my words underneath, as the crust keeps the fire under the brown.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Bake before light and say the stations while the loaves are still closed up in the warmth of the mixing bench. Once the bread is cut it is somebody’s dinner, and a saying over a man’s dinner is a blessing, which is another trade.

\item Say it to the dough, the peel or the oven mouth. Said looking at a woman it becomes a question, and there is always a woman who will answer it, and then the room has two griefs instead of one.

\item Break a loaf at the brown edge, never through the crumb. The crust stood in the fire. The crumb was carried over it.

\item Give the browned crust to the child. It is the part we can give without asking where the rest of the loaf went.

\item Leave the ridge of grey along the skirting board. On this one morning it is the only thing in the room that has been where the person was, and nobody sweeps a witness into a fire before it has been spoken to.

\item Four loaves to the four corners and a fifth place at the end of the bench. Do not set a loaf there and do not call it empty. A place at a bench is not a vacancy; a bench has no column.

\item When the bell comes up from the Cross, stop. It goes four, four and a gap, and the gap is not in this room. Begin again after and do not fill it with a word of ours.

\item If a man from Greybank comes with a slate, give him the flour-tally and not the leaf. The tally is a document and the flour has a figure. The leaf is a saying and has none.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{One woman reads from the tally. The room answers. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not an argument.}

\subsection*{I. Of the grain}

\begin{quote}\itshape The field was before the bakehouse and will be after it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone goes round and the grist comes out of it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with no hands in the figure and no name on the sack.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We wet what was ground and cover it and wait.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The waiting is not the work.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{II. Of the rising}

\begin{quote}\itshape Flour alone is a white dust and water alone is a river.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Put them together in a covered bowl and the bowl swells\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way a house swells in winter with everybody in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not lift the cloth to see. A thing looked at too early\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape goes down in the middle.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the reader lays her hand on the cloth over the bowl and does not lift it.}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{III. Of the firing}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was fired whole and the lid lifted in one anger.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The warm went out where no wall held it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and ran into the country that keeps nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The crack has a name. Say it once to the oven mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and do not go looking for it in the floor of your own house.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{IV. Of the oven}

\begin{quote}\itshape In Stone we keep the bread in a warmed box\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and in the Five we light the year from the year before.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire in this oven has never been asked who pays for it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the only courtesy we have shown it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the peel steady. A loaf put in crooked comes out crooked\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and is eaten anyway, as crooked things are in this street.\end{quote}

\emph{The loaves go in. Nobody speaks while the oven mouth is open.}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{V. Of the crust}

\begin{quote}\itshape Give the browned edge to the child and keep the crumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The crust took the fire and the crumb was carried over it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two gifts, and we have learned to give only one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A child come back who wants the crust before the breast\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is not asking for his former name. He is asking for the brown.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Give it to him. He will not know why, and neither do we.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the loaves come out. The first crust is broken off and held a moment in the reader’s fingers.}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{VI. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says. Read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for them that came up the road late.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure read over the basket and the figure paid out of the house\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape are two loaves set down side by side; nobody here has made them agree.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The other figure is left in the dough,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where it goes soft in winter and comes back in the thaw.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the reader touches the tally. The other figure is not written on the leaf and has never been entered where a woman can ask about it.}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{VII. Of the grey}

\begin{quote}\itshape The grey lies along the skirting board where a promise stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We leave it on the Last Day and burn it in the morning\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and say it is dealt with, which is what people say\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape when they have no other word for an end.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the name into the corner before the morning comes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name said into the corner stays where the person sat.\end{quote}

\emph{The reader turns toward the corner and does not sweep it. The ridge there is the width of a finger, the colour of the road after rain.}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{VIII. Of the coming back}

\begin{quote}\itshape Break at the brown edge and not through the crumb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The part that took the fire goes first to the child.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the name once for the house and once for the one\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape who stood at the end of the bench and was not given a place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If you have no name, leave the length of one on the bench\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and pass the crust along it to whoever is sitting there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The loaf is made for this. The warm was here before the counting.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the leaf leaves a space the length of a small loaf. It is not a loaf forgotten. It is the fifth place, which this bench keeps and the oven keeps and nobody cuts.}

\emph{Answer:} Break the loaf. Pass the crust. The warm goes round.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s office come up from Greybank borrowed the leaf while the flour was being weighed. He writes in the narrow upright hand they teach in the College and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a woman could hide in her sleeve. He laid his hand on the leaf before he looked at me, which is the manner of that office.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the warm goes round}, he wrote \emph{the measure is in circulation} above, underlined twice. Underneath, in mine: \emph{That is the account of a loaf going from one hand to another. I have watched it go. I have never seen the figure carry it.} Both stand.

\item At \emph{give the browned edge to the child}, he wrote \emph{transfer: no value entered}. It is true in the figure. The green bead left on the leaf came off a girl from the Cross who leaned to see what he had written and put her thumb down instead of asking. She was not entered either.

\item At \emph{a thing looked at too early goes down in the middle}, he set \emph{not a stable condition of a vessel} above, in the hand that has never stood at a mixing bench in a cold room. He has entered the dough and left the woman who covered it outside the sentence.

\item At the space the length of a small loaf he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. A nought is a number and a bench has no column. I have left his nought in the space and my space standing around it, as a crack shows under a keying.

\item At the close he wrote \emph{return recorded, one entry} against the four loaves and the fifth place, a true thing in a language nobody here speaks. The four went home with four households and the fifth went nowhere, and both are entered the same.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing, his hand above mine and mine underneath, as the brown keeps the fire. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman with flour to her elbow wants to know which hand broke the loaf and which passed it.

\subsection*{What a woman put in the margin}

The charcoal is thick and slips at the \emph{th}, being letters learned off a tally and not off a book. A woman of the low yard whose boy came back quiet in the Thin Year came in after the loaves were cut and read what I had written, standing where I could not see her face.

At V: “He put his mouth to the crust before his eyes found me. I had been told he would not know me. He knew the brown. I have not told the clerk which of the three he was.”

At VI: “They read their figure twice over the basket. I was at the basket. It went down the same road I walked home and came to my door before I did.”

At VII: “I did not say his name into the corner that year. I said it into the dough because the dough was warm and the corner was not. If that was the wrong place I should like somebody to tell me the right one.”

At the answer: “Say it for the ones that come back and want the brown. I do not say it for the ones that went in. A refrain will not bring them up out of the measure.”

Then, underneath and very small: “I have baked for them every Last Day since. That is not the same as having them at the table.”

I have left both lines standing. A bakehouse that scores itself will soon be a counting room, and I have seen how those rooms go.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The flour at the head is mine and dries bone-pale, the colour of a potter’s forearms at the end of a day in the pits; it is how this bakehouse signs anything it has touched. The crumb in the fold came off the first loaf of the Thin Year and has gone hard and will not crumble further, which is more than can be said for the loaf it came from. The scorch is where the oven mouth took the corner while I held the leaf near to read; the fire took the corner and not the word. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had been in a corner where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it and nobody will own it. The green is not ours; bread takes no glaze. A girl with the sweetness still at her mouth leaned to see the stations and touched the leaf. The tallow is off the lamp I keep low so the women at the bench will not know I am writing down what they say and change their words. The grey wool came off a cradle blanket and goes on coming off, though I have shaken the leaf four times. The damp is from the mixing bench, which takes the water out of everything left on it overnight. The square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with the back of the peel before I knew what I had written. I have not put it back or forgotten it. There is no Last Day for a bakehouse. The corners are swept here on the morning after and what is found in them is burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not the woman’s, struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The oven gives back the brown and keeps the rest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cradle gives back the shape and keeps the rest.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, the woman of the low yard, the girl from the Cross and a man with a sack of grist, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the sacking and under the loaf shelf. Next Last Day the four loaves will be set to the four corners before light and the fifth place left at the end of the bench; the clerk will come up from Greybank with his soft cuff and take the verbs out, and I shall put them back. Some child in this street will put his mouth to the brown before his eyes find anybody, and no figure in any book will tell his mother why. The bench stays where it stands. The bread goes on being made.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Carried Forward, Being a Page from the Roll of the Dead in the Bank at the Hearthseat, with the Measures Pressed into Newborn Vessels, the Figures Unspent, and the Line Which Is Never Closed}
\CRsheetheading{The Carried Forward, Being a Page from the Roll of the Dead in the Bank at the Hearthseat, with the Measures Pressed into Newborn Vessels, the Figures Unspent, and the Line Which Is Never Closed}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the bank’s own roll, kept under the counter by the clerk who writes the dead; figures in Ledgerhand set from the district slates, the remarks in the hand that carries a name forward, two corrections in borrowed hands, a column struck by the College and drawn back, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the bank at the Hearthseat on the Keel in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, through the Five and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept under the counter in a board cover and taken down when a figure is disputed or a kinsman comes to close an account, which no kinsman has yet done. It survives as two leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with an iron-gall thumb at the head, slate dust worked into the gutter, a tallow print from the lamp, a pressed grey Ash print from a district bundle laid on the counter, a small square of bare paper where a name was scraped away, a corner gone soft from the cold of the sealed-file room, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I write the dead into this book. The bank stands on the Keel, over the Hearth, and the room is warm in a way that has nothing in it of kindness; a man comes in off the road with a figure in his mouth, and the figure is entered, and his name is carried forward. There is no closing column. A clerk come down from the College asked me last tend where the closed accounts were kept. I showed him the empty shelf. He wrote \emph{no dispositions recorded} in his own book and went back up the road, which was true and cost him nothing.

There is a thing about this bank a clerk gets used to and never gets used to. A measure drawn in a district is pressed here into a newborn vessel, and the figure that stood in the dead man’s row comes out in the living one with no mark between to say it travelled. I enter both. I do not enter what it is that travels. A clerk who writes that down is writing a prayer, and prayers are copied by hands that do not sign them.

The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, made by holding a quire open through a market morning. It will not come out of the creases, which is how the Steward knows I have copied a thing before he asks me for it. What follows is one leaf of the roll, from the last tend of Stone through the Five and into the first tend of Ilmen.

\subsection*{The rates of this bank}

Entry — As the bank has it\par

Copper bit — twelve to a silver mark\par

Silver mark — twenty to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not stay in Grath\par

Ember — five marks, by the Court’s book; no man has exchanged one for the other\par

Newborn vessel — twelve to fifteen embers\par

Labourer in good case — forty to sixty embers\par

One of the Kept — three hundred; fewer than twenty in the rooms near the fire\par

Deduction — one in twelve, as the notice says\par
