Whole return — one measure poured into one vessel, booked at the figure\par

Thin return — many measures pooled and divided, figure entered by lot\par

Dead vessel — carried forward; never closed\par

An ember is five marks in this room. In the districts a woman trades six eels for five marks or five for six and makes nothing of it, which is a fact about eels and not about embers. I have set both and joined neither.

\subsection*{The leaf, as it stands}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand, set from the district slates. The remarks are mine, in the hand that carries the name forward, and are not part of the account. The last column has no heading; a heading would make it an account.}

Vessel, as the roll has it — Last measure — Deduction — Return — Pressed into — Carried forward — Remark\par

A widow of Low Kiln. \emph{Loaf} — 33 — 1 in 12 — — — A vessel born in Sill, Reed — yes — Figure read 41 at the last market; this is the district’s later figure. House roll kept close.\par

A clay-bound hand, the terraces — 44 — 1 in 12 — thin — A vessel of the Weir — yes — Six years entered. The seventh not. Still owing when the vessel went.\par

A girl of the Glaze Room, High Kiln — 38 — 1 in 12 — thin — A vessel of Mud End — yes — Pale line at the gum. The name given was not the name on the roll. Entered as given.\par

A child three days returned, Low Kiln — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — — — none — yes — Entered as a birth and a worsening in the same tend. Both figures stand.\par

A man of the Weir — 52 — 1 in 12 — thin — A vessel born below the sill — yes — Drawn before light. The eels went on being sold over the top of the morning.\par

Forty of Low Kiln. One line for the batch, by lot — — — 1 in 12 — whole — Forty vessels, districts not entered — yes — Birth-names not taken. Carried as forty, not as forty names.\par

A vessel returned three times — 29 — 1 in 12 — whole — A vessel of the terraces — yes — Smaller each time. No note made of why the figure went down.\par

A man of Low Kiln, uncollected in the Long Cold — — — — — — — — — yes — No tube came. The figure is the district’s own and is not ours. Carried with the rest.\par

One of the Kept, in passing — 300 — none — none — none — struck — Not dead. Entered in error. I have left the row and the striking both standing.\par

Draws booked on this leaf: eight. Rows struck: one. Columns struck by the College: one. Accounts closed: none, and none sought.

\subsection*{On the carrying forward}

An account is never closed. It is carried forward. The College has eleven words for a deduction and none for a carrying, which is why its clerk puts a nought in the last column and calls the roll balanced. A nought is a figure. The dead are not a figure that has become nothing, though the column is tidier with it, and a tidier column is what the College sends a man down for.

The batch of forty is the row he counts longest. He counts it once at the door and again at the foot before he strikes it, and I know he has looked because a man does not strike what he has not looked at. When he wrote \emph{nil} against it I asked him what had been done with the forty, and he said a disposition had not been recorded, which is a true thing to say about a room with an empty shelf. He was not unkind. He had a cuff gone soft from washing and ink on two fingers, and he went down the Hearth Road before I had put the verbs back.

The column I keep with no heading holds the vessel born. I set the district and the tend and no name, because a name in that column would let a kinsman walk from a cradle to a coffin with one figure in his hand, and there is no road in Sarn a man should walk with that figure. The College has struck the column twice in four years. It is still here.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The College clerk struck \emph{carried forward} wherever it stood and set \emph{was transferred} above, as though a man could be moved from one column to another by a verbless sentence. Against the widow’s row he set a nought where the district’s figure stood and wrote \emph{nothing further arises}. At the head of the last column he wrote \emph{No such column}. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words above it.

The other hand is tall and leaning and comes from the Steward’s room. Against the batch of forty it wrote \emph{the purchaser is not entered here}, which is true, and against the newborn \emph{vessel not on the roll}, which is also true, in the same ink that enters whole returns for persons not in the room. I have not contested either. A hand that writes whole returns knows the difference between a person in a room and a person spoken of in one, and has made a trade of not saying which.

\subsection*{The verse at the counter}

\emph{Said low at the turning of a tend, while the leaf is carried from the counter to the shelf. It is not sung at the Weighing and has never been read aloud in the Weighing Hall.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the drawing and two for the pressing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand that sets the figure down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape carry it, carry it, into the new year,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate keeps the number and the cradle the heat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve for the fire, the rest for the vessel,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody enters what it cost to keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three on the roll and a fourth in the gutter\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the clerk’s nought went when the damp took it.\end{quote}

The second verse is not old. It came in with the Thin Year and I have heard it said twice, both times by men who would not say it while the Steward’s clerk stood at the door. I have copied it as it came.

\subsection*{In the margins}

The slate dust in the gutter came off a district slate laid on this counter while a collector come up from the Ferr told me a figure in a voice that had been talking all morning. The tallow print is mine, from holding the lamp low over a row when somebody behind me was saying something I wanted the end of. The grey print at the foot came off a bundle set down where no bundle should lie, from a house three districts away that had wrapped its dead in a cloth and carried them to the road; the Ash came through the cloth and took the shape of a thumb, and I have not swept it. The small square of bare paper is where I scraped a name away with a knife and put no other in its place. It is the only name I have taken out of this book and I have not forgotten the length of it. The corner gone soft is from the sealed-file room, which is colder than the rest of the Hearthseat and always has been; the leaves take the damp when they lie against that wall, and the ink goes first where the figures are.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The roll keeps the figure. The cradle keeps the warmth. Nobody enters the road between.\end{quote}

I asked the College clerk, a man from the Steward’s room and a woman who came to ask after a vessel of Low Kiln, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back under the counter. On the Remembering a clean voice will read whole returns for persons not in the room, and the names of the dead will be spoken, and the roll will be carried forward one more tend with no disposition recorded. A kinsman may come in the morning to close an account. He has never come yet. The shelf is empty and the bank is warm, and the warmth is booked in a hand that will not sign it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Chamber Found Warm, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Hearth Concerning the Lighting, the First Returns, the Three Offices, the Fixing of the Deduction and the Four Sealed Wells; with the Line as the Copyists Smoothed It, the Kindling Verse, and Two Hands of Correction}
\CRsheetheading{The Chamber Found Warm, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Hearth Concerning the Lighting, the First Returns, the Three Offices, the Fixing of the Deduction and the Four Sealed Wells; with the Line as the Copyists Smoothed It, the Kindling Verse, and Two Hands of Correction}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A Hearthseat annalist’s extract from the low chronicle kept in the Weighing Hall, being the first hundred and twenty years after the lighting; the year-entries in a small close clerk’s hand, the line of the lighting in four successive copies set side by side, the offices entered in the order they were founded, the deduction set out against the notice that carries it, the kindling verse taken down from the keepers at the grating, one struck word restored from underneath, and two corrections in borrowed hands · Written in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Senn, a keeper of the low roll in the Weighing Hall of the Hearthseat, who signs with his name and not with the office, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. Copied from the low chronicle begun in the roll-room in Y.H. 120 and carried forward at each Opening since; the original is kept in the lower drawer beneath the fire-tongs and shown to no one below the rank of keeper. It survives as eight leaves of the thin ruled roll-paper sewn with iron wire into a slate-coloured board cover, soft at the fold: slate dust worked into the gutter, a coal pressed into the wax of the sewing by a keeper who had no business pressing it, a scorch along the third leaf where it lay against the grating, a tallow thumb at the head, a flake of cold-iron scale in the lower margin, grey Ash in the crease of the fourth leaf which no keeper sweeps during the Five, one word struck through and restored from underneath in the writer’s own hand, a correction in the narrow upright hand of the College and one in a temple hand that writes without verbs, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the low chronicle in the Weighing Hall, in the drawer beneath the fire-tongs, where the paper takes the warm off the grating and goes soft at the fold. It is not the book the steward’s clerk carries under his arm, nor the clean roll the factor reads from at the Weighing. Those books have had somebody taken out of them. This one has not, which is why it is kept where a man must kneel to reach it.

I sign with my name, Senn, and not with the office, because a name can be called to account and an office cannot. The roll-room would prefer the office. I have written the name at the head of every copy since I took the drawer, and at the foot of this extract, and in neither place has anybody corrected me, which I take to mean that nobody has read the foot.

This extract is the first hundred and twenty years. The temple calls them the mercy. The roll-room calls them the lighting. The low chronicle, which is older than either name, calls them the years in which the chamber was found. \emph{Found.} I have kept the word. A man who writes \emph{lit} in place of \emph{found} has put a hand into the story that was never there, and in this country a hand is never harmless.

\subsection*{The line, and the four times it was written}

\emph{The four copies stand on one leaf in the order they were made. I have not cleaned the earlier ones off. A line that has been copied four times is a line that somebody wanted changed.}

Copy — Hand — What the leaf says\par

First — a hard hand, not Court, every verb standing — The chamber was found already warm.\par

Second — an early roll hand, the word pressed small and close — The chamber was found warm.\par

Third — a tidy College hand, the finder gone out of it — The chamber was warm when we came to it.\par

Fourth — the clean hand now read at the Weighing — The Hearth was lit in the first year by the Nine Who Kept.\par

The first has a man in it. The second has lost a word. The third has lost the finder. The fourth has lost the finding. The temple tells the children that the Nine Who Kept lit the Hearth with a coal brought out of the first fire, and the children grow up and repeat it, and the clean hand reads it at the Weighing, and the chamber keeps its warmth and says nothing about how it came by it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College, against the first copy:} An account of a tradition, not an entry. Enter as the lighting. Strike \emph{already}.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left \emph{already} standing. It is the whole of the first copy. A chamber found warm is a report; a chamber found \emph{already} warm is a report made by a man who had expected it cold, and had gone in with a tool to see.\end{quote}

I asked a keeper of the grating why the copies had grown smoother. He said a thing copied often enough becomes true, which is not an answer and is the belief of the building. I have set it above the table and not beneath it, so that a reader knows which of us said it.

\subsection*{The years as the low roll has them}

\emph{Copied out of the drawer leaf by leaf. The Court hand stands above; mine stands beneath. Where they agree I have said nothing.}

\textbf{Y.H. 1.} The chamber was found already warm. No ember entered, no figure, no name of a finder. A coal was taken up at the grating, carried out of the hall, and brought back before the tend was out; the roll does not say why, and I have not asked the grating.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Court hand:} The Hearth kindled by the Nine. Strike \emph{found}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 3.} The first Returns recorded: six measures drawn whole and pressed into six newborn vessels, with the names entered before any face was looked at. This is the year the roll begins to have something in it worth counting.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Court hand:} Six whole returns recorded. Strike \emph{before any face was looked at}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 9.} Three offices set in the Hearthseat: assessors to value a life, collectors to draw the measure, bankers to press it into a vessel. Entered in the low chronicle as \emph{three clerks and a table}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Court hand:} The offices of the Keeping established. Strike \emph{table}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 40.} The deduction fixed at one part in twelve and printed upon the Weighing notices. The figure has not moved in seven hundred and seventy-two years.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Court hand:} The deduction fixed at one in twelve throughout the bowl. Entered and confirmed.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 62.} Four of the Nine Wells sealed in the Keel and the keys hung in the steward’s room. Entered as \emph{four sealed, the keys kept}. No reason given on either side. A fifth was sealed in Y.H. 618 and is written in another book; the low chronicle does not follow it, being a record of the beginning and not of the middle.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Court hand:} Four springs reserved to the Hearth. Strike \emph{sealed}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 88.} The first bank opened in the Hearthseat, the second at Greybank. Greybank keeps a Court’s hours and speaks a Court’s voice, and the clay towns have never quite forgiven it for either.

\textbf{Y.H. 120.} Here the chronicle begins. The hand changes. What stands before was copied out of a book with no cover and no first leaf; what follows was entered in the year it happened, by men who were there. I have kept the change of hand. It is the only honest thing in these years.

The cost of those first whole returns was paid by a province. The roll has a line of figures for it and then a line of squares, and I have copied the squares as squares, which is a thing no clerk of this building does twice. The province has a name in the temple and no name in the roll. What I know of it I have set in another extract and will not repeat here; a chronicler who says the same thing in two books has written a sermon, and a sermon in this country is always copied more often than an account.

\subsection*{The three offices, as the keepers speak of them}

The assessor asks what a life was worth. The collector draws it. The banker presses it into the next vessel that opens its mouth. The order matters: a man must be valued before he is drawn, and drawn before he is spent, or the account will not balance and somebody will be made to stand at the Weighing until it does.

There is a saying among the keepers at the grating, said into the iron and not at a person: \emph{The assessor counts, the collector takes, the banker gives, and the Hearth is thanked for all three.} I asked whether the Hearth gave anything back. The keeper said that was a question for the temple, and went on polishing the bars. He had the answer and had put it where I could not reach it, which is the usual way of answers in this building.

\subsection*{The figure on the notice}

One in twelve. It is printed large on the Weighing notices and read aloud at the Weighing in a voice that does not hurry, and a household goes home believing it has paid one in twelve because it heard one in twelve and the slate was in front of it. The tube does not read the notice. A printed figure is a promise and a drawn figure is a fact, and the two have never been introduced to one another.

I have heard another figure spoken in the yards of the clay country when the slate is put away. It is not on any notice and has never been entered in this hall. I have left it out of the years and put it here in the margin, where a figure can be kept without being made a promise. If it is true, it has been true a long time and has managed very well without me.

\subsection*{The four sealed Wells}

Four springs in the Keel give back more than they take, and the Court sealed four and kept the keys, which is a strange thing to do with a source and a reasonable thing to do with a key. The keepers say the Wells were sealed to keep the Warm in. A surveyor come up from Keld and drunk enough to speak said they were sealed to keep the amount of it a secret, and then turned his slate face down. I have set both sayings here. One of them has a key in it and one does not, and I have no way of weighing a key.

\subsection*{The kindling verse}

\emph{Sung by the keepers at the grating on Kindling, before the year-fire is carried out. It is not a prayer; the litany belongs to the Weighing, and the keepers do not sing it. I took it down from a junior who sang the first two lines and would not sing the third while I had a slate out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape We found it warm and left it so,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and counted what the flame would keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the first fire came from no first fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the coal came back to sleep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four wells are shut and four keys hung,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ninth runs where no key is kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the assessor writes, the collector draws,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Hearth is thanked as if it slept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The line grows smooth the more ‘tis said;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I keep the rough one where it lay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the chamber, not the coal,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape how warmth came in and stayed.\end{quote}

He said the third line was not a verse but a thing a keeper once wrote in the margin of a book, and had been sung ever since because men will sing what they are afraid to say. I have left it where I found it, in the middle, where a clerk correcting the leaves is least likely to put his hand.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

Two hands have been at this extract besides mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The College hand, narrow and upright, takes the verbs out. Where I wrote \emph{the chamber was found already warm}, it set \emph{the lighting is recorded in the first year}. Where I wrote \emph{a keeper pressed a coal into the wax}, it set \emph{a coal was pressed into the binding}. A verb with nobody in it is a verb that cannot be argued with, which is why they take them out. I have put mine back underneath and left theirs standing above, as the first copy stands under the fourth.

\item A temple hand, softer and rounder, wrote \emph{were gathered into the Hearth} across the line about the first Returns. It did not strike anything. It wrote across, which is a gentler way of taking a sentence away and a harder one to argue with, because the old words can still be read if a man is willing to lean over them and put a thumb on the leaf. I have left the thumb-print where it fell.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slate dust in the gutter has been there since the drawer was a drawer. The coal pressed into the wax of the sewing was put there by a keeper who had come off the grating with a coal in his fingers and had nowhere clean to set it; it is not part of the binding and never was. The scorch along the third leaf is where the leaf lay against the grating before I took the drawer, and it has not grown and will not go. The tallow at the head is mine; I turn the leaves by the light of a tallow end and have never managed to hold the book and the light with two hands. The flake of cold-iron scale in the lower margin came off the bars when a keeper struck one to show me where the fire comes up, and I kept it rather than ask him to strike another. The grey in the crease of the fourth leaf is Ash, and no keeper sweeps it during the Five, and no keeper has ever said why. The word struck through in the year-entries is mine: I wrote \emph{taken} where the Court hand had \emph{drawn}, and set \emph{drawn} above, because the book holds what was entered. What the tube did is in the verb underneath, where the College hand does not reach.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The line grew smooth and the smooth line stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rough one stays where the coal was pressed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four keys in a room and a fifth elsewhere,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a figure on paper the tube never reads.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the chamber. It has not forgotten.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It was warm before we came.\end{quote}

I asked a keeper of the grating, a clerk of the College, and a surveyor up from Keld who would not give his name, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the drawer under the fire-tongs. At the Opening of the Slates I copy them forward and put the four copies in again with my own hand, in the order they were made, so that the smooth one never sits alone on the leaf. The chronicle goes on. Next tend I copy the Weighing figures from the clean roll, and I shall put the verbs back there too, and set them under the Court’s hand, where a man must kneel to read them.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Clay-Yard Book of Remedies, Being What a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln Sets to the Second Chill, the Sweet Sickness, the Kiln-Burn, the Cord That Will Not Fall and the Cold That Stays, Written Down in Grathic with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Clay-Yard Book of Remedies, Being What a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln Sets to the Second Chill, the Sweet Sickness, the Kiln-Burn, the Cord That Will Not Fall and the Cold That Stays, Written Down in Grathic with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A midwife’s and healer’s book of remedies in the Grathic clay-yard manner, the cures in a hearth-maid’s hand with the verbs left in, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed in the margin, the corrections of a College clerk in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Low Kiln in Sill between Ash of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Hedda of the Clay Yard, a hearth-maid who caught children in the slip pits and laid out the dead of the kiln terraces for twenty-six years; begun on the back of a glaze-house tally spoiled by a fall of slip, folded into four and carried in the breast of her apron against a square of birth-cloth washed so often there is no birth left in it, and copied at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a rent-roll gone soft. It survives with a thumb of tallow at the head, grey Ash worked into the gutter, brick dust ground into the fold, a wet smear of slip that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a ring of barley-water, a scorch where a spark off the kiln caught the corner, a long hair the colour of wet wool caught in the seam, objections in the hand of a Greybank physician, corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I am a hearth-maid of the Clay Yard and I have caught children in it for twenty-six years. Nobody asked me for this book. I write it because a girl came to me in the lean week with a foot gone dark inside three turns of wool and asked me what I did for the second chill, and I heard myself answer her the way my mother answered me, and did not know whether I believed it. A remedy you have to say in your mother’s voice is a remedy that has not been looked at in a long while. I have looked at some of mine here. I have left the others standing, because a woman at three in the morning wants a hand more than she wants a correction.

I write on the back of a glaze-house tally that a fall of slip spoiled. The figures went before anyone could price them, which is a mercy of a kind: a figure that will not read cannot be entered. The tallow at the head is mine. The grey in the gutter came off my cuff when I measured a corner in a house two doors down and came back to write. I have not swept it off. The district burns its grey on the morning after the Last Day and calls it dealt with. I have kept mine, which is the only part of this book I have not copied forward.

\subsection*{The order of a birth-room}

\emph{Written small, with one word gone over in slip.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the slate face down before you go to the child. I have no slate-name and never shall; a midwife who writes the child before she looks at it has written the wrong one already, and a wrong one is hard to get off a slate.

\item Keep the door latched but not held. A woman who is watched through the door will hold her breath, and a held breath is a poor thing to bring a child on.

\item Put the stone in wool at the small of the back, never at the feet. Try it on your own wrist first. The stone takes from somebody’s fire, and somebody in the terraces paid for that fire.

\item Do not wash the red branch. Cross two fingers over it and say the word the mother gives you, and no other.

\item When the second chill comes, count with her. Do not count for her.

\end{itemize}

I asked a woman of the Weir what the red branch meant and she crossed two fingers and gave me a date. A date is an answer that does not spoil in the mouth. I have put the date in the margin and left the question standing, which is where it was when I asked it.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who goes thin\par

The second chill — Warmth, barley water, a watch kept to the fourth day — It comes after the warming, not before. We walk her, believing a moving woman cannot go cold. A physician come down from Greybank says a body made warm spends faster and that walking spends it quicker still; he has seen a woman go stiller by evening and be gone by morning. I have seen the same and I have walked her. Both stand. — The household, one night’s sleep and, sometimes, the woman.\par

The sweet sickness (the line at the gum) — A spoon of sour barley-water; the gum rubbed with a pinch of wood-ash — The glaze girls taste the mix to get the colour, and the sweetness answers sweetness, we say. The physician says it is lead in the glaze and that sour water does nothing but trouble the teeth. I have seen the pale line go off a girl who left the glaze room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A kiln-burn — Tallow first, then a clean fold; a damper-key laid across it to draw the heat — We say the iron draws. The physician says cold iron takes the measure as well as the heat, and that a burn can lose a hand by being made cold. I have set the key on a burn and watched the skin below it go the colour of old rope. I have not done it a second time. — The burn, and the hand if the iron stays.\par

Milk that will not come — Another woman to hold the child while the mother sleeps; clay-water to cool the breast — The favour is paid out of the other woman’s own house, and I say so before I ask it. The physician says clay-water dries the milk and feeds nobody. I have given it and watched a child cry over a dry breast. I have not given it since the third such child. — The other woman’s child, first.\par

The birth-flower — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — I have rubbed one with salt and one with slip and one with nothing, and the branch kept its shape in all three. A girl of the terraces told me her mother washed one and the child went flat by evening, and I have set that beside the three and not joined it, because a flower staying and a child going flat are two things in one room. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

The cold that stays (a foot out of the Slip Brook) — Wool, a stone at the belly, and work to keep the woman moving — The extremity goes first and the heart holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming when she gets worse. I have no name for that hour and have left the place where the name would stand the length a name of that kind wants. We walk her and set her to work. I have seen a foot go dark inside three turns of wool through a whole lean week and have gone on winding the wool. — The woman. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

A cord that will not fall — Wait. A hand on the belly and a hand kept still — A midwife of the Weir says never pull, and I have pulled once and had the cord come away with more than the cord. I have not written what came with it, because a thing with no name in Grath is a thing a clerk will put a figure to if you leave it lying. — The woman, in the lying-in.\par

A child that comes back with another house’s want — The name nine times at the door; a bowl of water under the bed; threshold clay rubbed at the wrist — She calls her mother by a name not given in this house and reaches for a door that is not in the room. We give the name back nine times and set water where the old water stood. The physician says a spoken name puts no shape back, and he is right as a man is right who has never held one of these children. One went off it by the ninth speaking and one kept it a year. I have entered neither in the birth-slate. — Nobody. The house, in a year it cannot spend.\par

A cut from a pot-shard — Tallow first, then a clean fold; never the grey — The women of the yard sprinkle Ash into a cut to dry it, believing the grey takes the wet. I have dressed three such cuts and found the grey under the skin in all three when they came back to me, and have not been able to get it out. That is as much as I know and as much as I shall write. — The cut.\par

Nothing in this book is free. That is the only thing I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The second chill}

The second chill comes on the third night, after the warm has come back into the room. The district calls it the child’s own work and says it goes off by the fourth morning. I have said that for twenty-six years. A body that has been warmed gives heat away faster than one never warmed, and the hour on the far side of the warming is the hour to be afraid of. I know it and I still walk her.

The physician told me to hold her instead and count with her, and not set her on her feet till the fourth day. I have held two women and walked twenty. Both were up on the fourth morning. Of the twenty, three went thin and one did not get up. Three and one are not a number a district will let you use: two is a coincidence, twenty is a habit, and a habit is what the district calls an answer. I have left the place where the count should stand, the length a count of that kind wants.

\subsection*{The note under the thumb}

Tap a sound cup with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. The kiln-masters keep this to themselves, which is their trade, and I have borrowed it from the rack where the cups dry.

I do not tap a woman to hear her. I did once, on a girl gone thin after a return, and the flat I thought I heard was not in her. A body is not a cup. But a house is: I can tell by the note in the pot on the bench whether the room held its warm through the night, and set the stone by that and not by a clock, for there is no clock in Low Kiln and no Court figure that will tell you what a pot knows.

\subsection*{The watch-song}

\emph{Sung low at the third night, to the woman and not to the child. The room says the last line with her.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The coals are banked, the water thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the child is come, the door shut fast;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the wrist and count the breath\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the place where two should be.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The red branch keeps what the water takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name comes late, the figure soon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a slate is a stone with a neat hand on it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a hand is a thing that can go cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The chill comes after the warm is back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is not the water, it is not the night;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape walk her soft, or hold her still ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fourth morning knows which one was right.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sing to the coals, sing to the child,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the woman counting under wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as it can.\end{quote}

I have changed one line in thirty years. I sang \emph{walk her soft} and now sing \emph{hold her still}, and the women singing with me have not noticed, which is how I know it was needed. A line said over a hundred births belongs to the room, not to me.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

The physician came down from Greybank in Ember of Y.H. 811 with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote in the margin without asking. He set \emph{a common settling} over my \emph{second chill} and struck the nine speakings of the name and wrote \emph{no efficacy} above them, then went off with a purse. I have put the nine back underneath. He was right about the lead and wrong about the name, and I have kept both sentences so the next reader can tell which is which.

A clerk of the College borrowed the leaf when it went to Greybank in Ilmen. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who goes thin} and wrote \emph{No cost entered} above it, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Against the space where I had left the name of what a returned child wants, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath it. A nought is a figure and can be entered; a want cannot. He took the verbs out of \emph{the child comes when the kiln does} and wrote \emph{the child is come when the kiln is} above, saying a thing always true has no need of a verb. I have put \emph{comes} back underneath. A clerk can speak without verbs because he is never in the room; a woman at three in the morning wants to know whether the child is coming now.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head came off the lamp I held low while a woman was saying something I wanted the end of. The grey is off my cuff. The brick dust in the fold is off the rack where the cups dry and is the only thing in this book put there by the trade and not by a person. The wet slip took two words clean off the second leaf, and I have not written them back: a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly, and everything here is said slowly. The ring of barley-water came from a cup set down while I was telling a girl to drink and she would not. The scorch is a spark off the kiln that went out under my hand, and I have not entered the burn. The hair in the seam is the colour of wet wool and is not mine, and I have left it where it caught.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the name. The clay keeps the print.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The warm that came between them is kept in no house.\end{quote}

I asked a physician, a clerk of the College, and a woman of the Weir, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The cloth goes back over the book in my apron. Tomorrow a girl will come to the door with a foot gone dark or a child that will not come, and I shall put the verbs back where the clerk took them out, and set the slate face down before I look at the child, because a child is not an account and a woman at three in the morning has a hand that wants holding.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Glass Eel, Being a Trapper’s Field Notes on the Eel of the Lower Ilm and the Silt Below the North Bridge}
\CRsheetheading{The Glass Eel, Being a Trapper’s Field Notes on the Eel of the Lower Ilm and the Silt Below the North Bridge}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hunter’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of nights at the trap and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fish-tallies, an eel-song as it is sung, a Greybank skin-buyer’s price pressed in the margin, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk, and one line in pale ink from a hearth-maid at the Fish Blessing · Written in Ilmen of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the first warm days after the Long Cold, by Tibb of the Fishstairs, who sets eel-traps at the Weir and fishes the silt below the north bridge; set down at the end of nights with a tallow lamp guttering in a clay dish, first on the backs of fish-tallies spoiled by river water and then on two folds of oiled eel-skin, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a clay tube stoppered with wool. Copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a salt warrant voided by the damp. It survives with dried eel slime along the fore-edge, grey silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head blown up from the Sallow, a lamp-scorch on the second leaf where the dish overturned, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, one eel-scale pressed flat in the fold, a tar thumb at the head, a brown tideline where the river stood on it through a night, a green bead of lead glaze from a woman who leaned to see the tally, a grey Ash print nobody will own, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a price in the blocky hand of the skin-buyer, a line in pale ink from a hearth-maid, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I trap eels at the Weir and fish the first warm silt below the north bridge. That is my trade and the whole of what I know, and I have set down only what I have put a hand to. A man who writes what he has heard at a hearth is writing a hearth, not a beast. I have known both kinds of book and this is the sort a man can use with wet hands.

The slime on the fore-edge is eel and the silt in the gutter is the Ilm. I have not cleaned either off. A book that has never been down to the Fishstairs was never taken on watch.

\subsection*{The run}

They come up in Ilmen when the water turns and the ice is gone from the middle of the river, and they come up out of the Sallow, which is a thing every trapper on the Ilm knows and no clerk has ever had to enter. The traps at the Weir are set with their mouths upriver, so a thing going with the water goes in and cannot find the way back out. On Ilmen fifteen the hearth-maids stand on the flat stone and bless the weirs and the traps, and speak the words over the boards; the eels run on that day and they run on the day after whether the words were spoken or not. I have set down both things and joined neither.

In the first warm days they lie in the silt of the Fishstairs, under the north bridge, where the water goes flat and brown and glossy. At night they come to a lamp and to a stone that has held warmth. This is the whole of the hunting: a lamp on a stone, a trap with its mouth upriver, and a man who keeps his hands out of the water until he knows where the eels are.

I tap a basket the way a potter taps a pot. A basket with eels in it answers full; an empty one answers flat and small. It is the only account on this river that I trust, and it cannot be carried into a counting room because there is nothing on it to write.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is an eel. I will set that down first, because the old women will not. It has an eel’s length and an eel’s way of going, and it is the colour of the Sallow on a dull morning, grey with a thin glass shine along the back. In the hand it is cold and slippery and stronger than a thing of that thickness has any right to be.

I have opened nine. In each I found an eel and nothing else, and behind the head a small clear place, no bigger than a pea split in two, with a little warmth shut in it. I have no name for that place and I have not asked for one. A man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in a clay tube is a man who will be asked for the cause by somebody with a slate, and the answer will be entered and the eel will go on being an eel.

\subsection*{The stop}

The danger is not the bite. It has no bite worth writing of. The danger is the stop it puts through the water.

A man wading at night with a lamp will feel it before he sees anything: the ways in him stop as though a clamp had closed on them, and there is no iron to see and no mark on the skin. It lasts a moment on dry ground. In water that is up to a man’s calf it lasts long enough. He cannot lift his foot. The water does the rest, quietly and without haste, the way the Ilm takes a step at the Fishstairs and goes on being a river.

I have seen it once only and I will set that down plainly. It was Ilmen twenty-two, a man of the Weir wading below the bridge with a lamp on a stone and his creel at his hip. He was a man who carried more than his natural measure — a Held man, the sort who can stand a great deal — and I thought he would stand this. He went down at the knee in three feet of water and his hands came up empty and would not close. We had him out in the time it takes to cross oneself, which was not a short time. His fingertips were grey for a tend after and he did not get his warmth back all at once. He has never said what it felt like and I have not asked him. A physician at Sill would call it the cold that stays. I have called it the stop because that is what it did.

A Thin man in that water would not have come up. I have no doubt of it and no wish to test it. The thing has no malice that I could see. It stops what is in front of it, the way the draw stops at a sluice, and goes on with its own business.

\subsection*{The lamp and the trap}

Set at dusk, mouth upriver, the lamp on a stone to the lee side and never against the chest. A lamp against the chest brings the eel to the man instead of to the stone, which is a distinction a new man learns once. Work in pairs where the silt is deep. Smoke what you take at the Fishstairs and sell it for three bits a basket; salted it goes for two, and the women there set their own figure and do not say it aloud.

The skins go a different way. A man comes up from Greybank in a coat with the cuff gone soft from washing and buys the skins dried, a mark apiece, which is four baskets of eels for the skin of one and a figure I have never been able to argue with. He told me the dried skin carries a flow a little farther than the hand can carry it, which is a trade I do not follow and have no wish to follow. A mark is a mark and a question is a question with a figure hanging off it. I have written his price where he set it and have not added a reason to it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pressed in the blocky hand of the Greybank buyer, in the margin beside the price:} A mark a skin, dried whole, no holes. Twelve to the bundle, entered at the tally house. The flow is not explained at this price. --- G.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He paid and I have no quarrel with a man who pays.

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Sung setting the traps at dusk, not lifting them at dawn. The third line is the old line and the men at the Weir sing it wrong on purpose, because a song that tells a man why the eel comes is a song he can carry home and set by his own fire. I have set it down as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the Sallow and one for the draw,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the run that comes up in the thaw;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes to the lamp and it comes to the stone\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes the warm that the stone has known.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four in the silt and four in the run,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mouth upriver and the lamp on the bight;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape if the stop comes, let the man go down ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river keeps what the river has found.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three bits a basket and a mark for the skin;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we sing the old line wrong and leave the gap\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the sixth eel rose and no hand went in.\end{quote}

The gap is where the sixth eel rose on Ilmen twenty-two. The men know it and sing it and have never once said why it is the sixth. There is a man at the Weir who sings the last line twice and will not say what for, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the nights I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine.

Night — Place — Lamp — Taken — Stopped — Entered\par

Ilmen 3 — Weir, west mouth — one — four — none — 12\par

Ilmen 8 — Silt below the north bridge — one — seven — none — 21\par

Ilmen 13 — Fishstairs, second step — two — five — none — 15\par

Ilmen 15 — Weir, after the blessing — one — nine — none — 27\par

Ilmen 22 — Below the bridge, deep silt — one — two — one man — 6\par

Ilmen 27 — Weir, east mouth — one — six — none — 18\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, struck through the “Stopped” column:} Persons stopped: not entered. Stop not a vessel. No deduction arises. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change. But the man on Ilmen twenty-two was grey at the fingertips through the whole of Ilmen and went on selling eels over the top of it, and the clerk has put \emph{nil} against him with a neat instrument and no name on it. I have written the grey in the margin below, where his column cannot reach, and set my own mark beside it in charcoal.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in my hand:} One man, grey ten days. Paid for at the Weir and not on any slate. Missed by nobody but me.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the old women say}

They say the glass eels are the shadows of star-rivets that fell into the river, and that each one is the dark of a rivet that could not bear the light where it was driven. There are songs for it with a woman’s name in them and a wrong done at a weir. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have opened nine and found an eel each time, and a small clear place behind the head with a little warmth in it, and nothing that would cast a shadow in daylight.

The stars are rivets in the great repair, so the old women say, and I have no learning to set against it. But a rivet that fell into the Ilmen would not come up as an eel. It would come up as a thing a man could not close his hand around, and there would be a figure in the slate for it before the water had gone down. I have written that sentence once and crossed it out twice, because it is the kind of sentence that gets a man called a natural philosopher, and natural philosophers are not set to trap eels at the Weir in Ilmen.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The slime at the fore-edge is mine, from holding a basket still while I wrote with the other hand. The silt in the gutter came up over the second step below the north bridge and has never come out. The salt bloom at the head came up out of the paper on a wind off the Sallow and comes and goes with the weather, which is more than can be said for the clerk’s figure. The scorch on the second leaf is where the lamp went over on Ilmen twenty-two, while I was down at the man in the water; the hand that set the dish upright was mine and has not been entered. The hook nick is from a creel at the Fishstairs. The scale in the fold came off a fish that went into the basket and not into the song. The tar is off the wrap. The tideline is the Ilm’s own hand on the leaf, and it has taken two of my words and left the clerk’s figures standing, which is a small injustice in the ordering of things. The green bead is lead glaze off a woman who leaned to see the tally with the sweetness at one corner of her mouth; she said nothing and went off with the light. The grey print nobody will own I have not swept. There is no Last Day on a river, and nothing here is burnt and called dealt with.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In pale ink on the corner of the fourth leaf, in the hand of a hearth-maid who stood on the flat stone at the blessing:} We say the words over the traps on Ilmen fifteen. The eels run whether we say them or not. I have spoken them for two and thirty years and have never once been told what they do, which is a mercy, because a blessing that does something has a price, and there is no house in Sill that wants a price on a blessing.\end{quote}

I have put her line above my own. She wrote it at the Weir and I wrote mine in the silt, and neither of us has asked the eel anything.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river keeps what it is given. It gives nothing back.\end{quote}

I asked a clerk, a buyer, a hearth-maid and a man who went grey at the fingertips, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

Next Ilmen I will go down to the Fishstairs before the blessing with a fresh lamp and two folds of eel-skin, and I will count them going and count them back, and if the clear place behind the head is full in one and empty in another I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb left in it and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Clicking in the Reed, Being a Hunter’s Notes on the Reed-Wolf of the East Marsh}
\CRsheetheading{The Clicking in the Reed, Being a Hunter’s Notes on the Reed-Wolf of the East Marsh}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A reed-cutter’s field book on one beast, set down as a record of hunts and not a book of natural philosophy; the calls and the counting-song in Grathic, the tally in charcoal and reed-sap, with a Stonemouth tooth-buyer’s corrections in Ledgerhand in the margin · Written in the hunting month of Bone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a reed-cutter of Reedholt who went into the east marsh with a spear and a knot of cord, and who hunts still; copied forward in Bone, Y.H. 813. Set on the backs of Stonemouth weigh-slips gone soft with damp and on two folded sheets of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a bark wrap under a loose board of the hunter’s hut. It survives stained and used: a tooth-grey smear along the fore-edge where the book was wiped on a sleeve after a kill, a press of wet reed across the first leaf, a brown peat thumb at the tally, a small round mark where a buyer set a two-mark piece down and left it, and a line of figures in the narrow hand of the Stonemouth weigh-clerk who counted and paid for the teeth. The hunter has answered that clerk in the foot and has not struck a word of his out.\par}\medskip
I cut reed at the east marsh and I have kept this book three winters. It is not a book of natural philosophy. I have no slate-name and no learning, and I set down only what I have put my hand to. A man who writes what he has heard from a hearth is writing a hearth, not a beast. I have known both kinds of book and this is the second sort, being the sort a man can use.

The brown thumb at the tally is peat, not Ash. There is Ash enough on the beast without bringing it into the book. I have not washed any of it off. A book that has never been wiped on a sleeve was never taken into the marsh.

\subsection*{The voice of it}

It does not howl. This is the first thing a new man gets wrong and the thing that gets him bitten. A wolf that howls is a wolf you can walk away from; you know where it stands and it knows you know. The mouth in the reed makes a low clicking with the tongue, under the water’s noise, so that you hear it in your boots before you hear it in the air. It carries over water as a man’s talk carries over a floor. Four clicks, then a gap, then four again, and the gap is where it is listening.

I have set the call down below as we use it, answered across the water to draw them to a stand. It is not a song for a fire. It is a thing said under the breath with the tongue behind the teeth, and the words are only there to keep the count for the men who cannot click true.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the mud and one for the slack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes to the warm and it comes to the crack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes not for singing, it comes for the place\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the way runs shallow and under the face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Click once in the reed, then hold, then click:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man who runs is a man they pick.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand to the elbow. Show them the bare.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It wants the one place and it finds it there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five in the open and nine in the wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one goes still and the rest go yet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the fourth for the man who lacked.\end{quote}

A reed-cutter goes in pairs. This is not a kindness. If a man goes alone into the east marsh in Bone he will come back with one arm or he will not come back, and the pairs are because a beast that has opened a way in one man must be driven off the other before it finishes. The last line of the song is for the one who does not come back. We leave the fourth click for him and we do not say his name at it. There is a man at Reedholt with two fingers gone who clicks four for himself and a fifth he will not explain, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{How it kills}

It goes for the throat and the inside of the elbow. That is the whole of it; there is no wrestling and no throwing down. I have seen a Held man, a man who carried more than his natural measure and was twice the weight of me, go into the mud under one of these and be under before he could shape a shout. The mud did as much as the beast. A pack can pull down a Held man in mud, which is why we cut reed in pairs and why I have no fine opinion of my own standing among them.

It does not worry a victim. This is what the hearths get wrong when they say it worries. It opens one place and waits at it. I have watched from a stand with my spear across my knee and seen a beast open a man’s elbow and then lie with its jaw against the place and wait, as steady as a collector with a tube against a wrist. The man stopped struggling. The beast did not shake him or worry him or drag him. It kept the one place, and the warm went out of it, and when I drove it off the man was already a thing I would not have sent for a physician to save.

I will set down what I have seen and not what it means. It killed quickly, at one place, and there was no anger in it that I could see. A collector’s draw is the same work done with iron and a slate. I have stood near enough to a draw to know the smell of the cold iron and I have stood near enough to one of these to smell the wet wool and the mud, and the two smells are not the same, but the work is. I have thought about that more than is good for a reed-cutter and I have not written a cause.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the hunts I kept a true account of. Some nights I did not write because my hands were full and some I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The figure in the fifth column is the Stonemouth figure, not mine. I counted teeth; the clerk counted marks.

Night — Place — Heard — Taken — Teeth — Marks — Lost\par

Bone 4 — East bank below Reedholt — five — two — six — 12 — a dog, bitten in the elbow, shot at dusk\par

Bone 9 — The marsh road cut — seven — three — nine — 18 — none\par

Bone 14 — Standing water north of Mud End — nine — two — five — 10 — one of ours, hand taken, lived\par

Bone 20 — The lower Ilm, silt side — five — one — three — 6 — none; the wind turned and we were heard\par

Bone 27 — Old run east of the reedbeds — seven — four — eleven — 22 — spear lost in the mud, not recovered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The narrow hand wrote against the “Heard” column:} five, seven, nine are not a number. Enter as 7. Average 7 to a pack, 6 teeth to a hunt. This is the figure the factor will ask for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And along the foot of the “Marks” column, in the same hand:} 12+18+10+6+22 = 68. Received. Account stands.\end{quote}

I had the book out at Stonemouth on Bone 30 and the weigh-clerk laid his cuff on the leaf before he looked at me, the way they do, and set the figures down. He is a clerk and I am a reed-cutter and the account is his, so I have left his hand standing. But a pack is five or seven or nine according to the night and there is no factor in the marsh to give it a number. He has put seven where I put three figures, and under it he has written \emph{average}, which is a word that means nothing to a man standing in water up to his calf with nine of them clicking in the dark.

\subsection*{The teeth and the pelt}

The teeth are set into clamp-handles, and a good tooth is worth two marks at Stonemouth. This is not a pretty trade and I have never pretended it is one. A tooth remembers the shape of a way; that is what the clamp-men say when they buy, and they pay for the saying. I have seen a handle set with one of these teeth bite true where an iron one would slip, and I have no explanation for it and no wish to make one. I took eleven teeth on Bone 27 and I would take the same again if it bought the winter.

The pelt is worth nothing. The hair carries Ash, and a coat of it makes a man go thin by degrees without his knowing how. I have seen a Fen trader try to sell one in Mud End with the Ash worked out of it, and he could not, because you cannot work Ash out of a thing, you can only move it somewhere else. We burn the pelts. We do not sell them and we do not keep them and we say so plainly when a man asks, because a man who buys a reed-wolf pelt is a man who will come back for another.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

The hearths say it is a drowned man’s grudge that has Learnt to click. There are songs about it in the Fenmarch with a man’s name in them and a wrong done at a weir. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. But I have taken six-and-thirty of these in three winters and opened most of them, and what I found was a wolf. It is a wolf that took to the water and stayed there, and the cold of the water has gone into it the way the wet goes into a coat. It kills the way water kills, at one place and without wanting anything from the man it kills. I have written \emph{no anger} in the margin and the clerk has written over it:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the clerk’s hand:} Malice: not entered. Sentiment is not a figure and has no place in a tally.\end{quote}

I did not write that it had no malice because I forgave it. I wrote it because I watched. Those are different things and a clerk’s hand cannot tell them apart, which is the whole reason I keep this book in a bark wrap under a board instead of on a slate in Stonemouth.

Two winters ago a man of Reedholt went in alone and came back walking in the direction he had been facing, and his mother lived in the next hut and did not know him. We did not send for a collector because there was nothing in him to draw, and because the collectors do not come into the east marsh in Bone. He walked to the water and stood, and in the morning he was not there. I have set this down because it happened and not because it explains anything. The hearths will make a song of it and put a name in it and the name will be wrong.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The tooth-grey along the fore-edge is from Bone 27, when I wiped my hand on the leaf before I could find a rag. The round mark is a two-mark piece the buyer set down and forgot; I have left it where it fell. The wet reed across the first leaf is from the morning the wind turned on us and we lay flat in the cut until the clicking went away. The peat thumb is mine. The clerk’s figures I have not touched, and the hunter’s hand that wrote \emph{no anger} under them is my own and will not be struck.

There is a new run east of the reeds that I have not walked. The water stands in it when it should have drained and the clicks come from it in fours with a longer gap than I have heard before. I do not know what the longer gap means. I will go in at the next Bone with a pair of cord and a fresh spear, and I will count them going and count them back, and if there are nine where there should be five I will set that down too, in my own hand, with the verb left in it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cold in One Foot, Being a Hunter’s Field Notes on the Silt-Leach of the Lower Ilm and the Ferr Shallows}
\CRsheetheading{The Cold in One Foot, Being a Hunter’s Field Notes on the Silt-Leach of the Lower Ilm and the Ferr Shallows}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hunter’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of wades and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled eel-bills, a blessing verse as it is said on the bank, one ruling in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a line in the pale ink of a hearth-maid, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Ember and Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a hunter of the Fishstairs who waded the shallows of the lower Ilm and the Ferr for eels and for leeches, and was paid by the dozen; set down at the end of wades on the bank with a tallow end in a dish and the cold still in one foot, first on the backs of eel-bills gone soft with river water and then on two folds of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket against a twist of tallow. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with grey silt worked into the head, an iron-brown tideline along the gutter from the Ferr, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a woman who leaned to see the tally, a cuff-grey smear where a collector set his slate down and took it up again, a singe where the tallow caught the third leaf, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one ruling in the clerk’s Ledgerhand, one line in the pale ink of a hearth-maid, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I wade the shallows below the Weir and the Ferr at Stonemouth, and I take the leach out of the mud for the women at the Fishstairs. It is a poor trade and an honest one, which is more than I can say of most. A dozen dried fetch three bits and no questions, and the questions are the part that costs a man. I write this at the end of a wade with the water still in my boots and the tallow down to a knuckle, because a man forgets a cold foot once he is out of the river, and the forgetting is how he loses the count.

The grey at the head is silt and went into the fibre the first morning I set a leaf down on the bank. The brown along the gutter is iron out of the Ferr, and it stains a hand the colour of an old copper coin and does not wash off before the next wade. I have cleaned neither off. A book that has never been in the water was never used for anything.

\subsection*{Where it sets}

It comes in the low water, when the shallows smell of iron and mud and a man can see his own toes through the brown. In Ilmen the river is up and the leach is nowhere to be found; by Ember the water has gone down a hand’s breadth and the Ferr comes off the Lead Run blue-grey, and they are there. They set against the ankle of a wader and against the legs of the eel-men at the Weir, which is why an eel-man will not stand still in one place to mend a trap. They are very near the colour of the silt, so that a man sees them only when he lifts his foot and looks at what he has brought up, and by then it has been a while.

They are thickest where the water comes through slowly and stands. I have waded the same reach of the lower Ilm three Grains running and taken nine one year and four the next and none the third, and I have not found the rule in it and do not pretend to. A man who writes a rule into a book he carries in his pocket is a man who will be asked for the use of it by somebody with a slate.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a leach. I will set that down before anything else, because the blessing verse does not and because a thing a man can hold in his fingers should be called by the name he would use for it in a kitchen. It is the length of a thumbnail and the colour of wet mud, with a mouth at the head end that does not let go once it has set, and a ways of going along the bottom that I have watched and cannot describe without making it sound like something it is not. It does not swim. It reaches and holds and draws itself along, the way a wetted finger draws along a table.

I have opened four. In each I found mud and a little blood and a small knot the colour of tallow behind the mouth, and nothing with a name in it that I could set down. I have put the colour where I found it and have not written what the knot is for. A man who has taken leeches for nine winters knows when to stop opening them.

\subsection*{The cold foot}

It does not bite. A man feels nothing while it works, and that is the whole danger of it. It sets its mouth to a way near the skin and draws slowly, the way a collector’s tube draws when the collector has all day, and a wader feels only a cold in one foot that does not go away when he leaves the water. I have kept that cold for a tend. I have known a man keep it for a month, and go to the physician about it, and be told there is nothing there to see.

It is the number that does the work. One leach on a grown man is a cold foot and an annoyance. A handful on a child is an hour, and at the end of the hour the child is cold all through and does not want anything. In Grain a woman came down to the Fishstairs with a child of two who had been set in the silt at the edge while she washed. There were six on the child’s ankles. I took them off into a dish and salted the feet, which troubles a leach but does not give back what one has already taken. The child was warm when I lifted her. She was cold by the time we reached the steps, and she did not cry at the steps. I have not put her cost in the tally because there is no figure for a child and because a figure would make it look as though somebody had paid.

I have set the verse down below as it is said on the bank at the Blessing, with the line the women sing wrong left standing. They sing it wrong on purpose. A song that tells a man why a thing takes his warmth is a song he can carry home and set by his own fire and be done with.

\subsection*{The verse}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the shallows and one for the bank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it sets where the iron comes up through the silt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not bite like a dog and it does not bark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it keeps to the ankle and keeps to the warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cold in one foot and a cold that stays,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a child in an hour and a fistful of them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the fifth for the one we did not lift.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three bits a dozen and no name on the bag,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a greyed hand for the man who lets the slate have them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we sing it gives to the river, and sing it wrong ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gap is the foot that does not come home.\end{quote}

The gap is a foot. The women know it and sing it and have never once said whose foot it is. There is an eel-man at the Weir who says the fifth line twice and will not say why, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the wades I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine; I counted what I took off, he entered what could be paid.

Wade — Place — Taken — Cold feet — Dozens — Entered\par

Ember 6 — Ferr below Stonemouth — eleven — one — none — 0\par

Ember 14 — Lower Ilm, below the Weir — nine — none — one — 3\par

Ember 22 — Ferr, the iron reach — fourteen — two — two — 6\par

Grain 3 — Silt side above the Fishstairs — seven — none — none — 0\par

Grain 11 — Lower Ilm, after rain — twelve — one — three — nil\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, struck through the “Cold feet” column:} Leeches not a vessel. Cold in a foot: not entered. Warm in the shallows: no deduction arises. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change. But the child of Grain 3 is in no column of his and in no column of mine, and the cold that stayed in my foot through the whole of Ember is written nowhere he can reach. I have put both in the margin below, where his ruler cannot go, and set my own mark beside them in charcoal.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Below, in my hand:} Six taken off. One child. No figure. The cold went on after the wade and I did not write it at the time because my hands were full. I write it now with the verb left in it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dozen and the greyed hand}

Dried leeches fetch three bits a dozen at the Fishstairs and nobody asks what they were taken from. This is a trade and I have never pretended it was a kindly one. I take them, I dry them on a strip of bark, I sell them, and the money goes into the house. What a man does with them after is not in my book.

But there is a use that is not mine to be nice about. A collector will buy them dried and set them on a wrist or a throat instead of iron and slate, and draw what he wants without entering it, and the law calls that theft and the fact calls it a greyed hand. I have seen the hand. It is the man who set the leeches who goes grey at the fingertips, not the man who sold them, which is a mercy of a kind and not one I like to think about on the walk home. I have sold four dozen in nine years and I have asked twice where they went and been told twice not to ask, and I have not asked a third time.

Salt does not stop the draw once it has begun. It only makes the foot smart, which a physician will tell you is a sign and a Fen trader will tell you is the cure. Both are paid for their answerings.

\subsection*{What they say at the Blessing}

They say at the Fish Blessing that the leach takes the warmth and gives it to the river, and that the river is honest with what it is given. I have put my hand in the water where a leach stood and where none stood, and the water is the same cold in both, and a river that had been given a hundred winters of warmth would not hide it so well. I have sung the line with the rest of them and I have left the sentence standing without a cause beside it. The women at the Fishstairs bless the traps in Ilmen and sell the leeches in Ember and will not hold both things in the same hand at the same time. I understand this better than I understand the leach.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the pale ink of a hearth-maid, on the corner of a leaf gone soft where the river touched it:} It gives to the water, they say. I have laid a bowl of water by a child who was emptied and the water in the bowl was cold by morning, and so was the child, and I do not know which of them gave to which. Bless the trap. Say nothing at the selling.\end{quote}

I have put her line above my own. She wrote it at the Weir and I wrote mine in the mud below it, and neither of us has asked the leach anything.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The silt at the head is mine and off the bank at Stonemouth; it is grey here and brown when it dries, and it has gone into the grain the way the iron has into the gutter. The sedge across the first leaf came off the bank the morning the river came up a hand and I lay flat with the book under me and the eels gone. The nick at the fore-edge is a fish-hook, from the wade when I lost the hook and found it in the cover. The green in the lower corner was pressed there by a woman who leaned to see the tally with the sweetness of the glaze at one corner of her mouth; she did not say where it came from and I did not ask. The cuff-grey at the head is off a collector who set his slate on my leaf while he asked me a question about a wrist and took the slate up again without waiting for the answer. I have not wiped it off and I have not entered him. The singe on the third leaf is my own tallow end and the Ash print nobody will own has been there since Greybank. The clerk’s ruling I have not touched. The verse is as the women sang it, with the wrong line standing and the gap the length they leave it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river is the road. It is not the house.\end{quote}

I asked an eel-man, a hearth-maid, a woman who washed at the Fishstairs, and a man with a grey hand, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

There is a reach of the Ferr above the Lead Run where the water comes down blue-grey and smells of iron even in Grain, and no eel-man sets a trap in it. Next Ember I will take a dish of salt and a coil of cord and wade it, and I will count them going and count them back, and if the cold stays in my foot for a tend after I have come out I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the cause left out and no figure at the end of the row.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cold-Iron Letter, Being a Letter from the Smithy at Low Kiln to His Sister at the Greybank Quay, Concerning the Tubes He Is Sent to Mend, the Iron That Comes Down from Keld, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Counting Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Cold-Iron Letter, Being a Letter from the Smithy at Low Kiln to His Sister at the Greybank Quay, Concerning the Tubes He Is Sent to Mend, the Iron That Comes Down from Keld, and the Figure Nobody Writes; with the Answers in the Margin, a Clerk’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Counting Song in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on a strip of oiled packing-paper, written in charcoal and iron-gall, folded thrice and tied with a bit of wire; carried downriver from Sill to Greybank on an eel barge, answered in the margin, corrected on the back at the factor’s house, and kept since in a dry tin among the quay’s iron tallies · Written at the smithy east of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, Sill, in the last tend of Silt, Y.H. 813, by Harn, a smith who mends kiln irons, barrow irons and the collectors’ cold-iron tubes, to Nessa his sister, who keeps the iron tally at the Greybank quay; carried eighteen leagues downriver on the eel barge, answered in her hand along the margin, and borrowed at the Court’s factor’s house, where a clerk set a correction on the back in Ledgerhand. It survives folded and wired in a tin of iron tallies, the charcoal rubbed thin at the folds, a thumb of brick-dust at the head, a tallow mark at the outer fold, a grey Ash print along the gutter where the writer’s cuff passed, a smear of cold-iron scale at the foot, a strip torn from the second fold, one word struck through with a chisel-point and written again underneath in the recipient’s hand, and a line on the back in a hand nobody has claimed.\par}\medskip
To Nessa at the quay, who keeps the iron tally and will not call a figure a figure before company. From Harn at the smithy east of the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill.

I write on the back of a packing-sheet because there is no slate in this shop that I would put a sentence on. A slate is a thing a man reads to you. I have set my count in notches on the bench with a chisel-point for eleven years and no officer has ever asked me what the notches were, which is how I know they are not a figure. The charcoal takes badly on the oil and I have gone over every other word twice. Don’t rub the fold. It comes apart in the hand if you rub it.

The barge goes on the ebb the day after Account-day and the carrier says a thing said in Silt does not travel well once the mud takes it, so I am putting down what matters first. It is this. I mended nine tubes in the last tend and eleven in the one before, and I did not mend them faster or slower than they came in.
