\emph{Taken down beyond the post, from a man who would sing it only while he was walking and not while he stood still. It is said to the ground and not to a person. The last line is said twice; the second time is for those who went in and did not come back to say why.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cold is not empty;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is a room with a name in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We set the dead to face the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and put no cloth on them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape whatever they came for, they can see it still.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone is given and no thanks entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name is given and no man keeps it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the warm man what he carries ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he will carry it back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is no Last Day out here.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing is swept. Nothing is owed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cold keeps what nobody kept.\end{quote}

He would not give the name of the man who made it, and said that songs from that country are made by the country, which is an answer of the kind the coast gives and the clay countries do not. I have put the song where I heard it, walking, and away from the post.

\subsection*{What the clerk did at Greybank}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaves on a market morning. He writes upright and narrow and has ink settled in two fingers of his cuff that will not come out. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at me, which is the manner of that table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{a space where a day stood} he wrote \emph{nought}, and beneath that, \emph{no entry lies}. I have put the space back under the figure. A nought can be carried into a court room; a space cannot, which is why one of them is honest.

\item Against \emph{I do not remember why I went} he wrote \emph{motive not entered}, which is true in the language of his office and false in mine. I did not fail to enter it. It is not in me to enter.

\item Against \emph{they gave and asked nothing for it} he wrote \emph{no consideration recorded; gift void}. Perhaps it is void. I have kept the stone sewn into the corner, and it has never once been entered.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the thin one under the neat one, as a quarryman leaves the old cut showing in a face of stone. A clerk who takes the man out of a sentence leaves the road standing by itself, and a road standing by itself has carried nobody, cost nobody, and has no figure in it to argue with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The frost at the head came up out of the paper on the climb and was gone before noon; it kept no figure and asked for none. The lime in the gutter is mine, off the load I took up and did not bring back. The tallow at the fold is my lamp, set too near the leaf because the light goes early up there. The grey stone in the lower corner came from beyond the post and has never been warm and never will be. The flake in the fourth leaf was warm-stone once and is cold now, and I have kept it because a man should be able to see the price he paid even after the price has gone out of it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s. I have not swept it. Beyond the post there is no Last Day on which a man might sweep, and I have not found one since I came back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A post and no gate, and a road that ends in stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man gave me a name I cannot say.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried warmth up and came back with a cold stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reason went somewhere I cannot find.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the man seated what he waits for.\end{quote}

I asked a Wasteling, a surveyor come up from the Keep, and a clerk at Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the tin, into the pocket the strap has worn. Tomorrow I take the cart down to the lime-yard and enter nothing, which is the only entry the road beyond the post has ever asked of me.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Country That Empties, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere Set Down by Tavi Salt, a Tally-Clerk of Vhal, Who Went Down with Glass and Salt and Came Back with Crowns He Could Not Spend; with the Prices of the South, the Four Bowls, the Song of the Wine-Press, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Country That Empties, Being an Account of the Southern Empire of Sere Set Down by Tavi Salt, a Tally-Clerk of Vhal, Who Went Down with Glass and Salt and Came Back with Crowns He Could Not Spend; with the Prices of the South, the Four Bowls, the Song of the Wine-Press, Three Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A travelling tally-clerk’s account, kept dry in a tarred tin and written first on salt-paper, then copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold; the figures in a sloped tally hand, the southern sayings kept in the hearing and not translated, the verbs put back underneath every borrowed correction, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward · Written in Grain and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the Bowl of Sere and at a provincial bowl on the south road, by Tavi Salt, a tally-clerk out of the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal, who went south in Reed with two chests of Cliffs glass and a consignment of Sallow salt for a house of the Ten Bowls and came back in Ash with three gold crowns, a jar of wine whose contract had perished on the Salt Road, and a green-glazed bowl that cracked on the second morning at home. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a voided grain-warrant and carried up the Salt Road to Vhal. It survives soft at the fore-edge and sour with salt, with a white bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the sewing, a ring of warm wine at the third hour, a thumb of olive oil, myrrh worked into the grain, the fibre of a wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a green bead of Cliffs glass flattened into the lower corner, a gold crown pressed flat between the fourth and fifth leaves, a husk of southern grain stuck fast in the gutter, a scorched corner, one small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, three corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep tallies on the Quay at Vhal in a room that smells of tar and wet rope. In our country a contract is written on salt-paper, and if the rain gets at it the debt is made nothing, and we call that a virtue. I went south with two chests of Cliffs glass and a consignment of Sallow salt for a house of the Ten Bowls, and came back with three gold crowns, a jar of wine whose paper had perished on the road, and a green bowl that cracked the second morning at home. I have set down what I saw. Where the south and my book disagree I have left both standing, which is what a tally-man does when he wishes to be honest and does not wish to be dismissed.

\subsection*{The road, and how the paper fared}

I took the Salt Road up to Greybank with the glass riding high and the salt riding low, because salt wets paper and glass breaks it and a man must choose which of his goods he will let suffer. The factor’s man there wrote \emph{salt} against a figure and did not look at the team. Below the coast pass the clay gives way to reeds, and at the Standing Post a reeve fined me a bit for asking which of the boards would bear me, which was within his right. The Fenfolk say a dry man is a dangerous man, and lodge him accordingly, and we learned why.

Beyond the Peat Line the villages stand empty in the middle of the day, and in their doorways are squares of bare clay where house-rolls once hung. A guide of ours asked whether the people had gone south or north. The reeve said they had gone where the account went, and would not say which that was.

I carried my paper in a tarred tin inside my coat and opened it only at the third hour, when the south does its business. At Greybank a clerk told me that paper made to rot was no way to carry a debt three hundred leagues. I told him it was the only way to carry one that could be honestly lost. He wrote it down and I have left it standing.

\subsection*{The heat, and the dust}

The south is warm the way a kiln is warm with the door standing open. I have sat out a Stone at the Sallow with the eels frozen in the baskets and never wanted water as I wanted it there. The burning winds come yellow off the east and take the skin off a traveller’s lips and leave the grain standing, which is a trick of the wind I have no learning in and several reasons to believe. My lips went first. The grain stood.

The courts have no walls. There is a fire in the middle of each and men sit in the heat of it with their coats on the ground beside them, and the dust comes down into their hair, and nobody brushes it off. I brushed mine off on the first day and was noticed. A man beside me said that a man who brushes the dust has decided he is only passing through, and a man only passing through may be charged for the hour. I let it lie after that. There is yellow of it ground into the sewing of this book, which I have not shaken out, because a clerk who shakes a leaf is a clerk who wants to pretend he has been somewhere else.

\subsection*{What I carried and what it fetched}

\emph{Figures as the house gave them at the third hour, set above what I entered on the Quay. The left column is the figure a man carries. The right is the figure he brings home, which is never the same figure and is never the same coin.}

Article — Entered at Vhal — Given in Sere — What I set on the back\par

Cliffs glass, a sheet, green — 2 marks at the ebb — 4 crowns — Crowns. They do not change on the Quay.\par

Sallow salt, a sack — 3 marks — 1 crown and a promise — The promise is not current. I entered it anyway.\par

Tallow-wasp resin, a nest — 4 marks — 4 crowns, to a bowl-surgeon — A surgeon, not a nest. I have set both.\par

Rope, tarred, a coil — 1 mark — 2 crowns — The tar came home with the figure, on my hands.\par

Dried fish, a string — 1 bit — not taken — A country that has fish will not pay for fish.\par

Keldish iron, a bar — 2 marks at Greybank — 3 crowns — The bar stood in four hands. The crowns stood in none.\par

A coarse bowl out of Nine Pots — 4 bits — 1 crown, for the curiosity — It cracked on the second morning at home.\par

Red wine, a jar, coming north — 2 marks at the Quay — — — Salt on the rim, and no charge for the salt.\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning counting-hand of a clerk of the house, written in thin gold: against the glass row he set “market rate, current”; against the bowl row, “inspection fee received.”} Underneath, in mine, The bowl cracked and the fee stands. There is always a hand, and a hand is what the gold leaves out.\end{quote}

Twelve bits to the silver mark and twenty marks to the gold crown. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is worth five marks; no man I have ever met has exchanged one for the other, south or north. I left the embers off. A column with nothing in it is an honest column, and there is no column at all for the promise.

\subsection*{The courts, and the four bowls}

At the feast of a house of the Ten Bowls I counted four bowls set on a board. I asked which of them was mine, having been told I was a customer and therefore welcome. They said the third, and that the fourth was not anybody’s and would be carried away full when the feasting was done. A sailor counts what is carried off a ship. I counted four and could not make them balance, and said so, and was answered with great courtesy in a sentence that had the shape of an answer and no figure in it.

Three went round and were poured. The fourth stood where it stood and was carried away still full, and nobody poured it and nobody said whose debt it held. I have set the bowl in the margin where a figure should be, and the gold clerk has set a figure beside it, and the two have not touched.

\subsection*{The burning}

At the end of a feast the debt-slates of one household, chosen by lot, go into the fire. New slates are written before the wine is cold. A woman whose slate burned wept, and the company was kind to her, and then applauded the new one.

I asked a clerk which of the two accounts was the true one. He said yes. When I asked which he meant, he said measure for measure and went back to his wine. In Vhal a debt goes damp and is gone, and everyone knows it is gone. Here they burn it in front of everyone and write it again, and everyone knows it is back. I have carried both kinds of paper. The damp one is the honest one, and I have never heard either of them called a kindness by anybody who had paid it.

\subsection*{The people who are bowls}

A thin northerner is a curiosity in Sere. I was asked to stand at a feast after the third bowl and was given three copper bits for standing, which I have not entered. They are in the tin with the crowns, where no figure is asked for. A man of that house called it an honour and a living, and said it without laughing.

Slaves there are called bowls. A slave is given a clay-name by the household and the old name is forbidden; in some houses the forbidden name is written on the inside of a bowl which the slave is never allowed to look into. A beautiful house-slave may be given a whole return and exhibited as proof of the owner’s generosity. A slave who runs is returned thin, shown at a feast, and set to the grain mills. There is a door to the room where the numbers of a house are read. A woman of that house may own the bowls and the slaves and her husband’s debt; she may not go through the door. I looked at it. It was an ordinary door, with ordinary wood in it, and I have thought about that door more than I have thought about the fires.

The bowl-surgeons buy the resin and set grafts, and a grafted person may be shown at a feast and given small coins. What a person is called in law and what a person is called at the table are two different names, and a visitor who joins them is told that there is no rudeness in Sere, only a person who has not yet been told. I was told, and have written it as it was said, with the end of the sentence thrown away, which is how those sentences are spoken.

\subsection*{A song from the press}

\emph{Taken down at a wine-press outside the Bowl of Sere, while the tread was going. The third verse is said to the bowl and not to the company. The singer would not give it while a clerk of the house stood by, so we went and stood at the press.}

\begin{quote}\itshape We tread the press and the wine comes warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a jar for the north and a jar for the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate goes on at the third hour\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth goes up to the shelf.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wind comes yellow and takes the lip;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grain stands where the lip was bare;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a crowd may burn what a crowd has written\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and clap at the writing that is not there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt went south and came back a crown;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape glass went south and came back a look;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the bowl which of them it poured\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bowl will keep its answer.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

Three hands have been at these leaves besides mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The clerk of the house, in thin gold, took the verbs out. Where I wrote \emph{a man carried it} he wrote \emph{delivery recorded}; where I wrote \emph{they burn a slate} he wrote \emph{instrument discharged by lot}; where I wrote \emph{a woman wept} he wrote \emph{affect observed, not entered}. I put my words back underneath. A verb is the difference between a thing that happened to somebody and a thing that happened in a counting room.

\item The Council clerk at Vhal, to whom I showed the perished wine contract, wrote \emph{instrument void by exposure; no claim lies}. He is right in the language of the pans. The wine was drunk and the paper is gone and there is nobody to ask. I left his line above mine. It is the only line in this account that I did not wish to argue with.

\item The factor’s clerk at Greybank, in the narrow upright hand, set \emph{figures of account, not of price} against my table, and put a round nought in the margin beside the fourth bowl. He has never been south and has strong views about dust. A nought is a figure; the bowl was not, and nobody has poured it.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt bloom off the dockets and comes and goes with the weather. The tar at the fold is mine, from the tin; I have never got it out of the crease and have stopped trying. The yellow in the sewing is the burning wind, ground in at the fold on the road down; it is the colour of the dust in a court and I should rather it stayed. The wine-ring is small and belongs to the third hour. The olive thumb is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I carry the bowl with. The myrrh came off a fold of cloth in a court where a man had been cremated the night before, and the family had bought back the ash at the price they were asked, and the house was ruined by degrees and called generous. I put my hand on the cloth because a woman there put hers there first. I have not washed the smell out and have not written what I think of it. The green bead is Cliffs glass, pressed on me by a girl at the furnace for a bit and a promise I have not kept. The crown between the fourth and fifth leaves is the only coin in this book nobody has tried to enter; it will not change on the Quay. The grain husk in the gutter came from a loaf sent north and left uneaten. The scorched corner is where the leaf lay near the court fire. The bare square is the word I scraped out with a knife and have not written back. I have not forgotten it either.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three are poured and the fourth stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the south keeps nothing and writes it down.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried paper the rain could undo\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and came home with gold that the rain could not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the bowl what it poured. Ask the door.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk of the house, the woman at the press, and a factor come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back into the tin, into the pocket the strap has worn. Tomorrow I take my book to the tide-tally house and enter what I paid for salt, on paper made to rot, and the Council will call it a virtue, and by evening it will be a debt that no man can prove. I have travelled three hundred leagues and I have never seen that art done better than in the south, where they burn the proof in front of everybody and applaud.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of the Open Table, Being the Figures Entered at the Court’s Table Set at the Fringe of the Cross in Sill on the Three Account-Days of Ember, with the Bell Told Beside the Bell Heard, the Figure Read Beside the Figure Paid, and the Place Where a Number Went That Nobody Entered}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of the Open Table, Being the Figures Entered at the Court’s Table Set at the Fringe of the Cross in Sill on the Three Account-Days of Ember, with the Bell Told Beside the Bell Heard, the Figure Read Beside the Figure Paid, and the Place Where a Number Went That Nobody Entered}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A Court assessor’s clerk’s day-book kept at the table set in the open air at the Cross; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand that touches the top slate before it looks at the woman waiting, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back underneath, noughts set beside blanks in a borrowed hand, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at Sill at the Court’s table at the Slate Row fringe of the Cross on the Account-days of Ember, Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year --- Ember 10, 20 and 30 --- and carried forward into the first tend of Grain; kept in the bottom drawer of the table under a loose slate and taken down when a figure is disputed, which on these three days it was not. It survives as one leaf of foolscap folded to the pocket, with an iron-gall thumb at the head, grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a tallow print where the lamp was held low, a pale streak of slip down the gutter, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a brown barley crust gone stiff in the fold, a pale round ring where a cold iron tube was set down and taken up, a damp tide-line from a board standing overnight in the rain, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, a column struck and drawn back, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, noughts set by a hand that is not mine, and one line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the Court’s table at the fringe of the Cross. It is set out on market mornings in the open air, between the direction that is Slate Row and the square where two hundred lean over a block to hear a figure. There is no room and no door. A woman comes and stands before me with her house roll in her hand, and I touch the top slate before I look at her, and say \emph{it’s entered as it stands}. That is the whole of the office. The assessor in his house sets the worth upon a figure; the man at the block reads it twice; I enter what is brought and say it stands. Between the three of us a life is carried the length of this square and nobody in it has carried the life.

There is an order to the reaching, and it is the one thing this table teaches. Hand to the slate, then eye to the woman, then mouth. If a figure is in her mouth before my hand is on the slate I will have to answer for the figure and for her together, and no table in Grath is furnished to answer for a person. I have watched the thane pass a finger over a number before he looked at the crowd, and the collector wipe his thumb twice before he touched nothing, and the eel-women set a hand to a cord before they lifted a creel. I do not say what this order means. A clerk who explains his own hand has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that comes north because it must and does not stay. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember. No man has exchanged one for the other under this table, and I have left no ember column on the leaf I hand to the drawer.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk come down from the College:} Ember: five marks. Reckoning entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written it as though a mark could be poured into an ember by a man standing in the rain. I have put \emph{called} back under his line. It is the Court that calls it five marks; the coin does not agree.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The leaf, as it stood in Ember}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are mine, in the hand that held the slate, and are not part of the account. The last column has no heading.}

Day — What stood at the table — Embers — Deduction — Entered as — Remark\par

Ember 10 — Eight pigs over the weighing board; the levy called for the kiln month — — — 1 in 12 — read twice — One in twelve, as the notice says, once for the moot and once for those who came late. A man brought a number in his fist and asked what the firing would cost now that hands had been in it. Sent to a slate at the watch.\par

Ember 10 — A woman of Low Kiln with a house roll; asked what her house was worth — 33 — 1 in 12 — as it stands — Read her the figure the notice gives, which is the only figure she can carry away. Green at one corner of her mouth; a pale line across the back of one hand. A colour entered, no name.\par

Ember 10 — A narrow slate taken up the clay road before noon, writing turned to the sleeve — — — — — not read — The runner said she carries and does not read, and that the road does not care which. No figure came off the slate at this table.\par

Ember 20 — Second Account-day. Eight pigs; the bell gone four, four and a gap — — — 1 in 12 — read twice — Nobody crossed himself at either bell. The heard bell kept beside the told; a man who wanted them to agree would have had to put a hand to both.\par

Ember 20 — A man carried out of the clay yard on the ninth, going up the road breathing — — — — — — — No collector called, no figure entered, no cause named in this square. Asked three ways and had no slate. I have left the row empty and not set a nought in it.\par

Ember 20 — A woman at the pot board turned a cup a quarter and set it back where it stood — — — — — — — Green in the crease beside the mouth, clay under the nails, a pale line where something had been worn tight and long. A colour joined to no name, held on a place of its own.\par

Ember 30 — Third and last Account-day of the kiln month. Eight pigs over wet boards — — — 1 in 12 — read twice — The district’s arithmetic changed a third time and cannot be changed back. The printed figure stood unchallenged.\par

Ember 30 — A basket set in the moot-post’s finger’s-width of shade and carried home at the going of the light — — — — — — — No slate opened near it. I set down the shade and not what was in it, which is the only thing this table is fit to set down.\par

Ember 30 — Below the north bridge, a clerk set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called — — — — — — — Cuff grey from washing; hand to slate before eyes to stalls; writing turned inward. Not one of ours. The market sold over the top of him.\par

Ember 30 — At the market’s edge, a shape in cast-off clothes with a green sliver on a string at the throat — — — — — — — No loaf passed, no sale, no slate came near. It caught the light on the sliver and went dull. I have not called it a seventh of anything.\par

Figures entered on this leaf: none that were not read. Lines with no figure: five. Rows struck: none. Columns struck: one, drawn back. Noughts set by another hand where I left a place: four.

\subsection*{The two readings}

I keep a place beside the figure the notice gives for the figure the household actually gave. I have set no heading over it. A heading would make it an account, and an account is a thing a man may be called to answer for, and this table has answered for enough this year.

On Ember 10 the number came up out of a fist and went to my mouth and then to the shoulder of a man going up toward High Kiln, and arrived nowhere. I entered the figure the notice prints, the only one a woman can carry away, and in the place beside it set the fist and the mouth and the shoulder, which are not figures and cannot be added. On Ember 30 a woman asked what the kiln month would take and was told a number goes into a slate and not a bundle, and that there would be a slate at the watch. No number came off the slate. I have written the sentence down and not the number, because there was no number to write.

The bell is kept the same way. I write four, four and a gap as I heard it, above the four, four and a gap that was told to me later by a man who had not been in the square. Both are true. A clerk who makes one out of the two has begun to keep an account of a rumour, and the Court pays for those by the page.

\subsection*{What the College hand did}

The man from the College borrowed the leaf on Ember 20, with his cuff gone soft from washing and ink settled in two fingers. He did not sit. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at the woman standing at my elbow, which is the order of that office and not the order of this table.

Where I wrote \emph{I entered} he set \emph{was entered} above, and above that \emph{the figure stands recorded}, which is further from the woman than the first. I have put \emph{I entered} back underneath and left his words standing over it. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these entries in the end, always after the slate is shut.

Against the man carried out of the yard he wrote \emph{no charge arising}, which is true of this table and cost him one glance at the empty row. Against the pale line at the back of the woman’s hand he wrote \emph{no entry}, and I have left it. He struck the column with no heading from the first row to the last and wrote \emph{No such column} above it in the same upright hand he uses for the deduction. He had to count the rows before he wrote that there were none worth entering. A man does not count what he has not looked at. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words where he put them.

The numbering hand is not the College’s. It is narrow and leaning and came down the clay road. Against four places where I had left the \emph{Entered as} column bare it set a round nought apiece. I have not struck the noughts out and I have not set them above my blanks either; they stand beside them. A nought is a figure and a blank is a place, and this leaf now holds both. A man who wanted those noughts to be true had to write them himself, and he did it in the hour before the last pigs went over.

\subsection*{The verse the table-keepers say}

\emph{Said low while the block is scraping, never while a slate lies open and never facing the direction of Slate Row. The last line is said to the table.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hand to the slate and then to the eye,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mouth comes last, as the mouth should do;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read twice over a basket and once over you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four and a place at the end\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the driver sets down what the clerk won’t take;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the thane wipes his thumb, the runner turns her sleeve,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the table keeps the shape of what they gave.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

A woman who stood here about her house said the first lines while she waited for me to finish, and would not say the last while a man from the factor’s office stood at the square’s edge, which is how I know the line matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it.

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, made by holding a quire open through a market morning; there are clerks in Slate Row who can tell a table-clerk by his thumb before he has spoken. The Ash in the outer fold came off my own cuff going through the square after the pigs, where I put my hand into a corner I had no business putting it into. They sweep the corners of houses on the Last Day and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a table set out in the rain.

The tallow print is mine, from holding the lamp low under the table’s edge while a woman at my elbow was saying something I wanted the end of. She did not tell me the end. The streak of slip came off the forearms of a thrower who set her slate beside mine to wait and left a pale mark along the gutter. The green bead is not slip; it is lead glaze from a woman who leaned to see the writing with the sweetness still at one corner of her mouth, touched the paper, said nothing, and went back across the square to her cup. I have left it where she put it. The brown crust gone stiff in the fold was laid down by a woman whose child would not eat it; a crust put down and not eaten is a thing this square knows how to read. The pale ring was made by setting a cold iron tube on the leaf while I reached for a slate. The tube was not used at this table and the ring is not a wound, but it is the thinnest paper on the page. The tide-line along the foot came from a board left standing overnight against the table leg. The small bare square is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I have not written it back and have not forgotten it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The table keeps the figure. The yard keeps the place where the figure stood. The two never meet, and there is no column for the road between.\end{quote}

I asked the man at the block, a woman who came to ask after her house, and a runner come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

In the first tend of Grain a word went over the boards that a slate had burned in the night, and went again, and came a third time from the direction of Slate Row on the breath of barley price and weather. I have set it in the remarks as a telling and not as a fire. No slate burned under any table I have kept, and a word about a slate is not a word about a pot. The leaf goes back into the drawer under the loose slate. Tomorrow the tenth of Grain will bring the boards up the clay road and the pigs over the wet boards, and a man will bring a number in his fist and ask what the month will take, and I shall touch the top slate before I look at him and enter the figure as it stands, and set the fist and the mouth and the shoulder in the column with no heading, where the noughts stand beside the blanks. Nothing has been joined or closed. The table stays in the open air, and the figure stays where it was entered.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Cup in the Dark, Being Five Tellings of the Return at the Alehouse Called the Wet Wool in Low Kiln, Set Down the Morning After While the Dead Were Named in the Street}
\CRsheetheading{The Cup in the Dark, Being Five Tellings of the Return at the Alehouse Called the Wet Wool in Low Kiln, Set Down the Morning After While the Dead Were Named in the Street}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A housekeeper’s record of a Long Night, written by daylight because nothing could be written in the dark; the order of the tellers in the house’s hand, the tellings in the words they were told, a charcoal count of the cups, a clerk’s figures entered over them and a carter’s gloss beneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written on the Remembering, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the alehouse called the Wet Wool in Low Kiln of Sill, by the woman who keeps the room and takes the kiln hands’ washing; set down from the dark of the Long Night before, on the back of a drying-tally spoiled when a wet hem went over it, in charcoal and pipe-clay, the house keeping no ink, sewn with a strand of grey wool into a fold of oiled sackcloth and kept in the meal crock behind the door, where nothing is kept dry. It survives with white pipe-clay ground into the head, a thumb of tallow, a ring of small ale gone dark, the press of a wet wool sleeve across the first leaf, a crust of frost along the outer edge gone soft, grey Ash worked into the gutter, the charcoal rubbed thin where a hand has gone over it, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank on the next market morning, one gloss in the thick charcoal of a carter, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the Wet Wool, a room on the south bank where the kiln hands leave their wet coats and come back for them after the firing, and where I take washing and give back names at the end of a tend when the factor’s man comes up from Greybank. On the Long Night there is no fire after dusk and no names given, and the room fills with people who have come in out of the cold to say things they would not say by daylight. I have set them down this morning, while they are naming the dead up the street, because a thing said in the dark has no owner once the light comes into the room. There is no ink in this house. Ink wants a steady hand, and there is no such thing in the dark. I write in charcoal and pipe-clay, which is what the house signs with.

The white at the head is pipe-clay, not Ash. There is Ash enough in the corners without bringing it into a book, and on the morning after the Last Day I burn it as everybody does and it is back on the bench by noon. I have not swept either. The house keeps its own counsel about the corners, and I have no wish to argue with it.

\subsection*{The manner of the night}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The coals go blind by dusk and the pot is set on the floor under the bench. A man who brings a lamp puts it out before he sits down.

\item The cup goes round from hand to hand and nobody pours for himself. In the dark nobody can see who pours, which is the whole of it. A man who pours for himself on this night drinks alone, and the room lets him.

\item A telling starts with \emph{I saw} or \emph{I carried}. A man who starts with \emph{they say} is told to begin again. The house wants witnesses on this night and has no use for news.

\item The cup comes back to the teller’s hand and the telling ends there. No clapping, no \emph{well said}; there is always another man sitting in his wet coat.

\item No name is spoken over a telling. Names are for the morning, and the morning has enough to do with them.

\item If a man in a clean coat comes in off the road, stop where you are. He will ask what was entered and the answer is nothing, and he will write that down as though it were a great deal.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The five that were told}

There were eleven coats on the pegs and five of the eleven told. I have set the tellings in the order they were said and not in the order of their worth, which the cup has no way of measuring.

The first was put by a carter come up from Greybank with clay dry on his boots.

\begin{quote}\itshape I was on the Clay Road when the ice set, and there were nineteen of us at the road house and one bed among us. The woman set a pot on the floor and told us to knock it, one after another, and never said what she was listening for. Eighteen answered full and one answered flat, and the man whose pot answered flat was given the bed, because she said a man who has lost his note has need of a place to lie down. He was gone by morning. The pot went back on its shelf and I have knocked at that shelf twice since and never heard anything.\end{quote}

He said it to the bench and not to the room. A man who has told a thing about a bed does not want ale afterward. He took his coat and went out, and the cold came in past him and went round the room looking for the place he had left.

The second was put by a girl who works the drying racks two doors up.

\begin{quote}\itshape In the Long Cold my brother and I slept against the bank wall. Each night I put my hand between his back and the stone to see that the stone was warm, and one night the stone was cold and he was warm. I did not tell him. In the morning the stone had its heat back and he had gone thin in his sleep, and my mother wrapped him in a coat she had kept folded for nine years. He is alive. He does not know the coat was kept for him, and I have never had the heart to say whose it was before.\end{quote}

Somebody asked her whose, which was against the rule, and she answered the cup instead, which is the proper way to answer in this house. She drank standing, with her sleeve over the rim, and there was a wet mark on the bench where her coat had been.

The third was put by a woman from the Fishstairs who had come up with a creel and would not set it down.

\begin{quote}\itshape We sold eels under the ice. A man came with a sack of salt and said the river had given him the eels, so he would take three pair for nothing. I told him the river gives nothing and takes everything, which is a thing my mother said to the bucket and not to me. He said it was the same sentence said twice. I let him have the three pair and would not take the salt. In the morning there was a thin white line on the step where he had stood, and it went when the sun came on it. I have swept that step every day for eleven years and it has not come back.\end{quote}

She asked for no ale and was given a cup by the man next her, which is how it goes when a person has told a thing and the room wants to put something between itself and the telling. She held the cup a moment and set it down again with the ale in it.

The fourth was put by a woman who had been a hearth-maid in High Kiln before she came down to the washing.

\begin{quote}\itshape I carried a coal from my mistress’s fire to my sister’s in a clay dish under my coat, with a fold of ash over it the way we do. There were three doors between and I lifted the lid at each, and at each the coal was there and a little less of it, which is how a coal behaves. At my sister’s the fire took. When I got home my mistress asked whether I had been out and I said no, and she said nothing and set the dish back on its shelf. She knew. She had put the ash on it herself.\end{quote}

This one the room heard out in silence, and then the cup went round faster, as it does when a thing has been said that everybody has done and nobody has owned to.

The fifth was put by a clay-hand from the yard, a young man with the grey worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts.

\begin{quote}\itshape In the Long Cold the pit was hard as a flagstone and we warmed the spade under our coats between strokes. There was a woman on the firing who counted the pots by knocking them as they came off, and she never knocked the last pot of any firing. I asked her why. She said the last pot belongs to the count that goes round the yard and is not asked anything, because a thing you knock has to answer and that one has not been asked yet. I have worked eleven years and I have never knocked it. Neither has anybody who learned from her.\end{quote}

He said the last words to the floor. I have set them down as he said them. No one in this house has ever knocked a last pot and no one here has ever claimed the habit as his own, which is two ways of keeping the same thing.

\subsection*{The tally, in charcoal}

Teller — What was told — The cup — Note\par

Carter from Greybank — The pot and the one bed — set down, not lifted — clay dry on his boots\par

Girl of the rack bank — The wall and the coat — lifted, drunk standing — sleeve over the rim\par

Woman of the Fishstairs — The white on the step — given, not asked for — creel on her knee throughout\par

Hearth-maid, now of the washing — The coal in the clay dish — went round twice — said it to the bench\par

Clay-hand of the yard — The pot not knocked — lifted — said it to the floor\par

Eleven coats, five tellings, and the cup came back to my hand with a dark ring in the wood where I could not remember setting it. I have counted the rings by daylight and got the number of tellings. I counted them in the dark and got one more. Both counts are mine and I have kept them side by side, the way the board keeps what the cup forgets.

\subsection*{The low verse, said at the end of the Long Night}

\emph{Not sung. Said low, to the pot, the floor and the door, in that order, and to a person last. There is no verse for Kindling in this house; the fire comes up from somewhere else and wants no help from us.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The coals lie blind and the coat hangs wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five have told and the sixth sits yet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cup goes round and the cup comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the board keeps a ring that the hand forgot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name them in the morning. Name them once.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The year was lit before the dark came down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the thing that was said in the dark goes round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the ale, and stays where the ale has gone.\end{quote}

The second line is the one people change when they say it, putting \emph{six} or \emph{nine} or the count of coats on the pegs. I have left \emph{five} where it stood, because it was five this year. Next year a hand will put another figure over it and leave mine underneath, which is how a verse gets said in this room.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor came up from Greybank on the market morning, with a cuff gone soft at the edge from washing and two fingers of it the colour of the slop-pail. He laid his hand on the leaf before his eye went to me, which is the manner of that table. He set the five tellings down as \emph{narratives of the Return, five received}; struck the sixth place and wrote \emph{no telling tendered} against it, which is true in the way an empty chair is true; and wrote \emph{five quarts small ale, watered; levy one in twelve}, and a figure against the clay dish as if a man could pay for a coal that way. At the dark ring he could not leave it alone. He put a nought under it and wrote \emph{vacancy}, and a nought is a figure and a figure travels well.

I have put my words back underneath his and left his standing, the way the board keeps a dark ring under a spilled quart. He has entered the five and struck the sixth. The sixth was not struck: it sat in a wet coat on the bench and went home when the rest did, and I have never asked which of the eleven it was.

\subsection*{The carter’s gloss}

Against the telling about the bed, in thick charcoal, in a hand that presses hard at the ends of words:

\begin{quote}\itshape I knocked that shelf twice. It never answered. I did not say so at the time.\end{quote}

He brought the leaf back himself and stood at the door while I read it, and went out without his ale. I have kept his two knocks where he set them. A man who says a thing in the morning that he did not say in the dark has paid something for it, and I have no slate on which to put the payment.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The pipe-clay at the head is mine. I held the leaf down with my whole hand because the draught comes under the door and takes paper before it takes a coat, and clay goes into the grain where nothing will get it out. The tallow thumb is off the lamp I wrote by this morning, with the street full of people naming the dead. The dark ring came off a cup that stood from the first telling to the fifth and was drunk by nobody, which is how small ale is drunk in this room when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The press of wet wool across the first leaf is the girl of the racks leaning over to see what I was writing; I have not brushed it, because she would only lean over again. The frost along the outer edge came up out of the paper on the walk from the wringing-board and went soft by noon; the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The Ash in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and nobody will own it. The charcoal is rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over the tally. There is no Last Day in a room where names are taken for ale and given back at the turning of a tend.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is said in the dark keeps its heat till morning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is written in the morning goes cold on the shelf.\end{quote}

I asked the girl of the racks, the woman of the Fishstairs and a man who takes in washing, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the meal crock behind the door. Tomorrow the bank wall will be warm again and the room will be full of wet coats, and a year from now, when the coals go blind and the cup goes round, somebody will begin with \emph{I saw} or \emph{I carried} and the sixth place will be there for whoever sits in it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Dish of Salt, Being a Guessing-Night at the Head of the Quay in the Long Cold, Four Questions Put to the Brazier, the Answers Said to the Dish, and What a Council Clerk Made of the Morning}
\CRsheetheading{The Dish of Salt, Being a Guessing-Night at the Head of the Quay in the Long Cold, Four Questions Put to the Brazier, the Answers Said to the Dish, and What a Council Clerk Made of the Morning}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A room-keeper’s account of one winter night, set down for the settling of a wager and not for the improvement of the reader; the questions in the words they were spoken, the wagers in pinches of salt in a dish, the tally taken off the dish at dawn, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, a salt-wife’s gloss pressed into the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that nobody will claim · Set down at the head of the Quay in Vhal in Stone of Y.H. 811, the Long Cold, when the coast pass was shut and no cart came down from Greybank in nine days, by the woman who keeps the brazier room there; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoil Council salt warrant, sewn with tarred thread into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a tin above the brazier, which is the only dry place in the house. It survives with a white salt bloom in the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a wine ring near the fourth question, wet wool pressed across the first leaf, a crust of frost along the outer edge, a green bead of cliff-glass folded into the second fold, a fish-hook nick, a grey print nobody will own, the clerk’s correction standing above the room’s words, the salt-wife’s gloss standing in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the brazier room at the head of the Quay. It is a narrow house with the water going under it, and in Stone the frost takes the iron ring at the landing, so that a man puts his boot against it before he will believe it is iron. The boats lie high. The pass is shut and no cart has come down from Greybank in nine days, which means no clay ware, no wool, and nothing to argue about over a fire. So we guess.

A guess here is a question said to the fire. Said to a person, an answer becomes an argument, and an argument in Vhal is a debt with no date on it, which is the one thing this house will not carry through the winter. We put four questions. The wagers are pinches of salt laid in a dish. Salt is the only thing in the room a man can taste and cannot spend, so it is the right stake for a night when there is nothing to buy. The dish goes from hand to hand and the answer is said to the dish. No slate lies where the dish lies. A man who wants a thing entered can go up to the tide-tally house and sit with people colder than himself.

The coal is paid for by the boat-house at the step, which enters it against the share in the spring. Thus a man warms himself before he owes for the warming, which is the ordinary order here and the reason the fire stays lit. I have no word in Vhaleni for a person who sits by a fire without an account. I have a word for a person whose account is current, and I used it of everyone who came that night.

\subsection*{The night as it went}

It was the ninth night of the shut pass. The Sallow came in against the wind and went out against the wind, as it does, and the frost stood on the Quay boards in feathers where the Warm had lately gone out of the stone. There were six of us and a boy who swept the landing. A question is put once; ask for it again and you owe a pinch, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the dish. Four are scored. A fifth may be said from the door and is not counted, being a thing said by a man who has not sat down.

The first went to a salt-wife of the third pan, with the salt worked white into the creases of her hands.

\begin{quote}\itshape Written to be lost, and lost is how I keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a wet morning is my ending\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Council calls it a virtue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A contract on salt-paper,” she said, and said it to the dish. She did not look at the man from the tide-tally house, who had not yet put his slate down. He put a pinch in all the same, which is the sort of thing a clerk does when he wants it known that he can lose a wager and still be paid.

The second went to a man come aboard at the step, whose opinion on the boat is counted at half and who knows it.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am held by a mother and not by me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape my word on the boat goes in at half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am married to the account\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and may never own it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A man come aboard,” he said to the dish, which is how a man says a thing about himself in Vhal without claiming it. His wife’s sister laughed, and he said nothing, and the dish went on. That is the whole of a marriage at the head of the Quay, and it is not a sad thing unless you have watched it.

The third I put myself, because the room had got loud and wanted quieting, and a question put by the fire is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape I steal a coal and leave no track but a warm crop;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am a bird with a borrowed name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pan-master counts me as weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A brine-gull,” said the glass-woman from the furnaces. She had the sweetness of the cliff at one corner of her mouth. After she had said it she wiped that corner with the back of her hand, though there was nothing there to wipe, and held the dish a moment longer than the passing needed. The salt-wife put a pinch in for her.

The fourth went to the boy who swept the landing, and he answered before the verse was done, which is why he never wins anything and is always first.

\begin{quote}\itshape I tap from below where the warm is kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the boat looks the same when I have done;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no hole in her, and no heat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A salt-thing,” he said to the dish. He had seen one tap his mother’s boat in the summer, and nobody in the room said the boat’s name. He set his pinch on the dish and did not take it up again, though nobody had asked him to pay, and I have left it lying where he put it.

\subsection*{The tally, taken off the dish at dawn}

Question — Put to — Answer, said to the dish — Salt laid down\par

The written thing — the fire — a contract on salt-paper — one pinch\par

The half word — the fire — a man come aboard — one pinch\par

The bird — the fire — a brine-gull — one, laid by another hand\par

The tap below — the fire — a salt-thing — one, not taken up\par

Four answered. Nothing was drunk, and the cup that stood by the brazier from the first question to the fourth went back on the shelf with the ale still in it, which is how small ale is drunk in this house when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it.

\subsection*{The salt-wife’s gloss, pressed into the margin in charcoal}

She borrowed the leaf before the clerk came and put her mark against the bird:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The gull took from the Council’s brazier at the pan gate, not from ours. It has been doing it eleven years and the Council has never once entered the coal. Say which fire you mean.}\end{quote}

Underneath, in mine: \emph{Both stand. A gull carries whatever is not watched, and a fire that is paid for by nobody is the kind a bird will always choose.} She came back for the leaf at noon and read what I had written below hers and said I had put it rightly, which she would not have said if I had put it wrongly, and went away with her hands white to the wrist.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council came with the light, being a man who cannot leave paper lying. He laid his hand on the leaf before his eyes went to the room, which is the manner of that house. He set the four questions down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses recorded}, valued each pinch of salt at a twentieth of a bit, and wrote \emph{gaming, not commercial} across the head of the tally, so that a night of guessing came out as a night of trading with the profit left off. Against the boy he wrote \emph{no standing party}, and against the coal, \emph{fire privately maintained; no public charge}, which is true and is the whole of what the Council cares to know about a fire.

In this room — In the Council hand\par

A pinch of salt, tasted and not spent — One twentieth of a bit\par

An answer said to the dish — A response recorded\par

The boy who swept the landing — No standing party\par

A fire paid for by a house that is not here — No public charge\par

He asked me what a guess was worth. I told him nothing a clerk could carry, which is the first true thing I have said to that table in two winters. I have put the room’s words underneath and left his standing above, as salt lies under ink and shows through when the paper wets. He has entered four answers and struck the boy, and the boy was not struck: he said a thing he had seen and took nothing for it, and that is the only answer of the four that cost the speaker anything.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom came up out of the paper itself and I have not brushed it off. The tar at the head is mine, off the coil I keep by the door for the boats in winter. The wine ring near the fourth question belongs to the glass-woman, who set her cup down and did not take it up until the salt-wife had paid for her; I have not washed it out. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the man come aboard, who held the door while the clerk read and did not let go when he was done. The crust along the outer edge came up out of the paper on the ninth night, when I carried the leaves inside my coat and the coat froze to my back; I have not scraped it off, because a guessing kept in a warm room would be a different guessing. The green bead in the second fold is cliff-glass; the girl pressed it in with her thumb and did not say what it was for, and I have not turned it to the light. The fish-hook nick came off a man paying for eels with the hook still in his hand. The grey print came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day here and nothing anywhere gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four answers went out on the ebb. The fire did not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish came back empty and the place by it stayed warm.\end{quote}

I asked the salt-wife, the man come aboard and the boy who sweeps, and had three names and no hand, and none of the three was in the room when the line was written. I have left it where it stands. The leaf goes back in the tin above the brazier, which is the only dry place I have, and tomorrow the pass will still be shut and the boats will still lie high, and if a man asks what there is to do of an evening I shall tell him to ask the dish.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Drawing Book, Being the Measures of the Sill District Entered at Greybank in the Last Tends of Stone, Y.H. 812}
\CRsheetheading{The Drawing Book, Being the Measures of the Sill District Entered at Greybank in the Last Tends of Stone, Y.H. 812}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the tally-book of the Court’s collector’s clerk at Greybank; figures in Ledgerhand, with the officer’s remarks in the hand that made the draw · Written in the factor’s house at Greybank in Y.H. 812, the year the clay towns call the Thin Year, by the clerk who keeps the tally for Sill and the villages about; the officers are entered on the leaf and the clerk is not. Copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. It survives as a quire of paper soft at the fore-edge in a tin on the factor’s shelf: a grey thumb at the head of the ember column, a streak of slip down the gutter, a green bead of glaze in the lower corner, a drag of Ash along the foot, one figure struck through and set above in a second hand, and a line at the foot which the factor’s clerk did not write.\par}\medskip
I keep the tally for the Sill district in the factor’s house at Greybank. The officer makes the draw and gives me the figure; I set it down. The figures go in Ledgerhand, without verbs, because a figure with a verb in it can be argued with and one without cannot. The remarks are the officer’s own, in the hand that held the tube, and I have not changed a word of them. The College would take the verbs out of those as well if it knew they were there. The factor allows them. He says a remark is not part of the account, which is his way of saying that a thing may be written down so long as it is never entered.

The grey at the head of the ember column came off on the officer’s fingers. He laid them on the page while he gave me the number and did not know he had marked it. I have not rubbed it out. It is the only mark on the leaf that I did not set here of purpose, and it is the one the factor’s clerk asked me about.

Day entered — Vessel, as the slate has it — Embers — Deduction — Banked to — Officer’s remark\par

Stone 12 — A man of the Weir. Birth-name not taken; entered as \emph{Eel} — 52 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Drawn before light. Pale round place left on the arm.\par

Stone 12 — A child three days returned, Low Kiln. Entered as \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Worse before dusk. Entered as a birth, not a worsening.\par

Stone 20 — A woman of the glaze room, High Kiln. Entered as \emph{Sweet} — 38 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Pale line at the gum. Asked after her girl; not entered.\par

Stone 20 — A clay-bound hand of the terraces. Entered as \emph{Seven} — 44 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Consent withheld. Clip-held by the wrist until consent entered.\par

Stone 22 — A man of Mud End. Entered as \emph{Peat} — 47 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Kiln’s breath. The neighbours called it merciful.\par

Stone 25 — A girl of the slip pits, Low Kiln. Entered as \emph{Nineteen} — 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Birth-slate laid face down on the bench before the child was turned.\par

Stone 30 — A widow of the lower town. Entered as \emph{Loaf} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Four loaves baked; three to the levy. Figure read twice, once for those that came late.\par

Stone 30 — Forty of Low Kiln. One slate for the batch, entered by lot — — — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Held overnight in the Waiting Room. Birth-names not taken. A barrow of grey went out through the north gate.\par

\subsection*{The column of embers}

An ember is said to be worth five marks and a newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen. A labourer in good case carries forty to sixty and does not know it. The book does not ask what the walls are like; it asks only what went through them and where it was put. I have set the figures down as they were given. I have not added them, because adding is a thing the College does in the Hearthseat and not a thing a tally-clerk does at Greybank, and because the last time I added a column I got a number that would not agree with the printed one and the factor told me to copy the printed one again.

The officer gave me thirteen for the child on Stone 12. The factor’s clerk struck it and set twelve above in his own narrow hand, saying a vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw. Both figures stand. I have asked which is right and neither of them has told me, and I have stopped asking, because a clerk who asks after a correction is a clerk who will soon be correcting next.

\subsection*{The remarks}

I struck out one of my own words on this leaf. Where the officer said \emph{the warmth was drawn}, I had written \emph{taken}, and he looked at the word and said a draw is not a taking when there is a slate. I set \emph{drawn} above and left \emph{taken} standing under it, which is the only honest thing on the page. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way; the slate is the difference, and the slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it.

The remarks are the only place in this book where a person appears, and even there they appear as a pale round place on an arm, a line at the gum, a word not entered, a wrist held until consent. The officer writes a good remark. He does not explain himself in them and does not plead. \emph{The neighbours called it merciful.} That is all he set down for the man of Mud End, and it is more than the ordinance would allow and less than a man would say.

\subsection*{What I did not enter}

The streak of slip in the gutter came off the forearms of a thrower who came in from Sill while I was copying the Stone 20 figures. She stood at the counter with her hands held away from her coat and waited for the figure, and the grey came off on the edge of the quire when she set her slate beside it. The green bead in the lower corner is not slip. It came from a girl who leaned over to see the writing with sweetness still at her mouth, and touched the paper and said nothing. I have left it where she put it. The drag of Ash along the foot was there when I opened the tin; it is not mine and not the factor’s clerk’s. I have not swept it. On the Last Day they sweep the corners of the houses and burn what they find there in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a tally-book.

One in twelve is printed on the notice and I have copied it eight times in these two tends. I have not checked it against the roll, and the officer has not asked me to. The figure goes into the book as it comes off the notice and out of the book into the Weighing, and a district hears it read in a clean voice and goes home knowing what it owes without having been told what it paid.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The factor’s clerk has written a line here that is not mine and is not in Ledgerhand:

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing is lost that we have kept.\end{quote}

I have not struck it out. It is not a figure and has no business on a tally; but it is in the book now, and when I copy the leaf on Ilmen 1 I shall copy it again, in his hand and not my own, as it stands. The tin goes back on the shelf between the salt scales and the damp copies from the coast. The grey thumb will come off on the next leaf. I shall not rub that out either.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Drawing Table, Being the Standing Rules of the Collectors of Sill and Greybank for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Table in Slate Row and on the Clay Road, with the Table of Years, the Wrapping-Song Pasted Inside the Wool Sleeve, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Drawing Table, Being the Standing Rules of the Collectors of Sill and Greybank for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Table in Slate Row and on the Clay Road, with the Table of Years, the Wrapping-Song Pasted Inside the Wool Sleeve, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A table-copy of the collectors’ standing rules in the hand of an old officer who keeps the wool sleeves and the roll of hands behind the collector’s table in Slate Row; the articles in short road sayings, the years and the faults in tables, the wrapping-song pasted inside a wool sleeve, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a College clerk, one in the soft-cuffed hand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, three lines in the thick charcoal of a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln, and a line at the foot nobody will own · First gathered at Greybank in Y.H. 719, the year the factor’s house began to keep a roll of hands beside its roll of measures, and copied forward from the sleeve and not from a book, which is why the rule about the grey is rubbed nearly through at the corner and the rule about the wool is as sharp as the day it was set down; this leaf written in Smoke of Y.H. 813 by a collector who has drawn on the Clay Road for twenty-six years and keeps the table’s sleeves and its roll of hands, after the Thin Year and the Opening of the Slates. It survives folded small enough for a coat pocket, carried in the wool sleeve of a tube that has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper: grey worked under the nails at the head, iron filings ground into the gutter off the tube’s wrap, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner by a girl at the Cross with the sweetness still at her mouth, frost-crisp along one edge from a morning on the Rim Road, a tallow thumb, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room along the foot, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away and no other put in its place, two corrections in borrowed hands, three lines in the margin, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the sleeves and the roll of hands behind the table in Slate Row. A boy comes up from Greybank with a house-name and goes back with a slate-name and a wool sleeve. I draw the measure. The clerk at Greybank writes the figure. There is a difference between the two. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way; the slate is the difference.

The table is a guild of a sort, though the word is a clay-country one and is not used in Slate Row. These articles were first gathered at Greybank in Y.H. 719, when the factor’s house found it had two sorts of men to count. A rule with no grey on it is a rule nobody has had to use. These have been used.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the table}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The table takes an apprentice, not a house. A house may bring him, or the Temple’s poor may be sent, or a collector may take him off a doorstep where a draw has left nobody to answer for him. From the day he first wraps a tube the table answers for his hand. A house that will not give up the years has given nothing.

\item He is taken at fifteen, or at sixteen if the house has kept him through a hard year. A boy who cannot carry a wrapped tube to the Waiting Room and set it down without letting the iron show has no business on the road; he will spend the wool on his sleeves and call the road’s.

\item His birth-name is said once at the taking and kept in the mouth afterward. A slate-name is entered in the roll in its place, in the same hand as the figures, so that no man can tell by looking which of the two was written first. A name in the mouth cannot be entered, and there is nothing in this country the Court has not tried to enter.

\item He is kept, not hired. He eats from the table’s dish and sleeps in the room above the Waiting Room, and what he earns goes into the table and comes back as bread and a sleeve, neither of which is written down. An officer who tells a boy he is paid tells a true thing about a figure and a false thing about a living.

\item No boy is asked whether he wants the iron. He is asked whether he understands what is carried: a tube wrapped in wool, a knuckle laid to the wall, a hiss, a figure read twice, and a grey that comes up under the nails before he has learned to read the slate. The wanting comes after, or it does not come.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, against rule 4:} Retained by the table; no wage arising. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that he is fed. He is fed, and the feeding goes into no figure, which is why it can be done. I have left my word where his was set above it, as a man leaves the crack showing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the wool and the note}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wrap the tube before you take it up, not after. A boy can hold iron while he speaks, but he will not speak well with his fingers going the colour of the sky before snow. The wool keeps the hand one draw and lets the heat go, which is as much as any sleeve of mine is owed.

\item Set the knuckle to the wall before the iron goes to the arm. A whole vessel answers full; one cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. Write the note before the figure, and write \emph{none} where there was no note and not a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not. The kiln-masters of Sill keep the full note to themselves, which is their trade; I know it from rooms where a pot was set down and the house talked over the sound. A collector who draws blind still brings back a figure. That is the trouble with figures.

\item Look at the arm, where the ways run near the skin. Do not look at the face. A face tells you nothing you can use, and a thing you cannot use is a thing you will remember, which is worse on the road.

\item Count the draws on the fingers afterwards, never before. A figure counted before the draw is a figure already decided, and a decided figure is the same thing as a false one with the ink dry.

\item Say the four sayings in the order the road comes to them, not the order the notice prints. In the room they begin with \emph{nothing is lost that we have kept} and end with the taking; on the road the record comes first, so it cannot comfort, and the banking comes last, because it is the true one and the one we do the most. Say them into the wool, not the air, where words go up and get entered.

\item One in twelve, as the notice says, read twice: once for the moot and once for those who came late up the road. The boy reads what is printed. What the district pays is not his hand, and the man who sets the other figure has gone up the Clay Road with it and does not carry it in the open. An apprentice who asks after that figure is told that a collector who asks after a correction will soon be making one.

\item Never say the prayer twice over one man. A second prayer argues with the first, and the first was honest, being said before he knew how much the man had. If the bell comes off the Cross four and four and a gap, stop at the gap. The gap belongs to somebody else.

\item Consent is recorded; the table writes the word as the slate has it. A boy is taught to say \emph{lawful draw; consent recorded} and not to ask recorded by whom, because a collector who asks it in a room will ask it at a door, and a door is where a man loses his cuff. A refusal is not entered. The clip belongs to the Court’s room, not to this table, and the room has its own hand for it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, against rule 11:} Printed deduction, read twice; no second figure arises. \emph{In mine, underneath:} Both figures arise. One is carried in the open and one under a coat. Both stand, and I have stopped asking the clerk which of the two he means by \emph{arises}.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The years at the table}

\emph{Kept behind the sleeves. What is written is the work that came up, in a hand that does not change between one line and the next.}

Year — At the table — What is taken\par

Fifteen — Wrap the tubes, sweep, keep the sleeves dry, carry the slate edge-on — The birth-name, said once and kept in the mouth\par

Sixteen — Walk with an old collector; set the knuckle; say the note into the wool — The habit of counting before the draw\par

Seventeen — Set the iron under an eye that has drawn forty times; read the figure twice — The face of the person on the pallet, which is not looked at again\par

Eighteen — Take a pot alone through a draw and read the grey in his own hand — The last of a boy’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Eighteen is the common end of a keeping and not a short one. He stays where the table sends him, at Sill or Greybank or a district he has not heard of. The table’s figure for him is one apprentice, current, no wage arising. What stands beneath that figure is a boy who eats from the dish. The College does not choose where he goes. The roll does, and the road after it. His hand goes grey under the nails first and comes up into the creases by the second year, and after that a man may wash till the water freezes and nothing changes. Collectors say the grey comes off in a day. I have had it last six, and no clerk has asked after the sixth. A collector who says the cost is nothing has not looked at his own hand, which is the only looking he does not do.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the table\par

Iron taken up before the wool — The tube wrapped in the boy’s sight; the draw put off a tend\par

Knuckle not set before the tube — The note entered as \emph{none}, which is not a nought\par

A figure counted before the draw — The figure struck; the boy set to counting sleeves for a tend\par

The face looked at — No punishment. The boy is told what he has kept and sends it nowhere\par

A prayer said twice over one man — The second struck; the first left standing\par

A birth-name written on a travelling leaf — Scraped away; no other word put in its place\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in one tend is a fault the boy has not understood, and the old collector sits with him behind the table until he has. The tube is not a rod and the slate is not a confession.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The wrapping-song, pasted inside the wool sleeve}

\emph{Sung low going up the Clay Road, with the tube wrapped and not in the hand. Nobody sings it in a house and nobody sings it at the Weighing. The boy whose sleeve is new says the middle verse, and nobody says his name.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wool on the iron, iron on the arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the note comes first and the figure after;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the moot and four for the late,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth goes by.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Grey in the nail, grey in the crease,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand goes home ahead of the man;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wrap the iron, turn the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape wipe the hand and say no name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wool on the iron, iron on the arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road goes up and the figure goes down;\end{quote}
