\begin{quote}\itshape the note stays where the knuckle left it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap in the bell is nobody’s.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the College borrowed the leaf at Sill with ink in two fingers of a soft cuff, and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh. Against \emph{I set the knuckle to the wall} he wrote \emph{the vessel was assessed}, true of every vessel in Sill and therefore of none; I have put my hand back underneath. Against \emph{what the district pays is not his hand} he wrote \emph{the deduction is one in twelve for every vessel of the Keeping}, which is what the notice says. I have left it standing; a clerk’s true sentence is not always an honest one. Where the space stands before the last verse he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a number. The place was not.

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank wrote \emph{no cost to officer} against the grey. I have not struck him out. A clerk’s false line is what the next reader ought to see.

The hearth-maid came up from Low Kiln with a birth-slate under her shawl and waited until the pigs were weighed before she put charcoal to the leaf. Her thick letters tore the paper in two places.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{look at the arm, not the face}: “I have washed that arm and held it when it was warm. You will not know whose it was. I shall.”

\item At \emph{write none and not a nought}: “We put the date where the word would go, and the date is not the word.”

\item At \emph{the hand goes home ahead of the man}: “There’s a stone in my house kept for whoever comes in behind. It isn’t for you. Don’t ask who it was for.”

\end{itemize}

I have set her words in the margin where she put them, because she would not have them on the face of the leaf where an officer might read them going past.

\subsection*{At the head and in the folds}

The grey at the head is mine, off the fingers I gave the figure to at Greybank, and it has gone in under the nails and will not come out. The filings in the gutter came out of the wool sleeve; there is always iron in the fold, and it has never drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the one kindness iron has shown this leaf. The green bead came off a girl at the Cross who leaned over with the sweetness still at her mouth and touched the corner; it tastes sweet in wet weather, and I have not washed it. The frost along one edge is from the Rim Road in Stone, and I have not gone over the words it thinned; a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The tallow thumb is mine. The tide-line along the foot came from the Waiting Room, where the collected are kept overnight and the damp gets into everything on a bench. The bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I have not written it back, and I have not forgotten it.

On the Last Day they burn the corners and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a sleeve.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wool keeps the heat out of the hand for one draw.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing else in this trade is kept.\end{quote}

I asked an old collector, a clerk from the College and a woman at my counter, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the two lines where they were written. The leaf goes back behind the table and the tube into its wool. Tomorrow a boy will come up from Greybank with a name he will not use on the road, and I shall set the knuckle to the wall before the iron and write the note before the College can strike it out. The grey will come off on the next leaf. I have stopped washing it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Price of a Dry Foot, Being the Market of the Standing Post and the Dues of the Boardwalks, the Peat Paths and the Marsh Roads, Cut on Count-Sticks and Copied into the South’s Letters}
\CRsheetheading{The Price of a Dry Foot, Being the Market of the Standing Post and the Dues of the Boardwalks, the Peat Paths and the Marsh Roads, Cut on Count-Sticks and Copied into the South’s Letters}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A board-man’s tally of the marsh’s prices and road-dues, cut as notches in a count-stick and written on oiled reed for a factor who cannot read a notch; the figure told below set above the figure taken here, one place left smooth and not noughted, the verbs put back where a borrowed hand took them out, two corrections in other hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch by Wade, who cuts the reeves’ sticks there and learned his south’s letters off a peat-tally clerk at Greybank, though he keeps his own accounts in notches; begun in Reed of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the Reed Cut of that year. It survives as one strip of oiled reed and two leaves of birch bark sewn with eel-sinew, folded and kept in a dry tin under the loose board at the Post; with a cross-notch cut at the head for a fine paid, a dry-mud thumb, a bog-water tideline along the gutter that has taken two figures clean off, a cross-cut from a reeve’s point, a reed-wolf’s tooth nick at the second corner, eel slime at the foot, the dark wet mark of a board laid across the third leaf, a grey Ash smear nobody will own, one knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first strip which the writer will not untie, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
I keep the boards at the Standing Post. Four planks lie across a cut no man has sounded, and a fifth place where no plank is laid, and a stick in my coat with a notch for every foot that went over and a mark for what it gave. A stranger comes up the marsh road, sets his boot on the first plank and asks what the crossing costs. I tell him the crossing costs nothing and the ground costs a bit. He takes this for a jest, because he is a dry man and believes ground lies still under him. I have watched dry men go down at the third plank. The water does not argue. It takes the boot and leaves the man to explain it to a reeve.

Fen Cant is not written. What is owed is cut in a stick: one notch for a bit, a deep notch for a mark, a cross-cut for a term, and a smooth place where nothing is entered. A factor’s clerk at Greybank can read my notches and cannot read what they are for, which is how I know they are honest. I write in the south’s letters so a reeve’s daughter may read this. The words that will not go into them I have tied in the margin, with no word for what the knots are for.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown, which comes north with the buyers, will not change at Greybank, and goes south again with them. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember. I have cut no notch for one. In sixteen years I have never seen an ember paid, and have seen a man try.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, written above my first line:} Ember: five marks. Reckoning entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left his figure standing and cut a smooth place beneath it. A thing nobody pays has no notch. A smooth place is where it belongs.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the Post keeps, and what it sells}

\emph{The left figure is what a man is told in Sill or at the Greybank beam. The right is what is given here, at the boards or in the cut. Nothing in the right column is weighed where a clerk can stand.}

Article — As told below — As given here\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone — a barrow cut by the buyer, or a day of bought breath; never by the stack, for a stack is a house’s winter\par

A winter stack for two rooms — not cried on any board — thirty marks below; here a term paid in work, and the term has a hook in its mouth\par

Reed bundle, an armful — not on any board — ask the arm that cut it; the arm knows weight and not cost\par

Hemp, a hank — 1 mark at Greybank — 3 bits, in kind; wet hemp weighs more and no buyer has ever noticed why\par

Eels, a basket — 3 bits smoked, 2 salted, at the Fishstairs — 2 bits at the boards, or a stick notched under an apron; the eel-women set their own figure and do not say it\par

Eel-sinew, a hank — not on any board — 1 bit; it sewed these leaves, and the seller would not take the bit back\par

Bog-cow, a milking — 24 marks below for the cow — a share of the morning’s milk, by the morning; no cow has ever stood on a board in this marsh\par

Salt herring — 2 bits at Sill — 3 bits; the salt has been up from the Sallow and knows it\par

Dried leeches, a dozen — 3 bits at the Fishstairs — not sold here; taken off children and counted, which is a different trade\par

Grey, a thimble, bottled — 60 marks in a Court jar, licensed — 4 bits at the Post, in an unmarked jar; the same grey in two vessels, one with a Court name and one with none\par

Thin return, paid by a household — 30 marks to the Court, in labour — a third of that, in eels and peat, and no questions about the source; what comes back is a stranger the house keeps\par

Bought breath, a season — not spoken of below — a term paid in iron or peat, entered in months; the hook is in the word the seller cannot say\par

A child named before the collector comes — no figure — a name said three times into the ground under the boards, which no stick can hold\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Cut deep in the margin:} The thin-return row is the only figure on this strip that a man from the Court asked me to change. He wrote \emph{one third of the Court tariff, subject to licence} above it. I cut \emph{no questions} beneath. A man who asks where the warmth came from has decided not to hear it.\end{quote}

There is a figure spoken in the yards at Mud End which is not the printed one. I have heard it and cut nothing for it. I have no beam to weigh it on, and a figure cut without a beam will be asked to read itself aloud at the Cross. Nobody in this marsh wants to stand under that bell.

\subsection*{What is paid in the mud and not entered}

What is taken — What I cut\par

A fine at the reeve’s post — peat to the winter stack — a notch; unpaid, it becomes a term, and the term becomes a measure\par

A feud settled by standing — the side that stands longest is called right by the mud — no figure; a reeve is chosen the same way\par

The draining of a cut — fever follows the ditch up into the water — nothing; the ditch pays and no slate carries it\par

A collector’s boots — children are taught those before their own names — not a due, but a thing every hut knows the price of\par

A name said at home — kept in the house, not entered on any roll — a door, which a knot in the margin stands for\par

The grey in the corner — gathered, bottled and sold at the Post — nothing swept and burnt and called dealt with; there is no Last Day under a board\par

A dry man is a dangerous man, we say, and say it to the water and not to him. He thinks a promise is a thing with a weight he can carry. Here a promise is tied in wool and left where the water can find it.

\subsection*{The dues of the marsh roads}

\emph{The figure asked is what a man is told at the road’s end. The notch is what left his pocket, or what left his back, which is the dearer of the two.}

Road and place — As asked — As cut on my stick\par

Boardwalk from the marsh road to the Post — 1 bit for a dry foot — 1 bit, or a stick notched for a wet one; I do not tell a stranger which planks bear\par

The fifth place at the Post — no plank, no crossing — a smooth place, not a nought; nobody steps on it and nobody’s foot is entered\par

East marsh road to Reedholt, a beast — 1 bit — 1 bit; a man on foot gives a date where a figure is asked and is let go on\par

The peat paths through the cut — paid in peat, by the arm-load — paid in peat, and the load is heavier going out than it came in\par

The smugglers’ paths — no name on any board — a stick left at the cut, notched by the bunch; no questions, and no name\par

The road up to Mud End and Sill, a beast — 1 bit at the marsh road — 1 bit, and the same beast weighed again at the Cross; a road has two ends and both have a hand\par

The road into the Quiet Acre — no gate, no due — nothing cut; there are wells and doorways there and nobody to come back through them\par

The Peat Line, going south into Sere — tribute in eels, paid at the Line — eels by the basket; the South calls it a tariff, and north of it a man is a neighbour, which costs less\par

The drain cuts, after the ditch — no figure — fever, paid by whoever dug and by nobody who entered it\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, against the fifth place:} Vacancy. Nil. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A nought is a notch cut deep enough to hold a figure. The fifth is a smooth place. I have not cut it, and he has not made it agree with anything.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a hand with a little gold in the ink, come down from Sere:} Bought breath entered as seasonal labour; thin return as a graded return, rate one third. \emph{In mine:} A season is a term with a hook in it, and a graded return is a stranger a house must keep. I have left both readings standing, as a board keeps the mark of the water under the mark of the foot.\end{quote}

The roads have two ends and the figures do not agree between them. The tally-man at Greybank cuts what goes out on the quay, the clerk at the Cross cuts what is paid under the pig-board, and I cut what is taken here. Between us a basket of eels is counted twice and a man once, which is the proportion the Court has always liked. The Hearth Road takes nothing at any gate, having taken it at home; the Salt Road calls its toll a contribution freely entered. I have cut neither. They are not roads of this marsh.

\subsection*{The song the board-men carry}

\emph{Said low going in over the Post, never coming out, and said to the plank or the water and not to a man. The last word falls and is not finished.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the dry foot and one for the wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a notch for the peat and a cross for the debt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the boards and a smooth for the fifth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mud keeps the count that the reeve does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bit at the Line and a bit at the plank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stick for the eels and a term for the stack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court writes the return and the river writes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who comes over is dry till he is not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say it to the board, say it down to the water,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the last word falls where the board has no foot;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name said at home is a door in the mud,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a notch in a stick is the whole of the account.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the factor’s hand, against the last line:} Three figures entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are four, and the fourth is a smooth place. He has put a nought where I left the stick bare. A nought can be carried away. The smooth place stays where it is.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The hands that are not mine}

The factor’s clerk writes upright and narrow and leaves the doer out of every sentence, as though a bit could pay itself and a foot could cross a board without a man in it. He put \emph{vacancy} where I keep a place and \emph{subject to licence} where I keep \emph{no questions}. I have set my notches under his words and left both standing. The Sere hand calls a term a season, which is a thing a house can empty and refill; I have called it a term, which a man carries in his mouth and cannot put down. A strip with three hands on it is the only kind a man at these boards will believe. A strip with one hand is a Court notice, and a Court notice has never told a man which plank will bear him.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The cross-notch at the head is the fine I paid last Reed, cut with the reeve’s own point so no wet sleeve takes it out; I have not said what it was for, and a cross-cut is the only signature this Post allows. The brown at my thumb is dry mud, not peat; I know the two the way a woman knows her own debt from another’s. The tideline in the gutter is bog-water from the morning the Post stood under and has taken two figures clean off the second leaf. I have not written them back, because a figure with two notches gone is a figure cut slowly, and everything here is cut slowly. The nick is a reed-wolf’s tooth, from a man who paid with his hand still on the knife. The slime at the foot came off a basket set down while a buyer was counting and a seller was not. The dark mark across the third leaf is the wet board laid on the strip to keep it from curling; it looks like a figure and is not one. The grey in the gutter is not mine and not the Court’s, and I have not swept it. The knot through the hole is mine, and holds the word that does not go into the south’s letters. There is no Last Day in a tin under a board.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps the foot. The stick keeps the debt. The mud keeps both and asks no figure.\end{quote}

I asked the reeve, an eel-trader, and a man come up from Greybank to count the winter peat, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The strip goes back into the tin under the loose board. Tomorrow a man will come up the marsh road, give me a date where I ask for a figure, set his foot where I do not tell him, and pay a bit for the dry and a notch for the wet, and by evening it will be a thing that was true. I shall cut it under the figure they told him and leave the space between the two.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Dry Tally at Reedholt, Being the Market of the East Marsh in Bits, Sticks and Kind, with the Dues of the Marsh Road, the Boardwalks and the Cuts, Kept Under an Apron and Copied at Greybank}
\CRsheetheading{The Dry Tally at Reedholt, Being the Market of the East Marsh in Bits, Sticks and Kind, with the Dues of the Marsh Road, the Boardwalks and the Cuts, Kept Under an Apron and Copied at Greybank}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An eel-trader’s tally of what the east marsh fetches and what the ways between its villages take, the figures named into an apron and not across a table, peat weighed at the dry set beside the same peat weighed at the quay, with a column left as a place and not a nought, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Kept by Meg Sedge, who buys eels on the marsh road and weighs peat at the dry in Reedholt, in the east marsh four leagues east of Sill; set down first in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, onto the back of a spoiled peat-tally at Greybank. It survives folded into oiled sacking under a loose board at the dry, sewn with eel-sinew, with a peat thumb ground into the head, a bog-water tideline that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, dried eel slime at the fore-edge, a fish-hook nick at the head, a grey Ash print along the gutter nobody will own, a press of wet sedge across the third leaf, a knot of grey wool tied through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, a small pale round place where a collector’s cuff was laid, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
I buy eels on the marsh road and weigh peat at the dry, and I keep the tally under my apron. A figure named aloud in this country grows legs. It walks to Greybank before the man who said it has got his boots dry, and comes back wearing somebody else’s debt. I say mine into the apron, to the creel, to the board under my foot; said looking at a person it becomes a bargain, and I have made enough bargains to know which of them I wanted.

The stick is the honest witness. A notch is still there when the paper has gone soft. Fen Cant is not written, so I set what I can in the south’s letters, learned off an eel-trader who could tally and could not read what he wrote. Where a word will not come I tie a knot in the margin and cut a notch in the edge. A notch is not a letter and a knot is not a figure. Both keep longer than a name.

Nothing here is free. A thing that costs nobody in a marsh has usually cost somebody who cannot write.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk out of Greybank, written above my first line:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written an ember as though a man could carry one up the marsh road in his boot. I have carried peat in my boot and never an ember. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of anybody in it. I put them back because a woman standing in water to her calf wants to know who is doing the keeping.\end{quote}

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty silver marks to a gold crown. Crowns come north with the Sere factor and will not change at Greybank, so a man takes the eels and leaves the crown, which is neither generosity nor an insult but the only arithmetic the marsh has ever understood. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember; no man has ever exchanged one, and I have left no column for them on my board.

\subsection*{The market at the dry}

\emph{What things fetched at the east-march dry between the last market of Stone and the Opening of the Slates. The left figure is what a man is told at Sill or the quay. The right is what is taken here, with the water still on the boots of the man who brought it.}

Article — As told below — As taken here\par

Peat, a barrow at the dry — 2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone — 1 bit in Grain, 3 in Stone; dear again at Greybank\par

Reed bundle, an armful, at the Reed Cut — not on any board — ask the arm that carried it; it knows weight and not cost\par

Hemp, a hank, from the east cut — not cried — 2 bits, and the hank goes soft if it has lain\par

Eels, a basket at the boards — 3 bits smoked, 2 salted — 2 smoked, 1 salted, named under the apron and never the same twice\par

Salt, a sack, up from the pans by Greybank — 3 marks at the quay — 4 marks; the extra mark is the road and nobody calls it a tax\par

Dried leeches, a dozen — 3 bits at the Fishstairs — 4 bits here, no questions; no slate asks where they came from\par

Grey, a phial, gathered and bottled at the dry — not sold in Grath — 4 bits, no name; the Court seals the same grey and sells it for sixty\par

Thin return, bought from a household — 30 marks, paid by the district — 10 marks, in peat and iron and labour, which is a third and still a return\par

Bought breath, a season — not spoken of below — paid in iron or in a term of peat; entered in months, not in marks\par

A child’s first bundle, cut in the dark at the Reed Cut — no figure — no figure; the child is not yet of the bog and goes again\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The peat row at Greybank stands at five bits in Stone and the same barrow is three here. The carter who pays both says the coal did not change and the road did. I have not set his words on the board.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I scraped a word I wrote beside the grey row and left the bare square where it was, which is the length of it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Paid in kind, and not entered}

These stand on the board with a space where the figure should be. The factor’s clerk has more than once put a nought in the space. A nought is a figure and can be carried away; the things below cannot, which is why the marsh keeps them.

What passes — What is given — What I write\par

A knot of grey wool tied for a debt — untied when the debt is paid — the knot, in kind; a knot has no ear and no rate\par

A count-stick cut at the dry — a notch for each barrow — the notch, which the rain does not take out\par

A name said at home before the collector comes — said into the ground beside the hut — nothing; a name at home is a door and not a figure\par

A reed-name said three times to the ground — once to the child, once to the pot, once under the boards — nothing; the third saying is for the child who cannot yet say it\par

A gold crown that will not change at Greybank — left in the coat and carried home — nothing; a thing nobody can spend is a thing somebody has paid for\par

\subsection*{The dues of the roads}

There are no roads in the Fen, only ways trodden long enough to be called roads by people who do not have to walk them. What follows is what the reeve’s man takes, or the factor’s, or the water. The difference between the two is the whole art of crossing a marsh.

\subsection*{The marsh road, east to Greybank}

Peat and eels go up it and salt and iron come back, and the factor’s clerk arrives with his soft cuffs. A cart makes it slowly in Silt and not at all when the high way is under.

Due\par

Cart with a load — 2 bits at the dry, 2 bits more at the quay\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Foot passenger — nothing on a dry day; 1 bit in Silt, when there is a bank to walk on\par

A drove of bog-cows — 4 bits, and the hides counted twice, once at each end\par

\subsection*{The boardwalks to the Standing Post}

The boards bear ten thousand feet and will bear a man’s if he puts his foot where the others went. Outsiders are put up on the walk and are not told which boards are safe, which is not cruelty but information nobody here has had reason to sell.

Due\par

A dry foot — 1 bit to the reeve’s man\par

A wet foot — a marked stick; a notch and no figure\par

A man who stands where he was shown to stand — nothing; the board minds him\par

A man from the Court asking which boards bear — 2 marks, paid before the question, not returned with the answer\par

\subsection*{The dry ways and the cuts}

No gate stands at any of them. Where the cart goes twice, the peat is counted twice, which the factor calls a load and the cut calls weather.

Due\par

Barrow going out to a cut — no gate; weighed at the dry\par

The same barrow weighed again at Greybank — 2 bits, which is the second weighing and not a second barrow\par

A drainage cut — no due; the fever that comes up after it is not entered\par

A ferry over a cut — 1 bit for the boat, nothing for the water\par

\subsection*{The road over the Quiet Acre}

North toward Mud End and Grath the way runs through the ground the Court calls the Empty Cantons and we call the Quiet Acre: wells with no hands at them and doorways in walls nobody lives behind. No reeve sits on that road and no due is asked, which is not the same thing as a road being free.

Due\par

Cart, beast or foot — nothing at any post, there being no post\par

A slate carried across the Acre — no fee; the figure arrives where the slate arrives\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A due is a figure somebody will stand behind and this road has nobody on it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Peat Line, south}

Sere’s northern advance stopped at the Line in Y.H. 634 and the reeves have paid tribute in eels ever since. A man goes down a neighbour and is counted a bowl when he gets there, and the crowns come back north and will not change at Greybank.

Due\par

Tribute in eels, at the Line — a basket of eels, paid by the reeves, entered by nobody\par

A man going south with a hide — 1 bit at the Acre end, and whatever the bowl asks at the other\par

Gold crown carried south — no due; the bowl takes it by emptying it\par

A man coming back from the Line — no due and no guarantee\par

\subsection*{The smuggler’s path, and the winter way}

Due\par

The path through the reedbed — no due and no guarantee; a man comes back with wet boots and no figure\par

The bog when it bears ice — nothing; no reeve will stand on it\par

The post at the Standing Post — no gate, only a board and a post cut with reeves’ marks\par

\subsection*{What no road charges}

These are not dues. No slate takes them and no factor enters them, and they are the reason a book like this has to be kept.

The mire-fever comes up after a drainage cut and burns a household in turns; a silt-leach draws as a collector’s tube draws, without the slate; a foot gone dark inside three turns of wool belongs to the woman who cannot stop working for it; a bought breath has a hook in the mouth that keeps a person from the word she would need to complain of it. No slate will stand behind these, and they are the only charges a household always meets.

\subsection*{The song the dry-keepers carry}

\emph{Sung low through the nose on the marsh road, with the last word dropped into the mud and not finished. Never sung at the dry while the factor’s clerk is in hearing of the second part.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to the mark and twenty to the crown,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the crown stays north and the eel goes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the board and a stick for the wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dry foot pays what the dry foot gets.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A barrow at the dry and a barrow at the bank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the factor counts twice and the reeve counts once;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a knot in the wool and a notch in the stick,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name said at home where the slate cannot pick.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the boards and a fifth for the slack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is a place and not a toll to pay;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Line takes an eel and the Court takes a figure,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mud takes the rest and wants no slate.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk strikes the verbs out. Where I write \emph{the marsh takes}, he writes \emph{was taken}, as though a cold had no hand in it. I put my words back underneath. A figure with nobody in it is a figure that will be paid twice.

The Sere factor writes in ink with a little gold in it and calls everything a rate: \emph{seasonal rate} against the peat, \emph{market rate} against the eels, figures where I had put an apron. I left both standing. A house of Sere has never stood in water to its calf at three in the morning.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is peat and I know it from Ash the way a woman knows her own debt from another’s: both stick to the hand, and one stays in the house after you have gone. I have not washed it off. The tideline took two words clean off the second leaf; I have not written them back, because a tally with two words gone is a tally said slowly, which is how everything here is said. The eel slime at the fore-edge is mine, from holding the leaf with the hand that held the creel. The fish-hook nick came off a man paying for six eels and charged for five, or the other way, which he never settled and I never entered. The press of sedge is from the morning we lay flat in the cut until a beast’s pushing had gone past. The knot through the hole holds a word that will not go into the south’s letters; I will not untie it. The small pale round place is where a collector’s cuff was laid while I told a girl to eat and she would not. There is no Last Day under a loose board at the dry.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tally keeps what was weighed. The knot keeps what was owed. The road keeps the boot and gives back the man, or a thinner one.\end{quote}

I asked a reeve, an eel-trader come up from the quay, and a woman whose term is not out, and had three answers and no hand.

The leaf goes back into the sacking under the board. Tomorrow the carts come east with salt and a Sere factor with gold he cannot spend, and a number named under an apron will by evening be a thing that was true. I shall set it beside the figure they told and leave the space between them as it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Ebb, Being the Order of the Return as the Quay of Vhal Keeps It}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Ebb, Being the Order of the Return as the Quay of Vhal Keeps It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said over the salted boat at the turning of the ebb, the dipper reading from the bollard and the women of the boats answering; with the rubrics of the quay, seven stations and their answer, a Council clerk’s correction, and two sayings at the foot that will not agree · Written at the Quay in Vhal in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Ova Rill, a dipper of the Salt Pans under Neri Sail, on the back of a tide-tally spoiled by a wet thumb in the tide-tally house; borrowed on a market morning in Ash and corrected by a clerk of the Council of Tides; copied forward in Silt of Y.H. 813 into a quire of salt-paper kept in a dry tin among what the house calls nothing. It survives soft at the fold and furred with white salt, with a tar thumb at the head, the print of a wet rope along the gutter, a nick from a fish-hook, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the lower corner, a peck from a brine-gull that took the corner and not the word, and one line of the fourth station eaten away by damp, which the writer has not tried to write again.\par}\medskip
I am the second dipper at the pans and I have written this where I was told not to, on the back of a tally Kett spoiled with a wet thumb. A dipper’s business is nets at dawn and the draw; a net is blessed by being trailed in the sea, not by having words said over it. The women of the boats asked me for a saying they could keep in a dry place, because a prayer carried in the mouth changes in a wet season and a prayer on salt-paper goes the way of a law, which everybody in this port calls a virtue and I call weather. What follows is what we say over a boat going out on the ebb. The clerk’s words are left standing under mine, where he put them.

The tar at the head is my own; I hold the leaf with the hand I use for the net-rope and did not know I had marked it. The rope print came off the bollard when a woman leaned over to see what the fourth station said. The hook nick is not mine and I have left it. The green bead came off the Glaze Cliffs in a girl’s palm and stayed in the fold when she closed it. The gull took the upper corner while the leaf lay on the stone and brought back a peck the width of a nail; he took no word, which was a mercy and cost somebody a crust. The damp has eaten the sixth line of the fourth station. I know what it said. Knowing a thing is not the same as having it, and I have not written it again.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The boat is sealed before anyone speaks. Salt in the seams, weight in the belly, and not a word over the salt until the seams are stopped.

\item Read at the turning of the ebb, not at the flood. The flood brings things back. We are not asking for that.

\item The dipper stands at the bollard with the net-rope in her hand. Do not trail the net in the ebb. Nets are blessed at dawn, when the draw runs against the wind.

\item The answer belongs to the women who held the share. A man come aboard has half an opinion; say his answer twice and count it once.

\item Watch until the boat is out of sight. That is held to be enough. Watching longer is another trade and has no name in this port.

\item If an officer of the Court is on the Quay, give him the tally and not the leaf. The leaf is not a document and the tide will not authenticate it.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{The dipper reads. The women answer. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not an argument.}

\subsection*{I. Of the salt}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Sallow was before the quay and will be after it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It lies the colour of skimmed milk and gives back nothing white.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt was here before anybody entered a share.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pan takes what the wind leaves and writes no figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A thing with no figure cannot be owed.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The sea keeps its own account. We have watched him out of sight.

\subsection*{II. Of the draw}

\begin{quote}\itshape The warm goes out on the draw, against the wind, every year,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and every year the Council is told it is a surprise.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At dawn we trail the net and do not ask it to come back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes seaward is not stolen. It has gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who has gone is a man who is not here to be entered.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The sea keeps its own account. We have watched him out of sight.

\subsection*{III. Of the boat}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seal him in a boat and not in a slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt in the seams, weight in the belly, his share at the stern.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boat has no house and no roll, only a share and an ebb.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What kept him up while he lived now carries him where he goes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not scrape the salt off when the boat comes back empty. It was his.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The sea keeps its own account. We have watched him out of sight.

\subsection*{IV. Of the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape On land they bring a cold tube and call it the Return.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Here is no arm to set the iron to and no slate that will stay dry.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write him on the water, where the writing is true and goes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clean hand cannot follow him. The wave has no cuff to wash.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the damp has taken the sixth line. I have left the space the length of it. A clerk put a figure in that space once and the rain had it away before noon, which is the ordinary order of things here.}

\emph{Answer:} The sea keeps its own account. We have watched him out of sight.

\subsection*{V. Of what takes}

\begin{quote}\itshape The gull takes the coal and enters nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The salt-thing taps the hull where the store lies.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Waste takes what nobody kept and has no clerk to answer to.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A boat goes out warm and comes to nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody pays for the going. That is the whole of the bargain.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The sea keeps its own account. We have watched him out of sight.

\subsection*{VI. Of the watching}

\begin{quote}\itshape Watch until the boat is out of sight. That is held to be enough.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Watch no longer. A sea that keeps a man is not a sea that gives him back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the tide-name over the water. If you have none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave the place where the name would stand and let the ebb take the place too.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name kept by the water is kept somewhere, which is not the same as kept.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The sea keeps its own account. We have watched him out of sight.

\subsection*{VII. Of the coming back}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who dies at sea has already returned.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He comes back as the tide comes: at the hour, not in the body.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He comes back to the Quay and not to a house.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not set a place for him. Do not sweep the salt where he stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We say the words, turn from the bollard and go home to our own fires.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The sea keeps its own account. We have watched him out of sight.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning with ink in two fingers and the cuffs of his coat gone soft from washing. He took the verbs out, which is what they teach in the counting house, and set a mark against what was not for sale.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At I, against \emph{the sea keeps its own account}, he wrote: \emph{No entry required.} Under it, in mine: \emph{That is what the sea says. I have heard it said at this bollard for thirty years and never once by a clerk.} Both stand.

\item At III, against \emph{a boat has no house and no roll}, he wrote: \emph{one boat-share, current; holder deceased, share not returned.} Under mine: \emph{The share goes to the daughter and the man goes to the Sallow. Those are two journeys and only one of them has an entry.}

\item At IV, against \emph{no slate that will stay dry}, he put a small stop and wrote: \emph{witness sufficient}. Under mine: \emph{We watched him out of sight. The Council has made that sufficient, which is the same thing said by a man who was not there.}

\item At V, against \emph{nobody pays for the going}, he wrote: \emph{cost to district, nil}. It is true in the figure and false in the room. I have left it.

\item At the answer, where I had set seven answers, he put a round nought and wrote: \emph{one answer, entered seven times}, which is a true thing in a language nobody on the boats speaks.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them; I put them back because a woman at the bollard wants to know which hand to take the rope with. He has entered the share and not the going, which is exactly what the Council does with both.

\subsection*{What the women put in the margin}

The thick hand is Omra’s, who holds an eighth through her mother and will not say how many before company. I have copied it as it stands.

At III, against \emph{his share at the stern}: \emph{The stern was her mother’s before him. Put him where she sat.}

At IV, where the line is gone, she wrote a tide-name and pressed it with a nail so the damp would not take it. I cannot read it and she has not written it again.

At VII: \emph{We said this of my brother. We meant we should not have to enter him. That is a mercy and it is not one.}

At the answer: \emph{He did not come back. We watched him out of sight. I have said both and will not make them agree.}

\subsection*{At the head and along the gutter}

The white along the gutter is salt and not Ash; there is no Ash in Vhal that has not been bought and sold. A factor come up from Greybank asked me once whether it was the grey the northern houses leave in their corners. I told him it was salt. He said he could sell me either, and laughed as though he had invented the weather. The green at the lower corner is not glass from our furnaces, which is blown clear; it came off the Cliffs and was sweet on the girl’s tongue before she put it in the fold. I have not washed it. A girl who tastes the Cliffs is either very young or very tired of being warned.

\subsection*{At the foot}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ebb takes and does not keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea keeps its own account.\end{quote}

Both lines are struck and both stand. I have asked three people whose hand it was and had two answers and no hand. The leaf goes back into the tin with the tide-name pressed deep and the damp where the damp has always been. Next ebb we shall read the seven stations and watch a boat out of sight, and the clerk will come with his wet thumb and take the tally, and the tide will do what it has always done, which is go out and not come back the same.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Eleven Months, Being the Sayings of the Under-Vessed of Keld, Gathered at the Shaft Mouth and Glossed for a Man Who Has Never Been Bought}
\CRsheetheading{The Eleven Months, Being the Sayings of the Under-Vessed of Keld, Gathered at the Shaft Mouth and Glossed for a Man Who Has Never Been Bought}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A windlass-man’s gathering of the proverbs, month-words, rope-maxims and bitter small sayings of the bought hands of the First Seam, set in Grathic letters though the sayings come in four tongues; the sayings in the short speech of the deep, the glosses in the writer’s own charcoal, a mine-reeve’s red cross, a Court survey-clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a southern word left standing where no northern word would come, one note in a clamp-master’s coal, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at Keld Keep in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Orv of the Rope, a windlass-man who has lowered and raised men at the shaft mouth for two and thirty years, from bought hands waiting their turn at the weigh and from those who sat by the lamp-room door with a month left in them; written in charcoal on the back of a spoiled month-tally, cut once at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, carried down the Rim Road with the first carts of Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a voided grain-warrant. It survives folded into a tarred rope-glove, with coal smut ground into the head, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, iron filings caught in the gutter off the clamps, a warm-stone shaving that kept a little heat through a night on the stone floor, a frost-feather pressed flat that was gone by noon, a tallow thumb, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the knife-cut standing in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s\par}\medskip
I work the windlass at the mouth. Two and thirty years I have let men down and drawn them up, and never once asked a man his name before I had him by the rope. The rope comes first. After that there is time enough for the slate.

Below the floor they work the stone with men bought for a term, condemned men and bought breath, whom the Grathic buyers call under-vessed. Their lives are reckoned at eleven months, a year with the month of the buying taken off. I asked the mine-reeve once what became of a man at the end of the eleven and he said the term was expiring, a phrase that lets a man go on writing. The men say other things. A saying said at the weigh goes up with the figure and is not entered, and the figure goes up alone.

Keldish is cut in bone and does not travel, and the men below speak four tongues besides. I have put everything in Grathic letters and left a southern word standing where ours would not come. Say these to the rope, the iron, the lamp, the floor, never to a man who is standing in front of a slate. Said looking at a buyer, a sentence becomes a petition, and there is no petition in any of them.

\subsection*{Of the eleven months}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “They buy eleven months and call it a year. The month of the buying is the one you keep.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A life bought for the deep is entered at eleven, and a man who lasts fourteen is entered at eleven still, because the figure is for the life bought and not the life lived. The month taken off at the buying is the only one he keeps, and no slate has found where he put it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A month paid for before you warm it is a month already gone.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said of advances, of grain, and of a man given his term in the morning and sent down before he has eaten. The buyers below do not cheat by false figures. They cheat by early ones.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A term is a rope with a knot at the far end. You cannot see the knot from this side.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — I have watched a man count his months on one hand and keep the other shut. When the mine-reeve says a term is expiring, he is not lying; it is the only word the roll has for a thing that ends.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Eleven in the slate and one in the mouth. The one in the mouth is not entered.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The twelfth is a man’s own because nobody thought to ask for it. It is spent saying the sayings, which is perhaps why the sayings matter to them.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, written above this one:} Term eleven. Value retained.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has taken the buying and the keeping out and put a value where a month stood. The value travels well. The month stays where the man said it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the rope and the count}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The rope asks your weight. It does not ask your name.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the weigh the name goes down on a slate and the body goes down on the rope, and the two arrive in different places. A man who steps off the board is counted by whatever the board says.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Give your number before your name if you have one. If you have none, give the month.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A free Keldishman states what he holds before he says who he is, and is sent back to the foot of the post if he forgets. A bought man has no number to give, his measure being held in law by the man who paid for him, so he gives the term. The same courtesy, at a higher price.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} No measure arises.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine:} True in his hand. In this one the man is standing here, which is a thing his sentence has no room for.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A clay-name is a pot with another man’s mark fired into it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A bought hand is named by the house that holds him and the old name is forbidden. I have heard a man answer to a name the way a pot answers flat: the sound comes, and nothing is behind it. A southern man said the forbidden name is written inside a bowl that the slave is never allowed to look into. I have left his word standing.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Ask the arm that carried it. The arm knows the weight and not the buyer.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — This one came up from the reed country and has been said in the deep ever since. An arm that has carried a shift knows what went into it and nothing of the man who sold the season. An honest answer, useless at a weigh.}

\subsection*{Of the iron and the stone}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Cold iron takes from a bought man and takes from a free man. It does not ask which account to enter.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The tube, the clamp, the blade across a fever: one iron, one hunger. A free man’s loss goes into a slate. A bought man’s goes nowhere, there being no account of his to carry it, which is the cheapest way of taking a thing there is.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A clamp on a free hand is a trade. A clamp on a bought hand is holding.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The same iron, the same bite, the same fortnight in which the arm is of no use. The free man has chosen it and the bought man has not, and the floor calls both by one name. Nobody on the floor has ever corrected that sentence.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Nine clamps go to the floor. The tenth goes to the stone. We are the tenth.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The tenth hangs behind the board and is not taken down, and no man below will say what it does at the stone. The bought hands say this of themselves. The masters do not agree and do not forbid it, which is how a floor keeps two readings of one thing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a clamp-master’s coal, the letters wide apart as though cut with a chisel:} A bought man is not a floor man. Keep him off my board. I have had one die on it and will not have another.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He is right about the board and wrong about the men. They were on it before he was. I have left the line where he put it.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The lamp is paid for out of somebody’s month. Do not warm your hands at it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A warm-stone takes from the lamp’s account and somebody down the shaft paid for the lamp. A bought man has no account to pay with, so he warms at another man’s cost and knows it. Said to the lamp, not to the man holding it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “When the lead smells sweet, the mountain has made up its mind already.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In the lower galleries the Warm comes up through the stone in a lethal flood and the only warning is the smell of hot lead. A man who has smelt it does not say the saying again.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The stone coughs and the man coughs. The stone is not asked to stop.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The dust of the Ninth gets into a man and he brings it up in the morning in a colour he will not discuss. The leech steams it under a cloth and sends him back to the same gallery.}

\subsection*{Of who pays and who is named}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Sere buys a man whole. Keld buys him by the month. Both pay somebody else.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Crowns come north with the mercenaries and go south again with them, and a crown will not buy a month in this mountain. The southern buyers want the shape of a life; the northern buyers want eleven pieces of one. Neither asks the man which he would rather be.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A Fen man sells a season. A Keldishman buys one. Neither asks the man what a season is.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Bought breath is common in the Fenmarch, a term of a season or a year to repay a peat-debt, and the hook in it is in the mouth so a man cannot say the word he would need to complain. I have had Fenny men down here counting by the drying of peat and northern men counting by the swell of a hand.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The clay man says one in twelve. The stone man says the number first. The bought man says yes.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — This is the dry joke of the shaft mouth and nobody laughs at it twice. The printed figure belongs to the low countries, the number cut in the arm belongs to Keld, and the bought man has neither. He has the yes, which is the only thing of his that is never entered.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} Consent is recorded.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine:} He has entered the yes and left out the man who had no other word. That is the whole talent of that hand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the dead who stay down}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “They wall the dead in facing the deep seam and add a number to a slate nobody reads aloud.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — There is no drawing and no pouring below the Keep. The mountain keeps its own, the surveyors say, and the figure goes into a book turned face down. A bought man says the mountain keeps its own and does not keep him, which is the same sentence turned over.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “No return for a man who was never banked. The stone has him and the slate has a figure.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The dead of the deep are not brought up for the Weighing. Somewhere above a household may be paid for a life it never saw; I have never asked who. The stone has the better claim of the two.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A man goes down by the rope and comes up by the count. There is a third way and nobody speaks of it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — I know the two ways of this windlass. The men below know a third and have a sentence for it, but they say it only when the lamp is out, and I have not set it here. A saying that needs the dark to be said is not a saying for a book.}

\subsection*{The month-song}

\emph{Said low at the weigh, going down and not coming up, by men whose term has less than a tend in it. The place after the last line is the length of a name, and no singer has filled it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the month they paid and one for the month they kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope goes down and the rope comes up and neither knows a name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine on the board and one at the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tenth is the one that stays below.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven in the slate and one in the teeth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cold comes up and the warm goes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the lamp who paid --- it will not say,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that held it knows.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We give no number, we give no name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we give the month we have left to stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the deep seam keeps what the deep seam takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure goes up where the man does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{[a place the length of a name]}\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The place is left because a name said below travels up the rope and arrives at a slate, which is a journey no bought name is permitted to make. A survey-clerk of the Court put a round nought in it and wrote vacancy underneath. A nought is a number. He has made a month into a figure and a name into a hole, and both travel well and arrive empty.}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A survey-clerk borrowed the leaves at Greybank with ink settled in two fingers of his soft cuff. He strikes the doer out as though a doer were a thing a man could spill. At \emph{the month of the buying is the one you keep} he set \emph{term: eleven; value retained}. At \emph{we give no number} he wrote \emph{no measure arises}. At \emph{the bought man says yes}, \emph{consent is recorded}, the truest and coldest sentence on the leaf.

The mine-reeve set a red cross against the eleven, meaning the figure has been checked and is to stand. It does not mean the man stood it. The clamp-master’s coal is the only hand down here that argues with the floor instead of the paper. I have set it above the saying and mine under it, as a board keeps two weights and chooses neither.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is coal off the sleeve I wipe the rope with, and no wet sleeve takes it out. The lead bead in the fold rolled out of the Ninth Gallery and was laid here by a man who went away without it. The filings in the gutter are off the clamps. The shaving kept its heat through one night on the stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The frost was a feather on the well lip and was gone by the time I found the leaf. The tallow thumb is mine, from holding the tally down in the draught up the shaft. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying in a room where men are counted; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day under the Keep. The knife-cut is where a word would not come, and a notch is still there when paper has gone soft.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape They bought the month. They did not buy the sentence.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rope carries the weight. The saying carries the name.\end{quote}

I asked a man with a month left, a surveyor come down from the stones, and the master of the floor, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaves go back into the rope-glove and the glove on its nail beside the windlass. Tomorrow the carts come up with the winter’s lead, and a man will give me a month where another man would give a number, and I shall write down what he gives and not ask him which he means.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Eleven Weeks, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Keeping Concerning the Rising in Low Kiln and the Forty-One, with the List Set Against the Corners That Were Not Swept}
\CRsheetheading{The Eleven Weeks, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Keeping Concerning the Rising in Low Kiln and the Forty-One, with the List Set Against the Corners That Were Not Swept}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A chronicler’s extract from the annals of the Keeping, copied from a Hearthseat original; the year-entries in Ledgerhand, Pell Varr’s list entered as it stands, the answer of the hearth-maids kept in the margin, one song carried out of Low Kiln, and two hands of correction, one of which no hand will own · Written at the Hearthseat in the College of Assessors in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the chronicle of the Keeping, who signs nothing and calls himself only the continuator; copied from an original of Y.H. 669 kept face down in the roll-room and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the chronicle drawer under the narrow window that looks toward the Keel: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a soot print where a leaf was held too near the Hearth grate, a drip of tallow gone hard as a fingernail, slate dust in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the continuator did not make and will not sweep, one line struck through and written again underneath in his own hand, and one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College which takes the verbs out.\par}\medskip
I keep the chronicle of the Keeping, which is not the same thing as the chronicle of Grath. Grath writes what happened, when it can get a man to stand still long enough to ask. We write what was entered. Where the two disagree we set the entry down and leave the gap where it fell, because a chronicler who closes a gap has begun to write a sermon, and a sermon gets copied oftener than an account and lasts longer.

This chapter is the hardest in the book to copy, and not because of the figures. The figures are neat. It is the things that stand beside them that will not go into a year-entry, and so I have put them in the margin. A margin is the only place in a chronicle where a silence is allowed to stand.

\subsection*{The years as the roll-room has them}

\emph{Copied from the Hearthseat original, kept face down. The entries are in Ledgerhand. I have put the verbs back where I found them taken out and left the College’s hand standing above mine.}

\textbf{Y.H. 668.} In Low Kiln a levy was taken of ninety children’s warmth, for one whole return. No household in Sill could say whose return it was. There followed eleven weeks of disorder in the district, in the course of which the peace of the Keeping was disturbed and certain collectors were prevented from the discharge of their office. Entered as \emph{a disturbance of the peace}.

\textbf{Y.H. 669.} Assessor-Marshal Pell Varr came up from the Hearthseat with twelve collectors and a list. Forty-one persons dead, all of them spent in the keeping of the peace. The rising ended in the ninth week of his sitting. Entered as \emph{peace restored, account standing}.

\textbf{Y.H. 675.} Certain survivors of the rising first named in a Court file as being of the sealed opinion.

\textbf{Y.H. 683.} Quiet ash sold openly in the Hearthseat for the first time, by licence of the factor.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of the College, against the first entry:} The levy was for a whole return. The return is entered at Greybank. Strike \emph{no household could say whose}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. The return is entered at Greybank, which is true, and no household in Sill could say whose it was, which is also true, and the two truths have different shapes and must not be laid over one another. A man who writes the annals learns early that the word \emph{disturbance} costs less than the word \emph{children}. The word is chosen for the same reason a potter chooses a thin glaze, because it covers and because it is cheap.

\subsection*{The list}

Varr came with twelve collectors and a list. The list was the heavier thing he carried, and the only one he ever set down. It was made in the Hearthseat before he left, so that the names stood in a clean hand while the men who bore them were still going about their work in Low Kiln. This is not a cruelty. It is a method, and the method has a name in the College, which is \emph{economy of office}. I entered the words as they were spoken to me by a clerk who was present at the reading and has since been returned whole.

The list, as it stands in the roll-room, has four headings.

Heading — Number entered — What the heading covers\par

Persons taken for the whole return — 90 — Children of Low Kiln, entered under their houses\par

Collectors detailed to the district — 12 — Named, with their districts after them\par

Persons spent in the keeping of the peace — 41 — Named in the body of the report, not on the list\par

Weeks from the levy to the restoring of the peace — 11 — Entered as nine weeks sitting, plus two weeks travelling\par

Forty-one dead, all of them spent in the keeping of the peace. The phrase is exact, and it is the only phrase in these annals I have ever had to read twice to believe. A man spent in the keeping of the peace is a man who died while other men were being made to keep it. The College has weighed the phrase and finds it sound. I set it down as it came and have not tried to make it kinder.

There is one line in the report that I cannot place. It stands between the twelve names and the forty-one, in Varr’s own hand, and it reads \emph{and the corners also}. I asked three men of the College what the corners were, and got the same answer three times, which was that a corner is where two walls meet. This is true and is not an answer.

\subsection*{The corners that were not swept}

The hearth-maids of Low Kiln say nothing. I have tried four times to get it onto the page. Silence is not an entry, and the College takes verbs out of anything that is not one; in the end I wrote the only thing I could write, which is what the district does with the grey.

On the Last Day the ash in a Grath corner is left where it lies and burnt in the morning. That is the ordinance and the observance both. In the years after Y.H. 669, word came up from Sill that in the houses of Low Kiln the grey was not burnt in the morning either, but left in its ridge along the skirting board into Seed and past it. I could not get a man to say this before a witness. I asked a woman who had carried birth-slates in that district for thirty years and she gave me a date for answer, which is what they do when the thing asked for is not a date.

In the chronicle of the Keeping — What came up from Low Kiln\par

Forty-one spent in the keeping of the peace — Ninety taken, and no household paid them back\par

Eleven weeks of disorder — The kilns stood cold eleven weeks\par

Peace restored, account standing — The corners were not swept\par

The matter is closed — The grey is still there\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of the College, against the third row of the right-hand column:} Corners are swept in due order on the morning after the Last Day. Enter as observance kept.\end{quote}

He has entered it as observance kept. Both rows stand. The ridge of Ash is the only entry in this chapter that cannot be corrected, because it is not a figure and not a word and has no verbs for him to take out. It is a grey line about two thumbs wide which turns the corner of a room without a break, and which somebody has to have put there, because Ash does not lay itself along a skirting board in the shape of a kept thing.

I set the hearth-maids’ answer in the margin rather than under the heading, because it is not an answer to the question the chronicle asks. The chronicle asks how many and when. They answer with a corner. It is the custom of that district to answer a number with an object, and an officer who does not know the custom goes away thinking he has been refused, when in fact he has been given the only true thing that was in the room.

\subsection*{The song out of Low Kiln}

\emph{Taken down from a woman of the drying racks who had not been in the district in Y.H. 668 and had learned the song from those who were. Sung low, at the washing, not at the fire.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ninety went up in a grain-cart’s belly,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven weeks and the kilns stood cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve came up with a list in a clean hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the list had the names before they were told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Forty-one spent in the keeping of the peace,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says, in a hand that never shook;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners and four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where the ninety stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not sweep. We do not burn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We lay the grey where the promise fell.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Court has a word for the thing we keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we have a corner, and that serves as well.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back, come back, little pot of the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the seam keeps the word that the mouth denied;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey is not dirt and the corner is not dumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it holds the count that the slate would not hold.\end{quote}

The woman would not sing the last verse until the fire was banked, and would not say who made the song. I have left both things as I found them. A song that is sung at the washing and not at the fire is a song about work, and work is a thing a household can remember without being told to remember it, which is more than can be said of an entry.

\subsection*{The sealed opinion}

From the survivors of those eleven weeks came the people the Court calls Unbanked. They call themselves nothing at all, which is a hard thing for an office to enter, and the College has entered it as \emph{refusal of designation}. Their argument is old and I have set it down once, plainly, because it is the only part of this chapter that the chronicle has had to make room for: if the world must be kept, let it be kept perfectly, so that nothing leaks, nothing is owed, and no one can give anything away. A world of unbreakable vessels would be a world of the walking dead. That is their saying, not mine. The Court’s public answer is that they are mad, and the answer is entered in the Weighing notices, where the figure one in twelve is also printed.

The Court’s private answer is in a sealed file in this building, two rooms from where I write. I have not opened it and am not likely to be asked to. There are doors in the Hearthseat that a chronicler passes every day and is never required to go through, and a man who keeps the annals learns to measure a room by the doors it has as well as by the walls.

In Y.H. 683 quiet ash was sold openly here for the first time. I am old enough to have seen the first phial go over the counter and to have known the woman it was for. I have not put her name in the entry. She paid in marks, which is a thing anyone can write down, and with something she said at the counter, which is not.

\subsection*{What the College hand did}

Where I wrote of the ninety children that they were taken and not returned, a narrower hand set \emph{the account stands} above and left mine under it, in the manner that takes a verb for a thing a man might smuggle in a cuff. Where I wrote \emph{the corners were not swept}, it wrote \emph{observance kept}. Where I wrote that Pell Varr came with a list already made, it wrote \emph{precautions taken}. It is a careful hand and a clean one, and it has never once in this chapter changed a figure.

There is a line at the foot in a hand I do not know, struck through twice and written again underneath, and it says: \emph{They took the warmth and left the account, and the account is the only thing that came back whole.} I have copied it as it stands. The hand that wrote it wanted to be found and did not want to be known, which is the state of most hands that write in the margin of this book.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The iron-gall at the head is mine; a chronicler who keeps a quire open through a tend marks himself before he marks the page. The soot came off the grate on a night when the Hearth was low and I held a leaf too near to read it. The hard drop of tallow is from the lamp in the roll-room and has been there since the first copy. The slate dust in the gutter came off a surveyor come up from Keld who leaned over my table with the Rim still on his cuffs and would not sit down. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and is not the College’s. I have had this leaf four years and have never swept it, and if the factor asks me why a chronicler leaves dirt on a chronicle I shall tell him it is entered as observance kept, which is a phrase he will accept without looking up.

The leaves go back into the drawer. The annals go on, as annals do, and next tend I copy the quay tallies from Greybank and after that the Weighing figures. The ninety have no row in the figures and the corners have no heading, but the grey turns the corner without a break and the levy is still read at one in twelve in every Court room in Sarn. I have put both down where they stand. A chronicler does not settle a thing by writing it. He keeps the place where it stood, so that the next hand has something to copy besides the clean version.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Line of Figures and the Line of Squares, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Cantons}
\CRsheetheading{The Line of Figures and the Line of Squares, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Cantons}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An annalist’s extract from the chronicle of the Keeping, being the account of the Empty Cantons; copied from a Hearthseat original and set beside a surveyor’s field note, a Fen song, and two hands of correction in the margin · Written at Greybank in the factor’s house in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by the keeper of the annals there (the office stands on the roll, the hand does not); copied from an original kept face down in the roll-room of the Hearthseat. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the annals drawer beside the winter tallies: a brown iron-gall thumb at the head, slate dust in the gutter, a tar print from the quay along the fore-edge, a dried Fen reed folded between the second and third leaves, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, one correction in the narrow hand of a clerk of the College and one in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the annals in the factor’s house at Greybank. The office stands on the roll and the hand does not; when the factor wants a name for the hand he writes \emph{the roll-room}, which is as much a name as a man with no house is allowed to have. What follows I copied in the last tend of Stone, in the Thin Year, from an original kept face down in the Hearthseat, because the man who set it there did not care to have it read standing up. I have put verbs back where I found them taken out. A chronicle with no verbs in it is a thing a man can read aloud in a clean voice and go home believing, and I have had to stand at this table and listen to too many clean voices.

The Empty Cantons lie sixty leagues south of Sill, between Grath and the Fenmarch, on no road a cart can make in a day. A man can walk into them, and several have, and come back with nothing to tell except the lie of the ground. There are roads still rutted where no wheel has gone in eight hundred years; wells with the stones laid tidy about them and the water down out of sight; doorways standing where the walls have gone; and in every third doorway a square of bare clay where something used to hang. The Fen reeves call the place the Quiet Acre. The Court calls it the Empty Cantons. The temple calls it nothing at all, and that is how a place is made to disappear.

\subsection*{The account as it stands in the roll-room}

\emph{Copied from the Hearthseat original, Title the First, Of the Cantons Beyond the South Road. The figures are in Ledgerhand. The squares are in the original; I have set the word square within them so that no copyist fills them with a nought.}

Year — Hearth-fires — Souls on the roll — Embers entered — Whole returns\par

Y.H. 1 — 1,204 — 6,110 — — — —\par

Y.H. 3 — 1,204 — 6,106 — 36 — 6\par

Y.H. 12 — 1,198 — 6,088 — 192 — 41\par

Y.H. 40 — 1,190 — 6,061 — 240 — 60\par

Y.H. 41 — square — square — square — square\par

Y.H. 100 — square — square — square — square\par

Y.H. 418 — square — square — square — square\par

Y.H. 812 — square — square — square — square\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of a clerk of the College, against the five rows of squares:} Squares are not entries. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A square is where a figure stood and was taken away; a nought is a figure put in its place. He has put noughts in the squares and the column balances. That is how I know it does not.\end{quote}

The figure the College likes is six whole returns in the third year after the lighting, which is the year the first Returns were recorded and the year the roll begins to have something in it worth counting. I have not checked the addition of that column, and I have learned not to.
