The last time a clerk of this office added a column he got a number that would not agree with the printed one, and the factor told him to copy the printed one again, in a better hand.

\subsection*{What the temple tells the children}

The temple tells it this way. The Cantons were taken up in the first Returns, and their people are whole somewhere, though no record says where. The cost of those first whole returns was entered against a province, and the province is this one. I set that down because it is written in the roll-room and not because I can say what it means. A chronicler who explains a figure has begun to write a sermon, and a sermon is a thing that gets copied more often than an account.

The oldest ledger says only that the fires went out in a season of no frost. The words \emph{returned elsewhere} were added by a hand that writes with its verbs taken out, and every copy since has been smoother than the one before. I have set the smooth words under the rough ones and left both standing. When the temple voice reads them at a Weighing it makes a mercy of a line of squares, and a household hears a mercy and goes home, which is the whole art of that voice.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a hand I take to be a temple hand, struck through} went out in a season of no frost \emph{and written above,} were gathered into the Hearth. \emph{Both stand. A hand that strikes a thing out and writes above it is a hand that wants the thing gone and cannot bear to lose the place where it was.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the ground keeps}

Three surveyors have walked the Cantons that I know of. Two went for the Court and one went for the Keldish, and none put his name to the account, which is the first thing the three accounts agree on.

The river road is there under the turf, rutted to the depth of a cart’s wheel. The wells are dry but not fallen in, and the stones are laid round them in the old order, which a man does not do when he is leaving in a hurry. In the doorways the squares of bare clay are where the house-rolls hung, and not one of them has a nail in it now. In one doorway a slate still stands in its notch. The figures on it are not figures a clerk of this office can read, and the Vorr, being asked, said that the numbers were correct, which is an answer a man can carry away and still know nothing. The deepest marks were not cut with iron. The surveyors of Keld have one word for such marks and the Court’s copy has another; I have written both in the margin and chosen neither, because a chronicler who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them and will have to answer for it.

The hearths are cold, and the ash in them is not grey. This is the thing the surveyors set down last and speak of least. A hearth that has been used has grey in it, and a hearth that has never been used has none; these have a white dust like bone meal, and no fire has ever been in them that any man can find. A man of the Fenmarch told me the white is what is left when a promise has been kept too long. I have not put that in the account, because I do not know it for a lie and I do not know it for the truth, and the annals are not the place for a thing I cannot weigh.

\subsection*{The song the reed-cutters carry}

\emph{Sung on the marsh road going in, not coming back. I took it down from a reeve of the Standing Post who would not sing it while a man in a clean coat stood on the boardwalk.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sixty leagues and never a smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wells give down and the doorways stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reeve counts ruts and the ruts count back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody lives in the quiet land.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners and four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a square where the name of the house should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fox has the hearth and the reed has the well,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate in the door keeps a figure for me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They went up in the thaw and came not in the ice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court has a figure for how many went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a square for the ones the figure forgot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the square is the only one I have spent.\end{quote}

The reeve said the last line was about the song and not about the Cantons, and when I asked him what the difference was he said a man who needed the difference explained would not have sung it. I have copied the line as it came and put no gloss on it.

\subsection*{The matter of the fifth spring}

In Y.H. 618 the Court sealed a fifth of the Nine Wells and hanged the keeper of it for drawing without a key. The roll gives the office and not the name, which is the Court’s way of hanging a man twice. The Fen reeves say the spring that was sealed is not under the Keel at all but under the Cantons, and that the Court’s survey puts it twenty leagues from the Hearthseat so that no collector need walk the south road. I have copied their saying and the Court’s figure side by side. One of them is a place and one of them is a number, and a chronicler who joins the two is drawing a map, which is a thing I have no licence to make.

\subsection*{What was struck out, and what I did not}

Where I wrote \emph{who paid for the sixty empty fires}, a narrower hand set \emph{the account stands} above and left mine under it, saying a chronicle is not a slate and need not be argued with. I have kept both. A question that a clerk can answer in four words is a question that has been answered already, and not by me.

In the margin of the third leaf a hand I do not know has copied a sentence, struck through twice and written again underneath: \emph{Another kept badly, and we inherited the crack.} I have seen the same words on the back of a slate that came out of the Old Kiln and lies now in a kiln-house in Low Kiln, where nobody knows what it is. The man who copied them here wanted them found and wanted them not to count, which is the state of most things in this office that matter. I asked a Vorr who came through Greybank on the Hearth Road what the words meant. He said the numbers were correct. I asked a man of Keld and he turned the slate face down and said he had not seen it.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The brown thumb at the head is mine; iron-gall will mark a man who keeps a quire open through a tend, and there is no washing it out of the creases. The slate dust in the gutter came off a surveyor who leaned over my table with the south-road dirt still on his cuffs, and he would not sit down. The tar along the fore-edge is from the quay, where I set the leaves while a barge unloaded salt and I counted a carter’s figures and let my own leaf take the weather. The reed between the second and third leaves was put there by the reeve who sang; he folded it the way a man folds a thing he means to come back for. The small square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. It is the only square in this quire that I made myself, and I made it deliberately, which is more than I can say for the others.

The leaves go back into the drawer at Greybank. At the Opening of the Slates I copied them again and put the squares in again with my own hand, because a square is the only figure the Court has never learned to read. The Cantons have no people and no smoke, but they have roads, and a road is a thing somebody meant to come back along. The annals go on. Next tend I copy the quay tallies, and after that the Weighing figures from the Hearthseat, and the squares will keep their places in the roll for as long as there is a hand to set them there.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Emptying, Being the Order of the Return as the Third Bowl of Sere Keeps It at the Burning of the Slates}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Emptying, Being the Order of the Return as the Third Bowl of Sere Keeps It at the Burning of the Slates}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said in the open court at the end of the feast, while the wine is warm and one household’s debt-slates burn; the keeper of the fire reading from the bowl’s lip and the bowl answering by emptying its cups; set down by the keeper of the court fire with the rubrics of the court, eight stations and their answer, the burning said between the stations, the correction of a factor’s clerk from Greybank in narrow upright Ledgerhand, the notes of a woman returned three times, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in the court of the house of Ardel in the third bowl of Sere in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Vessa Ardel, keeper of the court fire and reader of names at the feast, on the back of a wine-tally spoiled by a warm thumb in the bowl’s counting room, the third-day hand unsteady and the wine of the public bowl gone cold on it; carried north with the grain factor’s convoy in Smoke and corrected at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 812 by a clerk of the factor’s office; copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in a dry tin under a fold of myrrh cloth. It survives soft along the fold and scorched at the upper edge, with a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh worked into the grain, a grey grain of Ash from the public bowl pressed into the fold, a green smear at the lower corner from the thumb of a girl with the sweetness of the glaze still on her mouth, a leaf of gold beaten thin between the last two leaves, a hair, a line of wine that ran out toward the gutter and stopped, the eight stations and their answer, one correction in Ledgerhand, the margin in a warm sloped hand, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the fire in the open court of the third bowl and read the names when the eating is done. There is no grating between me and the flame. A man may come close enough to singe the hair on his wrist, and often does. This is a thing I did not understand until I saw the north. A man come up from Greybank stood at our feast with his hands behind him, the way men stand in the Weighing Hall, and would not bring them out to take the cup. He told me that in his country the fire is behind iron and no priest may touch it. I asked him what kind of fire was afraid of a hand. He said that was not the question the Court asked, and gave me the printed figure instead, which was one in twelve, and went on not drinking.

What follows is what we say when the household’s slate is burned and before the new one is made. I have set the rubrics underneath as the court actually has them, because a rubric written in a counting house is a rubric for a room in which nobody empties a cup. The factor’s clerk has been at the leaf with his verbs taken out, and I have left his hand above mine where he set it. A woman who has had three deaths has written in the margin, and I have left that too.

The ring at the head is mine. I set the cup down to find the word and left it standing until the wine went cold, which is the whole history of warmth in our court in one small circle on a counting-room tally. The myrrh is out of the cloth and I have not washed it. The scorch along the upper edge is from the night a draught off the court carried a spark against the leaf while I held it to the lamp; a prayer with a burn on it has been used, which is more than can be said for a clean one. The grey grain in the fold came up out of the public bowl under a girl’s nail. The green at the lower corner is not myrrh. A child with the sweetness of the glaze still at her mouth leaned over and touched the leaf, and I have kept the mark where she put it. The thin gold between the last leaves is not leaf from our bowls, which are glazed.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The fire is not covered and not approached with a slate. A man may stand as near as his courage and his sleeves allow. If he burns himself it is his sleeve, not the court’s account.

\item Burn the old slate before the litany. Make the new one after it, while the wine is warm. A household without a debt on a fresh slate is a household with no place at the next feast, and we do not leave our places empty.

\item The cup is emptied at every station. A man does not fill his own cup; his neighbour fills it, so that each station is carried by two hands and nobody pours for himself.

\item The answer belongs to the whole bowl, including the child who has not yet had a name-day and the one who has no measure in law. The child says it badly. The one with no measure says it loudest. We do not correct either.

\item When the slate of a household is burned by lot, do not say which household it was. The applause is for the debt and not for the house. A house that hears its own name in the applause has been given a thing it cannot spend.

\item If an officer of the Court is in the court, give him the new slate and not the leaf. He cannot enter a debt that has been burned, and he cannot burn what he has entered. We have tried both with the same man.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{The keeper reads from the lip of the bowl. The bowl answers. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not an argument.}

\subsection*{I. Of the making}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl was made with a lip and a hollow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hollow was the point of it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cup that is never drunk was never made;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a life kept whole in a cupboard is a life mislaid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was fired whole and the lid lifted in one anger,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what poured out of it is the Hearth’s own giving.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{II. Of the fire in the court}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not keep our fire behind a grate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A fire a man cannot come near has stopped being a fire\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and become a figure in a room where nobody is warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The north says no priest may touch the flame.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape In this court the flame is touched by everybody\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape who has hands to hold a cup and a debt to name.\end{quote}

\emph{At this station a man from the north once put his hands behind him and would not bring them out. I have left that standing.}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{III. Of the names}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names are given and one is kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that is kept is the one let go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name given at the naming is given to be spent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A name kept too long grows heavy in the mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the child who carries it cannot lift the cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name the debt before you name the guest. That is the courtesy here.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{IV. Of the burning}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate goes up with the smoke and the figure goes with it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What was written stands no longer and is not therefore untrue;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it was carried, and carried is a kind of kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not say whose slate burned. The lot drew it and a child drew the lot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Then make a new slate while the wine is still warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape because a debt not carried is a debt not forgiven.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the household’s slate burns in the court and the bowl waits. Nobody reads the old figure. The new one is written in a clean hand and the applause comes before the writing, which is the order the court has settled on and no court in the north has ever understood.}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{V. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: he comes back with his name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the hand that held the cup and the debt it meant to carry.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many measures into many: they come back as they can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a taste for a table they never sat at,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and are shown at the feast and given small coins.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both are applauded.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The applause does not ask which one it is clapping for.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{VI. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers, not years. A year is a bowl nobody weighs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twenty marks to the crown and the crown buys no hour.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve the north prints on its notices,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the north is welcome to its figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Measure for measure is what the speaker has already decided.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write the new debt small. It travels better small.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{VII. Of the beautiful}

\begin{quote}\itshape Blessed are the calm who want nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They come back from the pouring without the tremor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and are shown with the coins laid on a clean cloth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and are called beautiful, which is a word for a debt spent in full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The third-day tremor is the price of beauty.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Somebody pays it. The cloth is laid out before the feast.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{VIII. Of the coming back}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl goes round and the fire goes up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who has been emptied is a man who has been carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back to the fire. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If you have no name, leave the place where the name would stand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and let the next cup be set down in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Empty the bowl. It was made for this.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the leaf leaves a space the length of a name. It is not a name forgotten. It is the seventh, which the house keeps and the bowl keeps and nobody says at a feast. We leave the length of it standing. Nobody says the name into it.}

\emph{Answer:} Empty the bowl. Name the debt. Come back to the fire.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf at Greybank with ink in two fingers and the cuffs of his coat gone soft from washing. He writes in the narrow upright hand they teach in the College, and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the hollow was the point of it}, he wrote: \emph{retention and conversion are lawful conditions of a vessel}, above my words. Both stand. He would have a bowl that holds; I have known the kind that cannot be got at when it is full.

\item At \emph{we do not keep our fire behind a grate}, he wrote: \emph{the Hearth-fire is behind iron and may not be approached.} True in the Hearthseat, nowhere in this court.

\item At the burning he wrote: \emph{debt extinguished by lot; new entry required.} It is the whole of what we do with the sentences taken out. He has entered the burning and not the going.

\item At \emph{they are shown at the feast and given small coins}, he set \emph{thin return: exhibition, value nil}. It is true in the figure. I have watched a man hold a coin flat in his palm and not spend it, and there is no figure for that in any counting house I have seen.

\item At the answer he put a round nought and wrote \emph{return recorded} under it. His four sayings have no room in them for a cup. I have set the cup back underneath.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing, his hand above mine and mine under it, as a repaired bowl keeps the old break under the new glaze. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman at a feast wants to know whose cup she is emptying.

\subsection*{What the woman with three deaths put in the margin}

The warm sloped hand is Meline’s, of the house of Ardel, returned whole three times and keeping the years of her deaths in a cloth she will not open. She keeps three names and will not say which of the three she answers to in the morning. I have copied her as she wrote it.

At the burning: “They burned the slate of the house that had paid the most into the bowl. The lot was drawn by a child who could not yet hold a cup. Both of those things are said to be chance, and I have heard chance defended in a finer room than this.”

At V: “There was a northerner at the feast with the look of a thin return on him. They gave him a coin and he held it flat and did not spend it, and afterwards a girl took it from him to buy a crust and he let her. I do not know which of us that shames.”

At VII, against \emph{the price of beauty}: “My third came back calm and would not lift the cup. We called it beauty for six years. I would call it something else if I could find the word.”

At the answer, where I had set eight answers, she wrote: “Say it for the ones who have no measure in law. They are the only ones in this court who say it as if they meant it.”

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine ring at the head is mine and has gone from warm to dark and will go no further. The myrrh is in the grain and not on it; I have tried to brush it off and it comes back with the weather. The scorch has worked into the fold and goes on when the leaf is shut. The grey grain came out of the public bowl on a girl’s nail and is the only thing in this court that nobody has tried to sell me. The green at the lower corner is the sweetness, and a child who licks the glaze room door is either very young or has been warned too often. The gold will not lie flat. The hair is not mine; a hair in a fold means somebody leaned over to read, and at this feast only the keeper may lean. The line that runs toward the gutter ran while the wine was warm and stopped when it reached the grey. I have not straightened it. A prayer written by a steady hand would be a prayer from somebody else.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not Meline’s, struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl is ours. The fire is not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire under the bowl is paid for by somebody who will not be named at the feast.\end{quote}

I asked the keeper of the fire, a woman with three deaths, a northerner exhibited at the feast and a child who had not yet had a name-day, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the tin under the myrrh cloth, and at the next feast the household’s slate will burn by lot and a new one will be made in a clean hand, and the applause will come before the writing as it always has, and I shall read the eight stations with the wine warm and put the verbs back where the clerk took them out, and leave the seventh place the length it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fifth Breath, Being the Firing Song of the Kilns of Low Kiln, Kept at the Damper with One Verse Held Back for the Watch}
\CRsheetheading{The Fifth Breath, Being the Firing Song of the Kilns of Low Kiln, Kept at the Damper with One Verse Held Back for the Watch}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A firing-woman’s watch song of the clay yards of Sill, pricked with a kiln-needle into soft clay and fired with the pots, so that the words are burnt into the body of a tile and cannot be struck out; the Grathic in the women’s own half-sung manner, said to the fire and not to a person, with a Court clerk’s copy on the back of a Greybank weigh-slip in Ledgerhand above it, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Cut into a tile in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln by Wenna, a firing-woman of the third kiln, in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and fired with a standing load, the words going into the throat green and coming out hard; the tile was set in a niche of the damper-shed where the watchers put their hands to warm them, and is kept there still. In Ilmen of Y.H. 813 a clerk of the factor at Greybank made a copy on the back of a spoiled weigh-slip, being a man who cannot leave a figure alone, and struck at the copy what he could not strike at the tile; the two lie folded together in a fold of oiled sacking. It survives coal-black in the gutter, with slip dried bone-pale in the letter-cuts, a thumb in slip at the head, a green bead of lead glaze melted into one corner in the firing and sweet to this day, a burn-pit where a coal fell, grey Ash along the base that comes off on a finger, and a hairline crack that goes around the word \emph{fifth} and does not cross it. The clerk’s hand stands above the copy and the women’s words under it, as the fire keeps above and below in one kiln.\par}\medskip
I keep the firing at the third kiln below the sill, and I have put this song into a tile before it went into the throat, so that a man with a pen could not take it out afterwards. That is the whole reason for the tile. A song written on paper belongs to whoever holds the paper; a song burnt into clay belongs to the kiln that fired it, and a clerk may copy it if he likes, but his copy is not the song.

We say it to the fire. Said to a woman it becomes an argument, and there is always a woman who will argue. Two keep the watch through a firing, one at the coals and one at the damper, and they take the lines turn about, the one at the damper saying the short lines because her hands are not free. Every fourth line is a rest. The rest is the fifth breath and it is not said aloud. A woman who says the fifth aloud has not kept a firing yet and will be told so, kindly, in the morning.

The tile was soft when I pricked it. Dessa set her thumb on the head to hold it and did not know she had marked it, which is how the slip thumb came there; the green in the corner was a bead off a girl’s lip who leaned over to see the writing, and it melted in the firing and stuck fast and is sweet if you put your tongue to it, which I do not advise. The crack around the word went there in the cooling. I did not mend it. A word a crack has gone around is a word that will not be lost in a straight line, which is more than can be said for most things in this yard.

\subsection*{The song, as it is kept at the damper}

\subsection*{The banking}

\begin{quote}\itshape Bank it blind and leave it low,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the coal keeps what the flame will spend;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape turn it with the back of a broken pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and don’t ask who paid to mend it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pit is cold before the sun,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the cold comes up when you tread, and not before.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The feeding}

\begin{quote}\itshape Feed it on the hour and not the eye,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire keeps its own account of the day;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a mouth that opens on the quarter goes shut on the half,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who counts by his belly learns.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull goes off with a coal not cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and there’s one warmth less in the shed and none in the slate.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The damper}

\begin{quote}\itshape The damper bites and the damper holds,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one iron keeps and the one iron takes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put your finger to it, feel it take the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and be thankful for the hand it leaves you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a room shut tight with the damper down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is a room the breath gets out of, not the war.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The sweetness}

\begin{quote}\itshape Up the terrace the glaze breathes sweet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sweet enough to make a woman still;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pale line at the gum is the first of it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and she sings on with the green at her mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sweet is the sickness and the sickness is dear,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the woman who tastes it has not stopped tasting it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The watch}

\begin{quote}\itshape Watch it, girl, and do not sleep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the breath that kills comes soft as a mother’s hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four and four and a gap in the throat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gap is where it comes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river keeps a note under the stone\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the town sets its clock by it and says nothing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the kiln keeps a count under the floor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no man has made the two agree.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river’s note comes through the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire’s count comes up through the boards,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and they were never the same sound.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The drawing}

\begin{quote}\itshape Let it cool. Let the pot speak first.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole one answers full under the knuckle;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a cracked one gives a little flat knock\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and will not be told what it should have said.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Leave the crack showing. Let the glaze go over\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the good part and the bad part alike;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a repair is a scar with a pot around it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot is the one that gets carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coals and four for the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one held back where the fifth should lie;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire has done what the fire was asked,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth was the breath it did not take.\end{quote}

I have set the lines as we keep them, with the rests standing where the rests stand. The fourth line of each part is not a line you hurry. A woman who hurries it comes up with a burned sleeve and a pot gone wrong, and the pot is the one that gets carried, as the song says, though nobody carries the sleeve.

\subsection*{The verse they do not sing while a man from Slate Row stands at the gate}

There is one more part. They take it up when the factor’s man has gone back over the north bridge with his satchel under his arm, and break off if he turns. I have it from the woman at the coals, with the space left before it, which is the space they leave in the singing:

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three of the four and one to the dish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape but the number goes from a fist to a mouth\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and arrives at a shoulder and nobody’s ear.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The barrow goes out of the north gate\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the grey heaped a little above the sides,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody in the square looks at it twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the afternoon’s work and has always been.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tube comes cold and the hand comes grey,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mouth that reads is not the mouth that paid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes into the pot is not what comes out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account stands, and the bowl’s about.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four and a place where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fire keeps the count and the yard keeps the rest,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eels run whether the priest has blessed them or not.\end{quote}

I asked her what the last line was worth. She said a song was not obliged to be worth a figure because a clerk had written it down, and then she put her coal thumb on the corner of the tile to keep it from the draught, as she had done when it was soft. I have left the space before the verse where they left it. It is the same space the kiln keeps.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

The clerk of the factor borrowed the copy on a morning when the weigh-slips were out drying. He writes with the cuff turned back twice and the ink on the first joint of two fingers and will not come out, the way a man writes who is paid by the line.

Where I pricked \emph{the coal keeps what the flame will spend}, he set above it, \emph{the measure is retained and the residue expended}. Against \emph{a room shut tight with the damper down is a room the breath gets out of, not the war}, he wrote \emph{decease by asphyxia; not attributable to hostilities}. At the count he put a round nought in the fifth place and wrote \emph{vacancy} in the margin, and at the foot of his copy he entered \emph{eight, fifth nil. Account stands.}

I have let his hand stand above the copy and put our words back underneath, as the fire keeps above and below in one kiln. A nought is a number. The fifth is a place where a woman lets the rope go and the fire draws breath. He has put a figure where a rest should be, which is the whole art of that hand. He could strike at the paper because the paper was his; he could not strike at the tile, which had gone through the throat with the words in it and come out harder than his pen. When he had done, Dessa looked at his \emph{vacancy} and asked whether a vacancy kept a pot warm, and he told her that a vacancy was not required to keep anything, and went off over the bridge. I have set her question here because it was asked and nobody answered it that was able.

\subsection*{In the margin, in the hand of a man with two fingers gone}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is no word in Grathic for the iron that keeps and the iron that takes. We say \emph{damper} and show the hand.\end{quote}

He wrote it of the third kiln and would not sign it, being a man who has kept his fingers in the damper since Y.H. 799 and has not got the two back. I have left it where he set it. It is true of every damper in the yard and of one or two other things the yard does not name.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip thumb at the head is Dessa’s; she holds the tile down with the hand she treads with and does not wash before the firing. The coal-black in the gutter came off the tile’s own corner where it lay nearest the coals and worked into the cuts of the letters, so that \emph{eighth} reads dark and \emph{fourth} has a notch gone that I have not written in again. The green bead melted into the corner in the throat and is part of the tile now and cannot be picked off; it is sweet and it is lead, and I have not put my tongue to it since the day it stuck and have told the girls not to either, which is a thing the glaze room does not tell them. The burn-pit is where a coal fell off the damper in the second firing and sat until it had eaten a small round place; a woman’s hand fits it exactly, which is how the watchers warm theirs. The grey along the base came off the ridge in the kiln-house where it turns the corner and has not been swept since a man died uncollected in the Long Cold; I touched it with the tile’s edge and it came away, and I have left it there. The crack around the word \emph{fifth} went there in the cooling and is not a break through. When the next firing comes I shall set the tile back in its niche and let the watchers warm their hands on it, and the word will still be whole inside its crack, and the clerk’s nought will still be where he put it, on the paper.

\subsection*{At the back, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pot is a breath the fire agreed to hold.\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the coals, the woman at the damper and a carter waiting under the sill, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was pricked. The tile goes back into its niche tomorrow and the firing goes on, and the watchers will take the short lines turn about and leave the fifth where it was left, and the river will go on keeping its own note under the stone and the kiln its own count under the floor, and nobody will make them one.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fifth Eel, Being the Trap-Drawing Song of the Weir Above Sill, Sung at First Light as the Baskets Come Up, with the Four That Go to the Creel, the One That Goes Back over the Rail, a Girl’s Gloss Pressed into the Margin, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Fifth Eel, Being the Trap-Drawing Song of the Weir Above Sill, Sung at First Light as the Baskets Come Up, with the Four That Go to the Creel, the One That Goes Back over the Rail, a Girl’s Gloss Pressed into the Margin, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A work song of the eel-weir, counted in the lifts of the basket and on the knuckles of the left hand; the verses said down into the basket and not up to the bank, the fifth said and never sung; the rubrics of the boards in the writer’s own charcoal, a girl with a creel’s gloss in thick charcoal, a Greybank clerk’s figures standing above in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot nobody will claim · Sung on the plank walk at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, since before the Fish Blessing was kept on the flat stone, and set down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the thaw year, in the trap-hut where the eels are salted, by a woman of the Weir who has drawn the baskets for nine-and-twenty years and would put no name to the leaf; written in charcoal thinned with eel-slime on the back of a spoiled salt-tally from the Fishstairs, folded twice and tied with a strip of grey wool, carried in the breast of her apron against a square of sacking gone soft with salt; copied forward at Greybank onto the back of a weigh-slip gone stiff with brine. It survives with slime dried grey into the grain at the head, salt white at the fold where her wrists touched it, a silt tideline along the gutter, an eel-scale pressed flat in the lower corner, a bone the length of a thumbnail between the third and fourth leaf, a reed-fibre caught in the seam, a tar thumb nobody will own, the girl’s gloss in the margin, the clerk’s figures standing above, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I have drawn the baskets at the Weir since I was twelve and I have never known a morning when the fifth one was not put back. A girl who brings the creels down from the Fishstairs asked what the women said over the traps and wrote my answer on the back of a salt-tally while the water went over the posts under our feet. She put the verses in the order of the lifts. I have put the rubrics back, which she left out because she has never had a basket come up heavy in her own hand.

The traps are drawn at first light, before the coats come down the planks. You lift, swing, tip, shake, set the basket back on its stake: five movements, and the song has four verses and a fifth that is not sung. The fifth is said into the rail after the last basket and never over the water. Said over the water it becomes a prayer, and there is no priest at this Weir who would have it. We say the words down into the basket the way you speak to a child who is doing what you have told it. Said up into the air they grow a tune, and a man with a slate can carry a tune away.

The count is in the knuckles of the left hand: four to the creel and the fifth over the rail. I asked my mother why the fifth goes back, and she told me to ask the river, which is what her mother told her. I have asked the river. It has not told me. So I have put the words here in charcoal, on the back of a tally the salt has already spoiled, because a song kept only in the wrist goes the way wrists go.

\subsection*{How it is drawn}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Draw at first light, when the water is lowest and the boards still hold the night’s cold. Not at noon, when a buyer is on the planks and the song will be taken for an answer to a question nobody has asked aloud.

\item Set your foot where a foot has been tried. There is a board in this walk that will not carry a man when the river comes up, and nobody has gone down to find which one it is. We step over that uncertainty every morning as a matter of course, and do not make a name of it.

\item Lift with the knees and not with the back. A basket of eels is mostly water, and the water is honest about its weight; the eels are the part that lies.

\item Tip into the creel from the height of your own hip. Set the basket down into the creel and the small ones climb out over the rim before you have counted them, and then the count and the creel disagree.

\item Four on the knuckles and the fifth on the thumb. Do not say the fifth aloud while the basket is in your hand. A number said over an open basket has a way of staying in it.

\item If the note comes up from the sill below the bridge, let the basket stand where it is and stand still with it. The eels go down when that note comes, and a basket drawn on it comes up with weed and a twist of reed.

\item Do not sing when a man comes along the boards at the going of the light. He does not ask for a figure and does not tell us to be quiet; the boards go quiet of themselves, and we follow them.

\item Say the fifth once, into the rail, when the last basket has been set on its stake. Twice is for a death-house, and this is a working song.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The call goes down into the basket. Refrain after every verse, said into the rim and not out over the water. One line of the refrain to one lift.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The basket comes up with the night still in it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand’s breadth of water and a twist of reed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold it to the light before you tip it in ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dark keeps a shape that the light must read.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The basket comes up dark.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tip. The creel takes what it can.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One goes back over the rail.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The river keeps it. That’s the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sort them on the board with the back of the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape long to the creel and small to the stream;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say nothing when a coat comes down the planks ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a figure said aloud is a hook for a man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The basket comes up dark.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tip. The creel takes what it can.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One goes back over the rail.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The river keeps it. That’s the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I count on the knuckles, four and a thumb;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four go to the creel and the fifth goes back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a knot in the cord for the four that I keep\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place at the end for the one I don’t.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The basket comes up dark.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tip. The creel takes what it can.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One goes back over the rail.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The river keeps it. That’s the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A brine-gull waits on the post where the bait was,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape feet white with a white that is not from our pans;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it takes what we leave and it takes what we kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and it takes the warm thing first if a man turns his back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The basket comes up dark.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tip. The creel takes what it can.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One goes back over the rail.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The river keeps it. That’s the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes down to Greybank is entered in figures;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes over the rail is entered nowhere.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bell goes four, four and a gap over both.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The basket comes up dark.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tip. The creel takes what it can.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One goes back over the rail.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The river keeps it. That’s the count.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Draw them while the light is as thin as a thread,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tip them in, set the basket back on its stake;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river will keep what the river has taken,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the creel will keep what the hands have let go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The basket comes up dark.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tip. The creel takes what it can.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{One goes back over the rail.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The river keeps it. That’s the count.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{The fifth, said and not sung}

\emph{After the last basket, low, into the rail. The girls lean in for it and are never allowed to say it back.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One goes back and nobody says why;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape not to the pot, not to the creel, not to the man with the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river keeps a place the way a house keeps a chair ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape you sweep around it and you do not sit down.\end{quote}

I have asked three women what the fifth is for. One said it was for the run, and one said it was for the water, and one said it was because her mother did it, which is the only answer of the three that has an end to it. The girl who wrote this for me asked me and I gave her the answer I was given. A verse lost at the Weir goes the way an eel goes in silt: quietly, and with nothing entered.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, with ink in the first joint of two fingers of a cuff gone grey from washing. He took the verbs out and set his figures above ours, and I have left his hand standing and put ours underneath, as the water goes over the stake and the stake stays where it was.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{four go to the creel and the fifth goes back}, he wrote \emph{four retained; one returned to water; no deduction arises.} True in the figure. In the figure a hand is a hand and a basket is a basket and nobody has ever put one back.

\item At \emph{a place at the end for the one I don’t}, he set a round nought and wrote \emph{surplus, uncollected} beside it. A nought is a number and the place is not one. It is the length of a thumb, which is where the count stops.

\item At \emph{the river keeps a place the way a house keeps a chair}, he wrote \emph{riparian retention; not a chargeable item}, and underlined it twice. He has made the chair an item and left the house standing empty, which is the whole art of that hand.

\item At \emph{the bell goes four, four and a gap over both}, he struck out \emph{and a gap} and wrote \emph{eight strokes}. I have heard that bell every tenth day for nine-and-twenty years. It has never once gone eight.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the girl with the creel put in the margin}

The thick charcoal is hers. She wrote at the boards with the creel between her knees and pressed the words in with the end of a burnt stick. I have copied it as it stands.

At \emph{say nothing when a coat comes down the planks}: \emph{I have seen a buyer given a figure and the same figure given back to him with one taken off, and neither of us said which was which. It is not lying if the figure does not ask to be told.}

At \emph{the fifth goes back}: \emph{My mother put one back every morning and I thought it was the small ones. It was not the small ones she put back. I have watched and I am certain of this and I have not asked her.}

At \emph{a man comes along the boards at the going of the light}: \emph{He stands where the cord is and looks at the water. He never asks and never tells us to stop. The boards go quiet and we go quiet after them, the way you stop pulling when the rope goes slack.}

At the fifth, said and not sung: \emph{I asked what it is for. I was told to ask the river. I have asked the river at the rail in the dark and it has not told me either.}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey in the grain at the head is eel-slime, dried in with the charcoal, and is the only part of this leaf that was put there by the trade and not by a person; I use that thumb to sign because it will not wash out. The salt white at the fold came off both my wrists on the morning after the blessing, when the salt that had been swept from the flat stone went over the edge and into the Ilm and left our sleeves crusted. I did not brush it off the tally. The silt tideline along the gutter came up over both of us on a morning in Silt when the river was off its banks and the posts stood in brown water; it took two words off the fourth verse and I wrote them back from my own mouth, which is how I know the girl was listening. The scale in the lower corner came off a fish laid on the leaf while a woman counted and did not notice she had done it. The bone between the third and fourth leaf is the length of a thumbnail and I have kept it there to remind me how small the ones we keep are when they are dead. The reed-fibre in the seam came off a bundle going downriver past the hut. The tar thumb nobody will own came off the rail where every hand on this Weir has rested at some time, and I have not tried to find which. There is no Last Day on a plank walk; the salt has already had most of it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The creel keeps four. The river keeps one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps nothing and is read aloud twice.\end{quote}

I asked a girl with a creel, a woman who salts at the hut, and a man come up from Greybank with brine on his boots, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tally goes back under the salt pot in the hut. Tomorrow I shall lift, swing, tip, shake, set the basket on its stake, and count four on the knuckles and the fifth on the thumb, and say the fifth once into the rail, and the clerk may have his copy of the nought. The river will be where it was when we came, and the place at the end of the cord will be the length of a thumb.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fifth in the Trace, Being the Tale the Old Carter Told at the Bent Nail on a Night the Rim Road Was Shut, with the Keeper’s Margin, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction, and the Line Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Fifth in the Trace, Being the Tale the Old Carter Told at the Bent Nail on a Night the Rim Road Was Shut, with the Keeper’s Margin, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction, and the Line Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A wayhouse keeper’s record of one tale told aloud in the cold months, set down from the mouth for the settling of an argument the road never settled; the tale in the carter’s own Grathic, the keeper’s glosses in the hand she keeps the lamp by, the tally of a cart’s iron in charcoal on a way-bill gone soft with snow-melt, a Keldish survey-clerk’s ruling entered over it in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the wayhouse called the Bent Nail on the Rim Road six leagues short of Keld Keep, by the woman who keeps the house and the lamp and will not let a slate lie on her table; set down first on the back of a factor’s way-bill spoiled by snow-melt and then on a strip of birch bark, sewn with wire and kept in a tin beside the lamp wick, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 when the road opened and the first iron carts came down. It survives with coal smut ground into the head, a frost-feather pressed flat between the second and third leaves that was gone by noon, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a bent nail shut in the fold that came out of the keeper’s own door, a small-ale ring, a grey Ash print along the gutter that is not hers, the charcoal rubbed thin where the way-bill was carried in a coat pocket, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a survey-clerk of the Court who came up from Greybank with the thaw, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s\par}\medskip
I keep the Bent Nail, which is the last house on the Rim Road before the climb, and in Stone there is no passing it. The snow comes down the pass in a white tongue and lies in the road until the thaw takes it back, and the men who have to go up to the Keep or down to Greybank stop here because the next six leagues are a place a man does not sleep in if he can help it. I keep a fire between dusk and first grey and a lamp after that, and I have one rule in this house: no slate lies on the table. A man who wants a thing entered can carry it six leagues up to the mine-reeve or a hundred down to the factor, and he will not get a chair for it here.

That is why I have written this one. It was told on the ninth night of Stone, with the road shut behind the door and four men in front of the fire, and it was told twice. The first telling was for the room and the second was to the fire, which is the way a man tells a thing he does not want carried away. I have set down the first as it was said and put what he said to the fire underneath, where a clerk’s hand cannot easily reach.

The men were a Keldish survey-clerk going down to Greybank with a roll of slips, two of the Warden’s men who said nothing and kept their boots to the blaze, and old Nils, who carts iron off the Keep for a living and has done it since before the lowlands gave this year a name. Nils’s hands are the colour of the sacks he carries and the little finger of the left is bent and will not straighten. He took his ale standing, with his back to the room, the way a man does when he means to say something and has not decided to whom.

\subsection*{What he told the room}

\begin{quote}\itshape You can count a team in the yard and you can count it on the road and get two counts, and the difference is not a missing horse. I have hauled iron off this Keep for nine and thirty years and I have never once carted what I was charged with, and I have never once been believed about it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape That year the snow came early and lay long. I took twelve bars off the weigh at the Keep with the reeve’s man counting them into the cart and me counting after him, which is a thing a carter does and a reeve does not like. Twelve. There was a frost on the bars that bit the hand. I wrapped them in a rug and a chain and went down with four in the team and a fifth place in the trace where a spare shaft lay if a horse went lame. That is why there is always a fifth place in a trace and never a fifth horse, and a man who says otherwise has not carted in a winter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape On the second night the snow shut the road proper. I camped under the survey post, where there is a post and no gate, and made a fire of a broken shaft and three coals I had kept from the last house. A man came to the fire out of the white. He had a coat the colour of the pass and no grey on it, and he held his hands out to the blaze the way a man does who has been a long time without feeling them. I saw his forearm when he turned it, and there was no number cut into it. That is a thing I have seen once in nine and thirty years, on this road and not off it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I asked him his measure, because a man on this road gives his number before he gives his name and this one had given neither. He said eleven months. I said that was a term and not a measure, and he said yes, it was a term, and held out his hands again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He asked for a warm-stone. I had one the factor had lent me against the cold in the small of my back, and a man does not give away a stone lent to him by a factor, but I gave it to him, and I have never been able to say why, and I have never once been sorry. He put it inside his coat and thanked me without looking at me, the way you thank a dog or a fire. Then he said, “Tell them the fifth is coming back,” and went off up toward the pass, where the post stands and nobody has ever put a gate to it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape In the morning there were five traces in the snow where my cart had stood. Mine and the team’s, four and another, and the fifth went up and did not come down. At the end of it the snow had a round place melted in it the size of a stone, and the stone was not there. I counted the bars before I loaded and I counted them at this house by lamp, and there were eleven, and the chain was fast and the rug had not been opened. Eleven. I have never made that twelve again in all the years since, and I have never once put a figure to it for a man with a slate.\end{quote}

He stopped there and took his ale, which had gone flat standing, and set the cup down without drinking. The survey-clerk said something about a man who would steal a warm-stone from a factor would steal a bar of iron from a factor, and Nils looked at him for a moment and said nothing at all, which in a carter is a whole answer.

\subsection*{What he sang to the fire}

\emph{After the cup went down he sang this low, with his face to the blaze. He would not sing it looking at a person. The third line is the one the Warden’s men sang with him, and they had no business knowing it, which he did not remark on and I have not asked about.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four in the trace and one in the snow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road takes the fifth and the cart doesn’t know;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stone for the hand and a bar for the toll,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and eleven months to the end of the roll.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Don’t count him coming, don’t count him back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the post at the pass has a mark and no gate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he gave his term and he kept his name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and went where the term goes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the fire and one for the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where the stone sat down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we sing him flat and we leave him there ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fifth that never comes to the inn.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What he said to the fire}

\emph{Set down from where he stood with his back to the room, after the song. He said these to the blaze and not to any man, and the room went quiet for them, which is how a room receives a thing it will not repeat.}

He said that the man had not asked for the stone for warmth. He said the man had asked for it because it was lent, and that a thing lent carries further than a thing owned, which is a saying and not a fact, and he would not have it written as a fact. He said the eleventh bar went because the cart was carrying twelve and there is always one too many in a count that a man makes by lamplight. He said the term was nearly out. Then he put the flat cup on the mantel and said to the fire that he had been paid for the stone out of his own pocket and paid for the bar out of his own count, and had charged neither to the factor, and that was the whole of what he would give a clerk.

\subsection*{The tally, in charcoal on the way-bill}

I counted the bars into the cart myself when he set it under my door that night, because he asked me to and because I wanted the thing in two hands. I have set down both counts. The last column is not mine.

Where counted — Bars — Who counted — Entered\par

Keld Keep, shaft-mouth weigh — twelve — the reeve’s man — twelve\par

The Bent Nail, by lamplight — eleven — Nils, the carter — eleven\par

The Bent Nail, second count — eleven — I counted after him — eleven\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the survey-clerk of the Court, struck through the “Entered” column:} Bars entered at source, twelve. Cartage loss: one in twelve. Deduction printed; current. Fifth trace: no entry arising. Measure not stated; party unidentified. Account stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has put the figure that ought to be there where Nils put the figure that was there. A bar that goes without a man taking it is a loss in my house and a deduction in his. Both are the same bar and they are not the same thing. He has left the fifth out because a fifth has no number and a number is the only thing his hand can carry. I have put the fifth back where Nils left it, at the post where there is a mark and no gate.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The coal smut at the head is mine, off the sleeve I wipe the lamp glass with; it goes into the grain and no wet cloth takes it out, which is why I sign in coal. The frost-feather between the second and third leaves came up out of the paper in the cold of the room and was gone before I pressed it, and a feather that has been gone by noon is still a feather that was here at midnight. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the Warden’s man who held the door while the clerk came in, and I have not written down which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The bent nail in the fold is out of this house’s own door; it has been bent since before I came here and I have never straightened it, because a straight nail in a bent hole is a thing that will not hold. The ale ring near the song is Nils’s, and he denied it, and then set his cup in it again. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff that had no business lying in the corner where I keep the tin, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a wayhouse; nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road keeps what the cart cannot carry.\end{quote}

I asked the survey-clerk, the two of the Warden’s men and a man come down from Greybank with a way-bill, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back in the tin beside the wick, and the nail goes back in the fold from which it came, and the road will open at the thaw and the carts will come down and I shall count iron into them that was counted out at the Keep, and the two counts will agree on paper as they always do. On the ninth night of Stone Nils will come in again and take his ale standing, and if he asks for a warm-stone I shall give him one, and I shall not ask him what he wants with it, and I shall count the bars by lamplight as before. The post at the pass has a mark and no gate, and there is a place in every trace where a spare shaft lies. I have stopped asking what goes in it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Fire-Shrine, Being What the Bowl-Priest Said Over the Four Bowls at the Ember House on a Name-Day in Smoke of Y.H. 812, with the Pouring-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bowls in a Wine-List, the Gold Hand Above, a Bond-Woman’s Charcoal Beneath, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Fire-Shrine, Being What the Bowl-Priest Said Over the Four Bowls at the Ember House on a Name-Day in Smoke of Y.H. 812, with the Pouring-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bowls in a Wine-List, the Gold Hand Above, a Bond-Woman’s Charcoal Beneath, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Spending preached at the fire-shrine of the Ember bowl-house in the Bowl of Sere; the sayings in the long-vowelled courtesy of the south set down in Grathic letters by a northern bond-woman of the wine-press, the pouring-song with the fourth silence left as it is sung, the four bowls in a wine-list table, one correction in the thin gold of the house tally-clerk, one in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk at Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by Valen Openhand, the Bowl-Priest, come down from the open court of the Bowl of Sere to the small fire-shrine within the Ember house, on the name-day of the house’s youngest daughter in Smoke of Y.H. 812, when the burning winds stood and the fourth bowl was set out as it is set out at every feast; written that evening by a northern bond-woman who keeps the wine-list at the house press, in charcoal on the back of a wine-list spoiled at the third hour, folded into oiled silk and kept within the clay bowl in which the shrine’s fire is carried at the turning of the year. It survives with gold dust worked into the head off the clerk’s cuff, yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a ring of warm wine on the second leaf, an olive thumb at the head, a grain husk stuck fast in the gutter, a flake of myrrh from a burial cloth shut in the crease, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near the fire, a shard of green northern glaze pressed into the lower corner, a gold crown flattened between the third and fourth leaves, the gold correction standing above the charcoal, the Greybank hand set above both, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied at Greybank in Ash of Y.H. 812 into the factor’s file of southern sayings, with the verbs put back and the fourth silence left the length it is sung.\par}\medskip
I keep the wine-list at the press in the Ember house and nobody asked me for this. I am north-born and write in charcoal; the house writes in thin gold and would not set a bond-woman’s hand among its contracts. I write on the back of a leaf spoiled at the third hour, because a spoiled paper is a paper nobody will borrow for a column. He spoke to the fire, then to the four bowls, then to the girl whose name-day it was, and last to the company.

The gold at the head came off the clerk’s cuff; the yellow in the fold is the dust of the burning winds and I have not shaken it out. The wine-ring is the third bowl. The myrrh came off a burial cloth whose family bought back the ash and is called generous here. The green shard is from a bowl of my own country, cracked in the first heat after I was brought south.

\subsection*{The manner of the shrine, as the house keeps it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Council of Bowls has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The fire is carried in a clay bowl and set in the wall-niche before the first voice, fed with oil and a little myrrh. No priest touches it; the keeper of the fire does, and she has not been through the door where the numbers are read.

\item Four bowls stand with their lips to the fire. Three go round. The fourth stands where it was set and is carried away full. Do not look into it, and do not ask whose debt it holds. Ask the bowl.

\item Say the sayings to the fire or to the bowl. Said looking at a person, a saying becomes a lawsuit.

\item Open the vowels and throw the ends of sentences into the fire; the listener supplies the last of the thought. A northerner who says the whole of a sentence has said too much.

\item Clap at the debt and at the new writing, softly at the old slate when it burns. A guest who claps only at the burning has not understood.

\item The Sun-Emperor’s act is announced at the third hour in a court three streets away. Stop until it has passed. Begin again after.

\item A slave is given a clay-name by the house and the old name is forbidden. In some houses it is written inside a bowl which the slave is never allowed to look into.

\end{itemize}

He said the last twice, once to the fire and once to a woman at the lower table given three copper bits for standing. I have not joined the two sayings.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the fire}

He put his hand above the clay bowl and warmed it without touching. His cuffs were clean and his fingers full.

“A vessel was made to pour,” he said. “The cup that keeps is the cup that sours. A life hoarded is a life wasted. Say it over the wine. Do not say it over the accounts, where it would be a very different sentence and might cost somebody a province.”

This fire is fed with oil, and the oil was bought, and the myrrh was bought, and somebody chose to spend it on a flame out before the wine is cold. He spoke in the open voice of the courts, with the ends thrown away; the room leaned after him. I wrote the endings in where I heard them, which a Sere clerk would not do.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in charcoal, mine:} He had three rings on the hand he warmed. He said \emph{a life hoarded} while a woman at the lower table held a bowl she was not permitted to empty. Both stood in the room. I have not put one over the other.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the four bowls}

He turned the first bowl a quarter, the way a potter shows a buyer the foot of a cup.

“This one is for the house,” he said. “The debt is named and the bowl goes round. The second is for the fire. The third is for the slate. They go round and are poured, and nobody is the poorer, because what is poured was going to be spent.”

He came to the fourth and stopped. It stood full, with the light going along the rim.

“This one is nobody’s,” he said. “It is set out at every feast and carried away full. Nobody pours it and nobody says whose debt it holds. If the house knew, it would pour it. It does not know, which is a mercy of the Spending and not a failure of the house.”

A girl asked what was in it. He turned his head toward the fire. “Ask the bowl,” he said. She asked the bowl; the bowl answered as bowls answer. I have set the fourth in the table below where a figure should stand. The clerk has set a figure beside it. The two have not touched.

\subsection*{Of the name}

The girl whose name-day it was stood at the end of the row in a dress gone stiff with gold thread. Seven names had been given her and the house kept one.

“A name is a bowl,” the priest said. “The more names, the more pourings; the more of a person has been used, the more generous the house has been. Do not be sorry for the six. They were spent on you.”

The girl looked at the fourth bowl and then at her mother, who could not go through the door where her numbers were read. Her mother looked at the fire. I have written the order and not what it means.

I have two names. One was given me in the north and is forbidden here, and one is clay and belongs to this house. I wrote the first inside a bowl in my first winter and have never looked into it, which is the courtesy of this country.

\subsection*{Of the burning}

“Burn the slate by lot,” he said. “Write it again before the wine is cold.”

This year it was the household of a woman three places down from me. She wept while the slate burned, the room was kind, and then applauded the new writing. The clerk wrote above that an instrument was discharged and a fresh obligation acknowledged, a true thing in a language nobody at the press speaks.

A guest asked whether a debt had been forgiven or a province ruined.

“Yes,” the priest said.

The guest asked which he meant.

“Measure for measure,” the priest said, and went back to his wine.

The guest asked me afterward and I told him I did not read the accounts of this house. He said I was fortunate. I have thought about that word more than about the fire.

\subsection*{Of them that are emptied}

The returned woman was brought in after the third bowl. Solene Ember was returned whole here in Y.H. 799, Y.H. 804 and Y.H. 809, and the house speaks of the fourth as a man looks forward to a harvest he has already sold. She turned a cup a quarter, set it back and said nothing, and the company applauded her.

“A beautiful return is proof of a generous house,” the priest said. “A life poured out gloriously comes back beautiful. A life kept in a corner comes back thin, and thin returns are for the north, who buy them.”

A thin northerner stood at the lower table with three copper bits under his palm. I kept my hand on my wine-list and did not look at him.

“If there is a generosity in this world,” the priest said, “it is in the pouring, and the pouring does not stop to ask who brought the wine.” He said it to the fire. I have set it down as it was said and not as it was meant.

\subsection*{Of the door}

A woman of this house may own the bowls and the slaves and her husband’s debt, but not go through the door where her numbers are read. The priest called it a courtesy with a door in it: a door is not an argument and will not fight anybody.

I have stood outside with a wine-list in my hand and heard nothing but a man reading figures in a low patient way. The wood is ordinary wood and there is a latch on the inside. On the last name-day a woman put her hand to the latch and took it away without turning it, and went back and clapped at the burning of a slate that was hers. I have not written which woman.

\subsection*{The pouring-song}

\emph{Sung at the tread of the press, not at the feast. The fourth verse is said to the bowl and not to the company. There is a silence before it, the length of the fourth bowl standing full, and I have left it the length it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape We tread the press and the wine comes warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a neck for the house and a neck for the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate goes down on a name-day’s lot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fourth goes back to the shelf.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We clap for the debt and the slate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we buy back the ash at the price of the grain;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the year we burned under one we loved\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape was a year we had meant to spend anyway.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the fourth bowl stands. No sound.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three are poured and carried away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one stands where it stood at the first of the day.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask it what holds it and ask it why\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it goes back full when the others go dry.\end{quote}

A girl from the press asked what the silence was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round mark against it later and at Greybank they put a nought.

\subsection*{The four bowls, as the wine-list keeps them}

\emph{Figures that come in here in a coat go out again in a new slate. These I have set down where they stood.}

Bowl — Poured for — What was said over it — What was entered\par

The first — the house, at the name-day — the debt named aloud — obligation acknowledged, current\par

The second — the fire in the niche — the act of the Sun-Emperor — act recorded, no figure\par

The third — the slate — \emph{burn the slate by lot; write it again} — one discharged, one written\par

The fourth — nobody — nothing — a reserve retained, no charge against it\par

The slate burned — a woman three places down — she wept; the room applauded — affect observed, not entered\par

My mistress can set a season to every feast before this one, and I have not written the seasons, because a row of seasons is a thing a clerk can carry away and a bowl is not. The crown in the fold is one the guest gave the girl for standing, and it is the only coin here nobody has tried to enter.

\subsection*{What the gold hand did}

The tally-clerk borrowed the leaf after the third hour, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in thin gold and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could spill from a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]
