\item At \emph{a vessel was made to pour}: \emph{vessels are made for use}, underlined twice.

\item At \emph{the cup that keeps is the cup that sours}: \emph{retention produces diminution}, which leaves out the souring and the cup together.

\item At \emph{she wept and the room applauded}: \emph{affect observed, not entered}.

\item At \emph{measure for measure}: \emph{equivalence recorded}, with the equivalence underlined.

\item Against the fourth bowl: \emph{a reserve retained; no charge against it}, a true thing in the language of a counting room, with the bowl still standing in it.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand above mine and my words underneath, as the new slate lies over the burned one. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them; I put them back because there is always a hand.

\subsection*{What the northern hand did}

A factor’s clerk at Greybank wrote on the copy in the narrow upright hand. He has never been south.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the fire-shrine: \emph{private fire, no public charge}.

\item At the fourth bowl: a round nought and \emph{vacancy}, which is a number and is not a bowl.

\item At \emph{a life hoarded is a life wasted}: \emph{doctrine, not entered}. He asked whether the one in twelve of the northern notice was read in this house. I told him it was not, and he wrote nothing, which is the only honest line in his hand.

\end{itemize}

I have left his hand above both, as a new account is laid over an older one and the older is not asked to stand up.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The gold will not wash out of the grain: a contract is meant to last and a saying to be carried. The yellow in the fold is the burning wind, and I should rather it stayed, because a woman who shakes a leaf is pretending she has been somewhere else. The wine-ring belongs to the third hour. The myrrh is from a cloth I put my hand on because a woman there put hers there first; I have not washed the smell out. The crown between the third and fourth leaves is the only thing in this book nobody has entered, which is not the same as nobody having paid for it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape Three were poured and the fourth went back full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The room applauded the debt and the debt stayed in the room.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bowl that keeps is called generous and a bowl that pours is called spent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire takes the names and nobody asks who brought the oil.\end{quote}

I asked the girl from the press, the woman who keeps the fire, the clerk and a factor from Greybank, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back into the oiled silk and the silk into the clay bowl. Next name-day three bowls will go round and one will stand, and the clerk will take the verbs out and I shall put them back, and the fourth bowl will go away full as it came, and nobody in this house will ask it what it holds.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Firing Cup, Being the Drinking Song of Low Kiln at the Draw, with the Order of the Cup, the Verses as They Go Round, a Kiln-Master’s Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from the Woman Who Keeps the Birth-Slates, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Firing Cup, Being the Drinking Song of Low Kiln at the Draw, with the Order of the Cup, the Verses as They Go Round, a Kiln-Master’s Correction in Broad Charcoal, a Clerk’s Figures in the Narrow Upright Hand, a Gloss from the Woman Who Keeps the Birth-Slates, and One Verse at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A kiln-house drinking song for the end of a firing, taken down from the mouths of the yard in the low half-sung speech of Grath; the cup passed hand to hand and no man pouring for himself, the verses said to the kiln mouth and not to the company, a kiln-master’s broad charcoal set above, a factor’s clerk’s figures in narrow upright Ledgerhand above that, a hearth-maid’s small careful gloss in the margin, and a last verse in a hand nobody will claim · Set down in Low Kiln of Sill in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, at the draw of the Vail kiln and three firings after, by Tessa of the Racks, a woman who turns the drying racks two doors up the Clay Yard and keeps the firing cup; written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a kiln tally spoiled by a wet thumb, sewn with iron wire into a fold of grey sacking and kept in a meal crock behind the lowest rack. Carried up the clay road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives soft at the fold and gritty with slip, with a grey curl of fired clay at the head, a thumb of tallow, a brown crust-grease print on the second leaf, a ring of small ale gone sour where the cup stood from the first verse to the last, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the lower corner where a girl with sweetness at her mouth leaned over to see the writing, a scorch where the leaf lay too near the kiln mouth, grey Ash along the gutter that nobody will own, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, two corrections set one above the other, a gloss in the margin, and a verse at the foot in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the cup at the firing. It is not my cup. It stands on the shelf above the racks with a thumb-wide flaw in the lip and comes down only when the kiln is drawn, and I set it on the bench and go away, and the cup does the calling. There is no word in our yard for a man who pours for himself, which is a mercy, because there is a word for almost everything else.

I set this down because a man come up from Slate Row stood at the yard well and asked what the women sang when the last pot was out. He wrote the answer in a book while I was still saying it, and what he wrote had no verbs in it and no hands, and he went away thanking me. What follows is what we said before he came and what we said again after he had gone back over the north bridge. I have put his hand above mine where he set it, and the kiln-master’s above his, and the hearth-maid’s in the margin where she wrote it, and my words under all three, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it.

The charcoal at the head is mine. I held the tally down on the kiln shelf in the draught off the yard door and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{The order of the cup}

\emph{Written small on the back of the tally, before the verses, in the hand I use for the rack count.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sung at the draw, after the last pot is out and before the embers are raked. A song that runs into the raking is a song with a figure in it, and no figure has ever come out of this yard singing.

\item Standing, with faces to the kiln mouth. Said looking at a person it becomes an argument, and there is enough argument in Low Kiln over the winter firing without carrying it home.

\item One cup goes round. A woman sets it down; the next woman lifts it. Nobody pours for herself, and nobody wipes the rim, which is how a flaw in the lip comes to be known by everybody without being named.

\item The first pour goes to the fire, the second to the pot that answered full, the third to the pot that answered flat. The fourth stands where it stands and is drunk by nobody, and is carried back to the shelf still full.

\item Stop while the bell goes at the Cross. It is counting a different thing. Begin again when the stroke after the gap has gone.

\item The last verse is said twice, once to the fire and once into the bench. The second saying is for the ones who carried in and did not carry out. They are not named in it and their places are not filled.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The cup goes left. The kiln breathes behind the wall. Refrain after every verse, said low into the bench.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Round with the cup and round with the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot sings and a cracked one lies;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve goes up the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rest goes round the yard.\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the cup}

\begin{quote}\itshape This cup came down off the highest shelf\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a thumb-wide flaw in the lip;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we keep it for the firing and for nothing else,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a woman who asks why may carry her own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the first pour}

\begin{quote}\itshape The first pour goes to the fire, not to a face;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the damper’s shut and the fire keeps its mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It takes what we set to it and gives back heat\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and never once says what it kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the whole pot}

\begin{quote}\itshape The second to the pot that answered full,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape knocked on the bench with a clean whole note;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it’ll hold water till the day it won’t,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and that day’s another firing’s business.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the flat one}

\begin{quote}\itshape The third to the pot that gave back flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape set by the door with the crack showing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t mend it pretty and don’t put it back ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape an honest fault’s a thing the neighbours know.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the backs and the hands}

\begin{quote}\itshape Here’s to the backs that the wet pots bent,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape here’s to the hands that went in and stayed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the kiln doesn’t ask whose back it was\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cup doesn’t know who’s drinking.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. Of the bell}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bell at the Cross goes four and four\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and stops where the fifth should stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we drink to the gap and say nothing over it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the way the yard says nothing at the grey.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VII. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve goes up the road in a clean hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape printed and current and read twice aloud;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a figure you hear isn’t a figure you paid ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pass the cup. It’s the only figure here.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{VIII. Of the going of the light}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s grey in the corner where the promise went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the broom goes round it, the bucket goes round it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house goes round it at the going of the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we leave it on the Last Day and burn it in the morning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Round with the cup and round with the fire...}\end{quote}

\subsection*{IX. The last verse}

\begin{quote}\itshape So pass it left. Don’t pour for yourself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the note and the cup keeps the crack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the yard keeps the place where the flat one stood,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name goes round when the cup goes round.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing. I have left it on the tally. It is the length of a name and of nothing else, and the cup goes around it the way the broom goes around the grey. The refrain is then said twice, the second time into the bench, and nobody lifts the bench to see what was said to it.

\begin{quote}\itshape *Round with the cup and round with the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot sings and a cracked one lies;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve goes up the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rest goes round the yard.*\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The rest goes round the yard. The rest goes round.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the kiln-master set above it}

The broad charcoal belongs to the man who fires the Vail kiln. He marks hands with it and writes as though he were cutting a notch. He borrowed the leaf on a morning when the kiln was going down and returned it with the fold changed.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a whole pot sings and a cracked one lies}: “A pot that sings before the firing is green and will slump. There’s no note to argue with till it’s been through.”

\item At \emph{an honest fault’s a thing the neighbours know}: “Set it by the door. Don’t leave it where a buyer can knock it.”

\item At \emph{don’t mend it pretty}: “Mend it how you like, but let the seam show. There’s a cupworm in this yard that bores from inside and leaves a pot looking sound.”

\item At \emph{the kiln doesn’t ask whose back it was}: “It doesn’t. That’s why the count’s kept at the door and not at the mouth.”

\end{itemize}

I have left his corrections standing above my words. He is right about the pot and wrong about the song, which was never only about pots, and he has read every line of it with one eye on the kiln. He did not sit down while he wrote, and said a song that had never been in a kiln-house was not worth the paper.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He writes in the narrow upright hand, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could hide in a cuff and carry past a weigh.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the fire keeps its mouth} he wrote \emph{fuel consumed; no entry}, which leaves the fire standing and takes the mouth away.

\item At \emph{it takes what we set to it and gives back heat} he set \emph{heat transferred to chamber, current}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{one in twelve goes up the road} he wrote \emph{deduction one in twelfths, read twice, current}, as though the reading and the paying were the same act performed in two places.

\item At \emph{a figure you hear isn’t a figure you paid} he wrote \emph{figures of account, not of price}. I have never argued less with a sentence of his.

\item At \emph{the cup’s got a lip and the lip’s got a flaw} he set \emph{vessel fractured; retained in service}, which is the truest and coldest thing on the leaf.

\item Where the space stands before the last refrain he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a figure where a name should stand, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman at the end of a firing does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand held the cup before hers.

\subsection*{What the hearth-maid put in the margin}

The small careful hand is Alda’s, who keeps the birth-slates for the district and carries soap and warm milk in the same order every morning. She wrote in the margin because she would not have her words on the face of the leaf where a collector might read them going past. I have copied her as she set them down.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the first pour goes to the fire, not to a face}: “Same order at a birth. The hand goes to the slate before it goes to the child. Don’t make more of it than that.”

\item At \emph{here’s to the hands that went in and stayed}: “A round forgets who it was for by the third cup. Names are better. Ask me why I say that and I’ll give you a date.”

\item At \emph{we drink to the gap}: “The fifth isn’t a drink. It’s a place. Leave it the length it is.”

\item At \emph{an honest fault’s a thing the neighbours know}: “A child came back to us this year who liked the smell of wet clay before he had seen a pot. I have written that nowhere else. Keep it where a collector’s thumb won’t go.”

\item At the space before the last refrain: “The third saying is not for the pot and not for the fire. I have been asked whose it was and answered with a date. Both stand.”

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey curl at the head is off the kiln shelf and went into the grain when I held the leaf down. The tallow is mine, off the lamp I keep turned low behind the racks. The crust-grease on the second leaf is from a browned edge laid down while I was telling a girl to eat and she would not. The ring is small ale, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The green bead came off a woman from High Kiln who stood with the sweetness at one corner of her mouth, leaned over to see the writing, touched the leaf and went back up the terrace without buying. The scorch took one word off the sixth verse and I have not written it back, because a verse with a word gone is a verse said slowly, and ours are all said slowly. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind a rack. The twist of grey wool through the hole is mine, tied for the line I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps what it’s given. The pot keeps the note.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup goes round and the name goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate goes up the road with neither.\end{quote}

I asked a woman at the racks, the kiln-master and a man come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the verse where it was written.

The crock goes back behind the lowest rack and the cup goes back on its shelf with the thumb-wide flaw uppermost. Tomorrow the kiln will be drawn again and the cup will come down and go round, and the fourth pour will stand where it stood and be carried away full, and if the clerk borrows the leaf let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, and wet the rim before it sings.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The First Measure, Being the Collector’s Own Leaf for the Hearth Drawing in Low Kiln on Stone 12 of Y.H. 812, with the Embers, the Deduction, the Note the Room Gave, the Child Worse Before Dusk, and the Figure Read Twice at the Cross; Written in the Hand That Carried the Tube and Corrected in Two Others}
\CRsheetheading{The First Measure, Being the Collector’s Own Leaf for the Hearth Drawing in Low Kiln on Stone 12 of Y.H. 812, with the Embers, the Deduction, the Note the Room Gave, the Child Worse Before Dusk, and the Figure Read Twice at the Cross; Written in the Hand That Carried the Tube and Corrected in Two Others}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from a collector’s pocket ledger; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the day-slate, the remarks terse and in the hand that unwrapped the wool and held the tube, one column struck by a College clerk and drawn back beneath his words, a passive verb set above each of mine, one sentence written over by a factor’s man, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in the Clay Yard of Low Kiln and in the death-house two doors down from the Vail kiln-house on Stone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, the day of the Hearth Drawing; copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and carried in the oiled-paper wrap in the collector’s coat beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives with grey worked under the nails at the head, iron filings ground into the gutter off the tube’s wrap, a tallow thumb where the lamp was held low, a bone-pale streak of slip from a thrower’s forearm, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a pale round ring where a cold tube was set down on the leaf, the circle of a milk-cup pressed into the second fold, a damp tide-line along the foot out of a house where a pot was broken at the door, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with the tube’s edge, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a College clerk, one in the leaning hand of a factor’s man from Greybank, and one line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I draw the year’s first measure on a day before the year has turned, which is the Court’s way and not mine. Stone the twelfth, with the Ilm still under its skin of ice and the district saying three days to the Five while counting three Account-days and not three mornings. A collector may draw from the dying and from the newly born on the same day. The ordinance says \emph{may}; the district says \emph{must}; both are entered in the same neat hand by men who have stood in different rooms.

I set the slate down before I look at anybody. Hand to slate, then eyes to the bed, then the mouth to say what the slate has already said. If a woman tells me her mother’s name while I am writing the figure, I have the figure and not the name, which is what she wanted me to have, though she would deny it at her own door.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that comes north with the factor and will not stay in Grath. The Court books an ember at five marks and no man in this yard has exchanged one for the other. A newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen, a labourer in good case forty to sixty, one of the Kept three hundred, which is a figure no household can spend. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross, once for the moot and once for those who came late. I have set no second figure beside it. I have heard a figure spoken in the yards and not entered it, not being a figure I can weigh.

Draws on this leaf: five. Lines with no draw in them: three. Figures struck: one. Columns struck: one. Figures read twice: one, and both readings the same.

\subsection*{The leaf, as I set it down}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand, copied from the slate I carried. The remarks are mine, in the hand that unwrapped the wool, and are not part of the account. A dash is a place where nothing was drawn, not a nought.}

Day — Vessel, as the house has it — Embers — Deduction — Banked to — Note — Remark\par

Stone 12 — A neighbour two doors down, a man past speaking. \emph{Breath} — 44 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — none — Asked once while breath remained; the house answered. Wrote before unwrapping. Held the tube without pressing. A woman set a basket at the edge of the light; I did not ask whose.\par

Stone 12 — A child three days returned, the same room. \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — none — Worse before dusk. Entered as a return, not a worsening. Both figures stand.\par

Stone 12 — A hearth-maid’s slate, left at the threshold. \emph{Birth} — — — — — — — — — Name written before the face was looked at. No figure came off it. Not mine to enter.\par

Stone 12 — A thrower of the low yard, come for the year’s first. \emph{Nineteen} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Knuckle to the rim before the tube. Slip on both forearms; left a bone-pale streak on my cuff. Asked after her girl; not entered.\par

Stone 12 — A clay-bound hand of the terraces, sixth year of seven. \emph{Seven} — 43 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — nearly — Counted by the man, not by me. Air under the note; no Grathic word for it, so I have set the phrase as I heard it.\par

Stone 12 — A house of the terraces, disputed. \emph{Shoulder} — 52 — — — — — flat — Thumb wiped twice before touching nothing. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing.\par

Stone 12 — No vessel drawn. A house at the yard’s end — — — — — — — — — Breath had gone before I came through the door. Pot broken at the threshold after I wrapped the tube; heat went out with the shard and not into the account. No measure.\par

Stone 12 — The Cross, the figure read aloud — — — 1 in 12 — — — — — Read twice, once for the moot and once for the late households. The same figure I wrote by the bed. Both set; neither joined.\par

\subsection*{The order at a death-house}

\emph{Copied from what I was told at the table and have used for eleven years. The second column is mine and is not read at any Weighing.}

Step — As the notice has it — As I keep it\par

The asking — Put once while breath remains; the answer entered before the breathing is counted — I have asked twice in eleven years and entered both as fresh. Neither answer was worth the ink.\par

The answer — Where the vessel cannot speak, the house answers; entered to the house — The house is not asked whether it understood. A woman held her mother’s hand and said a sentence that was not an answer; I set it at the edge of the leaf, the length of it.\par

The tube — Unwrapped after the entry; of cold iron, wrapped in wool — The wool is for the hand that holds it. The ordinance has no place for such a hand. I hold without pressing.\par

The figure — One in twelve, as the notice says; not changed for the bed or the hour — Read twice at the Cross before I came down the yard; entered once at the bed. The same figure. I have not made one out of the two readings.\par

The pot — Broken at the door after the tube is wrapped, before the slate is carried away — Never entered. A pot is a piece of clay, and what was in it is not on any slate.\par

The shard — Not swept until the Last Day — This house swept its step in the afternoon. I asked who swept and entered the answer to the house, which was weather.\par

\subsection*{The note column, and why a man is not a cup}

Before the tube I set a knuckle on the rim or the bed-rail. A whole vessel answers full; one cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface; one with air under it answers nearly full, which the yards have no word for. A vessel turned toward in expectation may give nothing at all. I have entered that as \emph{none} and not as a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not.

At the death-house the room gave none. I did not tap the man. A man is not a cup, and I have learned not to set my knuckle to one. There was a cup on the bench by the bed and it had stood there long enough to take the room into itself; it answered nothing, and I wrote nothing beside it. The hearth-maid later turned a written note down under a milk cup, and the circle of that cup is pressed into the second fold of this leaf; it is her cup and her note and I have entered neither.

The College man came down from Slate Row with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing and struck the column through from the first row to the last, writing \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand. He drew his thumb down every row before he could write that there was nothing in any of them worth entering, and I watched him do it. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. A man does not count what he has not looked at.

\subsection*{The child on the third day}

The returned child in that room was three days back and worse before dusk. The women worked with the certain kindness of a thing they have known all their lives, warming from the outside and slowly, and saying almost nothing over the pallet. The physician come up from Low Kiln calls it the second chill; the hearth-maid calls it a graft settling. I have set both phrases in the remark and neither in a column. A child who comes back and then grows cold again is a thing the yards know and the slate has no place for. I entered the measure at thirteen, the clerk set twelve above it, and both stand, because a vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw and yet the slate beside the bed said thirteen when I read it.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College clerk struck \emph{I drew} against the man at the bed and set \emph{the measure was drawn} above it, and underneath that \emph{the warmth was entered}, which is further from the bed again. I have put \emph{I drew} back beneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these draws in the end, always at the door, always after the tube is put away.

A factor’s man from Greybank wrote in a leaning hand with a little gold in the ink. Against \emph{the house answered} he set \emph{the answer was entered}. Against \emph{the room called it merciful} he set \emph{the draw was lawful} and underlined it twice. Both stand. Lawful is true and does not mention a man on a board-bed; merciful is what the room said after I had wrapped the tube, and there is no column for what a room says. He struck the word \emph{none} in the note column and wrote \emph{vacancy} above it. A nought is a figure and can be carried out in a cuff. The silence at the bed stays where it was.

\subsection*{The verse the collectors say going down the yard}

\emph{Said low going down the Clay Yard after the tube is wrapped, never while the slate is open, and never twice in one house. The last line is said to the pot, and the man who said it to me would not say it while the factor’s man stood at the gate.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wool on the iron, slate on the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tube goes in where the breath would be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read twice at the Cross and once at the bed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four go down and four come up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth should stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot goes out with the house’s heat\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey goes home ahead of the hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The name goes down before the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the child comes back and wants no cup;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I write the note and not the room\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the room keeps what I never took down.\end{quote}

I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A collector who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{In the head and in the gutter}

The grey under the nails at the head came off my own fingers giving the figure to the clerk at Greybank last tend; it goes in under the nails first and comes up into the creases by the second year, and after that a man may wash until the water freezes and nothing changes. The filings in the gutter came out of the wool sleeve and have never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is the only mercy iron has shown this leaf. The tallow thumb is mine, from holding the lamp low while a woman in the death-house was telling me something I wanted the end of; she did not tell me the end, and went back to sitting. The bone-pale streak came off the thrower’s forearms when she set her slate beside mine to wait for a figure. The green bead is lead glaze and not slip; she leaned over with the sweetness still at her mouth, touched the paper, said nothing, and went back up the terrace. I have not washed it off.

The pale round ring was made by setting a cold tube down on the leaf while I reached for the slate, and the paper is thinner inside it. The tube was not used and the ring is not a wound, but it is the only mark on this page that looks like one. The circle in the second fold is the milk cup. The tide-line along the foot came up from the house where the pot was broken and comes back every wet month. The small bare square is where I scraped a word away with the edge of the tube and put no other in its place. I have not written the word back, and I have not forgotten its length.

On the Last Day the houses sweep their corners and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day in a coat.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the figure. The room keeps the answer. The pot keeps the heat that went out with the shard, and none of the three is entered to the same house.\end{quote}

I asked a hearth-maid, a factor’s man, and a collector’s boy come up from the yard, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the oiled paper and the tube into its wool sleeve. Tomorrow the district will go on saying three days to the Five and counting them its own way, and a figure will be read twice at the Cross, and I shall set the slate down before I look at the bed, and write the note before the College can strike it out. The grey will come off on the next leaf. I have stopped washing it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Five Days Outside the Months, Being Title the Third of the Ordinances of the Keeping: the Kindling, the Weighing, the Long Night, the Remembering and the Last Day; with the Table of Days, the Things Not Entered, the Fire-Carrying Verse, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Five Days Outside the Months, Being Title the Third of the Ordinances of the Keeping: the Kindling, the Weighing, the Long Night, the Remembering and the Last Day; with the Table of Days, the Things Not Entered, the Fire-Carrying Verse, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the counter of the Court’s room in Slate Row, Sill, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the five-day slate; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the days and the things not entered in a table, the carrying-verse as it is said under the covered pot, one line scored with a bread crust, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at Sill in Slate Row in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Third of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years and confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418, added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire in a slate-coloured board cover, kept in the drawer under the counter between the bell-cord and the tallow end and taken down when the months leave off: a tallow thumb at the head, grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a scorch along the first leaf where a covered pot was set down, a bead of lead glaze, a brown score where a crust was laid, a damp tideline along the foot, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the slate of the Five in the drawer under this counter, between the bell-cord and the tallow end, and take it down once a year when the months leave off and the days have names instead of numbers. Five days, and they belong to no month and no tend. A man comes in during them wanting a figure; I give him the day’s name instead. The ordinance is in Ledgerhand, with nobody in any of its sentences. I put the people back underneath, because a holy day with nobody in it is a day nobody kept, and that is the kind the Keeping likes best.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, written very small, in mine:} Copied for the counter and from the drawer. The verbs are mine and the absence of them is not. Let both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Third, as it stands in the Court’s room}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Third: Of the Five Days Outside the Months, their Observance and what is Entered Therein. Set down in the first years of the Keeping; confirmed to the factor at Greybank by the treaty of Y.H. 418; added to after the Rising of Y.H. 668, in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the days and their number}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A year has twelve months of thirty days and five days that belong to no month. The five are told after Stone and are named Kindling, Weighing, the Long Night, the Remembering and the Last Day, in that order and in no other.

\item No day is added to the count to make the sky agree with the slate. The Court teaches that the Warm holds the seasons in their places.

\item A tend has ten days and a month has three tends. The Five break the tend. On Ilmen 1 the count begins again at Firstday.

\item No market is held in the Five and no claim is taken and no account is opened. What would have been entered is carried forward into the Opening of the Slates.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A surveyor come up from Keld said, with the factor’s man at the trough, that the thaw had come in Ilmen for eight hundred years by the Keld count and the Court’s slate had never once had to agree with it; then he turned his slate face down and asked after the road. I have entered neither the eight hundred years nor the turning.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of Kindling}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item On Kindling every hearth in Sarn is lit from the Hearth-flame. The fire comes down the road under a covered pot, from hall to hall, and from this room to the houses of the low bank last of all. No priest touches the grating. The hand that carries is not the hand that kindles, and neither is entered.

\item Collectors take the first measure of the year’s roll on Kindling, before light, from the dying and from the newly born on the same day. The figure is copied into the roll in a clean hand and is not read aloud until Weighing.

\item A hearth lit from another hearth without the fire having been carried into it is entered as carried and not as lit. The house is not asked which it believes.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman came up from the low bank with a covered pot and asked whether the fire in it was still the Hall’s after three doors. I told her the ordinance asks where a fire was lit and not where it has been. She covered the pot again and went down the yard, and I have no article for the three doors. I carried such a pot once over ice; it warms the wrist through the cloth, and then it does not. There is no column for the carrying.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of Weighing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item On Weighing the year’s measures are read aloud from the clean roll in the Weighing Hall, in a voice that does not hurry. The figure printed on the notice is one in twelve, as the notice says. There is no other figure in the room.

\item The reading is given twice: once for those within the Hall and once for those who came up the road too late to get into it. The second reading is the same figure and is not corrected for the lateness.

\item A whole return may be announced for a person who is not in the room. The reader does not ask where the person is. The College keeps a second file for the answers to questions of that kind, and the second file is not read aloud.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I heard a figure in the yards that will not agree with this one, and have not entered it. A man from the College struck the word \emph{heard} from the line above and set \emph{a figure is current} over it, which is true of the notice and false of the yard. I have put \emph{heard} back underneath and left his above, where a man must lean to read both.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the Long Night}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item On the Long Night no fire is lit after dusk. Fires are banked and hearths covered; no light is carried between houses. What is spent in the night is not entered in the morning.

\item The stories of the Return are told in the dark. What is said in the dark is not entered, and the telling of it is not a claim upon any house.

\item No collection is made between dusk and morning and no slate is opened by firelight.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} In the Long Night of the Thin Year a woman sat in the low bank with a pot between her and the door and would not say what she had set there. I have no article for a pot in the dark and no column for the time she kept her hand on the lid. The bell at the Cross goes four, four and a gap on an Account-day; in the Five it is not rung at all, which is the one account this year kept its own silence without a clerk to enter it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the Remembering}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item On the Remembering the names of the dead are spoken in the order of the roll. The roll is carried forward and never closed. A name spoken is not a return entered, and a return entered is not a name brought back.

\item Where a whole return is announced, the reader gives the figure and the name together in a clean voice. Where a household disputes the name, the figure stands and the name is not changed.

\item No article provides for a name that a household will not have spoken.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have carried one name forward for eleven years after the house that gave it was empty of people. Nobody came to close it and I did not close it. A woman stood here with her thumb at the middle of her palm where a ring had once been worn tight and long, and asked whether the dead came back whole. I read her the figure the notice gives, which is the only figure I can read here. She went away with her thumb still on the place. There is no line in this Title for a place on a palm.\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. Of the Last Day}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item On the Last Day bread is baked in every house and nothing is swept from the corners before the day is out. The grey that gathers there is left where it gathered and is not called dirt in the hearing of a child.

\item On the morning after, the grey is swept up and burnt and called dealt with. Where the factor has licensed the gathering, what is bottled and sealed is done before the burning and is entered to the licence and not to the house.

\item A pot is broken at the door of a death-house to let the heat out. The breaking is not entered and the pot is not counted among the household’s goods afterward.

\item What is given at a house door in the Five is given and not entered, which is the same rule as in the months and more necessary here, where a man has no figure to defend himself with.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, scored with the edge of a bread crust:} A woman laid a crust here while she told me where her child had been found and would not say the name of the house. I have left the grease where it fell; the brown has eaten two letters without taking the sense. A crust keeps the place where it was set down, which is more than this article does. A man asked whether the pot broken at a death-house was paid for out of the household’s measure. I told him the breaking was not entered. He said that was an answer with nobody in it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{VII. The table of the days}

\emph{The third column is the ordinance. The last is mine and has no standing at any Weighing.}

Day — What is done — As the ordinance has it — What is not entered\par

Kindling — Hearth lit from the carried fire; first measure taken — Fire carried under a pot; figure copied in a clean hand — The three doors the pot came through; the wrist that carried it\par

Weighing — Year’s measures read; whole returns announced — One in twelve, as the notice says; read twice — The figure heard in the yards; where the absent person is\par

the Long Night — Fires banked; stories told in the dark — No fire after dusk; no slate by firelight — The pot at the door; the hand upon the lid\par

the Remembering — Names spoken in the order of the roll — Roll carried forward and never closed — The thumb at the palm; what the house would not have spoken\par

the Last Day — Bread baked; corners left; pot broken — Grey swept and burnt on the morning after — The crust laid here; the giving at the door\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I drew the last column and a College clerk struck it out, writing \emph{No such column} above in a hand so upright it hurts the eye. I struck his striking out and left it where I drew it. The College teaches eleven words for a deduction and none for a place.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The carrying-verse}

\emph{Said low under the covered pot on Kindling, before the fire has crossed the yard. Not at the Weighing and not while the collector’s tube is out of its wool. The last line is said to the pot and not to the person who carries it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five days and no month to their name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a fire goes out and a fire comes home;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure is read and the figure is paid,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the corner keeps what the broom has stayed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Kindling gives and the Weighing tells,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Long Night keeps what the dark keeps well;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four in the bell and a gap where the fifth should be ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that’s for the market, not for these.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A house keeps warm what the pot has known.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a narrow upright hand:} One observance entered; no deduction arises. \emph{In mine:} He has put a figure where I put a house. A house can be asked about; an observance cannot. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from the Hearthseat with ink in two fingers and a cuff gone soft from washing. He struck \emph{the fire comes down the road} and set \emph{the fire is transmitted} above, as though a pot could go from hall to hall without a wrist under it. I put the road back underneath. On the Remembering he struck \emph{the names of the dead are spoken} and set \emph{the roll is recited} above, which leaves nobody in the room to say the name. Both stand.

The other hand is a factor’s from Greybank, leaning and brown at the edge. Against the scorch he wrote \emph{fire received in good order} and against the verse \emph{annual observance, current; no charge to the district}. I have left both. A factor may call a fire received because a fire is a thing that can be entered and handed on; a woman who has carried a pot over ice calls it something else and has no word for it this room will take.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head is mine, from holding the lamp low while a woman told me which door the pot had come through and I did not want her to see me writing it down. The grey in the outer fold is Ash, off my own cuff going down to the Cross on an Account-day, where I put my hand into a corner I had no business putting into; it will not come out of the creases. The scorch is where a covered pot was set down while I read the Kindling article. The bead in the lower corner is lead glaze, not slip; a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth touched the leaf and went back up the terrace without asking. The tideline along the foot is damp come up from the flagstones in a wet Five. On the Last Day the houses burn their corners and call it dealt with. This drawer is not a house and keeps what is left in it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire goes out from the Hall and comes back to every hearth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure goes out from the Hall and comes back to no household the same.\end{quote}

I asked a keeper of the grating, a woman who carried a pot up the yard on Kindling, and a clerk come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written.

The slate goes back into the drawer under the bell-cord. Next year the months will leave off on the thirtieth of Stone and the five days will come with names and no tend-days among them, and I shall take this down and put the verbs back where another hand has taken them out. The fire will come in under a covered pot and go out to the low bank. The roll will stay open. That is my trade here: to write down what was done, and leave a place the length of what was not.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Flat Stone, Being What Was Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 812, with the Old Words Left in Knots Because Fen Cant Will Not Write}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Flat Stone, Being What Was Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 812, with the Old Words Left in Knots Because Fen Cant Will Not Write}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Weir preached at the blessing stone on the north bank at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill; the saying in Grathic, the three old lines held in the margin as knots of grey wool, with the tally-keeper’s corrections, a Court clerk’s in Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached at the Fish Blessing by an old woman of the Weir who had stood at the stone at thirty blessings, over the traps lifted and set on their sides on the plank walk, on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year; written that evening by a woman of the Weir who keeps the eel tally and has no slate-name, on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by a wet figure out of Greybank, and sewn with eel-sinew into the folded reed wrapper that holds the knot-accounts in the Eel House. It survives with a salt crust at the head where a flat hand was set to brush the grit from the cut, a silt tideline along the gutter from a morning the plank walk stood under water, eel slime on the second leaf, a fish-hook nick nobody will own, a grey Ash print from a cuff at the stone, three knots left over right with the tail under against the three old lines, and a fourth knot tied through a hole in the first leaf for a word the preacher would not give out. Copied once at Greybank in Silt, Y.H. 812, and again in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the knots left as they were tied.\par}\medskip
I keep the eel tally at the Weir and nobody asked me for this. I write because the old woman’s words went into the water and the water kept them, and I wanted something on dry paper that a clerk could not carry away in a cuff. She stood on the flat stone with her sleeves salt to the elbow and spoke to the stone, the traps, the river, and last of all to us, which is the order the women of this place use when there is work to be done and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set down what she said in Grathic. The three old lines are not Grathic and are not written anywhere; I have tied three knots in the margin against them, left over right with the tail under, which is how we keep a thing here that we cannot spell.

The salt crust at the head came off her hand when she flattened it on the stone to brush the grit from the cut. The silt tideline along the gutter is from the morning the plank walk stood under water and I carried the leaf under my apron. The eel slime is mine: I set the leaf down on the bench to count and a fish came out of the basket onto it, which the old woman called a blessing, and I did not argue. The fish-hook nick is not mine and I don’t know whose. The grey print came off a cuff at the stone and nobody will own it; I have not swept it. The knot through the hole in the first leaf is the fourth, and I tied it for the word she would not give out.

\subsection*{The order of the blessing, as the stone actually has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Brush the stone free of grit so the cut shows. Do not ask what the cut is. It was here before the tally and it will be here after.

\item Stand with your sleeves damp and salt in the creases of your hands. Salt on the stone and along the weir head, with a flat hand. Not on the traps. The traps have their own business.

\item Say the old words low, facing the water. A woman who says them looking at her neighbour is making an argument, and there is argument enough at the Cross without bringing it upriver.

\item Lift the traps and set them on their sides. Count them if you must, but do not say the number where a man with a slate is standing.

\item When the bell comes upriver from the Cross, stop. It is counting something that is not your river. Begin again after. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not ours to fill.

\item The eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. This is the first thing she says every year and the last thing she will have written down, which is nothing at all.

\end{itemize}

I asked her why we bless them if they run without it. She gave me three answers: because they run; because a woman must do something with her hands on a cold morning; and because if we did not bless them, somebody from Greybank would come upriver and enter the blessing for us, and then we would owe for it. I asked for a fourth. She stood on the stone and looked at the water and did not give me one.

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the mouth}

She squatted by a trap on its side and put her finger into the mouth of it, the way you would show a child where a thing goes in.

“Look at it,” she said. “The mouth points upriver. That is the whole of the contrivance. An eel swims looking for the current and the current takes him in, and the basket narrows behind him, and there he is. He has not been bad. He has not been called. He followed the water, which is what eels do and what water does.

“Set it down among you now and tap it. It answers full when the wicker is sound and flat when it has a hole. That is all the preaching I have. A thing that holds, holds. A thing that leaks, leaks. We do not ask the pot why it cracked.

“Away up the river they read a figure over a basket and call the basket full because the figure says so. I have stood at the Cross and heard it done twice, once for the moot and once for them that came late. I do not know what figure goes with an eel. Nobody has ever told me, and I have never asked a man who was carrying a slate.”

Here she stopped and crossed two fingers at the cut in the stone and covered the act with a date, which is what the women here do.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} She gave me Y.H. 418, the year the Clay Road was made a Court road. I asked her again in a different way and she gave me the same year. I have set it down and left the question standing. Dates are safe. The Court likes a date and does not ask what it covers.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the blessing}

“Do not say I made the eels come,” she said. “I did not. Say the words with me, and then go and look at the traps. They came because they came.

“A priest come up from Greybank told us the blessing is a mercy of the Hearth and that the Hearth keeps what it is given. I have heard the same man read a whole return for a person not in the room. I believed him once. Then I tied a cord and counted what came back into this house, and the cord and the house did not agree with him.

“Here is what I know of keeping. The river keeps what falls in it. The mud keeps what the river puts down. A knot keeps what a woman tied and will not tell you. None of these three writes it down and none of them sends a collector.

“Say the old words. Put the salt on. Stand where your mother stood. That is the blessing. It does not make the eels run and it does not make them stay. It makes us stand in the same place on the same morning, which is more than most households in Sill can say for themselves.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk who came upriver on the fourth day and borrowed the leaf:} The rite is observed by long custom and is efficacious thereby. The measure is retained in the silt. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have put \emph{keeps} and \emph{stand} back under his. A sentence with the verbs taken out travels well and arrives empty, which is what a man wants who has to carry it a league to a table. I have left his hand standing and my words below it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the figure}

“I will give you no number,” she said to me, when I asked what went into the cord. “Ask Orra. She will tell you which night the collector’s boat came and how many oars it had, and you may put that in your tally if you like.

“There is a number goes around this Weir from mouth to mouth and nobody gives it out. It gets into a fist and then a mouth and then a shoulder, and by the time it reaches the Eel House it has turned into weather. We say the river is up. We say the eels are running late. We say the book is lost. All true. None of them a figure.

“One in twelve is printed on the notice and read at the Cross and is not a lie. It is a true thing said to a room that is not this one. I have never seen the other figure and I have never wanted to see it. A figure is a thing a man can carry away in a cuff. A knot has to be looked at by the woman who tied it.”

\subsection*{Of the mark}

I asked her about the cut in the stone, which the chart draws and does not explain.

She put her thumb in it and said: “It was here before the stone was flat.”

“That is not a date,” I said.

“It is older than a date,” she said. “Your clerk will want a year. Give him Y.H. 418 and be shut of him.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the clerk’s hand at this place:} cut of uncertain antiquity; assign to the treaty-year, Y.H. 747. He wrote this above and underlined it twice, and set Y.H. 418 beneath it in a small stop. Both years stand, and the cut stands under both of them.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of them that come back}

“They tell us the dead come back warm,” she said. “I have stood at four returns in this district. Three came back as other people, with a hankering for a table they never sat at. One came back and said a word in a language I knew once and have forgot. The Court calls it a settling.

“I am not saying the Return is a lie. I am saying I have not seen the thing they say it is. There is a difference, and the difference has a place in the cord where nobody puts a figure.

“When my neighbour’s girl came back thin she went to the door and looked at the eel baskets and said she had been here before, which was true and no comfort to her mother. We gave her a crust. We did not read her a figure. If there is a mercy in this world it is in the crust and not in the reading.”

\subsection*{The old words}

\emph{Three lines said low, facing the water, in Fen Cant, which is not written. I have tied three knots in the margin against them, left over right, tail under, and set the sound of them here as well as I can hear it:}

\begin{quote}\itshape The eels run whether we bless them or not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the river keeps what the river got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a way in is a way in and no way out —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the oars and one for the doubt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the flat and salt on the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mouth points up and the basket stands;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we say the words and we say no more —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water does what the water bore.\end{quote}

I have put \emph{doubt} where I heard a word I cannot spell. It may be \emph{debt}. Orra says it is neither and will not say which. Two women have told me the last line means the same thing in Fen as it does in Grathic, which I do not believe, because a thing that means the same thing in two languages would have been written down by now.

\subsection*{The account of the morning}

\emph{Written as a tally, because that is the hand I keep.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Salt: a handful, from the Vhaleni jar in the Eel House. Berr Clay bought eels for the levy feast and paid two marks short; the trap-keeper has served him the same short measure ever since, and I keep the count of it. That is not a debt. It is an account no slate will take.

\item Rushes: a bundle cut above the plank walk. Nobody paid. They grow.

\item Words: three old lines and the Grathic saying after them. They cost the old woman her breath and cost me the afternoon. Not entered.

\item Eels: the traps came up full. I had the count in my mouth and put it in the water before anyone with a slate came round the bend. The second basket I did not count.

\item The stone: brushed, salted, stood upon, left as it was. It has never been entered and has never asked to be.

\end{itemize}

Nothing on this leaf was carried into the square. That is the only figure the Weir has ever agreed on.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came upriver on the fourth day with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers, borrowed the leaf at the Eel House, and gave it back with the verbs taken out. Where I wrote \emph{the river keeps what falls in it}, he set \emph{the measure is retained in the silt} above and left mine below. Where I wrote \emph{we say the river is up}, he wrote \emph{the figure is withheld pending the thaw}, which is the same sentence said by a man who has never stood in water. At the three knots he put a round nought and wrote \emph{nil} beside it, and when I asked him what a knot was worth he said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning.

I have tied the verbs back in wool. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them; I tie them in because a woman standing on a wet stone wants to know who is doing the keeping, and whether she will get it back.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the old woman’s and not the clerk’s, struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape A way in is not a way out. The stone knows this and says nothing.\end{quote}

I asked the old woman, Orra, the girl who brings the salt, and a man come up from Greybank, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the wrapper with the knot-accounts. Next Ilmen the women will brush the stone and stand on it and say the three old lines into the water, and the eels will run as they always run. If the clerk comes again I shall let him take the verbs out; I shall tie them back as I did this time, and keep the fourth knot through the hole in the first leaf, which is the one I tied for the word she would not give out.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fourth Name, Being a Letter from a Room with Good Light in Greybank to a Sister of the Ember House in the Bowl of Sere, with the Three Deaths Set Down, the Bowl-Song, a Factor’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and the Answer Left in the Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Fourth Name, Being a Letter from a Room with Good Light in Greybank to a Sister of the Ember House in the Bowl of Sere, with the Three Deaths Set Down, the Bowl-Song, a Factor’s Correction in Ledgerhand, and the Answer Left in the Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A letter between two women of one great house, the one written in the open courtesy of Sere and the other answered in the same warm hand; a tally of three names against three deaths, the feast-song in verse, the correction of a factor’s clerk laid over both, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a room with good light in the counting house at Greybank, eighteen leagues east downriver of Sill, by Solene Ember, returned whole in Y.H. 799, 804 and 809, to her sister of House Ember in the Bowl of Sere; written on the back of a spoiled grain docket from the Court’s granaries, the third-day hand unsteady and the wine of the public bowl gone cold on it. Carried south with the grain factor’s convoy in Smoke, answered in the margin at the Bowl in Ash, and brought north again with the glass in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. Kept since in a dry tin in the room with good light, under a fold of cloth that smells of myrrh. It survives with a ring of warm wine at the head, myrrh worked into the grain, a grey bead of Ash from a public bowl pressed into the fold, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a greenish mark where a ring lay on the leaf, a line that runs out toward the gutter and stops, the three deaths set down in a small table, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk of the factor’s office, the sister’s answer in a warm sloped hand in the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
To my sister of the Ember house, who keeps the seventh name and will not say which of the seven she kept. From the north, from a room with good light that I am not permitted to enjoy, in the counting house of the man who brought me.

Sister, I have taken the first ring off before I began, and the second is off and lying by the ink, and the third I have left on because I have not yet decided whether what follows is true enough to cost it. You know the habit. You have watched me remove them one at a time since we were girls, and you have never once asked why, which is a kinder thing than asking and being told.

I write on the back of a grain docket from the factor’s granary, because there is no paper in this room that is mine, and a letter on a man’s paper is a thing a man may read if he has a mind to. The smell on it is myrrh. I have begun to smell of it myself, which in the Bowl would make you laugh and here makes the serving women put a hand to their mouths, the way these lowland folk cross themselves when a thing is said badly. I have not crossed myself. I am a woman of the Ten Bowls and I know what a bowl is for.

It is the third day after a feast and my hand is not steady. Look at the line that runs out toward the gutter and then stops. I have not straightened it, and I have not written the word again. The priests at home call the third-day tremor the price of beauty. Here they say nothing at all, because nobody in Greybank has ever seen a beautiful return and would not know a price if one were laid in their hand. The wine on the leaf came from the public bowl and went cold while I was finding the word I wanted, which is the whole history of warmth in the north in one small circle on a counting-house docket.

\subsection*{Why I am writing, which is not the ring on my finger}

There are three of me and there may be no fourth. A woman with three deaths ought to set them down in her own hand before a clerk sets them down in his, because a clerk will write them as \emph{returns entered: three} and leave the deaths standing out of the sentence where they cannot be read. I was returned in the year of the green bowl. No --- the third one. I was returned in the year of the green bowl and I have had two since. You were at the first feast. You stood where the fire in the court lit the whole bowl of us, and you clapped for the debt and not for the girl, which was correct, and which I have never quite forgiven you for being correct about.

The name I answer to — The year — The death that belonged to it — What the new walls let me keep\par

Solene, the one I chose out of seven — Y.H. 799, the green bowl — the Spending fire, in the open court — the taste of the wine, and the applause for the debt\par

Ilyra, which was our mother’s — Y.H. 804 — the fall from the balcony at the feast of Grain; nobody pushed, which is why it was entered as a kindness — the fall itself, and the noise the bowls made below me\par

Vey, the shortest of the three — Y.H. 809 — quiet ash, given by a woman who smiled the whole while and said it was a mercy — the smile, and nothing at all of the face above it\par

The third one is the one I remember least and therefore the one I fear. When Valen Openhand asked me whether I was grateful, I said yes three times, and on the third I took a ring off before I said it, and he saw me do it and did not mention it, which was the only mercy in that court that had nobody’s name on it.

When you write back, ask me which death I mean, the way you used to. If I do not say \emph{the third one} inside a year, I shall know that the part of me that knows the difference has gone, and you may have the room and the light and the rings and welcome to them, but you will not have me to write to.

\subsection*{The song, as we sang it at the end of the feast}

They burn the debt-slates of one household by lot when the eating is done, and then they make new ones. I have set the song down as it is sung, going out from the bowl rather than coming back from it. The ends of the lines fall away in the court; I have put them back where I could hear them and left them gone where I could not.

\begin{quote}\itshape We emptied the bowl and the fire said yes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we burned the slate and we made it again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the debt we carried went up with the smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bowl stands full for the next of the house.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven names at the naming, one kept at the Bowl,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that we kept was the one we let go;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wine goes down and the fire goes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate goes where the slate is owed.\end{quote}

That is how we sang it. I used to think the last line was a courtesy. I have since seen a slate carried out of a room in this country with the same face on the man carrying it, and I no longer think it a courtesy.

\subsection*{What I ask you, which I ask everybody now}

What debt do you intend to carry? I ask it of everyone. In the north they think it is a question about money. It is not. When I asked it of a man who sits at a table in this house, he turned a slate face down before he answered me, so that I should understand I was not being entered, and then turned it face-up again when he had done, so that I should understand I had been. He has eleven words for a deduction and not one for \emph{sorry}. I have tried to teach him the word. He said it was the same absence wearing a different coat, and asked me to write the sentence again without the verb in it, which I did, and which is the most Sarnish thing that has ever been said in Sere.

There is a custom here of leaving the grey Ash in the corners on the last day of the year and burning it the next morning and calling it dealt with. In the Bowl we burn the slate and make a new one, and call that glory. I have stood between the two and cannot tell you which of us is the more honest. A woman here broke a pot at the door of a death-house so that the heat might get out. We would have poured a bowl. I have watched both and I have not decided which lets go the better.

\subsection*{What the factor’s clerk did to this leaf}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the narrow upright hand they teach in the College in the Hearthseat, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff. He set his hand on the top sheet before he looked at me, which is the manner of that table, and said that it was entered as it stood and there was nothing in it I need correct.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against the three names he wrote \emph{returns entered: three; fourth not entered}.

\item Against the deaths he set a figure for each, as though a fall from a balcony and a smiling woman with quiet ash were the same article at two prices.

\item Where I wrote that I am kept in a room with good light, he wrote \emph{the party is accommodated}, and underlined it twice.

\item Where I wrote that I have three deaths, he wrote \emph{measures current}.

\item Beside the name I left empty for the fourth he put a round nought. A nought is a number. The fourth has not come back to be one.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing, his hand above mine and mine under it, as a repaired pot keeps the old break under the new seam and does not pretend the first hand never touched the clay. He took the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman writing home wants to know who did what to her sister, and the answer is in the sentence if the sentence has someone in it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, warm and sloped, the long vowels open}

You always did name the death before you named the guest. Do not tell me you are kept. Tell me which room has the light and whether the window opens, and I shall know whether you can bear to sit in it. We burned the green bowl’s slate at the feast of Smoke and made a new one, and I put your name in it, which is no loss, because a slate that burns is a slate that cannot be read aloud by a man who never met you.

I have asked Valen Openhand what debt I intend to carry and he said \emph{the house’s}, which was correct and not an answer. Ask me again when the bowl is empty and I will tell you something else. Ask me on the third day and I will lie to you in the warmest voice I have, which you will believe, because you always do.

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the third ring. It was our mother’s before it was yours,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a thing that goes through a mother’s hands\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape does not stop being hers because a clerk has entered it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name the fourth when you have seen it. Not before.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A tide that has not come is still worth more\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape than a figure written in the rain.\end{quote}

The last of that is not mine; I copied it off a salt girl in a counting house and she charged me nothing and said so at once, so that I should know it was no favour. She is the only person I have met in the north who understands that a debt can be paid and still be owed.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wine ring at the head is mine; I set the cup down to find the word and left it standing until it went cold. The myrrh has come up out of the paper itself, or out of the cloth it was folded in, and I have not washed it. The grey bead in the fold is from the public bowl at Greybank, pressed there by a woman who leaned over to see what I was writing and said nothing; it is Ash, and in this country Ash is swept up and burned, and here it is in a letter going south. The green at the lower corner is not myrrh. A girl with the sweetness of the glaze still at one corner of her mouth touched the leaf with her thumb and went away, and I have kept the mark where she put it. The greenish print by the ink is where the third ring lay while I wrote the name Vey, and I have not lifted it or covered it. The line that runs toward the gutter is the third-day hand and I have left it running, because a letter written by a steady hand would be a letter from someone else.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three deaths entered, four names carried, and the bowl stands where it stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire under it is paid for by somebody who will not be named at the feast.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the fourth one when it comes what debt it intends to carry, and listen to what it says before you applaud.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fourth Phial, Being a Letter from the Licence-House at Greybank to a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln, Concerning the Ash That Is Sold to Stop a Voice, the Greyed Hand That Dispenses It, the Woman Who Came Back on the Ninth Day, and the Blank Where Her Name Should Stand; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, a Corking Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own, and a Line at the Foot}
\CRsheetheading{The Fourth Phial, Being a Letter from the Licence-House at Greybank to a Hearth-Maid of Low Kiln, Concerning the Ash That Is Sold to Stop a Voice, the Greyed Hand That Dispenses It, the Woman Who Came Back on the Ninth Day, and the Blank Where Her Name Should Stand; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, a Corking Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own, and a Line at the Foot}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the back of a licence for the buying of quiet ash spoiled by a wet thumb at the signing, written in iron-gall and pressed charcoal, folded three times and tied with the strip of grey wool that came off the stopper-bag; carried eighteen leagues down the Clay Road in a pot-carter’s empty bread-basket, answered along the margin at Low Kiln, borrowed at the Court’s table set at the fringe of the Cross where a clerk set a correction on the back, and kept since in the licence-house tin among the corks and the grey rags · Written at the factor’s house in Greybank in the second tend of Grain, Y.H. 813, by Renna, keeper of the licence for quiet ash, to Oda, a hearth-maid of Low Kiln in Sill who had taught her the three-day warming before she went up the road; carried down the Clay Road by a pot-carter going empty, answered at Low Kiln in the third tend of Grain, borrowed at the Court’s table at the Cross where a clerk of the assessor set a correction in the neat upright Ledgerhand.
