It survives folded and tied with the wool strip, with a grey thumb at the head where a stopper was set down unsealed, a cork-shaving caught in the second fold, a rain-line along the gutter from the carter’s basket, a small-ale ring on the third leaf, a tallow print at the outer fold, one word eaten clean out of the verse where the damp took it, the clerk’s correction standing above and the two hands of the women underneath, and one line at the foot that nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
To Oda at the birth-slates in Low Kiln, who puts the back of her wrist to a stone before she puts her hand to a child and has never once said which was warm. From Renna at the licence-house in Greybank, where the corks are kept in a tin and the ash in a drawer that will not shut in the damp.

I write on the back of a licence spoiled by a wet thumb at the signing. The paper is made to be kept, which is the opposite of salt-paper and a great deal less honest. A licence has a line for the buyer’s name and a line for the seller’s hand, and I have written across the buyer’s line, because I have never yet met a clerk who could read a blank the way it was meant. The factor here says a licence fulfilled is a licence closed. I say a licence with a name on it is a licence with a handle, and a thing with a handle can be carried into a room you did not mean to enter.

Do not rub the second fold. There is a cork-shaving in it that has been there since the first sealing of the tend and it will take your thumb.

I have sold eleven phials since the kiln month went out. A phial is sixty marks. You know what a mark is at the racks; I know what it is at the factor’s counter, and the two are the same coin with different hands. It comes to us as a grey powder in a clay bottle no bigger than a thumb. The physician’s order runs one phial for a voice that comes once in a dream, two for a voice that comes often, and three for a voice that has begun to ask for something. Three is the most the order allows. I have never seen a fourth written.

There is a woman in the upper street here who has never done a day’s work that anybody paid for. She came in the second tend of Grain with a green edge at one corner of her mouth from something she had tasted and set down, and asked for three phials, and asked me not to put her name on the line. I told her the line is the licence and the licence is the Court’s, and a name withheld is an unclosed account, and she said her husband had been banked these nine years and she had not been asked whether she consented to any of it. I sold her three. She came back on the ninth day and asked for a fourth.

The order allows three. I told her so. She said the order was written by men who had never been woken at the fourth hour by a voice asking for a fire. I have carried that sentence nine days and found no answer I would put on a slate, which is why it goes in a letter and into a pot-carter’s basket instead of into a clerk’s hand.

My right hand is the colour of wet ash from the cuff to the knuckle. They grey it at the College and call the greying a qualification; a seller who has not been greyed is a seller who has never handled the stuff, and a seller who has never handled it might as well be selling salt. When I stop a phial I use the left hand, because the right has no feeling in the cork and a cork set down by a hand that cannot feel is a cork that will not hold. There is a happiness in that, of a poor kind: the hand that cannot feel the cork is the hand that earns the keeping of it.

Now the asking. You have kept the birth-slates longer than I kept my first apprenticeship. When a child comes cold and is warmed and on the third day speaks in a voice that nobody in the house owns, what do you set down? I do not want the physician’s word for it. I want the word you use when there is no physician in the room and the woman who carried the child is standing there with her hands in her apron, waiting for the slate to tell her which hand held the stone.

\subsection*{The corking verse}

\emph{Sung low at the drawer, to the phial and not to the buyer. The third verse is the one the licence-house taught me; the fourth is mine, and I have never sung it where a clerk could hear it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the voice that comes to the bed,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the voice that comes to the chair,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the voice that has learned to ask;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ash is by the ounce and the ask is unpaid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Grey at the cuff and grey at the thumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the drawer shuts hard and the stopper holds;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what was a man is a pinch in a glass,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the buyer sleeps, or the buyer does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the woman who comes on the ninth,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no fourth in the book and no line for it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the licence has a place where her name should stand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and I have written across it in charcoal.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The house says the guest wants another house.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate says the day and says nothing else.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the stone which hand warmed it. It will not tell you,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and you will not ask a second time.\end{quote}

A clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaf on the morning the bread-basket went back, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the narrow upright hand, with the verbs taken out as though a verb were a thing a man could hide in a cuff. Against \emph{the voice asks for a fire} he set \emph{auditory disturbance, not entered}. Against \emph{a fourth phial refused} he wrote \emph{limit observed, account current}, which is true in the manner of a shut drawer. Against my charcoal across the buyer’s line he set \emph{name withheld, per licence}, and underlined it twice. Where I put the price in marks he wrote \emph{twelve embers, current}, which no market in Sarn has ever paid, and against \emph{what was a man is a pinch in a glass} he put \emph{residue, current}. I have put the verbs back underneath where I could still read them. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of verbs. I put them in because a woman at a drawer at the fourth hour wants to know whose hand stopped the cork.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, small, pressed hard at the ends of words, the letters leaning}

Renna. You have written across the line where her name should stand, which is the only sensible thing in the letter. Keep it. A name on a licence is a handle, and a woman woken at the fourth hour for nine years has had enough handles.

The physician’s order is a device of the College. We do not count voices at the bench. We count the third day. A child warm on the third day is entered as warm, and a child that speaks is entered as a child, and the house keeps the child and the woman keeps the question, and the slate has no column for either.

For the voice: we call it the guest, the one that wants another house. We do not write it on the slate. There is a column for the day and a column for the house and no column for the guest, and a woman who has carried a child three nights wants to know which hand held the stone, which the slate will never tell her. I have set a stone under eleven children and had a twelfth go cold while I was warming him. I have given up finding the figure that makes the two agree, which is not the same as not minding.

As for the fourth: sell it. Not because it will stop the voice --- I do not know that and you do not know that --- but because a woman who comes back on the ninth day has already paid for the coming back, and there is no column for the coming back. Put it where you put the charcoal and let the clerk strike it out; he will, and then it will be the only true figure on the sheet.

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the day and the wool keeps the warm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone goes in at the dark and comes out at the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the guest comes in where the column is not,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house keeps the child and says it is right.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the coming back and none in the book;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape you write across the name and I write the date.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A date is not an answer. It stays where you put it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is more than can be said of a voice.\end{quote}

I have put my verse under yours and left yours standing above, because a letter with two hands on it is the only kind I have ever known anybody believe.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is not the ash we sell. It is the powder off the stopper of the phial I set down unsealed on the second day, and it has gone into the grain so that the whole sheet smells faintly of the drawer. The cork-shaving in the second fold has been there since the first sealing and will not fall out; I have shaken the letter twice and it stays where the paper made room for it. The rain-line along the gutter came from the carter’s basket, which leaked onto the bread and then onto the licence, and he apologised to the bread and not to me. The ring on the third leaf is small ale from the counter, where I was counting the widow’s marks in the morning and did not notice the glass sitting there. The tallow at the outer fold is mine, off the lamp I keep turned down while I seal, so that the factor’s man will not come in and ask what I am doing with the drawer shut. One word has gone out of the corking verse where the damp took it clean, and I have not written it in again; a verse with a word gone is a verse said slowly, and a verse said slowly is a verse nobody can enter.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The drawer keeps the ash and gives no sleep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the date and gives no guest.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The licence keeps the blank and gives no name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sixty marks for a pinch of a man; ask who was paid.\end{quote}

I asked a physician of the factor’s house, a hearth-maid of Low Kiln and a clerk who could not leave paper alone, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back into the tin among the corks and the grey rags, and tomorrow a woman in the upper street will come for a fourth phial, and I will sell it to her and write across her name again, and neither of us will call it what it is, because a thing called by its right name is a thing the Court can enter.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fourth Poured Out, Being the Drinking Song of the Lamp-Women at the Tallow Works, Sung at the Turning of the Year with a Heel-Tap Under the Bench}
\CRsheetheading{The Fourth Poured Out, Being the Drinking Song of the Lamp-Women at the Tallow Works, Sung at the Turning of the Year with a Heel-Tap Under the Bench}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A lamp-woman’s drinking song, taken down from her own mouth at the fat-house and set in the low half-sung speech of the works; the verses with the ends let fall as they are sung, the order of the pouring in the writer’s own charcoal, a gloss pressed in the margin by a hearth-maid come up from Sill, the verbs taken out of two lines by a factor’s clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Sung at the turning of the year in the fat-house two leagues north-east of Sill, where sheep fat is rendered and the tallow poured into lamps, and set down in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the woman who keeps the lamps there, on the back of a tallow-chandler’s tally gone soft at the fold; written in charcoal and the dregs of a tallow-dip, sewn with a wick into a fold of grey wool and kept in the lamp-room under a cracked saucer. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant spoiled at one corner by the damp at Greybank. It survives with a thumb of tallow at the head, a scorch where a wick-end touched the second leaf, a ring of stale small ale near the refrain, a smear of bone-meal across the third leaf, a pressed sheep’s-ear mark in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a hearth-maid, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk, and a line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the lamps at the Tallow Works. That is my whole office: to pour the rendered fat while it is still running, to trim the wicks, to carry the light into the byre where the men sit at the turning of the year, and to know how much a flame takes before it gives. In Sill they know us by the smell when the wind is north. They do not know us by our names, and we have stopped minding.

I set this down because a man come up from the factor’s house at Greybank stood in the door of the fat-house with his cuff soft from washing and asked what we sang when we poured the fourth cup out. I told him we poured it on the floor. He wrote that down and went away satisfied, which is how I knew he had written the wrong thing. This is the song as we say it, with the fourth where we put it and not where he put it.

The brown at the head is tallow. I held the leaf down in the draught that comes up under the rendering pot and did not know I had marked it. A thing written in tallow keeps its mark when the words have gone, which is more than can be said for the Court’s paper.

\subsection*{When it is sung}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the turning of the year, after the last fat is run off and before the lamps go up, with the small ale watered the way we water it and the pot set on the floor between the feet. Not at the feast and not at the Weighing. This is a song for a room with smoke in it.

\item Pour the first three into cups. The fourth goes under the bench, on the trodden ash, and is not drunk. A cup poured out is not a cup wasted, and a man who calls it wasted has begun to count what he has not paid for.

\item Sing to the lamp and not to the company. Said to a man, the refrain becomes a question, and there is nobody in this room who can answer it without a slate in his hand.

\item The lamp stands with its wick trimmed to a fingernail. A flame that gutters while the fourth is poured is read as an answer and nobody says what the question was.

\item Say the last line twice. The second saying is for the one whose cup is under the bench, and the third, if anybody stays to say it, is for the one who poured the fat before us and never had a lamp of his own.

\item Do not sing it on the Long Night. On the Long Night there is no fire after dusk, and a song that mentions a flame is a song with a cost in it that the house cannot meet.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Sung low, with the ends of the words let fall as a tallow-drop falls. The refrain is said to the lamp. The cup goes under the bench on the fourth line of the last part and nobody watches where it goes.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the ewe and one for the pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the smoke that stands for Sill;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fourth we pour where the ash lies deep ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pass the cup and mind the wick.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ewe gave over what she kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we took the fat and left the name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a sheep has no slate and no return,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and goes on giving after death.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the cup and mind the wick.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fat remembers what the flame forgot.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Skim and skull and trotter go\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape into the pot and come out light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what sank comes up, and what came up\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape stands all night where a hand set it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the cup and mind the wick.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fat remembers what the flame forgot.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The north wind carries our smoke to town\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and Sill says tallow without a nose;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the only thing we make\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that nobody asks the price of.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the cup and mind the wick.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fat remembers what the flame forgot.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape On Kindling the coal comes up in clay\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and every hearth touches and passes on;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we pour our own out of the rendered pot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no man says what the first one cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the cup and mind the wick.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fat remembers what the flame forgot.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape On the Long Night we let the lamp speak last\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and sit with our hands where the light can see them;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three cups go round and a fourth goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the flame takes four and keeps a fifth for itself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Pass the cup and mind the wick.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fat remembers what the flame forgot.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The fourth is under the bench. The wick stands where it stood.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing, the length of the pause between the pouring and the wiping of the bench. I have left it on the leaf. It is the right length for a name and for nothing else.

\subsection*{A verse we do not sing when the factor’s man is in the room}

\emph{Said only when the door is shut and the lamp is down to a knuckle. There is no refrain. The last line is said to the floor.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The collector came on Kindling with a tube of iron\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and took the first measure of the year before the ewes were shorn;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve, he said, as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and wrote it in a hand that did not shake.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We poured the fourth on the ash beneath the bench\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and called it for the ewe, which was a lie we have kept for nineteen years;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a ewe has no account, and a man who wants one\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape may go to Greybank and ask the factor for it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lamp takes from the pot and gives to the room.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The room gives nothing back and is not asked to.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three go round and the fourth goes under,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name we do not say stands where we put it.\end{quote}

I have set this down because a woman who had been at the pouring told me that a verse with the factor’s man outside it is a verse that keeps, and a verse with him inside it is a line in a ledger, which does not. She would not give me her name and I have not asked twice.

\subsection*{What the hearth-maid put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman come up from Sill who keeps the birth-slates and crosses two fingers over a birth-flower and says nothing about the sign. She was at the turning of the year and carried a lamp home under her coat. I have copied her words as she set them.

At \emph{the fourth we pour where the ash lies deep}: \emph{I have kept slates at a birth for nineteen years and I have seen a hand go to the slate before it went to the child. This pouring is the same hand turned the other way. Both give what they cannot get back.}

At \emph{a sheep has no slate and no return}: \emph{We break a pot at a death-house door to let the heat out. We do not break one at a ewe’s throat. I asked a render-woman why, and she asked me whether I thought a ewe had a door.}

At \emph{no man says what the first one cost}: \emph{The year-fire is carried up the yard in a clay dish and every house touches its own to it. In our district nobody says where the flame was first lit. Here they say nothing either, but they say it standing over a pot, which is not the same nothing.}

At the space before the last refrain: \emph{The third saying is not for the one under the bench. I have asked whose it is and been given a date, which is a door that shuts.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank, being a man who cannot let paper lie. The ink sits in two fingers of his cuff and will not come out. He writes in the narrow upright hand and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{we took the fat and left the name}, he wrote \emph{the product was rendered and the donor is not entered}, which is true in the figure and false in the room I sang it in. I have left it.

\item At \emph{the fourth we pour where the ash lies deep} he wrote \emph{libation: nil}, and underlined it twice. A cup on the floor is nothing to a man who has never stood in a room that wanted the floor drank to.

\item At \emph{the lamp takes from the pot and gives to the room}, he struck out \emph{takes} and \emph{gives} and set above it \emph{transfer, current}, which leaves the lamp standing and takes the room out of it.

\item Where I had left the space before the last refrain, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a number where a name should stand, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman pouring the fourth cup at the turning of the year does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know who poured before her.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tallow at the head is mine and has gone into the grain, and no wet sleeve takes it out, which is why I sign with a dip and not with ink. The scorch on the second leaf is a wick-end that touched while I was writing and went out under my hand; the hand was mine and I have not entered the burn. The ring near the refrain is small ale, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the pot it stood against. The bone-meal across the third leaf came off the sleeve of a man carrying a skull to the pot, and when I asked him to stand clear he stood clear and said nothing, which was more politeness than I expected and less than I wanted. The sheep’s-ear mark in the gutter is a press from a fresh ear laid on the leaf while the tally was being made up; the edge of it took a little of the second verse and I have not written the words back in, because a song with two words gone is a song said slowly, and everything here is said slowly. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it and there is no Last Day in a lamp-room. The wick sewn through the fold is the one that burned down on the night the fourth was poured and would not stand again. I have kept it where it is.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the fat and the lamp keeps the flame.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The floor keeps the fourth and gives none back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and is read aloud all the same.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who pours, the hearth-maid who carries a lamp home under her coat, and a man who stood clear when I asked him, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back under the cracked saucer in the lamp-room. Tomorrow the wicks will be trimmed to a fingernail and the fat poured while it is still running, and the fourth will go under the bench for a name nobody says where a clerk can hear it. If an officer finds the leaf, let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, and will mind the wick.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Furnace Articles, Being the Standing Rules of the Furnace-Masters of Vhal for the Taking, Keeping, Trying and Paying Out of Apprentices at the Three Glass Furnaces, with the Table of Heats, the Tally of Hands, the Gathering-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Furnace Articles, Being the Standing Rules of the Furnace-Masters of Vhal for the Taking, Keeping, Trying and Paying Out of Apprentices at the Three Glass Furnaces, with the Table of Heats, the Tally of Hands, the Gathering-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A furnace-leaf of rules in the hand of the under-master who keeps the pipes and the anneal at the third furnace; the rules in the short sayings of the Quay, the heats and the hands in tables, the gathering-song pasted inside the cover, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk, one line struck in charcoal by a furnace-master, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · First gathered at Vhal in Y.H. 627, the year after the rising at the furnaces of Y.H. 626, when the masters found that a trade which could melt sand could also refuse to work, and set the rules down so that a refusal would have a place to be entered; copied forward from the anneal shelf and not from a book. This leaf written in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Riva of the Third Furnace, under-master, who has kept the pipes and taken the young at the gather for two and twenty years; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives on Council salt-paper furred white at the head and soft at the fold, with the lower edge gone over into a clear bead of glass under twenty years of anneal heat, so that the last two rules read best held up to the light, which is how furnace work is read; a thumb of tar at the fold off the pipe-rest, the press of a wet gathering-cloth across the song, a nick from a glass-cutter’s point, a ring of vinegar from a tasting cup set down by a girl who would not eat, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold by a girl with the sweetness still at her mouth, a grey thumb along the outer fold that a factor come up from Greybank called Ash, which in Vhal is a thing that must be bought and sold, and nobody bought this one; two corrections in the Council’s upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again beneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the pipes and the anneal at the third furnace. A house brings a child and goes away; the child stays with the fire. A clerk comes with a cuff soft from washing, writes what the pot was worth, and the pot is on a boat before he has finished. This leaf hangs on its wire beside the anneal shelf, where twenty years of heat have taken the lower edge into a clear bead of glass. The last two rules read best held up to the light. So does everything in this trade: a thing held to the light shows the bubble and the man who blew it, and the Council has never once asked to see the man.

I set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

They were gathered in Y.H. 627, the year after the rising of Y.H. 626, when the masters found that men who could melt sand could also stop melting it, and put the stopping into articles so that a refusal would have a place to be entered. A rule with no heat on it is a rule nobody has had to stand. These have been stood.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand at the third furnace}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The furnace takes a child, not a house. A house may bring him and feed him, but from the day he lifts a filled pipe he answers to the master. The Council takes the profit and leaves the child alone. This is the one thing in Vhal nobody has thought to tax.

\item Taken at twelve, set to the gather at thirteen, and not before he can lift a pipe and keep the end of it up. A child taken later is not made up the year he missed; the furnace keeps no count of the heats it did not make.

\item Kept, not hired. He eats from the furnace dish, sleeps in the loft, and what he makes goes to the furnace and comes back as bread and a place by the anneal, neither entered. A master who tells a girl she is paid tells a true thing about a figure and a false thing about a living.

\item His birth-name is said once at the taking and not used at the furnace. What he is called afterward is the heat, given at his first gather and kept in the mouth. A name in the mouth cannot be entered, and what cannot be entered is the last thing in this port the Council has not found a way to sell.

\item The gather comes before the name. A child gives what came up on his pipe before he gives who he is; a pipe that has gathered tells more about a boy than a boy at a gate does. A child who gives his name first is sent back to the pot, and the pot is not interested either.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the sand and the lead}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wash the sand in seawater and the sea takes the salt out of it and leaves the sand. The same sea takes the figures off a contract left in the damp, which the Council calls a virtue and the furnace calls a day’s work lost.

\item The lead comes out of the blue cliffs, blue-green and sweet in the heat. No child is sent to the cliffs. A girl who has once tasted the cliff will ask to go again, and that is the whole of the answer.

\item No child tastes the pot. The master tastes, with the side of the tongue, and spits it out. The pale line at the gum is lead and not a mark of skill; a master who calls it skill is selling the girl’s fingers one at a time and calling it a living.

\item A girl who rubs her gum with cliff-glass and says sweetness answers sweetness is not to be argued with before the young. Take the glass away, give her seawater, and let the sea be the one paid. We do not say kindly at a furnace; a kindness there is a debt with no date.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the pipe and the anneal}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Lift the end of the pipe and never point it at a man. A pipe pointed at a man has put out an eye in every generation, and the Council has never written a rule against it, which is how a man knows the rule is ours.

\item Roll on the marver and do not keep the glass on the pipe while you decide what it ought to be. Glass asked what it should be cools into what it was, and a thing only nearly what it should have been still goes to Sere with a figure on it.

\item The gather is taken from the pot and the pot is not left. A girl who leaves the pot to answer a question has given her heat to the question and taken it out of the glass. There is no figure for the heat that went into an answer, and no column where it would go.

\item The anneal is where a finished thing goes to stop being finished. Nothing is taken warm out of it to show a buyer. A thing cooled too soon keeps its heat in the wrong place and breaks a year later in a stranger’s hand, with no entry; the thing has crossed the sea and the hand belongs to somebody the Council never counted.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Struck hard in charcoal against rule 13, in a furnace-master’s hand, and written again underneath:} Do not take it warm. \emph{Written again above, the second time heavier:} Nobody takes it warm. \emph{In mine, below both:} The master has struck \emph{anybody} into \emph{nobody}, which is the same rule said to a person and said to a room. A girl does better with the person.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The table of heats}

\emph{Kept on the anneal shelf. What is written is the heat that came up, in a hand that does not change between one line and the next.}

Year — At the furnace — What is taken\par

Twelve — Carry sand, wash it, pile lead, sweep, hold the pipe-ends up — The birth-name, said once and not used again\par

Thirteen — The gather and the marver; the pipe kept level — The habit of asking what the glass ought to be\par

Fourteen — The first blow; the first heat named at the pot — The heat-name, given by what came up\par

Fifteen — The anneal; nothing taken out before its hour — The belief that a thing finished is done\par

Sixteen — Take a pot alone through a firing and read the green at the gum — The last of a girl’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sixteen is the common end of a heat and not a short one. A girl who has been through it is not paid out and sent away; she stays where the furnace needs her, at the third furnace or at the Quay or on a boat whose share goes through her mother. The master does not choose which. The pot does, and the Council after it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The tally of hands}

\emph{Kept by the under-master. The figure is the Council’s and is set first. What stands beneath it is mine and is not a figure.}

Condition — The Council’s figure — What stands beneath\par

Girl taken at twelve — one apprentice, current, no wage arising — A child who eats from the dish\par

First heat named — one decorative appellation, not a vessel — A name said to the pot and kept in the mouth\par

Green at the gum — occupational mark; no deduction arises — Lead. Paid out of the hand.\par

Hand that will not hold a pipe steady — one hand, current; measure not affected — The pipe taken from that hand; the hand kept\par

A thing broken in a year — breakage not entered — A stranger’s hand, in a house we have not seen\par

The end of the heat — discharged at sixteen — Paid out of nothing and sent where the pot needs her\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The green at the gum is entered as an occupational mark because an entry that says lead would want a payer, and no payer in Vhal will put his name to a girl’s hand. A physician came up from Greybank in Y.H. 798 and left a page saying the sweetness came from the lead; the word went out of it before the year was over, as though a word could be scraped off paper the way slip is scraped off a bench. I have put it back here, where a clerk can see it and choose not to read it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, against rule 15:} Occupational mark; no deduction arises. \emph{In mine, underneath:} It is lead. I did not learn it from a page, which is the only reason I can still say it. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the furnace\par

A hand put to the gum with cliff-glass — The glass taken away; seawater given; the word \emph{lead} said once\par

\emph{Skill} said of the green — The word struck in charcoal and \emph{lead} set above it, by a hand that will not sign\par

A warm thing taken from the anneal — Set back; the thing broken at the door and not sold\par

A heat-name written on salt-paper — The paper left out in the rain; the name said again to the pot\par

The pipe pointed at a man — The pipe taken away for a tend; the eye not put back\par

The Hearth beneath the salt asked about — Answered once: the Sallow has a Hearth under the salt; asked twice, send it to the dippers\par

A heat sold to the Council and the other kept — Not entered. There is no law against it, which is why the furnace does not speak of it\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in a firing is a fault the girl has not understood, and the master sits with her at the anneal until she has. The pot is not a rod.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The gathering-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung at the first gather, standing, with the pipe across the knee and the end up. Nobody sings it at the anneal and nobody sings it at the Council table. The third line of the second verse is the girls’ line and the masters sing it wrong on purpose.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lead from the blue and sand from the bay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sea takes the ink and the lead takes the day;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the end up, never point it at a man,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and take what comes up, not what you began.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The green comes up where the pale line was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the master calls skill what the girl calls hers;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name in the mouth is a name without sum ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk puts a nought where the heat should come.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lead from the blue and sand from the bay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one heat for the tally and one for the sea;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot keeps the flaw and the gum keeps the lead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the girl keeps the heat that was named for her.\end{quote}

The wet cloth across the song is from a girl singing in the rain at the outer furnace.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on the morning after the salt boats came down, ink in two fingers of a soft cuff, and took the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{he is kept, not hired} he set \emph{retained at the furnace, no wage arising}, true about a figure and false about a girl who eats from the dish. I have put mine back underneath.

\item Against the row about a hand that will not hold a pipe steady he wrote \emph{one hand, current; measure not affected}. I have set \emph{the hand kept} beneath it where a girl can read it.

\end{itemize}

The other hand is charcoal, a girl come down from High Kiln with the Glaze Room in her mouth. Against rule 8 she struck \emph{a mark of skill} and wrote \emph{It is lead. It is paid out of the hand}, and would not sign it. She has put the price where the proportion should have been, which is the only column in this trade that tells the truth. I have not asked her name and she has not given it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white at the head is salt and not Ash; there is no Ash in Vhal that has not been bought and sold. A factor from Greybank asked once if the grey thumb was northern Ash. I told him it was a thumb and had not been paid for. The tar at the fold is mine, off the pipe-rest I coil every dusk. The nick is from a glass-cutter’s point; the vinegar ring, set down by a girl who would not eat until a question about the green was answered, has taken two letters off the last line. The bead in the second fold is cliff-glass, pressed in by a girl who watched me write and said nothing; it has left a sweet smear two months dry. The lower edge has gone over into clear glass and will take no more ink; the words nearest it are the ones that matter most and the ones the light must be asked about. There is no Last Day on an anneal shelf; the heat does its own correcting and keeps no roll of it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the lead and the gum keeps the green.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The heat keeps the name that the tally left out.\end{quote}

I asked a furnace-master, a clerk come down from the Council room, and a woman who sells eels on the Quay, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaf goes back on its wire; the heat will take another word by the next firing and I shall not write it back. Tomorrow a child will be brought at twelve with a name she will not use at the furnace, and I shall lift the pipe-end, keep it level, and say what came up before I say who came.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Gallery Leech, Being Remedies for the Sweating, the Stone-Cough, the Clamp-Bite, the Hand Gone Rope-Coloured and the Cold That Stays, Set Down Under Keld Keep}
\CRsheetheading{The Gallery Leech, Being Remedies for the Sweating, the Stone-Cough, the Clamp-Bite, the Hand Gone Rope-Coloured and the Cold That Stays, Set Down Under Keld Keep}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A mine-leech’s book of remedies in the Keldish measure-first manner, set down in Grathic letters with the counts notched into the board cover in iron; the cures in a gallery-leech’s hand, the objections of a clamp-master pressed in coal, the corrections of a Court survey-clerk in Ledgerhand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Keld Keep in the First Seam between Y.H. 808 and Y.H. 812, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Dren of the Ninth Gallery, a leech who tended the clamp-hands and the stone-cough of the deep workings and went up and down the shaft by the same rope for nineteen years; written on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by a sweating in the Ninth Gallery and on four strips of birch bark, sewn with iron wire into a board cover and carried in a coat pocket against a splinter of warm-stone. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded tally-roll. It survives with coal dust ground into the head, a clear stain of lamp-oil down the fold that has made two words transparent, iron filings caught in the gutter off the Duelling Floor, a scorch where a lamp-spark took the corner of the second leaf, the splinter of warm-stone sewn into the cover which keeps the whole book a little warm, a ring of frost on the third leaf from the climb over the Cold Pass, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one note in the blocky coal-pressed hand of a clamp-master, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I write on the back of a survey sheet that spoiled in a sweating in the Ninth Gallery. The surveyor had set it down near a seam giving off the smell of hot lead, and the heat took the figures off before anybody could read them, which is a mercy of a kind: a figure that cannot be read cannot be entered. I have cut the counts into the board cover with a file, because a notch is still there when the paper has gone soft, which is more than can be said for the Court’s figures. I am a leech of the deep. I tend the clamp-hands and the stone-cough and men who come up from the lower galleries older than they went down. I have set down what I do and what the men before me did, and where the two disagree I have set them side by side, as the survey office keeps two readings of one seam.

Nothing in this book is free. That is the only thing I will stand behind.

The coal at the head is mine. I sign in coal because it goes into the grain and will not come out, and a leech who signs his cures in a hand a clerk can read is a leech who will be asked to answer for them.

\subsection*{The number before the name}

In Keld a man gives his number before he gives his name. At the lamp-room door I ask it too. A man with no number is come down from the low countries, and I tend him last, for I do not know what is owed against him and will not ask. This is not cruelty. It is the order of the room: the man with the least number goes first, for he has the least held between him and the cold.

If a man cannot say his number, look at the forearm. If there is a smooth place where a number was cut out, do not ask how it went. I have asked twice in nineteen years and had the same answer both times, a shrug and a look toward the shaft. A place the size of a thumb is the whole of what a man will tell you about it.

A survey-clerk from Greybank asked why I number the dying. I told him so the iron would know who to take from. He wrote it down and went away pleased, which is how I know he did not hear me.

\subsection*{The order of the lamp-room}

\emph{Cut into the first leaf, in the coal hand, with one word gone over in lamp-oil.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the lamp in the niche, never on the bench. A lamp on the bench will be knocked into a man’s wound, and then the wound has two troubles where it had one.

\item Lay the warm-stone in wool and try it on your own wrist before it goes to a hand or a belly. The stone takes from the lamp’s account, and somebody down the shaft paid for the lamp.

\item Ask the number before the name, and write it first, so that if the man goes while you are writing, the figure is the part that stays.

\item Look at the hand before the iron. A hand you cannot save is still a hand you must not make worse.

\item When the sweat comes sweetish with the smell of hot lead, get the men up. A man who stays to argue with such a gallery will not argue with you again.

\item Do not tap a man to hear him. A body is not a cup. I have seen a man do it and have not forgotten the sound he said he heard.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who burns\par

The Sweating — Get the men up the shaft; cold iron to the wrists, never the chest — Heat comes up through the stone and takes a man by the head. Iron at the wrist gives it somewhere to go. Whether out of him or only lower down him, I have never been able to say. — The gallery, which gives back nothing.\par

Stone-cough — Steam of lamp-oil and hot water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — To the mouth, not the face. The dust of the Ninth gets into a man and he coughs it up in the morning in a colour he will not discuss. — The lamp and the man’s own morning.\par

A hand gone rope-coloured below a clamp — Take the clamp off — Leave it to the sixth day, which is what we have always done. If the colour has not come back by then, the hand is gone; do not set the clamp again higher up and call it a second chance. — The hand. This is the honest row.\par

The cold that stays — Walk it off; rub with warm-stone; set the man to work — See what I have written below. I have done these three things and I have not stopped doing them. — Nobody knows.\par

A cut from the Duelling Floor, or a first way gone bad — Tallow first, then a clean fold — The clamp-master says cold iron to draw the heat out, and that the iron takes as well as draws. I have set his words above mine and both stand. — The man who opened the way.\par

A greyed hand, from years at the iron — Nothing I know. Keep him from cold iron for a tend — It does not come back with rest and it does not come back with warm-stone. A collector’s hand is paid partly out of other people’s heat, and the debt shows at the fingertips. — The collector who paid him.\par

A fever that cooks a man from within — Cold iron to the temple; bleed at the elbow to let the head fall — A physician come up from Greybank says bleeding lets the measure out and not the head, and the man is weaker after. I have watched four such men and two were quieter by evening; quiet is not the same as better, and I have set that down. — The man, in the arm.\par

A boy at the Descent — A warm-stone in the pocket and a number across the forearm — Thirteen is early to have a number cut in a bone that is still growing, but the Warden’s roll wants it and the roll gets what it wants. Give the stone after the knife, not before. — The boy, at thirteen.\par

A man come up from beyond the pass — A stone, a place by the lamp, and no questions — He will give you a number if he still has one and a name if he still has that. Take whichever he offers and do not ask for the other. — Nobody. He has paid already, and not here.\par

\subsection*{On the full note, and why a man is not a cup}

Tap a sound warm-stone with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. The surveyors of the First Seam use it on the stone of the shaft, and it is the one thing in this country that costs nothing and is still allowed to be true.

I knew a man who tapped the chest of a clamp-hand gone thin and said the note came back flat, and said it as though the man had refused him. The man had not refused him. There was simply nothing there for the knuckle to find. I did not say so at the time, because there was a slate in the room and a man who was going to be entered on it. I have written it here, which is a different matter.

The ways run down the arm the way a river runs, with smaller ways coming off it, and this is what every leech in the Keep believes and what I was taught at the Descent. I have put no drawing of them in this book, because a drawing is a thing that can be carried into a Court room and read aloud there. Whatever runs in a man was put there before the slate was, and the slate has never had the better of it yet.

\subsection*{The cold that stays}

Below the sill, and in the lower galleries where a man stands in water to the calf through a shift, a foot or a hand will come up cold and stay cold after the water has gone and the wool has gone on. In the low countries they call it the cold and go home warm on the word. We know it by the feel under the thumb: the extremity goes first and the heart holds out, and there is an hour on the far side of the warming when a man gets worse before he gets better, or does not.

I have no name for that hour. I have left the place where the name would stand, which is the right length for a name of that kind.

We walk it off. We rub it with warm-stone. We set the man to work, because a moving man does not notice how cold he is going and can finish his shift. I have done all three and seen a man lose two toes on the fourth day, and I have gone on doing them. There is no honest remedy in this book for the cold that stays, and this is the row where I have been least honest, so I have set it in the middle where nobody can miss it.

\subsection*{A song for the Descent}

\emph{Sung going down, not coming up, by a boy of thirteen with the number newly cut in the forearm. The last line is said twice, the second time for the one who has had his number taken out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lamp and one for the rope,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the stone that has kept the fire;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cut me a number across the arm\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and let the name wait till the shift is higher.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the lead and two for the sweat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the hand that holds the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Ninth Gallery takes and does not forget,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Warden counts us at night.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the going-down, three for the up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where the number was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask me my measure, I’ll give you my name ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the measure goes down and the name stays above.\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line in the singing, the length of the smooth place on the arm. No clerk has yet put a figure in it, which is the only reason it is still a space.

\subsection*{What the Court clerk did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaves at Greybank, being a man who cannot let paper lie. The ink sits in two fingers of his cuff and will not come out. He struck out my column headed \emph{Who burns} and wrote \emph{No cost entered} above it, which is a true thing in a dishonest place. Where I set that the gallery gives back nothing, he wrote \emph{The measure is retained in the stone.} Against the smooth place on a man’s arm he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, as though a place where a number had been were the same as zero.

I have filed the notches deeper in the cover. He can take a word off paper because paper is soft. He cannot file a notch out of a board without the board being the thinner for it, and then he has entered something of his own, which is the only kind of entering I have ever seen him avoid.

\subsection*{From the clamp-master}

\emph{At the foot of the remedies, in a blocky hand pressed in coal, the letters wide apart as though cut with a chisel.}

\begin{quote}\itshape On the fifth take the iron off. I have held it on the sixth and carried the hand away in a pail. What you have written is what we did. It is not what I do. --- H.\end{quote}

Hald Iron of the Duelling Floor borrowed the leaf before the clerk did and returned it with the fold changed. I have set his line above my row and mine under it, as the floor keeps the clamp and the hand that was in it. A man who has lost a hand to his own trade is allowed one sentence in a book of physic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head came off my own thumb setting down the sheet in the lamp-room and went into the grain before I knew I had touched it. The lamp-oil down the fold came from a lamp knocked over on the third night of a sweating, and has taken the ink clean off two words, which I have not written in again: a remedy with two words gone is a remedy said slowly, and everything down here is said slowly. The filings in the gutter are off the clamps on the Duelling Floor. The scorch on the second leaf is a spark that caught while I was writing and went out under my hand; the hand was mine and I have not entered the burn. The splinter sewn into the cover is warm-stone from the Ninth, and is why the book is a little warm in the morning, a kindness bought by somebody whose name is not in here. The frost on the third leaf came up out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass, and is the only thing in this book that entered itself. There is no Last Day under the Keep and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the heat and the iron keeps the number;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither of them asks who paid.\end{quote}

I asked a clamp-master, a survey-clerk, and a man with a smooth place on his arm, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back into the coat pocket against the splinter of warm-stone. Tomorrow a man will give his number before his name at the door, and I shall write the number down and cut another notch in the cover, and the notch outlasts the figure and the figure the man, which is the whole trade here.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Gate-Slate of Keld Keep, Being the Prices Current at the Shaft Mouth and the Dues of the Rim Road and the Cold Pass, Cut in Chalk by the Reeve’s Tally-Man and Never Washed Clean}
\CRsheetheading{The Gate-Slate of Keld Keep, Being the Prices Current at the Shaft Mouth and the Dues of the Rim Road and the Cold Pass, Cut in Chalk by the Reeve’s Tally-Man and Never Washed Clean}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tally-man’s cutting on a slate propped against the gate-post within the shaft mouth, being a market list of iron, lead, coal, warm-stone, clamps and hired lives set against what the same things fetch in the lowlands, with the road-dues cut beneath; scored in red by the mine-reeve, written over in a Greybank factor’s narrow hand, and left with one line at the foot that nobody will own · Cut first in Bone of Y.H. 812, the year the lowlands called the Thin Year, and cut forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, when the Rim Road opened and the first carts came up with the winter’s iron. Kept at Keld Keep in the lee of the gate-post, wiped at the end of each tend with a wet sleeve and never made clean, so that the figures of former years show through the current ones the way old repairs show through a vessel. It survives with coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red cross from the mine-reeve’s point, slate dust in the gutter, a warm-stone shaving shut in the fold, a bead of lead out of the Ninth Gallery, a frost-feather along the lower edge, a clamp-scratch across two columns, a thumb in coal dust nobody will claim, one correction in a factor’s narrow upright hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I cut the figures at the gate with a copper point on a slate that leans against the post. The wind comes down the shaft mouth and takes the chalk before it takes the snow, so I cut deep. At the end of every tend I wipe the face with a wet sleeve and go away, and by morning the old figures have come back through the new ones. A slate kept clean is a slate with no memory, and a road without memory is a road a man pays twice on.

My measure stands at fifty-two and my name is not cut here. At this gate a man states what he holds before he says who he is. A lowlander comes up and gives me his name and waits for me to ask the rest, and I send him back to the foot of the post to begin again. I am not shaming him. A name is a thing a man can change at the next well; a measure is what he carries into the dark, and the dark does not care what he calls himself. The mine-reeve checks a man who has lied about his number, and the checking is done in red, and there is no second asking.

What follows is the market at the shaft mouth --- what iron, lead, coal and warm-stone fetched here in Bone of the last year and in the first carts of this one --- and the dues of the roads by which a man comes up to the gate and goes on toward the pass. I set the lowland figure beside the figure taken here because a price carried up the Rim Road changes at every post, and a man who knows only one end of it will call the other a robbery.

Coin in Keld is scarce and iron is common. Twelve bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown, which comes north with the mercenaries and goes south again with them, a fine thing to hold and a poor thing to spend in a mountain. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is five marks. I have set no ember on this slate. In eleven years at this gate I have never seen one paid, and I have seen a man try.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a factor come up from Greybank, written above my own:} Ember: five marks. Reckoning entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have left his figure where he set it and put \emph{as told} beneath. He writes of an ember as though a man could carry one up the road in his boot. I have carried iron in my boot and never an ember.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The market at the shaft mouth}

\emph{Cut on the face of the slate. The first column is what a man is told in Sill or at the quay; the second is what is taken here, at the weigh beside the post.}

Article — As told below — As taken here\par

Good iron axe — 2 marks — half a mark\par

Iron bar, Keldish — 2 marks the bar — half a mark, by the load and not the bar\par

Lead, a pig — 6 marks at Greybank — 1 mark here; the seller below does not say which workings, and we do not ask\par

Coal, a sack — 3 bits in Sill — 1 bit; carried out in a coat and not entered\par

Warm-stone, a palm’s piece — not sold in Grath — 2 marks; it holds heat longer than anything else in Sarn, and is sold, never lent\par

Warm-stone shaving, for a brazier — --- — half a mark; swept up from the cutting floor, not given away\par

Cold-iron clamp, off the Duelling Floor — not sold — 3 marks; the bite that holds a vessel whole and the bite that takes a hand off a man\par

A mercenary, the season — hired by the Court and by Sere — 30 marks and keep; trusted by neither\par

Under-vessed hand, life reckoned at — eleven months — eleven months, whether he lasts them or not\par

Bought breath, a season — not spoken of below — paid in iron, entered in months\par

The Descent, at thirteen — no price — no price; the numbers cut into the forearm and a warm-stone given after the knife\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine, against the coal row:} A man from Sill paid three bits for a sack at this gate and asked why the same sack was a bit here. I told him the coal had not changed and the road had. He said that was a robbery done by a road, which is a true thing and not an entry I can make.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The mine-reeve’s red cross against the warm-stone row:} He set it there with his point while I was cutting the figure and said nothing. A cross in red on this slate means the figure has been checked and is to stand. It does not mean the stone is warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a sloping hand, a lowland carter’s:} Paid two marks for a bar here and was charged two again at Greybank, and the factor’s man said the second was for the road. \emph{In mine:} Both stand. I did not collect the second and cannot enter it. A man who carries iron down a road pays for the iron and again for having carried it.\end{quote}

A man who comes back from the Descent thin has the old numbers cut out of his forearm and new ones put in. Nobody asks him which count is his. I have seen a man with two sets of numbers, one over the other and the later cut deeper; the mine-reeve entered the later and left the earlier standing in the skin. The under-vessed are entered at eleven months as a matter of course, and a man who lasts fourteen is entered at eleven still, because the figure is for the life bought and not the life lived. I have kept the honest column where the honest figure is. It is a short column.

\subsection*{The dues of the roads}

Two roads are counted at this gate and a third that is not a road but a shaft. The Rim Road comes up from Sill, a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather; the Cold Pass lies ten leagues beyond the keep. Karric VII shut the pass in Y.H. 741, and the agreement of Y.H. 747 fixed it as the border. There is a post there and no gate. The Warden’s surveyors keep the record of the rim-seam and state a man’s measure before his name, which they do at this gate also, as a courtesy, so that no man can say he was not told.

Due cut at this gate\par

Surveyor’s mark upon a load going down — 2 bits; the load is not weighed again in Grath\par

Cart with iron, going down the Rim Road — 1 mark, or iron to the value\par

Beast on the hoof — half a mark\par

A man going up without a warm-stone — no stone lent here; he borrows from the next man who has one, or turns back\par

A man who has lied about his measure — the figure corrected in red by the mine-reeve; no second asking\par

Traveller going farther into the Rim — no due, and no guarantee\par

The Cold Pass — nothing at the post; there is no gate\par

A load going farther than the pass — not entered; the Warden’s surveyors do not promise to bring a man back\par

The shaft mouth — no toll; every Keldish child goes down at thirteen\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the carter’s sloping hand:} They asked me at the post what the pass cost and I said nothing, and they went through, and I never learned whether nothing was the right figure. \emph{In mine:} It is the right figure. There is no gate. A post is not a gate and a border is not a wall.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Greybank factor’s narrow hand, beneath the row about the liar:} Let the entry stand as \emph{measure misstated, corrected}. \emph{In mine:} I have set \emph{no second asking} beneath it, because the red cross was on the slate before his hand got here and the cross is the older figure.\end{quote}

The roads have two ends and the figures do not agree between them. The tally-man at Greybank cuts what goes out at the quay and the clerk at the Cross cuts what is paid at Sill; I cut what is taken at the post. Between the three of us a cart is counted twice and a man is counted once, which is the proportion the Court has always liked. The Hearth Road takes nothing at any gate, having taken it at home; the Salt Road calls its toll a contribution freely entered, which is a finer name for the same figure. I have not cut either on this slate. They are not roads of this keep.

\subsection*{What they chant at the post}

\emph{Said low by the men waiting their turn at the weigh, never within hearing of the mine-reeve. The crowd says the last line with the singer.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the gate and one for the name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the stone you carry in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hundred and twenty to the keep and ten\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape to the post where the counting stops.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hold the clamp and call it true ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the hand that holds it knows.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven months and a warm-stone too,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mountain keeps what the mountain owes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Greybank hand, against the first line:} One figure entered. \emph{In mine:} There are two roads and a border, and that line is a place where a count stops, not a number. A man who puts a nought in it has never been to the post.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The hands that are not mine}

The factor’s hand is narrow and upright and leaves the doer out of every sentence, as though a thing with nobody in it were truer than a thing a man had done. He set \emph{measure misstated, corrected} above mine and went away over the pass with a warm-stone charged to the account. I have set my words under his and left both standing. The red cross is the mine-reeve’s; the two marks are in the carter’s own mud. A slate with four hands on it is the only kind a man at this gate will believe. A slate with one hand on it is a Court notice, and a Court notice has never yet told a man what the road would charge him.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is coal off the sleeve I wipe with; it is in the grain of the slate and no wet sleeve takes it out. The red cross is iron oxide from the mine-reeve’s point and stays red in frost. The dust in the gutter is slate dust off my own cutting; it gathers at the foot and is swept onto the floor, where the men tread it into stone. The warm-stone shaving in the fold came off a piece a man set down while he counted his marks and went away without it; it is still warm on the coldest morning and I have not sold it. The bead is lead out of the Ninth Gallery, where the rock sweats and the smell of hot lead gives the only warning there is; a man laid it on the slate and did not take it up. The frost along the edge is a feather that grows where the Warm has lately gone out of the stone, and it is gone by noon. The clamp-scratch across the two columns was made by a man showing his brother how a clamp bites; both were honest men afterwards and one has a dead hand. The thumb in coal dust at the foot is not mine and not the mine-reeve’s. I have not wiped it away. There is no Last Day at a gate.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps the figure. The iron keeps the hand. The pass keeps the man who goes through it and does not come back.\end{quote}

I asked the tally-man at the quay, a surveyor come down from the Listening Stones, and a man who had been through the pass twice, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The slate goes back against the post. Tomorrow the carts come up with the winter’s coal and a lowlander will say his name before his measure, and I shall send him back to the foot of the post to begin again. The mountain sweats in the deep and the smell of hot lead gives what warning it gives, and the figures of the last tend show through the figures of this one, which is how a man reads a road: by what was cut here before him and not taken away.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Title the Seventh, Being the Ordinance of the Keeping Concerning Blent-Work, the Grafting of Beast-Clay into Human Wall, and the Measure of the Donor, Copied into a Back Room Behind the College in Slate Row of the Hearthseat with the Graft-Clerk’s Margin, a Sere Surgeon’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Title the Seventh, Being the Ordinance of the Keeping Concerning Blent-Work, the Grafting of Beast-Clay into Human Wall, and the Measure of the Donor, Copied into a Back Room Behind the College in Slate Row of the Hearthseat with the Graft-Clerk’s Margin, a Sere Surgeon’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the use of the back rooms behind the College of Assessors in the Hearthseat, with the marginal hand of the clerk who keeps the graft-book; the articles in Ledgerhand, the verbs set back beneath them, two tables, a form of entry left blank, the graft-song as it is said over the bench, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied in Slate Row of the Hearthseat in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Seventh of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the Hearthseat after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; it survives folded under a warm-stone in the back room behind the College, three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, with iron-gall in the creases of two fingers, warm-stone dust ground fine as meal in the gutter, a pale crescent of grease where a pad of beast-clay was laid, a green bead of lead glaze chipped from a bowl out of Sere, a grey Ash print along the outer fold, a small square of bare paper where a word was cut away with a knife, a tide-line along the foot from the sealed-file room, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the graft-book. It lies in the back room behind the College under a warm-stone the size of a loaf, in a room that smells of hot lead and tallow and of nothing that was ever entered. The College is a clean building and writes in a clean hand. Behind it there is a bench with a cut in it the shape of a small hand, and a stone that is warm at dawn and warm at dusk and has never once been asked where it got the heat. I copy the articles in the hand the ordinance uses, which has no person in it, and then set the person back underneath in mine. A law with nobody in it can be read at a Weighing. A law with somebody in it can be asked about, and then answered.

The ordinance condemns what this room does. That is the arrangement: the law says a blent person has the measure of the vessel its donor had, and the room goes on taking walls from beasts and setting them over the breaks of men, and both are written in the same neat hand. In nine years I have never entered a figure for a blent person that any bank would take. I enter the donor’s figure instead. It is small. A beast’s measure is small and simple, which the ordinance says elsewhere and here says nothing at all.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the head of the first leaf, in mine, written very small:} Copied in the room and for the room. The verbs are mine; their absence is not. If this leaf is read in the Weighing Hall, let it be seen that both hands were here and neither of them left.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Seventh, as it stands behind the College}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Seventh: Of Blent-Work, the Grafting of Beast-Clay into Human Wall, and the Measure of the Donor. Set down in the Hearthseat after the Rising of Y.H. 668; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the thing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wall taken from a beast and set over the break of a person is blent-work. It is condemned in the Keeping. The doing is not entered; the thing done is entered.

\item Blent-work is licensed in no district of the Keeping. It is done in the Bowl of Sere and is spoken of in the Hearthseat only behind the College.

\item A graft takes best where the donor’s measure was shaped like the recipient’s. A graft takes anyway where it was not.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The room says the third article to men who come in with a wall failing and money under a cuff. It is true. A graft takes, and then the person wants what he did not want before. The room calls it the graft settling, which is the phrase the ordinance allows. I have entered the phrase. I have entered the wanting underneath it, in the margin, where there is no column and no figure.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a narrow upright hand:} Article 3 was added in Y.H. 782. I have set \emph{takes anyway} above \emph{takes best}, which leaves two articles where the College meant one. Both stand. A man who has stood at this bench knows which of the two he is paying for, and the College does not know that he knows.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the donor}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The blent person has the measure of the vessel its donor had. The donor is a beast. The figure is entered in embers.

\item Where the donor is not entered, the figure is not entered. Where the figure is not entered, the account is not opened.

\item The donor pays. Where the donor is a beast and cannot consent, consent is entered by the hand of the officer.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have entered three such figures. Each was the donor’s, and each came to the same thing: three embers, four at the most, pressed into a man who walked out of this room with a wall that held. A man with three embers has no standing at any Weighing and no figure a bank will take. The ordinance gives him the donor’s measure. I have given him the donor’s figure. It is the same gift twice over and neither of them keeps him warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The officer enters consent for the beast and not for the man. The man is awake on the bench; the beast is in the yard with its throat cut; the hand that writes is the same for both. There is no word in this ordinance for the animal that did not agree, and I have not supplied one. A clerk who supplies a word has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the figure and the reading}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item One part in twelve of every measure banked is kept back for the Hearth, as the notice says. Where the measure is the donor’s, the deduction is entered against the donor.

\item A blent person has no standing to complain. Where a thing is taken from a wall that cannot speak, the house in which it stands is complainant. The blent person is not the house.

\item An account is never closed. The account of a blent person is carried forward at the donor’s figure.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have read one in twelve in this room and one in twelve at the Cross, and the two are the same figure and not the same weight. At the Cross a woman hears it over the pigs. Here a man hears it with a hand inside his forearm and a bowl of slip on the bench beside him. I have entered neither hearing, which is how the ordinance stays true.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in a leaning hand with a little gold in it:} Against article 7 a bowl-surgeon of the Ember house wrote \emph{a gift pays no deduction} and underlined it twice. I have left it. In Sere they empty a bowl and call a debt forgiven; here a figure goes down and is carried forward forever. Both are ways of not paying, and neither is entered as one.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of faults and their correcting}

\emph{The middle column is the figure. The last is mine and has no standing in any court in Sarn.}

Fault — As entered — What the margin keeps — Not entered\par

Wall taken from a beast — Blent-work; the donor’s figure — The sound the donor made — Consent\par

A graft that takes and then wants — The graft settling — The want, in another shape — The life it wanted\par

A blent person brought into the Keeping — Figure of the donor; carried forward — The name it answered to — The man it had been\par

A figure asked for and not given — A place left standing — The hand that asked — The figure\par

A word cut from an article — Bare paper — The length of the word — The word\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The last row is mine and has never been shown. The word I cut from the fourth article is the one this room uses for what comes back after a graft takes. It is not an allowed word, and when the College man comes he reads the bare place and does not ask how long it is. A man who has measured the place has looked at it, which is how I know he has read it. I have put the length in this table and not the word. A length can be carried; a word cannot.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the doing}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item No article provides for a wall that takes and will not hold. In the back rooms they try again.

\item No article provides for the man who comes back and wants a life that was not his. In the room they call it the graft settling and set a second wall over the first.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I saw a man come off this bench and turn his head toward a door he had never been taught to look at. He had the donor’s figure, which was three embers, and the donor’s want, which was a large want, and no name of his own on the slate he was entered upon. The room set another wall over the first. It took. He wanted the same thing afterward. There is no third article and no third wall that I know of.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The form of entry}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Seventh. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In nine years I have had no name for the last line that this room wanted spoken aloud.}
