It survives folded into a well-rope coil in a dry tin: a white dust like bone meal worked into the fold from the hearths, grey silt in the gutter off the road, a chip of slate pressed into the lower corner with a mark on it that is not a figure, a thumb of tallow at the head, a length of well-rope fibre caught in the sewing, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away with a knife-point, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that the writer did not make and has not swept, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I sink wells. There is one at Cold Acre that has never frozen, and I have kept it from the ice nineteen winters by knowing where the water goes under the ridge. A man who knows where water is knows where it is not, which is why the factor at Greybank sent for me. Three of us went south in Ash: a surveyor out of the factor’s house with a slate and a new coil of rope, a Fen man who would take us as far as the first doorway and no farther, and me. We went to measure the old wells of the Cantons. I had never measured a dry one.

I have measured six now. I have come back with nothing to tell except the lie of the ground, which is what men come back with from that place, and I had better set the ground down plain before it turns into a story.

\subsection*{The road in}

The Cantons lie sixty leagues south of Sill, and there is no road a cart can make in a day. We walked. On the third day the ruts came back under the turf, deep as a cart’s wheel and empty of anything a wheel had drawn through them in eight hundred years. A road is a thing somebody meant to come back along, and the ground had kept that much and let everything else go.

There is no gate and no due. The Fen man stopped where the first doorway stood and would not go past the shadow of it. He is a man of few words and gives them to the ground before he gives them to a person. He said a dry man is a dangerous man, and that he had stood on the boardwalk long enough to know one, and then he sat down on a stone and took no part in what followed, though he watched us the whole while with his back turned.

The first thing a well-sinker notices in a strange country is where the water would be if there were any. In the Cantons the low ground holds no damp, the ditches that were cut to drain it are dry cuts, and the clay underfoot has gone the colour of a pot fired too often.

There was no smoke. That is the thing every man writes down first, and I have written it down too, because it is true and because there is nothing else to write at that hour. In Grath a man can tell the hour by the smoke over a roof. Here the sky went on being a sky with nothing said in it, and the surveyor and I ate our bread standing up, though there was nowhere to sit that was not a step of somebody’s house.

\subsection*{The six wells}

\emph{Measured in the order we came to them. The rope’s figure is what my line brought up; the eye’s figure is what I saw at the mouth; the last column is what the surveyor wrote. I have set his hand above mine and left mine under it, which is the only way a man reads a slate in this country without lying.}

Well — What the rope said — What the eye saw — What was entered\par

First, by the road — full length down, dry coming up, iron on the wet end — stones laid round the mouth in the old order, every stone where a stone expects to be — dry; no entry\par

Second, in the doorway-yard — dry; the line came up with white dust on it — no mark of a bucket on the rim, and yet the rim worn smooth on one side — dry\par

Third, under the fallen wall — the rope fouled below and would not come back till I let the coil go — the mouth worn deep where a hand would rest and a hand would pull — dry; obstruction below, no value\par

Fourth, by the last standing hearth — dry — ash in it that is not grey — dry\par

Fifth — dry — a square of bare clay set into the stonework above it, where something had hung — dry\par

Sixth, beyond the doorways — dry — the stones laid so tidy that a man’s first thought is to ask who laid them — dry\par

A dry well is not a hole. A dry well is a statement made in stone, and I have no trade in answering it. In Cold Acre a well that fails is a well with a cause: a seam that has shifted, a taint, a nothing that the water used to do. These six had none. The water was down out of sight, which is a different thing from being gone, and the stones were laid round the mouths in the old order, which a man does not do when he is leaving in a hurry.

The surveyor wrote \emph{dry} against each and \emph{no entry} against the first. I asked him why the first was entered and the others not. He said the first stood nearest the road and a figure had to begin somewhere. Then he turned his slate face down, which is a thing men do here when they have seen enough and do not want to be asked what.

\subsection*{The doorways}

We counted nine doorways standing where the walls had gone. In three of them there was a square of bare clay above the lintel where a house-roll had hung, and there was no nail in any of the nine. A nail would have been pulled out and carried away, or would have rusted where it stood; there were no nails and no marks where nails had been, only the bare square as clean as the day the clay was laid.

In one doorway a slate still stands in its notch. The figures on it are not figures I could read, and I have set them down as shapes and not as numbers, because a man who calls a shape a figure has begun to explain it. One groove goes deeper than an iron point would cut, and I did not write how it was made, and would not know if I had.

A Vorr came through while we stood there, going north with a bag of nothing and a stick. The surveyor asked him about the slate. The Vorr looked at it a while and said the numbers were correct, and went on. He would not say what they counted. I have put his saying in the margin below rather than in the body of the account, because a sentence a man can carry away and still know nothing of is not an answer and should not be given the room of one.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in a small hard hand I took for the Vorr’s, four figures set down one under another, correctly made. I cannot match them to anything on the road: not to the wells, not to the doorways, not to the nine. I have left them standing where they were written.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{The hearths}

The hearths are cold, and the ash in them is not grey. It is a white dust like bone meal, fine and dry, lying in the hollow where a fire would have been. I have put my hand into four of them. In the fourth there was a little warmth still in the stone under the dust, no more than a stone keeps when the sun has been off it an hour, and I wrote that down and then crossed it out, because a well-sinker who writes a warmth where there should be none will be asked to find it again.

The Fen man said, from his stone with his back turned, that the white is what is left when a promise has been kept too long. I have set that down as it was said and have joined nothing to it. A man who joins a saying to a hollow full of white dust has made a story, and stories are what that country has no need of. In Grath we leave the grey in the corners on the Last Day and burn it in the morning. Here there is no Last Day that anybody keeps, and the white lies where it lies, and nobody sweeps.

\subsection*{The song of the dry road}

\emph{Sung by the Fen man going in, not coming back. He would not sing it within sight of the first doorway, and sang it on the third morning with his face to the north. The fourth line is his; there is a place in his singing of it where a word should stand, and I have set down what I heard rather than fill it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six wells and never a splash,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope goes down where the water was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stones keep house and the lintel keeps bare,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the road keeps the place where the step was.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners and one for the nail\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that was never driven and never pulled;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Fox has the hearth and the dust has the name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the well keeps the white that the hand never drew.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I went in dry and I came back dry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dry of the two is not the same;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one is a man and one is a ground,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and only the ground has a name for it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the rope what it brought back ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rope said nothing, and went on that way.\end{quote}

He said the last line was about the song and not about the wells, and when I asked him what the difference was he said a man who needed it explained would not have sung it. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it.

\subsection*{What the surveyor entered, and what I set under it}

At Greybank a clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaves while I was buying rope. He writes upright and narrow and leaves the doer out of every sentence, as though a well could dry itself and a man could walk sixty leagues without a pair of feet. He did not strike a word of mine. He put his words above and left mine where they stood, which is the readiest way of correcting a man I know.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the stones were laid in the old order} he wrote \emph{masonry, derelict}, which is a true description of stones and leaves out the order.

\item Against \emph{the rim was worn where a hand would pull} he wrote \emph{wear, cause unknown}. I have set \emph{cause: a hand} underneath in charcoal, which does not keep, and am content it should not.

\item Against \emph{the white dust in the hearths} he wrote \emph{residue, unclassified}, and against the Vorr’s saying, \emph{statement not entered}. He was right in the language of his office. A statement the office cannot enter is a statement the office need not answer.

\item Against my six rows he wrote \emph{six dry wells; no population; property unoccupied}, and underlined it twice. The wells are dry and the place is empty. I have never argued with either figure. What I cannot agree to is the word \emph{unoccupied}, which is a word for a house from which somebody has gone, and not for a house that has gone from somebody.

\end{itemize}

I have left both hands standing, his above and mine below, as a repaired vessel keeps the old break under the new staple and does not pretend the first hand never touched the clay. A clerk who takes the hand out of a well leaves the well standing by itself, and a well standing by itself has never dried anybody.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The white in the fold came off the hearths and is bone meal fine; it will not wash out and I have stopped trying. The grey in the gutter is silt off the south road and came honestly by its place, worked in on the walk back when the thaw had begun under the frost. The tallow at the head is my own lamp, set too near the leaf on the last night before we turned north. The rope-fibre in the sewing came off the coil that fouled in the third well; I cut it out with a knife and sewed it back, because a rope that has been down a well is not a rope to throw away. The chip in the lower corner is off the slate in the doorway. I prised it with a nail and it came away more easily than a chip should, and the mark on it is not a figure and I have never called it one. The square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with a knife-point and put no other in its place; it is the only square in this account I made myself. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the clerk’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in the Cantons and I have not found one since I came back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six wells and never a drop to count,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine doorways and no one to come through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope keeps the shape of what it didn’t bring up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate in the door keeps a figure for you.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the dust what it kept so long.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the stone why the water went.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the road whose wheel it was.\end{quote}

I asked the surveyor, the Fen man, and the Vorr who came through, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaves go back into the tin, and the tin into the coil, and the coil onto the shelf beside the rope I use at Cold Acre. Tomorrow I sink a well for a household on the ridge, and it will give water, and I shall be paid in marks for finding what the ground was willing to give. In the thaw I mean to walk south again with a longer line. I have not told the factor and do not know what I shall ask the well when I get there. A man who writes why before he goes has already decided what he will find, and I have made that mistake once, below the Old Kiln, and do not mean to make it twice.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Stonemouth Book of Remedies, Being What a Dresser of Stone Sets to the Lime-Burn, the White Cough, the Fall from the Bank, the Ferr-Thin, the Lead-Rat’s Bite, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Written in the Dust of the Lime Yard with the Errors Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Stonemouth Book of Remedies, Being What a Dresser of Stone Sets to the Lime-Burn, the White Cough, the Fall from the Bank, the Ferr-Thin, the Lead-Rat’s Bite, the Birth-Flower and the Child That Comes Cold, Written in the Dust of the Lime Yard with the Errors Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A quarry-leech’s book of remedies in the Stonemouth manner, set down on the back of a spoiled lime-warrant with the counts cut in the margin by a tally-point; the cures in a stone-dresser’s hand, the objections of a physician come down from Greybank pressed blue-grey into the gutter, the corrections of a College clerk in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a bank-master’s line in chalk at the foot of the remedies, a washing-song with the odd ones left standing, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at Stonemouth, where the Ferr joins the Ilm five leagues upriver of Sill, between Stone of Y.H. 811 and Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the Long Cold and the Thin Year, by Ivo of Stonemouth, a dresser of coarse sandstone who has set bones and caught children in the lime yard for three-and-twenty years; begun on the back of a lime-warrant spoiled by a wetting, cut at the edge with a tally-point, folded into oiled sailcloth and carried downriver at the Opening of the Slates, then copied at Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives with lime worked into the grain at the head, a blue-grey tideline off the Ferr that has taken two words clean off the second leaf, a reed-wolf’s tooth pressed into the lower corner by a buyer who paid two marks and did not stay to see it written, a ring of barley-water, a grey Ash print from a cuff nobody will own, a strip of salt-paper pasted over one correction and gone soft at the edge so that the correction shows through, three objections in the cold margin hand of the physician, the clerk’s upright hand above the cures, the bank-master’s chalk at the remedies, and the line at the foot\par}\medskip
I dress stone for a living and have set bones and caught children in this yard for three-and-twenty years. Nobody asked me for this book. A man came in off the bank in the lean week with both hands gone white to the wrist and asked what I did for the lime, and I heard myself answer in my father’s voice, and did not know whether I believed it. A remedy you have to say in your father’s voice is a remedy nobody has looked at in a long while. I have looked at some of mine here; the rest I have left standing, because a man at three in the morning wants a hand more than a correction.

I write on the back of a lime-warrant that a wetting spoiled. The figures went before anybody could charge them. The lime at the head is off the cuff I wipe the chisel with. The blue in the gutter came off the Ferr when I washed a man’s arm in it, which I have not done since. Nothing in this book is free. Here a thing that costs nothing has usually been paid for by whoever carried the lime.

\subsection*{The order of the dressing yard}

\emph{Cut small into the first leaf with the tally-point, with one word gone over in lime.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Lay the sick one on sacking, never on bare stone. Stone takes from a body faster than a bed does, and a man laid on it goes cold from the side he lies on. A physician from Greybank says a cold stone draws the heat out. I have set my line above his. Both stand.

\item Ask what he carried before you ask what ails him. A man who has carried lime knows where his back hurts; a man who has carried nothing will tell you where it ought to. This is not kindness. It is the order of the yard.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to a child. I have no slate-name and never shall; the weigh-clerk here sets his figure to a tooth before he looks at the man who brought it, and I have no wish to be taken for that kind of reader.

\item Put the warm stone in wool at the belly and try it on your own wrist first. The stone comes off the kiln bank, and somebody paid for the coal that warmed it.

\item Set the splint loose enough to see a finger under it.

\item When the third night comes, let the woman do the counting; a number counted for her belongs to whoever counted it.

\item Do not drink from the Ferr or wash a wound in it. We have said the opposite for four hundred years and have put the old line underneath rather than lose it.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is spent\par

The lime-burn (both hands, or the forearm where the sleeve rides back) — Tallow first, then a clean fold; never dry lime — The men shake lime on a burn to dry the wet, believing white is clean. The physician says lime eats and does not dry. I have dressed three such hands with lime on them and found a white line under the skin in all three, and have not done it a fourth time. — The hand; and the household that bought the lime.\par

The white cough — Steam of hot water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — We say the dust of the good stone cuts the dust of the bad. The physician says it is stone in the lung, and the only physic is to leave the yard, which no house here can do. I sent three up the ridge; two came back worse, because the ridge has stone of its own. — The man, in the morning he coughs up a colour he will not discuss.\par

The Ferr-thin (a season at the well) — Barley-water, a stone at the belly, and work — We say it is the cold of the water and that a warm body keeps it out. The physician says the water carries lead down off the old working and that warmth has nothing to do with it. I have sent men warm to the kiln and watched them go thinner by the fifth month; one went off it after his daughter took him up to Cold Acre. I have not sent anybody else. — The household, which cannot move six leagues to good water.\par

The sweet line at the gum — Sour barley-water; the gum rubbed with wood-ash — The pots from High Kiln carry the green, and the women taste the glaze to get the colour, and say a sweet answers a sweet. The physician says it is lead and that sour water only troubles the teeth. I have seen the line go off a girl who left the glaze room and come back on one who stayed. I have not seen the lead. — The glaze room, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A fall from the bank — Two hands, a lath of straight sandstone, a fold of wet cloth; set it before the swelling takes — We say a bone dressed green takes the tool the way a block does. The physician says wet cloth about a limb cools what should be kept warm. I have set eleven and had three come crooked; one hand I bound too tight for fear of its moving, and it did not come back. — The man, in the holding still. This is the row where I have been least honest.\par

A lead-rat’s bite — Tallow and a clean fold; burn the tails, two bits a score — We say one bite is nothing and a hundred make a thin child. The physician wrote the year Y.H. 641 in the margin, when this was known, and noted it was forgotten; he says the rat and the glaze carry the same lead. I have put the year where he wrote it and left the rat under it. — The household, whose children go thin by degrees; the catcher, paid by the tail.\par

The birth-flower (the red branch) — Nothing. Two fingers crossed, and the word the mother gives — A woman of the washing crossed two fingers at a child of this yard and covered it with a date, the way they do at Sill. I have put the date in the margin. The physician says it is a flowering of the blood and not a flower, and is right in a language nobody here speaks. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

A child that comes with the cold on it — A stone in wool at the belly, a living body under the fold, a watch to the fourth day — It comes when the birth is in Stone, and the hands go first. We walk them, believing a moving child keeps its heat. The physician says a child made warm spends faster and that a cold child cannot clot. I have watched nine and held two; all saw the fourth morning, and one went thin. I have left the count with the woman who did the watching. — The household, one night’s sleep, and sometimes the child.\par

Nothing here is given away. It is carried from one body into another and called a cure. That is the only sentence in this book I will stand behind.

\subsection*{The note in the block}

The masons tap a block with the butt of a hammer-handle before they dress a face. A sound one answers full and a flawed one answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the skin of the stone and will not go through. This is the one thing in this country that costs nothing and is still allowed to be true.

I tapped a man once, gone thin after a winter at the well, and put my ear to the little flat I thought I heard. The flat was not in him. A body is not a block. I did not say so at the time, because there was a weigh-clerk in the room. I have written it here, which is a different matter.

The cup on the bench knows more about whether a room held its warm through the night than the man in it, and I set the stone by the cup’s note and not by the yard bell, which counts something of its own.

\subsection*{What the well by the Ferr keeps}

The well was never sweetened. The clause is on the treaty slate and the factor at Greybank pasted his salt-paper over it, and the strip has lifted at one corner so that six words show and the rest do not. I have washed men at that well for three-and-twenty years and have never once tasted lead in it.

In the year of the water the households drank all winter and called it thin. The well-song, taken down at the washing from a woman who had learned it from women who had, says they did; the road-book at Sill entered three hundred households and no dead. A small hard hand put seventy-one against Stonemouth, and twenty-one went downriver and were not entered again.

The physician wrote \emph{visitation of the water} above our \emph{cold water}, true in a language nobody at this well speaks. He was right about the lead and had nothing to put in its place that a household here could pay for, and the well kept the larger part, as the song says. I have set his sentence above mine and left the twenty-one underneath, where a clerk carrying a round sum will not think to look.

\subsection*{The washing-song}

\emph{Sung low at the tubs, not at the kiln. There is a place after the second verse the length of a row that was never entered.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Ferr came down with a blue-grey skin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clause was pasted, the charge not paid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a pale line shows at the lip’s inner edge\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the pot from High Kiln has been tasted.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three hundred stand where a slate has them,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and seventy-one by the well we know;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man goes thin in the fifth month\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cup gives back what the water took.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sing to the tub, sing to the flat cup,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the woman who counts under wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and comes back as it can ---\end{quote}

A clerk of the College put a round nought in the place and wrote \emph{nil} beneath it. A nought is a figure. The twenty-one went downriver and stayed a row.

\subsection*{What the physician pressed in the margin}

He came down from Greybank in Smoke of Y.H. 811 with a book that had the word \emph{lead} in it and a hand that wrote without asking. Against the lime he set \emph{caustic; no efficacy}, against the birth-flower \emph{a mark in the blood, nothing more}, and against the white cough \emph{the dust of the stone, and no physic but departure}, which is true and of no use to a household whose living is cut out of that stone.

He was right about all three. I have left his sentences above mine, so the next reader can tell which is which, and put my words back underneath where a man at three in the morning will find them.

\subsection*{What the College clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf at Greybank when the winter lime was being counted.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against my column headed \emph{Who is spent} he wrote \emph{No cost entered}, which is a true thing in a dishonest place.

\item Where I wrote \emph{we drink all winter and call it thin}, he set \emph{a reduction in the measure was recorded} above, as though the drinker had gone out of the sentence and left the measure standing by itself.

\item Where I wrote \emph{the well was never sweetened}, he wrote \emph{the obligation remains outstanding}, which is the most beautiful sentence I have ever read in a hand that has never drawn water in the dark.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath. A clerk can speak without verbs because he is never in the yard; a man who has carried lime wants to know who paid for the coal.

\subsection*{In the margin, in chalk, the bank-master’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape A block tells you when it is dressed. A man does not. I have dressed four hundred blocks and two hands, and neither hand gave a note. --- R.\end{quote}

He wrote it at the foot of the remedies while I was at the well. I have set his line above my row and mine under it, as the yard keeps the old cut showing under the new dressing. A man who has lost a hand to his own trade is allowed one sentence in a book of physic.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime at the head is mine and will not wash out. The blue tideline came up the second leaf the morning I washed a Ferr-thin man’s arm and has taken two words clean off it; I have not written them back, because a remedy with two words gone is said slowly. A buyer pressed the tooth in the corner, paid two marks for it and said a good tooth remembers the shape of a way. The ring of barley-water came from a cup set down while I told a man to drink and he would not. The grey along the fold is not mine; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day in this yard. The salt-paper strip has lifted at one corner, so a correction shows through that was meant to be covered, which is the only honest thing that paper has done.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The block keeps the cut and the well keeps the dust;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither was asked who drank, or who paid.\end{quote}

I asked the physician, the College clerk and a woman at the washing, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. Tomorrow a man will come in off the bank with a hand gone white or a child that will not breathe, and I shall put the verbs back and turn the slate face down before I look at the child --- because a child is not a block and a body is not a cup, and the yard has room for both truths if a man leaves them side by side.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany Before the Grating, Being the Prayer of the Keepers of the Hearth-Fire at the Weighing, with the Voice’s Corrections and a Junior Keeper’s Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany Before the Grating, Being the Prayer of the Keepers of the Hearth-Fire at the Weighing, with the Voice’s Corrections and a Junior Keeper’s Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said by the keepers of the Hearth-fire in the Weighing Hall, the Voice reading and the keepers answering through the bars; set down by a keeper of the third watch who signs with a coal-cross, with the rubrics of the grating, the eight stations and their answer, the Voice’s struck corrections, the second watch’s note, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat on Weighing of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the junior keeper of the third watch, on the back of a spoiled slate-copy of the year’s first measure, and corrected by Hesta Clay, Voice of the Return, before the Remembering; carried through the Opening of the Slates and copied forward in Ash of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in the iron box under the grating ledge. It survives soft along the fold and scorched at the upper edge, with coal-dust worked into the creases of the first leaf, a lamp-black thumb, iron filings caught in the gutter from the grating hinge, a spot of tallow off the watch lamp, a hair, a grey Ash print from a cuff that had been in the residue room, and a small coal in the fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I am a keeper of the third watch at the grating and I write this where I stand, which is on the north side with my hands behind me. The Voice reads from the ledge in the clean voice, the one that takes her neatly out of her own sentences, and we answer through the bars. I have kept the answer as we say it and the rubrics as the room actually has them, because a rubric written in a clean hand is a rubric for a room with no fire in it. The Voice has borrowed the leaf and given it back with four of my lines struck through. I have left every struck line standing under her words, as a keeper leaves a repair showing.

The coal-dust at the head came off the grate when the hinge was worked on the morning of the Weighing; it goes into the grain and will not come out. The scorch along the upper edge is from a night when a draught came off the Keel and carried a spark against the leaf while I held it to the lamp. I have not cut the scorch away. A prayer with a burn on it has been used, which is more than can be said for a clean one. The filings in the gutter are off the hinge. The grey came off my cuff after I had been in the residue room, and I have not swept it off the leaf. The little coal in the fold is not mine and I have asked the second watch about it and had two answers, neither of which I have written down.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The grating is not opened. The fire is behind iron and no priest may touch it. We answer through the bars and keep our hands behind us.

\item Do not count the bars. There are nine on the north side and eight on the south; the ninth on the north is the one the fire leans against, and a keeper who counts from the wrong end will find eight and think he has lost one. He has not. Begin at the hinge.

\item The litany is read, not sung. A sung line travels up into the vault and comes back as something the keepers did not say, and the Voice does not answer to echoes.

\item When the Voice says the last line, lay the slate on the ledge face down. It has been read enough for one year.

\item The answer is said by every keeper present, including the one on the night stair who cannot see the ledge and says it a half-beat late. We do not correct him. He is counting a different thing.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{The Voice says. The keepers answer. The words between are mine where I have set them, and hers where she has struck them.}

\subsection*{I. Of the firing}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before the slate there was the clay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before the clay there was the fire in the dark,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dark had not yet been given a name to be afraid of.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was set up and fired whole.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It answered when it was tapped. The tap was not a hand.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{II. Of the Breaking}

\begin{quote}\itshape One anger, and the lid was off the pot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Warm went out where no wall held it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and ran into the country that keeps nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The crack has a name. Say it once. Do not go looking for it in the floor.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What went out is going still, and the going is not finished.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{III. Of the Nine}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hands went after what had run away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They drove the repairs home the way a potter drives a staple,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the staple is the same iron in a small vessel and a large one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name them by their number and not by their houses.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ninth repair is in the Hearth’s hand and is not finished.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine went. One is still abroad.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{IV. Of the iron and the gate}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is behind iron and no priest may touch it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron does not keep. It is a gate with a cold face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps. We stand where the grate lets us stand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give our answer through the bars.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Hands behind. A hand at the grate is a hand in the account.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{V. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers, not years. A year is a pot nobody weighs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says. Printed. Read twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The notice does not lean. It is the Hearth’s own hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate is a piece of stone with a clean figure on it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure does not sweat and the hand does not shake.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it small. A great thing written small still balances.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{VI. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: the shape comes back with its name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the price of bread and the handle of the cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many measures into many: the shape comes back as it can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a hankering for a table it never sat at.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both go into the same clean hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the one that wants. It is the one that can be kept.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{VII. Of the Kept}

\begin{quote}\itshape Blessed are they that are Kept. No want can reach them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They do not feel the cold and they do not ask for bread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There are fewer than twenty in the world.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand a moment at their place and do not ask them whether they are warm;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they will say no, and you will have spent your only question.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{VIII. Of the year}

\begin{quote}\itshape The year’s measures are read while the fire behind the grate\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape burns as it burned before the counting began.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The rich learn how whole they are. Low Kiln learns what it gives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both learn it from the same slate, which does not know the difference.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the name of each returned, once for the moot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and once for them that came up the road too late.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Keep the fire. Keep the account. Keep the name.

\subsection*{The close}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The Voice:} Nothing is lost that we have kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The keepers:} The measure is banked. The account stands. Your return is recorded.\end{quote}

Here I lay the slate face down on the ledge and take my hands out from behind me. The third watch ends with the fire not touched and the account not argued with, which is the whole of a keeper’s trade.

\subsection*{What the Voice struck out}

She borrowed the leaf on the morning after the Weighing, with the ink still wet in two fingers, and gave it back with four lines of mine under her own.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At II, against \emph{the crack has a name. Say it once. Do not go looking for it in the floor}, she wrote: \emph{The First Breaking is a mystery of the faith and not a place in a room.} Under that, in mine: \emph{It is a place in a room. I have seen the seam in the Keel behind the cistern, and it has been mended more than once.} Both stand.

\item At IV, against \emph{a hand at the grate is a hand in the account}, she wrote: \emph{The grating is not to be approached.} Mine stands below. She would have the rule and not the reason for it; I keep the reason, because a keeper on the night stair wants to know why he has his hands behind him.

\item At VI, against \emph{keep the one that wants}, she wrote: \emph{All returned measures are entered alike.} Under mine: \emph{A keeper can tell which child wants. The slate cannot. Both are true, and the second is the one that gets read.}

\item At VIII, against \emph{Low Kiln learns what it gives}, she wrote: \emph{The deduction is one in twelve for every vessel of the Keeping.} Under mine: \emph{I have copied the figure from the notice in the lower court. I have not copied the other. A keeper of the grating has no business with figures that are not printed, and I have kept my hands behind me.}

\end{itemize}

I have left her hand above mine and my words below it, which is the order the Hearthseat uses when it wants a thing looked at and not answered.

\subsection*{What the second watch put in the margin}

At VII, in a hand that writes with the ends of the words shaken, a keeper who stood at the Remembering has written:

\begin{quote}\itshape In the Remembering a whole return was announced for a name nobody in this hall had seen. She read it twice. I have kept the twice.\end{quote}

At the close, against \emph{your return is recorded}, the same hand has set a small coal-cross where a name would go and written no name beside it. I have asked him whose it was and he gave me the hour of the watch instead. A coal-cross is a keeper’s way of signing a thing he has stood at and will not carry out of the hall.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lamp-black thumb is mine; I held the leaf with the hand I write with and did not know I had marked it. The tallow is off the watch lamp, which stands on the ledge where the draught comes off the Keel and gutters down one side. The hair is not mine and I have left it where it fell, because a hair in a fold means somebody leaned over to see what was being written, and at the grating the only person who may lean is the Voice. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff that had been in the residue room and nobody will own the cuff. The filings have worked into the scorch and stay there. The coal in the fold I have not identified, and I have put it back each time I have taken the leaf out.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the Voice’s and not the second watch’s, struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire keeps what is given. The account keeps what is entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire is not an account.\end{quote}

I have asked three keepers and had two answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the iron box under the ledge, and next Weighing the Voice will read the eight stations and we shall answer through the bars, and the ninth repair will still be in the Hearth’s hand. I have copied this once into Ash of Y.H. 813 with the scorch left scorch and the struck lines left struck. On the day the ninth repair is finished the litany will be read no more, which is the one line in it I have never been able to say with my hands behind me.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Deep, Being the Order of the Return as the Surveyors of the First Seam Say It Over the Walling-In at Keld Keep}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Deep, Being the Order of the Return as the Surveyors of the First Seam Say It Over the Walling-In at Keld Keep}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return read from the walling-slate at the mouth of the First Seam, before the mortar is mixed and while the dead one still faces the deep seam; with the rubrics of the mouth, eight stations and their answer, the walling-slate for the season, a Court survey-clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a widow’s margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Senn, who keeps the walling-slate at the mouth of the First Seam at Keld Keep and has never been down the Descent, on the back of a walling-tally spoiled by a thumb of iron filings and a spill of lamp oil; folded into the flap of the slate satchel and kept on the nail beside the mouth, taken out only when there is a wall to make; borrowed at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 by a survey-clerk of the Court who set his hand above hers. It survives with clamp-filings ground into the head, pale lime from the walling mortar along the gutter, a thumb of tallow at the fold, a spot that came over the Cold Pass and has been water twice and frost twice, two words gone where the lamp oil ran across the fifth station, a notch cut at the edge with a tally-knife where a word would not come, the clerk’s correction standing above the words it corrects, a widow’s hand in the margin, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the walling-slate at the mouth of the First Seam and I have never been down the Descent, which is no disgrace above ground and is not mentioned below it. A man come up from Greybank in Bone with a clean cuff and asked what we said over a man who goes into the wall. I told him we said the Return. He asked me to say it. I said it, and he wrote it down and thanked me, and what he wrote had the verbs taken out and a figure standing where the man had been, and it is in the factor’s book by now, being truer than mine in the only room he knows. What follows is what we actually say, with the verbs put back and the space left the width it is.

There is a cold in this mouth that goes into slate and stays there. I have kept the leaf under the lamp while I wrote so that the charcoal would take, and the oil has run once and taken two words off the fifth station, and I have not written them back. A person who knows a thing is not therefore in possession of it; I know the two words and have left the space the length of them, as the wall leaves the length of a man.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Say it at the mouth, after the number is cut and before the lime is mixed. A man with wet mortar on his hands should not be asked to hold the slate; he will leave a pale print on it and the print will outlast the number.

\item The reader is whoever keeps the walling-slate. In my mother’s time it was a man of the Duelling Floor, and he said the words the way another man reads a charge-sheet, and the old women at the count answered for him because the row was too frightened to. I am not a woman of the Floor and I say them slower.

\item The answer belongs to the row at the mouth, including the boy who came up with the man and will go down in his place next year. The boy says it worst. We do not correct the saying, only the order.

\item Do not say it to the stone. Said to the stone it becomes a bargain, and the stone keeps bargains, which is more than can be said of the Hearth. Say it to the slate and let the slate hear what it cannot enter.

\item Set the dead one facing the seam. This is not part of the prayer. It is the part before, the way warming a stone is the part before in the low houses.

\item If an officer of the Court is at the mouth, give him the shift-tally and not the leaf. The leaf has no figure for a man who is not coming up, and he cannot enter a man who stays where he is put.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{I read from the walling-slate. The row answers. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not an argument with a mountain.}

\subsection*{I. Of the number}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say what you hold before you say who you are.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm gives the number; the mouth gives the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape At this mouth the order is the other way round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape because the wall has no ear for a name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate has no room for a person.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\subsection*{II. Of the breaking}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was fired whole and the lid went up in one anger.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The surveyors say the repairs lie one over another,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a new seam over an old seam, the newest over all,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape as a pot is mended until the first pot cannot be seen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not say this in front of an officer. Say it to the slate.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\subsection*{III. Of the Nine}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hands went after what had run away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine repairs were driven home and the ninth is not finished.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There is a paper in a tin lined with warm-stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read once a year by men who do not act on it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have not read it. I know the length of it.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\subsection*{IV. Of the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tube does not keep. The clamp does not keep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron opens a way and the way stays open.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One bite holds a vessel whole and one bite takes the hand off a man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is the same bite and it has never asked anybody’s opinion.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\subsection*{V. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve is printed on the notice and is read twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mine-reeve checks the figure in red and does not look at the man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve bits to the mark and twenty marks to the crown.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers, not years; a year is a stone nobody weighs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure that is not printed is the one this mouth pays.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the lamp oil ran. Two words are gone and I have left the space the length of them. A lowland clerk would write a figure into it and call the leaf whole. It is not whole. It is carried, which is a different thing and the only one known here.}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\subsection*{VI. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: he comes back with his name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the hand that held the cup and the price of bread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many: they come back as they can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a hankering for a table they never sat at.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both go into a clean hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Far beyond the Rim there is a people who say\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they were never owed, and no Court has entered it.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\subsection*{VII. Of the walling}

\begin{quote}\itshape Here is no tube and no cradle and no clean hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He goes in facing the seam with his number on the stone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lime in the joints and a flat chip at the head,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the surveyor adds a figure nobody reads aloud.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mountain does not fetch back what it has taken.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It does not say it has taken. That is the courtesy here.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\subsection*{VIII. Of the coming back}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not bring him up and do not say we have.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come up with the number you went down with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape or come up with the number the mountain gave.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two go down and the count comes two.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The count is made. That was always the promise.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} The number stands. The mountain keeps its own.

\emph{Here the leaf leaves a space the width of a number with no man under it. It is not a number forgotten. It is the one the slate will not take and the wall will. I have kept the space the width it is.}

\subsection*{The walling-slate, for this season, as I keep it}

Wall — Number cut in arm — Number on slate — Name said\par

North gallery, first — forty-one — forty-one — said twice, once to the row\par

Under the survey room — nine — nine, and a notch at the edge — not said; the boy asked\par

Third, beyond the cup — no arm to read — no figure entered — none given\par

\emph{The third row is not a debt. There is a cup at the end of the Duelling Floor that nobody takes, for the man whose number was changed twice. I have set the row down as it stands. An empty row is not the same as a crossed one, and there is no crossing out at this mouth. The mine-reeve entered the second man’s earlier number in red and left the later cut standing in the skin, which is how an honest clerk keeps two figures without calling either a lie.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaf at Greybank on a morning when the factor was weighing lead and his cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He writes in the narrow upright hand and takes the verbs out as another man might take the bones out of a fish.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the order is the other way round} he wrote \emph{the measure is declared and the person is identified}, underlined twice. Both stand. He has put the man after the number, which is where the mountain puts him and not where a mother does.

\item At \emph{the repairs lie one over another} he wrote \emph{the First Breaking is a single event of the faith} and struck my line through. I have put it back under his. He had to read the line before he could strike it, which is a thing a man does once and cannot do again without knowing what he struck.

\item At \emph{a paper read once a year} he wrote \emph{no such paper} above the line, and then, underneath, in the same hand, \emph{not for entry}. I have left both. The first is what he is paid to write and the second is what he believes, and a man who writes both on one leaf is not as stupid as his cuff makes him look.

\item At \emph{we do not bring him up} he wrote \emph{no return recorded; account closed}. It is the only honest sentence in his hand and it cost him nothing, because an account closed is a figure with a line under it and he has never stood at a mouth and watched the line drawn in lime.

\item At the answer he put a round nought against the space and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a number where a man would stand. That is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have left every line of his standing above mine and mine under it, the way a new seam lies over an old one and does not make the old one go away. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a boy at thirteen with a knife at his arm wants to know which hand to hold the stone with, and a woman at a mouth wants something to say to the boy after the knife.

\subsection*{What the widow put in the margin}

The leaning hand is Henna’s, whose man went into the wall under the survey room with a number cut into his arm that had belonged to somebody out of the Fenmarch in the year he came back thin from Sill. She has written where I set the sixth station, and I have copied her as she wrote it.

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel. That is what they say at Sill and what they print on the notice. My man came back from a pouring with a number in his arm that was not his, and he wanted a table he had never sat at, and the table was mine and he sat at it six years without knowing it was his. When he went into the wall the surveyor cut the number out and cut a new one in, and the old one is still under the skin. I have asked which of the two the wall will keep. Nobody has answered and I have stopped asking.\end{quote}

And at the space, underneath the clerk’s nought:

\begin{quote}\itshape Not a vacancy. He is where they put him. That is not the same as lost and it is not the same as kept, and I will not have your clerk choose between them.\end{quote}

I have copied her as she wrote it. She has taken her shawl home and I have not gone after her with a correction.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The filings at the head are off the clamp I set the leaf down on while the surveyor read the second number; they have gone into the grain and no wet sleeve takes them out, which is how iron signs. The pale along the gutter is lime off the walling mortar and is not Ash; there is Ash enough in this seam without bringing a stranger’s into a leaf. The tallow thumb is mine, off the lamp I keep turned low beside the slate. The spot at the lower corner came over the Cold Pass and has been water twice and frost twice and is still a spot. The oil ran across the fifth station on the night I copied after the second wall, and two words went with it; I have not gone over them, because a word written thin is a word said quietly and most of ours are. The notch I cut at the edge with my tally-knife where a word would not come. A notch is not a letter and it keeps better in the wet. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff that had no business lying where the slate is kept, and I have not swept it. There is a Last Day in the low houses and there is none above the shaft mouth, and even there the morning comes.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not Henna’s, struck through once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape We say the Return. The wall does the keeping.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Those are two trades. Only one of them has a slate.\end{quote}

I asked the surveyor who reads the numbers, a boy who came up from the second wall, and Henna at the mouth, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the satchel and the walling-slate goes back on its nail. Tomorrow a boy will state what he holds before he says who he is, the mine-reeve will check the figure in red, and the number will go on being called after the arm that carried it has gone into the wall.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Ground Pot, Being the Order of the Return as the Four Kilns of Nine Pots Keep It at the Opening of a Firing}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Ground Pot, Being the Order of the Return as the Four Kilns of Nine Pots Keep It at the Opening of a Firing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said to the clay at the shared pit and again over a child born under the fourth kiln, the tally-woman reading from the firing-tally and the women of the kilns answering; with the rubrics of the pit, eight stations and their answer, a road-clerk’s correction come up from Sill, a woman’s notes written in slip, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at Nine Pots in Ember of Y.H. 813, the year after the Thin Year, by Tessa of the Fourth Kiln, keeper of the firing-tally at the shared clay pit, on the back of a tally spoiled by a wet slip-thumb in the tally-shed; carried down to Sill on Account-day in a cart of coarse ware and corrected there by a clerk of the Court’s table in Slate Row, who had come up about the road; copied forward in Frost of Y.H. 813 into a quire wrapped in oiled sacking and kept in a hollow of the pit under a flat stone. It survives with bone-pale slip in every crease, brick-red kiln dust along the fore-edge, a broken sherd pressed into the fold with a cupworm’s bore through it, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl come up from the Cross, a press of wet wool across the second leaf, a small ale ring gone dark, the clerk’s upright hand above the talk, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed.\par}\medskip
I keep the firing-tally at the fourth kiln and I have set this down because the women at the pit asked for a saying they could use with their hands in the clay. A woman who has just lost a pot does not want an argument, and a woman who has just lost a person does not want a figure; both can stand a sentence said to the ground. The order that comes down from Sill is a good order for a room with a table in it. We have no table, only the wet bank and the boards laid across it, and a broken pot goes into the ball before the next firing as a matter of course. The Return seemed the same sort of work. We have said it so since the year of the flower, when three went in one tend and two names came back.

I have set the clerk’s words where he put them, above mine. He came up about the road, the quarrel between Nine Pots and Sill that outlives everybody who started it, and while he waited he borrowed the leaf and took the doing out of it. I have put the doing back underneath, as a potter puts the thumb back in a handle smoothed by somebody who never held a pot.

The slip at the head is mine and dries bone-pale, the colour of a potter’s forearms at the end of a day in the pits. The red dust came off the kiln crown when the fourth was drawn and has gone into the grain. The sherd in the fold came up with the cupworm’s bore already through it and lies over the word \emph{whole} in station III, so that the word shows hollow when the fold is shut; I have not written it again. The green is not ours, for our ware is coarse; a girl come up from the Cross with the sweetness at her mouth leaned to see the tally and left it. The wool is a woman’s, the ale ring has gone dark and will go no darker. None of it is a figure and none has been entered.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Open the kiln before you speak. A pot still in the fire has not answered, and a saying over it is a saying to the fire, which is done in Sill.

\item Say it to the clay, the boards or the bank. Said looking at a woman it becomes a question, and there is always a woman who will answer it.

\item Grind the broken pot small before the ball is made. A sherd ground fine cannot be told from the rest of the clay, which is the whole of what we mean by a return.

\item The answer belongs to everybody at the pit, including the child with no birth-slate and the one who came back quiet and does not know which name to answer to. Neither is corrected.

\item When a man comes up from Sill about the road, give him the tally and not the leaf. The tally is a document and the road has an entry. The leaf is a saying and has none.

\item If the bell at the Cross carries over the fields, stop. It is counting the pigs. Begin again after.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{One woman reads from the tally. The pit answers. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not a firing.}

\subsection*{I. Of the pit}

\begin{quote}\itshape Before the pot there was the bank, and before the bank\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clay lay wet with no shape laid on it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A shape is a thing done to clay. It is not the clay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We dig, we wet, we tread. The pit does not ask why.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{II. Of the firing}

\begin{quote}\itshape The world was fired whole and the lid lifted in one anger.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Warm went out where no wall held it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and ran into the country that keeps nothing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not ask where the country is. A potter knows\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a thing can be lost without leaving the yard.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The crack has a name. Say it once to the bank.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the fourth kiln is drawn and the pots come out hot. Nobody touches one before the station is said.}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{III. Of the nine}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine hands went after what had run away.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four kilns stand at this pit and a fifth never did;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the place where it would stand is the road to Sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and we do not fire upon the road.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine went. One is still abroad.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count the kilns from the west and you will get four.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count from the east and you will get four. The other is not here.\end{quote}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{IV. Of the grinding}

\begin{quote}\itshape The broken pot is ground back into the ball.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing is lost of it that was clay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lip that went first is in the new lip;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the belly that held is in the new belly.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It comes up out of the pit with another name on it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and answers when it is struck.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What was carried out is carried in. That is the Return.\end{quote}

\emph{Here a sherd is ground under the reader’s heel. It is not a ceremony. It is the work, and the work is the ceremony.}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{V. Of the note}

\begin{quote}\itshape Strike a sound pot and it answers full.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Strike a cracked one and it answers flat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cupworm goes in where the clay was worked too long\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot looks sound until the first pouring.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A flat note is a thing said plainly.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Carry it anyway. Set it where the light can find it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not glaze a crack and call it mended.\end{quote}

\emph{The sherd with the bore lies here. The hole covers a word; the reader says the word and the hole stays.}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{VI. Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says. Printed. Read twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The notice does not lean and the figure does not sweat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count pots, not years. A year is a kiln nobody weighs.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure read in the square and the figure the household pays\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape are two pots set down side by side;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody here has made them agree.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the reader touches the tally. The other figure is not said aloud, nor said quietly. It is left in the clay, where it goes soft in winter and comes back in the thaw.}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{VII. Of the pouring}

\begin{quote}\itshape One measure into one vessel: he comes back with his name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the hand that turned the wheel and the debt it carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many: they come back as they can,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with a taste for a table they never sat at\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a hand that goes out toward a cup already cracked.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are ground. Both are thrown. Both go into the same fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pit does not know which it has been given.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the leaf leaves a space the length of a name. It is not a name forgotten. The woman whose boy came back has written in it, and then written no more.}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{VIII. Of the coming back}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the name into the bank, not over the cradle.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Once for the house, once for the one who came up the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape after the kiln was closed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If you have no name, leave the place where the name would stand\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and set a pot down in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not sweep the bank. It is not dirt.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Open the kiln. Strike the pot. Carry it home.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the leaf ends and the firing begins. No clerk from Sill has ever understood why the reading comes before the heat.}

\emph{Answer:} Grind it small. Throw it new. Come back in the pot.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came up about the road on an Account-day with his cuff gone soft at the edge from washing and the ink settled in two fingers of it. He borrowed the leaf while a cart was being loaded and gave it back with the doing taken out, which is what they teach in the counting house at Sill. I have left his hand above mine and mine under it, as a repaired pot keeps the old break under the new slip.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At station IV, against \emph{what was carried out is carried in}, he wrote: \emph{the measure is drawn, banked and pressed into a newborn vessel.} Under it: \emph{That is the account of it. Ours is what the hands do, and the hands are in the pit.}

\item At station VI he put a small stop against \emph{the figure the household pays} and wrote the printed figure again above it, larger. It is the figure they like to see. I have left both, and nobody here has asked me to choose.

\item At station III, where the fifth kiln would stand, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it, which is a true figure about a road. Under mine: \emph{The road has a place and no fire. He has entered the place and not the quarrel, which is the whole art of that hand.}

\item At the answer he wrote \emph{one answer, entered eight times.} True in the figure and false at the pit, where eight mouths say it and the ninth, at the back, says it a half-beat late. We do not correct her. She is grinding something of her own.

\end{itemize}

He asked what the women learned by it. I told him the grinding and the note and the carrying home. He said that was the Return taught with a sherd in the hand, and wrote it down. We said it again after he went, because a saying said to a man goes off with the man.

\subsection*{What the woman whose boy came back put in the margin}

The hand is charcoal and slips at the \emph{th}, being letters learned off a tally and not off a book. She was at the pit when the fourth was drawn and came back in the dark to read what I had written.

At II: \emph{It was a good pot. It split at the lip, not in the belly. We ground it with the rest and made a cup out of it, and I have that cup by me. Nobody knows it was him but me, and the cup does not know either.}

At the worm: \emph{A worm does not break a pot. A pot breaks where the clay was worked too long and the worm goes in where it is already hollow. We say the worm did it because a worm is a thing you can point at.}

At VII: \emph{He came back quiet and wanted a cup. We gave him one with a crack in it and he held it the right way up. That was the only whole thing he did in six years, and we did not tell the clerk, because he would have entered it against him.}

At the answer: \emph{Say it for the pots. I do not say it for him. He is here and he is not the one we said it for.} Then, underneath and very small: \emph{I have ground him. That is not the same as having him back.}

I have left both lines standing. A pit that scores itself will soon be a Court, and I have seen how those rooms go.

\subsection*{At the head and in the fore-edge}

The slip thumb is mine and has dried the colour of old bone in every crease; it is how the fourth kiln signs anything it has touched. The red along the fore-edge is crown dust and comes off whenever the leaf is carried past the kiln mouth, which is every day in Ember. The sherd lies over the hollow word and I have not moved it, because a word with a hole in it is a word said through the teeth, and most of ours are. The green is not glaze of ours, for Nine Pots makes coarse ware; a girl who had tasted at the Cross left it and went back up the field without saying what she had seen. The wool is a woman’s; the dark of the ring came from a quart that stood from the first station to the eighth with nobody drinking it, which is how a quart usually goes at a pit in Ember.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not the woman’s, struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay keeps what it is given and gives it back in the pot.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Hearth keeps what it is given and gives it back when it is paid.\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the bank, the girl who carries pots down to Sill and a man who came up about the road, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the sacking and under the flat stone, and next Ember the fourth kiln will be drawn cold and we shall say the eight stations to the bank and grind the broken pots in before the ball, and the clerk will come up about the road with his soft cuff and put the doing back where the doing was, and I shall set it back as I did this year. The ninth has not come down the road yet, the fifth kiln has never been built, and the cup by the woman’s bed does not know what it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Litany of the Second Cutting, Being the Order of the Return as the Number-Cutters of Keld Keep Keep It Over the Returned Arm}
\CRsheetheading{The Litany of the Second Cutting, Being the Order of the Return as the Number-Cutters of Keld Keep Keep It Over the Returned Arm}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A litany of the Return said at the shaft mouth over a man come back thin from the bank, before the old numbers are cut out of the forearm and the new cut in; the cutter reading from the arm and the order answering by number, with the rubrics of the Keep, nine stations and their answer, the silence of the Vorr left standing, a factor’s clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand, the margin of a woman cut twice, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the cutter of numbers at the Descent in Keld Keep, who has set two counts where her name would stand, the first cut at thirteen and the second after the bank, on the back of a survey sheet spoiled in the First Seam; carried down the Rim Road in Stone of Y.H. 812 with a lead cart, corrected at Greybank in Kindling of Y.H. 812 by a clerk of the factor’s office, and copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 into a quire kept in a tin at the shaft mouth. It survives with coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red cross from the mine-reeve’s point, a warm-stone shaving still warm in the fold, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead, a frost-feather pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves and gone by noon, a clamp-scratch across the answer, grey Ash on the outer fold, a thumb in coal dust nobody will own, the nine stations, one correction in Ledgerhand, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath\par}\medskip
I cut numbers at the Descent and cut them again at the mouth. The first knife is at thirteen; the second is after the bank, when a man comes back with the old figures still on him and wants a place he cannot name. I have set two counts where a name would stand, because here a man states what he holds before he says who he is, and I am not going to break that rule in my own hand. Which of the two I answer to depends on who is calling.

This is what we say over the returned arm. We do not say it to the man: said to a man it becomes a question, and there is no figure for a question at this mouth, so the question goes away unanswered and the figure stays. The clerk from Greybank has been at the leaf with his verbs taken out, and his hand stands above mine where he set it. The iron-red hand in the margin belongs to a woman cut twice who keeps both counts in one skin. I have left all of it standing, as the earlier numbers are left showing under the later ones.

\subsection*{The manner of it, cut small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Bare the arm before the words. A man who cannot speak can still state what he holds, and the arm does it for him.

\item Do not cut the old numbers out until the answer has been said. They came back with him. They have a claim, even if the bank has entered them closed.

\item Give the warm-stone after the knife and never before. A stone given before the knife is a bribe to the arm, and the arm remembers who bribed it.

\item Where a man carries two sets, cut the later deeper and leave the earlier showing. The mine-reeve enters the later. We cut both.

\item The Vorr come down from the Stones and do not answer. Leave the length of their silence standing. Do not put a nought in it; a nought is a number, and they have refused the number.

\item Say it to the arm, low, the way you would speak to a pot before you knock it. If an officer of the Court is at the mouth, give him the new count and not the leaf. He can enter a figure. He cannot enter an arm.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The litany}

\emph{The cutter reads from the arm. The order answers by number. The answer is the same at every station, which is why it is a litany and not an argument.}

\subsection*{I. Of the number before the name}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes on the arm before the name goes in the mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A lowlander gives his name and waits for us to ask the other thing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We send him back to the foot of the post to begin again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dark does not care what a man calls himself.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It cares what he carries into it.\end{quote}

\emph{Here I turn the arm so the figures stand up. Nobody looks at the face.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{II. Of the mountain}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Hearth is under this mountain, as our people say.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Court’s fire is a candle lit from it, they say, and say it softly.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man came up with a slate and took the word out of our sentence\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the sentence stood up without it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the kind of standing a slate likes.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the mine-reeve touches the iron-red cross on the post. Neither man looks at the other.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{III. Of the first knife}

\begin{quote}\itshape At thirteen the knife goes in and the numbers come up on the skin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The boy holds the stone after, never before.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He holds it and does not know what has been cut into him.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody tells him twice. A thing cut once is told.\end{quote}

\emph{The boy is not in the room. He is at the Descent, holding the stone, finding out what the knife gave.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{IV. Of the second cutting}

\begin{quote}\itshape He comes back with the old figures on him\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a want for a table he never sat at.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We cut the old ones out. The new ones go in deeper.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mine-reeve enters the later. We leave the earlier showing in the skin.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two sets on one arm is not two men.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It is one man counted twice, which the Court has always liked.\end{quote}
