\emph{Here I cut. There is no ceremony in it, only a small knife, a hand that does not shake, and the time the figures take to come right. The arm knows the knife. The man does not watch.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{V. Of the eleven months}

\begin{quote}\itshape A bought breath is entered at eleven months,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape whether he lasts them or not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure is for the life bought and not the life lived.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who lasts fourteen is entered at eleven and is not corrected.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not correct him either. We give him the stone.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the under-vessed man at the back of the order puts out his arm. His figure was bought before he came up. The figure is not his and the arm is.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{VI. Of the clamp}

\begin{quote}\itshape One iron holds and one iron takes. Here they are the same bite.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man who holds a clamp to his palm without flinching\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape is called honest, and this Keep is full of honest men with dead hands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Say the number over the hand. It has earned the saying.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the hand whether it was worth it. It will not tell you.\end{quote}

\emph{A man who held a clamp at the Warden’s test lays his palm on the board. We say the number over the hand and not over the man. The hand knows the difference.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{VII. Of the sweating}

\begin{quote}\itshape The mountain sweats in the deep.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The smell of hot lead gives whatever warning it gives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing was said in the Ninth Gallery that could be written down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man went down and the lead told him, and he came up or did not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What the lead tells is not entered. What the lead takes is entered by nobody.\end{quote}

\emph{I stop while the rope moves over the mouth. There is no saying for the deep that has not had a man in it. I have tried to write one and left the place the length of it.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{VIII. Of those who do not answer}

\begin{quote}\itshape Across the Rim they sit against the Stones and come away with numbers.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They do not come down to the knife and do not answer at the mouth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They say they were never owed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We have left the length of their silence standing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not fill it. A filled place is an entered place.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the order turns toward the Rim. At this station the answer is said by nobody. I say it once into the arm, which is not the same as having it answered, and close the space the length of a man sitting against a stone.}

\textbf{The order answers:} \emph{Nothing is said here. The place is kept.}

\subsection*{IX. Of the stone after}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone is given after the knife and stays warm longer than the man expects.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape He will get worse before he gets better. That is the rule here as everywhere.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape If he comes back wrong, keep him. Keep him anyway.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the stone what it kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It will tell you the weather and nothing else.\end{quote}

\emph{I put the warm-stone in the hand that has just been cut. It is the whole of the mercy and the whole of the theft. Somebody paid to have it warm, and the man holding it does not ask, which is the only courtesy the mountain has ever been shown.}

\textbf{The order answers:} Cut the number. Keep the hand. Do not ask the stone what it kept.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the factor’s office came up with the lead cart and borrowed the leaf at the mouth on a morning when the rope was going down and nobody had a hand to spare. He writes narrow and upright and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry past a weigh in his boot. He laid his hand on the leaf before he looked at me, which is the manner of that office.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the number goes on the arm before the name}, he wrote: \emph{vessel identified by measure at entry.} He has left the mouth out, and the mouth is where the number has to go before anybody will hear it.

\item Against \emph{the Hearth is under this mountain}, he wrote: \emph{claim not admitted; the Hearth is entered under the Keel.} He has not argued with the mountain. He has entered somewhere else and gone away.

\item Against \emph{we leave the earlier showing in the skin}, he wrote: \emph{superseded entry retained, not current.} True in the figure. I have seen a man with two sets on one arm and both hands answered when his mother called, and there is no figure for that in a counting house.

\item Against \emph{two sets is not two men}, he wrote: \emph{duplicate entry. One to be struck.} He strikes men readily. The skin does not agree with him and has never been asked.

\item At the eighth station he put a round nought in the space and wrote \emph{no return required}. This is the truest thing he has written and the cruelest. A nought is a number. They refused the number. I have left his nought standing in the space and my space standing around it, as a crack is left showing under a keying.

\end{itemize}

I have left all of it standing, his hand above mine and mine under it, as an arm keeps the first figures under the second. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a man at the mouth wants to know which hand to hold out.

\subsection*{What the other hand put in the margin}

The iron-red hand is Nessa’s, of the Duelling Floor, cut at thirteen and cut again after the bank, who keeps both counts and has never said which she answers to when somebody calls across a room.

At IV: “My second was cut deeper and I still turn to the first when my mother calls. The mine-reeve entered the deeper. Both hands turned. I have never known which one she was calling to.”

At V: “My brother was entered at eleven and lasted fourteen. On the last morning he asked for the stone and they gave him the figures. I have set this here and not in the stations, because the stations are said over an arm and this is said over a man.”

At VI: “My father held the clamp and was called honest. He ate with the other hand for nine years and never once said the word they used of him.”

At VIII, against \emph{they were never owed}: “I asked one of them at the Stones whether they were cold. He asked me whether I had ever been cut. I did not ask him anything else.”

At the answer: “Say it over the hands. The rest of us are standing here and can hear.”

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is mine; I hold the leaf down with the hand I cut with and do not know I have marked it, and coal gets into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The red cross is iron oxide off the mine-reeve’s point and stays red in frost. The warm-stone shaving in the fold came off a piece set down and not taken up, and is still warm on the coldest morning, which is the whole argument about where warmth comes from and who paid. The lead bead rolled out of the Ninth Gallery and a surveyor laid it on the leaf and went away without it. The frost-feather grew on the survey stone after a warm night and was gone by noon. The clamp-scratch across the answer was made by a man showing his brother how a clamp bites; both were called honest afterwards and one has a dead hand. The grey on the outer fold came off a cuff that lay where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. The thumb in coal dust at the foot is not mine and not the mine-reeve’s. There is no Last Day at a shaft mouth.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not Nessa’s, struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape The knife gives before the bank takes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm keeps two counts. The slate keeps one. The stone keeps none, and is warm.\end{quote}

I asked the cutter at the Descent, a woman cut twice, a man entered at eleven who lasted fourteen, and one of the Vorr at the Stones, who answered me with a question, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the tin at the mouth. Tomorrow a boy will go down at thirteen and hold the stone after the knife, and a man come back thin will hold out his arm, and the old numbers will be cut out and the new cut in deeper, and the mine-reeve will enter the later and leave the earlier showing in the skin, and I shall say nine stations to the arm and keep the eighth place the length of a man sitting against a stone.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{A Letter from the Counting House at Greybank to the Ember Bowl in the Bowl of Sere, Concerning the Price of Northern Measures, the Forty That Are Not Found but Made, a Beautiful Return That Would Not Hold a Cup, and the Shape a House Must Buy; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Rowing Song from the Pulled Benches}
\CRsheetheading{A Letter from the Counting House at Greybank to the Ember Bowl in the Bowl of Sere, Concerning the Price of Northern Measures, the Forty That Are Not Found but Made, a Beautiful Return That Would Not Hold a Cup, and the Shape a House Must Buy; with the Answer in the Margin, a Correction in Ledgerhand, and a Rowing Song from the Pulled Benches}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A merchant’s letter in iron-gall on the back of a barley tally spoiled by damp, folded thrice and sealed with a thumb of red lead-glaze; carried south from Greybank by a grain factor’s clerk as far as the Peat Line and from there by a carrier of eels to the Bowl of Sere; answered in the recipient’s hand along the gutter, corrected on the outer fold at the Council room in Vhal, and kept since in the Ember house’s box of southern contracts · Written at the Sere counting house in Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, in the last tend of Grain, Y.H. 813, by Corven Dells, a factor’s under-clerk who buys northern measures for the Ten Bowls, to Ovia Gilded, keeper of the bowls in House Ember at the Bowl of Sere; answered in her hand in the gutter, borrowed at Vhal by a factor’s clerk who could not let paper lie, and returned to the box of contracts in the Bowl. It survives with barley dust worked into the head and the gutter, a round wine ring the width of a cup, a thumb of red seal at the outer fold that comes away on the finger, a pale tideline of salt along the lower margin, one figure gone over in the damp and written again underneath, an answer in a sloping southern hand, one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College, a round nought set in the place of a missing oar, and a line at the foot that nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
To Ovia Gilded, keeper of the bowls in the House Ember at the Bowl of Sere, from Corven Dells at the counting house in Greybank. Written on the back of a barley tally that spoiled in the damp and was given to me for nothing, which is the only paper in this house that has not already been told what to say.

I write in the southern hand because a northern one would be taken for a petition, and a petition in this country is a thing a man spends a mark to have lost. The damp got at the tally and took two figures clean off it. In Vhal that would be called a mercy and here it is called a waste of good paper. I have written over them. A figure that has gone soft is not a figure that has been forgiven; it is a figure with the number rubbed out and the debt standing all the same. Do not wet the fold. The seal is red lead and comes off on the thumb.

You write asking for a whole return before the first Frost, with the memory kept and the shape whole enough to be shown at a feast. I answer plainly, because the courtesy we use at this end of the trade is a courtesy with a bill inside it. It can be done. Twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures, as the Court books them; the marks go north to a household and the measures go south in a cradle, and nobody at this counter has ever seen the two things arrive at the same door. Your house wants remembering. What the north has to sell is remembering. That is the whole of our trade, and there is not a kind word in it that has not been priced.

The district is walking thin. The levy in Low Kiln is one in three and the notice in the Court room says one in twelve; I stood under the notice at the Cross last Account-day and heard the figure read twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for those who came late, and I know a figure read aloud is not the figure paid. I could not tell you which of the two goes into your cradle. That is not my department. In my department we write down what the Court gives us and do not ask the slate where it has been.

\subsection*{The measure as it comes to us, set against what goes south}

In the district — On the collector’s slate — In our letter to the Bowl — In the cradle\par

A widow of the lower bank. Two loaves — one in twelve — a whole measure, freely returned — the shape of a woman who wanted something\par

A glaze-room girl, sweet at the mouth — one mark, current — a vessel of good remembering — a mouth that turns toward the cup before the cup is shown\par

A clay-bound hand, term served out — term, not measure — a measure, term fulfilled — a hand that has forgotten the trade but not the reach\par

Six and twenty of the lower yard, by lot — one line for the batch — forty measures, purchased — forty, and no name among them\par

A man found in the yard at morning, no figure taken — not entered — nothing — nothing, and the slate shut\par

I keep the four columns apart because a man in a counting house can forget what a cradle is for if he writes the four in one line. The College would put them in one line. A College clerk borrowed this very leaf before it went south and put them in one line and took the verbs out of the whole of it, and I have set the verbs back underneath and left his line standing above, so that both may be read and neither mistaken for the other.

You ask why forty. I asked the same of a man who had stood at this counter longer than I had been alive, and he said \emph{because the account requires it}, which is a phrase that means \emph{because we have decided it}. A whole return wants one vessel that holds and remembers; it wants forty measures that will never be a vessel at all, that go into the account and stay there and are called unspent. They are not found in this district, lady. They are made. There are households below the sill with nothing left in them but the breathing, and out of those households the forty come, one line on a slate and a hand at a wrist that leaves a pale ring the neighbours call weather. I have written \emph{made} here and I will not strike it out. The borrowed hand above has written \emph{were banked}, which is true in the way a butcher’s floor is true.

\subsection*{The song the pulled benches keep}

\emph{Sung by the condemned at the oars of the salt galleys out of Vhal, to the stroke; put down here because it is the only account in this trade that counts the rower. The last line is said twice, the second time for the man whose hands give out before the seven years.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the clay and one for the chalk,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the hand that the salt took;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pull and the measure goes over the side,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pull and the measure stays inside.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four on the bench and four on the shore,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place where the fifth oar was before;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven years is a long, lean tide ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the lamp goes out and the hands abide.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We carry the warm that we never kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we row the road that the slate has cut;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the bowl what it wants of us ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it wants the shape, and it wants it shut.\end{quote}

You ask in the same hand after a fourth pouring for the woman of the green bowl, who was shown in that year and twice before, and you ask whether the shape will remember. I have seen the shape. It holds wine and does not spill, and it has not spilled at three feasts, and the applause for it is the cleanest applause in the empire because nobody in the room has to believe it. Whether there is anybody inside it on the third day is a question for your bowl-surgeons, not for a clerk at this counter. We can send the forty. We cannot send the wanting. That is the one part of the order the north cannot fill, and it is the part your house is buying.

\subsection*{In the gutter, in her hand, set close and small}

\emph{She writes on the diagonal, as the bowls write when they are crossed, and uses the plural of houses even where a single woman must have stood at the writing.}

We emptied the bowl on the first night of Grain and the debt-slates were burned by lot and new ones made, as you know, having once been at a feast in this room and applauded with the rest. Your four columns amuse me. We do not keep accounts of that kind here; we keep the bowl and the applause and the shape that comes back. Send the forty and send the cradle. As for the wanting, my house has never found it in the north, though we have bought north for nine generations and have had good value out of every district.

\emph{Below, in the same hand, a line she did not cross out:}

You were asked at sixteen what debt you meant to carry. I am asking you the same thing now, in a letter, because a debt named in a room is applauded and a debt named on paper has to be paid. Answer me on the back and not in the gutter, where the salt has got into everything.

\subsection*{What the clerk did at the Council room in Vhal}

A factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf in the tar-smelling room where the Council writes its decrees on salt-paper that goes soft in the rain and calls the softening a virtue. He writes in the narrow upright hand, with the verbs taken out and everything in the passive, as they teach it at the College and as the Council pretends not to need. Against \emph{they are made} he set \emph{forty unspent measures were banked}, and under that \emph{were lawfully purchased}, and underlined it twice. Against the rowing song he wrote \emph{no cost entered}, which is the neatest thing I have ever seen done to nine lines of a song. Against the woman of the green bowl he set \emph{a beautiful return, third pouring}, struck out \emph{wanting} wherever it stood, and wrote \emph{no want recorded} above it, because a thing a house has bought cannot be wanting. Where I left the place of the fifth oar he put a round nought and wrote \emph{nil} beneath it.

I have put my verbs back underneath and left his figures standing over them. He is right in the language he writes. In the language of the benches a nought is not a place where an oar was.

\subsection*{At the head and in the fold}

The barley dust at the head came off the tally when I turned it over, and there is more of it in the gutter than there should be, mixed now with her sloping hand, which is a thing I cannot separate and would not if I could. The round ring is wine from the feast at which the woman of the green bowl was shown, or from another feast; I did not mark which and will not guess at it. The red at the outer fold is the seal, lead and something else, and it comes away on the thumb with a sweetish taste if a man is fool enough to touch his tongue to it, which I have not done and the clerk from the College did, and was sick behind the tar-room door while the Council went on with its counting. The pale line along the lower margin is not the Ash, whatever a northerner would call it; it is the salt that gets into everything in this coast country, and I have not brushed it off. There is no Last Day on this counter. Paper goes into the box and the box goes south, and nobody burns it in the morning and calls it dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The north counts what it lost. The south counts what it kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bowl goes round and the account stays open.\end{quote}

I asked a factor, a clerk who cannot let paper lie, and a woman who rowed the pulled benches and now sells eels at the Peat Line, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the box of southern contracts. In the morning the grain goes south by the Peat Line and a tally goes up to the factor’s table, and the forty go where they go, which is not a place I have ever been allowed to name. Tomorrow another household below the sill will find it has had a good year and that the account has stood. That is the whole of the letter, and it goes on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Mercy Telling at Mud End, Being Six Stories Spoken on the Long Night in the Peat Byre, the One Told to the Floor, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Dead}
\CRsheetheading{The Mercy Telling at Mud End, Being Six Stories Spoken on the Long Night in the Peat Byre, the One Told to the Floor, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Dead}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A byre-keeper’s record of a winter telling, set down for the settling of which death was called merciful and not for the comfort of the reader; the rules in the hand the byre keeps, the stories in the words they were spoken, a score in peat-blocks on the trodden floor, the figures of a factor’s clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written on the Long Night of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the peat byre at Mud End three leagues downriver of Sill, by the woman who keeps the byre where the moot sits when the peat is too wet to stand on; copied out in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled winter-peat tally, folded into oiled sacking and kept in a wall-niche behind the peat-stack under a flat stone. It survives with a peat thumb at the head, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, a small ale ring, a grey Ash print along the gutter, frost-crisp at one edge, one sheep’s-wool fibre off the Tallow road, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the byre at Mud End where the moot sits in winter. There is a fire until dusk and none after, because this is the Long Night and the Keeping says a man may tell the Return in the dark and be heard the better for it. I have kept this byre eleven winters and I have never once seen anybody hear better in the dark. They hear the same. They hear it with nothing to look at, which is a different thing.

We hold the mercy-telling on this night. A person tells of a death the hamlet called merciful --- one that went quietly, where nobody had to be sent for and no collector came up from Greybank for it --- and the teller must give the dead one’s name. A story that keeps its name gets a peat-block set on the floor. A story that lets a figure into it gets nothing, and the teller owes a peat to the winter stack, which is the only fine this byre knows and the only one anybody pays without an argument. I do not say why a story served. A reason given is a story given away, and a person who has told one well can go home and sell it in Sill.

The moot meets here because the bog takes a man’s weight in Silt and his boots in Stone, and there is no dry room between us and the river but this one. Nine houses and their peat stacks, and one byre with a floor packed hard as old bread. On the Long Night the floor is the book. Nothing is written in it that a clerk can carry off, and in the morning I tread the blocks into the ash and there is no score left, which is the point of a byre and the difference between a byre and Slate Row.

\subsection*{The rules, as the byre keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Tell once. A story told twice is a different story and is not heard; the second telling is for the teller and he may pay for it himself.

\item Give a name. A figure is not a name. A figure travels; a name stays in the room where the person said it.

\item Four blocks lie in a row and a fifth lies by the wall. The fifth is not a prize and is not the best story’s block. It is for the one the year took and nobody in these nine houses could tell.

\item No fire after dusk. The last coal is banked before the first voice. A story told by firelight counts for nothing, being a story told twice --- once to the living and once to the coal.

\item Say it to the floor, the door, or the pot. Said looking at a person it becomes an argument, and there is enough argument in Mud End over the winter peat without bringing the dead into it.

\item The byre judges. I say whether a name was kept and I do not say which name I wanted.

\end{enumerate}

Before the first voice we sing the short song, standing, with our hands on the byre wall because it is the only warm thing in the room by then.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four blocks for the four that went quietly,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a fifth by the wall for the one not told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the peat keeps warm what the peat has held,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name goes round while the figure goes cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Tell it to the floor, tell it to the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tell it to the place where the fifth would stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk writes one and the house writes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and both go down in the same dry hand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The four that were told}

\textbf{Vey}, said the widow who cuts peat on the west bank. She said it to the pot. Her man went out after the frost with a spade and sat down in the cut and did not stand up again, and the district called it merciful because nobody had to go looking and no slate went up to Sill over it. She said his name three times, once for the byre, once for the floor, and once for the cut he sat in, and would not let me set a figure against it. “He’s Vey,” she said. “That’s the whole of it. A number’s what you write when you’ve lost the person.” She took her peat-block and went and stood by the door until the next story, which is how a widow stands in this hamlet.

The second was put by a woman come over from Cold Acre, where the well never freezes. She told of a child returned thin in the year of the flower, come back to a house where three had gone into the measure and the house could not say which of the three had come home. The child was quiet and wanted nothing and grew no shape, and the house called it merciful because it asked for no warmth and so cost nobody. She did not give the child’s name. She gave the name of the woman who kept it, said low into the pot, and said the child’s name was not for a byre where a clerk had been known to lean in the door. I set a block for the keeper’s name and none for the child’s, and we left it so. A name kept in one house is still a name kept.

The cooper told the third. He is the man the hamlet means when it says a cooper’s seventh, though he has never explained the seventh to anybody and gives a different date for it every time he is asked, which is a way of answering that costs him nothing. He told of the man they called merciful who slept before a banked kiln with the damper shut and did not wake, and he told it to the floor with his cap in his hand. “Merciful is the word the district used,” he said. “His name was Ansel. You can have the one or the other, but not both, and I’ll have the name.” There was a silence after that, the kind that has four in it and a gap where the fifth would be, and the bell from Sill came across the frozen fields four, four and a gap, and nobody crossed himself. I set the block. Ansel’s name went round the byre and came back to the cooper, and the figure never arrived.

The fourth I put myself, because the room had grown too quiet and a story put by the byre is not scored against anybody. I told of the year’s fire that comes up in a clay dish before light, house to house, each hearth touching its own flame to it, and the last house keeping what is left. There was a woman in this row who took the dish in and did not pass it on, and her house was warm all that winter and she went cold in the spring, and the hamlet called her merciful because she went in her sleep and nobody had to tell her the fire was spent. I did not say where the coal came from. She did not say either. That is the part we call merciful, or the part next to it. I set no block for my own story, because a byre that scores itself will soon be a Court, and I have seen how those rooms go.

\subsection*{The fifth by the wall}

The fifth block lay by the wall all night and nobody moved it. A girl from the Tallow road, who had come in with wool on her sleeves and stayed silent, put her hand toward it twice and took it back, and I have not written which girl, because she would stop coming if I did. In the morning there was a small grey print of Ash where the block had lain, the colour of the ridge that gathers where a promise is not kept, and I trod it in with the rest of the floor and called it the thaw, as we call everything in this hamlet that we do not want to name. The fifth was not a story that failed. It was the year’s taking that nobody in nine houses could put a name to, and a thing left in place is still a thing kept.

\subsection*{The score, in peat-blocks on the floor}

Story — Told by — Name kept — Block\par

The cut in the bog — Vey’s widow — Vey, said three times — set, paid\par

The thin child — Cold Acre woman — the keeper’s name only — set, child’s name not given\par

The banked kiln — the cooper — Ansel — set, figure refused\par

The dish not passed on — the byre — none; byre does not score — not scored\par

The year’s taking — nobody — none — by the wall, not moved\par

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat borrowed the leaf on a morning when the stacks were being measured and his cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He set the four tellings down as \emph{four merciful returns entered, nil deduction}, and put a figure of marks against each of the three names, which was more than the byre had scored, because the byre scores in whether a name comes back out of the room and he does not.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{he’s Vey, that’s the whole of it}, he wrote \emph{one life surrendered without claim}.

\item At the thin child he wrote \emph{third party unidentifiable; vacancy}, and put a round nought in the place where the child’s name would have stood.

\item Against \emph{his name was Ansel}, he struck the name and set above it \emph{the measure was voluntarily resigned}, and underlined it twice.

\item At the year’s fire he wrote \emph{the warmth was transferred by consent}, which is a true thing in a language nobody in this byre speaks. Consent of whom he did not write, and I have not asked him.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way the floor keeps a peat-block under a spilled quart. He has entered four and struck a name and numbered the empty place; I have kept three names and a place that is not a number. Both hands are on the leaf. Both will travel, his further than mine, which is the whole trouble with writing.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat thumb at the head is mine; I held the leaf down on the byre wall in the draught that comes under the door and did not know I had marked it. Peat goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the moot uses it to sign. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the girl from the Tallow road when she leaned over to see what the clerk had written; the sheep’s-wool fibre caught in the fold is off the same coat, and I have left it where it fell. The small ale ring is from a quart that stood from the first voice to the fifth and was drunk by nobody, which is how a quart usually goes in Mud End. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business in the corner where I keep the leaf, and I have not swept it. The frost-crisp at one edge is from the morning the leaf went out to be copied and was left under a stone too short for it; the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The block by the wall was never set. The Ash came where it stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four names went home. The fifth stayed where the year put it.\end{quote}

I asked the widow, the cooper and the girl from the Tallow road, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the sacking and under the stone, and the blocks go into the floor with the heel of a boot, and the byre is swept for the next moot as if nothing had been told in it. If the clerk comes again with his pen I shall give him the verbs to take out and keep the names underneath, as I did this year. On the next Long Night the fire will go out at dusk and the dark will come in, and I shall set four blocks in a row and one by the wall, and let whoever has a name to keep come in out of the cold and say it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Milk Sea, Being an Account of Vhalen and the Sallow Coast, Set Down by an Eel-Man of the Fishstairs Who Went Up the Salt Road with Smoked Eels and Coarse Pots and Came Back with Salt, Glass, and a Rope That Would Not Rot}
\CRsheetheading{The Milk Sea, Being an Account of Vhalen and the Sallow Coast, Set Down by an Eel-Man of the Fishstairs Who Went Up the Salt Road with Smoked Eels and Coarse Pots and Came Back with Salt, Glass, and a Rope That Would Not Rot}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A river-man’s travel account, set down first on the backs of dried eel-sacks and copied forward on the back of a spoiled Court salt warrant; part road-log, part inventory, part complaint, with the figure of a Council tally-clerk set in the margin, the verbs put back underneath in the writer’s own charcoal hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Quay in Vhal in the last tend of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by a man of the Fishstairs in Sill who went up the Salt Road in Stone of Y.H. 812 with two baskets of smoked eels, a cart of coarse ware from Nine Pots and two bales of wool, and came back at the turn of the year with a sack of salt, a bottle of cliff-glass, a coil of tarred rope and a silver mark that had been counted so often it had gone thin at the edge. Set down on the backs of eel-sacks, copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court salt warrant spoiled by the damp, sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sailcloth and carried upriver in a clay tube stoppered with wool. It survives with a white salt bloom in the gutter, a thumb of tar at the head, a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the second fold, a fish-hook nick, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a ring of warm wine near the song, a rope-burn along the outer edge, a grey Ash print nobody will own, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk, the writer’s charcoal words restored beneath it, and a line at the foot in a hand that answers to no name\par}\medskip
I am a man of the Fishstairs. I sell eels at dawn and know a river the way a potter knows a wheel: by the feel under the hand and the sound it makes when going wrong. In Stone of last year I took two baskets of smoked eel, a cart of coarse pots and two bales of wool up the Salt Road, and came back at the turn of the year with salt, a glass bottle, a rope and a mark gone thin at the edge. Where I wrote one thing and saw another I have left both standing. A river-man can do that. A clerk cannot.

\subsection*{The road up}

The Salt Road runs eighty leagues through Greybank and the coast pass. I went with a cart and came back with a cart, which is more than some do. At Greybank the Court’s granaries stand so tall that a man from the Fishstairs looks at them the way he looks at the falls: as a thing that will be cold and loud and go on without him. Past the pass the clay gives out. The road goes hard and white and the smell of wet wool goes out of it and the smell of salt comes in, and I have never got used to the exchange.

At the last stage I asked a man walking down what the sea was like. He said, \emph{Which tide?} I said, \emph{The sea.} He said there was no such thing in Vhal, only the one going out and the one coming in, and that a man who called them the same had never owned a boat. I did not tell him I had never owned one. He would have asked my account next, and there the question is not rudeness.

\subsection*{The milk sea}

They call it the Sallow. It is the colour of skimmed milk gone yellow at the edge, and cold in a way I had not met in the Ilm. The Ilm goes one way; a man of Sill can stand on the north bridge and watch his spit go downriver, and all his life that has been the arrangement. The Sallow will not do it. The tide comes in against the wind and goes out against the wind again, and a man new to it stands on the Quay with his coat blowing one way and the water the other and feels something go loose in him he had not known was tied. They say the tides follow the Warm and not the moon. I asked a dipper what the moon was for and he said the moon was for the fish, which may be true and is not an answer.

There is a thing in the water called a salt-thing. It taps the hull from under and draws the boat’s store away while the boat goes on looking the same. A man finds his warm gone and no hole in him to show where it went. In Sill we would call that a leak and put a hand over it. Here they write it in a tally and go on sailing.

\subsection*{What they write on}

Everything in Vhal is written on salt-paper, which is paper made to rot. A Council clerk told me this with a straight face and a cuff soft from washing. In the damp a contract goes soft and the writing comes up in pale islands, and the Council calls it a virtue, because a law that lasts too long has stopped earning. In Sill a thing left in the rain is spoiled. Here it is made nothing, which they hold a cleaner end. I have set the two side by side instead, the way our yard sets two figures on the heap of turnips without making them agree.

I kept a tally of my own on the back of a warrant the Court had spoiled. This is the account as I wrote it, and the Council clerk’s figure as he set it above.

What I took up — What I set down at the Quay — What I brought back — What the clerk entered\par

Two baskets smoked eel — sold before the third hour, at a figure I did not ask twice — one sack of salt, coarse, with the bloom on it — dried fish, current rate\par

Cart of coarse ware, Nine Pots — three pots cracked in the frost on the road, entered as broken — one bottle of cliff-glass, green at the lip — glass, as entered\par

Two bales of wool — paid in a silver mark, counted four times in my sight — a coil of tarred rope, which I have had six months and will not rot — wool at the crown rate\par

— — a tally-clerk read the draw against the contract; the contract had gone soft — one mark, thin at the edge — the figure is current\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, above the wool row:} Wool entered at the crown rate. The figure is current. The warmth was retained in the pens and transferred against the contract.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in my charcoal:} I carried the wool. They counted it in a room that smelled of tar and I stood in the doorway with my wet boots on the boards. A sentence with nobody in it travels well and arrives empty, which is what they want of a sentence here. I have put myself back in front of mine. The mark went thin because four men counted it and each took a little off the edge with his thumb. That is not a rate. That is four thumbs.\end{quote}

The Council room smells of tar and wet rope. The Council of Tides is elected by ship-owners and salt-masters for a year, and its decrees are written on paper that will not outlast the season, which is thought a good arrangement by anyone who has wanted to deny one. In the tide-tally house a man named Kett reads the draws against the contracts. A sheet left in the damp is a debt made nothing. I saw a man come in with a folded paper and go out with nothing in his hand, and lighter in the face too. Whether the paper freed him or only made him forget, I could not ask.

\subsection*{The dippers and the draw}

At dawn the dippers trail the nets and bless them and read the Sallow draw, which is the current of Warm going seaward, taxed by the Court and prayed over by the dippers, running against the wind as a matter of course. I stood at the pans before light and watched a dipper pull up a net and say a number, and the pan-master write it down and go on with his counting. Nobody thanked the water or the dipper. Here a man does a thing, the thing is entered, and that is the end of the conversation.

The salt-women at the pans sing while they rake. I asked one what the song was for and she said it was for keeping the count, and I asked what count, and she said that was the count the Court did not take, which is the nearest thing to an answer I got in eighty leagues. I have set the words down as she sang them, with the ends of the words let fall the way they let them fall.

\begin{quote}\itshape We rake at the fourth and the crust comes thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the gull takes a coal and the clerk takes a name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tide goes out where the wind comes in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the warm goes seaward all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the pans and one for the draw,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a place on the leaf where the ink won’t stay;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the paper keeps is the paper’s law,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what the water keeps, the water takes away.\end{quote}

She would not sing the last line while a man from the Council stood on the quay. That is how I knew it was the line that mattered.

\subsection*{Boats, shares and the half voice}

Boat shares pass through mothers in Vhal. A man who marries into a boat-owning family is said to be come aboard, and his opinion on the boat is counted at half. I asked a salt-wife whether a half opinion kept a man from being wrong; she said it kept him from being believed, which she said was a better thing. There is no word in Vhaleni for a guest or a friend, only for a man whose account is current. I was current for nine days. On the tenth I went up the road, which I think was why they were so pleasant to me on the ninth.

They say a stranger’s coin warms before his face. I put a copper bit on the counter my first morning and the woman looked at the coin and then at me, in that order, and I understood I had been read wrong and would spend the morning putting myself right. In Sill a woman looks at the face first and the coin after, which is a better custom and a poorer country.

The young walk the pans barefoot at low tide at fourteen and name a tide they have never seen. I watched a girl come in off the pans with her feet white and her head high, and an old woman ask what she had named it, and the girl tell her, and the old woman say nothing but take the girl’s hand, which was the only warmth I saw given freely in that town.

\subsection*{The pulled benches}

Condemned men row the salt galleys for seven years, or until their hands give out, whichever comes first. A Vhaleni hull is never long from the oars. I saw them at the pulled benches with their hands on the wood. I have not put down what I felt, only what I saw: seven years counted in advance and a man’s hands counted after.

Slaves may be bought in Vhal but may not be returned there. The Council will not pay for a thin return and will not house one. A man from Greybank asked a clerk what became of a bought person who died, and the clerk said the contract had ended, a sentence with the person taken clean out of it. I have set both down. In Sill we return a man thin to the district and the district pays thirty marks and goes on. Here they will not even pay. It is not kindness. It is a contract with the last line left out.

\subsection*{The cliffs and the glass}

The Glaze Cliffs stand a few leagues along the coast, blue-green with old lead, and smell faintly sweet in the heat. Children are told not to lick them. The furnaces take sand and lead and melt them into glass sold as far as Sere, and the women who work them rub their gums with the cliff and say sweetness answers sweetness, and their hands go slowly and they blame the cup. My mother tastes the glaze at the rim of every pot before it leaves our yard and will not say what she has tasted. I said nothing to the glass women.

The bottle I brought back is green at the lip. I keep it where the light comes in and have not entered it. The clerk at Greybank wanted a figure against it; I told him it was a bottle, and he wrote \emph{glass, as entered} above my words and left mine standing underneath.

\subsection*{What I brought back}

The rope has lasted six months in the wet and will last another six. In the Clay Yard a rope rots in a season and nobody is surprised. I keep it coiled by the door and touch it now and then with the back of the fingers the way a potter touches a pot come well from the fire. It is a thing that does not rot, and somebody paid to have it last, and I do not know who, and have stopped asking. The salt went on the eels. The mark is thin at the edge and will not change at the Cross; I keep it because I cannot spend it. The bottle stands in the light.

The eels went on being sold over the top of it all when I got back, and the Ilm went one way under the north bridge, and nobody asked me what the tide was like, which is the proper order of things and costs nothing.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom in the gutter came up out of the paper itself and I have not brushed it off. The tar at the head is mine, off the coil I carried in my coat. The green bead in the second fold is cliff-glass; a girl pressed it in with her thumb while I was writing and had the sweetness at her mouth and said nothing. Do not rub it, the edge will take you. The fish-hook nick came off a man paying me for eels with the hook still in his hand. The peck-hole is a brine-gull’s; he took the leaf for a crust and I took it back with one word gone clean through, and I have not written the word in again, because a word with a hole in it is a word said through the teeth, which is how a great deal was said in that country. The wine-ring near the song is small and belongs to the third hour. The rope-burn along the edge is where the coil lay against the leaf on the road up. The grey print nobody will own came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in Vhal and nothing anywhere gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape I went up with a river and came back with a sea.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river has one direction and the sea has two.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The debt was entered. The thumb was not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the rope what it kept, and the bottle what it held.\end{quote}

I asked the dipper, the tally-clerk and a woman at the pans, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. Tomorrow the eels will go on being sold at dawn and the Ilm will go the one way it has always gone, and I will not say which of the two I trust more, because a man who says it has begun to choose, and choosing is a thing the Court can enter against him.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Mixing Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Glaze-Mixers of High Kiln for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Glaze Room of House Clay, with the Years Set in a Table, the Tally of Hands, the Mixing-Song Pasted Inside the Lid, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Mixing Bench, Being the Standing Rules of the Glaze-Mixers of High Kiln for the Taking, Keeping and Trying of Apprentices at the Glaze Room of House Clay, with the Years Set in a Table, the Tally of Hands, the Mixing-Song Pasted Inside the Lid, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bench-copy of the room’s standing rules in the hand of the woman who keeps the mixing bench and the tasting-spoons; the rules in the short sayings of the terrace, the years and the faults in tables, the mixing-song pasted to the inside of the jar-lid, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk, one line struck in charcoal by a mixer who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed · First gathered at High Kiln in Y.H. 691, the year the house entered the sweet sickness in its own account and then wrote the word out of it again, and copied forward from the bench and the tasting-spoons and not from a book; this leaf written in Grain of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by the woman who has kept the mixing bench and the spoons for nineteen years, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813. It survives folded in a grey cloth under the jar that stands cold under its glaze, with the sweet green of lead glaze worked into the grain at the head and into the creases of the writer’s thumb, a white crust of dried slip at the fold, the sweetish edge of the mix still in the paper after a year, a ring where a tasting-cup of barley-water stood from one question to the next, a green bead pressed into the second fold by a girl with sweetness still at her mouth, a thumb of tallow, a grey print along the outer fold that is not hers and that she has not swept, two corrections in the Court’s upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again beneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the mixing bench and the tasting-spoons in the Glaze Room above Low Kiln. A woman from a house brings a girl and goes back down the terrace; the girl stays with the mix. A kiln-hand comes up with a pot gone wrong and asks what was put on it, and I tell him what went into the dish and not what it cost, because the cost is not in this room. There is a clay jar on the wall that is cold under its glaze and has been cold since before I came to the bench; nobody opens it and nobody says what it held. I set the rules down as they stand. Where a hand has corrected me I have left both readings.

They are not new rules. They were gathered in the year the house set the sweet sickness into its own account and then wrote the word out of it again, which is the way this trade has of keeping a thing and not having it read. A rule with no green on it is a rule nobody has had to taste. These have been tasted.

\subsection*{The articles as they stand on the bench}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The room takes a girl, not a house. A house may bring her and feed her and have her back at the end with a trade in her hands; from the day she first dips a spoon the room answers for what she mixes. A house that will not give her up for the years has given nothing.

\item She is taken at nine, or at ten if her house has kept her through a winter of sickness. Not before. A girl who cannot carry a dish of slip across the room and set it down without a rim of it on her sleeve has no business at the mix; she will spend the glaze on her clothes and call it the pot’s.

\item Her name is said once at the taking and kept in the mouth afterward, the way a heat-name is kept at a furnace. A name in the mouth cannot be entered, and there is nothing in this country the Court has not tried to enter.

\item She is kept, not hired. She eats from the room’s dish and sleeps under the room’s roof. What the room makes goes into the house’s pots and comes back to her as bread and a place at the bench, neither of which is written down. A mixer who tells a girl she is paid tells a true thing about a figure and a false thing about a living.

\item No girl is asked whether she wants the sweetness. She is asked whether she understands what is carried: a dish of lead, a spoon, a pale line that comes up where a person can see it, and the habit that grows in the mouth before the line does. The wanting comes after, or it does not come.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the lead and the tasting}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The lead comes up the Clay Road in a cask that the factor’s clerk does not open and does not ask to. It is blue-grey and sweet in the mix. A girl who has once tasted the dish will ask to taste it again, and that is the whole of the answer; send her back to the slip and let the slip be boring.

\item No child tastes the mix. The mixer tastes, with the side of the thumb and the back of the tongue, and spits it into the slop-pail. The pale line at the gum is lead and not a mark of industry. A mixer who calls it a good sign is selling the girl’s teeth one at a time and calling it a living.

\item A girl who rubs her gum with a green bead and says sweetness answers sweetness is not to be argued with before the young. Take the bead away, give her barley-water, and let the lead be the one that is paid. We do not say kindly in a Glaze Room; a kindness there is a debt with no date.

\item The slip is stirred down and the lead is stirred in, and the dish is covered between stirrings. A dish left open takes a skin, and a skin taken off a dish and put on a pot is a flaw that no knuckle will find and no firing will burn clean. Leave the skin where it formed; tell the pot nothing about it.

\item A pot is dipped and set up rim-down on the rack, and the rack is not crowded to make the day come out even. A crowded rack gives a thin coat, and a thin coat is a lie told in lead, which is the only lie a kiln cannot burn away.

\item The green at the mouth is entered as an occupational mark and no deduction arises. This is the house’s phrase and not mine. I have set what it is underneath it, where a clerk may see it and choose not to read it.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Struck hard in charcoal against rule 11, in a mixer’s hand that did not sign, and written again underneath:} It is lead. It is paid out of the mouth. \emph{Above it, heavier, the same hand:} No. It is paid out of the hand. I have left both strikes standing, one over the other, because a girl who has stood at this bench knows which of them is true and does not need me to choose for her.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The years at the dish}

\emph{Kept on the bench. What is written is the work that came up, in a hand that does not change between one line and the next.}

Year — At the bench — What is taken\par

First — Carry slip, wash the dishes, sweep, hold the spoon while the mixer tastes — The girl’s own hand, which learns to keep the spoon level\par

Second — Stir the lead in, skim nothing, dip under the mixer’s eye — The habit of asking what the glaze ought to be\par

Third — Cover the dish, tend the rack, name the coat on a cup with the green still at her mouth — The belief that a thing dipped is a thing done\par

Fourth — Taste the mix once, with the side of the thumb, and spit it out — The last of a girl’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Four years is the common end of a mixing and not a short one. A girl who has been through them is not paid out and sent down the terrace; she stays where the pots need her. The mixer does not choose where. The pot does, and the house after it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The tally of hands}

\emph{Kept by the bench. The figure is the house’s and is set first. What stands beneath it is mine and is not a figure.}

Condition — The house’s figure — What stands beneath\par

Girl taken at nine — one apprentice, current, no wage arising — A child who eats from the dish\par

First green at the mouth — occupational mark; no deduction arises — Lead. Paid out of the mouth.\par

A hand that will not keep the spoon level — one hand, current; measure not affected — The spoon taken from that hand; the hand kept\par

A pot dipped thin — not entered — A cup in a house we have not seen, that comes apart in a year\par

The clay jar on the wall — not entered — Cold. Nobody opens it.\par

The end of the mixing — discharged at the fourth year — Sent where the pots need her, out of nothing\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The sweet sickness is entered as an occupational mark because an entry that says lead would want a payer, and no payer on this terrace will put his name to a girl’s mouth. A physician came up from Greybank in Y.H. 798 with a page that said the sweetness came from the lead; the word went out of it before the year was over, as though a word could be scraped off paper the way slip is scraped off a bench. I have put it back here, where a clerk can read it and go on reading.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk, against rule 13:} Occupational mark; no deduction arises. \emph{In mine, beneath:} It is lead. I did not learn it from a page, which is the only reason I can still say it. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As corrected at the bench\par

A child tasted the mix — The spoon taken away; barley-water given; the word \emph{lead} said once\par

\emph{Skill} said of the green — The word struck in charcoal and \emph{lead} set above it, by a hand that will not sign\par

A skin skimmed off the dish — Put back where it formed; the cup dipped again and given no excuse\par

The rack crowded — The pots taken down and set up again with air between them\par

A heat or a figure brought up from Low Kiln in answer to a cost-question — Answered with the weather and the pots; no figure entered\par

The jar on the wall opened — Not entered. There is no rule against it, which is why nobody does it\par

A girl sent to taste a pot for a buyer — The buyer told the pot has no answer; the girl sent back to the slip\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A fault copied twice in the same firing is a fault the girl has not understood, and the mixer sits with her at the bench until she has. The spoon is not a rod.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The mixing-song, pasted inside the lid}

\emph{Sung at the second dipping, standing, with slip on the forearms. The room says the refrain together. Nobody sings it at the First Firing, and nobody says why. The third line of the second verse is the girls’ line and the mixers sing it wrong on purpose.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lead from the cask and slip from the pit,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the clerk writes nought where the green should sit;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape keep the spoon level, cover the dish,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and give what came up, not what you wish.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The green comes up where the pale line was;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mixer calls skill what the girl calls hers;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name in the mouth is a name without sum ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house puts a nought where the year should come.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lead from the cask and slip from the pit,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one coat for the tally and one for the kiln;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot keeps the flaw and the gum keeps the green,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the girl keeps the coat that went on unseen.\end{quote}

The press of wet reed across the second verse came from the song lying in the rain at the Weir while a blessing was said over the traps. I have flattened it as well as I could. The words are plain enough under it.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the Court came up from Greybank with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers. He struck \emph{the lead comes up} out of the first rule of the mix and set above it \emph{the material is delivered}, as though a cask could climb the Clay Road without a hand behind it. He put a round nought beside the green and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it, which is a number where a colour stood. I have put the lead and the green back beneath and left his above. A clerk who takes the lead out of a sentence leaves the room standing by itself, and a room standing by itself has poisoned nobody and cost nobody, and there is no figure in it to argue with.

The other hand is charcoal, a mixer come down from the firing with the sweetness at her mouth, who struck \emph{a mark of industry} and wrote \emph{It is lead} above it and would not sign. She has put the price where the proportion should have been, which is the only column in this trade that tells the truth. I have not asked her name and she has not given it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The green at the head is mine, off my thumb setting the leaf down on the bench with the mix still on it, and it has gone into the grain so that the whole sheet smells faintly of a firing and cannot be mistaken for a Court paper. The white crust at the fold is dried slip that stayed there instead of falling through, which is how I knew which hand held the leaf. The sweetish edge in the paper is the mix itself, a year old and still sweet, which nobody here has thought to call a virtue. The ring is barley-water from a cup set down while a girl asked why the green came up and I told her the weather. The bead was pressed in by that girl with the sweetness still at her mouth; it has left a smear two months dry. The tallow is off the lamp I keep low so a girl will not know I am writing and change the account for me. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a mixing bench; the green stays where it fell and goes into the next year under the cloth.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish keeps the green. The pot keeps the coat. Between the two a girl dips her spoon and sets it down, and goes to the next dish.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who brings the lead up, a girl new to the spoons, and a man who reads the notices at the Cross, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the jar and the jar stays cold. Tomorrow a woman will bring a girl down off the terrace, and I shall tell her what is carried before I tell her what is paid, and put the lead back where a borrowed hand took it out. The spoon will go into the dish level, and the green will come up where the pale line was, and nobody in this room will have entered either.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Moot Board at the Cross, Being the Prices Cried at Sill Market and the Dues of the Roads That Go Out of It, with the Counts That Go Round the Square Set Beside the Printed One}
\CRsheetheading{The Moot Board at the Cross, Being the Prices Cried at Sill Market and the Dues of the Roads That Go Out of It, with the Counts That Go Round the Square Set Beside the Printed One}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pig-weigher’s fair copy of the board at the moot-post, being the prices of the last market of Stone carried forward into Ilmen and the dues paid at this end of each road; corrected in a Court clerk’s soft-cuffed hand and a carter’s, with a third hand at the foot that nobody will own · Written and kept at the Cross in Sill by the man who weighs the pigs on Account-day, who has held the moot board since the year before the Long Cold; the figures taken at the last market of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and copied forward at the market mornings of Ilmen, Y.H. 813, as the levy was called for the thaw. Set on the back of a Court notice gone soft at one corner and kept under the moot-post’s nail in the finger’s width of shade, where a basket may be set beside it. It survives with pig-bristle in the head, a tallow thumb, barley grease from a crust laid down and not eaten, eel slime at the foot, a green bead of lead glaze from the Glaze Room rolled into the fold, marsh mud on the Reedholt corner, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first price to the last, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
They put me at the block on Account-day because I can lift a pig by the ear and not be argued out of the weight in my hand. That is the whole of my authority. I keep the moot board because somebody must, and a figure cried where two hundred people stand has a better chance of being true than one written in a room with the door shut. What follows is what things fetched at this square between the last market of Stone and these mornings of Ilmen, and what a man pays to leave Sill by the roads, set down so a carter may know his charge before he loads. The clerk down at Greybank keeps the far end of the figure. I keep the end shouted here, where the pigs go over the board and the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself.

Small coin is the bit, twelve to the silver mark; twenty marks make a Sere crown, which comes north because it must and cannot be spent here, so a man may be paid in one and go hungry all the same. The Court keeps its figures in embers and calls five marks an ember. I have left embers off the board. In six years of weighing I have never seen one change hands at the moot-post, and a column with nothing in it is a thing I will not put up on a wall in the rain.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk borrowed from Slate Row:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He set the figure down without the verbs, as though an ember were a thing a carter could put in his pocket. I have put \emph{called} back, because it is the Court that calls it five marks and not the coin that agrees.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board as it stood at the post}

\subsection*{Things cried at the block}

\emph{Account-day, the tenth, twentieth and thirtieth. Read twice: once for the moot, and again for those who came late.}

Article — Price\par

Brown-edged barley loaf — 1 bit\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit\par

Sour milk, a quart — 1 bit\par

Turnips, two — 1 bit\par

Salt herring — 2 bits\par

Smoked eel, at the Fishstairs before the bridge shade goes off — 3 bits; salted, 2\par

Eel skin, dried — 1 mark\par

Pig, over the weighing board — 6 marks, and a bit to the weigher to have it cried twice\par

Coarse pot off the racks — 4 bits the score\par

Barley gruel at a house door — not sold; given, and not entered\par

A brown crust laid in a basket — not sold, not lifted, not named\par

Barrow of grey going out through the north gate — not weighed, and no figure reaches it\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in mine:} The Slate Row clerk took the last three lines off, saying a thing not sold has no price. I have put them back. A bowl given at a door is the greater part of what Low Kiln eats and the whole of what it does not discuss. The grey goes out every market-day over the wet boards, heaped a little above the sides where the load has shifted, and nobody looks at it twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a tall leaning hand, with eel slime at the tail:} At the stairs they will sell you six eels for five marks or five for six, and call both the same bargain. Do not ask which. \emph{In mine:} I asked. They said a bargain was a bargain and went back to the water.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The counts that go round the square}

\emph{Not prices. I set them beside the prices because the district sets them beside everything.}

Count — Where it is said\par

One in twelve, as the notice says — Read from the block in a clean voice; the crowd leans in and goes back to the pigs\par

Four, four and a gap — The bell, morning and afternoon; let it go on\par

Nineteen out and nineteen back — The slip pits; put into a thumb and not said\par

The number for the thaw — Fist, then mouth, then shoulder; thought better of giving\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Slate Row hand:} Only the first is a figure. \emph{In mine:} He is right, and the square would not know what he means. A man who has stood here through a Long Cold knows four ways of counting and three of them are ways of not giving a number.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dues of the roads that go out of Sill}

Five ways leave the Cross. A man pays at four of them and at the fifth he pays the water. The quay clerk at Greybank keeps the far end; what is below is taken at this end, before the cart has begun to rut the clay.

\subsection*{The Clay Road, east to Greybank, eighteen leagues}

Packed clay over corduroy, a Court road since the treaty of Y.H. 418; five days by cart in Grain, six in Silt. An assessor may stop a cart on it without asking the thane, and does.

Due\par

Cart with a load, at this end — 2 bits\par

The same at the quay, by the factor’s man — 2 bits more\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Drove of pigs — 4 bits, and every pig weighed at the block besides\par

Foot passenger — 1 bit; nothing on Account-day, when a man may come to hear the figure\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The carters say they pay to travel one road and pay again for having travelled it. There is truth in it and I have not put it on the post.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The river road, to the Weir and Stonemouth}

One league upriver to the traps, four further to the quarry village at the meeting of the Ferr.

Due\par

Beast on the bank way — 1 bit\par

Foot passenger in Silt — nothing; the water has already charged him\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit; the boards are counted, but which will bear a man is not said\par

Basket of eels at the north bridge shade — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand:} Paid two bits at the Weir in Silt and was told it was the walk. The clerk sets nought against it. \emph{In the Slate Row hand:} No such due. \emph{In mine:} Both rows stand. The boards move after rain, which is more than can be said for a clerk’s figure.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The north gate road, to the Bone Orchard and Cold Acre}

One league to the orchard, another to the ridge and its well that never freezes. On market-days the barrow goes out through this gate in the afternoon.

Due\par

Barrow of grey going out — not weighed, not entered, nothing asked\par

Pot broken for the dead, on a cart — 1 bit; in the arms, nothing\par

Pig driven north to the ridge — 2 bits\par

Man going up for the never-freezing well — 1 bit; he brings back a common stone, which is not a warm-stone and is not called one\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A man asked why the grey goes out unpaid when a broken pot pays a bit. I told him the pot had been bought and the grey had not. He went away with his question, which I have kept here rather than my answer, being the better kept of the two.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Nine Pots and marsh roads}

Eight leagues west to the kiln village in permanent feud with Sill over the road; four east to the reed-cutters’ huts at Reedholt, three downriver to the peat hamlet of Mud End.

Due\par

Nine Pots road — no toll, and none ever collected; it is ours and theirs both, which is why neither mends it\par

Cart using it in Silt — a pot from the shared pit, or a knuckle; the two villages have never agreed which\par

Reedholt, firm boards pointed out to a stranger — half a bit, and half again after rain, because the firm boards move\par

Barrow of peat out of Mud End in Stone — 5 bits; no figure in the Long Cold, when there was none to sell\par

\subsection*{The Rim Road, the long roads, the bridges}

West-north-west to Keld Keep, a hundred and twenty leagues and worsening weather; the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond. The Hearth Road runs a hundred and forty leagues south-east to the Court, and the Salt Road north-east to Vhal.

Due at this end\par

Surveyor’s mark upon a load for the Rim Road — 2 bits; the load is not weighed again in Grath\par

Man going west without a warm-stone — not lent one here\par

Man going farther into the Rim — no due, and no guarantee\par

Grain going down the Hearth Road — weighed here, and the figure read to him twice\par

South bridge, loaded cart — 1 bit\par

North bridge, the winter ford under ice — nothing: the Fishstairs argued the bridge and won, and no collector crosses the ice\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter from High Kiln asked what the last of these cost and was shown \emph{no due, and no guarantee}, which he called the dearest figure on the board. The Court takes nothing at the gate because it has taken it at home. I have not put that on the board; it would stop nobody from loading. In the Long Cold the Ilm bore ice for ninety-four days and no collector crossed, so the ford’s nought is the only figure here that has never been paid.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse they tie to the board}

\emph{Sung at the block while the pigs go over, not while a man from Slate Row is within hearing. The crowd says the last line with the singer.}

\begin{quote}\itshape A loaf for the block and a crust for the fold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape an eel for the shade and a pig for the scale;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the roads and one for the ford,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth goes unpaid because it is water.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and four, and a place at the end\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the driver sets down what the clerk will not take;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell says come and the moot says paid,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the yard says come back as you can.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Slate Row hand:} Four roads entered. \emph{In mine:} There are five, and I have put nothing in the place. A nought is a number and the fifth is a way of going. A carter sang this with his back to the factor’s table and would not sing it facing it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The Slate Row clerk took the verbs out of everything, as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle through the north gate in his boot. Against the bowl given at a door he wrote \emph{nil}; against the grey, \emph{not weighed}; he put a nought in the place where the verse has a gap and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He asked what the board was for, and I told him so a man might know his charge before he loaded. He wrote \emph{figures published for the information of carriers} above my words and went back over the bridge with his cuff wet at the edge and ink in two fingers that will not come out.

I have put my words back under his and left his standing above, as a floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it. A sentence with its verbs taken out travels well and arrives empty, which is what a Court wants of a sentence and what a carter standing in the rain has no use for. The other hand is the carter’s, tall and leaning, with eel slime on it; he put his two bits at the Weir under the clerk’s nought, and I have not swept either away. A board with three hands on it is the only kind this square believes.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The bristle at the head is off a pig that went over with a driver holding one ear and me the other; it goes into the grain and will not come out. The tallow thumb is mine, from holding the notice down in the wind. The barley grease came from a crust laid on the leaf while a woman told a child to eat and the child would not; a crust put down and not eaten is a thing this square knows how to read. The slime at the foot came off a basket set down at the edge of the fish-trade, where no Court slate has ever reached. The green bead is lead glaze out of the Glaze Room; it rolled into the fold from a girl who leaned over to see the figures with sweetness at one corner of her mouth, and she said nothing and went back up the steep street. The marsh mud came off a man who stood too close with a bundle of wet reed. The grey along the margin is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a moot-post.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board has a figure for a pig and none for the warmth carried in a basket. The yard knows which is dearer and does not say it in the square.\end{quote}

I asked the carters, the eel-women and the man from Slate Row, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the post’s nail and the board onto the wall; tomorrow the pigs go over and the figures are scraped off, and a man will ask the morning price, and by afternoon it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Reedholt Mud-Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Mire-Fever, the Ankle-Cold, the Reed-Wolf’s Bite, the Birth-Print, the Bought Breath and the Third Night, Set Down in Grathic Letters Though Fen Cant Is Not Written, with a Physician’s Objections Pressed in the Margin, a Factor’s Clerk’s Corrections, and a Knot for the Word That Cannot Be Written}
