{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A survey-clerk’s extract from the annals of the Tenth Clamp, copied out of the tin lined with warm-stone that stands in the survey room off the Duelling Floor; the year-entries in the number-first hand, the propositions taken down from the paper itself with the Court’s corrections set above them, the nine readers entered by seat and not by name, a song taken down from a carrier who would not give his number, a curl of burnt paper pasted into the gutter, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written beneath Keld Keep in the First Seam in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the clerk who keeps the survey tally; he states his number before this and withholds both, which is the custom of the room. Copied from the paper in the tin on the Last Day, when the ash in the corners is not swept, and carried up the Rim Road with a lead cart, then entered forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: warm-stone dust ground into the inner margin off the tin, coal smut at the head, a curl of burnt paper from one of the eight copies pasted into the gutter, a smear of hot lead at the fold, a frost-feather pressed flat between the third and fourth leaves and gone by noon, a hard drop of tallow, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and has not swept, and a correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk which takes the verbs out.\par}\medskip
I keep the tally in the survey room off the Duelling Floor. The tin stands on the shelf above the survey sheets, and the key to the room hangs on a nail beside the clamps, but the key to the tin does not hang there and I have never held it. That is as it should be. A clerk copies what is put in front of him and asks for nothing that is kept from him; the floor has room for one answer and the room has room for one silence.

The tin is lined with warm-stone. On the Last Day, when the ash in the corners is left where it lies and nobody sweeps, the master takes the paper out and reads it standing and puts it back. He has never once said what he thinks of it, and I have never asked. I have copied it four times. On each copy the same thing happens: the seven propositions go in neatly, in a hand that wants to be read, and the hand that wrote them will not go in at all.

This is the chapter the Court clerk cannot find. He has asked for it twice, once at the survey table and once at Greybank with a soft cuff and a slate already open, and both times I have given him the roll of hands, which is a true account of every boy who came down, and is exactly what he came for under another name. What follows is not the roll of hands. It is what the tin keeps.

\subsection*{The years as the annals have them}

\emph{Copied from the floor’s roll and set beside what came down from the Hearthseat in a hand that writes with the verbs taken out. The entries are in the number-first hand. I have put nothing in from the temple tells, which have their own dates and a comfort in them.}

\textbf{Y.H. 702.} A keeper of the Hearthseat named Haldre set down a paper called \emph{The Sealed Vessel}. It was read by nine persons. The Hearthseat enters it as \emph{a paper concerning the retention of vessels}. The floor’s roll enters it nowhere, because the floor counts measures and a paper holds none. Entered here as \emph{nine readers}, and the nine set out below by seat.

\textbf{Y.H. 704.} The keeper disappears. The Court records that he died and was banked. No completed return is entered. The Unbanked say he crossed first. Entered as \emph{the keeper’s account carried forward}, and beneath it, in the same hand, a nought. There is no grave.

\textbf{Y.H. 710.} Nine copies ordered burnt. Eight went on the grate in this room and the ninth went into the tin. The Court’s entry stops at \emph{nine copies ordered burnt}, because an order is a thing a clerk can enter and a fire is not. Entered as \emph{order discharged}. The ninth is not entered, and the roll goes on to the next boy.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Court’s survey-clerk, against the entry of Y.H. 704:} The keeper’s return was not completed. Strike \emph{crossed first}.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have not struck it. The keeper’s return was not completed, which is true, and the Unbanked say he crossed first, which is also true, and the two have different shapes. A clerk who strikes the second has left the nought standing by itself, and a nought on its own is the readiest answer to a man there is.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The seven propositions, as the paper has them}

\emph{Taken out of the tin on the Last Day and copied while the master read from the other side of the table. The paper is in a hand like Ledgerhand and is not Ledgerhand: every verb in it is in the present, which is the way a man writes of a thing he has seen done and not a thing he hopes for. I have set the Court’s correction above each proposition and left the proposition standing beneath, as the old break is left under a new keying.}

No. — As the paper has it — What the Court’s hand set above\par

One — The world is a vessel and every vessel leaks. Leakage is a flaw in the making and not a law of it. — The world was made whole and cracked once. Enter as the First Breaking.\par

Two — A flaw may be stopped. The seam can be made to hold so that nothing passes through it, and the vessel need not be mended again. — The Return is the appointed repair. Strike \emph{need not}.\par

Three — Where nothing leaks, nothing is owed. Where nothing is owed, the deduction has no object. — The deduction is a tithe for the Hearth and is not a loss.\par

Four — The Return is not mercy but the consequence of a leak. A vessel that holds has no dead to send back. — The Return is mercy. Strike \emph{consequence}.\par

Five — The Want is a rate of loss and not a hunger. Stop the loss and the Want ceases of itself. — The Want is the portion kept back. Strike \emph{of itself}.\par

Six — A vessel that holds everything feels nothing. This is not a punishment but the end of accounting. — The Kept are not to be pitied. Enter as: the account is secure.\par

Seven — The Final Banking is not a drawing-in but a sealing. The world made retentive is the world at rest. — The Final Banking is in the hands of the Keeping. Strike \emph{at rest}.\par

The sixth is the one the master turns face down before he reads the seventh. I have seen him do it four times and have never seen him hurry. A man who keeps a paper he will not use will also take his time over it; there is no hurry in a room where nothing is going to be done.

The paper asks for no new way and opens no way in the arm. It asks for the stopping of every way there is. That is why an assessor can take the verbs out of it and still find something left to fear, which is the nouns: \emph{leak}, \emph{owe}, \emph{Want}, \emph{rest}. A verb can be struck; a noun has to be answered.

\subsection*{The nine who read it}

\emph{The tin’s copy gives seats and not names. I have not invented the names, and I have not asked the Vorr, who would say that the numbers are correct and turn the slate face down.}

Seat — What the tin sets beside it\par

The keeper who wrote it — gone in 704; no completed return\par

The Steward of the Hearth — the seat stands\par

The College of Assessors — three readers, not named\par

The bank at the Hearthseat — two readers, not named\par

The roll-room — one reader, not named\par

The keeper of the Hearth-fire\par

That is nine by seat, with the keeper counted at the head of them. Eight seats have a thing set beside them and the ninth has a line left blank. The blank stands where the keeper of the fire should have an answer; the fire is still burning, which is a fact and not a reader. A blank is not an absence in this room; it is a place where a clerk has put down his pen and gone to stand at the door. I have copied the blank as I found it.

\subsection*{The burning-song}

\emph{Taken down at the shaft mouth from a carrier come up with a lead cart, who would not give his number and said the numbers were correct. Sung going up, never going down. He said he had learned it from a man who carried in 710 and would not say which of the nine the man had carried.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine were written and nine were read,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one was read with a hand that shook;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the paper said a vessel might\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape be made to hold and never take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eight went on the grate in the survey room,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ninth went down in a tin of stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone keeps warm what the fire would not,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the tin keeps shut what the stone keeps warm.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape No leak, no owing, no coming back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no cold to count and no debt to keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the keeper said it would end the Want,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Vorr said the numbers were right.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s one went first and has no grave,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a tin on a shelf that is warm in Ash;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape read it on the Last Day, put it back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the numbers stand and the hand does not.\end{quote}

He would not sing the last verse until the cart was unloaded. I have set it where he put it, at the mouth and away from the table.

\subsection*{What the Court’s hand did}

A survey-clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf when the survey table sat at the Keep. He writes upright and narrow, and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man might smuggle past a weigh in the fold of a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{every vessel leaks}, he set \emph{the vessel is whole by ordinance}, which is a sentence true of no cup in Keld.

\item Against \emph{the deduction has no object}, he set \emph{the deduction is received in due order}. The order is due and the object is not named.

\item Against \emph{a vessel that holds everything feels nothing}, he set \emph{the account is secure}, and struck the word \emph{end}.

\item Against \emph{the world at rest}, he set \emph{the work continues}, which is the phrase the College teaches its own to write at the foot of every closed file.

\item Against the blank where the ninth reader stands he wrote nothing. The hand passed over it without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting a reader I have yet seen.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the paper under the neat hand, as the floor keeps the first number under the second when a boy’s measure changes and nobody scrapes the old one out. A clerk who takes the verbs out of a paper leaves the nouns standing, and the nouns in this paper are the only things in the First Seam that have ever frightened me.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal at the head came off the master’s sleeve when he leaned over to turn the sixth proposition face down and would not sit down to do it. The warm-stone dust in the inner margin comes off the tin every time the paper goes back in, and there is more of it on the seventh proposition than on the first, which tells a man nothing he should repeat. The curl of burnt paper in the gutter is from one of the eight; it curls inward, the way paper curls when the fire takes the edge and not the middle, and I have pasted it in with flour paste that has gone brittle. The hot lead at the fold came off a surveyor’s cuff on the day a passing was measured early; it has eaten the corner of the fourth proposition and I have not written the word back in. The frost-feather came up out of the paper on the climb over the Cold Pass and was gone by the time I found the leaf to press it in. The tallow is my lamp set too near the tally. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have had this leaf from the last Opening of the Slates and have not swept it, and if the factor asks why a clerk leaves dirt on a chronicle I shall tell him it is entered as observance kept, which is a phrase he will accept without looking up.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eight went to the fire and one to the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone keeps warm what the fire undid;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a world that holds is a world that feels,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the keeper who crossed has no name on the slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the tin what it keeps.\end{quote}

I have asked the master of the floor, a surveyor come up from the Ninth Gallery, and a Vorr who came through with a warm-stone and would not set it down, and had three answers and no hand. The Vorr said the numbers are correct. The surveyor turned the slate face down. The master cleaned a clamp and went on with the counting. I have left the line where it was written.

The tin goes back on the shelf and the key goes back on its nail. Tomorrow a boy will be brought down at thirteen and will give his number before his name, and the master will ask him the second question while he cleans the iron, and whatever the boy answers will be entered in the same neat hand as the boys who stayed warm. The paper in the tin will be a little warm in the dark. Somebody paid for that warmth and the payer is not entered in any roll I keep.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of the Open Bowl, Being the Seven Remedies of a House-Physician in the Bowl of Sere, with the Eighth Place Left Standing}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of the Open Bowl, Being the Seven Remedies of a House-Physician in the Bowl of Sere, with the Eighth Place Left Standing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A bowl-house physician’s book of remedies in the southern courtesy hand, written in the thin gold so that no clerk could mistake physic for a contract; the cures in a house-leech’s hand, the leaning entries of the tally-clerk above them, a northern bond-woman’s charcoal underneath, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own; with one song for the third hour and an eighth place kept empty · Written in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in a house of the Ten Bowls in the Bowl of Sere, by Orylla Vanee, a house-physician who kept the sick-bowls and attended both the slave births and the exhibited returns; set down in thin gold on prepared paper, the back of the leaf carrying the thick gold of a contract that was never signed. Carried north with a consignment of oil and tallow-wasp resin and copied at Greybank onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with the thin gold worn from half the remedies so that the uncleared contract shows through, the yellow dust of the burning winds worked into the sewing rather than lying on the face, a thumb of olive oil, a resin smear that caught dust and will not come out, a wine-ring at the foot, a scorched corner where the leaf lay near a court fire, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a grain of southern wheat stuck fast in the resin, and a single pale hair in the fold that is not gold. The corrections stand above in the leaning hand of the house tally-clerk and underneath in the charcoal of a woman of the grain mills who would not give her name.\par}\medskip
I keep the sick-bowls of this house. That is my office: to set a bowl of barley water at the head of a bed, to carry it away when it has been drunk, and to know which of a girl’s seven names to say when the household asks for somebody who is not in the room. I have kept these bowls eleven years and nobody has ever asked me which of the seven I meant, which tells a person how much a name is worth here and how much a bowl.

I write in the thin gold because thick gold is for contracts, and a contract is a thing said to a man who is not in the room. A remedy is said to the bowl. If the bowl answers, that is between them. The tally-clerk writes above my lines and a northern woman writes underneath, and I have left both standing, because a house that keeps only one hand in a book of physic has stopped learning, which is the same as a bowl that has stopped pouring.

The thin gold has gone off half the remedies, and where it has gone the uncleared contract shows through: nine marks, a date, a house-name grander than the house. I have not written over it. A physician who covers her leaf will soon be covering a patient.

\subsection*{The order of a sick-room}

\emph{Written small in the thin gold, with one word gone over in resin.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the bowl at the head, never at the feet. A person takes from the top down, as a bowl empties from the lip.

\item Leave the court door open. A sick one who cannot hear the third hour will die of wondering what the bell said, which is the more expensive death.

\item Ask whose bowl it is before you fill it. A slave’s warmth is the house’s holding and a free servant’s is her own, and a physician who gives the same physic to both has made a gift of goods that were never hers.

\item Pour for the house, not for the person. The person belongs to the house and the house knows what it wants. I have set down what I was told, not what I would choose, which is a physician’s whole art here.

\item When the burning winds come off the east, wet a cloth and lay it over the lips. The wind takes what is loose, and a man’s lips are the loosest thing he has.

\item At the third hour, stop. The bowl is being emptied in every court in the city and our small room is not behindhand.

\item Do not tap a person to hear whether they hold. A bowl-surgeon taps the clay; a man who taps a person is asking a question whose answer belongs to the owner.

\end{itemize}

I have set down more bowls than I can count, which is why I count them in sevens and leave the eighth place standing. A girl here may have seven names by the time she is grown and keep whichever the household prefers, and a book of remedies ought to be at least as honest as a household.

\subsection*{The seven remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who is emptied\par

A fever that burns — Bleed at the elbow; a bowl of wine at the head — Take from the arm while the head is still clear, and give the wine after, to fill what was taken. A physician of the north would leave the blood in and give water. I have set her words underneath mine and both stand. — The patient, in the arm, by the house’s leave.\par

The thirst of the south — Water, and a wet cloth over the lips — Not wine. Wine is for the third hour and for the emptying, and a man who drinks it in a sick-room is being emptied without a slate. The water-carrier brings it up from the court well and is not thanked. — The water-carrier, who carries it and is not entered.\par

A hand taken by the grain mills — Tallow, a clean fold, resin if a graft must hold — A nest of tallow-wasp resin costs four marks and holds a patch until the vessel takes. The bowl-surgeon lifts the nest to the light and listens to it before he buys, the way a potter listens to a pot. In Grath they burn the nests. I have never asked why. — The mill. It takes no account and names no names.\par

The stone-cough of the dust — Steam of hot water under a cloth; honey if the house has it — To the mouth, not the face. The burning winds put a yellow grit in everything, and a man coughs it up in the morning in a colour he will not discuss. The woman of the mills writes that no steam will bring it up and that I am treating the symptom of a wind. Both stand. — The wind, which does not answer.\par

A wall that has given way within — A living patch, held under pressure with resin — Take the wall from a donor whose measure was shaped like the sick one’s. A patch from a donor shaped otherwise takes anyway and goes on wanting, and a person who wants a life that was not theirs is unsafe to exhibit. The bowl-surgeons know this and the buyers do not. — The donor, first, and the buyer afterward.\par

A child that will not take milk — A wet-nurse come up from the mills, for a season — She was returned thin and has milk enough for one; the house has bought her for two. Give the child barley water when she sleeps and do not tell the house how little there is. — The other child at the mill, who was not bought.\par

A wound that will not close — A pinch of quiet ash, then a clean fold — The house buys back its own funeral ash, a year’s grain burnt under one person and the remainder sold at the price they ask. I have set a pinch in a wound gone three days yellow and watched it go quiet by evening. The Court licenses such ash only to the rich; the penalty for selling it unlicensed is a greyed hand. I have never sold any. I have set it in wounds. — Nobody. This is the row I keep turned down.\par

There is an eighth place in this book where a remedy would stand for the trouble a person has when they remember who they were. I have left it the length of a name. The tally-clerk has put a figure in it; the figure stood and the place stood beside it and the two did not touch.

\subsection*{On the full note}

Tap a sound bowl with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. The bowl-surgeons listen to the clay before they pour a graft into it. A green-glazed bowl bought from a northern potter gave a flat knock in its first frost and went from lip to foot without anything falling out that I could see. In the Clay Yard they would call it a bowl gone wrong and sweep around it. Here the house calls northern clay inferior, and I have not corrected the house.

A northern potter tapped the ribs of an exhibited man at a feast and said the man had gone flat. He was a guest in that court and I did not correct him; in this country a guest who is corrected stops being a guest and becomes a witness. I have written his words without his name, which is the only mercy a physician here can practise without a slate.

\subsection*{Of the beautiful return}

This is the part of the book the house would have me leave out, so I have set it in the middle where nobody skipping to a remedy can miss it.

When a person has been emptied and brought back thin, the bowl-surgeons warm them and pour until the head rises. The memory goes first, then the appetite, then the sense of self; what comes back is calm and wants nothing. The house calls this a beautiful return and exhibits it at feasts as proof of generosity. A woman with seven names came back from one and kept the name the house preferred, saying she had always been that one, and the house was well pleased.

A physician of the north wrote that the calm is a burn. The copy that came down to me had the word taken clean away, as though a word could be taken off paper the way wine is taken off a bowl. I have written it back in the thin gold. I have not seen the burn. I have seen the calm, and a woman who said she had always been the name the house kept. I have set both sentences down, because a book that holds only one of them is a ledger, and I would sooner be wrong in a book than right in a ledger.

\subsection*{The song for the third hour}

\emph{Sung at the wine-press, not at the feast, with the vowels open and the ends thrown into the fire. The last line of the third part is said to the bowl and not to the company.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wind comes yellow and takes the lip,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the mill turns under and takes the hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bowl goes round and a name goes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that is kept is the one that stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pour for the house and pour for the heat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pour for the ash that the house buys back;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the calm comes first and the wanting goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bowl goes dry and says no lack.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three at the board and a fourth on the shelf,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven on a girl and one on the slate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the ash comes back and the wine comes round,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what went out . . . . . . . . . . .\end{quote}

There is a space before the last line where a name would stand. I have left it the length it is. The tally-clerk has tried twice to fill it; both times the space stood under the figure, which is the only argument this house has ever lost and never admitted.

\subsection*{What the tally-clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf after the third hour, being a man who cannot let paper lie, and writes in the leaning counting-hand with the gold gone thin.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a house-leech’s mercy} he struck out \emph{mercy} and set above it \emph{return completed, current}.

\item Against the quiet ash he wrote \emph{licensed residue, market rate}, and put a figure in the margin where I had put a pinch.

\item Against the eighth place he set a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} underneath, as though a place where a name had been were the same as nothing.

\item He took the verbs out of two lines. A sentence with no verb travels through a counting room without catching on anything, which is what a counting room wants of a sentence.

\end{itemize}

I have put the words back underneath his and left his standing above. He can enter the ash at the market rate, for the house paid it. What he cannot enter is the space at the end of the song, which tells a person he knows the difference between a figure and a place better than a physician has any right to.

\subsection*{What the woman of the mills wrote underneath}

She is a bond-woman come up from the grain mills, returned thin, and she writes in charcoal on the backs of barley ration tallies with a hand that shakes at the ends of words. She would not let me put her name.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the bleeding:} I have seen four bled. Two were quieter by evening. Quiet is not better.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the beautiful return:} The calm is not peace. It is a room with the door shut and nobody in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Against the eighth place:} That is where my name was. I have not forgotten it. I have only stopped saying it where a clerk can hear.\end{quote}

I have left her words without a name, which is the only kindness in this house that a clerk cannot enter. She took her charcoal away and did not ask for the leaf back, which is how I know she meant it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The olive thumb at the head is mine; I turn the leaves with the hand I carry the bowl with. The dust of the burning winds has worked into the sewing rather than lying on the face, which is how a person tells a book carried in a coat from one read in a court. The resin smear caught dust in the third year and will not come out, and I have stopped trying. The wine-ring at the foot belongs to the third hour and is small. The scorched corner is where the leaf lay too near a court fire and went brown without burning through, so the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly and most of ours are. The grey print along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying, and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a house of the Ten Bowls and nothing gets swept. The grain of wheat in the resin came from a loaf sent north and returned uneaten. The pale hair in the fold is not gold and is not mine.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The fire takes the grain and the house buys back the smoke;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bowl takes the wine and nobody buys that back.\end{quote}

I asked the bowl-keeper, the tally-clerk and a woman who would not give her name, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The book goes back under the fourth bowl, where I can find it in the dark. Tomorrow the third hour will come, and I shall set a bowl down at the head of a bed and carry it away when it has been drunk, and if a girl has seven names I shall say the one the house keeps and leave the other six standing.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Prayer Before the Tube, Being What a Collector Says into the Wool on the Clay Road, with the Manner of It, the Four Sayings Turned End for End, the Answer Made with the Hands, a Clerk’s Correction and a Hearth-Maid’s Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Prayer Before the Tube, Being What a Collector Says into the Wool on the Clay Road, with the Manner of It, the Four Sayings Turned End for End, the Answer Made with the Hands, a Clerk’s Correction and a Hearth-Maid’s Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A collector’s own order of service, carried in the wool sleeve of the cold-iron tube and said low before the draw; written without a name, in charcoal on the back of a voided district tally, with the rubrics of the road, seven parts and the answer made after each, the four sayings in the order a collector comes to them rather than the order the notice prints, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk, the thick charcoal of a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln, and two lines at the foot that will not lie down together · Written between Greybank and Sill on the Clay Road in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a collector of the lower road who signs with a crossed tube and not with a name, and carried back through the Five in the wool sleeve of the tube, which is why there is iron in every fold; borrowed at Greybank by a clerk of the factor, who set the four sayings right at the head and wrote against the grey fingers, and read over by a hearth-maid from Low Kiln on a market morning at the Cross, who put four lines in the margin with a stick of charcoal. It survives as one leaf folded small enough for a coat pocket: cold-iron filings ground into the head, a grey wool fibre from the tube’s sleeve, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, frost-crisp along one edge where it lay against the outer fold of a coat on the Rim Road in Stone, a tallow thumb, a ring of small ale gone dark, silt in the gutter from the assessor’s step at Sill, and a grey Ash print along the foot that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I have drawn measure on this road for nine years and I have never once said the four sayings in the order they are printed. They are printed for a room. They are said in a clean voice by a clerk who has never held the tube, with the slate face up and the man already on the pallet and the door shut behind him. On the road we turn them end for end. It is not doctrine. It is the order in which a collector comes to them, which is a different thing and the only one I can answer for.

There is no name on this leaf. A collector’s name on a prayer is an entry, and an entry can be produced at a Weighing by a man who was not there and had not held the iron. I have set a crossed tube in the corner in charcoal, which is a mark and not a name. If the factor asks me what it is I shall tell him it is a stain.

I wrote this on the back of a district tally voided for a figure entered in the wrong column, between Greybank and Sill in the last tend of Ash, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year. It rode in the wool sleeve of the tube, which is why the iron is in every fold and why the leaf goes grey before the words do. A clerk of the factor set his hand above mine at the head; a hearth-maid come up from Low Kiln with a birth-slate put four lines in the margin, in letters pressed hard enough to tear the paper. I have left both where they were put. The leaf has never been read at a Weighing, which is the whole reason it has lasted.

\subsection*{The manner of it, written small at the head}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Wrap the tube before you say the prayer, not after. A man can hold iron while he speaks, but he will not speak well with his fingers going the colour of the sky before snow.

\item Stand with the road at your back and the house in front. The house is what you are about to take from. The road has no opinion and will not follow you home.

\item Do not look at the face. Look at the arm, where the ways run near the skin. A face will tell you nothing you can use, and a thing you cannot use is a thing you will remember, which is worse.

\item Say it into the wool, not into the air. Words said into the air go up and get entered somewhere. The wool keeps them one draw and lets them go, which is as much as any prayer of mine is owed.

\item Count the draws on the fingers afterwards, never before. A figure counted before the draw is a figure you have already decided, and a decided figure is the same thing as a false one with the ink dry.

\item If the bell comes off the Cross four and four and a gap, stop at the gap. The gap belongs to somebody else. Begin again when the bell has finished counting what it counts.

\item Never say it twice over one man. A second prayer argues with the first, and the first was honest, being said before I knew how much he had.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The prayer}

\emph{I say it into the wool. There is nobody present to answer. The answer is made with the hands after every part: wrap the iron, turn the slate, wipe the hand. I have written the answer down as it is done, because a thing done is the only answer this road gives.}

\subsection*{Before the iron}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron, you were cold when I took you out of the wool.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape You will be cold when I put you back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What you take does not stay in you. It goes where it is entered.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am the hand that holds you to the way. I am not the way,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and I am not the taking, whatever the slate may say later.\end{quote}

Here I draw the tube through the wool again, so the sleeve keeps its shape for the next man. A small care, and costs nothing, which is why I keep it and enter it nowhere.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the arm}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ways run near the skin here. A man’s face is no use to me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The arm tells where to set you; the slate tells what stood there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I do not ask the arm whether it consents. Nobody asks it in this country.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A good arm gives full and gives quickly. A worn arm gives flat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure is smaller, which is not smaller to the man.\end{quote}

Here I set the cold rim to the way and wait for the small hiss. There is iron, a smell like wet wool near a fire, and the time it takes to write a figure down.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the figure}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count embers. A year is a thing the household remembers\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate has no column for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, as the notice says. Printed. Read twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for those who came late up the road.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I write the printed figure. What the district pays is not my hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man who set the other figure has gone up the Clay Road with it\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and does not carry it in the open.\end{quote}

Here I read the figure twice, low, into the wool. The second is for the person at the door who came too late to be counted and stands in the draught.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{The four sayings, turned end for end}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Your return is recorded.} I say this first, so that it cannot comfort at the end.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Nothing is lost that we have kept.} Kept is not the same as held. I have held the iron and know the difference.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The account stands.} It stands after the man sits down. It does not stand while he is standing.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The measure is banked.} Last, because it is the true one and the one I do the most.\end{quote}

The clerk set these in their proper order above mine, with \emph{as appointed} against them. Both stand. His is the order a clerk prints for a room; mine begins with the record and ends with the taking. I have put my hand beside his, not under it.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the cradle}

\begin{quote}\itshape I never see the cradle. It is a room I am not paid to enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One into one: the name comes back with the shape,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape with the price of bread and the way a hand closes on a cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Many into many: what comes back wants a table it never sat at\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and goes toward a cup before the cup is shown.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Both are poured. Both are entered in the same clean hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have seen such children at the Cross and cannot tell you\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which draw of mine went into which of them.\end{quote}

Here I leave a space the length of a name. It is not a name forgotten. No name of mine belongs in it, and the clerk’s round nought is a figure, and a figure is a thing I have already used too much of this morning.

\emph{The answer is made: wrap the iron. Turn the slate. Wipe the hand.}

\subsection*{Of the hand after}

\begin{quote}\itshape The iron takes from the drawer as well as from the drawn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape By the third draw the fingers go the colour of ash water;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by the fifth they are as they were, or they are not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A collector who says the cost is nothing\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape has not looked at his own hand, which is the only looking\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape he does not do.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I marked forty draws on the bench in charcoal one tend\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and washed the bench before the factor came,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is not the same as not having made the marks.\end{quote}

Here I set the tube back in the sleeve and shut the slate. Collectors say the grey comes off in a day. I have had it last six, and no clerk has asked after the sixth.

\subsection*{What the clerk set at the head}

A clerk of the factor borrowed the leaf while the tube was being rewrapped, with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers. He did not take the verbs out. He took the man out instead, which is the stranger thing to do to a leaf written on a road.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{I am the hand that holds you to the way}, he wrote: \emph{the draw is performed by an officer of the Keeping.} Both stand. Mine has a hand in it, his an office, and the man on the pallet will be told about the office.

\item At \emph{I do not ask the arm whether it consents}, he wrote: \emph{lawful draw; consent recorded.} Underneath, in mine: \emph{Recorded by whom? The slate was face down and the man was looking at the wall.} His above, mine below; that is the order this road is read in.

\item At \emph{the figure is smaller} he wrote the printed figure above it, larger. It is the figure they like to see. Both stand.

\item Against the grey fingers he wrote \emph{no cost to officer}, true in the figure and false in the hand I wrote it with. I have not struck it out. A clerk’s false line is what the next reader ought to see.

\item In the space where a name would stand he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. A nought is a number. The place was not.

\end{itemize}

He asked what a collector learned by the prayer. I told him the order of the sayings and the wrapping of the tube. He entered both and went up the road with the tally he had come for. The leaf came back with his ink wet on it. I have kept the ink; a man who cannot help writing on a thing has let it be seen that he wrote.

\subsection*{What the hearth-maid put in the margin}

The letters are thick and lean, made with a charcoal stick and not a pen. She came up from Low Kiln with a birth-slate under her shawl and stood at the Cross until the pigs were weighed before she would touch the leaf, because a woman who touches a paper in the middle of a market will be asked what she had to do with it.

At \emph{the arm tells where to set you}: “It tells you nothing I have not told it. I held that arm last winter while it was still warm. You came up the road after I had carried the slate down it.”

At \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}: “The notice is not in our house. We give the other figure there, and you do not write it, and the house is cold in the morning. I have said this to a woman who was holding a child and had no word for the cold.”

At \emph{I never see the cradle}: “A child came back two doors down and went toward a cup before the cup was shown. I have not told you which of yours it was. I never shall.”

At \emph{sit down} — for she wrote this where I had set \emph{the fingers go the colour of ash water} — she put: “Sit down. I have kept a stone warm since before you came. It is not for you. It is for whoever comes in behind you.”

She would not say who that was, and I have not asked twice. There is always somebody at a market with a slate.

\subsection*{At the head and in the folds}

The filings came off the tube when I set it down hard on the assessor’s step at Sill and went in without apologising; they have worked into the grain and have never once drawn the warm out of the paper, which is the one kindness iron has shown this leaf. The grey wool is the same colour as the fingers it wraps, which I have noticed and not written into the prayer. The green bead is lead glaze from a girl at the Cross with the sweetness still at her mouth; she touched the corner and went back to her pot board without saying what she had seen, and the corner tastes sweet in wet weather, and I have not washed it. The frost along one edge is from the Rim Road in Stone, when the leaf lay against my coat and the writing went thin; I have not gone over those words, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The tallow thumb is mine. The ale ring stood from the first part to the seventh and went dark in the time it takes to draw and be corrected. The silt came up from the step on a wet morning and lies in the gutter with the clerk’s nought beside it, neither entered. The grey along the foot came off a cuff that had been in a corner where no cuff has business lying. There is no Last Day on this road, and nothing here is swept up and burnt in the morning and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot}

In a hand that is not mine, not the clerk’s and not the hearth-maid’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The room hears them in the right order and is comforted.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road hears them backwards and goes on working.\end{quote}

Struck once and written again underneath, very small:

\begin{quote}\itshape Neither order is said to the arm.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk, the hearth-maid and a slate-holder at the Cross, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the struck line where it was struck. The leaf goes back into the wool, the wool over the tube. At the Hearth Drawing the first measure of the year will come off this iron on this road, and I shall say the four sayings backwards into the wool, and the clerk will set them right above my words, and the hearth-maid will come up from Low Kiln with a stone in her hand and will not give it to me until I have finished, which is the only order of service I have kept nine years without correction.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Price Board at Greybank, Being the Rates for Goods, Carriage and the Tolls of the Four Roads, Copied from the Beam Beside the Quay}
\CRsheetheading{The Price Board at Greybank, Being the Rates for Goods, Carriage and the Tolls of the Four Roads, Copied from the Beam Beside the Quay}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A weigh-clerk’s fair copy of the public board, with the dues of the Clay, Salt, Rim and Hearth roads set after it, corrected in two borrowed hands and left standing in a third · Written and kept at Greybank, eighteen leagues downriver of Sill, by the clerk who tends the weighing beam on the quay; begun in Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. The board itself hung on the quay wall beside the grain doors and was scraped and rewritten each tend; this leaf was pinned inside the Vhaleni counting house for the factor’s use, and survives soft at the nail-hole, with a white salt bloom along the gutter, a tar thumb at the head, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a spot of barley grease, a grey Ash print along the margin, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the beam on the quay. A man brings a barrow of peat and wants a figure, and I give him the figure of that morning; by afternoon a barge has tied up and it is not the figure any more. The factor wants a number that will stand still. I have told him that a number which stands still is a lie told by a man with a roof over his goods, and he has told me to copy the board again in a better hand. I have copied it in the same hand. What follows is not what things are worth but what they fetched at the beam between the last market of Stone and the Opening of the Slates, set down so a carter may know his charge before he has unloaded.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark. Twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and does not stay in Grath. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is worth five marks; no man has ever exchanged one for the other, and I have not left a space for them on the board.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the Court’s factor’s clerk:} Coin and reckoning entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} An ember is a word the Court uses for warmth it has already counted. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them; I put them back because a carter standing in the rain does not know he is hearing something always true.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board, as it stood on the quay wall}

\subsection*{Bread and the pot}

\emph{Copied from the Cross at Sill, where the same figures are cried on Account-day. These do not move with the barges.}

Article — Price\par

Coarse barley loaf, brown-edged — 1 bit\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit\par

Sour milk, a quart — 1 bit\par

Salt herring — 2 bits\par

Smoked eel — 3 bits\par

Turnips, two — 1 bit\par

Barley gruel, a bowl at a house door — not sold; given, and not entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} The factor’s clerk took the last line off the board, saying a thing not sold has no price. I have put it back. In Low Kiln a bowl given at a door is the greater part of what the district eats and the whole of what it does not discuss.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Goods that go downriver and goods that come back}

\emph{Weighed at the beam on the north bank. Eels and coarse pots go down to Greybank; salt and iron come up. The figure is for the load at the beam, before the road takes its share.}

Article — Price\par

Coarse pots, the score — 4 bits\par

Tile, the hundred — 9 bits\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain; 5 bits in Stone\par

Eels, a basket at the Fishstairs — 3 bits the eel smoked; 2 bits salted\par

Eel skin, dried, at this quay — 1 mark\par

Salt, a sack from the pans — 3 marks\par

Iron, a bar, Keldish — 2 marks in the lowlands; half a mark in Keld\par

Glass from the Glaze Cliffs, a sheet — 2 marks\par

Rope, a coil — 1 mark\par

Tallow, a stone — 2 marks\par

Lead, a pig, from the western workings — 6 marks; the seller does not say which workings\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The peat row stood blank through the Long Cold of Y.H. 811; fuel doubled in Stone, then stopped being quoted, because there was none to sell. I have set two figures above it for the Thin Year and struck neither out. A man who buys in Grain and pays the Stone figure does not complain, which is how I know this is not a list of what things are worth.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Wages, hire and beasts}

Article — Price\par

A kiln hand, the day — 1 mark\par

A journeyman, the day — 2 marks\par

A child sweeping the yard, the day — 6 bits\par

A collector’s clerk, the day — 4 marks\par

A carter and cart, the day — 2 marks and the beast’s feed\par

Rent, two rooms in Low Kiln, the month — 8 marks\par

Fuel, the month — 4 marks\par

Food, the month — 12 marks\par

Sheepskin coat — 3 marks\par

Good axe — 2 marks\par

Pig — 6 marks\par

Cow — 24 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a tall upright hand, the letters leaning, the ink gone brown at the edges:} A sailor’s share is two marks a month and keep; a salt-worker gets one mark and a binding promise. The Council has instructed me to enter these beside the wages of the clay towns, so that a man may see which country feeds him. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I asked the gentleman whether a binding promise could be spent at this beam. He said it could not, and went on writing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Articles a man asks for after he has paid}

\emph{Not on the board. I keep the list behind the beam.}

Article — Price\par

Leeches, dried, by the dozen, Fishstairs — 3 bits; no questions\par

Ice-mouse skin — 1 bit in Sill; 1 mark in Keld\par

Brine-gull feathers, a bundle, at Vhal — 1 bit\par

Reed-wolf tooth, for a clamp-handle, Stonemouth — 2 marks\par

Ash-mite paste, a thimble, in Mud End — 4 bits\par

The same, in the Hearthseat — 60 marks, taxed\par

Tallow-wasp resin, a nest — 4 marks to a bowl-surgeon of Sere; burnt in Grath\par

Quiet ash, a phial, by the Court’s licence — 60 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The paste and the licensed medicine are the same grey in two jars, one with a Fen name and one with a Court name. I have not put that on the board. A clerk who writes it down does not last a tend at this quay.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Court’s figures, copied from the notice and not traded here}

Entry — Figure\par

Deduction, as printed on the Weighing notice — one in twelve\par

Thin return, paid by the district — 30 marks, in labour\par

Whole return, booked by the Court — 1,200 marks and forty unspent measures\par

Ember, as booked — 5 marks\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The factor keeps a damp leaf of these in his drawer and desires that the board agree. One in twelve is printed and unchallenged and I have put no other figure beside it. I have heard other figures spoken upriver and have not entered them, not being figures I can weigh.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The tolls of the roads}

Four roads leave Greybank, and a fifth, which is the river. The dues below are what the beam collects or what the factors at the far end collect, and the difference between the two is the whole art of travelling.

\subsection*{The Clay Road}

From the Cross at Sill to this quay, eighteen leagues, packed clay over corduroy, a Court road since the treaty of the Blue Cliff in Y.H. 418. Five days by cart in Grain, six in Silt; rutted and then clay again. Because the treaty made it a Court road, an assessor may stop a cart on it without asking the thane, and does.

Due\par

Cart with a load, at the Sill end — 2 bits\par

The same at this end, by the factor’s man — 2 bits\par

Beast on the hoof — 1 bit\par

Drove of pigs — 4 bits, and the pigs weighed at the Cross besides\par

Foot passenger — nothing on Account-day; 1 bit any other day\par

Barrow of grey going out through a north gate — not weighed, and not entered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The cartmen say they pay twice to travel one road, once to the moot and once to the Court, and that the road is in a better state before the payment than after. I have put the last row on my copy and not on the board. What goes out of Sill in a barrow is the afternoon’s work, and no figure reaches it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Salt Road}

From this quay north-east to Vhal, sixty-two leagues beyond the eighteen, eighty in all, by the coast pass. Salt, glass, rope and dried fish go out; coin and contracts on salt-paper come back, and the damp gets into both.

Due\par

Sack of salt, at the coast pass — a mark to the Council of Tides\par

Coil of rope, or a sheet of glass — 1 bit\par

Boat-share passing inland — paid in kind, by the lot and not the league\par

Contract written on salt-paper — no fee; it will not survive the journey, which the Council calls a virtue\par

Man going up with the glass at the turn of the month — 3 bits, returned if he comes back with the answer\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand:} \emph{toll} is struck and \emph{contribution freely entered} written over it. \emph{In mine:} He has left the figures standing. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a man pays it all the same.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Rim Road}

West-north-west from Sill to Keld Keep, a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather; the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond, at a hundred and thirty. Karric VII shut it in Y.H. 741 and the agreement of Y.H. 747 fixed it as the border. Keldish surveyors keep the record and state a man’s measure before his name.

Due\par

Cart, at the pass — 1 mark, or iron to the value\par

Beast on the hoof — half a mark\par

A man without a warm-stone — the stone off the next man who has one\par

Surveyor’s mark upon a load — 2 bits; the load is not weighed again in Grath\par

Traveller going farther into the Rim — no due, and no guarantee\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Only fools and factors travel it without a warm-stone, and the factors charge the stone to the account. I have kept the last row: the Warden’s surveyors do not promise to bring a man back.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Hearth Road}

South-east from this quay to the Hearthseat, a hundred and forty leagues, the merchants’ road to the Court, spoken of in Grath as if it were a fever. There is no barrier on it and no figure at any gate.

Due\par

Toll at the barrier — none; there is no barrier\par

Grain going south, weighed here — by the deduction, entered at this end\par

The same again at the Hearthseat — booked in embers\par

A man who asks what he has paid — the figure is read to him twice, once for the moot and once for those who came late\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter from High Kiln asked what the Hearth Road cost and I showed him the empty column. He said it was the most honest figure on the board and the dearest. The Court takes nothing at the gate because it has already taken it at home. I have not put that on the board; it would stop nobody from loading.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Bridges, ford and river road}

Due\par

South bridge at Sill, loaded cart — 1 bit\par

North bridge at Sill — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

River road to the Weir and Stonemouth — 1 bit a beast; passable on foot in Silt when the low way is under water\par

Winter ford at this quay — 1 bit, when there is water to cross\par

The ford when the Ilm bears ice — nothing, because no collector can cross\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit; the boards are counted and nobody says which will bear a man\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} In the Long Cold the Ilm bore ice for ninety-four days and no collector crossed from this quay. I have left the figure standing because the factor wishes the board to be complete. It is the only figure on it that has never been paid.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The verse the carters tie to the board}

Four roads out of Greybank and one road down, Clay to the bank and Salt to the sea; Rim to the stone and Hearth to the fire, and the four pay twice and the fifth pays free.

Four and four and a place where the fifth should be, the beam keeps the weight and the river the rest; a man goes up with a mark in his coat and comes back with a figure he cannot digest.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow Court hand, against the fifth line:} Four roads entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are five, and I have put nothing in the place. A carter sang this on the quay and would not sing it while the factor’s clerk was in hearing, which is how I know the fifth line matters.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The factor’s clerk struck \emph{brown-edged} before \emph{loaf}, saying a board has no use for a description. I put it back: no household in Low Kiln has seen a loaf without an edge. The Council clerk numbered the roads as three, leaving the river and bridges out; I wrote four above his three and left both standing. Where he put a nought against the fifth line I set nothing; a nought is a number, and that line is a place.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The road to the Hearth is paid at home. The road to the river is paid by the river.\end{quote}

I asked porters, carters and the clerk, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the counting house and the board onto the quay wall; tomorrow the barge comes in with salt from Vhal and the peat row wants copying again. A man will ask for the morning’s figure and I shall give it, and by afternoon it will be a thing that was true.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Quart Set Down at the Ninth Pot, Being a Winter Wager on the Nine Pots Road, the Road-Song as It Is Sung, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Frost}
\CRsheetheading{The Quart Set Down at the Ninth Pot, Being a Winter Wager on the Nine Pots Road, the Road-Song as It Is Sung, and the Figure a Clerk Set Against the Frost}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An alehouse keeper’s telling of a night in the deep cold, set down for the settling of an argument about a quart and not for the improvement of the reader; the five quarts in a charcoal column, the sayings in the words they were spoken, the road-song as it is sung, the figure of a clerk entered over them, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Ninth Pot in Nine Pots, eight leagues west of Sill, by Cilla who keeps the bench and the fire behind it; set down because a man came the next morning and asked whether a quart had been drunk at the end of the bench and she could not tell him. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a spoiled kiln tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled paper and kept in the jar beside the bench. It survives with a tallow thumb at the head, a small-ale ring, a press of wet wool across the first leaf, frost-crisp at the fore-edge, grey Ash in the gutter, a scorch where the leaf was held too near the fire, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Sill table, one saying in charcoal in a wheel-man’s hand, and one line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the Ninth Pot at Nine Pots, which is eight leagues west of Sill and a long day’s walk when the road is open. There are four kilns in this hamlet and nine pots in the name of it, and no living man will tell you which is the ninth. I have asked. I asked a man who had lived here sixty years, and he looked at the road the way a man looks at a thing he has been told not to touch, and said it was a question for somebody with a slate. There is no slate in this house. There is a bench black with the sleeves of forty winters, a fire behind it that is not mine to say where it came from, and one clay pot for the quart that stands between the first question and the last. That is the furniture, and a man may sit on all of it if he takes his boots off first, which nobody does.

The road to Sill is the quarrel of this place. It has outlived every man who began it. Sill says the road is ours to keep because the clay goes west on it; we say it is theirs to keep because the carts come back empty and leave the ruts for our women to walk in. Both sayings are true and neither has mended a yard. In Stone the drift takes it, and the road belongs to the frost, which is the only landlord in Grath that never sends a bill and never comes to collect one.

It took us in the Thin Year, on a Stone morning when the wind came over the Rim and shut the west road in a night. A carter out of Sill was caught on it with an empty cart and a horse that had gone lame somewhere short of the shared pit. He came into the Ninth Pot at dusk with the snow standing on his shoulders and did not take it off, nor ask for a seat, nor say whose horse it was. He stood with his back to the fire until the ice on his coat went grey at the edges, and then asked for a quart. I gave him one and he paid a bit for it, which is the price, and a carter who pays the price in this hamlet is a man who wants something.

There were three at the bench when he came: Radd the wheel-man, Onn who treads the shared pit, and Denn of the fourth kiln. They had been telling the road story as men tell it when the road has shut them in, each with the same saying he told last winter and will tell the next, and none of them hearing the others. The clerk of the Sill table sat in the corner with a slate to his forearm. He had come up before the frost to measure the road, which is a thing a clerk will do when two hamlets have been at a word for fifty years and nobody has thought to ask him; the drift had kept him where he sat. He had a pen and a narrow hand, and he had not once looked at the carter.

“I’ll stand four quarts,” the carter said, “to the man who tells me what this road is worth. One for each of you and one for the bench. Then I’ll drink my own and go to bed.”

Radd turned the wheel in his hands though there was no wheel there, the way a man will turn a thing that is out of reach. “A road’s worth the wheel that’s on it,” he said. “Take the wheel off and it’s a direction. I’ve sold directions. They don’t pay.”

Onn said the road was worth what it carried, and what it carried was mud, and he had trodden mud for nineteen years and could tell a man the weight of it and not the price. “A day’s back,” he said. “It’s worth a day’s back and nothing in coin.” He said it to the pot, which is where we say such things.

Denn of the fourth kiln said a road was worth the pot that went out on it and the state of the pot when it came back. “If it comes back whole, it’s worth the firing,” he said. “If it comes back flat, I’ve lost the firing and the road too, and that’s two losses with one name.”

The clerk did not put his pen to the slate. He said he was not a man to wager on a way and had no opinion of a road. He kept his eyes on his own hand, which is the manner of that table.

The fourth quart was mine, because a quart put to the bench is not scored against anybody. I set it down and said what I had. “A road is worth the man that’s on it,” I said. “A man on a road is worth more than the same man off one, and that’s the whole of what I know. Ask the road. It’ll tell you the weather.”

The carter drank his own without sitting down, wiped his mouth on the back of a glove, and then did a thing I have not seen a man do in this house before or since. He put a bit on the bench and pointed to the end of it where nobody sat. “There’s a fifth,” he said. “Stand it there. A man went out on this road before the drift and hasn’t come back. Set it where he’d have sat, and don’t let anybody drink it.”

Nobody asked who the man was. In this hamlet a question like that is answered with the weather and the road, and we had had enough of both. I set the pot down at the bench end. Radd looked at it and looked away. Onn shut both hands round his quart as though the heat were going out of it, which it was. Denn said nothing at all, which was the most he ever said. The clerk wrote two lines and I have left them standing.

Before the fire was banked we sang the road song, as we sing it when the frost has shut us in, standing with a hand on the bench because it is the only warm thing in the room by then. The second line is the potters’ error and I have set it down as they sing it. They will not have it changed.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four kilns cold and the west road fast,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nine pots and nobody knows the last;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the frost has drawn a line across\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a man goes out and a man comes back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Knuckle the pot and the pot will say\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which side the crack let the fire away;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the road what the carting cost ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road gives weather, the slate gives lost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the man that came in wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the man that hasn’t come back yet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one set down where the bench is bare:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house keeps it. Nobody’s there.\end{quote}

I have set the five quarts down as they stood, because of the man who came the next morning and asked whether a quart had been drunk at the end of the bench, and I could not tell him. This is the whole account the house keeps, in charcoal on the back of a spoiled kiln tally, because charcoal goes into the grain and a slate does not.

Quart — Set down for — Paid — Drunk\par

The first — the carter out of Sill — one bit — yes, standing\par

The second — Radd of the wheel — one bit — yes\par

The third — Onn of the shared pit — one bit — yes\par

The fourth — the bench, not scored — one bit — yes, by the room\par

The fifth — the bench end — one bit — nobody owned\par

The clerk’s lines stand above mine in the narrow upright hand he uses, which is a hand that travels further than mine ever will.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the hand of the clerk of the Sill table:} Way: no measure stands. No deduction arises. Ale sold: five. Consumed: four. Party at the bench end: unidentified.\end{quote}

I have not crossed him out. He is right about the four and wrong about the fifth, and he has put a figure where I put a man. A figure travels well and arrives empty. The fifth quart was drunk by somebody in this room or it was not drunk at all, and I will never know which, and I have left the column as it stands.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in charcoal, in Radd’s hand:} A direction’s not a road till a man’s been lost on it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He said that to the pot and not to the clerk, and the clerk did not take it, which is the one kindness I have ever seen him do.\end{quote}

The tallow thumb at the head is mine; I held the tally down in the draught that comes under the door and did not know I had marked it. The ring is a small-ale ring that stood from the first quart to the fifth and was not lifted until morning. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the carter when he leaned to see what the clerk had written, and I have not written down which man held the door for him. The fore-edge is frost-crisp where the leaf lay under a stone too short for it; the writing there has gone thin and I have not gone over it, because a word written thin is a word said quietly, and most of ours are. The scorch is where I held the tally too near the fire to read what the clerk had done. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business near the corner where I keep the leaf, and I have not swept it. The road opened at the thaw and the carter went east with his horse shod. He did not ask after the fifth quart again, because it was paid for.

At the foot, in a hand nobody will own:

\begin{quote}\itshape The ninth pot was on the bench all along. Nobody knocked it.\end{quote}

I asked Radd, Onn and Denn, and had three silences and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tally goes back into the jar and the fifth pot goes back on the bench, and on the next Stone night I shall set four quarts out and one at the end where nobody sits, and let whoever has a road to tell come in out of the cold and tell it to the pot.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Quay Tally at Vhal, Being the Rates of the Sallow Market at the Flood and at the Ebb, with the Dues of the Salt Road, the Coast Pass and the Waters of the Quay, Copied from the Board Beside the Tide-Tally House}
\CRsheetheading{The Quay Tally at Vhal, Being the Rates of the Sallow Market at the Flood and at the Ebb, with the Dues of the Salt Road, the Coast Pass and the Waters of the Quay, Copied from the Board Beside the Tide-Tally House}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tally-man’s fair copy of the shore-board, written on salt-paper he keeps dry against the practice of the country; the figures sloped as tallies are sloped, the verbs written back under the Council’s correction, one rate gone void by rain, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the tide-tally house on the Quay at Vhal by one of the men who read the draws under Kett of the Quay; begun in Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, after the Long Cold, copied forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the turn of Grain. It survives in a tarred tin lined with dry rushes, sewn with tarred net-twine, the leaves kept dry though the Council’s own paper is made to rot; with a white salt bloom at the head, a tar thumb at the fold, a fibre of wet rope pressed into the second leaf, a brine-gull’s peck through one figure, a fish-hook nick at the head, a wet corner where two rates have gone and are void by law, a green bead of Cliffs glass in the lower corner, a grey Ash print along the margin that nobody will own, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
I keep the shore-board beside the house where Kett reads the draws. A carter comes down the coast pass with salt in his load and asks the figure before he has unloaded, and I give him the figure of this water; by the turn of the tide it is not the figure any more. The factor at Greybank wants a number that will stand still, and I have told him that a number which stands still is a lie told by a man with a roof over his goods. He has told me to copy the board again in a better hand. I have copied it in the same hand and set the two waters against each other.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and comes north because it must, and cannot always be spent here. The Court books in embers and calls five marks an ember; no man has ever exchanged one for the other. I have left no column for them on the nailed board and kept the row here, because a carter who has walked eighty leagues is entitled to know which figure has a hand behind it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk out of Greybank:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written it as though a mark could be carried to the bank and poured into an ember. I have put the verb back. The Court calls it five marks. Nobody trades it, and a figure that nobody trades is a figure that gets read aloud.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board as it stands on the Quay}

\emph{The left figure is what a thing fetched at the head of the flood, when the boats are coming in and the buyers have not yet had the morning’s bread. The right is what it fetched at the turn of the ebb, when the same boats are loading out and the buyer knows he must pay for the road as well as the goods. Both were cried under the tide-tally house between the last market of Stone and the turn of Grain.}

Article — At the flood — At the ebb\par

Salt, a sack off the pans — 1 mark — 2 marks, and the carter does not complain\par

Glass, a sheet, green off the Cliffs — 1 mark — 2 marks after the Glaze boat has come in\par

Rope, a coil, tarred — 1 mark — 1 mark, and tar on the buyer’s hands before he pays\par

Tar, a pail — 4 bits — 1 mark when the galleys are refitting\par

Dried fish, a string — 1 bit — 1 bit, or two if the gulls have followed the boat in\par

Salt herring, a basket — 2 bits — 2 bits, and a third bit when the boat has been out longer than anyone says\par

Eel skin, dried, come down the river — 1 mark — 1 mark; it has been down the water to be sold back up it\par

Brine-gull feathers, a bundle — 1 bit — 1 bit; the bird is not consulted\par

Red wine, a jar, out of Sere — 2 marks — 2 marks; salt on the rim, and no charge for the salt\par

A bed in a house on the Quay, the month — 4 marks — 4 marks, and the floor is a bit\par

A boat, new, from the shipwright — 30 marks — 30 marks, and the curse is included, which no shipwright will enter on a tally\par

Grain going up the Salt Road, by the beam — by the deduction — read twice, once for the moot and once for those who came late\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The Council clerk took the two columns and made one, saying a board has no use for the weather. I put them back. Salt is not dearer at the ebb because the salt has changed; the boat must go out on the water that brought it in, and a man who has paid for the going out is in a hurry to be gone.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in the leaning hand:} A sailor’s share is two marks a month and keep; a salt-worker gets one mark and a binding promise. A man who marries into a boat-owning family is come aboard and his opinion counts at half, which is entered nowhere because it has never been a figure. \emph{In mine:} I asked a salt-worker whether a binding promise could be spent at this board. He said it could not, and went back to the pans.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Paid in kind, and not entered}

These stand on the board with a space where the figure should be. The Council has more than once put a nought in the space. A nought is a figure and can be entered; a boat-share is not, because it passes through the mother and a man cannot pay for what he was born beside.

What passes — What is given — What I write\par

A boat-share going inland — paid by the lot and not the league — the lot, in kind, no figure\par

A man come aboard — half a word on the boat — nothing; the half is not mine to enter\par

A shipwright’s curse — included in the thirty marks — nothing; it is the price of the boat and not the boat\par

A binding promise — one mark’s worth, said binding — one mark in the promise column, which the Council has no column for\par

Seven years at the pulled bench — a condemned man rows them and is paid nothing — seven years, which the Council calls a mercy\par

A dead man sealed in a salted boat and set on the ebb — the watching, until he is out of sight — no fee, and no collector\par

A contract on salt-paper left in the rain — a debt made nothing — nothing, which is held to be a virtue\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand, against the last row:} Instrument void by exposure; no claim can lie. \emph{In mine:} He is right in a language nobody at the pans uses. Half the fortunes of this port have turned on a contract going damp at the right moment, and the other half on somebody forgetting to bring it in.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The dues of the roads}

Four ways leave this Quay: the Salt Road down to the coast pass and on to Greybank, the shore road along the Cliffs, the water of the Sallow, and the road that is the tide itself. The figures below are what the Council asks or what the factor’s man asks at the far end. The difference between the two is the whole art of travelling.

\subsection*{The Salt Road, by the coast pass}

Eighty leagues to Greybank, sixty-two of them beyond the pass, where the clay country gives way to the salt; a day’s walk south-west of Vhal by the low road. Salt, glass, rope and dried fish go out; coin and contracts come back, and the damp gets into both.

Due\par

Sack of salt, at the coast pass — 1 mark to the Council of Tides\par

Coil of rope, or a sheet of glass — 1 bit\par

Cart with a load, at this end — 2 bits\par

The same at the factor’s beam at Greybank — 2 bits more\par

Contract written on salt-paper — no fee; it will not survive the journey, which the Council calls a virtue\par

Man going up with the glass at the turn of the month — 3 bits, returned if he comes back with the answer\par

Passage upriver for a man — 2 bits; his boat-share inland is settled by the lot\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand:} \emph{toll} is struck and \emph{contribution freely entered} written over it. \emph{In mine:} He has left the figure standing. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a man pays it all the same.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The shore road to the Glaze Cliffs}

Five leagues along the coast, where the old lead sweetens in the heat and the glass comes green off the rock. There is a path and no gate, and a due at the path’s end because a path in Vhalen is never left alone for long.

Due\par

Sheet of glass carried off the Cliffs — 1 bit at the quarry path\par

Pig of lead from the old workings — 2 marks; the seller does not say which workings\par

A man who licks the Cliffs — nothing, and the sweetness stays with him\par

Barrel of rain carried against the salt-thing — 1 bit; a man who does not carry it pays later\par

Winter, when the pass is shut — no figure; the road is a direction and nothing more\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A child is told not to lick the Cliffs and some do, for a child believes a warning about a taste before one about a poison. The due is nothing and the cost is not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The water roads}

Due\par

A keel at the Quay, the month — 2 marks, or a fish off the catch\par

A boat that comes in on the ebb and goes out on the flood — nothing; it has not stopped\par
