The first was put to the eel-woman from the Fishstairs, who smells of silt and answers a question with a question. She had given hers before the verse was finished, which is why she never wins anything and is always first.

\begin{quote}\itshape Mouth and no lip to speak with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape belly that gives nothing back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a door you cannot find from inside:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what goes in head-first stays?\end{quote}

“An eel basket,” she said, and laid a bit toward the pot though nobody had asked her to pay. The carter said a basket has no door. She told him to ask the eel, which is the whole of the answer and the proper way to give it.

The second was put to a girl who sweeps the yard for six bits a day.

\begin{quote}\itshape Carried in a clay dish before the light,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape given once and never twice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape every house has it by morning\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no house will say where it was lit.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What is it?\end{quote}

“The year’s fire,” she said, and I gave her a quart of small ale watered until it barely counted, which she drank standing with her sleeve over the rim because she had been told not to spill. Nobody asked her where she had learned it. A child of eight in this town knows which dish the coal comes in and which houses will not tell you who paid for it.

The third went to the man from the kiln, who had slip dried on both forearms to the colour of old bone.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am not a warm-stone and nobody calls me one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am borrowed from a neighbour’s fire and carried in wool;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am put under a head that cannot turn\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and by morning I am a stone again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A river stone,” he said, and there was an argument about whether a thing borrowed is the same thing when it is given back. I stopped it by setting the cup down. There is no winning an argument about a stone; there is only the stone, and it is cold by morning whichever way you decide it.

The fourth I put myself, because the room had got noisy and wanted quieting, and a riddle put by the bench is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing at noon and plain by tallow;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I gather where a promise was not kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they leave me lying on the Last Day,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape burn me in the morning and call it dealt with.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name me.\end{quote}

No one answered for a while. Then a clay-hand from the pits, with the grey worked into his knuckles that no scrubbing lifted, said the grey in the corner, and said it to the bench and not to the room. I passed him the pot. He set it down again without drinking and said it was a thing his mother said to the skirting board, and that he had said it to his own daughter the week before and had not known he was going to. That is the best answer I have heard in eleven winters and the only one that cost the man something.

\subsection*{The fifth, which was put from the door}

It was the middle of Stone, when the ice had set for good and the bit for a quart had gone up two and come down again. A man stood at the door and did not come in. He was dry, which a man cannot be in that weather without having come a long way or else not having come from the weather at all. He asked whether anybody here was warm. Nobody answered him, which is an answer in this town. Then he put the fifth:

\begin{quote}\itshape I go back to a house that knows my face and not my name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape my mother is glad of me and does not know me;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I want a thing I never wanted\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and cannot say what it is.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

The eel-woman said, “A thin return.” He said, “That is what the slate calls it,” and asked what it was to the house. The room went the way a room goes when everybody has the answer in their mouth and nobody will be the one to say it. He waited a little, and said, “Then you have not lost it,” and turned back into the cold. He did not come in and I did not ask him. Where he stood the boards were wet with the melt off every coat in the room, and in the morning there was a round dry place on the bench where no cup had stood. I rubbed the charcoal over it and it came back. I have stopped looking for the hand that did that.

\subsection*{The tally, in charcoal}

Question — Put by — Answer given — Score\par

The basket — the bench — an eel basket — one, paid\par

The dish — the bench — the year’s fire — one, drunk\par

The stone — the bench — a river stone — one, argued and allowed\par

The grey — the bench — the grey in the corner — one, not drunk\par

The face and the name — a man at the door — none served — not scored\par

The figure read at the Cross that morning was one in twelve, as the notice says, and it went over the bench with the ale and no one looked at it twice. There is a pause in that figure the length of a held breath, which the clerk reads past and I do not, but that is not a thing for a riddle night.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

A clerk of the Court’s table borrowed the leaf on a market morning when the square was full and his cuff was soft at the edge from washing. He set the riddles down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the four, which was more than I had scored, because the bench scores in whether a man sits down again and he does not. Against the fifth he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck}. He asked who had put it. I told him a man at the door. He asked for the man’s name, and I said the man had given none, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified}.

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way a bench keeps a charcoal score under a spilled quart. He has entered four answers and struck the fifth, and the fifth was not struck: it stands where a man stood and did not sit down. I asked him what a figure was for and he said a figure was for carrying away. He has carried away four and left the one that would not go.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The tallow thumb at the head is mine; I held the leaf down in the draught that comes under the door and did not know I had marked it. The ring came off a quart that stood from the first question to the fifth and was drunk by nobody; three men have claimed it and one woman has denied it and I have not given it to any of them. The press of wet wool across the first leaf came off the man who held the door while the stranger spoke, and I have not written down which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The barley grease is from a crust the sweeping girl set down on the leaf and took away again uneaten, which is how a crust is usually taken in this town. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff that had no business in the corner where I keep the leaf, and I have not swept it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four went home warm. The fifth went home with them.\end{quote}

I have asked the carter, the eel-woman and the clay-hand, and had three silences and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the jar and the charcoal goes off the bench with the heel of my hand. The road will open at the thaw and there will be more to do of an evening than ask one another what we already know, and the bench will be wanted for cups again. I will set the fifth where it was and let the next man stand in it. If he asks whether anyone here is warm, I shall tell him to ask the pot.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Roll of the Dead, the Remembering, and the Account Not Closed, Being Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Bank at the Hearthseat with the Roll-Clerk’s Margin, the Tallow Gone White, a Fish-Scale Pressed Flat, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Roll of the Dead, the Remembering, and the Account Not Closed, Being Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping, Copied into the Bank at the Hearthseat with the Roll-Clerk’s Margin, the Tallow Gone White, a Fish-Scale Pressed Flat, Two Corrections in Borrowed Hands, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An extract from the Court’s ordinances, written out for the roll-clerk’s counter at the bank in the Hearthseat, with the marginal hand of the clerk who carries names forward and reads them on the Remembering; the articles in Ledgerhand and the verbs restored beneath them, the roll set in a table, the form of a carry-forward left blank, the roll-song as it is said at the reading, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody has claimed · Copied at the bank in the Hearthseat in the last tend of Ash of the Thin Year, Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, from Title the Ninth of the Ordinances of the Keeping as set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668 and sent down to the factor at Greybank in Y.H. 418, added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year; survives as three leaves of foolscap sewn with wire, kept under the roll-sheet in the bank: a grey Ash thumb at the head, tallow gone white and hard in the gutter, a fish-scale pressed flat at the second fold, iron filings in the crease where a tube-wrap lay, a crumb of barley bread at the foot, a damp line along the lower margin where a pail stood, a bone-stylus score where a word was taken out, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the roll of the dead. It lies in a tin on this counter and it grows every tend and is never once emptied. A name goes in at the drawing, stays in at the pouring, and is still there when the house that gave it is a figure in the granary accounts and nothing else. On the Remembering I read the names in a clean voice, with the Hearth-fire behind the grating and nobody allowed to touch it. The ordinance is in Ledgerhand, with nobody in any of its sentences, which is the manner this Keeping has of making a death read as though it had happened to a roll and not to a person. I put the people back underneath.

\begin{quote}\itshape At the head, in mine, written small: Copied for the counter and from the roll. The verbs are mine. The absence of them is not. Let both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Title the Ninth, as it stands in the bank}

\emph{From the Ordinances of the Keeping, Title the Ninth: Of the Roll of the Dead, the Remembering, and the Account Not Closed. Set down in the first years after the Rising of Y.H. 668; sent down to the factor at Greybank in Y.H. 418; added to in Y.H. 782 and in the Thin Year, Y.H. 812.}

\subsection*{I. Of the roll}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Every vessel drawn is entered by slate-name and not by birth-name. The birth-name is turned face down at the entering and is not spoken at the Remembering. A name turned down is still a name, and the roll does not say so.

\item An account is never closed. It is carried forward. The name of a vessel already poured remains in the same hand as the names of vessels not yet drawn, and no column provides for an ending.

\item What is not entered did not happen. A death entered is a death that was collected; a death not collected is not entered, and the roll has no place for it.

\item Where the vessel is a foundling with no house, the name is written by the hand that writes the slate, and the house is the Keeping. Where the vessel has a house, the house is entered and not the person.

\item The measure is banked. The account stands. Nothing is lost that we have kept. Your return is recorded. These four sentences stand at the head of the roll and are read at no Weighing.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman stood here with her hand at the corner of her apron and asked whether her mother’s name was still on the roll, eleven years after the house that gave it was empty of people. I found the line and showed it to her, and the line was there. I have not entered what she said when she saw it, for there is no column for a daughter, and she took her hand off the counter before I could set a word down.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the Remembering}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item On the fourth day of the Five, being the Remembering, the names of the dead are spoken in a clean voice by an officer of the Keeping or the clerk he sends. The reader does not ask who is in the room.

\item A name is spoken once and is not explained. Where two names are alike, both are spoken, and the reader does not say which house is which.

\item Whole returns are announced on the same day. The figure is read in a clean voice and is not inspected. A whole return is entered at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures; the purchaser is entered where the Steward keeps his room and not upon this counter.

\item Where a name is disputed, the figure stands and the name is not changed. Where a name is not disputed, the figure still stands.

\item No fire is carried into the reading and no priest touches the grating. The reader stands with his back to the fire and his face to the roll.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have read eleven Rememberings at this counter and was never once told whether the names are called up or called back. A keeper of the Hearth-fire said to me that the fire does not care which, and would say no more. I have set that at the edge, where a keeper’s sentence has no column.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the returning}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where one measure is pressed into one newborn vessel, the return is whole and the person comes back with memory. Where many measures are pooled and divided among many, the return is thin, and what comes back is a stranger with a faint interest in a life it cannot name.

\item A thin return is paid by the district at thirty marks and is paid in labour. The figure is entered to the district and not to the vessel. The vessel is not asked.

\item A whole return is booked at twelve hundred marks and forty unspent measures. The difference between the two figures is not a tax. It is not entered as a tax.

\item After the pouring the name is carried forward and not struck out. The vessel that has been poured is the vessel that stands upon the roll, and no second line is begun.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman asked whether a whole return brings back the person or only the shape the cradle can hold. I read her the eleventh article. She said that was not an answer, and I said it was the ordinance. Both are true and I have entered neither. There is no column in this book for the thing a woman wants to know.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the death not collected}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A house that has a death in it sends for the collector before the pot is broken at the door. The pot is broken after the draw and not before. A pot broken first lets out what the ordinance has not entered.

\item Where no collector is called, the death is not entered, and the grey that gathers in the corner of that house is gathered in the ordinary course and carried forward like any other grey.

\item What is held in a vessel from which no draw was made is not metered by the Keeping and is not returned to any account. The house is not asked, and this article is not sent to the factor.

\item An officer of the Keeping has no house and no kin. The roll is his family. He is not corrected for a name he did not hear.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A woman broke a pot at her door before I came up the stair in Ash and told me the heat had gone out of him already. I entered the draw and not the pot, for the pot was the earlier thing and this ordinance reaches only the later. She held the broken rim against her apron all the while I wrote, the way a woman holds a cup she has not yet set down.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The roll, as it stands at the counter}

\emph{Copied from the roll-sheet. The middle figures are the figures entered. The last column is mine and has no standing at any Weighing.}

Tend — Names entered — Carried forward — Whole returns — Thin returns — What the counter kept\par

Ash 1–10 — 19 (14 house, 5 Keeping) — 611 — 1 — 6 — a scale pressed flat in the fold\par

Ash 11–20 — 23 — 634 — 0 — 9 — a crumb at the foot, gone white\par

Ash 21–30 — 17 — 651 — 2 — 7 — the score where a word came out\par

Kindling — 6 (the year’s first measure) — 657 — 0 — 0 — a scorch off the watch-fire\par

Weighing — 0 — 657 — 3 — 0 — the clean voice, twice\par

Names entered on this leaf: sixty-five. Names struck: none. Accounts closed: none. The word that was taken out stands scored in the lower margin, the length of it, and I have not written it back.

\subsection*{The form of a carry-forward}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Ninth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand. In eleven years no house has asked for the last line to be read twice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the name of ----------------------, slate-name ----------------------, the birth-name turned down at the entering and not spoken at the Remembering; the measure drawn, banked and pressed into ------- vessel(s); the return whole / thin as the case stands; the account not closed but carried forward to the roll; the figure ---------------------- as the notice says; read on the Remembering in a clean voice by ----------------------, who did not ask who was in the room. What the house asked at this counter ----------------------, which is not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The roll-song, said at the reading}

\emph{Said low at the counter on the Remembering, while the roll lies open and the reader stands with his back to the fire. Never at a Weighing, and never twice in one year.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name on the roll and a crumb on the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot at the door and the pail at the well;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they read the name and they leave the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house keeps the figure and not the place.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Whole for the one and thin for the crowd,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape forty unspent and a clean voice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cradle answers the way it can\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the roll goes on where the house gave out.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ash in the corner and tallow gone white,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name turned down and a figure read twice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the account stands open and the counter stands still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dead go forward because they must.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the last line of the second verse:} One figure entered; no deduction arises. \emph{In mine:} There is a cradle in that line and he has numbered it away. A cradle can be answered; a figure cannot. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man came down from the Hearthseat with ink in two fingers of a cuff gone soft from washing. On article two he struck \emph{carried forward} and set \emph{the account stands} above it, which is the same thing said by a man who has never had to find a name at the bottom of a leaf. I have put \emph{carried forward} back underneath. A standing account is a thing a man can argue with; a carried name is a thing somebody has to keep moving, and somebody does.

The other hand is a keeper’s from the Weighing Hall, narrow, with soot at the edge. Against article eight he wrote \emph{the purchaser is recorded} where I had written that the purchaser is entered in the room the Steward keeps. Both stand. A keeper who says a thing is recorded has never had to go and find where. I have left my line where it is, because my line is the one the next clerk at this counter will read.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The grey at the head is Ash off my own thumb, turning the leaf toward the lamp while I found a name; it is the colour of a corner swept too late and will not come out of the creases. The white in the gutter is tallow gone hard where a lamp was set down on the leaf at the Remembering and left until morning; it has taken the corner off a line without taking the sense and I have not picked it off. The fish-scale at the second fold came off a herring sent up from Greybank and laid beside the counter while I read; it has flattened into a little pale leaf of its own and has not been brushed away. The iron in the crease came off the tube-wrap an officer laid there and stood longer over than he needed to; there is always a little iron in the fold of this book and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper. The crumb at the foot is barley from a boy who held it while I read him his grandmother’s name and forgot to eat it. The damp along the foot is a pail set under the counter through a morning and has taken the corners off two lines. The score in the lower margin is a bone stylus drawn through the word \emph{died}, with \emph{was drawn} set above it; I have put \emph{died} back underneath and left the score standing, the length of the word they took out. There is no Last Day at a bank, and nothing here is swept up and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The roll keeps the name and the cradle keeps the warmth.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The space between them has no column.\end{quote}

I asked the keeper who reads the fire, a woman who came about her mother’s name, and a clerk come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the lines where they were written.

The roll goes back into its tin. In a few days the Five will come and the Remembering will be read, and I shall stand with my back to the fire and say sixty-five names in a clean voice, and the roll will be full when I have finished as it was when I began. A woman will come to ask whether her mother is still on it, and I shall find the line and show it to her, and the line will be there. That is my trade: to keep a name moving and not to say where it goes.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Of the Shutting of the Pass and the Seven Years, Being an Extract from the Roll of the Cold Pass Kept at Keld Keep, with the Warden’s Claim Entered in the Number-First Hand, the Reeves’ Answer Out of Grath, the Four Terms Cut on the Slate in Slate Row, the Road-Song Carried Down the Rim Road, the Corrections of a Court Clerk in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{Of the Shutting of the Pass and the Seven Years, Being an Extract from the Roll of the Cold Pass Kept at Keld Keep, with the Warden’s Claim Entered in the Number-First Hand, the Reeves’ Answer Out of Grath, the Four Terms Cut on the Slate in Slate Row, the Road-Song Carried Down the Rim Road, the Corrections of a Court Clerk in Ledgerhand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A survey-roll keeper’s extract from the Warden’s roll at the pass, copied into Grathic letters with the Keldish endings struck off; the seven years in the number-first hand, the claim set down as an entry with a nought beneath it, the reeves’ answer in a sloping margin hand, the four terms cut from the slate in Sill’s Slate Row, a carter’s song taken down at the post, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk, one nought cut in chalk, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the survey post in the Cold Pass, ten leagues beyond Keld Keep, in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the roll, who states his measure before this and has set no name to it: nine and twenty when he was put to the roll, and not the number he went down with. Copied from the Warden’s roll of Y.H. 741 to 747, carried down the Rim Road in Stone of the same year with a lead cart, copied at Greybank in the Five, and entered at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as six leaves of rough survey paper sewn with wire into a board cover gone soft at the seam: coal smut ground into the head, an iron-red thumb at the second corner, a nought cut in chalk at the foot of the figures column, a frost-feather pressed flat between the fourth and fifth leaves and gone by noon, a bead of Ninth Gallery lead shut in the fold, a hard drop of tallow, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the keeper did not make and has not swept. A factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank on a market morning and set his upright hand above two of the entries; the carter’s song was taken down from a man who would not give his number either.\par}\medskip
I keep the roll at the post. The post stands ten leagues beyond Keld Keep where the Rim Road goes through into Grath, and there is a post and no gate, which is the first thing a man from the south asks about and the last thing anybody tells him. The roll is not a history. It is a list of measures and of the days men went through, kept so that a reeve who says the pass was shut in the seventh year may be answered out of a book and not out of a memory. There is no quarrel about the figures at this post. Everything else is quarrelled about, and the quarrel is entered under the year in which it was written, not the year in which it happened.

I write in Grathic letters, because Keldish is cut in bone and a bone does not travel down a road in a pocket the way a letter does, and I have struck the endings off as our people do. My number stands where a name would stand: nine and twenty. I have put no name to this. A post keeps measures, not men.

This chapter is the one the factor’s clerk asks to see when he comes up from Greybank. I have copied it four times. On each copy the four terms stand as the slate cut them, and the one thing that will not go into a year-entry is the nought under the claim, which I have cut in chalk at the foot of the figures where a man looking for a gate will find it.

\subsection*{The years as the roll has them}

\emph{Copied from the Warden’s roll, which is kept face down in the survey room at the Keep and carried up to the post each Ash. The entries are in the number-first hand. I have put nothing in from the temple tells, which have their own dates and a comfort in them.}

\textbf{Y.H. 741.} The Cold Pass shut to Court traffic by Karric VII, Warden of the Rim. Entered as \emph{the pass is shut}. Beneath it, in the same hand: \emph{the true Hearth lies under this mountain}. Not entered again.

\textbf{Y.H. 742.} Assessors came up from the Hearthseat with slates and no soldiers. They wrote the claim down, took the verbs out of it, and went back. Entered as \emph{the matter is under consideration}.

\textbf{Y.H. 743.} Hired men came up the Rim Road from the coast with cold iron. Entered as \emph{precaution taken}. No dead entered.

\textbf{Y.H. 744.} A levy of clay-men out of Grath, who had no interest in the argument. They came because the levy was called and went up because it was called. Entered as \emph{the levy was answered}.

\textbf{Y.H. 745.} The road downriver stopped short of Greybank. Carts went by the river and took nine days where they took five. Entered as \emph{the road is otherwise engaged}.

\textbf{Y.H. 746.} Commissioners sat at the post with a slate and a piece of Keldish iron on one table. Entered as \emph{a conference at the post}, with no mention of who paid for the table.

\textbf{Y.H. 747.} Terms cut and the pass opened. Entered as \emph{peace, the road opened, the account standing}.

\textbf{Y.H. 749.} Grath, Keld, Vhalen and Sere set their marks to the neutrality of the Hearthseat. Entered as \emph{the fire is left standing}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of the factor’s clerk, against the entry of Y.H. 741:} An unauthorised claim is recorded. Strike \emph{true}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. The Hearth is under the Keel and the Warden’s mountain is under the Rim, and both men have been told this since they were boys. The word is the Warden’s, and I have not put it there. A surveyor who takes the adjective out of a claim has left the claim standing and taken away the only part of it that could be argued with, which is a great kindness to do an argument and a poor one to do a man.

\subsection*{The claim, set beside what came down from Grath}

\emph{The left column is the roll’s. The middle is the Court’s annals, read to me at Greybank by the clerk who took the verbs out. The right came up in a sloping hand on the back of a reeve’s weigh-slip, and I have set it where I found it.}

The roll at the post — The Court’s annals — What came down from the reeves\par

The true Hearth lies under this mountain — An unauthorised claim is recorded — The Hearth is under the Keel. We have seen it. This is under a mountain.\par

The pass is shut — The frontier was closed to traffic — There is a post and no gate. What was there to shut?\par

The levy was answered — Precautions were taken — The clay-men came because the levy was called. They asked whose war it was and were answered with the weather.\par

Peace, the road opened — The matter is closed, the account standing — The road is open. The toll is the toll of 740 still.\par

The reeve gave a date where a figure was asked, which is the custom of that country and not an evasion of it. He set down the fourth of Frost and said the ferries stopped on that day and the eels ran on every day after it, whether the pass was shut or not. I put his date in the margin where it stands. It is not an answer to the question the roll asks, and it is the only true thing that came down from Grath in those seven years.

\subsection*{The seven years in figures}

Year — Men entered at the post — Measures declared — Warm-stone sold, in embers — What the roll calls it\par

741 — 1,204 — 1,204 — 96 — The pass is shut\par

742 — 311 — 309 — 41 — The matter is under consideration\par

743 — 88 — 88 — 12 — Precaution taken\par

744 — 60 — 58 — 9 — The levy was answered\par

745 — 47 — 44 — 6 — The road is otherwise engaged\par

746 — 51 — 50 — 7 — A conference at the post\par

747 — 1,188 — 1,188 — 91 — Peace, the road opened\par

The figures are neat. The sixty of 744 were clay-men from Grath who had been levied to fight a Warden over a Hearth they had never seen, and the roll enters them as \emph{the levy was answered}, a phrase with no men in it and no cost. I asked the old tally-man what the sixty had been. He said they had been cold, and went on with his counting. I have put \emph{cold} in the margin and not in the table, because a table is a thing a clerk reads and a margin is the only place in a roll where a silence is allowed to stand.

Under the 744 row I have cut a nought in chalk. It was there when I came to the roll, and it is not a figure for men. In the old roll a gate was drawn in the margin where the post stands, and somebody cut the gate away and put a nought in its place. A nought is a number. A post is a place. The two have stood side by side in this book for seventy years and nobody has asked me to make them agree.

\subsection*{The four terms, cut on the slate in Slate Row}

\emph{The treaty slate stands in Slate Row in Sill, which is a Court street and not a Grathish one, and is read at the Cross on market morning. The thane of Clay was not asked. The Grathish say this is how all important treaties are made; the Court says the slate was cut in the presence of four powers and the thane’s absence is not an entry. I have copied the four terms as they are cut.}

Clause — As it is cut on the slate — What the roll set beside it\par

One — Keld keeps the pass and the survey shaft. — \emph{The post stands.} A surveyor goes down and comes up, or does not, and the Warden’s men do not promise the third thing.\par

Two — Grath keeps the road. — \emph{The road is open.} Open to whom is not cut, and the toll at the post is the toll of 740 still.\par

Three — The Hearthseat is neutral ground. — \emph{The fire is left standing.} None of ours has been allowed to stand near it, and none of ours has asked.\par

Four — The border is fixed at the survey post. — \emph{A post and no gate.} The reeve’s nought was cut at the slate’s foot and then scraped away, and the scrape is still there.\par

In Y.H. 749 the four powers set their marks to the neutrality the slate had only promised. I have copied the marks as four strokes and not as a word, because a stroke is the only part of a treaty a man at this post can check with his own eyes.

\subsection*{The road-song}

\emph{Taken down at the post from a carter going down with lead, who would not give his number and sang it instead. Sung going down the Rim Road, never going up.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Seven winters the pass stood shut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Warden’s fire under the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the assessor came with a slate and a word,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the word went down like rain.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the Warden’s mountain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the Keel beneath;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the powers that set their marks,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and none for the man between.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a post and there’s no gate,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a nought where the gate should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number goes on the arm, not the road,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mountain keeps its own.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay-men came and asked whose war,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and were told to ask the levy;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road stands open to every cart\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the toll stands where it stood.\end{quote}

He said he had learned it from his mother and she from a man who went up in 744 and came back in 747, and that the man never said which of the seven years he had spent in the pass. I have left that where he put it.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did, at Greybank}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning. He writes upright and narrow, and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a weigh. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at either of us, which is the manner of that table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{the true Hearth lies under this mountain}: \emph{an unauthorised claim is recorded}.

\item Against \emph{the pass is shut}: \emph{the frontier was closed to traffic}.

\item Against \emph{the levy was answered}: \emph{precautions were taken}.

\item Against \emph{peace, the road opened}: \emph{the matter is closed, the account standing}.

\item Against \emph{there is a post and no gate}: \emph{the frontier is unguarded}. There is no gate to guard and never was, but a sentence with a guard in it can be entered.

\item Against the nought I cut in chalk he wrote nothing at all. The hand passed over it without a stroke, which is the readiest way of correcting a figure I have yet seen.

\end{itemize}

I have left both readings everywhere, the thin one under the neat one, as a repaired wall keeps the old break under the new keying and does not pretend the first hand never touched the stone. A clerk who takes the men out of a sentence leaves the road standing by itself, and a road standing by itself has carried nobody and cost nobody, and there is no figure in it to argue with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The smut at the head is mine; I hold the leaves down with my whole hand because the draught at the post comes along the floor and takes paper before it takes a man. The iron-red at the second corner came off the mine-reeve’s point when he checked a man who had given a figure that would not hold; he did not look at me and I did not look at the man. The chalk at the foot of the figures is the nought, and it comes away on the cuff and is put back each Ash, which is more than can be said of the gate it replaced. The frost-feather was on the survey stone after a warm night and was gone by the time I found the leaf to press it in. The lead bead rolled out of the Ninth Gallery; a surveyor laid it on the leaf and went away without it. The tallow is my lamp set too near the roll. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at this post.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four powers set their marks to the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one man cut a nought in the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the road went open, the pass went shut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the account came back the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the post what it kept.\end{quote}

I asked the tally-man, a surveyor come up from the shaft, and a carter who had been down in 747, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The roll goes back to its nail beside the post. Tomorrow a man will state what he holds before he says who he is, the number will be entered, and the gate will still not be there.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt Walk, Being the Standing Rules of the Dippers of Vhalen for the Taking, Walking, Trying and Naming of Apprentices at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Table of Walkings, the Net-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Council Clerk’s Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt Walk, Being the Standing Rules of the Dippers of Vhalen for the Taking, Walking, Trying and Naming of Apprentices at the Pans Outside Vhal, with the Table of Walkings, the Net-Song Pasted Inside the Cover, Two Corrections in a Council Clerk’s Hand, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A dipper’s leaf of rules from the west pan, written in the leaning low hand with the ends of words let fall; the rules set in short sayings, the walkings and the faults in tables, the net-song pasted inside the cover, a tide-name written in salt in the margin and gone before noon, two corrections in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Council clerk, one line struck in charcoal by a pan-master who would not sign it, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Salt Pans outside Vhal in Frost of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813 by Halla Salt, a dipper of the west pan who has taken the young out barefoot at the Salt Walk for one and thirty years and keeps the pan’s leading rope and its tide-name in her mouth; written on salt-paper leaves she keeps dry in a tin that once held salt and has never been washed, sewn with tarred net-twine and carried up the Salt Road with a glass consignment, where a clerk of the Council corrected it at Greybank. It survives with a white salt bloom at the head that has taken the last letters off a word and left the rest readable, a thumb of tar at the fold off the leading rope, the press of a wet net across the song, a peck-hole where a brine-gull took the leaf for a crust, a fish-hook nick, a ring of small ale at the foot left by a ship’s master who would not drink with dippers, a grey Ash print along the outer fold that is not hers and that she has not swept, a tide-name written in salt in the margin which the sun took by noon and left a white place, two corrections in the Council’s upright hand, one charcoal line struck and written again beneath, and a line at the foot nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the west pan and the leading rope. When the young are taken out at the Salt Walk I go first and they come barefoot behind me, and when one of them names a tide nobody has seen I write it in salt on the crust and the sun takes it before they are back at the shed. That is the whole of the teaching, set down so that a girl at the pans and a girl at the Quay hear the same rule. I write on salt-paper and keep the leaves dry, which is against the practice of the country and I know it. A contract left in the rain is no contract here and we call that a virtue. A rule left in the rain is no rule either, and I have met no man who sees the virtue in that.

These rules were gathered before the Council had a name for the pans and are copied forward from the rope and not from a book. A rule that has never been walked is a rule nobody believes. These have been walked.

\subsection*{The rules as they stand at the west pan}

\subsection*{Of the taking}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item The pan takes a child, not a house. A house may bring him and a house may feed him, but from the day he first puts a foot on the crust he answers to the dipper who walks him. The Council takes the tide and leaves the child alone.

\item A child is taken at twelve and walked at fourteen. A child taken later is walked at the next low tide after his fourteenth year, and the year between is not made up to him. The salt does not make up a tide that was missed.

\item He is kept, not hired. He eats from the pan-house dish and sleeps under the pan-house roof, and what the pan gives back comes back as bread and a place by the fire, neither of which is entered. A dipper is paid by the pan-master in weather and never in ale. A man who offers ale is buying something; ask the price before you drink.

\item His birth-name is said once at the taking and not used at the pan. What he is called at the pan is a tide-name, and it is kept in the mouth and not on the leaf. A name in the mouth cannot be entered, and what cannot be entered is the only thing in Vhal the Council has never managed to tax.

\item The tide is said before the name, always. A name a man can change at a moot; a tide he cannot change at all. The day a child gives his name before his tide he is sent to the water’s edge and asked again, and the water does not answer him either.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a Council clerk, against rule 4:} The appellation is recorded. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I had written that the name is kept in the mouth. He strikes a mouth wherever he finds one. I have put the mouth back underneath, because a clerk who keeps a name on paper has never had to say it to the water at low tide.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the walk}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At fourteen the young go out barefoot on the crust at low tide, going out and not coming back until the water turns. Going back is the same walk and is called something else; nobody has ever told me what.

\item Each names a tide nobody has seen. Write the name in salt on the crust and let the sun have it. What is written in salt belongs to noon; what is said belongs to the person who said it. Do not write it on salt-paper. A thing that rots is no protection for a name that was never a contract.

\item Rake at the turn and rake at the fourth, and keep the rake going when there is nothing under it. A child who stops raking begins to ask what ought to come up, and a dipper who answers that question has begun to teach the wrong trade.

\item Do not look at the Glaze Cliffs while walking. They are sweet and they are lead, and a child who puts a green bead in his mouth is not long for the pans. Tell him why once. A warning about a taste is believed before a warning about a poison, which is the only useful thing I know about children.

\item The chief dipper keeps the names of the three great tides in his mouth and writes none of them. A child keeps the one he named himself until the sun takes it, and then keeps the place where it was.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the net and the draw}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Trail the net at dawn. The blessing is in the trailing and not in any word said over it. A net blessed at noon is a wet rope and nothing more, and the Council will pay the same for it, which is the difficulty.

\item Read what comes up. Do not read what ought to have come up. The Sallow runs against the wind and does not ask the moon, and a dipper who has learned what the tide should do has learned to miss the tide that did.

\item Bless the nets against the salt-thing, which follows boats at night and taps the hull where the store is. Carry a barrel of rain against it; fresh water stops it as a wall stops a man. Every captain denies the barrel and every captain carries one.

\item A brine-gull will lift a coal from the brazier and go off with it under its crop. No malice in it. Do not set a dipper to watch the coals in place of the net; the gull is honest and the net has a master.

\item We say the Sallow keeps a Hearth of its own beneath the salt and the Court’s fire is only its chimney. No one has taken me down to see the door of it, and I have stopped asking which way it opens. A dipper who claims to have seen it is selling something, generally a passage.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Of the tally and the paper}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Keep the tide-tallies on salt-paper and keep the paper dry. What Kett reads at the tide-tally house is the tide that was entered, and what the pan saw is another matter. Both are true; only one can be carried into a room with a Council table in it.

\item Write the draw and leave out what it meant. The Council pays for the first and has never asked for the second. A clerk who asks what a dipper meant has mistaken the tide for an account; there is no profit in answering him with another figure.

\item The assessors come against the pans with one in twelve as regular as gulls. Pay it out of the entered tide and never out of the seen one. This is not dishonesty; it is the arrangement by which a poor pan stays a pan and not an unclosed account.

\item A contract on salt-paper in wet weather is no contract, and half the port’s fortunes have turned on that. We do not say kindly to a pan-master, and a dipper who offers a favour without a price should be told that in Vhal a favour is a debt with no date, and a debt with no date keeps a man awake.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of walkings}

\emph{Kept by the girl who rakes the west pan. What is written is the tide that was seen and the day it was seen, in a hand that will not change between one line and the next.}

Year — The walking — What is taken\par

Twelve — The pan: rake, carry, mend net-rope with the old women — The birth-name, said once and not used again at the pan\par

Thirteen — The dawn net; hold the leading rope and say nothing — The habit of asking what ought to come up\par

Fourteen — The Salt Walk, barefoot on the crust at the turn — The tide-name, written in salt and gone by noon\par

Fifteen — The tally house; read the draw against the contract — The difference between the tide seen and the tide entered\par

Sixteen — Trail the net alone and bless it against the salt-thing — The last of the child’s account with any house\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sixteen is the common end of a walking and not a short one. A girl who has been walked is not paid out and sent away; she stays where the pan needs her, which may be at the west pan or at the Quay or on a boat whose share goes through her mother. The dipper does not choose which. The tide does, and the Council after it.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The table of faults}

Fault — As corrected at the pan\par

A tide-name written on salt-paper — The paper left out in the rain; the name said again to the water\par

A tide named that has already been seen — Sent out again at the next low tide, barefoot, going out\par

\emph{What ought to come up} spoken at the net — The net taken in; that day’s draw entered as nothing\par

A net set in the afternoon — The leading rope coiled and the child set to counting gulls for a tend\par

\emph{Kindly} said to a pan-master — Two bits owed, named on the spot, with a date\par

The Hearth beneath the salt asked about — Answered once: it is under the salt and the Court’s fire is its chimney. Asked twice: a barrel of rain carried three paces and set down\par

A tide sold to the Council and the other kept — Not entered. There is no law against it, which is why the pan does not speak of it\par

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item It is the only answer the pan has for a question the Council has never thought to ask, and a child who brings it up a second time is set to raking at the fourth where there is nothing under the rake.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The net-song, pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Sung at dawn, kneeling, with the leading rope in the hand and not yet in the water. The pan says the last line with the dipper. Nobody sings it at the Council table, and nobody sings it on the ebb.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rope in the hand and the salt on the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tide comes in where the wind isn’t;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape trail it low, trail it slow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and read what rises, not what should.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A coal goes up and a gull goes off,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a white bloom comes on the tarred board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pan keeps clean by what it takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk keeps what he can read.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Write it in salt, write it in sun,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name’s gone before the net comes in;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape carry the rain in a barrel by,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and speak to the water, not the men.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Rope in the hand and the salt on the knee,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one tide for the tally, one for the sea;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the one they pay for isn’t the one I saw ---\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one I saw is kept in me.\end{quote}

The press of the wet net across the second verse came from the song being sung in the rain at the outer pan, the rope laid on the leaf while a girl said the middle line. I have flattened it; the words hold.

\subsection*{What the borrowed hands did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf at Greybank, ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff, and struck the verbs out of it as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle past a table.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against rule 12 he set \emph{the draw was read} above my \emph{read what comes up}, which is a sentence true of every draw and therefore of none. I have put my words back underneath.

\item Against rule 4 he wrote \emph{the appellation is registered} and a round nought in the space where the tide-name had been. A nought is a figure. The tide was not a figure and has not come back to be entered.

\end{itemize}

A pan-master struck the line \emph{speak to the water, not the men} in charcoal and wrote above it \emph{and to the pan, which answers}. I have set his line above mine and struck it, and written mine under again, which is how a pan argues with a floor it cannot leave. The charcoal has come off on the fold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt bloom at the head came up in a wet week and has eaten the end of a word, which I have not written back; a word about a current that the weather has taken is truer than one a clerk can still read. The tar at the fold is mine, off the rope I coil every dusk. The peck-hole went through the first verse and nobody has claimed the bird. The fish-hook nick is from a basket set down over a disputed count of herrings. The ring of ale came off a ship’s master who would not drink until a question about the draw was answered; he has not been back. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Council’s, and I have not swept it. At the pans there is no Last Day and nothing gets burnt in the morning. The white place in the margin is where the tide-name was written. It was a good name and I will not write it in again, which is the same as saying it every morning.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The salt keeps the name till noon. The rope keeps what the net brings up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What was named and never came is kept in the mouth, and in no other place.\end{quote}

I asked a pan-master, a clerk of the Council and a woman who sells eels on the Quay, and got three answers and not one of them would put a name to his answer. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaves go back into the tin and the tin back on the shelf where it has never been washed; tomorrow the young go out barefoot at the turn, and I shall write what the water did and leave out what it meant, and be paid for the one and not asked for the other.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Salt Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Glass-Sickness, the Chill, the Bite and the Third Night, Set Down at the Quay in Vhal}
\CRsheetheading{The Salt Wife’s Book, Being Remedies for the Glass-Sickness, the Chill, the Bite and the Third Night, Set Down at the Quay in Vhal}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A boat-midwife’s and healer’s book of remedies in the Vhaleni tide-words, written in Grathic letters so a girl of the Quay could read it; the cures in a salt-wife’s hand, a lowland physician’s objections in the margin, and the corrections of a Council clerk set down on salt-paper that has since gone soft, with one song for the third night and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Quay in Vhal in Ember and Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Eda of the Quay, a midwife who went aboard with the eel-boats and kept the households of the glass-workers; begun on the back of a Council tide-table spoiled by rain and sewn with eel-sinew into an oiled sailcloth wrapper, carried up the Salt Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank onto the back of a discarded weigh-slip. It survives in a dry tin among a boat’s things, soft at the fold and sweet at the edges, with a green bead of cliff-glass pressed into the head, a thumb of tar, a white bloom of salt along the gutter, a ring of brine, a fish-hook nick, one correction the damp has eaten down to a figure with no verb, and a line struck through and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand.\par}\medskip
I write on the back of a tide-table the Council left out in the rain. The figures have gone where the Council’s figures go, which is nowhere a man can put his hand on, and what is left is paper enough for a book nobody has asked to see. I am a salt-wife of the Quay. I go aboard when a birth will not wait for the quay, and I keep the households of the glass women, who are the only people in Vhal who sweat sweetness. I have set down what we do and what the lowland physician at Greybank told me to do, and where the two disagree I have left both standing. A remedy is a thing the sea has been paid for already. A woman who takes a line out of a book of physic is answerable for the next body that takes it.

My hand is not a clerk’s. I put the verbs in because a direction without a verb is a thing a Council clerk can read aloud at a table and a woman cannot use at three in the morning with a boat coming up under her. The green at the head is not tar. It is a bead of cliff-glass a girl pressed into the leaf with her thumb while I was writing, and she had sweetness at her mouth and said nothing. The tar is mine, off the oar I held down in the wind. The salt along the gutter came up out of the paper itself. I have not washed any of it.

\subsection*{The order of a sick-room aboard}

\emph{Written small in the margin, with one word gone over in brine.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Get the brazier under the lee of the hold, not in the wind. A fire in a draught is a fire that has been taking warmth from somebody and giving it to the air. Nobody in this port will agree to pay for the air.

\item Set the sick one’s feet toward the ebb if the trouble is a chill, toward the flood if the trouble is a swelling. This is what we do. A lowland physician told me it should be toward the fire in either case, and both stand here.

\item Turn the slate face down before you go to the child, as the hearth-maids do in Grath. I have no slate-name and never shall; a salt-paper contract is a thing that rots in the damp, which is a virtue in this country and a folly in every other.

\item Salt the water before you wash a wound. The sea does it for nothing and we charge for it, which is the whole of our trade.

\item When the quay-crier calls the turn of the tide, stop and begin again after. He is counting something that is not in your room.

\end{itemize}

I have done three hundred births and I still look at the door before I look at the child. It is a trick the room plays on a woman. After the first hundred you stop calling it a habit and call it the order of things.

\subsection*{The remedies, as they are used}

Trouble — What is set to it — The manner of it — Who pays\par

Glass-sickness (the sweetness) — A draught of seawater, and cliff-glass scraped into it — The glass women rub their gums with it and say the sweetness answers sweetness. A lowland physician says it is the lead in the glaze and that the draught makes it worse. I have seen the pale line at the gum and the hand that cannot hold a cup. I have not seen the lead. — The glass furnace, which cannot stop and does not ask.\par

A chill off the water — A common stone warmed at the brazier, in a fold of wool; the feet to the ebb — To the belly, never the feet. Change it when it goes cold in your own hand, not when the child stops crying. A Grathic hearth-maid says a stone is a stone and not a kindness, and I have let her words stand. — The brazier, and whoever paid for the coal.\par

A hot wound, or a fever that burns — A cold-iron knife blade laid across it — We say the iron draws the heat out. A Keldish man at the quay told me cold iron draws and gives nothing back, and that a blade on a wound takes the measure as well as the heat. I have set his words beneath mine. — The wound. There is no other answer.\par

A bone set wrong — Two hands, a splint of straight reed, a fold of wet cloth — Set it while the vessel is quiet, before the swelling takes; leave the reed on till the third day. A bone-setter from Nine Pots says leave it a tend and a half. Both stand. — The patient, in the holding still.\par

A birth-flower — Salt, rubbed in — We call it the tide-mark and rub it with salt, believing the sea set it there. A Grathic woman crossed two fingers at the corner of one and gave me a date instead of an answer. I have put the date in the margin. — Nobody knows. The child’s skin, perhaps.\par

Milk that will not come — Another woman to hold the child while the mother sleeps — The favour is paid out of the other woman’s own house, and I say so before I ask it. — The other woman’s child.\par

A cut from glass — Tallow first, then a clean fold — Do not salt a glass cut if you can help it. The glass women salt everything, and their hands are mapped in white lines. — Whoever opened the furnace.\par

The bite of a salt-thing — Nothing I know — Keep her from the water at the turn. Salt does not hold that bite, and a brine-gull will take a coal off a brazier but will not take this. — Nobody. This is the honest column.\par

A child emptied by leeches — Nothing. Do not set them. — They draw through a small wound and leave the body thin; a collector would call it a draw and ask for a slate, and I have never seen one ask. If you find them on a child, take them off and count them, and do not put them back. — Whoever put them there.\par

The third-night chill — Warmth, quiet, and a watch kept till the fourth day — Keep her against a living body under the quilt and give barley water by the spoon. Do not leave her to sleep it off, and do not call a collector for the worsening; it is the night’s own work and goes off by the fourth morning. — The household, one night’s sleep and a loaf.\par

A lowland physician came up the Salt Road in Y.H. 798 with a book that said the sweetness came from the lead in the glaze. He left a page of it in the glass-house and went off with a purse. The page came back to me with the word taken clean away, as though a word could be taken off paper the way salt is taken off a net. I have written the word here in my own hand, which is a thing a salt-wife is not supposed to do. I have also left the draught of seawater standing under it, because it is what I have seen done for thirty years and I have not yet seen what it does to a person beyond the month.

\subsection*{The full note}

Tap a sound cup with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. The glass women know it in their cups and I have borrowed it from them. A girl of the furnace told me her mother used to tap the ribs of a sick man and say he had gone flat. I do not do it. A body is not a cup, and a cup’s answer is none of a person’s business.

The dippers say the Sallow gives back a note like a cup three-quarters full, and that the Council enters it as full because the difference is not worth a figure. I have left the three-quarters where I heard it. A figure a clerk can carry away in a cuff; a note is not.

\subsection*{The tide and the draw}

We say the draw runs seaward and a body empties into it. The dippers bless the nets at dawn so the eels will not notice, which is a kindness spent on eels. If the warm goes from the full to the empty, as the lowland books say, then a sick body turned to the ebb should lose what ails it. That is what I used to think. I have watched nine such bodies and eight of them went colder before the turn; the ninth did not, and she had been carried in the other direction by her daughter, who did not tell me. I have left the old line standing and set the nine beside it. When a thing has been done wrong nine times I want the ninth to keep her place.

There is a shape of salt and cold water in the Sallow that taps the hull and takes a boat’s store away. We call it the salt-thing. A healer who cannot tell a tide from a taking will set a sick man facing the water at the turn and wonder why he goes thin. I have done it. I do not say I was right.

\subsection*{The song for the third night}

\emph{Sung low, to the child, while the watch is kept. The room says the last line with her.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ebb takes and the ebb keeps,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the glass gives back what the furnace grieves;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a body is a boat with a seam\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seam is where the warmth leaves.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the brazier, two for the bite,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the hand that holds the light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the twelfth goes down and the twelfth comes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one goes out on a wind not seen.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three nights, three watches, a hand kept true;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what comes back is not what went;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape sing to the child, sing to the cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back on the flood. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

The twelfth is left where the twelfth should be. The Council would put a figure in it. A figure is a thing that can be written and then rained on and then entered again in a dry hand; a tide is not.

\subsection*{What the Council hand did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a market morning in Ember. He writes on salt-paper, and the salt-paper has taken the damp and let his hand go, so that of his three corrections only one figure and half a verb survive. Where I wrote \emph{the draught of seawater}, he set \emph{the measure is restored} above it, and the damp has eaten \emph{restored} so that only \emph{the measure is} stands. He put a round nought in the place of the unnamed tide and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it, and the vacancy has outlasted the nought, which is the Council’s own art in a small space.

I have put my words back under what is left of his. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them in because a woman on a boat at three in the morning does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand to hold the child with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The green bead at the head was pressed in with a thumb and has left a sweet smear that will not dry. The tar is off the oar, and came off when I held the sheet down on deck in a wind that was taking everything else. The bloom along the gutter is salt out of the paper and not out of the sea, which is a thing only a person who has kept salt-paper knows the difference of. The ring of brine came from a cup set down while I was telling a girl to eat and she would not; the hook nick came off a man paying me with his hook still in his hand, and he did not apologize. The grey print at the foot is not mine and not the Council’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a tin.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The sea keeps what it takes. It has no slate and no clerk, and it does not call it a debt.\end{quote}

I asked the dippers, the glass women and a factor come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The tin goes back among the boat’s things and the leaf goes aboard when the ebb comes. A girl will press another bead into it and say nothing, and I shall put the verbs back where the damp has taken them.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second Chill, Being a Letter from Wenna, an Old Hearth-Maid at Cold Acre, to Milla, Newly Set to the Birth-Slates in Low Kiln, on the Warming of Stones, the Three Days, the Collector’s Tube, and the Name Written Before the Face Is Looked At; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk’s Entry in Ledgerhand, and a Washing Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Second Chill, Being a Letter from Wenna, an Old Hearth-Maid at Cold Acre, to Milla, Newly Set to the Birth-Slates in Low Kiln, on the Warming of Stones, the Three Days, the Collector’s Tube, and the Name Written Before the Face Is Looked At; with the Answer in the Margin, a Clerk’s Entry in Ledgerhand, and a Washing Verse in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter in a hearth-maid’s small careful hand, written on the back of a birth-slate rubbing taken before the ink had set; folded thrice and tied with a twist of grey wool, carried down from the ridge in a potter’s wife’s apron, answered along the margin in a younger hand, corrected on the back at the Court’s table in Slate Row, and kept since in the birth-flower shrine’s slate-box among the slates that have been answered · Written at Cold Acre, two leagues north of Sill on the ridge where the one well does not freeze, in the last tend of Tallow, Y.H. 813, by Wenna, who has kept the birth-slates of that ridge for thirty-one years, to Milla, a maid newly set to the slates in Low Kiln after the kilns were brought up. Carried down the ridge road in a potter’s wife’s apron, answered in the margin, and borrowed at the Court’s table in Slate Row, where a clerk set a correction on the back in the neat upright Ledgerhand. It survives folded in the shrine’s slate-box: beeswax from the shrine candle worked into the grain at the head, a thumb of slip from the hand that held the rubbing, one drop of birth-water gone brown in the fold, grey Ash along the gutter where a cuff was laid, a curl of grey wool through the tie-hole which the writer will not untie, a tallow thumb at the outer fold, a tideline where well-water came up over the lower leaf, the clerk’s correction standing above the words, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
To Milla at the shrine in Low Kiln, who has begun to put her hand to the slate before she puts it to the child. From Wenna at Cold Acre, where the well has not frozen in thirty-one winters and nobody on the ridge has ever thought to say why.

I write on the back of a rubbing I took off a slate before the writing had set, so that you have the true hand and not a fair one. A fair copy is a thing a clerk makes. Do not rub the fold. The birth-water has eaten into it and it will come apart between your fingers if you rub it, and then you will have a clean piece of paper and nothing on it, which is what the Court would like every birth to end as.

You wrote to ask about the child who went worse on the third day. You wrote it down as a question about a child and I have read it three times and it is a question about a stone. I will answer the stone. The child will hear the answer over her mother’s shoulder and will not know she has heard it, which is the whole of our trade.

\subsection*{The stone}

Put it at the middle and not at the ends. A warmed stone goes to the belly, under the wool and against the skin, and stays there while you count three breaths and then three more. The hands and feet are wrapped and left. They are not rubbed and they are not set to the fire, and if a neighbour tells you to hold the foot to the hearth you say that the house has spoken and carry the stone back to the middle, because a woman who spends her heat on the extremity has none left for the part that can keep it. The chill comes up from the ends and settles in the middle on the second or third day, and it is the second chill and not a sickness and not a thing to be entered. Call it that where the mother can hear you and call it nothing where the father can. A name spoken in a room becomes a figure by supper in this country.

I have had thirty-one winters at this well and I have never once seen a stone that was too warm for a child and four that were too cold. A stone taken fresh from the fire will burn a belly as easily as it will burn a hand, so hold it to your own wrist before you put it to the child, the way you would taste a spoon of broth before you give it. The wrist knows. The eye does not.

\subsection*{The three days, as I keep them}

What is done to the child — What goes on the slate — What must not go on it\par

The first day — The stone to the belly; the child to the breast; the birth-flower covered — The house, the day, the hour before first grey — A name you would keep\par

The second day — Wrap and leave the cold ends; count the breaths; do not rub — The day again, in the same hand — What the child said in the night\par

The third day — Keep the stone if the chill came; give the child over — The name if the mother has given it; else the date and no more — The chill, the stone, the neighbour’s advice\par

A birth is entered within three days, which is a rule the College wrote and the hearth-maids keep because it was ours before it was theirs. A hand goes to the slate before it goes to the child, and a hand that goes the other way has already decided what the slate will say and will spend the rest of the evening making the child agree with it. Write the day first. The face will tell you the rest in its own time and will keep telling you for a year.

Alda Reed crossed two fingers over a birth-flower on the seventh day of Stone and would not say the word for it. I have crossed two fingers over nine children in this room and never once told a person what I saw under them, and I am not telling you now, though you are my maid and have a right to the practical part. Cross the fingers. Say nothing. The day you tell somebody what you saw is the day it gets written down, and a thing written down in this country does not stay a thing you saw. It becomes a figure in a column, and the column goes up the road.

\subsection*{The man with the tube}

He will come before the three days are out if the house has owed, which in Low Kiln is most houses. He takes the mother’s attention first, and that is a kindness the Court has never entered, because a woman who is being asked for her warmth will look at the man asking and not at the child, and the child is left to the stone and to you. Give him the mother and keep the child behind the slate. If he asks what the stone is for, tell him it is for the warmth. It is for the warmth. That is a true answer and has no figure in it and he cannot put it on a slate without putting a warmth on a slate, which no man does while he is standing in the room where the warmth is.

Do not say no to him. We do not say no. We put the pot between the child and the door and we talk to the pot about the weather until he has gone back over the bridge, and the pot has never once been asked what it held. If he leaves a pale ring on the mother’s wrist, do not rub it and do not cover it before he has gone. Cover it after. A thing covered too soon looks like a thing hidden, and a thing hidden is a thing that will be asked about twice.

\subsection*{The washing verse}

\emph{Sung low to the stone, with the child at the belly and the wool drawn up. Never across the room. The second verse is the one my mother sang and I have set it under yours so you can see where the words change.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stone from the hearth and wool from the ewe,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the second chill comes through and through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape warm the middle and wrap the end,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house will keep what the house can mend.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four at the well and one gone dry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hand on the slate before the eye;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name goes down and the face comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the stone keeps warm in the old tin’s cup.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Wash the pot and leave the ring,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate takes one and the child takes nothing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cross two fingers and hold your tongue,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the count comes back to the one it came from.\end{quote}

I keep a stone from every birth in a tin under the bench, thirty-one of them and not one marked. A clerk would look at that tin and call it a count and ask me for the figures, and when I gave him none he would write \emph{unentered residue} above it and go away satisfied, because a figure with nobody in it satisfies that kind of man more than a figure with a person in it. It is not a count. It is a tin of stones. If you keep such a thing, keep it where the light does not fall on it and never put a mark on any stone, for a marked stone is a slate and a slate can be read by anybody who can hold it.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a younger hand, set close to the lines}

It was the second day, not the third. I have struck your three through and put two underneath in your own iron-gall so that you cannot say a stranger wrote it. The child was cold in one foot and I wrapped it and did not rub it and did not set it to the fire, and the foot stayed dark until the morning and then came back of itself while I was counting breaths at the belly. I set the stone to my own wrist first, as you say, and it was too hot the first time and I waited. I did not cross two fingers over the mark on her skin because I did not know the sign was mine to make, and nobody at the shrine has told me whose it is. Tell me what to do when the man with the tube comes, because I do not know whether to give him the mother or the child and I cannot ask the mother in front of him and I will not ask him. I have kept the stone. It is under the bench and it is not marked.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did}

A clerk of the Court’s table borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. Against \emph{the second chill} he set \emph{a common event; no entry}. Against \emph{do not rub the foot} he wrote \emph{no remedy applied}, which is true and cold and leaves out the woman who did the not rubbing. Against \emph{give him the mother and keep the child behind the slate} he set \emph{the measure is drawn as provided}. Against the tin of stones he wrote \emph{residue unentered}. At the foot of the count he put a round nought and wrote \emph{no vacancy}, where I had written that the child came back of herself while I counted.

He takes the verbs out of a thing and leaves the figures standing, as though a thing always true had no need of anybody to do it. He can enter the chill as common and the stone as residue and the ring as a thing provided, because all of those have a place in his book. He cannot enter the wrist that tested the heat or the fingers that stayed crossed, and he has not tried. I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above, where they belong, the way the Ash is left in the corner until the morning after the Last Day and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The wax at the head is off the shrine candle I held over the rubbing while the ink was still wet; it went into the grain in a drop and no knife takes it out clean. The slip came off the hand that held the slate down, and it is the fine grey slip from the upper pit and not the coarse, which is why it stayed in the fold instead of falling through. The brown in the fold is birth-water and has eaten two words off the back; I have not written them in again, because a verse with two words gone is a verse said slowly and all of ours are said slowly. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it and there is no Last Day in a slate-box. The curl of grey wool through the tie-hole is mine and I tied it there for the word I could not put down, and I will not untie it.
