The tallow is off the lamp I kept low so that the mother would not know I was writing and change the account for me. The tideline is well-water, from the pail set down on the lower leaf while I was telling Milla about the stone, and it has taken the corners off two lines without taking the sense.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone keeps the belly and not the name; the slate keeps the name and not the cold. Between the two a woman carries the child, and sets it down, and goes to the next room.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who brings the well-water, a potter’s wife come up to have her mark confirmed, and a man who reads the notices at the Cross, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before about the grey print and the two words gone. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the slate-box with the slates that have been answered. Tomorrow there will be another child up the ridge and I will put a stone in the tin and not mark it, and Milla will put her hand to the slate before she puts it to the child, and neither of us will call the tin an account.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second File, Being the Names Removed from the Rolls at the College of Assessors in the Hearthseat, with the Figures Struck, the Figures Set Above, and the Reasons Not Entered}
\CRsheetheading{The Second File, Being the Names Removed from the Rolls at the College of Assessors in the Hearthseat, with the Figures Struck, the Figures Set Above, and the Reasons Not Entered}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A leaf copied forward from the College’s second file at the Opening of the Slates; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand of the junior set to the tin, the names withheld into another hand, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College, a column struck and drawn back, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Copied at the Hearthseat in Slate Row, in the College of Assessors, on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, the Opening of the Slates, from the tin that lies beside the sealed-file room; carried in the inner pocket of a junior’s coat until the copying was checked. It survives with slate dust worked into the gutter, an iron-gall thumb at the head, a damp tide-line along the foot out of the sealed-file room, a grey Ash print nobody will claim, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a small square of bare paper where a name was scraped away with a knife, one column struck and drawn back underneath, two corrections in the narrow upright hand, and one line at the foot that has never been owned\par}\medskip
I copy the second file forward. It lies in a tin beside the sealed-file room, and once a year at the Opening I take the leaves out, set them in order and copy them into a fresh hand. The names are not on the leaf I copy. They are kept in the tin in another hand, and I have never been shown which hand; the College holds that a boy who is set to copy removals has no need of the names he removes. I write the shape of each removal, the figure struck, the figure set above, and the remark. That is the whole of my office.

A removal is not a death and not a forgiveness. It is a correction to the roll. The roll is never wrong, so the person entered in it must be. I set that down because it is what the College does, not because I admire it; a clerk who admires his own work has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{The order of the file}

The name goes off the roll in the same hand that put it on. This is the first thing a junior is taught and the last thing he forgets: a hand that changes between one entry and the next is a hand that can be accused of feeling something. The figure is struck through and a figure set above it, or no figure set above and the place left standing. A reason is not entered. There is a column for the reason in the tin and it is blank from the first leaf to the last, which is a finer arrangement than a column struck out, because a struck column invites a man to ask what was in it.

Twelve bits to a mark; twenty marks to a Sere crown that does not stay in the Hearthseat. An ember is called five marks in this College and no junior has ever seen one exchanged. One in twelve is printed on the notice across the way and is the figure every boy in this room learns to write before he is allowed to write his own name. I have copied it into the removals more times than I can count and have never once set it against a removal, because a removal is not a deduction. A deduction takes a part of a measure. A removal takes the man who was carrying it.

\subsection*{The leaf, as I copied it}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are those set down in the tin, in the hand that kept the file, and are not part of the account. A dash is a place where no figure was set above, not a nought.}

Manner of removal — Figure struck — Figure set above — Remark\par

A boy who could not learn the hand — 19 — — — The hand was his own. No man took it from him. Entered in the same hand as those who stayed.\par

A vessel returned three times, entered whole by order — 29 — 30 — \emph{Whole} set above the earlier figure. The earlier figure kept here. Joined to neither.\par

A number cut out of an arm and a new number cut in — 41 — 39 — The later figure entered. The earlier stands in the skin. Nobody asked which count was his.\par

A debt bought before it was due — 52 — — — Assignee entered; debtor not asked. The debt kept its figure and lost its man.\par

A whole return announced for a person not in the room — 300 — — — Room empty. Name not spoken. The file does not say where the person was.\par

A sealed file carried beyond the room — — — — — Carrier’s own name set where the other stood. The first entry left standing beside it.\par

A hand greyed by cold work — 38 — — — The hand struck off the rolls; the fingers greyed. The figure is not struck.\par

Forty of Low Kiln, one slate for the batch, by lot — — — — — Names not taken. Figure entered elsewhere. Nothing carried up into this tin.\par

A foundling left at the mill, stone under him — 12 — — — No name to remove. Stands till a hearth claims him. Copied here and not entered.\par

A keeper who drew without authority, Y.H. 618 — 60 — — — An old leaf, carried forward every year. The figure stands and the name does not.\par

A measure entered in a house roll only — 33 — — — Court never picked it up. Struck by no hand, called forgiven by no hand.\par

Removals copied on this leaf: eleven. Figures struck: eight. Figures set above: two. Names set down: none. Reasons entered: none.

\subsection*{What the narrow hand did}

The Provost’s clerk borrowed the leaf after I had copied it and before it went back into the tin. He writes upright and takes the doer out of every sentence, as though a thing with nobody in it were truer than a thing a man had done.

Where I had copied \emph{they took his name off the roll}, he set \emph{the name was removed from the roll} above it, and above that \emph{the removal is recorded}. I have put my line back underneath and left his standing over it. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these removals in the end, always at a door, always after the tin is shut.

Against the vessel returned three times he struck my \emph{the earlier figure kept here} and wrote \emph{superseded} above it. Both stand. \emph{Superseded} is the word the Weighing uses and the word a household hears in a clean voice. \emph{Kept here} is the word I use when I am not reading anything aloud. I have not chosen between them, and would thank any man who told me I must.

He struck my last column and wrote \emph{No such column} over it. I drew the column back underneath. A man does not count the rows of a column before he writes that there is nothing in it unless the column has troubled him, and he counted every row.

\subsection*{The column with no heading}

I keep the figure that stood before the removal beside the figure the College will read. I have set no heading over it. A heading would make it an account, and an account is a thing a man may be called to answer for, and this College has answered for enough.

On the arm with two sets of numbers the older figure was thirty-nine and the later forty-one, and the file carries them in that order, which is the order in which the knife went into the skin. The roll carries forty-one alone. A surveyor would say the roll is right and the arm is wrong, because a roll has one figure and an arm can have two. I have set down both and joined neither. A clerk who joins two figures to make them agree has begun to keep an account of a man, and the College pays for those by the leaf.

The foundling has no removal. He has a figure and a stone and no name, which is a different absence from the absences in the rest of this tin, and I have kept it on its own line and not laid it across any of them. Seven absences standing in a row are seven; they do not become an account until somebody stands under them to pay, and nobody in this room has stood.

\subsection*{The verse the copyists say}

\emph{Said low at the Opening, while the tin is open and the ink is still wet, never in the Weighing Hall and never with the door toward Slate Row. The last line is said to the tin.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Strike the figure, set the other,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape leave the reason where it stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one in twelve as the notice says,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the roll is always good.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Name goes up and name goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape same neat hand from first to last;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what the arm keeps the roll forgets,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house keeps what the roll passed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four turns the wheel and the fifth held back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the tin keeps what the tin was told;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape hold the empty column open,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the only one we hold.\end{quote}

A junior who had been set three Openings to the file said the first two lines while I checked the counting and would not say the last while the Provost’s clerk was in the room, which is how I know the last line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A clerk who explains a verse has begun to write a sermon.

\subsection*{In the tin and in the gutter}

The slate dust in the gutter came off the floor of this room, where it gathers under the benches and goes into the grain of whatever is laid down. The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, from holding the quire open through an Opening morning; there are juniors in this College who can tell a copyist by his thumb before he has spoken a word. The damp line along the foot came out of the sealed-file room, which takes the damp in every season and gives it back to everything kept beside it. The grey print on the outer edge is Ash and is not mine; I found it on the leaf when I took the tin out and have not brushed it away. On the Last Day they sweep the corners of houses and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a tin beside a sealed room.

The green bead in the lower corner is lead glaze and not slip. A girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see the figures while I copied and touched the leaf and said nothing and went back down the road. I have left it where she put it. The small bare square is where a name was scraped off with a knife before this leaf was given to me. I did not cut it and cannot read what was there. I have not put a name back and have not tried to.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The first file keeps the name. The second keeps the place the name stood in. Neither of them keeps the man.\end{quote}

I asked the Provost’s clerk, a woman who came to ask after a house in the low country, and a collector come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the tin and the tin beside the sealed-file room. Tomorrow a boy will be taught to write a life with nobody in it, and a name will be taken off a roll in the same neat hand that put it on, and I shall copy the shape of it forward with the reason column standing blank. Nothing has been joined, named or closed. The empty column stays open, which is the only column in this College nobody has thought to strike.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Broken Pot, Being What Was Said at the Bone Orchard on the Remembering of Y.H. 812}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Broken Pot, Being What Was Said at the Bone Orchard on the Remembering of Y.H. 812}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pot-break sermon preached at the shrine of broken pots outside Sill’s north gate, over the year’s pots and the one pot nobody brought; the manner of the breaking in the niche-keeper’s hand, the sayings in Grathic, the breaking-song in verse, the row of pots in a tally, a factor’s clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand set above the keeper’s verbs, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached by an old woman of Sill who had broken pots at the Bone Orchard for one and thirty years, on the Remembering of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, over the pots set in the niche a league north of the Cross; written that evening by the woman who keeps the niche, in charcoal and with the point of a broken nail on the inner face of a grave-tile that came away whole when it should have broken, and kept under the flat stone among the sherds. It survives with grey Ash ground into the slip along the gutter, a salt bloom in a hairline at the head, a tallow thumb where the tile was held down on a man’s knee, a green bead of lead glaze caught in a chip of the rim, a morsel of dry clay in the fold, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a factor’s clerk come out from Greybank that takes the verbs out and numbers the nameless pot as nil, and one line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand nobody will own. Copied forward in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the empty place left the length it is.\par}\medskip
I keep the niche of broken pots at the Bone Orchard. It is my work to set the year’s pots in a row and lift the flat stone on the Remembering and put the sherds back. What follows is written on the back of a grave-tile that came away whole from the row and would not break, so I kept it, the way this ground keeps everything that fails at the work it was made for.

The old woman stood with her back to the north gate and spoke first to the pots, as potters do, and to the clay under them, and to the fire that had made them, and only at the end to the people standing in the row. She had broken pots here for one and thirty years and had never once broken one at the foot. She said the same things every year. I have written them as she said them, with the verbs where she put them, because a sermon said over a pot is a thing a household has to use.

The grey in the gutter came off my cuff when I measured the ridge two doors down in Low Kiln and came back to write, and I have not swept it. The salt at the head is from a woman’s hand laid flat on the tile to hold it still in the wind off the ridge. The tallow is mine. The green bead is not slip; a girl with sweetness still at her mouth leaned over to see what I was writing and touched the rim with her thumb. The tile has a chip at the upper right where somebody tapped it with a knuckle and did not say what answer it gave.

\subsection*{The manner of the breaking, as the niche keeps it}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Set the pots in a row on the flat stone with their lips to the north. Feet toward water is for the body; lips toward the Hearth is for the pot. Do not mix the two.

\item Tap each pot with the knuckle before you lift it. Listen for what it answers. Do not say what you heard where a man with a slate is standing.

\item Break at the lip with one blow. A blow at the foot sends the heat into the clay and the clay will keep it, which is a kind of burying twice.

\item Break it whole. A pot broken into dust has let the heat out through a hundred little doors and cannot say which way it went.

\item If a pot answers flat, break it gently. It has given already and asks no help from you.

\item When the bell comes up the north road from the Cross, stop. It has counted something that is not your pot. Begin again after. Four, four and a gap, and the gap is not ours to fill.

\item Break the nameless pot last. Do not let anybody bring it. It comes out of the niche by itself.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as she said it}

\subsection*{Of the lip and the foot}

She put her thumb in the chip at the rim of a milk pot and turned it so the row could see where the star was.

“You bring me a pot and you say, break this, it is my mother’s. I ask you nothing. I break it at the lip, because the lip is the mouth and the heat goes out of a mouth the way breath goes out of a person. Break it at the foot and you have put your mother’s warmth into the ground twice: once in the grave and once under the grave, where the clay keeps it and will not let it go.”

She struck the pot with the heel of her hand and it opened clean across, two pieces and a third small one that fell among the sherds.

“A whole pot keeps. A broken pot gives. That is the whole of my preaching and I have had one and thirty years to find another sentence and could not.”

\subsection*{Of the note}

“Before I break, I tap. You have all heard a pot tapped at the wheel. A sound one answers full and a cracked one answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. You bring me a pot that answered flat three days before the person went and you say nothing about it, and I say nothing either. We are not fools in this district. We know what a pot was doing while we were looking at the person.”

She tapped the cup with the cupworm in it. It gave nothing that I could hear from where I sat, and she put it down on its side.

“This one I break gently. It has been giving since it came off the wheel and there is no heat in it to let out. Do not break a pot that has given already as though it had held. That is a cruelty to the pot and a lie about the household.”

One of the women in the row said that a pot was only a pot. The old woman turned her head a degree toward her and said: “A body is only a body, too, and we wash it and put its feet to the water and send for a man with a tube. Do not tell me what a pot is. I have made them.”

\subsection*{Of the one nobody brought}

There is one pot in the niche that no household brings. It is a plain clay pot, smaller than a milk pot, with no mark on it and a lip worn smooth by hands that have lifted it every Remembering since I can remember. The old woman took it out from under the flat stone and held it a moment against her apron before she set it on the row.

“This is for them that have no house to break for them,” she said. “The little graves lie over there beyond the broken stake, shallow, because the clay was frozen when they were put in. You can walk past them and not see them, and people do, and I do not blame them, because a person can only look at so much in a winter.”

She struck it at the lip. It opened with a dry sound, smaller than the milk pot’s, and the three pieces lay where they fell.

“The Court reads a whole return at the Weighing in a clean voice for a person not in the room. I have heard it done. I have stood outside the door and heard it done, and come up here and broken this. Somebody has to break for the ones the clean voice does not name. That is not an argument with the Court. It is a pot with a name left out of it.”

She would not say how many graves lay beyond the broken stake, and when the clerk asked her she said the clay was frozen and she had not counted that year. A woman beside me wrote something in the margin of her tally and covered it with her thumb. I have not read it and it is not on this tile.

\subsection*{Of the keeping}

A factor’s clerk had come out from Greybank with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers, and stood at the end of the row with a slate held to his forearm. He asked the old woman what became of the heat once the pot was broken.

“It goes up,” she said. “That is what I know of it. It goes up out of the mouth and into the air and the air is bigger than the house. I have stood at more breakings than I could set a figure to, and never once seen it come back to the pot.”

“It is banked,” the clerk said.

“It is gone from the pot,” she said. “I have not said where from. Those are two sentences and I will not have one put over the other.”

“Nothing is lost that we have kept,” he said, in the voice that takes the speaker out of his sentence.

“I have never kept one,” she said. “I have let go of a great many. If the Hearth wants what went up, let the Hearth come out of its iron and fetch it. It has not come yet, and I have been waiting one and thirty years.”

After that she gave the mark on the niche the same answer she gives every year. The clerk asked what it was, the crossed thing cut in the stone above the pots, which the surveyor draws in the chart and does not explain. She said it was cut in Y.H. 668. He asked her again in a different way and she gave him the same year.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the margin, in my hand:} A date is safe. The factor’s clerk says so himself, and he is right, because a date is the only answer that cannot be argued with. I have set down her year and left the question standing.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The breaking-song}

\emph{Sung low, standing, while the nameless pot is lifted out of the niche. The row says the last line with her. There is a gap before the last line, the one the bell leaves, and I have left it here as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Break at the lip and not at the foot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the heat goes up and not into the root;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a whole pot holds and a cracked pot gives,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay keeps only what the clay receives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners, four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where a name should fall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell comes four and four and a gap,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the pot gives back what the pot had.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not ask the fire where the fire has gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape do not ask the ground what it stands upon;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say the name, or leave the place it had,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and come back warm, as the Keeping said.\end{quote}

A girl from High Kiln asked what the space before the last line was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it later, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The row, as the niche counts it}

Pot — Brought by — Broken — What was said over it\par

Milk pot, lip starred — a woman of High Kiln — at the lip, one blow — her mother’s name, said three times\par

Cup with a cupworm in it — a man of the Clay Yard — at the foot, by mistake — nothing; the heat went into the clay\par

The nameless pot — the niche — at the lip — no name; a place left the length of one\par

A grave-tile, came away whole — nobody — not broken — kept, and written on\par

There were two and twenty pots in the row besides these, and I have not set them down, because a tally of pots is a thing a clerk can carry away and a name is not. The two and twenty went into the barrow with the grey the next market-day and nobody in the square looked at it twice.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He borrowed the tile on the morning after and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where she said \emph{a whole pot keeps, a broken pot gives}, he wrote \emph{retention and leakage are lawful conditions of a vessel} above and left hers below.

\item Where she said \emph{the heat goes up}, he wrote \emph{the measure is released to the keeping} and underlined it twice.

\item At the nameless pot he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it, and when I asked him what a pot was worth that nobody had brought, he said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning.

\item At the line about the Hearth coming to fetch its heat he wrote \emph{claim not established}, and drew a small stop between two clusters of his neat dark hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath where she put them and left his hand standing above, as the flat stone leaves the sherds and the sherd leaves the clay. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman standing in the cold wants to know who did the letting go, and whether it was her own hand.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the old woman’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole pot is a lie told by a sound vessel.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole pot is a vessel that has not yet been asked.\end{quote}

I asked the old woman, the woman of High Kiln, the man who brought the cupworm cup, the girl who asked about the gap, and the clerk, and had five answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The tile goes back under the flat stone with the flat side down, so the writing is kept from the wet. Next Remembering I shall lift the stone and set the row out, and the nameless pot will come out of the niche and be broken at the lip as it is every year. If the clerk comes again I shall let him take the verbs out. I shall put them back.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What Iyn of the Listening Stone Said to a Boy at His First Sitting in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Sayings Said Twice, the Sitting-Song Left with a Season in It, the Sittings in a Register, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Counting Stone, Being What Iyn of the Listening Stone Said to a Boy at His First Sitting in Bone of Y.H. 812, with the Sayings Said Twice, the Sitting-Song Left with a Season in It, the Sittings in a Register, a Survey-Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Vorr preached at the shrine of the counting stones five leagues above Keld Keep in the high Rim; the sayings in the slow long-vowelled Rim speech set down in Grathic letters, the sitting-song with every line said twice and the season left the length it is kept, the sittings in a high-path register, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court survey-clerk come up from Greybank, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached on Bone 12, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at the third stone from the high path, by Iyn of the Listening Stone at the setting-out of a boy’s first Long Sitting; written that evening by the woman who keeps the sitting-register at Keld Keep, in charcoal on the back of a rim-seam rubbing spoiled by a wet slate, folded with a pinch of blighted-seam dust in the crease and sewn with wire into oiled survey-cloth, and kept in the register-box beside the high-path door. It survives with pale lichen worked into the head off the north stone, the print of a doubled last joint pressed in tallow at the second corner, rime from the high path ground into the fold, a warm-stone shaving that held its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, a thread of copper wire off the spoiled rubbing, a wet ring where a dish of meltwater stood from the first saying to the last, a grey Ash print nobody will own, the dust shut in the crease, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter lead, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the season left the length it is kept.\par}\medskip
I keep the sitting-register at Keld Keep, in a box beside the high-path door, and nobody asked me for this. There is no word for shrine in the Vorr tongue; they call the stones the stones, and a man below who says \emph{shrine} has named what he cannot see. I write because the boy had no name. A Vorr takes his name one at a time, many years apart, and is known until then by the stone he keeps, so I have entered him as the boy of the third stone and left the place where a name would stand the length a name would be.

He spoke to the stone, the dust, the dish of meltwater, and last to the boy, the order the Vorr use when a season is waiting and somebody below may be listening who wants a figure. He said every sentence twice. I have set the second beneath where it mattered and left it out where it did not, a freedom no Vorr would take and they have never asked me for this leaf.

The pale at the head is lichen scraped off the north stone; it goes into the grain and no wet sleeve takes it out. The doubled print at the second corner is his, pressed into my lamp’s tallow while he turned the leaf; a Vorr’s last joint is split in two and leaves a mark like a cleft hoof. The rime in the fold was on the path at first grey and was water by the time I folded. The shaving kept its heat one night on the stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The copper thread came off the spoiled rubbing and has nothing to do with the sermon. The ring is the dish, set down at the first saying and taken up before the boy saw it. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it; there is no Last Day above this Keep.

\subsection*{The manner of the sitting, as the stone has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Come at first grey, before the seam-tide turns. A boy who comes at noon sits in another man’s season and calls it his own, and the stone has never once corrected him.

\item Sit facing the way you came. An elder will turn a boy around without a word if he faces the road, and the road is not the direction this shrine keeps.

\item Put the dust on the palm, not on the stone. The stone marks what is kept; the hand marks who keeps it.

\item Say each sentence twice. Once for the stone and once for the boy. A third saying is the sayer’s fault; the stone has heard three before and will hear three thousand.

\item Do not say the number before the season ends. A number said early has a buyer, and a man from Greybank would pay for it and enter it wrongly.

\item The first sitting gives a number and not a name. A boy who asks for his name is given the number again, which is not anger but the arrangement of years this people keeps.

\item A season is not an hour. The impatient hear the stone scratch and bring home a number they could have had at home.

\item A number goes down the road. The dust stays. If a man from the Court writes one, let him write the number and not the sitting; the two have never agreed.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the dust}

He took a pinch of grey from a fold of his coat and pressed it into the boy’s palm with the doubled joint of his last finger. The dust is marked off a blighted seam and is not sold.

“This is put down. It is not given.”

\begin{quote}\itshape This is put down. It is not given.\end{quote}

“A thing given can be taken back. A thing put down stays where it was put. I have never given a boy anything in forty years and have had no cause to ask anything back.”

“The Court has a word for what is put down and a column to put it in. This has no column. If you find one on the road below, do not stand in it.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He used the word for \emph{put down} that the factor’s clerk at Greybank translates as \emph{retained}. I have left both standing, as the dust lies on the palm and not under it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the first sitting}

“You will sit until the number changes. It changes. That is the whole of the sitting.”

“Ask what it changes to and I will say the numbers are correct. That answers the numbers, not you. A third asking is yours.”

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask what it changes to and I will say the numbers are correct. That answers the numbers, not you. A third asking is yours.\end{quote}

“You want a name. The stone gives a number. Names come one at a time and many years apart, and a man here is known by the stone he keeps. I have kept this one forty years and have not been given the other word.”

A girl from the Keep asked what the boy was to be called. He gave her the number. She asked again in another way and he gave her the same number. I have set the two askings down and not joined them.

\subsection*{Of the bone}

“The count is in the bone. The tube finds nothing there.”

\begin{quote}\itshape The count is in the bone. The tube finds nothing there.\end{quote}

“They below take what is in the blood and write it on a slate. We keep ours where no iron reaches. A thing a man cannot take is a thing he will not call a gift.”

“We were never owed. We do not ask.”

\begin{quote}\itshape We were never owed. We do not ask.\end{quote}

A miner stood at the back with a pale ring at his wrist. When the elder said the last, the miner covered the ring and went down the path before the boy had heard the saying twice. I have written the hand and not the man.

\subsection*{Of what goes down}

“A stone is kept. A number is sold.”

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone is kept. A number is sold.\end{quote}

A Court survey-clerk had come up with ink in two fingers and held his slate inward so the row could not see the column.

“You will carry the number down in a clean hand and read it in a room I have never stood in,” the elder said to him. “I have given you the number and not the sitting. Do not lay one over the other.”

“The measure is declared and the person is identified,” the clerk said, in the voice that takes the speaker out of his own sentence. He wrote it down and put the boy in a column where no boy had stood before.

“If the Court’s fire is a candle lit from our mountain,” the elder said, turning toward the stone and not the clerk, “it has never been brought up here to light this one.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In my hand:} He said that to the stone. The clerk wrote \emph{claim not examined} against it, true of a man who has never climbed five leagues of scree. Both stand.\end{quote}

Higher on the path a body sat facing the way it had come, with no fire and no word read over it. The elder said: “He came from there. He faces there. The sitting is finished. No one goes up to bring him down. There is no slate at a Vorr death and no return, and we do not ask the account below to make one.”

\subsection*{The sitting-song}

\emph{Said low, facing the stone, the dust in the palm. The elder says each line twice and the boy says the last four twice after him. There is a season between the third part and the last, the length of a sitting, and I have left the space the length it is kept.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone was here before the sitting.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone was here before the sitting.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dust is on the hand and the hand is on the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dust is on the hand and the hand is on the stone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the way you came and one for the way you face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the way you came and one for the way you face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes in where the bone is old,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number goes in where the bone is old;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the count comes down and the stone stays up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the count comes down and the stone stays up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Here the boy sits for a season. No words are said. The space is the season and I have left it the length it is kept.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number changes. The stone does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number changes. The stone does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We were never owed. We do not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We were never owed. We do not ask.\end{quote}

A girl from the shift asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it and wrote \emph{vacancy}, which is the first figure of his that has ever fitted anything above this Keep, and still does not fit, because a nought is a number and the space is a season. I have left it where he set it.

\subsection*{The sittings, as the register keeps them}

\emph{The number goes down the high path in a coat and leaves nothing in the box. These I have set down where they stood, without saying what the numbers count, because I do not know and the Vorr have never told me.}

Who kept the stone — Count before — Count after — What was entered at Greybank\par

Iyn of the Listening Stone, at his third sitting — 41 — 41 — figures confirmed; no proceedings\par

A woman of the high path, at her second — 17 — 17 — number unchanged; no cause assigned\par

Ao of the Third Seam, before the Rim War — 9 — 14 — change entered; reason withheld\par

The boy of this morning, first sitting — not yet counted — the sitting continues — a column standing\par

One seated higher on the path facing the way he came — no count — no count — no entry; party not on the roll\par

There were sittings before these that I could set a season to, and I have not written them, because a row of seasons is a thing a clerk can carry away and a stone is not. The Vorr call no number a rise and no season a loss, and no boy has ever come down and thanked the stone for it.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He borrowed the leaf on the morning after while I was entering the boy in the register, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{this is put down, not given} he wrote \emph{the stone is the lawful custodian of the mark}, true in a room where a mark can pass from hand to hand and meaningless on a high path.

\item At \emph{the count is in the bone} he wrote \emph{the measure is not deposited; party difficult to draw}, and underlined \emph{difficult} twice, which is the only part he has ever understood.

\item At \emph{we were never owed} he wrote \emph{the party is not entered for a return}, leaving out the owing and keeping the party.

\item At \emph{the sitting continues} he wrote \emph{proceedings pending the season}, and put a season into a column where no season has ever stood.

\item At the gap in the song he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}. When I asked what a season was worth with no number in it, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he said all morning.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as a newer repair lies over an older one in the seam and the older is still there under it. He takes the doer out because a thing with nobody in it cannot be argued with. I put the doer back because a boy at forty with dust in his palm wants to know who put it there, and whether it was his own hand that will keep it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lichen is off the north stone and will not wash out of the grain, which is why the Vorr scrape with a thumb and not with cloth. The doubled print is Iyn’s and no other hand in this Keep could leave it. The rime was on the path at first grey and was gone before I folded; the writing there is thin and I have not gone over it, for a word written thin is a word said quietly. The shaving held one night and is cold, which the keeper of the warm-stone calls the order of things. The dish stood from the dust to the dead and was drunk by nobody. The grey came off a cuff and nobody will own it. The pinch of dust is shut in the crease and has never been sold or spent or put on a stone.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not Iyn’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone has kept every number that was ever brought up to it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It has never once been asked what the numbers were for.\end{quote}

I asked the girl from the shift, a surveyor who carries the numbers down, a miner who came up and went down again in one morning, and the clerk, and had four answerings and no hand. I have left the line struck through and standing, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back into the oiled cloth and the cloth into the register-box with the dust in its crease and the copper thread where it fell. Next Bone another boy will sit and come down with a number changed or unchanged, and the clerk will take the verbs out and put a nought in the season. I shall put them back as I did this time, and leave the nought in its place and the space the length the sitting is, and the place where the name would stand the length a name would be.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Glaze Cliffs, Being What an Old Dipper Said Over the Beads on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 812, with the Draw-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bead-Row in a Tally, a Court Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Glaze Cliffs, Being What an Old Dipper Said Over the Beads on a Morning in Ash of Y.H. 812, with the Draw-Song Left as It Is Sung, the Bead-Row in a Tally, a Court Clerk’s Correction, and a Line at the Foot in a Hand Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Sallow pans preached in the bead-niche under the blue-green cliff where the glass-sand is dug; the sayings in Vhaleni set down in Grathic as I heard them, the draw-song with the ebb-line left as it is sung, the beads in a tally, one correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a clerk come down from Greybank, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, on a morning when the draw ran seaward against the wind, by an old dipper of the pans who had trailed a net at dawn for more years than he would give; written that evening by the keeper of the glass tally in the shed below the cliffs, on the back of a salt-paper contract gone damp and therefore void, folded with a green bead in the crease and tied with a tarry end of net-cord. It survives with salt bloom worked into the head and the gutter, glass dust in the grain, a green stain along the fold that smells sweet in heat and is not sweet to the tongue, one brine-gull feather, a wet ring where a dish of sea-water stood from the first voice to the last, a tarry fibre at the tie, the damp of the voided contract eating the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk come down from Greybank to count the winter salt, and a line struck through and written again very small underneath in a hand that has never come forward. Copied once at Greybank in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the ebb-line left the length it is sung.\par}\medskip
I keep the glass tally in the shed under the cliffs and nobody asked me for this. I write because the old man spoke to the cliff, the net, the dish and last of all to us, which is the order the pans use when somebody may be listening who wants a figure. When a man asked him the year of some tide he gave the tide instead, which is the Vhaleni way of answering a question you do not mean to keep. I have set his words down in Grathic, which is not his tongue. Where he left a verb out I have left it out and put it back underneath in my own hand, because a saying said over a bead is a thing a person has to use.

The leaf is the back of a contract that went damp in the shed and is therefore no contract at all, which the Council calls a virtue and the clerk from Greybank does not. The salt at the head came off the old man’s hand when he flattened it on the niche; the glass in the grain is from the sand we dig and scratches a fingernail. The green along the fold is not slip and not salt. It came off a bead left in the crease in the sun and smells sweet when the shed is warm, and I have told the girls not to put a tongue to it. The feather is a brine-gull’s. The ring is the dish, set down at the first voice and taken up at the last. I have not washed any of it.

\subsection*{The manner of the dipping, as the pans keep it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Go down before the light and trail the net in the draw. Do not say what the draw is doing. A draw said aloud becomes an argument, and there is argument enough at the Quay.

\item Salt on the hand, never on the net. The net has its own business with the sea.

\item Leave a bead in the niche for every morning you dip. The sea cannot eat it and a clerk can carry it away, which is why we leave it in a hole in the cliff and not on a shelf.

\item Do not lick the cliff. In the heat it smells of sugar and in the cold of nothing, and children are told in both months. A child who licks it gets a pale line at the gum and in the end cannot hold a cup, and no dipper has known a cure.

\item If a brine-gull takes a bead, let it go. It has carried the keeping into the air, where it was going in any case. No slate in Vhal stands the poorer for a gull.

\item If the draw runs backward, do not correct it. We are the ones who are early or late.

\item When a man with a slate comes among the pans, stop, and begin again after. His figure is for another room. Do not lay the two together.

\end{itemize}

He said the last twice, once to the cliff and once to a man behind me with his hands in his sleeves. I have not put the sayings together.

\subsection*{The sermon, as he said it}

\subsection*{Of the green}

He put his palm flat on the cliff where the blue-green stain ran down like a glaze that had been poured and not stopped.

“Look at it,” he said. “Sweet in the heat. The children are told not to lick it and the glass-men not to breathe it, and still we dig the sand at its foot and make good glass and sell it to Sere, and Sere puts wine in it and empties the wine at a feast. There is no trick in this. A thing can be good to look at and bad to take in. That is the whole of my preaching and I could find no other sentence.”

There was green on the creases of his hand and he did not wipe it on his coat.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in my hand:} He used the Vhaleni word for \emph{sweet} that also means \emph{owed} when a debt is left too long. I have set \emph{sweet} because that is what the cliff does. He would not have the other word written, and that is a word with a use.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the bead}

“Every morning I leave one,” he said. “A green bead in a hole in the cliff. I have left them since before you were born and never counted them.

“A priest out of Greybank told me the bead is an offering to the Hearth and that the Hearth keeps what is given. I asked him what became of a bead in a crack no priest could reach without a rope. He said the offering was received, which a man says when he has not been down the cliff.

“Glass keeps its colour. Salt keeps nothing. A man who puts a bead in a hole and goes back to the pans has done something with his hands before the day took it from him. If the Hearth wants the bead, let it come down the cliff and fetch it. It has not come yet.”

A woman beside me said the beads were only beads. He turned his head without haste. “A net is only a net,” he said. “I have mended them for years. Do not tell me what a bead is.”

\subsection*{Of the draw}

“The water goes out with the warm in it,” he said to the dish. “That is the draw. It runs against the wind and has since my father’s father dipped, and we bless it at dawn so it will go on running and not turn and take what stands on the shore.

“They say there is a Hearth under the salt and the Court’s fire is only its chimney. I have been asked if this is true and I have given a tide for an answer, because a tide does not spoil in the mouth and a man with a slate likes a thing he can set in a column. Ask me what is under the salt and I will tell you which tide. There is always one more tide than there are questions.”

He put two fingers in the dish and lifted them out.

“I have dipped thirty years and never seen a measure come back out of the sea. Salt comes back. Glass comes back. A boat comes back if the wind is kind. A person does not, and the dippers do not say it, and I am saying it to a dish that will not carry it up the Salt Road.”

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a Court clerk who came down from Greybank on the third day and borrowed the leaf while I was at the pans:} The Sallow draw is a tide of the Keeping and is efficacious thereby. The measure is retained in the salt. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} I have put \emph{goes out} and \emph{comes back} under his \emph{is retained}. His sentence is true eighteen leagues inland and has no verbs for a woman standing in salt water.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the coin}

A man from a Sere ship had given a boy a coin, and the boy showed it to the dipper, because Vhaleni say a stranger’s coin warms before his face.

“It warms before his face,” the old man said. “So they say, and I have said it myself. But I have held a coin out of a counting-house fire and a coin that lay in a man’s pocket in the pulled benches for a term, and the two are not the same warmth. Somebody paid to make that coin warm. A coin has no fire of its own and neither has a stranger.

“When a man says a thing warms before your face, ask who paid. You will not get an answer at the Quay. You will get a contract on salt-paper, and if the weather is kind it is gone by morning, and that is called a virtue here.”

The boy kept the coin.

\subsection*{Of them that go out on the ebb}

“We seal them in a boat and push it out on the ebb,” he said. “We watch until it is out of sight, and that is held to be enough. I have stood at eleven of these and never seen a boat come back with the man in it.

“I am not saying the Return is a lie. I am saying this coast has the least to show of it. We put no slate at the boat and read no figure over the water. A Vhaleni who dies at sea is called already returned, which is a kind sentence and costs nothing.

“If there is a mercy in this world it is in standing until the boat is small, and then going back to the pans. We do not call it a keeping. We call it enough.”

\subsection*{The draw-song}

\emph{Sung low, facing the water, a bead held between the teeth. There is a line missing before the last four, the one the ebb leaves, and I have left the space the length it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt on the hand and the net in the dawn,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the draw goes out where the cold has gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cliff tastes sweet and the sweet is a lie,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bead in the niche will not say why.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the pans and three for the rain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the boat that comes back again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes one and the gull gives none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clerk writes nil when the count is done.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ebb takes what the tide would not keep —\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We watch till the sail is a speck and then\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it is enough, and go to the pans again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the sea keeps nothing and keeps on keeping,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the green in the crack is not for eating.\end{quote}

A girl from the glass shed asked what the space was for. Nobody answered her. The clerk put a round nought against it, which I have left where he set it.

\subsection*{The bead-row, as the niche keeps it}

\emph{A bead that goes into the crack is a bead no tally can reach, and a figure brought into the shed in a pocket goes out again in the glass and leaves nothing on the leaf.}

Bead — Left by — What was asked of the dipper — What the tide gave\par

Green, chipped at the rim — the old man, every morning — nothing; he set it in and went — another morning\par

Clear, with a tarry fibre shut in it — a man off the pulled benches — whether his term was kept — a tide named, no year\par

Green bead melted round a coal — a girl of the glaze works — whether the sweet would kill her — \emph{Ask the cliff}, which is no answer\par

The bead the gull took — nobody — nothing — a feather on the leaf\par

Nine beads under the loose stone — the pans, in the lean winters — one in twelve, read at the Quay — the printed figure, unchallenged\par

There were beads I did not set down, because a row of beads is a thing a clerk can carry away and a morning is not. The nine under the loose stone have no names.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He came down from Greybank on the third day with ink in two fingers, borrowed the leaf while I was at the pans, and gave it back with the verbs taken out.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Where the old man said \emph{the water goes out with the warm in it}, he wrote \emph{the measure is retained in the salt} above and left the old words below.

\item Where he said \emph{ask who paid for the warming}, he wrote \emph{claim not established} and drew a small stop between two clusters of his neat dark hand.

\item At the bead-row he put a round nought against the nine under the loose stone and wrote \emph{vacancy} where the tide should stand.

\item At the gap in the song he wrote \emph{vacancy} again, and when I asked what a line was worth with no words, he said nothing a clerk could enter, the first true thing he said all morning.

\end{itemize}

I have put the verbs back underneath and left his hand standing above, as the cliff keeps the green over the sand that made it. He takes them out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a woman in salt water wants to know who did the going out, and whether it was her own net.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The salt at the head is the old man’s and mine and will not wash out of grain this soft. The glass scratches a nail. The green on the fold is sweet in heat and I have kept the leaf out of the sun since it took. The feather lay on the niche when I came to write and I have not moved it. The ring is from the dish, which stood on the leaf while he spoke of them that go out on the ebb. The tar at the tie holds a knot the way a niche holds a bead. The damp at the lower corner is the voided contract showing through its own writing. The clerk did not notice any of these things, which is how I know he is a good clerk.

\subsection*{At the foot}

Struck through once and written again underneath, very small, in a hand that is not mine, not the old dipper’s and not the clerk’s:

\begin{quote}\itshape The beads are an account of warmth the Court did not take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The beads are the place where an account was refused.\end{quote}

I asked the old man, the girl from the glass shed and the clerk, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left it struck through and standing, the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

The leaf goes back in the shed with the bead in its crease and the cord tied as it was. Next Ash the dippers will trail their nets and leave their beads in the crack, and the draw will run out against the wind as always. If the clerk comes I shall let him take the verbs out and put them back, and leave the nought in its place and the green where it fell.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Bite, Being a Winter-Hunter’s Field Notes on the Ice-Mouse of the Frozen Ilm}
\CRsheetheading{The Sixth Bite, Being a Winter-Hunter’s Field Notes on the Ice-Mouse of the Frozen Ilm}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A trapper’s field book on one small beast, set down as a record of snares and not a book of reasons; the set-lines in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled fish-bills, the counting verse as it is said on the bank, a midwife’s note in a small hand, a collector’s ruling in Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Tebb of the north bank, a hunter of the frozen fields above Sill who set snares in the eaves and under the river ice and sold the skins for a bit apiece; set down on the backs of fish-bills gone stiff with frost and on one spoiled toll-tally, sewn with eel-sinew into a scrap of oiled sacking and carried in a coat pocket against a tallow end. Copied forward at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold. It survives with frost-white ground into the head, a thumb of dried silt at the fold, a mouse-drop the size of a barley grain on the second leaf, a singe where the tallow end caught the lower corner, a coin-rub where a bit was carried loose in the pocket, a collector’s ruling in narrow Ledgerhand across the fur column, a midwife’s note in a small hand beside the sixth bite, a grey Ash print nobody will own, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I have taken ice-mice for nine winters and kept this book for three. It is a record of snares. It is not a book of reasons. If a man wants reasons let him go to a College and ask them there, where they will write him one in a clean hand and charge him for the ink.

The paper is the backs of fish-bills from the north bank, gone stiff with frost and soft again in the thaw. A skin is worth a bit in Sill and a mark in Keld, and honest paper is worth a bit as well, so I write on what the eel-men throw away. The frost-white at the head is mine, off the thumb I set the sheet down with on Stone 9. I have not knocked it off.

\subsection*{Where it keeps}

It lives under the ice and in the thatch. In Stone, when the Ilm has lain frozen three tends and the eaves along the north bank have a white lip to them, it comes into the houses and nests in the clothes a man leaves hanging by the door. I have found one in the fold of a coat that had been worn down to the Fishstairs and back, and two in the straw of a bed whose occupant had not risen in a week. It does not come for the person. It comes for the place where the warmth has been, which is very often the same place, and the poor do not thank it for telling the difference.

You find it by the small cold patch. A man comes in off the bank, puts his hand to his own sleeve and says his arm has gone to sleep, and it has, but not from the sleeping. Where the mouse has sat there is a place the size of a thumb that does not warm when the rest of him does. It spreads if you leave it. Rub it toward the heart; do not cut it, for there is nothing in it to let out. I have seen a man put a knife to such a patch because he thought to drain it, and he drained nothing but the use of two fingers, which did not come back before the thaw.

\subsection*{The taking}

A noose of horsehair, set where the thatch has sagged and not where the frost sits highest. The mouse goes along the under edge of the eave where the house gives off a little warm through the roof, and a noose in the open gives you nothing but a dead bird and a cold hand. Under the ice you set a bent sliver in a crack and lead it with a crumb; the ice is clear in Stone and you can see the thing come to it. Do not crush it. A skin with a hole in it goes thin in the tanning and a thin skin will not come round, and there is no market for a skin that will not come round.

The fur is warm past its weight. A skin the size of a man’s palm will keep a cup from freezing on a shelf where a fold of good wool will not. This is the whole reason the trade exists, and the reason is not a pretty one. The skin goes into the lining of collectors’ coats, sewn there by a man who has never held a collector’s tube and has no wish to. The collectors say it is a good joke. I have stood by a brazier with one of them in a coat lined with nine or ten of my skins and watched him hold his grey fingers out to the coals, and he could not get them warm, and he said it was the weather. It was the weather. It is always the weather. I have never told him what was sewn into his coat and I never will, because a man who has been given a joke is allowed to keep it.

Stone — Set — Skins — Bitten — Entered\par

Stone 2 — Eaves, north bank, four lines — three — none — 3\par

Stone 8 — Under the ice below the Weir — five — one, a man’s thumb — 5\par

Stone 12, the Drawing — Eaves, three houses — two — none — 2\par

Stone 17 — Under the ice, bank above Sill — six — three, all in one house — 6\par

Stone 20 — The thatch by the Fishstairs road — four — one child, four bites — 4\par

Stone 26 — Eaves and ice together — seven — two, one not woken — 7\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a collector of Greybank, struck through the “Bitten” column:} Bites to persons not entered. No vessel. The measure stands where it is. Account stands.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And under the “Entered” column, in the same hand:} 3+5+2+6+4+7 = 27. Received.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He counted the skins; I counted what the skins cost, and the two columns are not the same column. A bit is a bit and a child that does not wake is not entered, which is the whole of the accounting in one line. I wrote the bites in the margin below where his column cannot reach, and put my own mark beside them in charcoal.

\subsection*{The verse}

\emph{Said on the bank when the lines are set, not at a fire. The fifth line is the one the old men leave out and the young ones put back.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the eave and one for the ice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the coat that has come home cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the thumb that will not come round\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the hand that could not hold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Set it where the thatch has sagged,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape not where the frost has made a crown;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a skin with a hole is a skin gone thin\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a thin skin will not come round.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six for the cradle, six for the bank,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the one who does not wake;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the last one for the snare to take.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A draft is a thing that a house can bear;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bite is a thing that a house can’t.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the window. Mind the coat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count the skins and let the child count.\end{quote}

I do not know why the old men leave out the fifth line. I have asked two of them and had two answers, and neither answer was about mice. I have set it down as it is said and let it stand.

\subsection*{The sixth bite}

It bites cold. There is no more to the bite than that: a small nick, not much blood, and a place that goes white around it. If the wound is warmed it comes back. If it is not warmed the whiteness travels, and a foot or a hand goes the way that the old people call the cold that stays, and stays. Salt does not hold it, and I have never found a physic that does. Keep the part warm, get the person to a fire, and do not put a knife to it.

A sleeping child bitten six times will not wake. This is not a saying. I have seen it in Stone 26 in a house above the Fishstairs road, and I had set the line myself and knew how many of the little bodies had gone into my hand that morning, which was seven, and one of them had already bit and I had not known it. The child had four nicks along the jaw and two at the wrist, and the sixth was the one at the wrist. There was no blood to speak of and no sound. The mother put a warm stone to him and would not take her hand away, and the midwife came and said the second chill had taken him, and said it in the voice midwives use when they have said a thing many times and have never once been thanked for it.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a small hand, in the margin beside this passage, pressed small and close as though the writer feared the room might read it:} The second chill comes to children who were never bit. I have laid out eleven. Do not let this book say six for the midwives. Four at the jaw and two at the wrist is a count, not a cause. --- A.\end{quote}

I have not struck her line out. I have not changed my count either. We are both right in the way that two people standing on opposite banks are both right about the river, which is a thing I have learned in this trade and nowhere else.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is the cold made small enough to be killed, a bit of winter that got legs and went looking for a coat. There are songs in the Fenmarch with a man’s name in them and a wrong done at a weir, and I have heard them and have no quarrel with a song. I have opened a great many of these and found a mouse. It is a field mouse that has lived where the cold comes up through the ice, and the cold has gone into it the way the smoke goes into a hound that lives by a kiln; the place changes the creature and then the creature carries the place about with it. I have written what it does and not what it wants. A man who writes what a mouse wants is a man who will be asked to write what a collector wants next, and there is no end to that sort of work.

What it does is take. It sits in the warm place and takes the warm out of it, and the place it has taken from stays cold after the mouse has gone. We say it takes the head from the place. A collector sets iron to a wrist and takes by the same road, only with a slate to make the taking look like keeping, and the collector’s fingers go grey where the mouse’s coat goes warm. I have set the two side by side below and I have not written a word between them. Let the College join them if it can get a figure out of it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The frost-white at the head is mine, and came off the ninth day of Stone when I set a sheet down on the step and picked it up again with the frost already in it. The silt thumb at the fold is from the bank above Sill, where I knelt in the grey to lead a line under the ice; it has dried into the grain and will not rub out. The mouse-drop on the second leaf is the only part of this book that has entered itself. The singe on the lower corner is where the tallow end caught while I was reading by it, and the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. The coin-rub is a bit I carried loose in that pocket for a month before I spent it; I do not remember what I bought, which is the common fate of bits. The grey print along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. I have not swept it and nobody will own it. The Last Day is kept at a fire, and a line set under the ice has no fire to keep it, so nothing in this book gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape It does not eat what it takes. Neither does the iron.\end{quote}

I asked a midwife, a collector who wears the coat, and a man who lost two fingers to a patch he cut, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written, which is the only honest way to keep a sentence you cannot sign.

Next Stone I will set a line in the eaves below the north bridge, where the ice comes up wrong in the thaw and the thatch stays wet when the rest has dried. I will count the bites as well as the skins, and if six come up together in one house I will set that down too, in charcoal, with the verb left in it, and let the collector take what figure he can out of it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Repair, Being a Letter from the First Seam to Nine Pots, Answered in the Margin and Entered Over by the Court}
\CRsheetheading{The Sixth Repair, Being a Letter from the First Seam to Nine Pots, Answered in the Margin and Entered Over by the Court}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A letter between brothers, the one hand Keldish and number-first, the other Grathic and given to proverbs; a tally of repairs set down in a small table, the sentence of the Vorr kept as it was spoken, the answers of the man addressed written in the margins, the corrections of a Court survey-clerk laid in Ledgerhand over both hands, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, in the survey room off the Duelling Floor beneath Keld Keep, by Varek of the First Seam, a clerk of the rim-seam tally, to Ollen of Nine Pots, a thrower, his brother by a mother who came down from the clay country and never learned to say a number before a noun. Set first on the back of a survey sheet spoiled by wet slate and carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Seed of Y.H. 813 with a survey party bound for Greybank; answered in the margins at Nine Pots and corrected at Greybank by a clerk of the factor’s office who borrowed the leaf on a market morning and would not give it back until the verbs were out of it. Kept since in a clay tube stoppered with wool on the shelf of the thrower’s shed in Nine Pots. It survives with coal dust at the head, a smear of hot lead at the fold where the leaf lay against a surveyor’s cuff, bone-coloured slip dust worked into the gutter, a thumb of tallow, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first question to the last, the figure for the sixth repair struck through and written again underneath in the writer’s own hand, and a grey Ash print along the outer fold that nobody will own.\par}\medskip
To Ollen, thrower, of Nine Pots, from Varek of the First Seam, his brother. Six repairs counted this week. One letter. No answer looked for.

I write from the room off the floor where the survey sheets are kept, which is warm in a way a room should not be warm. The stone sweats here in Bone and the smell comes up before anything shows, hot lead and a mineral sweetness like a glaze pot left too near the fire. Two men went out of this shaft in my first season and came back with their fingers the colour of a skimmed milk skin. I have counted the repairs in the wall behind the tally desk six times and got six each time, which is a small thing to be glad of. A number that comes back the same is the only honest company down here.

We had the same mother, who came down from Nine Pots with clay under her nails and a way of addressing the pot before she addressed the room. She taught you the wheel and taught me to hold a slate. I have kept the slate. You got the wheel, which is the better inheritance and I have never once said so in a letter until now, so you may put this down to the lead smell.

\subsection*{The tally, as I keep it}

The wall behind the desk is not the oldest in the seam. It is only the one I can see from my stool. I have entered what I can see and left the rest where it is, which is a rule the Order is not so strict about as it used to be.

Repair — What it is made of, by the Keldish translation — What the factor’s copy at Greybank calls it — How many times repaired\par

One — Stone, dressed and keyed — Stone — Twice\par

Two — Stone and iron pins — Stone, iron not entered — Once\par

Three — Stone — Stone — Three times; the third over the second\par

Four — Warm-stone dust in a clay bed — Material not entered — Once\par

Five — Stone — Stone — Once\par

Six — Not stone — Language — Once; crossed out and written again\par

Five of the six are stone and are no trouble. The fourth wants a word I will not use of a wall, because warm-stone is a thing a man carries against a child’s belly and not a thing he puts in a hole in the world. I have entered it as dust in a clay bed and let the translation stand beside it.

The sixth is the one I am writing to you about. The Keldish translation calls it Ash. The factor’s copy calls it language. I have copied both words into the margin and chosen neither, because a surveyor who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them and will have to answer for it at the Weighing. The Vorr were asked. One of them sat against a stone for a season and came back with three sentences, all the same sentence, which was that the numbers were correct. I have written that down too. It is a complete answer if you are a Vorr and a very thin one if you are a man trying to sleep above a seam that sweats.

\subsection*{The entry of Y.H. 588}

There is an entry in the old survey of a man with a branching red mark on his forearm and ribs. The entry is crossed out. It was crossed out before I came down the shaft and I do not know whose hand did it, which is a thing I have said to myself often enough that it now sounds like an answer.

I have copied the shape of the mark onto the back of this sheet so that you can look at it and tell me whether clay ever makes it. I do not want an opinion. I want to know whether you have seen it under a glaze or in the bottom of a jar, and if so, on what day and out of which pit. Give me the day and the pit and leave the rest where you found it.

There is a paper in a tin lined with warm-stone in the room off the floor. The men who keep the floor read it once a year and do not act on it, which I am told is a great skill and is certainly an old one. I have read it twice. The second time I found a line about a vessel that holds without leaking and went back to counting the wall, which was easier and paid the same.

\subsection*{What I want to know from you}

This is the question I cannot put to any man in Keld without being told to state my measure first and ask afterwards:

A pot that has cracked all the way through and been mended, does it hold the same as a pot that never cracked? I do not mean whether it holds water. I mean whether the holding is the same holding. Tap a sound pot with the knuckle and it answers full. Tap a cracked one and it answers flat, a little dead sound that stops at the surface. I know the two sounds as well as I know my own number, which was thirty-three when I went down and thirty-nine when they changed it, and has been cut out and written again twice since, so that my forearm reads like this letter does. But nobody has ever tapped a repaired pot for me and asked it the question twice, once before the mending and once after, and told me what changed.

You will say a pot is a pot. You will say this with slip on both forearms and the little finger bent where the splinter went in at eleven, and you will be right in the way that potters are always right, which is from the wrist and not from the mouth. Answer me from the wrist.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, the letters round and pressed hard, with slip in the strokes}

You always did ask the wrong question first. A pot that never cracked is a pot that has not been mended, and there is no holding to compare with it. Tap mine and it answers full because I set the seam myself and it sang when it went home. If it had not sung I would have sold it for a flower pot and said nothing. A crack that is mended keeps the crack. Ask it to be a pot it was not and you are asking a lie of the clay, which is a thing the clay charges for in the thaw.

On the red mark: third firing of Y.H. 806, a jar from the Old Kiln clay that would not take a glaze and went grey in the firing. The mark was on the bottom, branching like frost on a pane. A girl from the terrace crossed two fingers at it and said it was a flower. I asked her which flower. She gave me a date. I have kept the jar under the bench and I have never turned it up in company.

On the road: it is ours and Sill’s both, which is why neither of us mends it. Come down in Seed when the clay has set and bring the warm-stone if you are still carrying one. Six repairs in a wall is enough for a man to carry without a stone as well.

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the wheel and one for the fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the crack that the glaze won’t hide;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it at noon, it answers at night,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the seam keeps the word the potter denied.\end{quote}

I have never written a verse in my life and I would not begin now if there were not a man above me in a shaft who needs one. Put it under the numbers where it belongs.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did, at Greybank, in the second tend of Seed}

A clerk of the factor’s office borrowed the leaf on a market morning; his cuff was gone soft at the edge from washing and he had ink in the creases of two fingers. He laid his hand on the top sheet before he looked at either of us, which is the manner of that table. He took the verbs out of both hands as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff, and set a figure against each repair, and struck the question about the mended pot and wrote \emph{No such comparison} above it. Against the red shape he put a round nought and wrote \emph{mark, not entered}. Where my brother wrote that the seam keeps the word, the clerk wrote \emph{repair retained; material not entered} and left mine underneath, which is more than he usually leaves.

In my hand — In the Court hand\par

Six repairs counted this week — Repairs entered: six\par

The sixth is not stone — Material not entered\par

The Vorr said the numbers were correct — Figures confirmed\par

Does a mended pot hold the same? — No such comparison\par

A mark on the bottom of a jar — Mark, not entered\par
