The seam keeps the word — Repair retained\par

He asked me what a verse was worth and I said nothing a clerk could enter, which was the first true thing he said all morning. I have left both hands standing, mine under his and my brother’s under both, as a repaired wall keeps the old break under the new keying and does not pretend the first hand never touched it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal dust at the head is mine; I held the sheet down with my whole hand because the draught in the survey room comes along the floor and takes paper before it takes a man. The hot lead at the fold came off a cuff on the day a passing was measured two hours early and we all went up faster than we had any right to. The slip in the gutter is my brother’s and has gone bone-coloured with dry, which is the colour of his forearms by noon and of mine by never. The tallow thumb is mine. The ring came off a cup that stood from the first question to the verse and was drunk by neither of us, which is how small ale is drunk in Keld when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the Court’s. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in the First Seam.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six repairs in the wall and one with no name. The Court has entered the five it can spell. The wall keeps all six and has never once been asked to explain itself.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Slack Tide, Being a Winter Riddle Night on the Quay at Vhal, Five Questions Scored in Chalk on the Tarred Post, the One Put from the Door, and the Tide That Was Named and Has Not Come}
\CRsheetheading{The Slack Tide, Being a Winter Riddle Night on the Quay at Vhal, Five Questions Scored in Chalk on the Tarred Post, the One Put from the Door, and the Tide That Was Named and Has Not Come}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A tavern-keeper’s record of a cold-month contest, set down for the settling of arguments and not for the improvement of the reader; the rules in the hand the house keeps, the riddles in the words they were spoken, a score in chalk on the tarred door-post, the figures of a Council clerk entered over them, a boat-master’s note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year after the Long Cold, at the alehouse called the Slack Tide on the Quay at Vhal, by the woman who keeps the house and the lamp over the door; set first on the back of a spoiled tide-tally from the house beside the Council room and on two strips of salt-paper that would not hold ink, sewn with eel-sinew into a fold of oiled sailcloth and kept in a dry tin under the till, where nothing else in this house is kept dry. It survives with a thumb of tar at the head, a white salt bloom along the gutter, a press of frozen rope across the first leaf, a green bead of cliff-glass in the lower corner, a fish-hook nick, a coal-smudge near the fifth question, the chalk rubbed thin where a sleeve has gone over the post, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the Council of Tides, one note in the blunt hand of a boat-master, and a line at the foot in a hand that is nobody’s.\par}\medskip
I keep the Slack Tide on the Quay. It is a different work from keeping a tally, though both begin with the hand on the board and end with a figure somebody wants to carry away. In the cold months the east wind holds, the Sallow skins over at the edges, and the galleys lie up on the pulled benches with their oars in, and there is nothing to do of an evening but ask one another what we already know and call the asking a riddle. A question with an answer nobody knows is a bet, and there are men on this Quay who would bet on which way the wind will sit by morning.

The door-post is tarred and the chalk shows on it. I score the night there and take the score off in the morning with a wet rope-end, which is the only erasure this house has ever needed. Nothing is carried away from the Slack Tide on a slate. A man who wants a thing entered can go up to the Council room and sit with people warmer than himself, and the paper there will rot before he gets home, which the Council calls a virtue.

\subsection*{The rules, as the house keeps them}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A riddle is put once. Ask for it again and you owe a quart, because the second asking is for your own pleasure and not for the post.

\item Answer in one breath. A second answer is a different riddle and is not heard.

\item Five are chalked. A sixth may be put and is not scored, being a thing said from the door and not from a stool.

\item The house judges. I say whether an answer serves and I do not say why. A reason given is a riddle given away for nothing, and the giver can go home and sell it.

\item No paper lies on the board. A contract left here overnight is a debt the weather has settled, and this house does not settle debts for the Council.

\item A quart of small ale is set down before the first question and no one lifts it until the fifth. If a white bloom comes up on the board before then, the night’s answering will go badly. I have never known this to fail and I would not say so before a dipper.

\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{The five that were chalked}

The first went to a woman who holds a twelfth of a boat through her mother and will not say the fraction before company. She had her answer before the verse was fairly out, which is why she never takes the quart and is always asked first.

\begin{quote}\itshape I go from mother to daughter and never by buying;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man may come aboard and hold me in his hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and still his word upon the boat is counted half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I am not the hull, and I am not the sea.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“A share,” she said. “And the half is his opinion, not mine.” I gave her the quart and she drank standing with her sleeve over the rim, because she had been told not to spill. Nobody asked her how many twelfths she held, which is the proper way to ask nothing in this house.

The second went to Kett of the Quay, who reads the draws at the tide-tally house and keeps his cuffs dry by not touching anything.

\begin{quote}\itshape I am set down to be kept and I keep by going;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wetter the room, the less I owe;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council has made a virtue of my dying\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and hired a man in a clean coat to write it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

“Salt-paper,” he said, without looking up from his tally, which is how he answers everybody. The house allowed it. A man who reads the draws all day does not need to look at a person to know what that person has brought in.

The third was put to a dipper come in off the pans with salt dried white in the creases of her neck.

\begin{quote}\itshape I run against the wind and am blessed before light;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Council is surprised by me every year;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they tax me in a figure I never carried.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What runs seaward and is counted by men who never saw it?\end{quote}

“The draw,” she said, and said it to the pot and not to Kett, because a dipper does not argue with the tide-tally house before company. She took no quart. Dippers are paid by the pan-master, who pays in the weather and never in ale.

The fourth went to a boat-master who had lost a store below the waterline and had come back to sit down again, which not every man does after such a loss.

\begin{quote}\itshape I knock where no hand can reach, below the waterline;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I take the store and leave the rope behind;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the nets are blessed at dawn and I come all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What taps a hull and takes what the hull was holding?\end{quote}

“A salt-thing,” he said, and set the quart down again without drinking, which in this house is how a man says he has already paid for the answer. There was an argument about whether a blessing that does not keep a store is a blessing at all. I stopped it by touching the post, because there is no winning an argument about a blessing and there is only the thing that came in the night and the store that is not in the boat.

The fifth I put myself, because the room had grown noisy and wanted quieting, and a riddle put by the house is not scored against anybody.

\begin{quote}\itshape I steal the warm and do not eat it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I go up the wind with a coal under my crop;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no tally in this town stands one mark the poorer.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What carries the fire out of the account?\end{quote}

An old woman who mends nets said “a brine-gull” and said it low, the way people say things they have said to the fire at home. I passed her the pot. She set it down again and told me a gull had taken a coal off her brazier the week before and she had not gone after it, because a thing that goes up the wind with your coal has already been paid and there is nobody to charge. That is the best answer I have heard in nine winters and the only one that cost the teller nothing by telling it.

\subsection*{The sixth, which was put from the door}

Toward the end of the night a girl came to the door and did not step over it. There was salt dried white on her shins and at the hem of her coat, as if she had come up off the pans and walked the Salt Road without putting her shoes back on, which nobody does who owns a pair of shoes. She asked whether anybody in the house had seen the tide she named at the Salt Walk. Nobody said yes, which is a way of saying no that costs nobody anything. Then she put the sixth:

\begin{quote}\itshape I was named at fourteen with my feet in the pan\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and written in salt where the dippers could read;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape by noon there was no word, and the pan kept nothing;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have carried the shape of it all winter, not the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What am I?\end{quote}

Kett said, “A tide not yet seen.” The girl said that was what the dippers wrote in the salt and asked what the house called it. The room went the way a room goes when everybody has the answer in their mouths and nobody will be the one to say it, which is the same in Vhal as in any town with a Council. She waited a little. “Then leave it where it is,” she said, and went back into the wind. Where she stood there was a small drift of salt on the boards. In the morning it was gone, and I have not swept the place where it lay, because the wind does the sweeping on this Quay and always has.

\subsection*{The score, in chalk on the tarred post}

Question — Put by — Answer given — Score\par

The share — the woman with the twelfth — a share — one, drunk\par

The paper — Kett of the Quay — salt-paper — one, allowed\par

The draw — a dipper — the draw — one, to the pot\par

The tap — the boat-master — a salt-thing — one, not drunk\par

The coal — the house — a brine-gull — one, given low\par

The named tide — a girl at the door — none served — not scored\par

The Council’s figure for the draw went up on the tally board that morning and came down by noon, which is what the Council’s figures do. It went over the post with the ale and nobody looked at it twice, which is how figures go in this house.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the leaf on a morning when the till was being counted and his cuff was soft at the edge from the damp, which is the only way a Council cuff ever gets soft. He set the riddles down as \emph{queries entered} and the answers as \emph{responses entered}, and put a figure of marks against each of the five, which was more than I had scored, because the house scores in whether a person sits down again and he does not. Against the sixth he wrote \emph{no answer tendered; struck.} He asked who had put it. I told him a girl at the door. He asked for the girl’s name, and I said she had given none, which is a true thing and not the thing he wanted, and he wrote \emph{party unidentified; interest in a tide not entered.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Against \emph{a share, and the half is his opinion, not mine}, he wrote \emph{one-half interest, contingent}.

\item At the salt-paper he wrote \emph{instrument voided by damp}, and underlined it twice, which is what the Council does when it wants a thing to look like a mercy.

\item Against the draw he wrote \emph{current taxed at source}, which is true in a language nobody on this Quay speaks unless they are being paid to.

\item At the salt-thing he wrote \emph{loss not entered}, and put a round nought in the place where the store had stood.

\item Against the brine-gull he wrote \emph{no value transferred}, which is the only one of his answers I have ever wanted to keep.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words under his and left his standing, the way a tarred post keeps the chalk under the salt. He has entered five and struck the sixth, and the sixth was not struck: it went out on the wind with the girl and is still going.

\subsection*{From the boat-master}

At the foot of the scored leaves, in the blunt hand of the man who had lost his store and sat down again:

\begin{quote}\itshape A man’s word on a boat is counted at half. His loss is entered whole.\end{quote}

He says he wrote it about the salt-thing and not about his wife, and I have let him say so. A man who has married aboard is allowed one sentence in a book he did not write, which is more than the Council allows him anywhere else.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The tar thumb at the head is mine. I held the leaf down on the Quay in the wind and did not know I had marked it; tar goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the Council room uses it for a seal and this house uses it for nothing. The salt bloom along the gutter came up out of the paper on the third night, when I carried the leaf inside my coat and the coat crusted white at the fold. I have not brushed it off. A bloom written by the weather is the only writing in Vhal that a clerk cannot strike. The press of frozen rope across the first leaf came off the man who held the door while the girl spoke, and I have not written which man, because he would stop holding doors if I did. The green bead in the lower corner came off a string of cliff-glass a carrier left on the till; it has the colour of the Glaze Cliffs after rain and I have kept it where it fell. The fish-hook nick is from a hook set in the edge by a man paying for his quart, and he did not apologize, which is how hooks are paid for here. The coal-smudge near the fifth question is from the brazier, where the leaf lay too close while the net-mender was telling us about her gull; the coal was ours and the answer was not. The grey print along the outer fold is not mine and nobody has claimed it. Nothing on this Quay is swept until the wind does it, so the print is still there.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pan keeps the shape and the sea keeps the name;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape neither gives back what was made in it.\end{quote}

I asked the woman with the twelfth, Kett and the boat-master, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back in the tin and the chalk goes off the post with a wet rope-end, and in the morning the Council clerk will come for the till and find nothing in it that rots. Next winter the galleys will lie up again and the east wind will hold, and I shall set five questions on the post and leave the sixth standing at the door, for whoever it is to come in out of the wind or not, as they please.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Smoke-Side Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Kiln-Hound at the Old Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The Smoke-Side Dog, Being a Soldier’s Field Notes on the Kiln-Hound at the Old Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch and not natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on a spoiled levy-roll, a watch-song as it is sung, a kiln-master’s correction in slip-white, a clerk’s ruling in Ledgerhand · Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Hobb of Sill, one of the Thane’s men watching the Old Kiln road, in the watch-shed with a tallow end; set down on three levy-rolls spoiled by rain, then on the back of a granary docket, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with soot ground into the head, a brown spot on the second leaf, a wet boot-print from the Slip Brook, a singe from the fire-pot, the charcoal rubbed thin, two corrections from the factor’s clerk, one line in slip-white from the kiln-master, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I keep the road to the Old Kiln for the Thane. It is no post a man writes home about. The ruin stands one league south of Sill where the clay has gone grey and will not take a glaze, and the ash in its throat is deeper than a man is tall. I am set there to see that no one digs the grey in the dark and that no one lies down in it and stays there. I carry a short spear with the head gone blue on the quay stone and a fire-pot of coals under ash, and I write these lines at the end of a watch with the tallow down to a knuckle and the cold coming up through the soles.

The rolls I wrote on first were spoiled in a rain that took the figures clean off, which was a mercy of a kind: a figure the rain has eaten cannot be entered. I write in charcoal now, because charcoal goes into the grain and a clerk cannot take it off with a cuff. The soot at the head is my own thumb setting the sheet down on the watch-shed bench. I have not knocked it off.

\subsection*{The road and the river}

The hound keeps to the smoke side. That is the first thing a new man must learn and the thing that costs him a night’s sleep. It will lie all watch on the side of the ruin where the warm comes up through the clay and the air moves, and it will not come round to the cold side though a man stand there with his coat open and his pot hanging. The folk of High Kiln say the river is a wall. I thought it was a saying until the night I watched one stand in the mud at the Slip Brook with its nose across the water and a man lying three paces beyond on the other bank. It stood. It did not go over. The man was not saved by it, but he was not eaten either, and in this trade a man takes what the night gives.

It comes off the smoke side in the second watch, when the tallow is low and the kiln-yards down at Sill have stopped their shouting. It does not bark. The sound it makes is low in the throat, like a man clearing himself in his sleep, and you hear it in your boots before you hear it in the air. I have set the watch-song down below with the hearths’ words standing where the watchmen put them, which is not where I would have put them.

\subsection*{What it is}

It is a dog. I will set that down before anything else, because the hearths will not. It has a dog’s teeth and a dog’s neck and a dog’s way of putting its head on one side when it listens. It is bigger than the yard hounds at the Tallow Works and thinner, with a coat the colour of wet clay and no grey on the outside. The grey is in the mouth and under the nails. Behind the ears it is hot to the back of the hand, hotter than a beast that has merely been near a fire should be. It smells of smoke and hot clay, and when it has been lying in the throat a man smells of it too, for a day after.

I have opened three. Two were brought down on the road and one was found dead at the mouth of the old flue, where it had gone in after the warmth and not come out. In all three I found a dog altered by the place it lived in, the way a potter’s hands are altered by the wheel. I found no more than that and I have not put a cause beside it. A man who writes a cause into a book he keeps in his pocket is a man who will be asked for it by somebody with a slate.

\subsection*{The breath}

The danger is the air. The dog is the thing that brings a man to where the air is.

I have stood on both sides of it. A man who stays in the throat with his head low will come out with a headache and a thirst that outlasts the watch, and his lips are a little too red, which is all the evidence there is. There was a potter of Low Kiln came up in Ash to look at the grey and went down on the second morning in his own house with the window shut, and the physician said it was a merciful death, which is a thing physicians say when they have not had to lay the body out. He had never seen a hound in his life. The potters leave a window open in a firing though the draft spoils the glaze. A spoiled glaze is a loss a man can count. A man is not.

I have written the air where the watchmen write the dog, and I have left both standing.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the blocky hand of the kiln-master of Low Kiln, written in slip-white with a potter’s stylus, down the margin of this leaf:} It is the air. I have buried two who never saw a dog. Leave the window. The glaze can bear it. --- K.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The bite}

It does not bite a man on his feet. I have stood within two paces with the spear down and it went on with its own work. But let a man go down and it comes for the face, and it does not shake him or drag him. It puts its mouth to him and waits, the way a collector sets a tube and waits, and the waiting is the part I cannot write about without my hand going still.

The boy they set with me in the second watch went in at Ash 5 after a man we had heard in the grey. We found him face down with the hound at the cheek. I struck it across the back with the spear-shaft and it went three paces off and stood, which is what it does; it does not run and it does not come back at a man who has hit it. The boy’s cheek was two small holes and not much blood, and his lip was red on the side next the ground. I washed with water and bound it. At the end of the tend the holes were closed and the lip was still red and he was asking for water at every watch. He has never said what he saw down there and I have not asked him. Salt does not hold that bite and there is no physic for it that I know. Keep the man out of the close air and let him ask for water. That is the whole of what I have.

The tongue, dried, is bought by Fenfolk to test a close room, for it discolours where the breath is. Two bits a tongue and no questions. The hide is too smoky to sell, so we burn it. A man who tells you he has found a use for a kiln-hound hide is a man who wants another one, and you should keep your coals between you and him.

\subsection*{The watch-song}

\emph{Sung going in at the first watch, not coming back. The fourth line is the hearths’ line and every watchman sings it wrong on purpose. I have set it down as it is sung.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the clay and one for the smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dog keeps the side where the fire has been;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it does not bark at a man on his feet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the kiln’s own breath that comes to him.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Keep the window. Let the glaze go bad.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A draft is a thing a man can pay.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The lips go red where the head lay down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the next day’s water is never enough.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the watch and one for the road\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the man who did not come back to it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not name him at the singing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we leave his place where the gap should be.\end{quote}

The gap is the fifth breath the old kiln does not take. The watchmen know it and sing it and have never once said what it is a gap in. There is a man at Sill who sings the last line twice and will not say why, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the nights I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The last column is the clerk’s, not mine.

Night — Place — Hounds — Overcome — Tongues — Entered\par

Bone 6 — South road at the broken flue — one — one — one — 2\par

Bone 12 — The throat, east side — two — none — none — 0\par

Bone 19 — Smoke side below the ash-heap — one — one — one — 2\par

Bone 28 — Old damper, not gone in — three — none — none — 0\par

Ash 5 — The throat, where the boy went down — one — one — one — nil\par

Ash 14 — North bank of the Slip Brook — one — none — none — 0\par

Ash 26 — The road, after the rain — two — one — two — 4\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, struck through the “Overcome” column:} Persons overcome: not entered. Air not a vessel. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change. But the boy asked for water through the whole of Ash and the clerk has put \emph{nil} against him with a neat instrument and no name on it. I have written the thirst in the margin below, where his column cannot reach, and I have put my own mark beside it in charcoal.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is the kiln’s breath given legs, a thing that got up and went walking because the fire was put out unkindly. There are songs in the Fenmarch with a man’s name in them and a wrong done at a flue. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. I have opened three of these and found a dog, and a dog is the least of what is wrong with that place. If the breath has legs, then it is the room that does the work and the legs only carry a man into it. I have written that last sentence out once and crossed it out twice, because it is the kind of sentence that gets a man called a natural philosopher, and natural philosophers are not set to watch roads in Bone.

I do not know what the hound wants in the throat. I know the order it goes in: the ash-heap first, then the broken flue, then the old damper if the watch is long and the tallow is low. I have set the order down and no cause. The complexion of the place is not mine to explain and I have never been paid to explain it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The soot at the head is mine. The brown spot on the second leaf fell there from the boy’s cheek when he sat down to have the rag changed, and I have not scraped it, because it is the only entry on this leaf that cost anybody anything. The boot-print across the foot came off the morning I crossed the Slip Brook after the rain and came up to the calf in grey silt; it has dried into the grain and will not rub out. The singe on the lower corner is where the leaf caught when I held it over the fire-pot to read, and the hand that pulled it back was mine and is not entered. The charcoal is rubbed thin where I carried the roll against my thigh. The clerk’s line I have not touched. The slip-white line is the kiln-master’s and will fade before the charcoal does, which is a small kindness in the ordering of things. The song is as they sang it, with the hearths’ lie left standing in the fourth line.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape What kills in the room was there before the dog came in.\end{quote}

There is a place down in the throat where the ash stands deeper than my spear and the air comes up warm on the stillest day of Ash. I have not gone in. Next Bone I will take a fire-pot and a coil of cord and go down to where the old damper was, and if the breath comes up in a place where no kiln has burned in a hundred years I will set that down too, in charcoal, and let the clerk take what figure he can out of it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Song of the Borrowed Ground, Being a Drinking-Song of the Peat-Dries on the Peat Line, Sung Sitting with the Cup Passed Hand to Hand and Nobody Pouring for Himself; the Verses Said to the Fire and the Last Word Let Fall into the Floor, with a Knot in the Margin for the Word That Cannot Be Written, a Reeve’s Score in Peat, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figure Set Above, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
\CRsheetheading{The Song of the Borrowed Ground, Being a Drinking-Song of the Peat-Dries on the Peat Line, Sung Sitting with the Cup Passed Hand to Hand and Nobody Pouring for Himself; the Verses Said to the Fire and the Last Word Let Fall into the Floor, with a Knot in the Margin for the Word That Cannot Be Written, a Reeve’s Score in Peat, a Factor’s Clerk’s Figure Set Above, and a Line at the Foot Nobody Will Own}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A peat-dry woman’s drinking-song, set down in Grathic letters though Fen Cant is not written; the words in the thick half-sung speech of the dry, the refrain kept by the table, a knot tied through a hole for the word that goes out at the back of the throat, a reeve’s score in peat along the head, a factor’s clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand above the lines, a mud-wife’s small gloss pressed into the margin, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at a peat-dry on the Peat Line three leagues in from the Standing Post in Reed and Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, by Oda Sedge, a woman who keeps the cup and the coals at the dry and has cut peat there since the Glaze Wars were ended; set down because a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat asked what was sung when the cutting was done and the cup went round, and wrote the answer down with the verbs taken out. Written first on a leaf of oiled reed and the back of a spoiled peat-tally, sewn with eel-sinew and tied with grey wool, carried under the boards to Greybank at the Opening of the Slates in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied onto the back of a factor’s voided grain-warrant. It survives with a peat thumb worked into the head, a bog-water tideline that has eaten two words clean off the third verse, the press of wet sedge across the second leaf, a small-ale ring gone sour at the foot, a smear of eel slime at the fore-edge where a man set the cup down with his hands still wet, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which a collector’s cuff left and nobody will own, a knot of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the reeve’s peat score standing above the clerk’s figure standing above the words, and one line at the foot that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the cup at a peat-dry three leagues in from the Post. That is my office, such as it is: to see the coals are blind by morning and the cup goes round and round and nobody pours for himself. A man who pours for himself in a dry drinks alone, and a man who drinks alone in the Fen is a man the water has begun to mark. I have kept the cup since the Glaze Wars were ended and I have never once seen a man refuse it, which is not the same thing as saying he wanted it.

I set this down because a clerk come up from Greybank to count the winter peat stood at the dry with a cuff soft from washing and asked what the women sang when the cutting was done. I told him. He wrote it in a book while I was still saying it, and what he wrote had the doing taken out of it and a figure put where a place should stand, and he thanked me and went back over the boards with his boots clean. So I have set down what we said before he came and what we said again after he had gone. His hand stands above mine where he set it, and the reeve’s peat score stands above his, and the mud-wife’s gloss is pressed in where she wrote it, and my words lie under all three, as the dry keeps the old cut under the new turf.

The thumb at the head is mine. I held the reed down on the bench in a wind off the bog and did not know I had marked it. Peat goes into the grain and no damp takes it out, which is why we sign with it here and not with ink.

\subsection*{How it is sung}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Sitting, never standing. The cup goes to the left, and the man whose turn it is does not pour; his neighbour pours for him, so that no man holds his own drinking in his own hand. Said standing, it becomes a grace, and we have no grace in a dry that the Court has not already entered.

\item Said to the fire, not to the company. The last word of every verse is let fall into the floor and not finished. A verse said looking at a man becomes an argument, and there is enough arguing at the Post without carrying it three leagues in.

\item Through the nose, slow, half-sung. Where a word cannot be written I have tied a knot in the margin; it is made at the back of the throat with the nose shut and does not go into Grathic. A clerk can carry a figure away. He cannot carry a knot away, which is the whole reason for knots.

\item One verse for the ground, one for the warmth, one for the boots, one for the Mother, one for the grey. There is a place where a sixth should stand and it is not scored and not filled. The factor’s clerk has put a nought in it; the nought is his and the place is ours.

\item Not sung on the Post and not sung at a death. There is a different thing said at a death and it is said to the water.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{Said low to the fire, sitting. The table keeps the refrain; one voice begins it and the rest come in on the second line. The bracelet of grey wool goes round with the cup.}

The refrain, as the table keeps it after every verse:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Drink to the dry. It’s lent.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Drink to the warm. It’s spent.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{What the cup forgets the mud keeps,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and gives it back to whom it wants.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{I. Of the ground}

\begin{quote}\itshape We stand on a loan. The water calls it in\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape when it has a mind to, which is most years;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the board’s a promise the bog has not kept,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and dry’s a thing we rent by the hour.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Gloss, in the mud-wife’s small hand:} The last word is let go into the floor. Do not say hour as though it had an end to it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{II. Of the warmth}

\begin{quote}\itshape They sell it whole in the south and dear;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we buy it thin and ask whose, and don’t know;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a third of the figure, a quarter of the account,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the child comes quiet, and likes the fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, written above:} The deduction is retained. No vendor arises.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A vendor arises in the house that got the child. He is not named here because a name said in a dry travels with the cup, and the cup goes as far as the Post.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the boots}

\begin{quote}\itshape Our young know a collector by the boot\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape before they know the word for their own name:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no peat on the heel, no water to the cuff,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a slate held level, the way you’d hold a knife.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Gloss:} The knife is not drawn. It is held the way a man holds a thing he has put away and may take up again. Children are not told this part and learn it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of the Mother}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Mother keeps it warm under a skin of water\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and hands it up to whoever can reach;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t ask her who paid --- she’ll tell the mud,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the mud has kept the answer since the First.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} The measure is retained in the peat.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has taken the verbs out again. \emph{Keeps} and \emph{hands up} are in my mouth and in theirs, and a woman lying face down in the cut wants to know whose hands are doing it. Both stand.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of the grey}

\begin{quote}\itshape In Grath they leave the grey where it fell\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and burn it on the morning after the Last;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we jar it and cork it and sell it south,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is a kind of sweeping, the reeve says.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Gloss:} He says it with a straight face and a dry one, which is the same face he uses for the fines. Nobody has bought our grey back and nobody has asked to.\end{quote}

\subsection*{VI. The place that is not a verse}

\emph{Here the leaf has a hole worked in it and a knot of grey wool tied through. There are no words to the sixth place. The reel of the cup goes round once more with the knot standing.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the hole:} nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape *\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In mine:} A nought is a figure and can be carried away. The sixth is a place and stays where it is. I have not untied the knot and I will not.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

He struck out three verbs and numbered the sixth place and wrote \emph{vacancy} under his nought. When I asked him what he wanted with a drinking-song, he said the factor wanted to know what the Fenfolk owed. A man who asks what you owe has written the answer before you open your mouth; all that is left him is to watch where you put your stop. I have put my verbs back under his and left his above, as a dry keeps the old cut showing under the new turf. A sentence with the doing taken out travels well and arrives empty, which is what the Court wants of a sentence. A knot arrives as it was tied.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The peat thumb at the head is mine and has gone into the grain. The tideline came up the second leaf the morning the Post stood under and has taken two words clean off the third verse; I have not written them back, because a song with two words gone is a song said slowly, and ours are all said slowly. The press of wet sedge is from the morning we lay flat in the cut until a beast’s pushing had gone past. The sour ring at the foot is small ale, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last by which time it had gone the colour of the floor it stood on. The eel slime at the fore-edge came off a man who set his cup down with his hands still wet from the baskets; he did not stay and I have not washed it. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at a peat-dry and nothing here is gathered and bottled and called dealt with. The knot of grey wool through the hole is mine and holds a word that does not go into Grathic. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cup goes round and comes back empty.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The ground it stood on is still owed.\end{quote}

I asked the reeve, the mud-wife out of Reedholt and a woman whose term is not out, and had three answerings and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the boards and the cup goes back on its nail. Tomorrow the cutting begins again and the cup will go round and nobody will pour for himself; and if the clerk comes up again from Greybank with his soft cuff and his pen, I shall put the verbs back and tie another knot for the word he cannot hear.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Song of the Fold, Being the Lullaby a Woman of Low Kiln Sang to a Child Come Back from the Bank}
\CRsheetheading{The Song of the Fold, Being the Lullaby a Woman of Low Kiln Sang to a Child Come Back from the Bank}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A mother’s lullaby for the third watch, taken down from her own mouth by a woman who keeps the drying racks; the song in the low half-sung speech of the yard, the rubrics of the room in the writer’s charcoal hand, a Court clerk’s correction in Ledgerhand, a gloss pressed into the margin by a hearth-maid who used the words at bedsides, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will claim · Sung in a kiln-house two doors up the Clay Yard in Low Kiln of Sill and set down in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a woman of the drying racks who had had a child come back to her from the bank in the Reed before; written in charcoal and tallow on the back of a birth-slate spoiled by a late entry, sewn with wire into a fold of grey birth-cloth and kept in a meal crock behind the lowest rack. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto a strip of sauce-paper from the factor’s house at Greybank. It survives soft at the fold with a tallow thumb at the head, a crust-grease print on the second leaf, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a ring where a cup of barley water stood from the first verse to the last, a green bead of glaze pressed into the lower corner, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court clerk who borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, a gloss in the thick charcoal hand of a hearth-maid who carried the words to bedsides, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own\par}\medskip
I sing this in a kiln-house two doors up the Clay Yard, and I have set it down because a man come up from Slate Row asked a woman at the well what the mothers sang when a child would not settle, and wrote the answer in a book before she had finished saying it. A lullaby is not a prayer. A prayer can be said in the clean voice, which takes the speaker neatly out of his own sentence; this has to be said in the voice the child has heard since it had ears, low, with the last word falling into the fold of the shawl. I have written it as we say it and put the verbs back where the clerk took them out.

I had a child come back to me from the bank in the Reed, warm and quiet, and he turned his face toward the pot when I set a cup down, which my first did not do at that age. I have never known whether that was the bank or the child, and I have not put either answer in the margin, because a margin is where a woman writes what she can bear to have read aloud.

The tallow at the head is mine. I held the slate down in the draught under the door and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How it is sung}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the third watch, after the fire has been turned with the back of a broken pot and the house has given its last instruction to the wind. Not at the first watch; a child at the first watch is still arguing with the day.

\item Warm the stone on your own wrist before it goes to the belly. A stone cold in your own hand is a stone and not a kindness, and no house here owns a Keldish one.

\item Set the child on the bed and not by the fire. Sing with your face turned toward the wall. Said looking into a face, the song becomes a question, and a child who has come back from the bank cannot answer it.

\item If a slate lies open on the bench, turn it face down first. A name said in the same room as an open slate travels, and a name that travels arrives somewhere the mother will not be told of.

\item Say the last line twice. The second saying is for the child who cannot say it yet, and the third, if there is one, is for the one who has forgotten how.

\item Do not sing it at a death-house door. That is a different song and belongs to the pot.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The stone goes to the belly before the first line. The hand that holds the child does not hold the slate. Refrain after every verse, said into the fold.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The stone came out of our neighbour’s fire,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I tried it on my wrist before I tried it on you;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a stone that’s cold in the hand is a stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a warm one is a kindness somebody paid for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The dark has no slate and no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The name goes in where the number can’t.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot on the shelf answers full to the knuckle,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pot by the door gives back flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I tap the one by the door because it’s ours,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the crack showing so the neighbours can see it was handled.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The dark has no slate and no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The name goes in where the number can’t.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s grey in the corner where the promise went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape don’t put your hand there, and don’t ask me whose;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the broom goes around it, the bucket goes around it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the house goes around it, which is the same thing said kindly.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The dark has no slate and no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The name goes in where the number can’t.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape You came with a red branch from the third rib down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I crossed two fingers at the edge of it and gave a date;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a date is an answer with nothing in it to argue with,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the edge of the branch is not to be washed.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The dark has no slate and no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The name goes in where the number can’t.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The tube went in at the arm and the slate took the figure,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the iron only opened the way, as they tell us;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape you came back warm and you did not come back knowing,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and which of them kept the knowing, nobody says.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The dark has no slate and no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The name goes in where the number can’t.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The loaf has a brown edge and the brown goes to you,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the crust is the kind part and the crumb is the rest;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eat what they give you and leave the place at the end\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape of the row where a loaf stood and nobody says why.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The dark has no slate and no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The name goes in where the number can’t.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape So lie still. I’ll say it where no clerk can hear.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The name’s in the fold and the fold’s in the bed;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the number stops at the door and the name goes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the dark keeps it over till you want it again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Lie still. The dark has no slate and no hand.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The child cannot say it. The dark says it twice.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the singing. I have left it on the slate. It is the space where a name would be said if the child could say it, and it is the right length for a name and for nothing else.

\subsection*{What the hearth-maid put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman who carried words between bedsides in the district and would not have them on a slate where a collector might see them. I have copied it as it stands.

At \emph{I crossed two fingers at the edge of it and gave a date}: \emph{She gave the date I had given her mother. Two women gave the same date in one room and neither looked at the other. A date is a door that shuts.}

At \emph{you did not come back knowing}: \emph{Said over a child of House Silt who came back in the year of the flower. The child lay warm and wanted nothing. The mother sang the old words to it every night for a tend, and the child never once turned at them, and she never once missed a night. Both stand.}

At \emph{the dark has no slate and no hand}: \emph{There was a hand in the room that night and it went to the slate before it went to the child. I have put no name to it. It was not the mother’s hand.}

At the space before the last refrain: \emph{The third saying is not for the child. I have asked whose it is and been given a date.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A Court clerk borrowed the leaf on an Account-day, with a cuff gone soft from washing and ink sitting in two fingers of it that would not come out. He took the verbs out of the verses and set his words above mine.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{a warm one is a kindness somebody paid for}, he wrote \emph{the stone was transferred by consent; cost to district, nil}. It is true in the figure and false in the room I sang it in. I have left it.

\item At \emph{the pot by the door gives back flat}, he wrote \emph{the vessel failed, having reached its term}, and underlined it twice.

\item At \emph{the house goes around it}, he wrote \emph{no entry required}, which is what the Court says when it wants a thing left alone.

\item At \emph{which of them kept the knowing, nobody says}, he wrote \emph{thin return, entered}, and put a figure against it that was not in my song.

\item Where I had left the space before the last refrain, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beside it. He has put a number where a name should stand, which is the whole art of that hand.

\end{itemize}

I have put my words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child at the third watch does not know he is hearing something always true, and wants to know which hand will hold him.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The crust-grease on the second leaf is from a browned edge laid down while I was telling a child to eat and it would not. I left it where it fell. The ring is barley water, set down at the first verse and taken up at the last, by which time it had gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The green bead came off a girl with sweetness still at her mouth who leaned over to see the writing and touched the cloth and said nothing and went back to the rack. I have not washed it and would not if I knew how. The grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind a rack. The thread drawn through the hole in the fold is grey wool, tied for the word I could not write down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pot keeps the crack. The bed keeps the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and is read aloud all the same.\end{quote}

I asked a woman at the well, the clerk and a hearth-maid who came through with a bundle, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The crock goes back behind the rack. Tomorrow the fire will be turned with the back of a broken pot and I shall sing the same words into the same fold, and a child who cannot yet say them will hear them for the third time. If an officer finds the leaf, let him take the verbs out. The next hand will put them back, and will warm the stone on its own wrist before it reads.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The South Beam at the Peat Line, Being the Price-list of the Border Market and the Dues of the Grain Road, the Wine Road, the Mill Road and the Crossing, Set Down by a Clerk Who Keeps Both Ends of a Figure}
\CRsheetheading{The South Beam at the Peat Line, Being the Price-list of the Border Market and the Dues of the Grain Road, the Wine Road, the Mill Road and the Crossing, Set Down by a Clerk Who Keeps Both Ends of a Figure}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A market clerk’s fair copy of the board that hangs over the southern beam, with the figure asked set above the figure taken, the goods of the empire priced against the goods that come north out of the mud, the tolls of four posted roads and a fifth that is the drain, two corrections in borrowed hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written at the Peat Line in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, in the first market after the Long Cold, by the clerk who keeps the south beam for a factor of the Ten Bowls; carried north with a tally of eels at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again at the third Account-day of Grain. It survives on the back of a grain-warrant discharged at the Line, sewn with a thread of grey wool into a fold of oiled silk and kept in the breast pocket against a wooden counting peg, with the yellow dust of the burning winds ground into the fold, a ring of warm wine the width of a cup at the head, a smear of myrrh across the second leaf, a white salt bloom along the lower margin, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a thumb of oil from the wine jars, a small square scraped bare where a word would not stand, two corrections in hands that are not the writer’s, and one line at the foot that nobody will claim.\par}\medskip
I keep the beam on the southern bank of the Line, where the peat water stands between the two countries and neither will say whose water it is. The army stopped here in Y.H. 634 and the arguing has gone on longer than the army did. A factor’s man comes down out of the north with eels and asks the figure before he has unloaded; by the time the eels are counted the figure has changed, because a man with a roof over his goods does not pay for the weather. I write the figure asked and the figure taken in two columns. The house calls this double entry. I call it keeping both ends of a figure in sight.

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, which is our coin and travels north as far as Greybank and then stops, being too bright for that country. The Court books an ember at five marks. I have kept no column for embers. In nine years at this beam I have never held one, and I have held a man’s collar while he was counted.

The north prints one in twelve on its notice and reads it twice over a basket. I have heard another figure spoken under the boards below the sill, which I have no beam to weigh and have not entered here. A figure I cannot weigh is a figure somebody will want me to read aloud.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a clerk come up from Greybank, written above my first column:} Coin and reckoning entered. Ember: five marks. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} He has written it as though an ember could be carried across the Line in a coat. I have carried eels across it and never an ember. I have left his figure standing and put the verb back.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The board as it hangs over the beam}

\emph{The first figure is what is said at the household door or on the factor’s counter. The second is what is taken here, where the load is set down. Both were cried between the last market of Stone and the third Account-day of Grain.}

Article — As it is said — As it is taken here\par

Barley, a sack, dressed and dry — 1 mark — 1 mark, and a handful off the crown of the sack at the twelfth post, which is not entered\par

Red wine, a jar, first pouring — 2 marks — 2 marks; the jar is not returned, which nobody calls a charge\par

Oil, a jar — 2 marks — 2 marks, and a finger of it on this leaf\par

Glazed bowl, green, off a southern wheel — 2 marks — 2 marks here; 3 in the Bowl, where the colour is praised before the price\par

Salt herring, a basket out of the Sallow — 2 bits — 3 bits; the salt has been all the way up the Salt Road and knows it\par

Eels, smoked, by the basket — 3 bits — 2 bits at the southern boards; the same eels are counted again on the northern bank\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone — the Stone figure, paid in Grain, without complaint, as in the north\par

Reed bundle, an armful — not on any board — ask the arm that carried it; the arm knows weight and not cost\par

Field hand, sound of wind, the season — 12 marks — 12 marks; the season begins the day before it is named\par

House-born hand who can read a tally — 40 marks — 40 marks; the seller counts her years twice and the buyer does not correct him\par

Northern shape, whole, with memory — not cried at any board — 1,200 marks and forty unspent measures, as it is written in the factor’s room; it does not cross this beam\par

Debt-slates, burned by lot after a feast — no figure — the fire; the slates are made new before the wine is cold\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin, in mine:} The factor’s clerk struck out \emph{sound of wind}, saying a board has no use for a description. I put it back. No row here is a person’s name. That is not the same as saying no person stands behind it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} There is a figure spoken in the yards north of the Line which is not the printed one. I have heard it and set down nothing. A clerk who enters a figure he has not weighed will be asked to read it aloud at a feast.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Paid in the mud and not entered}

What is given — What I write\par

A wet foot — a stick notched by the bunch — no figure; the boards are counted and nobody says which will bear\par

Tribute in eels, going north — eels by the basket — the basket, in kind; north of here a man is a neighbour, which costs less\par

A name said over a child before the collector comes — a name said three times into the ground under the boards — nothing; no stick can hold it and no court has asked\par

A cup set at a cradle’s head — the cup stands full and is not drunk — nothing; it is not the child’s cup and it is not the woman’s\par

The seventh name — kept empty for the household to choose — a space, the length of a name, not a nought\par

The yellow dust of the burning winds — breathed through a season — nothing; a man comes back thin and no post charges it\par

A nought is a figure that can be spent somewhere else. A space is where it stands. I have kept the space.

\subsection*{The dues of the roads}

Four roads are posted at this market and a fifth is the drain, which has no post and is the dearest of them. The figures on the left are what a man is told at the road’s end. The figures on the right are what left his hand.

\subsection*{The Grain Road}

Two hundred leagues south to the Bowl of Sere, through eleven grain posts and a twelfth that is painted and charges nothing. Grain and people go down it. Crowns come up, and eels, and the news that a household has had a good year.

As told at the post — As taken\par

A cart of grain going south — 2 bits at the Line — 2 bits, and a handful off the top at the twelfth post\par

A sack passing a grain post — 1 bit at each — 1 bit at each of eleven; at the twelfth a hand goes into the sack and no receipt is given\par

A crown going north — no due — no due; the Emperor’s face is sufficient\par

A person in a cord going south — 2 marks at the Line — 2 marks here and 2 again at the Bowl Gate; the second is for the road, which has no slate\par

A cart coming north with eels — 3 bits — 3 bits, and the eels weighed again on the northern bank, where the reeve uses a different beam\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter asked why a sack pays eleven times to travel one road. I told him the twelfth is a place and not a charge. He said a place was the dearest thing on any road, which is true and not an entry I can make.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The Wine Road}

It comes in from the east, where the wine is made, and runs to the east gate of the Bowl and from there to the coast, where the Vhaleni buy it. The road is paid in wine when the factor’s man is thirsty, which is often.

As told — As taken\par

A jar at the east gate — 1 bit on the jar — 1 bit on the jar, 2 marks on the wine\par

A broken jar — nothing; there is no wine to carry — 1 bit for the pieces, which are swept into the road and paid for twice\par

A bowl emptied in public at a feast — no toll — no toll; the applause is entered in the household and the slate is burnt afterward\par

A man who licks the rim of a green cup at the gate — nothing — nothing, and the sweetness stays with him for the length of the road\par

\subsection*{The Mill Road}

A day’s dust from the Bowl to the grain mills. A person sent to the mills when the term is called goes down this road, and the road is paid by whoever called the term, which is the cleanest figure in the empire.

As told — As taken\par

A sack of grain going down to the mills — 1 bit at the mill door — 1 bit, and a tenth of the grinding, which the mill calls the fire\par

A sack coming back — 1 bit for the sack — 2 bits if it comes back empty, having used the road twice and carried nothing either time\par

A person sent when the term is called — no toll at the gate — nothing here; the price is written in the house that called the term\par

\subsection*{The crossing of the Line}

The water between the countries has two banks and two hands on it, and the hands are paid at different hours.

As told — As taken\par

A basket of eels going north — tribute — 3 bits to the reeve, in eels, by the basket\par

A dry foot — 1 bit each way — 1 bit to each bank, and the two agree on nothing but the coin\par

A person counted in the south and carried north — no due at the water — the paper that names him is left in the rain, which is a virtue in Vhalen and a convenience everywhere else\par

\subsection*{The drain cuts}

No post, no figure, no hand. Fever follows the ditch up into the water in both directions, and whichever country dug pays it. I have set this under the roads and not among them: a due is a figure somebody will stand behind and the ditch has nobody.

\subsection*{The song the drivers carry}

\emph{Sung going down the Grain Road with the empty carts, never coming back up with grain. Said to the posts, not to one another.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to the mark and twenty to the crown,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the north counts what it lost and the south what it kept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the foot and a bit for the cart,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a third for the road that has no slate.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Eleven posts and a twelfth where the grain goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two marks for a cord and two for the gate;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wine goes up and the eels come down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the man in the middle is counted twice.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four roads are posted and a fifth is the drain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a sixth has no name and no hand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the beam keeps what the cart brought over,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Line keeps the rest in the mud.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of a bowl-house tally-clerk, against the last part:} Five roads entered. Nil. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are six, and the sixth is a place. A nought is a figure that can be carried away. The sixth stays where it is.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two hands did}

The clerk from Greybank writes upright and narrow and leaves the doer out: against \emph{a hand goes into the sack} he wrote \emph{a levy is applied at the twelfth post}. The bowl-house man, who writes leaning with gold at the ends of the strokes, put \emph{contractual person} where I put \emph{a person in a cord}, and a nought where the song keeps a place. I have left both readings standing above mine. A verb is the difference between a price and a debt.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The yellow at the head and in the fold is off the burning winds and has worked into the grain of the warrant; no damp takes it out, and it is the only mark here that came without a hand. The wine ring is the width of the cup they carry down from the court at the third hour. The myrrh came off a phial set beside a cradle while the woman who owns neither spoke to a child who is not hers. The salt bloom has eaten the figure against \emph{salt herring}, so that I cannot read whether it stood at two bits or three; a price the weather has taken is truer than one a clerk can still read, and I have not written it in again. The eel slime at the foot is mine, from holding the basket still while the reeve counted. The green bead is lead glaze off a cup whose rim had gone thin; a buyer set it on the leaf and went back to the wine. The grey wool caught in the sewing came off a northern coat when a man leaned to see the figures; he did not see it go. There is no Last Day at this beam. The board is scraped and written again every tend, and nothing here is burnt in the morning and called dealt with except the slates at a feast, which are made new before the wine is cold.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps what the cart carried. The mud keeps what the road took. The bowl keeps what nobody paid for.\end{quote}

I asked a carter of the Grain Road, a woman who holds a share in a boat on the Quay at Vhal, and a reeve’s man from the Standing Post, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the oiled silk and the silk into the breast pocket. Tomorrow the eels come up out of the north and the grain goes down, and a figure will be asked at this beam that by evening will be a thing that was true for a morning. I shall set it under the figure they gave and leave the space between them as it is.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Stand in the Peat, Being a Bog-Hunter’s Field Notes on the Fen-Leech or Bog-Cow of the East Marsh}
\CRsheetheading{The Stand in the Peat, Being a Bog-Hunter’s Field Notes on the Fen-Leech or Bog-Cow of the East Marsh}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hunter’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of stands and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the backs of spoiled peat-tallies, a peat-cutter’s song in the words it is sung, two rulings in the narrow upright hand of the reeve’s counting-man, a line in the pale salt-paper ink of a Vhaleni hide-buyer, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Reed and Tallow of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a hunter of the Standing Post who kept the east-marsh peat-dries for the reeve and took the beast for its hide and its horn; set down at the end of stands in the peat-hut with a peat-fire under a pot, first on spoiled peat-tallies and then on three folded strips of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket against a flint and a twist of tallow. Copied forward in Reed of Y.H. 813. It survives with peat worked into the head in a brown thumb, a press of wet sedge across the first leaf, a spot the size of a fingernail on the second leaf where a boy’s blood fell, a horn-shaving caught in the gutter of the tally, a scorch where a coal from the peat-fire took the corner of the third leaf, the charcoal rubbed thin where the book was carried against the thigh, two rulings in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the reeve’s counting-man, a line in the pale ink of a Vhaleni hide-buyer written on salt-paper gone soft at one corner, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the peat-dries east of Reedholt for the reeve, and I take the cow when the Standing Post wants a hide or a horn. It is not a trade a man puts on a slate. The reeve’s counting-man writes what is paid and I write what I have put my hand to, and the two have never agreed and were never meant to. I set this down at the end of a stand in the peat-hut with a peat-fire under a pot and the tallow down to a knuckle, and the cold comes up through the boardwalk and takes a man by the ankles before it takes him anywhere else.

The brown at the head is peat. I know the difference between peat and Ash the way a man knows the difference between his own debt and another man’s: both stick to the hand, and one of them stays in the house after you have gone. There is Ash enough on this beast without my bringing it into the book. I have not washed the peat off.

\subsection*{Where it stands}

The cow stands in the black peat east of the marsh road where the ground gives a little under the boot and comes back warm. I have laid the back of my hand on the peat where one has stood and on peat a spear-cast away, and the two are not the same. Under the beast the peat is warm as a banked coal under its skin of grey; a spear-cast off it is cold water and sedge. I have set that down and put no cause beside it. The reeve says it is the Marsh Mother keeping her own down there. A Vhaleni hide-man says warm water comes up through the bog and the beast has found where it comes. Both men said it standing on the boardwalk, which is a dry place to say anything.

It stands until only the head shows. I have watched one hold the same place through a tend and part of another, and the sedge about it flattened and the water went still, and I went away and came back and found it there with the same set of the head. It does not chew. It does not lie down. It takes in through the hide, which is a thing a man can feel at the back of the hand without seeing it, the way he can feel a fire in the next room before he sees the flame. I have no word for that in Grathic and I have not made one.

\subsection*{The push}

It lowers its head and pushes. That is the whole of the danger, and a man who has never stood in peat will not believe how much of a man a beast can take with a push when the ground will not hold his foot. On hard ground you step aside. In the bog your foot goes in to the calf and stays, and the beast does not hurry. I saw a Held man --- a man who carried more than his natural measure and could lift a peat-bale above his head --- go down under one because he braced his legs, and bracing was the thing that took him. The peat did the rest. The beast stood over him and held him where he fell. It did not eat him. It kept him there until he stopped wanting, and when we got him out he was a man who would not say what had been done to him and asked only for the warm.

The order of it I have set in the tally. The why I have left standing where I found it, which is in the peat. There is no anger in the push. It is the same work the tide does when it takes a boardwalk up and leaves it somewhere a man cannot reach. I have written that sentence out once and not crossed it out, which is more than I did in the last book I kept, and I am not sure it was wisdom.

A Drawn man came up from the Post in Tallow and walked round one of these with his coat open and did not quicken. To him it is an obstacle in the ground, not a fight. I have set that beside the Held man going down and left the two where they fell, because they are both true and a man must choose which one he is before he goes out, not after.

\subsection*{The song}

Sung by the peat-cutters going out to the dries at first light, not coming back. The third line is the Marsh Mother’s line and every cutter sings it wrong on purpose, because a song that gives the cow a reason is a song a man can carry home and set by the fire. I have set it down as it is sung, with the wrong line standing.

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the mud and one for the stand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cow keeps her head where the warm came up;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape she lows to the Mother and she lies in the peat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape she takes through the hide and gives nothing back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Three for the push and three for the bog,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the man who braced and could not;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Mother counts what her cattle take\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and never counts what they leave in the ground.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count the horns and count the hide,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count the days that the beast stood still;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reeve takes one and the salt-man one,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one stays where the standing was.\end{quote}

She does not low and she does not lie down. I have stood within three paces of six of them and never heard a sound out of one, and I have never found a place where one has lain. The cutters know this as well as I do. They sing it that way because a beast with no reason in it is a beast a man cannot forgive for what it did to his brother, and a man who cannot forgive has to carry something home.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the stands I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had the fever and had forgotten the day. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The counting-man’s figures are his, not mine. I counted what stood and what came walking back; he counted what the Post could sell.

Stand — Place — Stood — Taken — Hides — Horns — Lost\par

Reed 3 — East of the marsh road — one — one — one — two — none\par

Reed 11 — Old cut beyond the sedge — two — one — one — three — spear lost in the peat\par

Reed 20 — Warm place under the alder — one — none — none — none — a boy, taken by the leg, lived\par

Tallow 4 — Black stand south of the Post — three — two — two — five — none; wind turned, we were heard\par

Tallow 16 — New ground, no name yet — two — one — one — two — one of ours, braced, did not come back\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright Ledgerhand of the reeve’s counting-man, written along the margin:} Enter as: three hides, twelve horns. One hide and four horn to a beast; this is the figure the Post will ask for. Loss of persons: not entered. The bog is not a vessel. Account stands.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. He has set \emph{not entered} over the boy’s leg and over the man who did not come back, and \emph{the bog is not a vessel} over the warm place under my hand, which is the neatest piece of work I have seen out of the Standing Post. A count-stick can settle a fine and a fine unpaid can become a term and a term unpaid can become a measure, so there is a kind of justice in it, if the stick is held by the right hand. I have written the leg and the man under his line in charcoal, where his column cannot reach.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the pale ink of a Vhaleni hide-buyer, on a corner of salt-paper gone soft:} Three marks paid and received at Vhal. The water keeps out. --- K.\end{quote}

Three marks is thirty-six bits and a bit is a loaf and a quart of small ale, so a hide is most of a winter to a household that has one. K. has never asked where the stand was that gave the hide. I have sold him three. There is a fourth hide lying in the peat-hut that I have not sold, and I have not set a figure against it.

\subsection*{The hide and the horn}

The hide, dried over peat, keeps out water better than anything else in Sarn, which is a strange thing when you consider that it came out of water. The buyer comes up the marsh road in Tallow with his salt-paper in his pocket and his hands always warm, and he pays in marks and counts them twice, and I have never known him to short a man and never known him to overpay one either. I have never sold him the hide of a beast I found standing where a man had gone down. He has asked for it and the reeve has told me to take what is offered, and I keep the hide under the bench and the reeve’s word on the boardwalk where it was said.

The horns go to the Standing Post and are cut into count-sticks. A horn takes a notch differently from bone: the reeve can tell his own stick by the feel of the notch in the dark, which he says is the reason for it and not the price. I have cut the horns and notched nothing. Who the sticks count is not a thing a hunter asks when the counting-man is standing over him with a cuff gone soft at the wrist and a hand that goes to the stick before it goes to the man.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

They say it is the Marsh Mother’s own cattle, set in the bog to keep the warm down where her people can lie face down in it and find it. There are songs in the Fenmarch with a woman’s name in them and a kindness done at a peat-cutting. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. But I have put my hand on the peat where one has stood and on peat where none has, and I have watched a beast driven off a warm place go and stand in another warm place, and if these are the Mother’s cattle then she keeps them in particular places, and the particular place is the whole of what I can see. What it wants there I have left where I found it.

There was a man of Mud End went into the black stand after a hide in Tallow of Y.H. 811 and came out with the fever that burns a man and then leaves him colder than he went, each turn taking a little head. There is no physic for it but keeping warm, which is a thing the poor cannot do, and he went home and did. I have not put his name in this book. The reeve’s stick knows it, I daresay, in its own way.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The peat thumb at the head is mine, from setting the leaf down on the hut bench and not knowing I had marked it. The wet sedge across the first leaf came off the morning the wind turned on us and we lay flat in the cut until the push had gone past, and I have left the press of it where it fell.
