\begin{quote}\itshape three for the green we get off the Cliffs,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the coal the gull has got;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the bench that rows seven years,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the wine with salt on the rim;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the share that goes down the mother,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the word that is counted at half;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine for the pan where the water comes in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ten for the step where it turns and goes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven for the slate they keep in the house,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve for the mark that goes into the fist.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The half that is not a share}

A child whose father came aboard jumps at the half. She goes on one foot and says \emph{half} under her breath on every line, and the others allow it, because half is what he brought and half is what this house has always given her. She does not get to shut the mark in her fist at the twelfth; the mark is a whole thing and she has not got a whole one. She stands aside at the turn and comes in again on the ebb, which is the only tide that ever brought anything back to this coast. If she argues, they tell her the boat was here before her word, which is a hard saying to a child and a true one.

\subsection*{The gull’s edge}

A child who puts a foot wrong goes to the gull. The gull is the far edge of the pan, where the salt is too thin to bear a weight; the child sits there and watches the others jump. She is brought back by three bits of salt put into her open hand, one after another, with nothing said. A child sent to the gull is brought back by the salt and not by a name, because a name called across the pans travels and comes back with a figure on it. This is the children’s own law and I have never once known them to break it. They stop when the crust goes soft or a dipper tells them off the pan, and the last thing said is always the bringing-back, never the count. A child left sitting at the gull’s edge when they stop is not counted as having played, which is a kindness the Council would not understand.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man from the Council is on the Quay}

\emph{I have it from the child who keeps the cord, with the space left before it. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it with him in hearing. She said it to the crust with her back turned and made me put it down as I have it, with none of my verbs in it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The draw takes the Warm and the tax takes the draw,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rain takes the paper and calls it the law;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the pan keeps the salt and the tide keeps the count,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat comes back on the water it spent.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the half that is not a share,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the mark that is not a debt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say it to the crust and jump it through,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and no man in a clean cuff knows what it cost.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A clerk of the Council borrowed the sheet on the morning he came down, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He writes in the leaning hand they use in the Council room, where it smells of tar and wet rope, and the ink sits in two fingers of his cuff and will not come out. He numbered the twelve lines in the margin. At \emph{the mark that goes into the fist} he wrote above, \emph{the measure is retained by the counter and not entered}. At \emph{the tide takes it} he wrote \emph{instrument void by exposure to water; no value attaches}, and underneath, \emph{no claim can lie against a lost mark, which is fortunate for all parties}. Against the half he set \emph{the fractional interest is rated at one half and does not constitute a share}. At the foot of the count he put a round nought and wrote \emph{nil} against it, where the children’s game ends with salt in an open hand.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child up to her ankle in the salt of the pan does not know she is jumping something always true, and wants to know which foot to lift. A nought is a number. The half is a place at the table. The fist is not a bank. He has put a figure where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned by it. I told him the count and the turn and the bringing-back, and he said it was the whole doctrine of returns taught before a child could hold a slate, and he entered it. The children stop jumping when a man from the Council comes onto the crust and take it up again when he is past the shore road, and they never once change the twelve.

\subsection*{In the dipper’s charcoal}

At the foot of the first leaf, in thick charcoal that has rubbed onto the fold, in the hand of a dipper who borrowed the sheet while the net was mending:

\begin{quote}\itshape We read the flood at dawn and tell the Council what it is worth. The ebb brings the boat back and nobody puts a figure on it. The children put a figure on it and then give it to the tide. That is why I let them have my old cord. A cord that counts and then loses is the only honest cord on this coast.\end{quote}

When I asked him why he wrote it on a children’s game he said a game is the only paper in Vhal that a Council man never thinks to read. I have left the charcoal where he put it and not washed the fold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The salt crust at the head and along the gutter has gone into the grain of the paper and will not come out. The tar thumb is mine; I held the leaf down in a wind off the Sallow and did not know I had marked it. The fibre of net-cord in the second fold came off the cord the children use and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the tin. The green bead came off a girl’s hair as she leaned over to see the writing, and she did not ask for it back. The gull’s peck went through the word \emph{flood} in the verse and I have left the hole standing, because a verse about the tide with a word taken out by a bird is in better order than I could have made it. The wet corner took two lines of the verse and they are void by the Council’s own law, which is a virtue; I have left the space the length of them and written nothing in it, because a verse with two lines gone is a verse said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The grey print along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it and there is no Last Day at the pans. I keep this leaf dry in a tin lined with rushes, which is a strange thing to do in Vhal, where paper is made to rot. A document the rain has not had is a document the Council can still read. That is the only reason I keep it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The pan keeps the salt and the tide keeps the count;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the half is a share and the share is a debt;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fist keeps the bit that the slate cannot keep,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the boat comes back on the water it spent.\end{quote}

I asked the child who keeps the cord, a dipper, a woman who holds a share from her mother, and a Council clerk come up from the Quay, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back into the tin I keep on the shelf with the paper I mean to let the rain take. Tomorrow the flood will come in over the third pan and the crust will bear a foot again, and the children will jump the twelve and give them back to the water, and the clerk will put a figure against the one thing in this port that was never for sale.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Turning of the Fire, Being the Watch-Song of the Kiln-Mouth in Low Kiln, Sung at the Firing and Again at the Second Firing}
\CRsheetheading{The Turning of the Fire, Being the Watch-Song of the Kiln-Mouth in Low Kiln, Sung at the Firing and Again at the Second Firing}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A firing song of the clay yard, called to the damper and answered into the mouth, the words in the low half-sung speech of the yard; written in charcoal thinned with brick-dust, the rubrics of the mouth in the same hand, a kiln-master’s correction in broad charcoal, a factor’s clerk’s figures in a narrow upright Ledgerhand, a gloss in the thick charcoal of a woman who rakes the lower fire, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Smoke of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by an old woman who turns the fire at a kiln two doors above the Vail in Low Kiln of Sill, who learned her letters off a tile-counter and has no slate in the yard; written on the back of a firing-tally spoiled by a wet thumb while the second firing was being counted, tied with grey wool to the handle of the damper under a broken pot turned mouth-down against the rain. Copied forward in Tallow of Y.H. 813 onto a strip of oiled paper from the wheel-shed after the first leaf scorched. It survives with a brick-dust thumb at the head, a long scorch along the lower edge where the leaf lay too near the mouth, a green bead of lead glaze pressed into the corner, a small-ale ring through the third verse, a grey Ash smear in the gutter that nobody will own, a sherd pressed between the fourth and fifth leaves, one line eaten away by the heat and not written in again, one correction in broad charcoal, four in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk at Greybank, a gloss from a woman at the tubs, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I have turned the fire at a kiln two doors above the Vail through nineteen firings and have never seen a man write down what we say at the mouth. A factor’s man came up off the north bridge with a cuff gone soft from washing and asked a girl at the tubs what the women sang when the fire was kept through the night; she began to tell him and he wrote before she had finished. I have set it down in her words and in mine, with the rests left in.

A firing song is not a tune. A tune wants a voice with nothing in its hands, and at the mouth every hand is full. It is said to the iron and to the coals, to keep the rake moving and the count honest. Sung at a table it grows a melody in it, and a man in a clean coat can carry that away and enter it as a custom. I have put the verbs back where the clerk took them out.

The brick-dust at the head is mine. I held the tally down on the flagstone with the hand I rake with and did not know I had marked it.

\subsection*{How the fire is kept}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Turn the coals with the back of a broken pot, never with iron. Iron remembers the heat and gives it back in a man’s face.

\item The call goes to the damper and the answer goes into the mouth. Said looking at a woman it becomes an argument, and an argument at the mouth ends with somebody setting the tongue wrong.

\item Four pulls to the rake and a rest at the turn of the tongue. The rest is not a pull and is not counted. It is where the iron is given its other bite.

\item The damper has two bites and no Grathic word that holds both. Hold one and the pot comes whole out of the firing; hold the other and a hand comes off a man. Call the iron by what it is doing that hour and do not ask it what it means.

\item A girl come up from the Glaze Room with green at one corner of her mouth and the pale line at her gum does not rake. Not a punishment. Sweetness makes a hand careless, and a careless hand turns the tongue too far.

\item If a slate lies on the bench, turn it face down before the first pull. A fire said over an open slate arrives somewhere the speaker did not send it, and gets entered there.

\item Do not sing when the Slip Brook is up brown. The water has its own note, and two notes over one mouth make two counts that will not agree, and the yard goes around both all day.

\item The last part is kept back. It is for when the man from Greybank has gone back over the bridge with his satchel under his arm and the yard can hear itself again.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\emph{The woman at the mouth calls the first line of each pair; the hands along the bank answer the second. The refrain is said low into the mouth at the turn of the tongue, and the last line is held until the rake is back on the iron.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The coal came down from the Last Day under ash,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we broke it out with a broken pot and gave it a name of our own;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it is the same fire in every house in the yard,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and every house says it kept it, and none says who lit it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate keeps neither, and is read in the morning.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Green clay will stand up straight all day\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and slump in the night with nobody to see it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape so will a promise, and so will a man\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape who has been told the thaw is only weather.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One iron holds the heat in and takes it out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape say which mercy you mean before you touch the tongue.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man with his finger in it holds his tongue instead,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is the answer most of us give.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The glaze goes on green and comes off with a sweetness;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the girl who tastes it has a pale line at her gum.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Do not let her rake. The lead does not care whose hand it takes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes the steadiest first.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The breath kills in sleep and leaves no mark worth speaking of;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape they call it merciful who have not gone in after breakfast.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We set a pot at the door of the house where it happened,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and say nothing to the pot, and the pot says nothing back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate keeps neither, and is read in the morning.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for them that came late;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the figure you heard is not the figure they paid.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Take nothing out while the hot is still in it.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A cup knocked at the draw answers full or answers flat;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the flat ones go by the road for the cart to crush,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape which is kinder than letting a buyer find them.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Keep it low. The mouth takes what the hand will give.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Four at the rake and a rest where the fifth should be;}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn,}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{and the slate keeps neither, and is read in the morning.}\end{quote}

There is a space before the last refrain in the keeping, the length of a turn of the tongue. I have left it on the tally. The clerk put a round nought in it once, which is a thing you can hold up and look at, and a rest is not.

\subsection*{The part they keep back}

\emph{Not said while the factor’s man is in the yard. Taken up after he has gone back over the bridge. The women say it to the damper and not across the square.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four at the mouth and a gap where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we do not name whose gap it is, and the house does not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The heat we keep was paid for somewhere before it came here,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a quiet man down at Mud End went in his sleep last week\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody made a lesson of him.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The number goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and arrives at nobody, and nobody asks where;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a brine-gull went off upriver with a coal from a banked fire\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape that was not yet cold, and carried it out of the account.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four and a rest. The iron keeps the other bite.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clerk has no word for a thing a woman does with her hand.\end{quote}

One line of this part is gone where the leaf lay too near the mouth. I know what it said. Knowing a thing is not the same as having it, and I have not written it in again.

\subsection*{What the kiln-master did}

He borrowed the leaf at the firing and wrote in broad charcoal over my small hand. He has read every line of it with one eye on the damper.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At} the glaze goes on green and comes off with a sweetness: \emph{Green ware, current. The sweetness is not entered.}\end{quote}

I have left it standing. He is right about the ware and wrong about the sweetness, which is entered somewhere, and not by him.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk took the leaf on the morning we drew the second firing, ink sitting in two fingers of it that would not come out. He took the heat out and set his figures above mine. I have left his hand standing and mine underneath, as the mouth keeps the pot’s heat and the flagstone keeps the scorch.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the pot keeps the note and the hand keeps the burn}, he wrote \emph{vessel sound, entered; quality not a figure. Labour, one mark; no deduction for injury}. True in the figure, false at the mouth, where the note is the whole of the quality and the burn is the whole of the price.

\item At \emph{four at the rake and a rest}, he wrote \emph{four pulls, fifth nil}. A nought is a number. The rest is where the iron changes hands.

\item At \emph{we do not name whose gap it is}, he wrote \emph{cost to district, nil}. It is true in the figure and false in the room that breathes through its mouth at the end of the yard.

\item At \emph{a quiet man down at Mud End went in his sleep}, he wrote \emph{one death, cause undetermined}, and drew a line under it as if a line could close it.

\item At \emph{carried it out of the account}, he wrote \emph{loss, nil; gain, nil}, and put the leaf face down, which is the only thing he has done all morning that the yard could agree with.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{What the woman at the tubs put in the margin}

The thick charcoal belongs to a woman below the racks who has raked more firings than she will count. I have copied it as it stands, without making the two hands agree.

At \emph{the same fire in every house}: \emph{We say it kept it because there is no other sentence. In my first winter I asked who lit the first one and was told to ask the fire, which is an answer given by people who asked the same thing at their own first firing.}

At \emph{say which mercy you mean}: \emph{A man held the cold side of that iron for twenty years and never once said which bite he meant. He is dead now and the pot he kept is still on the shelf.}

At \emph{the girl who tastes it}: \emph{I have held the pale line up to the light for three of them. Two went south. The third still rakes, and I have said nothing, which is a kindness and a fault in the same breath.}

At \emph{the flat ones go by the road}: \emph{My father set a flat cup by the road and a buyer took it up anyway and carried it three leagues before it broke. Somebody paid for those three leagues and it was not my father.}

At the kept-back part: \emph{The river takes what the Court does not. You can shout at either one. I have tried.}

\subsection*{At the head and along the gutter}

The brick-dust thumb at the head is mine and will not come out of the grain, which is why I use it to sign. The scorch along the lower edge is where I laid the fold on the flagstone while the mouth was open; it took the corner off two lines, and I have not written them in again, because a song with its corner gone is a song the yard has half forgotten, which is how most of them reach us. The green bead came off a girl who leaned to see the writing with sweetness still at her tongue; she touched the paper, said nothing, and went back to the Glaze Room. I have not washed it. The small-ale ring went through the third verse while a woman stood over me telling me to keep it low; she set her cup down and took it up when I had done, and the ring has gone the colour of the pot it stood on. The long grey along the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying on a kiln bench. Nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day behind a fire. The sherd between the fourth and fifth leaves answers flat when I knock it; I keep it there to remind me what flat is. The grey wool through the hole ties the leaf to the damper handle, and there is a knot in it for the one line I could not bring up and have not looked to see whether it has come back.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The clay keeps the thumb. The fire keeps the cost.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate keeps neither and is turned face up at the Weighing.\end{quote}

I asked the woman at the tubs, the kiln-master and a man who came up from Greybank with a satchel, and had a proverb, a figure and a date, and no hand to set over any of them. I have left the line where it was written.

The leaf goes back on the damper hook. There is a firing in Ember and another in Smoke, and the fire will be turned with the back of a broken pot, four pulls and a gap, and the gap will be left where it was found. If the factor’s clerk borrows the leaf again he may strike out the verbs. The fire does not care. The hands do.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Two Figures, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Standing Post Concerning the Thirty-One Years, the Figure Read at the Ferry and the Figure Paid at the Reed, with the Years as the Reeves Kept Them, the Court’s Annals Set Beside Them, the Fen Song, and the Corrections of a Factor’s Clerk}
\CRsheetheading{The Two Figures, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Standing Post Concerning the Thirty-One Years, the Figure Read at the Ferry and the Figure Paid at the Reed, with the Years as the Reeves Kept Them, the Court’s Annals Set Beside Them, the Fen Song, and the Corrections of a Factor’s Clerk}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A reeve’s-clerk’s extract from the chronicle of the Standing Post in the Fenmarch, copied out of the tarred box under the third board of the walk; the years in a broad standing hand gone stiff with peat water, the Court annals in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk come up from Greybank, the two figures entered in a column that no clerk of the Keeping has ever signed, one song taken down in Reed from a singer who would not give her name, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written at the Standing Post in the Fenmarch by the clerk who keeps the reeves’ chronicle, a man with no slate-name who signs with a thumb pressed into peat, in Reed and Ember of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813; copied from the post’s original begun in Y.H. 420 and kept since in a tarred box under the third board of the walk, where the peat water reaches the nails in the wet season. It survives as six leaves of stout foolscap sewn with wire and folded in oiled sailcloth, with black peat worked into the gutter and the creases of the thumb, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the clerk did not make and will not sweep, a twist of wet reed fibre pressed flat in the second leaf, a strip of Vhaleni salt-paper gone soft at the edge and pasted over the sixth clause, a dark streak of eel slime at the foot, a tallow thumb at the head, a bead of green cliff-glass in the lower corner, the broad reeve’s correction standing above the narrow Court correction standing above the text, and one line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the chronicle of the Standing Post. It is not a history of Sarn and does not pretend to be one. The reeves of the Fenmarch are chosen for standing longest in a bog, and a man who has stood longer than any other is asked to settle the fines and the feuds, which he does in a voice thinned by the waiting. Nobody writes down the years he gave to the standing. The post writes them down. I copy the post.

This extract is the Thirty-One Years, which the Court calls the War of Deductions and the fen has always called the taking. The Court’s annals place it among the Bowl Years, between the southern purchase of measures and the fixing of the borders. We kept it in a tarred box under the third board of the walk, where the water comes up to the nails in the wet season and no paper will hold a word for a tend. The Court buys its contracts on salt-paper from Vhal, and in Vhal a contract that rots is held to be a virtue. In the fen a contract that rots is a contract nobody trusted in the first place. I have copied what the water left.

\subsection*{The years as the post has them}

\emph{Copied out of the tarred box. The broad hand is the reeve’s and sets down what stood. The narrow upright hand beneath each year is the factor’s clerk, who came up from Greybank in Reed of Y.H. 813 and corrected the whole leaf while a boy held it against the wind. I have left both readings standing, as a mended pot keeps the old break showing.}

\textbf{Y.H. 420.} Agents of the Bowl of Sere bought measures in the fen at prices no household could refuse, and carried them south to be returned whole, beautiful and remembering, in the open courts. Entered as \emph{the southern trade}, with the prices set against the eel-count of that year.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} A profitable commerce in measures, regulated by the Keeping. Strike \emph{carried}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 426.} A collector came up to the post with a cold iron tube and a slate. The reeve set him on the lowest board, where the water came over his boot tops, and asked him to state his office before he drew. He said his office was a taking. The reeve asked him to write that down, and he wrote \emph{a draw}. Entered as \emph{a drawing of the office}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} The office extended to the fen districts, peaceably received. Strike \emph{boot tops}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 429.} The collectors began to sit at the ferry and at the reed landings. A household of a recognised house in Grath paid one in twelve, as the notice says. A household of the fen paid one in three, and was told that the notice said one in twelve. Entered as \emph{the two figures}.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} The deduction fixed at one in twelve throughout the bowl. Strike the second figure.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 437.} Eels failed at the weirs in the lean week, and the levy was called on the standing crops of reed. A man brought the figure up out of his fist and asked which of the two the Court meant. The reeve told him the Court meant the one on the notice, and the collector drew the other. Entered as \emph{the figure said and the figure paid}.

\textbf{Y.H. 441.} The Court’s annals begin to call the thirty years a war. There was no battle in the fen and no dead man entered. What the fen lost went out through the tube and came back as a thin child who could not say whose warmth it carried. Entered as \emph{eleven empty places in the returning line}, with no names, because the collector did not give them and the reeve did not ask.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} Disturbance of the peace, occasioned by the southern trade. Strike \emph{empty}.\end{quote}

\textbf{Y.H. 449.} The collectors were withdrawn from the post for one tend and came back with a new slate. No reason was entered on either side. The reeds were cut that year by hands that had been in the strips and had not all come out again. The fen entered the number of hands. The Court entered the number of reeds.

\textbf{Y.H. 451.} The thirty-first year. The two figures stood as they stand now, and the notice still says one in twelve. Entered as \emph{peace, the account standing}. The reeve who stood out the last of the thirty-one years stepped down and could not say, when asked, how long he had stood. I have put his standing in the margin rather than in the year, because a figure that a man cannot carry away with him is not a figure the post can keep.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} Peace restored. The several rates of the deduction confirmed. Strike the margin.\end{quote}

I have not struck anything. The factor’s clerk takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them, and a deduction that was always one in twelve has no need of a fen, nor of a man to stand in it. I put the verbs back. A clerk who holds a leaf down for another man in a wind is not a man who believes the leaf is always true.

\subsection*{The two figures}

\emph{The column on the left is what is printed on the Weighing notice and read aloud at the ferry. The column on the right is what went out through the tube. Both stand in the box under the third board. Neither has ever been signed.}

Who stood — Figure read aloud — Figure drawn — Where it is entered\par

A house of Grath in good standing, clay or coin behind it — one in twelve — one in twelve — the notice, the slate, the annals\par

A household of the fen districts — one in twelve — one in three — the notice only\par

The clay-bound of the terraces — one in twelve — one in three — the notice only\par

The unhoused and the foundling with no house — one in twelve — one in three — nowhere at all\par

The difference between the two columns is three parts in twelve, which is a figure any child at the ferry can work out with eel-bones and does. It has never been entered. I have asked a man who copies the Court’s annals why a figure might be read in one place and paid in another, and he said a figure read aloud was a kindness and a figure paid was an account, and that a man who mixes the two has begun to write a sermon. I have set his sentence down. It is the only true sentence he gave me, and he did not know he had said it.

In Y.H. 612 the Fenmarch was made a confederacy under Court protection, and the cheap thin returns began in the same year. The post entered them without comment, which was a kindness to the box. I have copied the entry here because a reader who stops at Y.H. 451 will think the thirty-one years ended. They did not end. They were entered under another name.

\subsection*{The song of the two figures}

\emph{Taken down in Reed of Y.H. 813 at the third landing, from a woman who would not give a name and asked that the last line be left unsung. She said a song with its last line sung is a contract, and contracts in the fen are carried away by the damp. I have set a rule in its place, because a rule is the only thing a Court clerk will copy without asking who said it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve in the mouth and three in the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water takes what the slate won’t stand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A whole comes back with its face on plain,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a thin comes back and asks for its name again.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The eel goes up and the eel goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the peat goes up and the peat lies dry;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Hearth keeps one and the Hearth keeps two,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and who keeps three will not say why.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand on the board till the board stands still,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count what you gave on the nails of the walk;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a figure said is a figure paid\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the water ends and the boardwalk stops.\end{quote}

\emph{Here the singer stopped. In the place of the last line she put her thumb into the wet boards and left it there until the print filled with water. I have set the rule down as she gave it, and I have left the print where it fell.}

\subsection*{What the clerk wrote above the song}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, written across the third stanza:} The Hearth keeps nothing that is not given. Strike \emph{who keeps three}.\end{quote}

The factor’s clerk has a clean way with a line of verse, and no ear for the water under it. The Hearth keeps what is given, which is true, and somebody in that stanza keeps three, which is also true, and the two truths are not the same shape. He has taken the second one out because it has no name to stand behind it. I have put it back. When he came down the plank walk with his slate I asked him whether the figure on the notice was the figure the Hearth received, and he said the account stood, which is the Court’s way of closing a door without saying which side of it a man is on.

\subsection*{The reeve’s correction}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the broad standing hand, written above both the song and the Court hand:} Nine went out of the fen in Y.H. 429 and six came back, and the three who did not come back are not entered as dead, because no collector wrote them down and no slate was opened over them. We stood them at the post. That is the whole of what we could do.\end{quote}

I have left the reeve’s hand standing above the Court’s, and the Court’s above the text, and the text above the peat. A leaf kept under a board in a bog does not lie flat, and nothing written on it lies flat either.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{At the foot, in a hand that has never been claimed:} We paid the third. We stood and let it go, which is not the same as giving it, and is the only thing in this box that I would swear to.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Unstruck Stroke, Being a Letter from the Bell-Founder at Keld Keep to the Man Who Rings the Market Bell at Sill, Concerning the Fifth That Is Not Struck, the Counting of the Strokes, the Song of the Bell, the Answer Written in the Margin in Charcoal, and What the Court Entered Over Both}
\CRsheetheading{The Unstruck Stroke, Being a Letter from the Bell-Founder at Keld Keep to the Man Who Rings the Market Bell at Sill, Concerning the Fifth That Is Not Struck, the Counting of the Strokes, the Song of the Bell, the Answer Written in the Margin in Charcoal, and What the Court Entered Over Both}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A private letter on the back of a bell-founder’s charge-sheet gone stiff with tallow, written in iron-gall and the point of a chisel, folded thrice and sewn with a fibre of bell-rope; carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a consignment of clamps, answered at Sill in Reed of Y.H. 813 on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice, borrowed at the factor’s house at Greybank, and kept since in a dry tin among the founder’s small tools · Written in Bone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, in the foundry under the west wall of Keld Keep, by Vesk, a founder who casts and recasts the bells of the Rim and the Clay Road, to Bram, who rings the market bell at the Cross in Sill; set first on the back of a charge-sheet spoiled by a spill of tallow, carried down the Rim Road and the Clay Road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 with a survey party’s clamps, answered at Sill in Reed of Y.H. 813, and borrowed at the factor’s house at Greybank, where a clerk of the College set a correction in Ledgerhand. It survives sewn with a fibre of bell-rope: bell-metal filings worked into the head, a thumb of tallow at the outer fold, a greenish shaving of the same metal pressed flat into the second fold, a frayed strand of rope caught in the stitch, a grey Ash print along the gutter where a cuff passed, a ring where a cup of small ale stood from the first counting to the verse, a bloom of frost from the Cold Pass gone soft on the last leaf, one word struck through with a chisel-point and written beneath in the recipient’s charcoal hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody has claimed.\par}\medskip
To Bram at the Cross, who keeps the bell and will not be told what it is for. From Vesk of the foundry under the west wall of Keld Keep, who counts the metal before he counts the man.

I write number-first because that is how the foundry keeps its charges and how I was taught to keep them. Four figures to this letter. One, the metal. Two, the strokes. Three, what has come up the Clay Road about the bell at your Cross. Four, what I want from you, which is a number and not an opinion. I have no opinion. Opinions are what men sell when they have no figure to give.

\subsection*{One: the metal}

I cast by the ear and not by the scale. A bell is a vessel with a mouth, and the note is the thing I sell; the metal is only the note made to stand still until a rope finds it. A bell with a flaw answers flat. I have cast thirty-one bells and never sold one that answered flat, and I have never once been asked to.

That is the whole of my trade and it is a small thing to put in a letter. The trouble began when a man came into the foundry off the Clay Road with a tale that the bell at Sill wants recasting with the fifth stroke put in, so that it may ring whole. He had the figure in a fist and would not say who had given it to him. He said a bell that rang whole would be worth a full note to the district. I asked him which district. He said all of them, which is an answer a man gives when he has never stood under a bell.

\subsection*{Two: the strokes as I count them}

Stroke — What the hand does — What the district hears — What I was paid to make\par

First — Rope taken, weight given — A full note — Sound\par

Second — Rope taken — A full note — Sound\par

Third — Rope taken — A full note — Sound\par

Fourth — Rope taken — A full note — Sound\par

Fifth — Rope held; no stroke — A place where a stroke should be — Nothing\par

Four strokes I can cast. The fifth I cannot cast, because there is no metal in a silence. I asked the man from the Clay Road what metal he proposed to put into the fifth. He said that was a question for the founder. I told him I was the founder and the question was mine, and we sat a while without either of us getting the better of it.

I have struck through the figure nine above, where I wrote that I had cast nine bells this year. It is eight. The ninth was a pot-bellied thing for a shrine beyond the Cold Pass and went back into the pot before it ever went into a mould, which is a casting that does not count. I have put eight beneath in my own iron-gall so that you cannot say a stranger did it.

\subsection*{Three: what has come up the Clay Road}

There is a bell you tell of on the Long Night and a bell you hear at the market. Which is it that wants mending? I am not asking to be difficult. A bell that is told of needs no metal and no rope; men sit in the dark and tell it, and it answers out of their mouths. A bell that is heard wants a hand on a rope twice a market-day, morning and afternoon, and wants it to go on wanting for as long as the market stands. Those are two trades and I keep only one of them.

I am told your bell is longer than a church bell and that nobody crosses himself at it. I have seen men cross themselves at a bell in the Bowl country; they do it quickly and with the whole hand, as if to brush something off the face. If your bell rang five, would they begin to do it there? That is the question I would put to a man from Sill if I had one in the foundry who had been to one of your markets. Give me the number and leave the reason at home. I have small use for reasons and a great use for counts.

\subsection*{Four: what I want}

Send me a figure. If it is five I will cast five and thicken nothing. If it is four I will cast four and leave the lip thick where the fifth would have bitten, which is a thing I can do and still call the bell sound; a thick lip answers a little later than a thin one, and a late note is a note that can be stopped. Do not send me a saying. Sayings do not go into a mould.

\subsection*{The song I keep at the foundry, said to the metal and not to a person}

\begin{quote}\itshape Two to the fire and two to the floor,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fifth to the place where the stroke was before;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the rope takes four and the hand takes none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the bell keeps the note that the hand never won.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Iron comes up and the warm goes down,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a flaw in the lip is a flaw in the town;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape tap it at morning, it answers at night,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fifth is a hole that the market keeps right.\end{quote}

I have never written a verse in my life and I would not begin now if there were not a man at the other end of two roads who has heard a bell I have only made. Put it under the numbers where it belongs. If a clerk borrows this leaf, let him take the verbs out; he will have to take the metal out too, and then there will be nothing left for him to enter.

Vesk, at the foundry under Keld Keep, Bone of Y.H. 812.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a second hand, small, in charcoal, the letters round and pressed hard}

You asked for a figure and I have set you one in your own table; look at the fifth row, where under \emph{what I was paid to make} you have written \emph{nothing}. That is the figure. Four strokes and a place. I have struck your \emph{five} through with the point you left in the fold and put the other underneath, in charcoal, which does not keep; I could not find your iron-gall and would not have borrowed it if I had.

Do not recast it. A bell that rings five would set the market crossing itself, and this district does not cross itself at a bell. It has stood over the reading block these twenty years and nobody has once put a hand to his face at it. I have kept the rope through three Account-days in the wet and a fourth when the boards stood under brown water, and the gap has come back with the bell every time, the same finger’s width of nothing. I have never measured it and would not know how.

Your trade and mine are the same trade with the tool changed. You tap a bell where the lip is thick and I tap a pot where the crack was mended. A sound one answers full, a cracked one answers flat, and a mended one answers what it answers; I have never known a pot to lie about itself, which is more than I can say for the men who set them on the board. Strike our bell five times and the fifth would be a true note and the first four would be true notes, and the two truths would not agree. The yard has made its bed on the one that does not happen. Leave the lip thick. Leave it.

There is a bell we tell of on the Long Night and a bell we hear at the Cross. I keep the one we hear. The other is kept by people sitting in the dark, and when they have told it they go to their beds and it goes nowhere. If you must cast for someone, cast for them; they have no rope to wear out and no market to go up and down over the gap.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the market and four for the bell,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fifth for the place that the market knows well;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask the rope what it wants, said the rope to the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the clay said nothing, and went on that way.\end{quote}

I do not write verses. I have set this one down because you set yours down and because a man who makes a thing and a man who rings it should not both be left with only figures between them. Put it under your eight where it belongs, and keep the eighth where you put it; a pot-bellied shrine bell that never went into the mould is a bell too, and there is no column for the ones that do not get made.

Bram, at the Cross, Sill, Reed of Y.H. 813.

\subsection*{What the Court hand did, at Greybank, in the second tend of Reed}

A clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaf on a market morning; his cuff was gone soft at the edge from washing and he had the top sheet in his hand before he looked at either of us, which is the manner of that table. He writes in the neat upright hand they teach at the College, with the verbs taken out and everything in the passive. He took the verbs out of both hands as though a verb were a thing a man could smuggle in a cuff, and set a round figure against the casting, and struck the fifth row of the table and wrote \emph{fifth stroke: not entered} above it. Against \emph{a place where a stroke should be} he wrote \emph{vacancy}. Where Bram wrote that the two truths would not agree he wrote \emph{figures reconciled}, which is the Court’s own art in a small space, and left the charcoal underneath.

In the founder’s hand — In the ringer’s hand — In the Court hand\par

Four strokes cast; the fifth is silence — Four strokes and a place — Four strokes, sound\par

A gap is a fault in the casting — The gap keeps the bell honest — Vacancy; not entered\par

The lip thickened where the fifth would bite — A thick lip answers full — Material not entered\par

Two truths that will not agree — Leave it; leave it — Figures reconciled\par

Eight bells this year — The eighth was never cast — Castings entered: eight\par

He asked me what a verse was worth and I said nothing a clerk could enter, which is the first true thing he said all morning. I have left both hands standing, his above ours and ours beneath, as a repaired wall keeps the old break under the new keying and does not pretend the first hand never touched it. We have never entered one another. I would rather the foundry forgot my name than have it stand beside his on a slate with a figure after it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The filings at the head are mine and came off the lip on the day I thickened the last one; I held the sheet down with my whole hand because the draught along the foundry floor takes paper before it takes a man. The tallow thumb is mine. The greenish shaving in the second fold is of the same metal as the bell at your Cross, or near enough; a shaving does not answer when you tap it, which is a thing I have often thought about and never said in company. The fibre in the stitch is your rope, not mine; it came away in my hand at Greybank and I sewed it back rather than let it go, because a rope that has been on a bell is not a rope to throw out. The ring is off a cup that stood from the first counting to the verse and was drunk by neither of us, which is how small ale is drunk in Keld when there is a thing to say and no proper word for it. The frost bloom came over the Cold Pass and has gone soft. The grey along the gutter is not mine and not the Court’s. I burn my grey on the morning after the Last Day like everybody else, and it is back on the bench by noon, which is why this leaf lives in a tin and not under a stone.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody has claimed}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four, four, and the place kept clean.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bell rings whole; the market does not.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the metal what it wants: the fire.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the rope what it wants: a hand that will stop.\end{quote}

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Untaken Turn, Being the Well-Game of Cold Acre, with the Passing, the Bringing Back, and What a Clerk of the Factor Made of the Warm That Is Not Counted}
\CRsheetheading{The Untaken Turn, Being the Well-Game of Cold Acre, with the Passing, the Bringing Back, and What a Clerk of the Factor Made of the Warm That Is Not Counted}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A well-woman’s setting-down of a children’s passing-game in the Cold Acre speech, written with a charred stick on the back of a meal-mill tally gone soft at one corner; the verses in the children’s own half-sung words, the manner of the play in the writer’s hand, a correction in the margin by the woman who winds the well-rope, the factor’s clerk’s ruling in Ledgerhand above the eighth line, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Set down in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, at Cold Acre on the ridge two leagues north of Sill, by the woman who keeps the well-rope there, on the back of a barley tally from the meal mill that had given up its figures at one corner; carried down the ridge road in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 and copied at Greybank, where a clerk of the factor’s house borrowed the leaf for a morning and gave it back with the verbs taken out. Kept since under the loose stone of the well-curb, in the nick where the rope is coiled, which the children do not lift. It survives with a thumb of well-clay at the head, a grey Ash print nobody will own along the gutter, a white frost-ring that has eaten two words off the fourth line, a barley awn stiff in the fold, a nick from a turnip knife at the fore-edge, a thread of sacking caught in the second leaf, the rope-woman’s correction standing in the margin, the clerk’s ruling standing above the eighth line, and the line at the foot that has never been claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the well-rope at Cold Acre and have drawn at this curb for thirty-one winters. I set this down because a man come up from Slate Row stood on the ridge in Stone and asked what the children said when they passed the stone round the well. He wanted a figure for the warmth. I told him there was a turn in it and no figure, which is the truth of the thing, and he went away and sent a clerk, which is what a man does when he has been given an answer he cannot carry back.

The leaf is the back of a mill tally whose figures had gone soft at one corner, and I wrote with a charred stick out of the barley kiln, because ink will not stay on a paper that goes into a bucket. The children’s words I have set as they came, half-sung and with nothing mended in them. What they do not say before a man with a clean cuff I have put at the end, where such things belong. I have left the clerk’s hand standing where he set it and the children’s words under it, as the curb keeps both the rope’s mark and the water’s.

\subsection*{Where it is played}

In Stone and Frost, on the bare ring of ground that goes around the well, where the frost will not hold. The river lies ice at the Sill and the Singing Sill keeps its note under the ice, but the ground at our well stays dark and a little soft to the boot, and the children say it is because the well is breathing. I have heard men say it is a current under the ridge. Nobody has asked it with a slate in his hand, and I have not asked either.

They do not play in the Five, because in the Five a child stands and listens and there is no round for it. They do not play on a market-day while the barrow goes out of the north gate and along the ridge on its way to the Bone Orchard, heaped a finger above the sides where the load has shifted. The children stand and let it pass and say nothing, and take up the stone when the road is empty again. This is not a rule anybody taught them.

\subsection*{The choosing, said before the stone is taken up}

\emph{The children stand in a ring with their hands behind their backs. One among them, facing the well, passes the stone from fist to fist behind the ring and says the words. She does not look at the faces. On the last word the child who has the stone takes the first turn. Said to the well. Said looking at a child, it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six houses and a well,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a well and six houses;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape stone in the fist and thumb on the stone,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one it stops with starts the round.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The passing, as it is played}

\emph{Eight lines, one line to each passing of the stone from hand to hand round the ring. The words go low and are mostly sung. A child who passes late has let the turn go and is cold at once; a child who passes early has taken a turn that was not hers, and must give the stone back and breathe on it herself before the round can go on. At the eighth line the passing stops, whoever holds the stone. That hand is the untaken turn. The child shuts her fist on the stone, sets the fist on the curb, and does not open it. She is the turn that stands.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the north road where the barrow goes,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the gate that lets it through;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the turnips under the snow,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the stubble the frost holds to;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape five for the rope too stiff to bend,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the breath that warms it again;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the curb where the bare ground is,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a turn for the water that comes without a hand.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well gives. It does not ask.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Let the stone go. Let the turn stand.\end{quote}

The eighth is not a number. I have asked them why and they say it is the turn, and if I ask what the turn is they ask me why a woman wants to know what a well does when nobody is at it. There is always a child who will say the water comes up because somebody let the rope go, and there is always another child who will say no, the water came up first and the rope went after it. The argument never settles and the game goes on all the same.

\subsection*{The bringing back}

A child who stands on the curb with a shut fist is brought back in one way only. Another child takes the stone out of her hand — she does not give it, it is taken — breathes on it twice, and puts it into her hand again. Nobody says who gave the warmth and the child who was cold says nothing when she comes in. If the stone is breathed on three times and still nobody takes it, the standing child stays where she is until the well-rope is let down and drawn up again, which the children call the ebb, and the ebb takes a while.

I have seen a child go to the curb on purpose on a morning when there was no fire in her house and the bare ring held more warmth than the hearth did. I have set that down and have not mended the sense of it. A gift on this ridge is not a thing that gets entered, and a child who has never been given a figure knows where to stand in a game about giving.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man from Slate Row is on the ridge}

\emph{From the child who keeps the curb, with her back to the road. She would not say it to the clerk and would not say it within sight of his cuff. She said it to the well.}

\begin{quote}\itshape The barrow goes out and the well stays in,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says six and the ridge says none;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a breath is a gift and a gift’s a debt\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in the hand that writes in the town.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The turn stands where the fingers let go;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape nobody took it, nobody owes;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water comes up when the river is ice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court has never asked its price.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Pass it behind and pass it back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and warm the one you left in the cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone says nothing, the well says less,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the well gives still, and asks no more.\end{quote}

\subsection*{In the margin, in the hand of the woman who winds the rope}

Against \emph{a turn for the water that comes without a hand}, in a small hard hand pressed close to the gutter:

\begin{quote}\itshape Not without a hand. I have let go at this curb and the bucket has come up all the same, full, with nobody standing to it. There is a hand somewhere, only it is not mine.\end{quote}

Underneath, in mine: \emph{She has put a hand back into a line where I put none, and both stand. A well that gives when nobody winds is a thing a woman will argue about, and a thing a woman will not let a clerk enter.}

\subsection*{What the clerk wrote above the eighth line}

A clerk of the factor’s house at Greybank borrowed the leaf on a morning in Ilmen, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits on the first joint of two fingers and will not come out. He wrote above \emph{and a turn for the water that comes without a hand}: \emph{one turn unperformed; unmeasured yield; presumed to accrue to the Keeping}. Against \emph{The well gives. It does not ask} he set \emph{source unentered; no deduction arises}. At \emph{six for the breath that warms it again} he wrote \emph{warmth passed between vessels without slate; no value attaches}. At the foot, where the child is brought back with a breath, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{one restored, nil}.

I have put the children’s words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child with a shut fist on a cold curb does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know whose hand will warm the stone. He has made a giving into a yield and a turn into a nought, and the nought belongs to the Keeping while the turn belongs to nobody. That is the whole art of that hand. He said the game was an account of the Return taught before a child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when the soft cuff comes along the ridge. They take it up when he is back down the road, and they never once change the eighth.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The thumb of well-clay at the head is mine. I sign in clay because a wet hand will not take ink and because this curb is the only thing in Cold Acre that keeps a print the whole winter through. The grey along the gutter came off the barrow road, where I laid the leaf down while the Ash went past on its way to the north gate; I have not swept it, and there is no Last Day on a ridge. The white ring took two words off the fourth line one night when the leaf lay outside the door on the frost; I have not written them back, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The barley awn in the fold came off a sack by the door and has gone stiff as a splinter. The nick at the fore-edge is the turnip knife’s, and the thread in the second leaf is sacking, which is the only sort of clothing this hamlet has ever had. Frost is the only clerk Cold Acre ever had, and it takes two words where the factor’s clerk takes the verbs.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The well kept its own account before there was a slate. It has never entered it, and it has never once run short.\end{quote}

I asked the rope-woman, the children, a man come up from Greybank and a neighbour who carries turnips to the north gate, and had four answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaf goes back under the loose stone in the nick where the rope is coiled. Tomorrow the children will draw their ring on the bare ground and pass the stone and leave the turn standing where it stands now, and the bucket will come up with nobody at the rope, and the Court’s figure will stay where the Court put it, which is not at the well.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Up-Haul, Being the Bank-Rope Song of the Ilm, Sung Going Up from Greybank with Salt and Iron, Set Down from a Towman’s Mouth with the Rest Beats Kept and a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Margin}
\CRsheetheading{The Up-Haul, Being the Bank-Rope Song of the Ilm, Sung Going Up from Greybank with Salt and Iron, Set Down from a Towman’s Mouth with the Rest Beats Kept and a Factor’s Clerk’s Figures in the Margin}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A work song of the towpath, counted in the feet and not in the hands; the verses in the low hard Grathic of the bank, said into the rope; the rubrics and the unsung fourth verse in the charcoal hand of a girl at the eel-stalls who wrote what was dictated to her; a factor’s clerk’s figures in a narrow upright hand down the margin; a grey Ash print nobody will own · Sung on the up-haul between Greybank and Sill since before the Glaze Wars and set down in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, the thaw year, by a bank-walker out of the Fishstairs who had begun to lose the fourth verse and the use of her left hand, dictated to a girl at the eel-stalls who wrote it on the back of a weigh-slip from the factor’s house at Greybank gone soft with salt. The girl put the verses in the order of the pulls and left the rubrics out, having never hauled. The slip survives folded twice against a storm, tied with tarred twine nobody will own, with a tar thumb at the head, a silt tideline along the gutter, a crust of salt on the second leaf, a rope-burn across the third verse, a fish-scale pressed flat in the lower corner, a splinter of corduroy from the Clay Road in the fold, the clerk’s figures standing in the margin, and the fourth verse in a hand that is neither the walker’s nor the girl’s\par}\medskip
I have walked the bank between Greybank and Sill for nineteen springs, with a three-strand rope laid across the heart of my right shoulder and a barge behind me that somebody else has packed. I did not set this down. A girl at the eel-stalls wrote it for me because I had begun to lose the fourth verse in the same year I began to lose the use of my left hand, and a verse lost at fifty is lost for good. She put my words in the order of the pulls. I have put the rubrics back, which she left out because she has never hauled.

A hauling song is not like a yard song. A yard song can be sung while the hands go on doing something else. This one is counted in the feet, and if you sing it out of time the rope takes up the slack on your own shoulder, which is the only correction a river makes. We do not sing going down. A boat going down wants a hand at the tiller and a woman at the bight, and no words.

\subsection*{How it is sung}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At the first pull after the boat comes off the mud at Greybank, not before. The first pull is the one that tells you what the barge weighs, and a song sung before it is a song sung to nothing.

\item Lay the heart of the rope to the shoulder, not a strand. A strand across the shoulder will roll and take the skin off; a heart lies still and tells you by its pull when you are about to be wrong.

\item Put your foot where a foot went before you. The Clay Road is packed clay over corduroy in the wet places, and the corduroy is under the silt, and a man who steps beside it instead of on it spends the morning finding his ground again.

\item Refrain after every verse, into the rope and not into the air. Said into the air it becomes a song for listening to, which is a different thing and belongs to the Cross.

\item Do not take up the song under the sill at Sill in Ilmen. The stone gives its low note under the water when the Warm comes up, and the old of Sill set their clocks by it, and a man who pulls against a note that is not his own loses his breath. Let the stone have that stretch of river.

\item Not on thin ice, and not in the Breaking. In those weeks the bank is a different country and the song does not know its roads.

\item Rest on the rest, even when there is time to make up. The count is in the pull and the resting, and a man who eats his resting to get home early pays it on the next haul with his shoulder.

\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The song}

\begin{quote}\itshape Salt up from Greybank and iron up with it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three strands and a heart, and the heart to the shoulder;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape put your foot where a foot went before you,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and draw.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The wind comes down off the Sallow and the water comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the two never agree, and the boat goes between;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape do not ask the river which one owes the other,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it has no slate and it will not be told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The factor writes what goes into the hold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the silt writes what comes off it in a year;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one hand in a clean cuff and one hand in the mud,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the same boat goes up in the morning.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape [The fourth verse is given below in another hand. I have never been able to say it, and the girl wrote a line of dots where it stood.]\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape There’s a step short at the Fishstairs and nobody mends it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water put it back a hand’s breadth out of line;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape step where the others step and do not look down at it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and draw.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape In Stone the rope is a piece of iron with no heat in it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and keeps the print of your shoulder after you are gone;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape in Silt it’s a snake in the mud and wants to go downriver,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and you must want it up more than it wants to go.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A brine-gull took a coal off a banked fire last spring,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape warm and not yet cold, and went upriver with it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no slate in Sill stood one mark the poorer,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the fire went on taking its breath in fours and a gap.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The notice says one in twelve, and the clerk reads it twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape once for the moot and once for them that came late;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the bank keeps a count that will not stand still to be entered,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and I have not put it here, and neither has the girl.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape When the rope goes slack and the barge lies at the stair,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape shake the water out of it and coil it against the wall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what we brought up will be spent by evening,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the river will be where it was when we came.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The rope takes it.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Draw. The bank gives it back.}\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Rest. The water goes on without us.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{The fourth verse, above the line of dots, in a hand that is not mine}

\begin{quote}\itshape There was a man went under at the Weir in the flood year,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the rope came back with a knot in it we had not tied;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we did not undo it and we did not sing it,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the next boat went up with one less hand.\end{quote}

It is said once, low, when a boat goes out with fewer hands than came up, and then the rope is shaken out and the song begins again at the first line. I asked the girl who wrote it. She said she had not. The eel-women at the Weir say their mothers sang it, which is an answer that does not spoil in the mouth. I have left the knot where the words put it and have not looked to see whether the rope still has one.

\subsection*{What the clerk did at Greybank}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the slip when the salt tally went up. He set a figure against each verse, as if a verse were a basket of tile, and struck the verbs out of two lines. \emph{The water goes on without us} became \emph{the current is constant}. \emph{The silt writes what comes off it in a year} became \emph{loss is entered annually}. Where the fourth verse stood he ruled a line and wrote \emph{no entry} against it, which is a true thing in a place that has never had a man come back up a rope.

I have left his figures standing above and put my words underneath. A clerk can write a current that is constant because he has never had one on his shoulder. He has put a number where a man’s breathing goes, and the number will travel as far as Greybank and arrive as light as salt-paper. When a rope goes slack it does not care what has been entered.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The tar at the head is my thumb; I held the slip down on the bight while the girl wrote and did not know I had marked it. The silt tideline along the gutter came up over both of us on the third pull out of Greybank and took two words off the second verse, and the girl wrote them back from my mouth, which is how I know she was listening. The salt crust is from the weigh-slip itself and has eaten one of the clerk’s figures half away, which I have not mourned. The rope-burn across the third verse is where the slip lay inside my coat against the heart-strand. The fish-scale came off a woman’s creel at the Fishstairs when she leaned over to see the writing; she did not stay, and I have kept it where it fell. The splinter of corduroy in the fold is off the Clay Road and got there when the slip was opened in a wind, which is the only part of this paper that has walked the towpath on its own. The grey along the lower edge came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; nobody will own it, and there is no Last Day on a river. The tarred twine through the hole at the fold is not mine and not the girl’s and I have not untied it to find out who tied it.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The song belongs to the rope and not to me. I have lost the fourth verse and the use of my left hand, but the right shoulder still knows where the heart lies, and it will know after I have given the rope up. When that day comes another woman will take the bight and a girl, or a girl’s girl, will write down what she hears in the order of the pulls. If the clerk gets the leaf again he may have the figures. The pulls will be there underneath, and the water will go on without us, as it has done since before there were slates at Greybank to write it on.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Want in the Count, Being the Hopping Game of the Drying Racks in Low Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{The Want in the Count, Being the Hopping Game of the Drying Racks in Low Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A children’s counting game, set out with its words, the scored ground, the forfeits, and the two hands that disagree over the empty place · Set down by an old woman of the drying racks in the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, in Ilmen of Y.H. 813, having no slate-name and signing with a thumb pressed into slip; written in charcoal on the back of a spoiled drying tally and kept folded in the band of a cast-off apron. It survives with the score of a knuckle in slate dust, a tallow thumb, a drop of barley grease, a green bead of lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the writing, a grey print of Ash, and one correction in the narrow hand of a clerk borrowed from Slate Row. The game is held to be older than the bell at the Cross.\par}\medskip
I have no slate-name. The rack has one, and the kiln has one, and a pot has a number chalked on its foot where the thrower puts her thumb, but I have never been entered in anything that I can read. So I have set my thumb in slip at the foot of this leaf, which is how we sign a pot in this yard, and if a man come down from Slate Row wants a name for the hand, let him write \emph{the racks} and be done.

I write it because the little ones have begun to leave the want out. They hop the eight and stop, and say the count is finished, and stand looking at the bare clay where the ninth score should be, waiting for somebody to tell them it is finished. It is not finished. A count that closes is a Court count. I have taught them the words before they had the legs, and now I set the words down, because a thing carried only in the legs goes out with the legs.

\subsection*{The words}

\emph{Said while hopping. The row says the refrain; the hopper says the lines. No one says the want alone.}

One for the stone that was warmed at the fire, two for the pot that answers full, three for the grey that turns the corner, four for the loaves that go on the levy. Four and no more before the want.

Five is the bell that is longer than a church bell, six is the step that is not at the landing, seven the eels in the bridge’s shade, eight the pots on the rack, bone-pale. Four and four, and a place where the fifth should be.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Refrain, all together, stamping:} Hop it, hop it, call it out — four and four and a want. Put your foot where the foot should be and the whole count comes to nought. Hop the want and come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

If you set down in the want you are gone wrong, a flat note under the heel; go stand in the grey where it turns the corner and do not answer when they say your name. Bide till the bell goes. Then come back warm. Come back as you can.

The big ones carry nineteen out and nineteen back from the pit to the rack and again; we carry eight and the place where a step should be, which is as much as our legs can hold. When your legs are long enough the want becomes a step and you go on.

One in twelve, as the notice says, four and four as the kiln breathes, nineteen as the women tread — three counts and never one agreement. The Court has a figure for every place. We have a place with no figure in it. That is the one we keep.

\emph{The calling at the end, which is not a verse but the way they end:}

\begin{quote}\itshape Who is not in the row? — One that was not in the room.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What do we call her? — Kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape What do we say to her? — Come back warm. Come back as you can.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The ground, and how it is scored}

Eight places are scored in the trodden ash beside the racks, a hand’s breadth apart, with the end of a broken pot or a bit of slate. The ninth is not scored. On the Last Day the ash is not swept, and there is no need to score anything, because the grey shows the places of its own accord; after it is burned the game is played on the bare clay and the want is marked with a chip of pot set on its edge, so that it can be moved aside and put back.

Where there is a cord, two of the bigger ones turn it and the hopper runs in on the first line.
