Her reading is better than mine. A hand on the rim is a hand that might lift the slate; a hand over the writing is a hand that has already decided what the slate will say. I have left both lines standing, hers in the margin and mine underneath, as a kept thing is left where it fell.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He numbered the twelve lines in the margin, struck through \emph{the one kept out} and wrote above it, \emph{the deduction is one in twelfths, the residue is nil, the young are instructed}. Against \emph{twelve for the dish} he wrote \emph{the twelfth is retained for the Hearth}. At the foot of the count he put a round nought and wrote \emph{absence} beside it, where the children’s game ends with a name said three times.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child up to her ankle in the grey of the yard does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which foot to lift. A nought is a number. The dish is a place at the table. He has put a figure where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned from it. I told him the count and the fault and the bringing back, and he said that was an account of the Return taught before the child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes into the yard. They take it up again when he is past the bridge, and they never once change the twelfth.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man from Slate Row is in the square}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lean and two for the thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the loaves that go on the dish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says one and the yard says none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name said at home is the only one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish goes round and the dish comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was kept is counted as lack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners and one for the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place where the twelfth stood is standing still.\end{quote}

I have it from the child who keeps the crack, with the proper space left before it, which is the space they leave in the hopping. She would not say it while the clerk had his pen out, and would not say it to him at all. She said it to the floor with her back turned and made me put it down as I have it, with none of my verbs in it, because a verse said to the floor wants nothing added, and a verse said to a man wants everything taken away.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is off the hand that drew the line; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard uses it to mark a place. The green bead came off a pot broken in the glaze room and rolled as far as the fold before anybody saw it. The tallow thumb is mine: I held the notice down in the draught under the shrine door and did not know I had marked it. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it and there is no Last Day in a slate-box. The tideline took two words off the back of the notice and I have not written them in again, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The twist of grey wool through the hole is mine, tied for the word I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey chalk, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I kept the crack and nobody came.\end{quote}

No hand will own it. The letters are set down as they were made, hard at the \emph{th} and one of them backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a slate and not off a book. I asked whose it was and had three answers and no hand, as I did with the grey print. I have left it where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the slate-box with the birth-slates that have been answered. Tomorrow the yard will draw its line again, and one in twelve will be read in a clean voice at the notice-board, and the twelfth will be kept out of the count and brought back at the end of it, which is more than can be said for the district’s own twelfth. The children will go on saying the name three times. I have kept their words and I have not joined them to anything.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Cord Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Eel-Folk of the Weir, Gathered in the Trap-House a League Above Sill and Glossed for a Girl Come Up from Low Kiln}
\CRsheetheading{What the Cord Keeps, Being the Sayings of the Eel-Folk of the Weir, Gathered in the Trap-House a League Above Sill and Glossed for a Girl Come Up from Low Kiln}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A trap-woman’s gathering of the proverbs, plank-maxims, eel-counts and river-curses of the Weir, set in Grathic letters on the backs of spoiled trap-tallies because the counts here are tied in cord and a cord will not lie flat on a clerk’s table; the sayings in the short wet speech of the weir with the ends let drop into the water, the glosses in the writer’s own charcoal, a knot tied in the margin where no Grathic word will come, a factor’s clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a slate-runner’s line in the slant of a carried hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Gathered at the Weir in Ilmen and Silt of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year of the Long Cold, and written up in the trap-house through the high water by a woman who lifts the baskets at the turn and keeps the leading cord and the count of them in her sleeve; set down first in charcoal on the backs of trap-tallies spoiled by wet hands, carried downriver to Greybank in Grain of Y.H. 813 with a consignment of eels and copied there onto the back of a Court grain-warrant voided by the Long Cold, where a factor’s clerk borrowed the leaves and set his hand above hers. It survives folded into a strip of oiled eel-skin and tied with a loop of grey wool, with river silt dried pale in the grain at the head, eel slime worked into the fold off the leading cord, a fish-hook nick at the fore-edge, a brine-gull’s peck through one word of the song, a glass-eel thread fine as a hair in the lower gutter, a pressed reed across the third leaf, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the writer did not make and has not swept, the knot standing in the margin, the clerk’s narrow correction above the charcoal, the runner’s sloping line below it, and the line at the foot which nobody has claimed\par}\medskip
I lift the baskets at the turn and keep the leading cord. There are four traps below the plank and a fifth set where the water goes quick, which nobody admits to setting. A girl came up from Low Kiln this spring who can hear a pot before a knuckle touches it and cannot tell which way the water runs under her own feet. She is our kin and she is not ours, and what the weir can give her is the old sentences. A saying said to the water stays at the water. A saying tied in a cord goes on with her without a figure.

Our counts are not written. They are tied in grey wool and reed-fibre, at arm’s length, with one tied low by teeth and thumb where the hand that made it cannot see. A knot keeps when paper has gone soft, and no clerk at Greybank has ever read one, which we did not think of first and have since come to value. Where a sound has no word I have tied a knot in the margin. Do not put a word into it. A man come down from the Cross asked what we say when there is nothing to say. I told him we say it to the water. He went away believing he had learned the Weir, which is the usual end of such a conversation.

Say these to the plank, the basket, the water under the plank, and to a person last. Said looking at a person, a saying becomes an argument, and there is enough arguing at the Cross without carrying it upriver.

\subsection*{Of the water under the plank}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Ask the water what it took. It will tell you where it put it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — At the Fishstairs they ask what the water cost and are given the weather. Here we ask where it went. The leach takes the Warm out of a thing and hands it to the Sallow draw; the river is only the road. A man wants a figure. The water has a direction. Both are true, and only one can be carried into a room with a table.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The ice is a lid. Do not trust a lid.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Two or three children a winter go through the skin of the Ilm. The old women say the ice-mouse is the cold made small enough to be killed, which is a comfort that kills no fewer children. We say it of the water and of a man who promises what he has not stood on.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The sill sings before it breaks. Nobody sets a clock by the song.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — When the Warm rises in Ilmen the stone under the falls gives a low note that carries to the Fishstairs. The town sets its clocks by it and does not explain it. We say the river clears its throat before the Breaking. A man from Greybank wanted the hour entered; we told him the hour was the note, and the note was not entered.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The Breaking comes up the same steps every year and takes a different house.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In Silt the Ilm comes over the Fishstairs and leaves silt waist-deep in the lower town. The water is the same water; the door is never the same door. We say it of the river and of the levy, which comes on the same day of the month and takes a different household each time. Neither is malicious. Both are habitual, which costs more.}

\subsection*{Of the eel and the basket}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The eel keeps its heat behind the head. Cut there and you learn nothing.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The old women say glass eels are the shadows of the rivets that hold the lid on the world. There is a sac behind the head where the eel keeps a little of the Warm; a boy who cuts one open to find the heat finds it gone into the water, which is where it was going. Say this of a man who opens a thing to look for the feeling in it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Count them going in. Count them coming out. The basket has no column.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The traps are lifted at the turn and the eels counted by the hand that lifts them, not the eye that prices them. A tally at the Fishstairs takes your figure and gives another by the tide’s turn. We keep the going-in count in the cord and let the buyer have the other, which is not dishonesty but an arrangement two people can live with.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A gull will take a coal and leave you colder. It will not take a wet eel.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The brine-gull lifts what is warm and light enough, with no malice in it. Say this of a man who has taken something and calls it borrowing. The eel is safe because it is cold and wet and no bird wants it, which is a poor safety and the only kind the basket has.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Tied in the margin, where the word for the little green eel-thread would stand: a knot low down, made with teeth and thumb.} It has come loose twice and I have tied it twice. I have not written the word in.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Of the cord and the count}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A knot remembers what the hand forgets.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We tie grey wool when a thing is owed and untie it when paid; the sleeve-cord has one knot tied low where the hand could not see. A knot keeps longer than a name and does not care who tied it. A factor’s clerk entered our knots as nil, because a knot is not a figure. Right by his law, wrong about the cord.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Do not read a cord. Ask the woman who tied it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A man from the Court held up a reed-cutter’s cord and asked what it counted. She told him to ask the water, and then to ask her, in that order. He wrote “no entry lies,” which is true of the cord and false of the woman, who had carried the count eleven years and knew every knot by her thumb.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Forty and one. The one has no name and is not a debt.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In the year of the flower a woman at these traps tied forty knots for the children of Low Kiln taken in the levy, and a forty-first she cannot account for. She has never untied it. When she says the word low into a basket, the child looks at her and cannot answer, which is the answer given by people who asked the same question at their own first tying.}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, written against this saying:} Figure entered as nil. Vacancy. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A nought is a number. The forty-first is a place. He has made the place smaller by writing in it, which is the whole art of that hand.\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The slate goes by edge-on. Ask the carrier, not the slate.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The runner who carries the thane’s slate between the Cross and Greybank holds the writing turned into her sleeve and will not read it. “I don’t read it. I carry it,” she says; “there’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which.” A man who wants the figure must walk to Greybank for a number that was not true when it left the basket.}

\subsection*{Of the collector and the figure}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “You hear the collector on the plank before you see his slate.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — His boots have never been in the water. Children here are taught to know the sound of them before their own names, a grim kindness and the only warning the weir gives. He comes with a cold tube and a clean figure, and the figure does not get wet.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Cold iron takes. The water takes. Only one of them writes it down.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The brand for a stolen cup of warmth goes on the wrist, and the district pays in cold for what the river carries off without a slate. Ask a woman which is the kinder and she will ask why a man wants a kind way to be emptied. There is no feast at the Weir in Silt.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “One in twelve is printed. The other goes up the Clay Road in a box.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Read twice at the Cross, once for the moot and once for those who came late. The reader says the levy is called and not called by him, taking himself out of his own sentence. What goes up the road in his locked box is a different figure, and the two have never agreed here.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A name said to the water is not entered.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The slate takes a number and the house takes a name, and both travel where the person does not. What is said at the trap stays there. A woman whose child came back from another hearth keeps one name at home and one for the officer, and has never joined them, which is the only kindness her house can manage.}

\subsection*{Of the dead and the plank}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Feet to the river. Pot at the door. Sherd on the plank.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — We break a pot at the door of a death-house as they do in Sill, so the heat may get out, and set one sherd on the plank afterward, facing upriver. A threshold is a thing a house can step back over; a plank has only one way off it. Nobody says who the sherd is for, and nobody takes it up.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Nothing is swept off a plank.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — In Sill they leave the grey in the corners on the Last Day, burn it in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no corner on a plank. What falls off goes into the water and becomes somebody else’s weather, a difference no clerk has entered.}

\subsection*{The basket-song}

\emph{Sung lifting the traps at the turn of the water, going out and not coming back. The fourth line of the second part is held, and the space after it is the length of a knot. Nobody fills it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the baskets and one set out,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the cord that the thumb knows;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the water goes where the wind isn’t\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the eel goes where the water goes.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the basket, a bit for the board;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the gull takes the coal and the clerk takes the mark\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one I keep\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cord goes home in a sleeve, unread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The slate goes up in a hand, unread.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The river reads both and says neither,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the water keeps what the water took.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — The held line is not a fifth basket or a fifth trap. Children ask and are told to ask the cord, which is the answer their mothers were given. A tally-man from Greybank put a nought in the space and wrote vacancy beneath it. A nought is a figure. The space was a place.}

\subsection*{What the borrowed hand did}

A factor’s clerk borrowed the leaves at Greybank on a market morning, with ink settled in two fingers of a soft cuff. He writes narrow and upright and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in his sleeve.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{the water will tell you where it put it}, he wrote \emph{the loss is not ascertained}, which leaves the water out and the loss in.

\item At \emph{count them going in}, he set \emph{two tallies entered; discrepancy nil}, joining the count I kept to the count the buyer paid, which is the whole art of that hand.

\item At \emph{a knot remembers}, he wrote \emph{no instrument recorded}, true in his language and of no use to a woman with a cord in her sleeve.

\item At \emph{forty and one}, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy}, which is a figure where a place stood.

\end{itemize}

I have put the sayings back under his hand. He takes the doers out because a thing always true has no need of anybody doing it. I put them back because a girl from Low Kiln wants to know whose hand lifted the basket, and there is always a hand.

\subsection*{In the margin, in a slate-runner’s sloping hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry the slate edge-on and never look at what is on it. The figure that goes up to Greybank does not know what came out of any basket on this river. I have walked that road eleven years and never once opened one.\end{quote}

Below, in mine: she said it to the plank and would not say it twice. I have not asked. A person who carries a slate is not one who reads it, and the road cares about neither.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The silt at the head came off the hand that held the tally down on the rail in high water; no wet sleeve takes it out, which is why we use charcoal. The slime at the fold is off the leading cord and goes soft when the weather goes soft, which tells me when to shut the tin. The hook nick is from a basket set down by a man paying for six eels and charged for five, or the other way, which he has not settled. The gull’s peck went through one word of the song and nobody has claimed the bird. The green thread in the gutter is a glass eel, fine as a hair, left where it fell. The pressed reed came from a bundle set down while a woman decided whether to sell. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and not the factor’s. I have not swept it. There is a Last Day downriver; there is none on a plank.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The water takes and does not enter.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cord keeps and cannot be read.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man is what he has carried to the basket and not yet let go.\end{quote}

I asked a woman who lifts the traps, a slate-runner, and a factor’s man out of Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The leaves go back into the eel-skin under the board. Tomorrow the water turns at the fourth and the baskets go down; I shall count them going in, say nothing of what came out, and tie one knot low where my thumb cannot see it, which is the whole of the trade at the Weir.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Cold Is Full Of, Being the Sayings of the Wastelings, Gathered at the Survey Post Beyond the Cold Pass and Glossed for a Man Who Still Carried a Name}
\CRsheetheading{What the Cold Is Full Of, Being the Sayings of the Wastelings, Gathered at the Survey Post Beyond the Cold Pass and Glossed for a Man Who Still Carried a Name}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A post-keeper’s gathering of the grunts, borrowed Grathic, gift-words, answers and refusals of the Waste, set in Grathic letters on the back of a spoiled rim-seam sheet because Waste Cant is not written and has no hand; the sayings in the few words the country uses, with a blank left where a sound has no word, the glosses in the keeper’s own charcoal, a survey-clerk’s correction in narrow upright Ledgerhand, a Keldish tally-man’s line cut into the edge with a knife, and one line at the back in a hand nobody will own · Gathered over nine winters at the survey post in the Cold Pass, ten leagues beyond Keld Keep, in Ash and Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Vek of the Post, a Keldishman who came up with a lime cart in Y.H. 800 and was left to count the men who go through and the men who come back; first set in charcoal on the backs of spoiled survey sheets, then copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a requisition for warm-stone voided by the Long Cold, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled survey-cloth and carried down the Rim Road. It survives with frost raised out of the grain on the first leaf and gone by noon, coal smut at the fold, a flake of warm-stone that kept its heat one night on a stone floor and is cold now, a small grey stone stitched into the lower gutter, a white hair pressed between the third and fourth leaf, the Ash of an uncollected man along the outer fold which leaves no stain, the clerk’s narrow correction standing above the keeper’s words, the tally-man’s line cut into the edge, and a line at the foot in a hand that has never come forward\par}\medskip
I keep the post. There is a post and no gate, and the surveyors who set me here count men through it: those who go up and those who come down. When the party turns back I stay with the counting. Nine winters I have heard what the people beyond it say, and this winter I put it down, because a keeper who stays long enough becomes the only man who remembers a sentence that the country it came from has let go.

I write in Grathic letters because Waste Cant is not written. It is a handful of borrowed words and a way of letting the ends fall away, and what cannot be done with the mouth is not done with a hand. Where a sound has no word I have left a blank. Do not put a word into the blank. A man come up with lime from Stonemouth asked me what they say when there is nothing to say. I told him they say it to the cold. He went away believing he had learned the Waste, which is the usual end of such a conversation.

Say these to the ground or to the stone you are sitting against, never to the person who has just said them. Said to a person, one of these sentences becomes a question with an answer owed, and there is not one sentence here with an answer owed in it.

\subsection*{Of the question, which is the whole of their information}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Warm?”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Ask a Wasteling what he fears and he asks whether you are warm. I took it for evasion the first winter. In the fourth I understood that it was all the information he had, and the only question worth asking a man who has come that far. It is not asked about the weather. A man may be asked it three times; the third asking is for the child who has not yet learned to be cold, who cannot answer and is asked all the same. I have set that down as I heard it and have not made a lesson of it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Then you have not come far enough.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said to a man who showed a warm-stone in his coat and thought it counted as an answer. Out there a stone is a thing you carry and not a thing you have. The man who sold it to him at the Keep had told him the price and not the debt, which is the whole of that trade. They do not say the second sentence unkindly. They say it the way a man at the bottom of a stair says there are more steps.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “It does not change. That is not weather.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — There is no weather beyond the Rim. Weather is a change, and the cold there does not change: it is an even, patient cold with nowhere to go and all the time in the world to get there. A man does not freeze in it so much as come gradually to agree with it. This is the hardest saying on the leaf for a man from the clay countries, because it leaves out the thing he would recognize.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Coming to agree.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — What they call it when a traveller stops being warm and starts being quiet. I have put Grathic words round a phrase with no grammar in it. A surveyor come up from the shaft told me travellers go back older and thinner and cannot say what they went for, and that the Court sends no collectors past the post. He said both in one breath and turned the slate face down.}

\subsection*{Of what is carried, and what is let go}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “What is in your hands.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — A Wasteling owns what he is still carrying and nothing else. This makes for a short inventory and a long silence. A man of Keld states his number before his name and has the number cut into his arm; a man out here holds out his hands, and if they are empty there is nothing to state and no shame in stating it. I have seen an officer ask after a man’s holding and been given the palm of a hand to look at, which is an answer in that country and an insult in every other.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “A stone. A name. A day. No figure.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — They will give any of the three and ask nothing back. The factor’s man at Greybank could not leave this sentence alone; see below. A gift that expects nothing is the one thing a lowland household cannot enter, and so it calls it theft, or folly, or a virtue done badly. Out here there is no word for a debt and no use for one. They are not the people the Court’s sealed rooms argue about. They are simply the spent.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “I put my hand on yours and let go.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The giving of a day’s warmth. A man told me he offered his palm to one of them and felt nothing come or go, and yet came back a day short somewhere he never found. I have set it as it happened and not as a bargain: a bargain is a thing two men remember, and he remembered only the hand.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Keep it. I have gone out of it.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said when a name is given. A Wasteling takes one word for a name and changes it when it stops fitting; asked for a second name he will point at the cold. When he gives the word away he does not lend it, and the man who receives it cannot return it to him, because the giver has gone out of it. I asked a woman who had given me a word what I owed her for it and she asked me if I was warm. I did not ask twice.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “—”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — There was a sound before the last sentence that I could not write, and she would not make it again. It was not Grathic and not Keldish, and it asked for nothing, which may be why I wanted it down. The blank is where it was. Men put words into blanks because a blank troubles them. A page is not troubled. Only men are.}

\subsection*{Of the dead, and the road they came by}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “He faces the way he came.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The dead are set upright facing the way they came and left uncovered. A woman who had stood beside one all morning said a man who had come that far had a right to be seen off toward the road he had travelled, and that covering him would be an argument with him, and they did not argue with the dead. In Grath they break a pot at the door to let the heat out. Both are kindnesses; I have never seen two so unlike and so complete.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Do not cover him.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The same saying said to the living, at a man who has stopped walking and is still sitting. It is not a refusal to help. It is a refusal to ask a question of a vessel that has no answer left in it. A hearth-maid from Sill who came up with a survey party crossed two fingers over the face and gave me a date instead of an answer; I have left the date out, because she would not have it entered.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Nothing swept. No Last Day.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — There is no day on which the grey is gathered and burnt, because there is no morning after out here to burn it in. The Ash of a person whose warmth was never taken is gathered by Wastelings and given away. I put my hand on such a place and it left no mark on me or the leaf; that is the stain along this fold, which nobody has owned and which I have not swept.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The cold is not empty.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — It is full of what nobody kept. Every traveller brings back this sentence and every clerk tries to enter it; I have heard it oftenest and understood it least. A Vorr says of his dead that they were never owed and leaves it standing; out here there is no word for owing, so the sentence cannot even be refused. What comes in is not called kept or lost. It is called there.}

\subsection*{Of the thing that comes close}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “It stands. You go.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — The cold-eater comes toward any vessel with a head. It has no language and no appetite a visitor can recognise; it does not kill, it takes. Lowlanders say it is the Waste come to fetch what is owed. That is a lowland sentence. There is nothing owed out here, and they do not fight the shape because there is nothing among them worth owning. A man who stands his ground against it is not brave; he has not understood the arrangement. I have left the sentence where it was said and made no rule of it.}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “That is what it is for.”

\end{enumerate}

\emph{Gloss — Said of a cold-eater by a woman I asked why they did not drive it off. I took it for an answer about the creature and saw it was an answer about everything: the post, the counting, the sitting dead, the things given away. I have kept it because it is the only sentence in this country that sounds like a reason and refuses to be one.}

\subsection*{What they say when a man goes on ahead}

\emph{Said to the ground, walking, by a man who would not sing it standing still. The place before the last line is left as it was left; nobody fills it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stone in the hand and the road in the face,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a name let go where the name stood;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape one for the man who goes on ahead\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the man who does not come back.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape No mark, no debt, no fire to carry,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no door to break and nothing swept;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cold keeps what nobody kept\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and does not ask to be paid.\end{quote}

\emph{Gloss — There is a space where a third line of the first part would stand. I asked a man what went in it and he said it was not a man but the place a man leaves, and that a place has no name and cannot be carried. The surveyor who took the leaf up the Rim Road put a notch in that space, because a notch is the nearest his trade comes to a place. I have left the notch standing and the space under it.}

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

A survey-clerk of the factor at Greybank borrowed the leaves on a market morning. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and ink in two fingers that will not come out. He writes upright and narrow and takes the verbs out as though a verb were a thing he could carry off in a cuff.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item At \emph{warm?} he set \emph{the thermal condition of the party is not entered}, which is a sentence true of every man alive and therefore of none.

\item At \emph{a stone, a name, a day, no figure} he wrote \emph{no consideration recorded; three gifts void}. He was right by his own law and has entered the three things as nothing, which is what the country does and what the country does not call nothing.

\item At \emph{the cold is not empty} he wrote \emph{the Waste is occupied}, which is a word for a room and not a word for a sink, and is the nearest I have ever known him come to agreeing with them.

\item At the space in the verse he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} beneath. A nought is a figure. The space was a man’s place, and the clerk has made it smaller by writing in it.

\end{itemize}

I have put the words back underneath and left his above, the way a newer survey line lies over an older one on the rim-seam. He takes the doer out so that a thing always true can be carried into a counting room. I put the doer back because a keeper at a post wants to know which way a man was facing when he stopped.

\subsection*{Cut into the edge, in a Keldish tally-man’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask one of them what his measure is and he will hold out his hands. Our numbers are on the arm and theirs are in what they have not let go. Both can be read. Only one can be entered.\end{quote}

He cut it with his tally-knife and would not write it, the manner of a man who has been up to the stones. The cut has gone grey in the fold.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The frost at the head came up out of the grain in the ninth winter and pressed the first two sayings together, so that \emph{warm?} and \emph{not far enough} stand closer here than they were said. I have not prised them apart; they are generally said in one breath. The coal smut at the fold is mine, off the sleeve I wipe the tally with. The flake of warm-stone kept its heat through one night on the stone floor and is cold now, which is the order of things here. The grey stone in the lower gutter was given by a woman who would not take a bowl for it; I stitched it in so the account and the thing it accounts for travel together. The white hair between the third and fourth leaves is not mine, and I have left it where it lay. The Ash along the outer fold leaves no stain and I have not swept it. There is no Last Day at this post, and I have not found one since I came up.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man is what he has not yet given.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape When he has given it, he is the road.\end{quote}

I asked a Wasteling who came through with no stone, a surveyor come down from the stones, and a clerk at Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the lines where they were written. The sheets go back into the oiled cloth and the cloth under the board at the post. Tomorrow the party will come up and count the men, and I shall count with them, and the people beyond the post will go past it without asking what the counting is for, which is the only honest answer any post has had.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Cold Keeps, Being an Account of the Country Beyond the Cold Pass}
\CRsheetheading{What the Cold Keeps, Being an Account of the Country Beyond the Cold Pass}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A quarryman’s itinerary and travel account, set down on the back of a spoiled Keldish survey sheet and a strip of birch bark; part road-log, part inventory of what came back, part complaint, with the corrections of a Court survey-clerk in Ledgerhand, a Keldish surveyor’s note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 811 at Keld Keep, on the Rim Road and beyond the Cold Pass, by Orrel of Stonemouth, a quarryman who went west as a hired guide to a survey party and came back down the Rim Road in Seed of Y.H. 812 with a stone in his pocket, one year gone by the slate and three by his face, and no memory of the debt he went to recover. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded tally-roll, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sailcloth and carried in a tin. It survives with coal dust ground into the head, a smear of hot lead at the fold that has burnt through one word, a crust of white frost along the gutter, a single white hair pressed between the second and third leaves, a small grey stone folded into the gutter, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one note in the broad slow hand of the Keldish surveyor who borrowed the leaves, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I went west to recover a debt and came back with a stone. The debt had a name on it when I left and no name when I returned, and I have left the place where the name stood rather than put a figure in it. A figure would stand. I have seen what stands and what does not out there, and I am not the man to say which of the two is true.

I am a quarryman of Stonemouth. I cut lime and coarse sandstone out of the bank where the Ferr comes down, and I know the weight of a stone by the hand before I know it by the eye. In Seed of Y.H. 811 a surveyor come through the village hired me to carry instruments and guide a party up the Rim Road, and there was a debt between us that I thought a man could collect if he walked far enough behind it. This is the account I kept. I have set down what happened and what did not, and where the two disagree I have left both standing, which is a thing a clerk cannot do and a quarryman can, because stone does not care which of your accounts it lies under.

\subsection*{The road as far as the last pass}

From Sill to Keld Keep is a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather. Only fools and factors travel it without a warm-stone. I went with one in a fold of wool against my belly and another in the cart, and I do not say now who paid for the second, because I have asked and the answer comes back in a voice I do not recognise.

At Keld Keep a man states his measure before he states his name. I stated mine and was told it was a lowland figure and would not carry me ten leagues beyond the pass, which was true: it did not. The survey-clerk who hired me wrote this down in the margin as a kindness, since it cost him nothing. In that city a man’s number is cut into his forearm at thirteen and cut out again when he comes back thin, and I saw three men with smooth places on their arms where a number had been, and I saw a fourth who had had his changed twice and could not say which of the two he had been born to. None of them asked me my name. All of them asked my measure. This is a difference a Grath man notices and does not enjoy noticing.

Ten leagues beyond the Keep the road goes through the Cold Pass, which Karric VII shut in Y.H. 741 and the agreement of Y.H. 747 fixed as the border. There is a survey post there and no gate. The Warden’s surveyors do not promise to bring a man back, and this also was written down, in the same hand. I asked the clerk whether a promise not made was a promise kept, and he said that was a question for a lowland moot, and went on writing.

Past the last pass no map is honest. I carried that sentence out of Keld and set it here because it was the only true thing anybody told me in that country. The survey party turned back at the post. I went on, because the debt was on that side and because a man who has come a hundred and thirty leagues to collect a thing is a fool in exactly the way that keeps him walking.

\subsection*{The country itself}

There is no weather in the Waste. Weather is a change, and the cold there does not change. It is not a great cold, the way Stone is cold in Sill; it is an even, patient cold that has nowhere to go and all the time in the world to get there. A man does not freeze in it so much as come gradually to agree with it.

The Keeping teaches that the Waste is the sink where everything unheld goes. I have no quarrel with that; a man who has worked a quarry knows about sinks. What the Keeping does not teach is that a sink is a country, and a country has people in it, and those people have no use for a slate. There is nothing to count out there. No ember changes hands, no mark is made, no collector comes with his iron tube and his clean figure. The Court has never opened an account beyond the pass, which is the only mercy in this world that costs the Court nothing.

They say the cold is not empty. They say it is full of what nobody kept. I have no reason to disbelieve them and several to believe them, and one of those reasons is in my pocket.

\subsection*{The people, and what they give}

The bands beyond the Rim are called Wastelings. They have no banks, no Returns and no word for a debt. They are not the Unbanked the Court speaks of, who have a design and a name and people to argue with; they are simply the spent. A man there owns what he is still carrying and nothing else, which makes for a short inventory and a long silence.

They leave their dead sitting upright facing the way they came. They do not cover them. I asked why, and a woman who had stood beside one for a morning said that a man who had come that far had a right to be seen off in the direction he had travelled, and that covering him would be a sort of argument with him, and they did not argue with the dead. I set that down as she said it. A Grathic hearth-maid would have covered the body with a fold and crossed two fingers and given me a date. Both acts are kindnesses. I have never seen two kindnesses so unlike and so complete.

A Wasteling will give a stone, or a name, or a day’s warmth, and expect nothing back. This stopped me longer than anything else in that country, because in Stonemouth a gift that expects nothing is the one thing a man cannot enter, and a thing a man cannot enter is a thing he cannot afford. I took the stone. I have not entered it. The woman who gave it to me wanted nothing, and I still do not know what to do with that.

Ask a Wasteling what he fears and he will ask whether you are warm. At first I took this for evasion. On the ninth day I understood it was the whole of his information, and the only question worth asking a man who has come that far.

\subsection*{The ninth day}

I went out with a porter of Keld who had opened a way in his forearm and had the numbers cut out and put in again twice. He was a man of few sentences and those all about the road. On the ninth morning out he stood close to my little fire, closer than a man stands to warm himself, and I thought he was warming himself. He was not warming himself.

The Keldish call such a shape a cold-eater. It stands close to a vessel and draws its Warm away; it takes and does not give. There was no struggle and no sound. In the afternoon his fingers were the colour of skimmed milk gone off, and by the third watch he had forgotten his numbers, and by morning he had forgotten that he had ever had a name. We did not say the thing’s name aloud, because a name gives a thing a place in an account, and there is no account out there.

The cost is the part the books leave out. I carried one warm-stone out and brought two back, and one of them is his. I have not given it to anybody because there is nobody to give it to, and because if I set it down I should have to say what it cost. It sits in the gutter of this account where a figure should be, and the Clerk has been at it, as you will see.

\subsection*{A song they sing at the sitting-down}

\emph{Set down in Grathic letters from the mouth of the woman who gave the stone. The last line is said three times, and the third time is for the one who cannot say it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Beyond the last pass there is no weather,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no mark, no debt, no name to spend;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dead sit facing the way they came\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cold keeps what nobody kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone for a stone and a name for a name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a day’s warmth for whoever can carry it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask me what I fear and I will ask you this:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape are you warm? are you warm? are you warm?\end{quote}

I asked her what the third asking was for. She said it was for the child who had not yet learned to be cold, and that a child could not answer and the question was asked anyway, which is the way the world treats a child. I have left that in, though a clerk would take it out.

\subsection*{What went out and what came back}

Went out with — Came back with\par

One warm-stone in a fold of wool — Two stones; the second is not mine and I have not entered it\par

A clay cup out of the meal mill at Sill — A cup, cold, that answers flat when set down, and nobody to tap it\par

A slate with a name and a debt on it — The same slate, one year older, with the name gone and a figure in another hand\par

A porter of Keld with numbers on his forearm — A man with a smooth arm who answered to no number and went on walking\par

A year by the slate, Seed of Y.H. 811 to Seed of Y.H. 812 — Three years by my face, and a morning I cannot account for\par

A debt to collect — A stone to keep\par

There is a place in this table where a line should stand and does not. I have set the stone in it. If you hold the leaf to the lamp you can feel the stone through the paper, which is more than I can say for the figure.

\subsection*{What the Clerk did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaves at Greybank. He struck out \emph{the cold keeps what nobody kept} and set above it, \emph{The measure is retained in the Waste.} Against the second warm-stone he wrote \emph{no value entered.} Where I had left the place where the porter’s name stood, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it.

Against the debt he set a figure and wrote \emph{satisfied} beside it. It is the only satisfaction I have ever been given that I did not receive. I have left his hand standing and mine under it, the way a quarry leaves the spoil above the stone.

\subsection*{From the man who hired me}

At the foot of the second leaf, in the broad slow hand of the Keldish surveyor, who borrowed the leaves before the Clerk did and returned them with the fold changed:

\begin{quote}\itshape The numbers are correct.\end{quote}

He was asked, beyond the post, to translate a marking cut in a stone that was not cut with iron. He gave that answer and turned the slate face down. I asked him twice and got the same words both times. In Keld that is an answer a man can carry away and learn nothing from, and it is the sort of answer that keeps. I have set it where he wrote it and added nothing.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal dust at the head came off the surveyor’s cuff in the lamp-room at Keld Keep; he leaned over my sheet and would not sit down. The hot lead at the fold came from a sample wrapped in the same paper. It has burnt a small hole clean through the word \emph{pass}, and I have not written the word in again, because a hole in that word is the honest state of it.

The frost-crust in the gutter came up out of the paper on the ninth morning, when I carried the leaves inside my coat and the coat froze to my chest. The white hair is not mine and is not the porter’s; it lay pressed between the leaves when I found them in the snow, and I have kept it there. The small grey stone is the one I came back with; I have folded it into the gutter so that the account and the thing it accounts for travel together. The grey print along the outer fold is not mine. There is no Last Day out there and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man is a vessel set down facing the way he came.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody covers him, and the cold does not lose him.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who gave the stone, the survey-clerk and a factor come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back in the tin, and the tin goes under the bench at Stonemouth where I keep the things I cannot enter. If I am asked what I went for I shall say a debt, because that is the word I was taught. If I am asked what I brought back I shall say a stone, and put my hand in my pocket to feel it, as I have done every morning since Seed of Y.H. 812.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Dog Ate, Being a Grave-Guard’s Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Greybank Burial Grounds}
\CRsheetheading{What the Dog Ate, Being a Grave-Guard’s Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Greybank Burial Grounds}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the back of a spoiled granary docket, a digger’s song in the words it is sung, the factor’s clerk’s corrections in Ledgerhand in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Watt of Greybank, one of the factor’s men paid by the tend to keep the south-bank burial ground; set down at the end of watches in the watch-hut with a tallow end in a pot, first on three dry grain-dockets from the Court’s granaries and then on the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at one corner, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a grey Ash thumb ground into the head, a brown spot the size of a fingernail where a man’s blood fell on the second leaf, a wet boot-print across the foot from a morning crossing the ford, a nick from a billhook at the fore-edge, the charcoal rubbed thin where the leaf was carried, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the south ground at Greybank for the factor. It is not a post a man boasts of. The dead laid there are mostly such as came back thin out of the district, and they go into shallow clay with a potsherd at the head and no slate read aloud over them. My work is to see that they are not opened twice. Once is the hearth-maids and the diggers; the second is somebody else, and it is the second I am paid to stand against. I carry a billhook and a short spear with the head gone grey on the quay stone, and I write this at the end of a watch with a tallow end in a pot and the cold coming up through the soles of my boots.

The grey thumb at the head is Ash. I have tried to knock it off and it went into the fibre. That is what Ash does. There is nothing mysterious in it, except that a man who has never held a pot over a room where a promise was not kept will call it dirt and be done with it.

\subsection*{The ground}

The ground lies south of the town beyond the Ilm, a short way past the winter ford, and in Stone you may cross on the ice if you know where the ice is sound. There are two sorts of grave. The old ones are long and set in rows with a headboard gone soft at the foot. The new ones are small and close under the south fence, dug by Mott, who is paid by the grave and not by the hour, so that he has an interest in their being shallow. I have no quarrel with him. A deep grave in this clay costs a man his winter.

What I noticed first, and wrote down before I knew what to call it, is that the new small graves do not take the frost like the old ones. On a morning in Bone I laid the back of my hand on six mounds in the row. Four were cold clay and two had a little softness under the crust, the way a banked coal is soft under its skin of grey. I have no name for that and I have set no cause beside it. Mott says it is warmth rising off the river. The diggers say the clay was turned late. Both may be true. I have kept the shape of it, which is the only work a watchman has.

\subsection*{What comes}

It is a dog. I will set that down first, because the hearths will not. It has a dog’s teeth, a dog’s neck, a dog’s way of putting its head on one side when it listens, and the long narrow muzzle of a dog that has been fed out of a ditch. It is bigger than the yard hounds at the Tallow Works and thinner. Its coat is the colour of wet clay and carries no grey on the outside; the grey is in the mouth and under the nails, and a man who has opened one will know where I mean.

It comes out of the low ground south of the fence in the second watch, which is when the tallow in the hut is down to a knuckle and the men on the quay have stopped shouting at one another. It does not bark. The diggers have a song about the barking which is wrong in every particular, and I have set the song down below with the wrong part standing, because a thing sung wrong for twenty years is part of the ground as much as the graves are.

It does not attack a man. I have stood within two paces of one with my spear down and it went on with its work and never looked at me. But put a man between it and a grave it has chosen and it will bite. That is the whole rule, and there is no courage in testing it twice.

\subsection*{The bite}

Mott put his foot in a hole at Ash 5 and came down on one knee with his hand in the clay, and the dog was already there. I struck it across the back with the spear-shaft. It went away three paces and stood, which is what it does; it does not run off and it does not come back at a man who has hit it. Mott’s bite was two small holes on the thumb-side of the hand, grey at the edges, and not much blood. We washed with salt and water and bound it. At the end of the tend it was still open, with the grey where the edges had been.

Salt does not hold that bite. The physician at Greybank told Mott to keep it warm, which is what physicians say when they have nothing else to say, and Mott kept it warm and the hand went on being a hand with a hole in it. He has a rag on it now and will not show it at the market. I put the size of the holes in the margin because a man cannot close his hand and I have had to watch him try. The clerk has written over them, which I did not ask him to do.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, written along the margin:} Wound: not entered. No deduction arises.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand is an iron thing and has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change.

\subsection*{The song}

Sung by the diggers going out to the south ground in the dark, not coming back. The second line is their error and not mine. I have not corrected it, because Mott sings it loudest and would take it ill.

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the big and three for the small,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it barks at the wall and it comes to the wall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it puts its nose to the new-turned ground\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes what the ground has not yet made cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a horn for the reeve and a phial for the jar;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey in the mouth and the grey on the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one that is kept and not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the nights I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The figure in the last column is mine, not the clerk’s.

Night — Place — Opened — Grey gathered — Lost\par

Bone 4 — Small row, south fence — one — one — none\par

Bone 13 — Small row, west end — two — one — none; wind off the river\par

Bone 22 — Old grave under the alder — none — none — spear lost in the clay\par

Ash 5 — Small row, third mound — one — one — Mott’s hand\par

Ash 16 — Two graves, the old ground — two — two — none\par

Ash 27 — New ground beyond the fence — three — one — dog stood and did not go\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} Openings: six. Loss of property: nil. No entry arises.\end{quote}

There is no property in a grave, so he is right, and he has written \emph{nil} where I wrote Mott’s hand. I have set my line under his and left both where they fell, the way a digger leaves the clay on top of the pot and knows what is underneath it.

\subsection*{The jar and the horn}

There is a man comes up the south road at the dusk of Account-day with a jar under his coat and no horse. He is of the fen people and speaks little. He pays five bits a phial and asks no questions, which is the price of quiet ash in the Fenmarch and the reason a man asks no questions at it. I do not know what dog it was that gave the grey, and I have never asked him what house will buy it. I have held the jar while he filled it from the thing we scrape out of the beast when one is taken. I have never taken the bits. A man may say that and still know it is not enough.

The horns go a different way. A reeve of the Standing Post came in Frost and paid two bits a horn, and the horns went south to be cut into count-sticks. I asked him what a stick counts that a slate cannot. He said a stick cannot be read by a man who is not standing over it, which seemed to him a virtue and to me a great deal of trouble. But the diggers like them. Mott keeps one in his belt and turns it when he is deciding which row to open, and it has more notches than there are graves, which I have not asked him to explain.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

The hearths say the dog guards the graves. I have stood and watched it go to the small new ones first and pass the old ones by, and I have seen what it leaves in the clay. A thing that guards is not a thing that eats; but those are words too fine for me, and I have written only the order in which it went. From the south fence to the third mound, then the west end, then the old rows if the watch is long and the tallow is low. That is the whole of what I know. I have not written why.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The Ash thumb at the head is mine; I held the docket down in the draught that comes under the watch-hut door and did not know I had marked it. The brown spot on the second leaf fell there from Mott’s hand when he sat down to have the rag changed, and I have not scraped it, because it is the only entry on this leaf that cost anybody anything. The boot-print across the foot came off the morning I crossed the ford after the ice went thin and came up to the calf in silt; it has dried into the grain and will not rub out. The nick at the fore-edge is the billhook, from the night the dog stood at Ash 27 and I struck at it and missed. The charcoal is rubbed thin where I carried the leaf in my pocket against my thigh. The clerk’s two lines I have not touched. The song is as the diggers sang it, barking and all.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes into the ground is kept by somebody else. Ask the jar.\end{quote}

There is new low ground beyond the south fence that I have not walked, and the dog comes out of it with clay on its chest that is not the clay of these graves. I will go in next Bone with a fresh spear and Mott’s counting-stick, and I will count them going and count them back, and if the grey comes from a grave nobody laid I will set that down too, in my own hand, with the verb left in it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Road Took and the Market Gave, Being a Chapman’s Book of Rates for the Ilm Circuit and the Roads Upon It, Copied into No Counting House}
\CRsheetheading{What the Road Took and the Market Gave, Being a Chapman’s Book of Rates for the Ilm Circuit and the Roads Upon It, Copied into No Counting House}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A pedlar’s pocket-book of prices and road-dues, the board’s figure set above the figure actually paid; figures in a rough travelling hand, one column left as a place and not a nought, the verbs put back where a borrowed hand took them out, two corrections in other hands, and a line at the foot nobody will own · Written on the circuit between Sill, the Weir, Stonemouth, Nine Pots, Mud End and the Standing Post in the Thin Year Y.H. 812, after the Long Cold; carried forward at the Opening of the Slates, Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and written up again in Reed of that year. It is a chapman’s book, kept in the inner coat pocket where the pack-strap has worn a place through the leather, and it survives soft at the fore-edge with dried eel slime, grey silt worked into the gutter, a white salt bloom at the head, tar at the fold, a docken leaf pressed flat between two leaves, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a bit gone verdigris in the bottom margin, an Ash thumb at the head, iron-gall in two fingers, a small bare square where a word was scraped away, two corrections in borrowed hands, and one line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I carry a pack on the Ilm circuit and have done these nineteen years, which is longer than most men last at the Court’s work. Every market morning I hear a figure cried that I have already paid for in shoe leather, and every evening I set down what I gave, and the two never agree. This book is the second figure. The board on the quay tells what a thing fetched under the beam; it cannot tell what it cost to bring there, because no man behind a beam has walked the road.

There is a saying among the reed-cutters that a bundle is counted in the arm that carries it, and that the arm knows weight and not cost. My back knows the weight. This book knows the cost. I have never got the two to sit at one table.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of a man from the College, written above my first line:} Figures entered in the ordinary way. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There is nothing ordinary about a figure that has walked eighty leagues. I have put the verbs back.\end{quote}

Twelve copper bits to a silver mark. Twenty silver marks to a gold crown, which is a Sere coin and does not stay in Grath. The Court books in embers and will tell a man an ember is five marks; no man has ever exchanged one for the other, and I have left no column for them. A bit, in this book, is a bit I parted with. A mark is a mark I did not want to part with.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the College hand, struck through and written above:} An ember is valued at five marks. \emph{In mine, restored underneath:} The Court values it. I do not. A verb with nobody in it is a verb that cannot be argued with, which is why they take them out.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The pack, and what it fetched}

\emph{Figures cried at the Cross on Account-day set against what I actually put down between the last market of Stone and the Reed Account-days. The left column is what a man with a roof over his goods calls the price. The right is what I carried away less than I brought.}

Article — As it is cried — As I paid\par

Coarse barley loaf, brown-edged — 1 bit — 1 bit, and a crust over at a door where nobody entered it\par

Quart of small ale, watered — 1 bit — 1 bit at Sill; 2 at the Weir, where they know it is watered\par

Salt herring — 2 bits — 2 bits, or 3 when the boat has been in and nobody says why\par

Eels, by the basket, at the boards — 3 bits smoked, 2 salted — a figure named under an apron, never the same twice\par

Coarse pots, the score — 4 bits — 4 bits at Sill; a pot broken at the feud post costs the seller\par

Tile, the hundred — 9 bits — 9 bits, and two hollow ones put in that I set out again\par

Peat, a barrow — 2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone — the Stone figure, in Seed, without complaint\par

Salt, a sack off the pans — 3 marks — 3 marks, and a mark again at the coast pass\par

Iron, a bar, Keldish — 2 marks in the lowlands — 2 marks here; half a mark in Keld, where the road costs more than the bar\par

Glass, a sheet from the cliffs — 2 marks — 2 marks, and it broke before Stonemouth\par

Rope, a coil — 1 mark — 1 mark, and it left tar on this leaf\par

Sheepskin coat — 3 marks — 3 marks, or two and a promise in a hard year\par

Good axe — 2 marks — 2 marks; half a mark in Keld, which is the same axe\par

Ash-mite paste, a thimble, at Mud End — not on any board — 4 bits, no questions; the same grey in a Court jar is sixty marks and sealed\par

Reed bundle, an armful, at the Weir — not on any board — ask the arm that carried it; the arm does not know cost\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} I have set the eel row without a figure of my own, which is a place and not a nought. A buyer names a number under an apron; the seller puts her thumb to a cord and keeps it there longer than the number wants. There is no figure in that. A chapman who explains a stall does not last a tend at these boards.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The paste and the sealed jar are the same grey in two vessels, one with a Fen name and one with a Court name. I carry neither. A man I drank with keeps a hand in a glove. I have not joined the jars, and have scraped out the word I wrote beside them; the bare square is the length of it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The markets of the circuit}

The Cross at Sill holds its market on the tenth, twentieth and thirtieth, when the bell goes four, four and a gap and nobody crosses himself, and the slate is read twice, once for the moot and once for those who came late. I have stood under that bell in nineteen years of weather and never heard a figure that agreed with the one I paid at the stall. At Greybank the market is every day and the beam is always warm. At the Weir the eels are sold at dawn and the traps blessed on Ilmen fifteenth, and the eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. Stonemouth sells lime, sandstone and a reed-wolf tooth for a clamp-handle. Nine Pots sells pots and has never sold Sill a road.

There is a figure spoken in the yards of Low Kiln which is not the printed one. I have heard it and have not set it here. I have no beam to weigh it on, and a man who writes a figure he cannot weigh will be asked to read it aloud.

\subsection*{The tolls of the roads}

\emph{The gate figure is what is demanded. The last column is what left my pocket. Four great roads and a fifth which is the river, and a handful of little roads that no board has ever heard of.}

Road and place — As demanded — As I gave\par

Clay Road, Sill end, loaded cart — 2 bits — 2 bits, and 2 more at the factor’s man at Greybank\par

Clay Road, foot passenger — 1 bit; nothing on Account-day — 1 bit; on Account-day I walk with the crowd and pay nothing\par

River road to the Weir and Stonemouth, a beast — 1 bit — 1 bit; passable on foot in Silt when the low way is under\par

Plank walk at the Weir — 1 bit — 1 bit, and I took the board that was trodden flat\par

South bridge at Sill, loaded cart — 1 bit — 1 bit\par

North bridge at Sill — nothing — nothing; the Fishstairs folk argued it and won\par

The Nine Pots road, west from Sill — no gate — a pot set down at the feud post, which Sill calls an insult and the potters call a toll\par

Fen boardwalks to the Standing Post — 1 bit for a dry foot — a marked stick for a wet one; outsiders are not told which boards bear\par

Salt Road, a sack of salt at the coast pass — 1 mark to the Council of Tides — 1 mark, freely entered, which is what they call it\par

Rim Road, a cart at the pass — 1 mark, or iron to the value — 1 mark in iron, the iron being heavier than the mark\par

Rim Road, a beast on the hoof — half a mark — half a mark, and a warm-stone off the next man who has one\par

Hearth Road, at the barrier — none; there is no barrier — none; the figure was read to me twice at home\par

The ford when the Ilm bears ice — nothing, because no collector can cross — nothing, for ninety-four days in the Long Cold\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the Council clerk’s leaning hand, against the salt row:} toll is struck and contribution freely entered written over it. \emph{In mine:} The figures stand. A Council that cannot charge a toll has found a finer name for one, and a man pays it all the same.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A carter from High Kiln asked what the Hearth Road cost and I showed him the empty column. He said it was the most honest figure on the page and the dearest. The Court takes nothing at the gate because it has taken it at home. I did not put that in the demanded column; it would stop nobody from loading.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What no gate charges}

These are not dues. No slate takes them and no factor enters them, and they are the reason a book like this has to be kept.

The Ferr runs lead dust off the western workings, and a man who drinks it through a season comes back thin; there is no figure at Stonemouth for that. The sweet sickness from bad glaze shows first as a pale line at the gum and ends with a man who cannot hold a cup, and the glaze-mixers of High Kiln taste it every morning and call it their work. A brine-gull went off below the north bridge with a coal not yet cold, and no slate in Sill stood one mark the poorer. Beyond the Cold Pass the cold takes a year and gives back a thinner man who has forgotten what he went for. A woman at the lower boards gave me a date where I asked for a figure and said I could shout at either one.

I have set all this under the roads and not among them. A due is a figure somebody will stand behind. These have nobody behind them, which is why they are the ones that get paid.

\subsection*{The verse the chapmen carry}

\emph{Sung under the breath on the Clay Road, never at the Cross while a slate is out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Twelve to the mark and twenty to the crown,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and five to the ember the Court books down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the board keeps the figure the beam can hold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the road keeps the rest in the soles of a man.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A pot at Nine Pots and a bit at the Weir,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a bit for the bridge and a mark at the pass;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Clay pays twice and the Salt pays twice,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Hearth pays at home where the fire lies.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ask the arm, ask the cord, ask the running river,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court has a figure for all of the three;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I have a book with the figures I gave\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a column kept empty for what the road took.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the College hand, against the last line:} Three figures entered. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} There are four, and I have set nothing in the place of the fourth. A nought is a figure. That line is a place.\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The College man strikes the verbs out. Where I set \emph{I paid}, he sets \emph{was paid}, as though a mark could pay itself and nobody carry it; where I set \emph{the road took}, he sets \emph{was taken}, as though a cold had no hand in it. I put both back underneath and leave his words above. A verb is the difference between a price and a debt, and a man who loses the verb has lost the man who owed.

The other hand is a counting house hand out of Sere, with a little gold in the ink. Against \emph{2 bits in Grain, 5 in Stone} it wrote \emph{seasonal rate}, and against the eel row, \emph{market rate}, and put figures in the margin where I had put the price. I left both standing. A house of Sere can call a figure a rate, because a rate is a thing that can be emptied and refilled. I have held peat in a barrow in Silt and called it what it was.

\subsection*{In the margins}

The eel slime on the fore-edge is mine, from holding the board still at the Fishstairs with the hand that held the book. The silt in the gutter came off the second step below the north bridge and I have never got it out. The white at the head is salt bloom blown up from the Sallow; it comes and goes with the weather and is never entered. The tar at the fold came off a Vhaleni coil. The green bead is lead glaze from a woman who leaned to see the figures with the sweetness still at her mouth, and touched the paper, and said nothing. The docken leaf I pressed flat on the Cold Acre road for a blister; the bit gone verdigris in the bottom margin has been there since the Long Cold and is the only coin in the book never spent. The Ash at the head is off my own thumb turning the leaf toward the light; the iron-gall is in two fingers and will not come out. The bare square is the word I scraped away. There is no Last Day for a chapman’s pocket, and nothing here is swept and burnt and called dealt with.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The board keeps the figure the beam held. The book keeps the figure the man carried. The difference has no column and no name.\end{quote}

I asked a carter, a stall-keeper at the boards, and a clerk come down from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back into the inner pocket, against the place the strap has worn. Tomorrow I take the Clay Road up to Sill with salt and rope and a sheet of glass not yet broken, and a figure will be cried at the Cross that I shall pay in coin and in leather and in a day I shall not get back. By evening it will be a thing that was true. I shall set it under the figure they cried and leave the space between them as it is.

\chapter*{The Reckoning of Days}
\markboth{The Reckoning of Days}{The Reckoning of Days}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Reckoning of Days}
\begin{CRtimeline}
\CRday{Day 1}{Stone 7, Y.H. 812 (Seventhday)  —  the birth room off the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Corin is born two hours old with Daniel Marchetti’s whole memory and a branching red flower on his ribs; the stone Dessa warmed at the Vail fire goes cold at his belly while a name is entered in a neat dark hand on Alda’s slate before anyone has looked at his face, Mira gives bread and keeps her back to the writing, and Sella’s door-burned hand feels for the warmth, hovers over the bundle and withdraws with the third day still to come.}
\CRday{Day 2}{Stone 8, Y.H. 812 (Eighthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and wheel-shed, and the birth room of House Silt, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  In the kiln-house the fire keeps its four-and-four-and-a-gap breath around Garl’s hollow wheel-seat, salt coat and unswept Ash ridge while Tarn pockets and returns the bench knife and Jorra declares the foundling is not Vail to a Sella who answers the pot instead, and three doors down Corin, two days old, hears the flat note of a cup he cannot reach, feels the warmed stone go past temperature, endures Alda’s ordered washing and unasked-for dates and Des’s laugh from a Chicago car park, while Dessa calls her cough weather, counts nineteen steps and refuses his name as the room arranges an unspoken question about who pays to keep him.}
\CRday{Day 3}{Stone 9, Y.H. 812 (Ninthday)  —  the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house with its wheel-shed and Debt Loft, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella carries the covered bundle up the icy yard with the burn-door closing on its weight and the boy counting her steps, while Dessa stands at the end of nineteen steps she does not take with her thumb on the sieve-wire scar and Alda tells her he went in the levy among the children taken for the account and lets unasked-for dates settle over an unspoken figure, leaving the cold stone behind on the abandoned bed, and under the Vail roof the boy is laid on fresh straw with heat returning painfully to his hands and feet, hears Jorra’s sentence sealed and Tarn’s I’m-a-debt-not-a-foundling and a second flat note from a pot, and sees the charred edge of a slate in the kiln ash that he cannot reach, the market and the Cross still ahead.}
