\textbf{Kind.} Female order of midwives, collectors’ assistants and keepers of the birth-slates. \textbf{Seat.} Scattered through every Grathic village; the birth-slate book is kept in the hearth-maid’s own house. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Alda Reed}, who attended Corin’s birth, crossed herself at the birth-flower, and told nobody what she had seen. \textbf{Goals.} To deliver children, record births within three days, and keep the small domestic knowledge of the afterdrop and the warmed stone alive. \textbf{Methods.} Practical instruction in proverbs and half-sentences; the stone against the belly; the slate; the crossed sign at a birth-flower. \textbf{Resources.} Access to every newborn vessel in Grath, the trust of households that would not let an officer into the room, and the memory of the second chill before the Court struck its name from the record. \textbf{Enemies.} The collectors, who arrive with a tube and take the mother’s attention. The College, which tried in Y.H. 782 to make every birth a Court entry and succeeded by paying them. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The maids have kept a second set of notes since Y.H. 651: every infant who grew worse on the third day and spoke words in an unknown language. The notes are not in the Court’s file. Alda Reed’s is the fullest.

\section*{The Vorr of the Listening Stones}

\textbf{Kind.} Ancient people and keepers of numbers; a lineage rather than a school. \textbf{Seat.} The Listening Stones, five leagues above Keld Keep; a few seats at the Court’s survey table. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ao of the Third Seam}, \textbf{Iyn of the Listening Stone}, \textbf{Eru Who Counts}. \textbf{Goals.} To sit until the stones give up their numbers and to keep the record of the repairs without selling it. \textbf{Methods.} The Long Sitting at forty; a life’s patience; answers of one sentence, usually \emph{the numbers are correct}, which is not a translation. \textbf{Resources.} The Deep Hand’s numerals, a memory of the unnumbered ages, and four thousand people who cannot be banked in the ordinary way. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, which employs them and watches them. Anyone impatient. The age of the world, which is longer than any Vorr’s attention. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They know the oldest repairs are not clay and have known for centuries. They will not say what they are, because the last surveyor who wrote it down was removed from the shaft in Y.H. 717.

\section*{The Dippers of Vhalen}

\textbf{Kind.} Salt priesthood and practical school of tide-lore. \textbf{Seat.} The salt pans outside Vhal, and the Council’s tar-smelling room in bad weather. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Neri Sail}, chief dipper; \textbf{Kett of the Quay}, who keeps the tide-tallies. \textbf{Goals.} To bless the nets, read the Sallow draw, and keep Vhalen’s warmth from going out with the cold tides. \textbf{Methods.} Trailing a net in the sea at dawn; contracts on salt-paper that rot in the rain, which is considered a virtue; a law that lasts too long is a law that has stopped earning. \textbf{Resources.} The pans, the boats, the glass of the Glaze Cliffs, and a people who can turn a wet document into a fortune. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s assessors with their lists of deductions. The salt-thing. The winter. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The dippers know that Vhalen’s Sallow has no separate Hearth, whatever the priests say. They have measured the draw. They tell the Council only what is profitable.

\CRrule

\section*{II. Houses, churches and powers}

\section*{House Vail of Low Kiln}

\textbf{Kind.} Kiln-house; the closest thing Grath has to a noble family. \textbf{Seat.} The Vail kiln-house in the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, beside the Slip Brook. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Sella Vail}, keeper of the fire; \textbf{Jorra Vail}, her son; the household’s dead, whose names are kept on the roll. \textbf{Goals.} To hold the fire, keep the wheel, and see that a Vail name is written on the birth-slate of every child born under the Vail roof. \textbf{Methods.} A widow’s mark, four generations of standing, inheritances settled by who has the stronger hands, and a practical refusal to discuss anything that matters. \textbf{Resources.} One kiln, the slip pits, a house of clay-daubed rooms, and the attention of the whole district. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, which levy one in three. Nine Pots. The cupworm. The Ash ridge that grows along the skirting board in a bad year. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} Sella took Corin in as a foundling because a slate-name with no house can be used by anyone. She has kept the boy close and has never once asked where his memory came from. She is waiting to see what he will become.

\section*{The Sunbowl houses of Sere}

\textbf{Kind.} Great slave-owning houses; the nobility of the southern empire. \textbf{Seat.} The Bowl of Sere, three hundred leagues south of Sill; provincial bowls throughout the empire. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Alessa Sunbowl}, \textbf{Rial of the Ten Bowls}, \textbf{Ilyra Gilded}. \textbf{Goals.} To empty vessels gloriously, to own beautiful returned slaves as proof of generosity, and to keep the northern measures flowing south at a price no poor household can refuse. \textbf{Methods.} The public Bowl feast, the burning of debt-slates by lot, open chattel slavery, and a law in which \emph{measure for measure} means whatever the speaker has already decided. \textbf{Resources.} Grain, wine, oil, gold crowns, the largest slave population in the world, and the warmest funerals in Sarn, which can ruin a house. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s deduction on their grain. The Fenmarch at the Peat Line. Any slave who remembers enough to want something. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The houses buy poor measures to make beautiful whole returns for their own exhibits, which means a Sere household is a machine for turning a district of thin people into one decorative person. The order is intentional and is never spoken of in the counting room, where a woman’s numbers must be read by a man.

\section*{The Temple of the Return}

\textbf{Kind.} Public church of the Keeping; the faith taught to children. \textbf{Seat.} Temples in every town; the Weighing Hall in the Hearthseat is its altar. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Hesta Clay, Voice of the Return}, with the keepers of the Hearth-fire beneath her. \textbf{Goals.} To teach that the world was made whole, cracked once, and is being mended by the mercy of the Hearth; to make the Return the first thing a child learns and the last thing a dying person hears. \textbf{Methods.} Temple walls showing the single breaking; the Nine Who Kept as figures of pity and reverence; the phrase \emph{nothing is lost that we have kept}; the fire behind a grating that no priest is allowed to touch. \textbf{Resources.} Every childhood in Sarn, the Five Cold Days, and an institution that has never needed an argument because it got there first. \textbf{Enemies.} The surveyors of Keld, who have seen the layers in the rim-seam. The Deep Hand. Anyone who reads the oldest repairs as language. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The founding story is an invoice. The temple’s own oldest slate shows the repairs laid one over another, and the oldest of all are not the work of any god that can be named. The temple keeps the slate face down.

\section*{The Marsh Mother}

\textbf{Kind.} Peat cult of the Fenmarch; a church of the mud. \textbf{Seat.} The Standing Post and the peat-dries; rites performed face down in peat. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Bogga of the Reed}, \textbf{Mudge Peat}, who sells the Ash the Court will not license. \textbf{Goals.} To keep warmth in the mud and to take it back when the household needs it; to sell cheap thin returns and ask no questions about the source. \textbf{Methods.} Lying face down in peat until the cold becomes ordinary; knot-sticks instead of writing; a child named by its mother before the collector arrives, which is the closest thing the Fenmarch has to a declaration of war. \textbf{Resources.} The peat-dries, the smugglers’ paths, cheap returns at a third of the Court’s price, and a population that can identify a collector by his boots before it can name its own children. \textbf{Enemies.} The draining of the fens. The Court’s lists. A winter in which the peat does not dry. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The cult knows where the Ash goes, because it sells the Ash. It does not care what the Ash is, which is why it has survived where more squeamish institutions have not.

\section*{The Spending}

\textbf{Kind.} Fire church of Sere; the doctrine of glorious emptying. \textbf{Seat.} Open courts with a fire in the middle, in every bowl of the empire. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Valen Openhand, the Bowl-Priest}. \textbf{Goals.} To teach that a vessel was made to be emptied and that a life hoarded is a life wasted. \textbf{Methods.} Feasting, the emptying of a public bowl of wine to announce an act of state, and the burning of one household’s debt-slates by lot at the end of a feast, after which new ones are made. \textbf{Resources.} Wine, music, public fires, and an audience that applauds a debt carried as heartily as a debt forgiven. \textbf{Enemies.} The northern habit of calling Sere spendthrifts. The Court’s tax on funeral ash. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The Spending teaches that emptiness is generous so that the poor will volunteer to be emptied. The priests who teach it are among the fullest vessels in the empire.

\section*{The Council of Tides}

\textbf{Kind.} Merchant republic; the foreign power of the Sallow coast. \textbf{Seat.} Vhal, in a room that smells of tar and wet rope. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Avis Wake}, \textbf{Mav Hull}, \textbf{Dolf Brine}, elected for a year at a time by ship-owners and salt-masters. \textbf{Goals.} To keep the salt and glass trades moving, to avoid being taxed into the Keeping, and to make sure no law lasts long enough to stop earning. \textbf{Methods.} Contracts written on salt-paper that rot in damp, which is considered a virtue; the pulled benches for condemned criminals; a slave who can be bought in Vhal but cannot be returned there. \textbf{Resources.} Ships, salt, glass, rope, dried fish, and a council that can turn a wet document into a fortune or the loss of one. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s assessors. The winter. The salt-thing. Sere’s buyers when they arrive with gold. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The Council has never paid for a thin return and never will, which is why returned slaves are not housed in Vhalen. It has calculated that a person with no account is cheaper than a person with one, and calls this civility.

\CRrule

\section*{III. Criminals, rebels and secret societies}

\section*{The Ash-runners}

\textbf{Kind.} Criminal network; smugglers of warmth and quiet ash. \textbf{Seat.} The Fenmarch boardwalks and the Waiting Room at Sill, where a clerk can be paid to look away. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Slog Eel}, \textbf{Hobb Mud}, and a collector’s clerk in Slate Row whose name is not on any roll. \textbf{Goals.} To move Warm where the Court would not allow it and to sell forgetting to anyone who can pay. \textbf{Methods.} Cheap thin returns with no questions; quiet ash by the thimble; bone-hound ash from the shallow graves; a slate corrected in a second hand. \textbf{Resources.} The Fen paths, the peat-dries, a market in forgotten lives, and the complicity of people whose accounts are already damaged beyond repair. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, which punishes the unlicensed sale of quiet ash with a greyed hand. The collectors, who are sometimes customers. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} One of their customers in Y.H. 812 paid for a whole return with the warmth of forty children of Low Kiln, and the runner who carried the slate has never been able to spell the buyer’s name. The name was Corin.

\section*{The Sere factors}

\textbf{Kind.} Slavers and buyers of measures; the empire’s advance guard in the north. \textbf{Seat.} A counting house in Greybank and a shipping quay in Vhal; the Bowl of Sere behind them. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ilyra Gilded}, \textbf{Rial of the Ten Bowls}, with agents in Low Kiln who never give their names. \textbf{Goals.} To buy poor measures at prices no household can refuse and ship them south as beautiful whole returns for the great houses. \textbf{Methods.} Credit, the kindness of advances, the purchase of a debt before it is due, and the quiet conversion of a district into one decorated person. \textbf{Resources.} Gold crowns, grain, and the cooperation of households that have already sold next year’s warmth. \textbf{Enemies.} Grath, which hates Sere traders and sells to them anyway. The Court, which fought a thirty-one-year War of Deductions over the same trade. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} A factor does not want the poor person’s warmth for its own sake. He wants the shape of it, because a beautiful whole return must remember enough to be exhibited, and only certain lives make a good show.

\section*{The Broken Slates}

\textbf{Kind.} Rebel network in Low Kiln; descendants of the Ash Rising. \textbf{Seat.} The back rooms of the Vail kiln-house and the Fishstairs in Sill. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ennit of Low Kiln}, whose family was taken in the levy of Y.H. 668; \textbf{Jorra Vail}, who has never said whether he is with them. \textbf{Goals.} To destroy the slates, stop the levy, and make it impossible to bank a person who does not consent. \textbf{Methods.} Broken birth-slates, a year in the clay yard for the offender, ash on the doorstep of an assessor, and a refusal that is just short of an unclosed account. \textbf{Resources.} The memory of ninety children taken in one levy, the silence of the hearth-maids, and the fact that a slate can be destroyed in a kiln in four minutes. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, Pell Varr’s list, and the collectors who come with a slate already written. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They want the Return abolished, which in Sarn means the end of the economy. They have not worked out what comes after. Their best argument is that nothing could be worse, and the Court’s sealed file suggests that they may be right.

\section*{The Unbanked}

\textbf{Kind.} Secret faction inside the Keeping, descended from the Ash Rising and named in a Court file of Y.H. 675 as \emph{persons of the sealed opinion}. \textbf{Seat.} No fixed seat. A locked drawer in Rusk’s room above the Fishstairs; a sealed file in the Hearthseat; the margin of a slate in Greybank signed M. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Rusk of the Weir}, who teaches a strange boy to listen to vessels; \textbf{Collector Marra}, who pays for a whole return with her own fingers; \textbf{Haldre}, whose paper \emph{The Sealed Vessel} was read by nine people in Y.H. 702 and who disappeared in Y.H. 704. \textbf{Goals.} The Final Banking: make every vessel perfectly retentive, so that nothing leaks, nothing is owed, and no one can ever give anything away. A sealed world is an unbreakable world. \textbf{Methods.} Recruitment through apprenticeship, the forgery of assessments, the purchase of whole returns with memory intact, and the long cultivation of a man who can look at a dying body and decide without prayer. \textbf{Resources.} A collector inside the Keeping, a teacher inside the Clay Yard, a cold iron tube, a locked drawer, and a hot trace that crossed between worlds. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s public answer is that they are mad. The Court’s private answer is in the sealed file. Their real enemy is want itself, which they mean to abolish. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They did not make the blizzard and they did not put the minivan on the ice. They wanted a vessel that gave at the moment of breaking, and found one in a country they could not have named. They paid to have the memories left in, which is the most expensive single purchase a banker in Sarn can make. Rusk taught Corin to make him the instrument. Marra has been paying for it ever since.

\section*{The Deep Hand}

\textbf{Kind.} Secret society of scholars; a reading of the oldest slates. \textbf{Seat.} A back table in the Keld survey shaft, and one room in the Hearthseat whose key is held by an assessor. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Ludo of the Old Kiln}, a Grathic scholar who found a slate in the ash throat; \textbf{Derren the Younger}, an officer’s son with access to the sealed file. \textbf{Goals.} To read the Deep Hand and learn what the oldest repairs were made of. \textbf{Methods.} Copying slates that are not meant to leave the shaft; comparing the Keld translation \emph{Ash} with the Court’s translation \emph{language}; asking the Vorr the wrong question and recording that the numbers are correct. \textbf{Resources.} One slate from the Old Kiln, a crossed-out page from Y.H. 588, and the observation that a pot mended many times is not the pot it was. \textbf{Enemies.} The College of Assessors. The Court, which removed a surveyor from the shaft in Y.H. 717 for writing \emph{words that hold}. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} They believe the oldest repairs are made of promises that were never kept, made solid. If this is true then the world is being held together by the very thing the Court’s economy produces, and the Keeping cannot be abolished without finding out what holds the walls up.

\CRrule

\section*{IV. Foreign powers at the border}

\section*{Keld — the Warden of the Rim}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power; mountain kingdom of iron, lead, coal and warm-stone. \textbf{Seat.} Keld Keep, with the First Seam beneath it and the Cold Pass ten leagues beyond. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Karric VII, Warden of the Rim}, who shut the Cold Pass in Y.H. 741; the mine-reeves beneath him. \textbf{Goals.} To hold the passes, keep the true Hearth claim alive, and sell iron and warm-stone to whoever pays without becoming anyone’s subject. \textbf{Methods.} Mercenaries, the Descent at thirteen, a measure stated before a name, and a treaty enforced at the point of a surveyor’s slate. \textbf{Resources.} Iron, lead, coal, warm-stone, the survey shaft, and a population that can hold a hot clamp against its palm without flinching. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court, which has never accepted the Hearth claim and has never bothered to argue it. The Sweating. Grathish clay-men levied into a war they did not choose. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The Warden knows the true Hearth is not under his mountain. He keeps the claim because it keeps the Court out of the shafts, and because a kingdom that believes it owns the source can charge more for its stone.

\section*{Sere — the Sun-Emperor}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power; hot empire of grain, wine, bowls and open slavery. \textbf{Seat.} The Bowl of Sere, three hundred leagues south of Sill. \textbf{Named leaders.} The \textbf{Sun-Emperor}, whose acts are announced by the emptying of a public bowl of wine; the Council of Bowls beneath him. \textbf{Goals.} To grow north by purchase rather than conquest, to buy measures cheaply, and to keep the Peat Line from becoming a border it has to defend. \textbf{Methods.} Agents with credit, the Bowl feast, a public burning of debt-slates followed by the making of new ones, and a phrase \emph{measure for measure} that means whatever the emperor has already decided. \textbf{Resources.} Gold crowns, grain, oil, wine, fine glazed ware, and the largest slave population in the world. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s deduction on grain. The Fenmarch. The northern habit of calling Sere spendthrifts. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} The empire does not want territory in Grath. It wants the poor. A northern district that has been bought is more useful than a northern district that has been conquered, because nobody in a conquered district signs a contract.

\section*{Vhalen — the Council of Tides (as foreign power)}

\textbf{Kind.} Foreign power and trading republic; the gate between Grath and the Sallow Sea. \textbf{Seat.} Vhal, eighty leagues north-east of Sill by the Salt Road. \textbf{Named leaders.} \textbf{Avis Wake}, \textbf{Mav Hull}, \textbf{Dolf Brine}, rotating yearly. \textbf{Goals.} To keep the Salt Road open, to tax nothing that can be avoided, and to make the Court’s assessors feel poor in a room full of salt-paper. \textbf{Methods.} Contracts that rot in damp, a welcome for any traveller who pays, and the pulled benches for those who do not. \textbf{Resources.} Ships, salt, glass, rope, dried fish, and a legal system in which a wet document is no document at all. \textbf{Enemies.} The Court’s lists. The salt-thing. A hard winter that closes the coast pass. \textbf{Hidden agenda.} Half the port’s fortunes have turned on a contract going damp at the right moment. The Council’s real doctrine is not the Sallow Hearth but the convenient disappearance of evidence, which it has elevated into an art and a foreign policy.

\chapter*{Glossary}
\markboth{Glossary}{Glossary}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Glossary}
\section*{Glossary of Sarn}

\emph{Entries for the reader. Every coined name set down in the Compendium so far is gathered here, in alphabetical order. Where a thing is known by different names in different countries, the common Grathic name is given first. A term whose deeper meaning is will be found in its own place in the Compendium; this glossary gives only what a traveller may hear in a market or a hearth.}

\CRrule

\section*{A}

\textbf{Account-day.} The tenth, twentieth and thirtieth day of every tend, when the slate is read aloud. In Grath these are also market-days. On Tallow 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 159), the first Account-day of the firing month, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} at the Cross, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; a figure read aloud was not the figure paid. On Tallow 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 169), the second Account-day, he read the same figure again under the moot-post, called the levy and said it was not called by him, and sent a man with a number in his fist to a slate at the watch with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}; the printed figure stood unchallenged, the true subtraction went back up the clay road in the locked box and Hessa Rale carried his narrow slate up the road edge-on without reading it. On Tallow 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 179), the third Account-day and the last market of the firing month, he read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} for the third time, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 189), the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure, read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. Two hundred leaned over the reading block and eight pigs went over the wet boards. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell. The reading did not answer the man carried out on Day 188: no figure, collector or slate knew what he cost (T015/T041/T047/T077).

On Ember 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 199), the second Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off up the clay road with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic for the month changed for the second time and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. Hessa Rale carried his narrow slate up the road unread, and no figure, collector or slate knew what the man carried out on Day 188 had cost.

On Ember 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 209), the third and last Account-day and the last market of the kiln month, two hundred leaned to the reading block under the moot-post while eight pigs went over the wet boards. Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the third time in the kiln month and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. Hessa Rale took the slate up the clay road toward Greybank unread, the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called, and the reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 (T015/T041/T047/T077).

On Grain 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 219), the first Account-day and market of Grain, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner. He wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and sent a man’s number from fist to mouth to shoulder into a slate at the watch. The district’s arithmetic changed for Grain and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. Hessa Rale carried the narrow slate up the clay road unread, the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called, and the reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188. Grain 20 (Day 229) is the second Account-day of the month. Ch 56.

On Grain 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 229), the second Account-day and market of Grain, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, sent a man’s number from fist to mouth to shoulder into a slate at the watch, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the second time in Grain and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, and the reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back. The year’s dressed grain lay covered under wool near the Vail hearth and was read over by a figure that did not know what it cost. Hessa Rale carried his narrow slate up the clay road toward Greybank edge-on and unread, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing below the north bridge for a measure nobody called. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off and carried him home at midday saying nothing of what had been read over him. Grain 30 (Day 239) is the third and last Account-day of the month. Ch 59.

On Grain 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 239), the third and last Account-day and market of Grain, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road to the reading block under the moot-post with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the third time in Grain and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. The year’s dressed grain lay covered under wool near the hearth and was read over by a figure that did not know what it cost, and the reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back (T015/T041/T047, T077, T098 carried). The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, and no figure came off it (T080); the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called (T090); the seventh green stayed a colour at the pot board and the seventh shape a shape at the market’s edge, with no eighth of either (T050/T051, T033/T034 held). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off and gave no instruction or reason to the basket, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Grain went out without a boundary drawn in the narration and neither of the district’s two month-names was corrected. Ch 62.

On Smoke 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 249), the first Account-day and market of the second firing, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the first time in Smoke and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and the figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, answering nothing for the man carried out on Day 188 or the hand that went in on Seed 15. The dressed grain lay covered under wool near the Vail hearth and was read over by a number that did not know what it cost, so the space between the figure read over the covered grain and the price of that grain had no signature. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the clay road toward Greybank edge-on and unread, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing below the north bridge for a measure nobody called. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Ch 66.

On Smoke 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 259), the second Account-day and market of the second firing, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, passed a finger over a narrow slate and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy, denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed a second time in Smoke and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and the figure read was still not the figure paid. The dressed grain lay covered under wool on the cool stone at the rack end at home and was read over by a figure that did not know what it cost, so the space between the figure read over the grain and the price of that grain had no signature. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the clay road toward Greybank unread and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Smoke 30 (Day 269) is the third and last Account-day of the month. Ch 69.

On Smoke 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 269), the third and last Account-day and market of the second firing, two hundred leaned over the reading block and eight pigs went over the wet boards. Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd, the figure going twice over the basket, once for the moot and once for the households that came late; he called the levy and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the third true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the third time in Smoke and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged, the figure read was still not the figure paid, and the dressed grain lying covered under wool on the cool stone at the rack end was read over by a figure that did not know what it cost, the space between the figure and its price unsigned. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called. At the pot board and the market’s edge a silent woman’s seventh green stayed a colour and a foundling’s seventh shape a shape, with no eighth of either and neither named, joined or entered (T050/T051, T033/T034 held). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Ch 72.

On Frost 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 279), the first Account-day and market of the ninth month, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of the two hundred, the figure going over the basket once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the first true subtraction of Frost inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the new month and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, and the reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188, the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, or the dressed grain covered under wool at the rack end, which was read over by a number that did not know what it cost. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, and the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set below the north bridge at the out-of-line landing for a measure nobody called. At the pot board a woman’s green stayed a colour and at the market’s edge a foundling’s shape a shape, with no eighth of either. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Frost 20 (Day 289) was the second Account-day of the month. Ch 76.

On Frost 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 289), the second Account-day and the month’s second market, Berr Clay came up short off the clay road with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the two hundred, the figure going over the basket once for the moot and once for the households that came late. He called the levy for Frost and denied it with \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, and went off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the second true subtraction of Frost inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed a second time for the month and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stands unchallenged and the figure read is still not the figure paid, and the twice-read figure is two accounts and not one. The reading answered nothing for the man carried out on Day 188, the hand that went in on Seed 15 or the dressed grain covered under wool at the rack end, which was read over by a number that did not know what it cost, the space between unsigned. Eight pigs went over the wet boards and two hundred leaned in; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself; Hessa Rale carried the slate up the clay road toward Greybank before noon, edge-on and writing to her sleeve, and no figure came off it; the soft-cuffed clerk stayed set at the out-of-line landing below the north bridge for a measure nobody called; the seventh green stayed a colour at the pot board and the seventh shape a shape at the market’s edge, with no eighth of either. Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of thin shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the reading and the bell, carrying him home at the going of the light saying nothing of what had been read over him. Frost 30 (Day 299) is the third and last Account-day of the month. Ch 79.

\textbf{A firing opens the kiln. A week of tending settles nothing.} A saying of the drying racks in Low Kiln, told after the first firing of a month: \emph{A firing opens the kiln. A week of tending settles nothing. The hand goes to the mark before the fire, and to no shelf, no bed, no basket after it.} It is a rule about the widow’s mark and a refusal to turn an opening into a doctrine: the first firing of Frost on Frost 2, Y.H. 813 (Day 271) was done with Sella Vail’s hand to the mark for one breath and at no other hour, and through Frost 4–6 nobody made a lesson, sign, mending or payer of it. Four openings in four months are four and not a rule; the next stands in a later month’s first firing, far off (T058/T079). Ch 74.

\textbf{The Afterdrop.} The worsening before recovery in a rekindled or rewarmed vessel. The ordinary cause is a graft settling; midwives call it the second chill.

\textbf{The Ash.} Grey silt that gathers where promises are unkept, in corners and under beds, invisible in daylight and plain by tallow-light. The poor leave it on the Last Day and burn it next morning. On Stone 29, Y.H. 812 a woman at the tubs told a girl beside her that the grey would be left where it lay until the Last Day and burned the morning afterward and called dealt with.

\textbf{Ash-mite.} A small grey mite that lives in the Ash and drinks the thin edge of a sleeper’s measure. Invisible by day; troublesome in poor rooms.

\textbf{Ash-runners.} Criminal smugglers of the Fenmarch who move Warm and sell quiet ash without a Court licence.

\textbf{Ash Rising.} The rising in Low Kiln in Y.H. 668 after ninety children’s warmth was taken for a private account; put down by Assessor-Marshal Pell Varr.

\textbf{Ash-sickness.} The condition of dreaming in another person’s voice after long exposure to an Ash-wraith.

\textbf{Ash-wraith.} A grey shape seen by tallow-light where many have been spent; it follows the Ash ridge from room to room.

\textbf{Ask the arm that carried it.} A reed-cutter’s answer to a girl at the Clay Yard who asked what a bundle held: \emph{Ask the arm that carried it. It’ll tell you.} The arm judges by the weight settling into the forearm and tells what was carried and not what it cost; the cutter lifted the next armful before a second question could be got out. It is the same answer as \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it} in another mouth, filed by the boy on the tray of directions answered with directions. On Reed 7, Y.H. 813 the girl went off with the creel on her hip and no figure went with her. On Reed 13, Y.H. 813 a cutter told a girl with a creel at the Clay Yard to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}; to a man who asked what the work would want he gave the weather and the river, never a figure. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it} and \textbf{A record kept in muscle}. On Reed 16, Y.H. 813 a cutter going down past the racks told a girl with a creel to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}; to a second question he said \emph{It doesn’t know cost. Ask it how heavy it is}, and went on downriver with another armful. A woman at the racks who asked what the hands would be paid was told the weather and the river and shut two fingers out of a fist as she went. See \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

On Reed 25, Y.H. 813 the last bundles were judged by the arm that carried them, and a cutter told a girl with a creel to lift her bundle and let her arm tell her what went into it, \emph{and that’s the whole of what it knows}; a man who asked what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river, never a figure. See \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

\textbf{Ask the pot.} An answer given to a question about cost in the Vail kiln-house of Low Kiln: \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} The question is carried away held level, the way a woman carries a full pot, and arrives at a thing that has no answer in it; nothing is priced and nothing is refused. On Reed 4 and Reed 6, Y.H. 813 a woman asking what the reeds would cost now the hands were out of them was sent to the pot with these words, and a man asking what the beds would want was told to ask the beds and the weather. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}.

On Reed 10, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with a wet pot at the Vail kiln-house asked what the loaf row would want before the tend was out; Sella’s hand went toward the clay jar on the wall and came away, and the woman was sent to the pot with these words, carrying the question away level with nothing slopped and nothing given. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}. On Reed 16, Y.H. 813 a neighbour come up from the strips with a wet pot asked what the loaf row would want before the tend was out and was sent to the pot with these words, carrying the question away level and nothing slopped.

On Tallow 2, Y.H. 813 a woman come up from the firing work asked what a firing cost set down in the Vail kiln-house; Sella glanced once at the clay jar, sent her to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level with nothing slopped. At the Weir the same day a woman asking what the hands would be paid for the going down and the coming back was answered with the going down and the coming back and then the river, so that a cost asked as a direction was answered with a direction and left no entry (T077). On Tallow 8, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with wet sleeves at the Vail kiln-house asked what a firing cost set down there; Sella sent her to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level so that nothing slopped. See \textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it}. On Tallow 11 and Tallow 12, Y.H. 813 a neighbour with a wet pot at the Vail kiln-house asked what a firing cost set down there; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, sent her to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level with nothing slopped and no figure given. On Tallow 17 a neighbour with a wet pot asked the same question in the third working week and was sent to the pot with the same words; nothing was priced, nothing was refused and no figure was given. On Tallow 21 a neighbour with a wet pot asked what a firing cost set down in the Vail house; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, did not touch it, and sent the woman to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level. On Tallow 22 and Tallow 23 the same answer went to neighbours who asked what the kilns would want now the last week was in: \emph{The weather’s set it. Ask the pot. It’s had the heat and kept it. The river’ll take what’s over.} Nothing was priced and nothing was refused in the firing month’s last tend. On Ember 2 and Ember 3, Y.H. 813 (Days 181–182) a neighbour asking what the newly opened firing cost and another asking what the second day’s firing wanted with the kiln newly open were both sent to the pot and the weather; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, and each question went away level and arrived nowhere, nothing priced, nothing refused and no entry left (T077, T058/T079). On Ember 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 184) a neighbour come up from the tubs with a wet pot asked what the firing cost now the kiln month’s second week was on; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without touching it, and sent the question to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}. The woman carried the question away level, nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079).

On Ember 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 187) a neighbour come up from the tubs with a wet pot asked what the firing cost now the kiln month’s middle days were on; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without touching it, and sent her to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079).

On Ember 11 and Ember 12, Y.H. 813 (Days 190–191), women who asked what the firing would want before the kiln month’s tend was out were sent to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and carried the questions away level with nothing priced, refused or entered. One came up from the drying racks with slip dried pale in the creases of her wrists (T077, T058/T079). Through Ember 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 192–194) the answer went out three more times under the Vail roof: to a neighbour with dry scurf of mud on her hem who asked what the firing would want now the account had gone up the road, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the kiln month was out, to a woman with a wet pot who asked what a wet thing cost set down in the dry heat, and to a man come off the clay road with the morning’s figure still moving in his mouth who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up the road. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction sat in a locked box up the road, out of reach of every hand in the yard (T077, T015/T041/T047). Through Ember 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 195–197) the answer went out again under the Vail roof: to a neighbour with dry mud-scurf on her hem who asked what the firing would want now the account had gone up the road, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the kiln month was out, and to a man come off the clay road who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up the road. Each carried the question away level, nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction still in the locked box out of reach of every hand in the yard (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Ember 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 198–200) the answer went out three more times under the Vail roof: to a neighbour with dry mud-scurf on her hem who asked what the firing would want with the second reading a day off, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the kiln month was out, and to a man come off the clay road who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up twice. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction sat in a locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079).

Through Ember 22–24, Y.H. 813 (Days 201–203) the kiln month’s last tend ran into its third working day with the answer going out as before: to a neighbour with dry mud-scurf on her hem who asked what the firing would want now the last tend was in, to a rack-woman with slip dried pale in her wrists who asked what the pots would want before the month was out, to a man come off the clay road with a number in his fist who asked what the kiln would want now the figure had gone up twice, and to a neighbour with a cost-question at the door. Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it and sent each to the pot and the weather; every question went away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Ember 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 204–206) the kiln month’s last working week ran on with the answer going out as before: to a neighbour at the door, to a rack woman at the yard well with slip dried pale in her wrists, to a man come off the clay road with a number shut in his fist, and to a neighbour at the door with dry scurf on her hem and a pot against her hip. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Ember 28–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 207–209) the kiln month’s last working week ran out with the answer going out as before: to a neighbour with a cost-question at the door, to a rack woman at the yard well with slip dried pale in her wrists, and to a man off the clay road with a number shut in his fist who paid nothing. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 1–3, Y.H. 813 (Days 210–212) the answer went out again under the Vail roof as the firing thinned into the ordinary tending of the year: to a neighbour with a cost-question at the door (Days 210 and 212) and to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists and a man who kept a number shut in his fist at the well (Day 211). Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction still out of reach in the locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047). There was no market and no Account-day in these three days; Grain 10 (Day 219) is the first.

Through Grain 4–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 213–215) the answer went out through the first working week to a neighbour with a pot in her hands at the threshold (Day 213), to a neighbour at the door and a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists and a man with a number shut in his fist at the well (Day 214), and again to a neighbour at the door with a question about the mid-tend work and a rack woman at the well (Day 215). Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, and the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged with the true subtraction out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road. There was no market and no Account-day in these three days; Grain 10 (Day 219) is the first (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 216–218) the answer went out through the second working week to a neighbour at the door (Days 216 and 218), to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists at the yard well and a man who kept a number shut in his fist (Day 216), and to the rack woman again at the well (Day 217). Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; the man kept his number in his fist and paid nothing, while the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road. There was no market and no Account-day in these three days; Grain 10 (Day 219) is the first (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 219–221) the answer went out under the Vail roof on the two tending days after Grain’s first market: to a neighbour at the door and to a rack woman at the yard well with slip dried pale in her wrists, and in the morning of the market day to a man who brought a number in his fist to the reading rail. Each carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without a touch, and sent each to the pot and the weather. The printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 222–224) the answer went out under the Vail roof with the harvest: to a neighbour at the door with a pot against her hip, to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists at the yard well and to a neighbour who asked what the reaping would take now that hands were back in the strips. Each question was carried away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered; a man off the clay road brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it and put it back in his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere. The printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047).

Through Grain 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 228–230) the answer went out under the Vail roof now that the grain was dressed and covered: to a neighbour at the door with a pot hitched against her hip, to a woman at the threshold asking what the storing would take now the grain was under wool, and to a rack woman with slip dried pale in her wrists at the yard well. Sella did not turn from the coals; each went away level with nothing priced, refused or entered. A man come down the clay road stood at the well with a number brought up out of a fist toward the water, looked at it as a man looks at a thing he has not decided to keep, and put it back into his sleeve so the figure arrived nowhere and was entered against nothing. The dressed grain lay covered near the hearth with no figure over it, read over on Grain 20 by a number that did not know what it cost; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047). Ch 59.

Through Grain 22–24, Y.H. 813 (Days 231–233) the answer went out under the Vail roof now that the grain was dressed and stored: to a neighbour at the threshold on each of the three mornings who asked what the storing would take, and on the afternoon of Grain 23 to the ownerless voice that asked over the boards which row the pot went quiet on. Sella did not turn from the fire; she sent the cost-questions to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot... The weather knows the rest}, and the ownerless question was answered with the weather first and the price of barley after it, the voice going off up the terrace with the row standing where it stood. A man come down the clay road brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it and put it back into his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere and no row, witness, cause or figure was entered. The dressed grain was turned for damp, spread thin and gathered back under the fold, counted in glances and handfuls and by the carrying arm’s weight that knows weight and not cost, given no figure and entered on no slate; the printed one in twelve stood unchallenged and the true subtraction stayed out of reach in Berr’s locked box up the road (T077, T058/T079, T015/T041/T047, T101 advanced and unpaid). Ch 60.

Through Smoke 2 and Smoke 3, Y.H. 813 (Days 241–242) the answer went out twice more under the Vail roof: a neighbour at the threshold with a pot asked what the storing would take and another what the keeping would take now the grain was under wool, and each was sent to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot... The weather knows the rest}, going away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). No cost-question came on Smoke 1, the morning of the opening; a man come down the clay road with a number in his fist toward the yard well looked at it and put it back into his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere and was entered by nobody (T015/T041/T047 held).

Through Smoke 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 249–251) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the storing or the keeping would take now the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent each question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Smoke 11 a woman of the firing work at the yard well, Ilva, answered a question about the cost of the firings with her hand still in her sleeve: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off her strip and the ninth record-first hand stayed nine (T080 held). At the Cross on Smoke 10 the figure read over the basket was still not the figure paid and the space between the figure read over the covered grain and its cost had no signature. Ch 66.

Through Smoke 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 252–254) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent each question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). At the yard well on Smoke 13 Ilva answered a question about the firings with her hand in her sleeve: \emph{I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off her strip and the ninth record-first hand stayed nine (T080 held). At the Cross on Smoke 10 the figure read over the basket was still not the figure paid, and the space between the figure read over the covered grain and its cost had no signature. Ch 67.

Through Smoke 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 255–257) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now that the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent the question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Smoke 16 the grain was turned under wool for damp, spread thin, gathered by the handful and set flat; on Smoke 17 it was gathered in by the handful for the last time before Smoke’s second reading, covered under wool and set away from the hearth on the cool stone at the rack end with no figure; on Smoke 18 it was turned once under the wool and drawn back smooth, with no fifth gathering (T077 advanced, unpaid). At the yard well on Smoke 16 Ilva answered a question about the firings with her hand in her sleeve: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}; no figure came off her strip and the ninth record-first hand stayed nine (T080 held). The figure that will be read over the covered grain on Smoke 20 will not know what it cost, and the space between the two stays unsigned. Ch 68.

Through Smoke 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 258–260) the answer went out under the Vail roof on the mornings of the 19th and 21st: to a neighbour at the threshold with a pot who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now that the dressed grain was under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing and sent the question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Smoke 19 the grain was lifted at a corner for damp and laid back with no figure; on Smoke 20 the district’s arithmetic changed a second time up the road and was read over the covered grain by a number that did not know its cost; on Smoke 21 the grain was turned under the wool for damp and laid back, still with no figure. At the yard well on Smoke 19 Ilva answered a question about the firings with her hand in her sleeve and her strip unread: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} (T080 held at nine). Ch 69.

Through Frost 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 288–290) the answer went out under the Vail roof on all three mornings: to a neighbour at the threshold who asked what the keeping or the storing would take now the dressed grain lay covered under wool, and Sella glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, shut her hand half over nothing without touching it, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and sent the question to the pot and the weather with nothing priced, refused or entered (T077, T058/T079). On Frost 20 the second arithmetic went up the road in Berr’s locked box and was read over the covered grain by a figure that did not know what it cost; the space between the figure and its price stayed unsigned, and nothing of the reading was brought under the roof as lesson, figure, mending or payment. Ilva was offstage on all three days and no figure came to her well, the notches staying in wood (T080 held at nine). Ch 79.

\textbf{Assessor.} An officer of the Warm Court who decides what a life was worth and how much of its measure may be kept back.

\section*{B}

\textbf{The bell at the Cross.} A bell struck at market morning and afternoon, longer than a church bell; nobody crosses himself at it. The boy counts four strokes, four, and a place where the fifth should be. No one in Sill explains what it is for. On Seed 10, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Seed, it went four, four and a gap over the market while Berr Clay read one in twelve twice over the basket, and nobody crossed himself; the heard bell stayed in its own place beside the told bell of the Long Night. The phrase \emph{the bell’s fourth stroke had been missing} in one paragraph of that day is a slip: the missing stroke is the fifth.

On Reed 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of Reed, it went four, four and a gap at the reading block with nobody crossing himself; the heard bell stayed in its own place beside the told bell of the Long Night and was not added to the hearings of the full note. On Reed 20, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of Reed, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the six stoppings of the near-saying. On Reed 30, Y.H. 813, the third Account-day and the last market of Reed, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying. On Tallow 20, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of the firing month, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and its missing fifth not laid across the kiln’s missing pull or the boards’ knot. On Tallow 30, Y.H. 813, the third Account-day and last market, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of the kiln month, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078).

On Ember 20, Y.H. 813, the second Account-day of the kiln month, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself while Berr Clay read the figure twice over the basket; the heard bell stayed beside the told bell and was counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078).

On Ember 30, Y.H. 813, the third Account-day and last market of the kiln month, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself while the figure went twice over the basket; the heard bell stayed beside the told bell and was counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078).

On Grain 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 219), the first Account-day and market of Grain, it went four, four and a gap at the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself; four was four in the fire under the floor, four in the nails overhead and four in the bell, and the gap stood where a fifth should have stood in each of the three places and rose up in none of them. The heard bell stayed beside the told bell and was counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying (T078, T061/T082).

On Grain 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 229), the second Account-day and market of Grain, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell and counted among neither the hearings of the full note nor the nine stoppings of the near-saying, while Berr Clay read the figure twice over the basket and carried the true subtraction away in the locked box (T078, T061/T082). Ch 59.

On Smoke 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 249), the first Account-day and market of the second firing, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note; the boy held it through the missing stroke and came down on the next sound in the square, filing the answer as an interval against an absent stroke and not a hearing (T078, T061/T082). Ch 66.

On Smoke 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 259), the second Account-day and market of the second firing, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note or laid across the fire’s missing fifth; the boy held his inch through the stroke that did not come and came down on the stroke after it, supplying no stroke to fill the gap (T078, T061/T082). Ch 69.

On Smoke 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 269), the third Account-day and last market of the second firing, it went four, four and a gap over the square with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note or laid across the fire’s missing fifth or the boards’ thumb-width knot; three counts stood in three places and did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood. The boy held his inch through the bell’s missing stroke and came down on the stroke after it, supplying no stroke to agree any three; on the hundred and fourteenth answer the hand carried two of the house’s rhythms across the empty interval and left the bell’s gap in the square with a finger between (T061/T082, T078). Ch 72.

On Frost 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 279), the first Account-day and market of the ninth month, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note, a fifth of the fire or an agreement with the boards’ thumb-width knot; three counts stood in three places and did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood. On the hundred and thirty-fourth answer the hand set the small intake of the heard bell’s gap beside the hold of one counted breath with a finger between, the heard bell kept beside the told and not agreed with the figure read over the basket (T078, T061/T082). Ch 76.

On Frost 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 289), the second Account-day and market of the month, it went four, four and a gap over the reading block under the moot-post with nobody crossing himself, the heard bell kept beside the told bell of the Long Night and its gap not made a seventh of the full note, a fifth of the fire or an agreement with the boards’ thumb-width knot; three counts stood in three places and did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood. On the hundred and fifty-fourth answer the hand set the heard bell’s gap beside a counted breath from the room whose floor does not touch his, with a finger between, the heard bell kept beside the told and not made to agree with the figure read twice over the basket (T078, T061/T082). Ch 79.

\textbf{Birth-flower.} The branching red mark some infants are born with, shaped like frost on a pane or a burn gone into the skin. Hearth-maids call it a flower, cross two fingers over it and say nothing about the sign. Alda Reed crossed herself over Corin’s on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, and covered the act with the word.

\textbf{Birth-slate.} The flat slate a hearth-maid keeps within reach at a birth, on which the child and the day are entered. In Low Kiln it lies on the bench, and a midwife’s hand goes to it before it goes to the child. A second hand may have written on it before anyone looked at the face.

\textbf{The Bowl.} The Sere coming-of-age feast at sixteen, where a young person empties a bowl of warm wine and names a debt they intend to carry.

\textbf{Bought breath.} A person sold for a term, usually a season or a year, to repay a debt. The common form of slavery in the Fenmarch.

\textbf{The Breaking.} The spring flood, when the Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs and takes the low houses; also the Silt thaw itself. The year’s flood of Silt 9–15, Y.H. 813 came up in a thin brown sheet, stood on the Fishstairs and went around both the Vail corner and the burned ridge two doors down, then went off into mud; the district called it weather and then the thaw that was. It is not the great Breaking of later years, when the low houses are taken and the town’s thin place is named.

\textbf{Brine-gull.} A Sallow-coast gull that steals anything warm: a loaf, a warmed stone, a coal not yet out. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 one went off upriver below the north bridge with a coal from somebody’s banked fire that was not yet cold, carrying the warmth out of the fire’s account; no slate in Sill stood one mark the poorer for it.

\textbf{Broken Slates.} A rebel network of Low Kiln, descended from survivors of the Ash Rising, which seeks to destroy the slates and end the levy.

\textbf{A bundle’s counted in the arm that carries it.} A saying of the reed-cutters at the Weir: \emph{A bundle is counted in the arm that carries it. The hands that cut it are counted in nothing at all.} On Reed 1, Y.H. 813 a reed-cutter told a woman at the racks that a bundle was counted in the arm that brought it, and when she asked about the hands that cut it he went past her with another armful and let the question go down the yard unanswered --- not refused, only never put into words that would stay put long enough to be entered. A day’s cutting was a direction downriver and a coming-back at dusk; nobody set a figure on a bundle standing in the mud. On Reed 4 the cutter said it again in the yard at Low Kiln, wiping his palms down his thighs; a woman at the racks asked \emph{And the hands that cut it?} and he went past with another armful and let the question lie where it fell, not refused and never entered. See \textbf{The hands go in by the look} and \textbf{The reed-cutter’s cord}.

On Reed 25, Y.H. 813 the saying was heard again over the last bundles of the reed month: the arm that carries a bundle knows what went into it and that is the whole of what it knows, while the hands that cut it are counted in nothing at all; a man who asked what those hands would be paid was given the weather and the river. The boy filed the exchange on the tray of directions answered with directions and entered nothing. On Tallow 13, Y.H. 813 the reed work was finished and had become a direction counted in the carrying arm, which keeps the weight and not the cost; a cost asked as a direction was answered with the river and the weather and left no entry (T077, T071/T072). On Tallow 18 the finished reeds were only a memory in the carrying arm, which kept the weight and not the cost, and a cost asked as a direction was answered with the river and the weather and left no entry. See \textbf{Ask the arm that carried it} and \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

\textbf{Burned slate (a direction from Slate Row).} A word that goes around the yard of Low Kiln as a direction and not as a visit: \emph{a slate has burned in the night}, spoken over the boards on the same breath as the price of barley and the weather, with no owner named, no room, no hand at the flame and no reason. It is not a body, not a slate brought near the basket, not a cause and not a hearing, and nobody in the yard turns it into one. On Ember 26, Y.H. 813 (Day 205) it came over the boards a first time and on Ember 29–30 a second; on Grain 6, Y.H. 813 (Day 215) it came a third and on Grain 9 (Day 218) a fourth, each arrival going nowhere and deepening the claim of the Broken Slates on Jorra Vail without a fact anybody can carry into a chart. A fourth voice going around the boards is not a fourth witness to one fire, for a witness stands somewhere and can be asked; the voice stood a quarter league off in Slate Row and went on to the price of barley. A fourth telling of the burned slate is \textbf{not} a third telling of the counting room shut in the war: the two Greybank tellings of that room stay at two (see \textbf{Closed counting room}), and no slate burned under any roof and no new fire was lit at the kiln mouth on the morning of the fourth telling. Jorra grows quieter whenever it goes around and the household straightens around the quiet without an order; \emph{he’s not Vail} stays sealed and the promise of the boy’s name to the men who burn slates stays ungiven (T035/T031/T065/T095 advanced, not paid). No fifth telling came through Grain 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 219–221); the fourth telling from Grain 9 stayed a direction arrived nowhere, held with a hand between it and the three shapings of the pot saying, and still not a third telling of the counting room shut in the war (T035/T031/T065/T095 held, not paid). Through Grain 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 228–230) the word stood at four tellings and no fifth came; it came over the boards from Slate Row and arrived nowhere, still not a third telling of the counting room shut in the war, with Jorra growing quieter whenever it went around and the household straightening around the quiet without an order. On Grain 21 a different voice, with no owner, room, hand at the kiln or cause, asked which row the pot went quiet on; that question is a thing of its own and not a fifth telling of the slate (T101 planted, T035/T031/T065/T095 held). See \textbf{Broken Slates}, \textbf{Closed counting room}, \textbf{Slate Row} and \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?}
