\textbf{C}

\textbf{The carried fire (the year’s fire).} The new fire taken into every house on Kindling: a coal under ash comes up the yard in a clay dish, each hearth touches its own flame to it and passes it on, and the last house keeps what is left. In Low Kiln nobody says where the flame was first lit or what it cost, and the Vail house keeps it banked under ash and never answers a question about its payer. On Ilmen 16, Y.H. 813 a brine-gull carried off one of its coals, not yet cold, upriver; one warmth less went out of the house’s account and was missed in no account, and the fire went on taking its breath in fours and a gap. Through Ilmen 19–25, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four; the coal the gull took was entered in no slate and missed in no account.

Through Silt 2–8, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed; the coal a brine-gull took on Ilmen 16 was twenty-two days gone and entered in no slate. Through Silt 9–15 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed; the coal the gull took was twenty-nine days gone and entered in no slate. Through Silt 16–18 it still lay at four, four and a gap under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed; the door stood a finger’s width open and the river’s note came through the gap, kept apart from the fire’s four-four-and-a-gap as it had been for seventy-seven days. Through Silt 19–25, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed; the mud of the lean week went around the two lines in the corner and the fire’s gap came up through the floor while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door, the two sounds kept in two places. Through Silt 26–30 and Seed 1 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees; its payer had gone unnamed for ninety days and the coal the brine-gull took upriver was entered in no slate and missed in none. Through Seed 2–4 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for ninety-three days; Sella told it the thaw each day and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot. Through Seed 5–11 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four and warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and touched no widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The river’s low note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s gap came up through the floor, in two separate places as for a hundred days. Through Seed 2–4 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for ninety-three days; through Seed 5–11 it was unnamed for a hundred days; and through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, warming the boards by degrees and missing one breath in every four, its payer unnamed for a hundred and three days. Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, and touched no widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a basket and a bed are not openings. Through Seed 15–17, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and six days; Sella told it the thaw each day and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. Through Seed 18–20 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and stood a moment at the fire counting something under her breath, joined to no opening. Through Seed 21–23, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twelve days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and fed them, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. Through Seed 24–26 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and fifteen days; Sella told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the fire gave back four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the two counts did not meet. Through Seed 27–30 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nineteen days; on all four days Sella told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and at the going of the light on Seed 30 the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the two counts did not meet.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twenty-two days; Sella told it the thaw each day, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. The river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s gap through the floor under blind ash, the boards overhead keeping four nails, four, and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb: three counts in three places that did not become one. Through Reed 4–6, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twenty-five days; Sella told it the thaw on all three days, turned the coals and said \emph{The house will keep it}, and the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been while the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the boards kept their knot --- three counts in three places that did not become one.

Through Reed 7–9, Y.H. 813 it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twenty-six, seven and eight days; Sella told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand and did not look toward the bed. The fire gave back four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been; the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the boards overhead kept four nails, four, and a knot the width of a thumb. Three counts in three places, and none became one.

On Smoke 2 and 3 the dressed grain was turned under wool for damp, spread thin and gathered back by the handful, changed in state and given no figure, entered on no slate (T077); a wrong wind off High Kiln on Smoke 3 brought the sweet edge of lead glaze over the boards, touched the fold and went out on the wind that brought it, a direction arrived nowhere and not a second edge paid (T064). In the small hours of Smoke 3 the boy’s sixtieth answer went up an inch toward the river’s low note, through the small intake, the hold and the letting-go of one of Sella’s breaths in the room that does not touch his, kept through the little silence after her count had ended and down on the river’s next low note — two rhythms crossing in the inch, remembered, filed on the sixth place with no payer named and not a change made again (T061/T082).

Through Smoke 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 249–251) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty-nine, fifty and fifty-one days; Sella told it the thaw on all three mornings, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, and at the close the fire stopped at four while the silence where the fifth should have stood stood where it stood. The river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept two other counts in three places that did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood to any; the bell’s four, four and a gap from Smoke 10 stayed beside the told bell and was not folded into the three or heard as a seventh of the full note. The one opening before Smoke 1 was behind the household and made into no lesson, sign, mending or payment; the next real opening is the first firing of Frost, far off and unbrought. Ch 66.

Through Smoke 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 252–254) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for two hundred and fifty-two, fifty-three and fifty-four days; Sella came to the fire before the basket each morning, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, and at the close the fire stopped at four while the silence where the fifth should have stood stood where it stood. The river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four, and a thumb-width knot kept two other counts in three places that did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood to any. The sweet edge of lead glaze came over the boards on a wrong wind off High Kiln on Smoke 14, touched the fold of dressed grain and went out on the wind that brought it, a direction arrived nowhere and not a second edge paid. No collector came up or went down the clay road on Smoke 13, 14 or 15; the widow’s mark stayed untouched and the one opening before Smoke 1 was not looked at again. Ch 67.

Through Smoke 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 255–257) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for two hundred and fifty-five, fifty-six and fifty-seven days; Sella came to the fire before the basket each morning, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, and set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. The river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four, and a thumb-width knot kept two other counts in three places that did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood to any. On Smoke 18 frost-bloom wrote white on the stone lip of the yard well where the Warm had lately gone out, and the bucket knocked it grey and the yard called it weather; a well is not an opening and the white lip was kept on a place of its own with no cause. The widow’s mark stayed untouched and the one opening before Smoke 1 was not looked at again; the next real opening was the first firing of Frost, far off and unbrought. No collector came up or went down the clay road on Smoke 16, 17 or 18. Ch 68.

Through Smoke 19–21, Y.H. 813 (Days 258–260) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four, four and a gap, warming the boards by degrees, its payer unnamed for two hundred and fifty-eight, fifty-nine and sixty days; Sella came to the fire before the basket each morning, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, and set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. The river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept two other counts in three places that did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood to any. On the 20th the district’s arithmetic changed a second time in the square up the clay road and the bell went four, four and a gap, the heard bell kept beside the told and not folded into the three; on the 19th and 21st frost went out of the well lip under the bucket and the yard called it weather, a well not being an opening. The widow’s mark stayed untouched since before the kiln on Smoke 1, the one opening before Smoke 1 was not made into a lesson, sign, mending or payment, and the next real opening was the first firing of Frost, far off and unbrought. No collector came up or went down the clay road on Smoke 19, 20 or 21. Ch 69.

Through Smoke 28–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 267–269) it still lay under blind ash and the back of a broken pot at four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for two hundred and sixty-seven, sixty-eight and sixty-nine days; Sella came to the fire before the basket each morning, told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, kept her finger on top of the shelf’s front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, and set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with a half-beat and no look toward the bed. The river’s note of water over water through the finger’s-width door and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot kept two other counts in three places that did not become one, for agreeing any two would want a payer and none stood to any. The widow’s mark stayed untouched since before the kiln on Smoke 1, because a rack, a well, a basket, a market, a reading and a bed are not openings; the third arithmetic went up the clay road in Berr’s box on the 30th and changed nothing under this roof, and the next real opening, the first firing of Frost, stood far off and unbrought. No collector came up or went down the clay road on Smoke 28, 29 or 30. Ch 72.

\textbf{Clay-bound.} A debt-servant working off a term, commonly seven years, with interest gathering as grey Ash in the household accounts.

\textbf{Clay-name.} The name a slave is given by the household that owns them; the old name is forbidden.

\textbf{Clay Road.} The packed-clay road from the Cross at Sill to Greybank, eighteen leagues; a Court road since the treaty of Y.H. 418.

\textbf{Clay Yard.} The slip pits, wheel shed, drying racks and kiln in Low Kiln; the whole world of a clay child.

\textbf{The clinical ear.} The ability to hear a faulty vessel before touching it. Dan possesses it to an unnatural degree; the Kiln-Masters of Sill have quietly noted it.

\textbf{Closed counting room (the Greybank saying).} A counting room shut during the last war with the damper closed, in which the men inside died of the breath rather than of the war’s hand. On Ilmen 26, Y.H. 813 a man come downriver from Greybank told it at the Low Kiln well as a curiosity with a date, eighteen leagues east; the yard took it for history and nobody joined it to any kiln in the district. In houses that keep their breath in fours and a gap the saying is heard differently, though no one says so aloud. On Silt 25, Y.H. 813 a second man come downriver from Greybank repeated it at the same well as a curiosity with a date, and the yard took it as history again; the boy filed the second telling on the same tray as the first without letting the two touch, keeping the likeness and the difference --- breath through the nose against breath in the throat, both saying \emph{not the war’s hand} --- and joined neither to any kiln. No third telling came in the last five days of Silt or on Seed 1, and the two stayed on their own tray beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap, likeness and difference kept and joined to no kiln. Sella, who lost a husband to that danger, heard both and told the fire it was the thaw, and never once described it that way herself. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 a neighbour at the bucket-round only mentioned a counting room shut in the war with the men inside dead of the breath — a mention with a date in it and none of the weight, not a telling — and no third telling came. The two earlier tellings stayed on their tray joined to no kiln, likeness and difference kept; Sella, who lost a husband to that danger, told the fire it was the thaw and never once described it that way herself.

No third telling came in Ember’s last working week (Days 207–209), and the boy kept the two tellings on their tray joined to no kiln while the burned-slate word from Slate Row went around the boards a second time as a separate direction arriving nowhere (T035/T031/T065/T095).

\textbf{The Cold.} The absence of Warm; a material substance in Sarn, with a place to put what is taken.

\textbf{Cold Acre.} A barley-and-turnip hamlet two leagues north of Sill on the ridge, with one well that never freezes.

\textbf{Cold iron.} Iron that draws Warm out of a vessel and gives none back; used in the collector’s tube and in clamps.

\textbf{Cold Pass.} The mountain pass beyond Keld Keep, closed in Y.H. 741 and fixed as Grath’s northern border by the agreement of Y.H. 747.

\textbf{The cold that stays.} A foot or hand that remains cold after the water around it has gone down and the person has been wrapped in wool and carried inside. On Silt 12, Y.H. 813 a child wading below the sill at Sill came up with a foot that stayed cold after the water fell; a woman wrapped it and called it the cold, while the yard called the water weather, so the two names never met. Nobody in the yard gave the staying cold a cause or a treatment, and it was entered in no account. A surgeon’s eye would read the extremity going before the core and the worse hour waiting on the far side of a warming. Through Silt 19–25, Y.H. 813 the foot stayed the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to the yard through the whole lean week, with no hand placed, no cause and no treatment; the boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the reading bought nothing. Through Silt 26–30 and onto Seed 1 it was still the cold to that woman and weather to the yard, carried across the turn of the month uncured, uncaused and unnamed; the surgeon’s reading of the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform worked perfectly and bought nothing. Through Seed 2–4 it was still the cold to one woman and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, while the first seed went into the strips; the boy’s reading had the usefulness of an instrument held behind glass. On Seed 9 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool, the woman wound it round and called it the cold and a neighbour at the tubs called the water weather, so the two facts went past each other and never met; the boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and had no hand two paces long. Through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill; the woman wound it round and called it the cold while a neighbour at the tubs called the water weather, so the two facts still went past each other and never met. The boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the reading bought nothing. Through Seed 18–20 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to one woman and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, and no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken. Through Seed 21–23, Y.H. 813 it was still the cold inside three turns of wool below the sill, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform; the boy’s reading of the extremity going before the core worked perfectly and bought nothing, and no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken. Through Seed 24–26 it was still the cold inside three turns of wool below the sill, cold to one woman and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed; the afterdrop waited past a warming nobody would perform and the reading bought nothing. Through Seed 27–30 it stayed dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, still the cold to one woman and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed; the boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting on the far side of a warming nobody would perform, and the perfect reading bought nothing.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed; the boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the perfect reading bought nothing (T093/T094/T096). Through Reed 4–6, Y.H. 813 the foot still stayed the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to the yard, dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, uncured, uncaused and unnamed; the boy’s reading of the extremity going before the core worked perfectly and bought nothing (T093/T094/T096). Through Reed 7–9 it was still the cold to that woman and weather to the yard, dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, and the boy kept it on a place of its own and did not lay it across the other absences (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid). Through Reed 19–21, Y.H. 813 it was still dark inside three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to a neighbour with a pail; the boy read the extremity going before the core, the almost-smile that was not peace and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the perfect reading bought nothing. No silt-leach, cause or cure was named and no door was knocked (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid).

Through Reed 10–12, Y.H. 813 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform. On Reed 11, below the fish-trade shade, the boy read the extremity going before the core and the perfect reading bought nothing; the two facts went past each other and never met, and no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken (T093/T094/T096 carried).

On Reed 15, Y.H. 813, below the sill, the child’s foot stayed dark inside three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to the yard; the two facts went past each other as they had gone past each other every morning of the child’s life and never met. The boy knew the whole order of it --- the extremity going before the core, the small almost-smile that was not peace, the afterdrop waiting on the far side of a warming nobody would perform --- and the reading worked perfectly and bought nothing: no beast, no cause, no cure, no recognition, no word for it in the language of the house, and no way to close two inches of his own hand on a fold. He did not lay it beside the green that had gone off with the light across the square (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid). On Reed 18, Y.H. 813 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to the woman who wrapped it and weather to a neighbour with a pail, so the two facts went past each other and never met; the boy read the extremity going before the core, the almost-smile that was not peace and the afterdrop waiting on the far side of a warming nobody would perform, and the reading bought nothing (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid). On Reed 24 the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to a neighbour with a pail; the boy’s reading of the extremity going before the core, the almost-smile that was not peace and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform worked perfectly and bought nothing, and no silt-leach, cause or cure was named (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid).

Through Reed 25–27, Y.H. 813 the foot stayed dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed; on Day 145 the boy read the extremity going before the core, the almost-smile that was not peace and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the perfect reading bought nothing (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid).

On Tallow 2, Y.H. 813, below the fish-trade shade at the Weir, the foot was still dark inside three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the neighbour with a pail who set her pail down without going near; the boy read the extremity going before the core, the almost-smile that is not peace but the shape a face makes when it is cold enough, and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody in the shade meant to perform, and the reading worked as perfectly as the day he learned it and bought him nothing. No silt-leach, cause, cure or recognition was written across it (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid). On Tallow 6, Y.H. 813, below the fish-trade shade, the foot was still dark in three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the neighbour with a pail who set hers down without going near; the boy read the extremity going before the core, the almost-smile that is not peace but the shape a face makes when it is cold enough, and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody meant to perform, and the perfect reading bought nothing. Through Tallow 11–13, Y.H. 813 the foot stayed dark inside three turns of wool below the sill, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the neighbour with a pail who set hers down without going near; a cold vessel cannot clot, a frozen foot is not rubbed or set to the fire, and the afterdrop waits past a warming nobody means to perform, so the perfect reading bought nothing at two paces and no silt-leach, cause or cure was spoken (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid). On Tallow 18 below the fish-trade shade it was still dark inside three turns of wool, the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the neighbour with a pail who set hers down without going near; the boy read the extremity going before the core, the almost-smile that was not peace and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody meant to perform, and the reading worked perfectly and bought nothing at two paces, with no silt-leach, cause or cure named (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid).

Through Ember 28–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 207–209) the foot stayed the cold to the woman who wound it and weather to the yard, uncured, uncaused and unnamed, below the sill and out of reach of every hand in the Vail kiln-house; the boy read the extremity going before the core and the afterdrop waiting past a warming nobody would perform, and the reading bought nothing (T093/T094/T096 carried, not paid).

\textbf{Cold work.} Work done in cold rooms, especially the greyed-finger labour of a collector; the Court’s phrase for a punishment that damages the hand.

\textbf{Cold-eater.} A Wasteling shape that stands close to a vessel and draws its Warm away; it takes, and does not give.

\textbf{Collector.} An officer of the Warm Court who draws the measure from the dying with a cold iron tube and records it on a slate.

\textbf{College of Assessors.} The academy in the Hearthseat that teaches Ledgerhand and the valuation of lives, and holds the only right to write a lawful deduction.

\textbf{The cord and the mouth.} A saying of the Weir, told sideways: \emph{The cord knows what the mouth will not say, and the mouth knows what the cord will not count. Keep the two apart. Laying them together is a trade no honest house makes.} On Reed 13, Y.H. 813 a reed-cutter at the Weir turned his grey cord once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and bit the end off, and answered a woman who could not read it with \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. The boy set the cord beside the charcoal under the Vail shelf and the empty place in the returning line --- three records in materials no Court thumb can spell --- and kept them side by side and not across. See \textbf{The reed-cutter’s cord (a tally in wool)} and \textbf{Knot-string}. On Reed 18, Y.H. 813 the cutter straightened his grey cord on the flat blessing stone, turned it so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and bit the end off; to a weir woman who said \emph{I can’t read a cord} he answered \emph{No more can the Court}. The cord went back inside his coat with the knots unread and was not laid beside the charcoal under the shelf, the empty place in the returning line or the word forty. On Reed 21, Y.H. 813 the same cutter came along the boards with a bundle, set it on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord oiled by a working thumb, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat, drawing it closed with the flat of his hand; to the woman who said \emph{I can’t read a cord} he answered \emph{No more can the Court} and went to lift a trap with the question going down into the water. No knot was counted, no figure read and no joining made to the missing hand, Mira’s cords or Orra’s knot-string (T099 carried, not paid). On Reed 24 the same cutter came along the plank walk in the morning with a bundle, set it on the flat blessing stone, straightened the grey cord oiled by a working thumb, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat, drawing it closed with the flat of his hand; to the woman who said \emph{I can’t read a cord} he said \emph{No more can the Court}, without anger or smile, and went up the boards with his knots unread, no figure, knot, name or joining (T099 carried, not paid).

On Reed 26 and Reed 27, Y.H. 813 the reed-cutter straightened his grey cord on the flat blessing stone, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and a pull of the thumb, bit the end off and put it back inside his coat with the flat of his hand; to the woman who could not read it he said \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. No figure, knot, name or joining, and the cord was not laid beside the charcoal under the shelf or the empty place in the returning line (T099 carried, not paid). On Tallow 18, Y.H. 813 the reed-cutter at the Weir straightened his grey cord on the flat blessing stone once more, turned it once so the knots stood, tied one low with his teeth and put it back inside his coat with the flat of his hand; to the woman who asked what it held he said \emph{You can ask the cord} and \emph{No more can the Court}. No knot was counted, no figure read and no joining made to the missing hand, Mira’s two cords or Orra’s knot-string (T099 carried, not paid).

\textbf{Council of Tides.} The elected government of Vhalen, composed of ship-owners and salt-masters, whose decrees are written on salt-paper that rots in damp.

\textbf{Court’s room.} The room in Slate Row where the slate is read aloud on market-day and the district’s measure is spoken for; in the Keeping, bank and church are one room. A neighbour come back from it on Stone 19, Y.H. 812 described a bench by the door, a pot on the bench, a draught under it going along the floor to the corner, and a place in the figures where a line should stand and does not --- the same furniture as a birth room, a kiln-house and a death-house, which the boy keeps in four separate places rather than call them one room.

\textbf{Crown.} A gold coin worth twenty silver marks, common in Sere and rarely seen in Grath.

\textbf{Cup-bank.} A procedure for storing Warm outside the body in clay or iron, to be spent later or by another.

\textbf{Cupworm.} A blind worm that bores clay from the inside, so that a pot looks sound and breaks at first pouring.

\textbf{D}

\textbf{Damper.} The iron gate across a kiln’s throat that stops the heat running and lets it out by degrees. The Grathic word carries only the holding; on Seed 3, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail put his bent finger into it ahead of an unfinished sentence, and the boy read it as the same bite that keeps a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man --- mercy and mutilation in one piece of iron, with no word in Grathic that holds both. It is the iron of the Greybank saying about a counting room shut with the damper closed, which the yard takes as history eighteen leagues east and the Vail house keeps under its own roof. On Seed 7, Y.H. 813, Jorra Vail put his bent finger into the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, the cold iron taking the cold out of his fingertip, and the household straightened around his silence as cloth straightens when a weight is lifted; the boy read the same bite that keeps a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no word in Grathic that holds both mercies, and filed the reading as an object worth nothing. On Seed 13, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail again put his bent finger into the damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, the cold iron taking the cold out of his fingertip, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted; he read the iron as the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no word in Grathic that holds both mercies, and filed the reading as an object worth nothing. On Seed 16 he put the bent finger into the cold iron ahead of her sentence again, the iron taking the cold out of his fingertip while the household straightened around his silence; the reading of the double bite was filed as an object, exact and worth nothing, joined to no kiln and still with no Grathic word for both mercies. On Seed 19 he did the same before first grey with men unnamed in the back room; the iron took the cold out of his fingertip, the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted, and the boy read the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man and filed it as an object joined to no kiln. On Seed 22, Y.H. 813 he put the bent finger into the cold iron ahead of her unfinished sentence once more, the iron taking the cold out of his fingertip and giving a little back in reverse of the core; the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence. \textbf{For the first time} Tarn’s broom checked half a beat behind the finger standing in the iron and then went on toward the road without a word or a turn of the head: the two silences stood in one room unjoined, the loan that can hear was not called, and the boy filed the half-check beside the bent finger on one tray without laying a finger across them. On Seed 28, Y.H. 813 he put the bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence again, the iron taking the cold out of his fingertip while the household straightened around his silence, and the boy read it once more as the bite that holds a vessel whole and the bite that can take the hand off a man, one piece of iron and two mercies with no Grathic word for both, filed as an object worth nothing joined to no firing; the debt’s stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check of Seed 22, the stones keeping the place where it had stopped, and the two silences stayed unjoined.

On Reed 2, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail again put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, the iron taking the cold out of his fingertip, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted. The boy read the same bite that keeps a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no word in Grathic for both mercies, and filed it as an object worth nothing, joined to no kiln; Tarn’s broom went on over the flagstones without the half-check while the stones kept the shallow bright patch where the stroke had stopped, and neither man named the other’s silence. On Reed 5, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail again put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, the iron taking the cold out of his fingertip and moving the tongue a hair’s breadth; the end of her instruction arrived at the pot, the household straightened around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted, and he neither answered nor looked at her. The boy read the same bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no Grathic word for both mercies, and filed it as an object worth nothing joined to no kiln; behind the standing finger Tarn’s stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check, the stones keeping the shallow bright patch where it had stopped, and neither man named the other’s silence.

On Reed 11, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted. The boy read once more the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no Grathic word for both mercies, and filed it as an object worth nothing joined to no kiln; Tarn’s stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check while the stones kept the shallow bright patch where it had stopped. On Reed 17, Y.H. 813 Jorra put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing; the boy read once more the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no Grathic word for both mercies, and filed it as an object joined to no kiln. On Reed 21 he did it before Sella had finished telling him the fire was low, moving the tongue a hair’s breadth and leaving it standing; the household straightened around his silence and the end of her instruction arrived at the pot, and the boy filed the double bite as an object joined to no kiln, worth nothing, with the two tellings of the shut counting room beside it and no third. On Reed 23 Jorra put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing, and the household straightened around his silence as cloth straightens when a weight is lifted; the boy read the same bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no Grathic word for both mercies, and filed it as an object worth nothing joined to no kiln.

On Reed 26, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail came through with fine grey slate dust ground small as meal into both forearms past the bent finger, spoke to the wheel before anyone and told a pot \emph{You’ll do}, withheld its full note from a High Kiln kiln-master who said it was singing before its time, and put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, moving the tongue a hair’s breadth and leaving it standing; the household straightened around his silence and the boy read once more the bite that holds a vessel whole and can take the hand off a man, with no Grathic word for both mercies, filed as an object joined to no kiln.

On Tallow 1 and Tallow 3, Y.H. 813, Jorra Vail again put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence; the boy read the one iron with two bites, the holding and the taking, with no Grathic word for both mercies, and filed it as an object worth nothing, joined to no kiln. The kilns had been brought up for the year’s last working season and the danger of the month was the kiln’s breath in fours with a gap, so that the damper’s bite stood in every room without being named twice. On Tallow 5 and 9, Y.H. 813 Jorra Vail again put his bent finger into the cold damper ahead of Sella’s unfinished sentence, moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence; the boy read one iron with two bites, the holding and the taking, with no Grathic word for both mercies, filed as an object worth nothing and joined to no kiln. The two tellings of the shut counting room stood beside it with no third. On Tallow 12, Y.H. 813 (Day 161), for the first time under the Vail roof, Jorra Vail put his bent finger to the cold iron and stopped there while Sella finished telling him the fire was low and wanted feeding; only then did he move the tongue a hair’s breadth and leave it standing. The household straightened around a sentence that had been allowed to finish and nobody said a word of the waiting; the boy read once more the bite that holds a vessel whole and the bite that can take the hand off a man, with no Grathic word for both mercies, and filed the fraction on a place of its own as a change held and unspoken --- not a reconciliation, not a hearing, not a payment, no payer named --- kept apart from Tarn’s unchecking stroke and the nine stoppings (T062/T035/T031, T061/T082). On Tallow 15 he went to the cold damper again with slate dust ground small as meal on both forearms, told a pot \emph{You’ll do}, withheld its full note from a High Kiln kiln-master who said it was singing before its time and that a pot which sings early generally sings itself out early, and held his bent finger at the iron until Sella’s instruction had finished; no pot was lost and nobody spoke of the waiting, the fraction held and unspoken as before and not made a pair with anything (T062, T061/T082). On Tallow 22, Y.H. 813 (Day 171), he went to the cold damper again with fine grey slate dust ground small as meal past the bent finger and under the nails, told a pot \emph{You’ll do}, knew its full note and withheld it from a High Kiln kiln-master who said a pot singing before its time generally sings itself out early, no pot lost; then his bent finger went to the cold iron and \textbf{held} while Sella finished \emph{It wants feeding}, then moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing. The fraction was remembered in the holding and not in a word, nobody spoke of the waiting, and no payer was named. While the finger still stood, Tarn’s broom checked half a beat behind it on the flagstones and went on without a word or a turn of the head; the boy filed the third movement of the equality under the roof on a place of its own beside the Day 161 fraction at the damper and the Day 166 held beat beneath the loaf shelf — three held changes on three places, not a pair, a doctrine or a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer (T062, T036/T076, T100, T061/T082). On Ember 2, Y.H. 813 (Day 181) Jorra Vail again put his bent finger to the cold damper and held it while Sella finished her unfinished sentence at the hearth, then moved the tongue a hair’s breadth and left it standing, so the end of her instruction arrived at the pot and the household straightened around his silence; nobody spoke of the waiting and no payer was named. On Ember 3 (Day 182) the holding was a remembered repetition and not a new change, and the fraction stayed held and unspoken, not paired with the Day 166 beat beneath the loaf shelf or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule. The boy read once more one piece of iron with two bites, the holding and the taking, with no Grathic word for both mercies, joined to no kiln and entered in no slate.

\textbf{Debt left lying.} A debt nobody has picked up, which is not the same as a debt forgiven; a saying kept in the Vail kiln-house in Silt, Y.H. 813, where Garl’s tile debt lay where it lay through seven days of higher water.

\textbf{Debt Loft.} The narrow sleeping loft above a potter’s wheel-shed in Low Kiln where a household’s clay-bound hands sleep. In a poor house a foundling may be given a bed under the roof while a debt is given the loft, and the difference is not argued about.

\textbf{Deep Hand.} The unread script of the oldest slates and seam records; the Vorr recognise its numbers but will not translate it in full.

\textbf{Deduction.} The portion of a banked measure kept back for the Hearth. Taught as one part in twelve and printed on the Weighing notices.

\textbf{Descent.} The Keldish coming-of-age at thirteen: one day down the mine, after which some have their number changed.

\textbf{Dippers.} The salt priests of Vhalen, who bless nets by trailing them in the sea at dawn and read the Sallow draw.

\textbf{E}

\textbf{Eel-bones.} The small bones a Fishstairs seller flicks against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, one put away when the deciding is done. Mira Silt’s are a tell the boy watches without anybody knowing he watches; the movement is entered nowhere.

\textbf{Eight at the Teeth.} A proverb of Low Kiln, said over the last bundles of Reed as the reed month goes out: \emph{Eight times a word may come to the teeth and go back, and eight times is a keeping and not a payment. The reed gives its last bundles to the water and keeps the count in the arm that carried them, and the arm does not know the figure. A word held at the teeth is a word still owed, and when the month goes out the account goes with it into the next house, unread.} It is the eighth of the fire’s proverbs in these tend-weeks: a thing held five times was kept and owed, a sixth stopping did not make it paid, and seven likenesses had still to be held apart by hand or they would stand up as an account with a payer. On Reed 26, Y.H. 813 the sentence about an ear under the Vail roof being worth more than the debt that holds it came to the teeth an eighth time — after Reed 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20 and 23 — and stopped at the word that would call the loan, with no figure and no name; Tarn drew the breath he did not spend and the boy filed eight stoppings on the interval tray as objects and not a rule, intervals and not payments, and would not let eight likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer and no payer had been named to any of the eight. The seventh year stood one tend from its end and had not given. On Reed 29, Y.H. 813 it came a ninth time — a keeping still and not a payment — and the boy filed nine stoppings on the interval tray and would not let nine likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine; see \textbf{Nine at the Teeth}. See \textbf{Five at the Teeth}, \textbf{Six at the Teeth}, \textbf{Seven at the Teeth}, \textbf{Near-saying}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}.

\textbf{Ember.} The Court’s unit of booked warmth, said to be worth five marks; a newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen embers.

\textbf{Empty Cantons.} A province sixty leagues south of Grath with roads, wells and doorways but no people after Y.H. 40.

\textbf{F}

\textbf{The Fenmarch.} The reed and peat confederacy south-west of Grath, governed by reeves chosen for standing longest in a bog.

\textbf{Fen-leech (bog-cow).} A large horned beast of the peat bogs that stands half-submerged and pushes a man down into the mud.

\textbf{The Ferr.} A cold tributary of the Ilm, about forty leagues long, carrying lead dust from the western workings.

\textbf{The field gives back what the fist would not count.} A saying of the Vail kiln-house kept over the middle tend of Grain: \emph{The field gives back what the fist would not count. The yard goes around the place in the returning line and calls it weather. A number goes from the strip to a man’s teeth and back again and is given to nobody. The house keeps its days in loaves and the fire keeps four, four and a gap. Ask the pot. Ask the weather. Nobody is told what the harvest cost.} Through Grain 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 222–224) the first cut grain came off the worked strips east of Low Kiln and the yard counted it in glances and handfuls and never in a figure; with the returning hands the yard went around the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number. The boy took the saying apart as a surgeon takes apart a wound and filed the harvest on a place of its own, with no figure for the grain and no name, cause, body or figure for the hand that did not come back (T098 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{The hands go in by the look} and \textbf{The hand that does not come back}.

\textbf{The Final Banking.} The Unbanked’s design for making every vessel perfectly retentive, so that nothing leaks, nothing is owed, and nothing can be given away.

\textbf{Three readings are three and not one account.} A saying of the rack end in Low Kiln, told in the last tend of Smoke: \emph{The tenth day reads what the ninth would not. The reader goes up the road with the box shut, and the wool lies where it lay. Three readings are three and not one account.} On Smoke 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 269) the third and last reading of the second firing was given over the basket at the Cross; the district’s arithmetic changed for the third time and cannot be changed back, the printed figure stood unchallenged, the figure read was still not the figure paid, and the dressed grain under wool at the rack end stayed unfigured with its price unsigned. The boy kept the finding that a figure read a third time over the same basket is no nearer the covered thing than a chart laid over a covered body is nearer the wound under it, that three readings are three and not one account, and that the not-knowing is as complete after the third as after the first — a finding with no payer, not a lesson, a grievance or a doctrine, and not laid across the house’s not-doings, the covered grain or his own kept gaps (T015/T041/T047, T077, T061/T082). Ch 72. See \textbf{A figure read over a covered thing}, \textbf{Account-day} and \textbf{Handling is not entry}.

\textbf{A figure read over a covered thing.} A saying of the Clay Yard, told at the first market of the second firing: \emph{The slate is read over what the wool covers, and the wool gives back no figure. A bell is four, four and a gap, and the gap has no payer until somebody puts a name under it.} On Smoke 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 249) the district’s arithmetic changed for the first time in Smoke when a figure was read twice over a basket holding a child, while the dressed grain lay covered under wool at home and the figure read over it knew the cover and not the thing; the space between that figure and what the grain had cost had no signature. The figure read was not the figure paid, and neither the gap in the bell nor the gap between the two figures became a hearing, a seventh, a cause or a payer. Ch 66.   On Smoke 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 259) the saying was lived again at the second reading of the second firing: the district’s arithmetic changed a second time and cannot be changed back, the figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, and the dressed grain lay covered under wool on the cool stone at the rack end while the figure read over it knew the cover and not the grain; the space between the figure and the grain’s price had no signature. The gap in the bell went unfilled and no stroke was supplied to make a row come out even, and no name was put under either gap (T015/T041/T047, T077, T078). Ch 69.   Through Smoke 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 264–266) the grain was lifted at a corner for damp on the 25th, drawn wholly out of the wool and turned piece by piece in the flat of a hand for damp and rot on the 26th, with each piece set down where it lay, and turned once with a lighter touch under the wool on the 27th; no figure was given on any day, and the arithmetic that will be read over it on Smoke 30 will still not know what it cost, the space between the figure and its price still unsigned (T077 advanced, unpaid). Ch 71. See \textbf{Account-day}, \textbf{The bell at the Cross}, \textbf{Handling is not entry} and \textbf{What is kept is kept by being covered}.

On Frost 10, Y.H. 813 (Day 279), the first Account-day of the ninth month, the saying was lived again: Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the basket and the dressed grain lay covered under wool on the cool stone at the rack end, read over by a figure that knew the cover and not what the grain had cost, so the space between figure and price had no signature. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself, and the gap was not made a payer or a seventh. Through Frost 11 and 12 the grain was turned once for damp under wool with a lighter touch each morning and given no figure. \emph{The slate is read twice and the grain is read over once, and neither of them knows what the other cost}, the market women said at the Cross on that first Account-day (T015/T041/T047, T077, T078, T080 held). Ch 76.

\textbf{A firing kept in wood (two counts in two materials).} A saying of the Clay Yard, told in the middle tend of Smoke: \emph{A firing kept in wood wants no figure put on it, and a pot set down wrong tells on itself before its time. Two counts in two materials, and neither asks the other what it cost.} The first clause is of a woman’s strip of notched birch, which keeps a count of firings and cannot be turned into an account; the second is of a vessel that gives its note before it has borne heat and is swept around rather than made an omen. Through Smoke 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 252–254) the boy kept three counts in three places — the carried fire’s four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should stand under the floor, the river’s note of water over water through a finger’s-width door, and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot — and would not agree any two, for agreeing them would want a payer and none stood to any. On Smoke 13 Ilva answered \emph{I keep the count, not the account} and no figure came off her strip; on Smoke 14 a pot set down wrong at the drying racks gave its high thin note before its time and was swept around with a practical word about the slip, so no pot was lost, no fourth likeness was made a cause and no name was given to what ailed the man carried out on Day 188 (T061/T082, T064, T080 held, unpaid). Ch 67. See \textbf{Firing-stick (a count kept in wood)}, \textbf{Pot singing early (a pot that sings before its time)} and \textbf{A figure read over a covered thing}.

Through Smoke 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 255–257) the boy kept three counts in three places — the carried fire’s four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should stand under the floor, the river’s note of water over water through a finger’s-width door, and the boards’ four nails, four and a thumb-width knot — and would not agree any two, for agreeing them would want a payer and none stood to any. On Smoke 16 Ilva answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} and no figure came off her strip; on Smoke 17 the dressed grain was gathered in by the handful for the last time before Smoke’s second reading, covered under wool and set away from the hearth with no figure, so the arithmetic read over it on Smoke 20 will not know what it cost; on Smoke 18 frost-bloom wrote white on the well lip and the yard called it weather. The boy’s file, turned out on the towel in the small hours, was exact, complete and worth nothing at two inches of air, with six hearings beside and never among and no seventh, nine stoppings and no tenth, and ninety honest answers on the sixth place, none a reach, a hearing, a key, a power or a rule (T061/T082, T064, T077, T080 held, T083/T085 carried). Ch 68.

\textbf{Firing-stick (a count kept in wood).} A short strip of birch bark notched along one edge, carried in the sleeve by a woman of the firing work in Low Kiln, on which the firings of the month are counted. The notches are pale where a thumb has rubbed them and dark in the uncut grain between. It is kept in wood because a slate would want a figure put on it and the yard has no wish to give the slate one: nothing on the stick waits to be read and no figure comes off it that a clerk could enter and carry up the road. On Smoke 5, Y.H. 813 (Day 244), at the yard well, Ilva drew her strip from her sleeve and passed her thumb-nail across the notches before her eyes went to the woman who had asked and before her mouth answered \emph{Five to this morning}, then put the strip back with the flat of her hand and went on with her water. The hand went to the record before it went to the person and to the pot not at all. The boy took that order of reaching and filed it as the ninth record-first hand on a place of its own beside the eighth, holding it apart from the charcoal under the loaf shelf, the reed-cutter’s cord, the knot-string, the six pages, the tins, the missing hand and the pale line, because two things kept from a slate are not therefore one keeping and nine likenesses must not stand up and call themselves a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood to any (T080 advanced, not paid). On Smoke 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 247) she was seen again at the yard well drawing water with the pail against her knee, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb. This time her hand stayed in her sleeve: she answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{It’s kept where it’s kept. Ask the pot what it cost} — and went on with her water while nobody turned twice. The boy filed no tenth hand-shape; the ninth stays on its own place with a finger between it and the eighth, the notches stay unread and no figure comes off the stick (T080 held, not paid). See \textbf{The tally under the shelf}, \textbf{The reed-cutter’s cord} and \textbf{A record kept in muscle}.

On Smoke 11, Y.H. 813 (Day 250) she was seen a third time at the yard well with the pail against her knee, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and grey rack dust in the seam of one thumb. Asked what the firings of Smoke had cost, she did not take the strip from her sleeve; her hand stayed where it was and she answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account} — and went on with her water while nobody turned to look at her twice. The boy filed no tenth hand-shape: the ninth stays on its own place with a finger between it and the eighth, the notches stay unread and no figure comes off the stick, and the strip is not joined to the charcoal, the cord, the knots, the pages, the tins, the missing hand or the pale line (T080 held at nine, not paid). Ch 66.

Through Smoke 25–27, Y.H. 813 (Days 264–266) she was glimpsed once at the yard well on the 26th, drawing with the pail against her knee, clay pale in her nail crescents and rack dust in one thumb seam; her hand stayed in her sleeve, the notched strip was not taken out or read, and she answered \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}. On the 25th and 27th she was offstage and no figure came to her well. The boy filed no tenth record-first hand; the ninth stayed on its own tray with a finger between it and the eighth, and the count stayed in wood where no slate could take a figure off it (T080 held at nine, not paid). Ch 71.

On Frost 11, Y.H. 813 (Day 280) she was seen once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, clay dried pale in the crescents of her nails and grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb, which she did not scrub out. Asked what the month’s firings had taken now the first reading had gone up the road and the district’s arithmetic changed for a new month that could not be changed back, her hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there; the strip was not taken out, read, asked about or joined to any private keeping, and her eyes went to the asker while her mouth answered the question put and not the one behind it — \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account}. On Frost 10 and 12 she was offstage; no figure came to her well and the firings still stood in wood where no clerk’s thumb could read them. The boy filed no tenth record-first hand; the ninth stayed nine with a finger between it and the eighth, and she does not know she was read (T080 held at nine, not paid). Ch 76.

On Smoke 29 (Day 268) she was glimpsed once at the yard well drawing with the pail against her knee, clay dried pale in her nail crescents and grey rack dust worked into the seam of one thumb. Asked what the firings of Smoke had cost, her hand went toward her sleeve and stayed there; the notched strip was not taken out, read, asked about or joined to the charcoal under the shelf, the cord, the knots, the pages, the tins or any other private keeping, and her mouth answered the question put and not the one behind it: \emph{Ask the pot what it cost. I keep the count, not the account.} On Smoke 28 and 30 she was offstage; no figure came to her well, including through Smoke’s third reading up the road. The boy filed no tenth record-first hand, the ninth stayed on its own tray with a finger between it and the eighth, and the firings stood in wood where no slate could take a figure off them (T080 held at nine, not paid). Ch 72.

\textbf{The First Breaking.} The temple’s name for the single moment of anger in which the world was cracked.

\textbf{The First Firing.} The Grathic coming-of-age at twelve: a child makes a pot, fires it, and knocks it with a knuckle. A clear note means a feast; a flat note means another year in the yard.

\textbf{The first grain (the year’s first cut grain).} The first barley cut off the worked strips east of Low Kiln and carried home under a roof. Through Grain 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 222–224) hands went back into the strips and the first grain of the year came out; Sella Vail took it at the edge of the Clay Yard, carried it under the Vail roof, set it near the hearth and covered it with a fold of wool. The carrying arm read its weight and not its cost, the yard counted it in glances and handfuls, nobody gave a figure and no slate was opened. It lay beside the loaf shelf’s two unnamed gaps without joining them or the fold’s one crust and its empty place, and the yard went around the returning-line place with a look and no number (T077, T098 advanced and unpaid). Through Grain 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 225–227) the bundle was taken out of its covering, beaten open on the flagstones with an ash-wood flail and winnowed so the chaff went up on the river wind; it was spread thin to finish drying, gathered by the handful and poured back near the hearth under wool --- dressed and stored, changed in state three times and given no figure. The arms read its weight and not its cost, the yard counted it in glances and handfuls, no slate was opened and no hand entered it, and the returning-line place was still gone around with a look and no number. It was filed on a place of its own, not across the shelf’s two gaps, the fold’s one crust and its empty place, the pan’s gone round ring or the field’s empty place. See \textbf{A record kept in muscle}, \textbf{The hands go in by the look} and \textbf{What is kept is kept by being covered}.

\textbf{The first opening.} The first firing of a new month under a kiln-house roof, when the keeper puts her hand to the widow’s mark \emph{before} the kiln mouth, holds it one breath and lets go, and tips the carried coal under the back of a broken pot. On Tallow 1, Y.H. 813, after a hundred and forty-nine days of going around every shelf, strip, rack, basket and dusk because none was an opening, Sella Vail performed the first opening of the firing month, and did not touch the mark again at a well, a shelf, an afternoon or a dusk; the rule held exactly with nobody to praise it and nobody to see it broken. The fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed. An opening is a thing done and gone past the way a door is gone past once a man is through it and has put his shoulder to the next. See \textbf{The widow’s mark}, \textbf{The carried fire} and \textbf{The damper}.

On Smoke 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 240), after sixty days of going around shelves, wells, racks, roads and baskets without a touch, Sella Vail performed the first opening of the second firing-month: before the kiln mouth she put her hand to the widow’s mark, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot. The fire took, still answering four low pulls with the fifth missing and no payer named; nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended, and the household put it behind them without a lesson, figure, slate, bond or payer. She did not touch the mark again at a shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on Smoke 1, 2 or 3, because the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. The next real opening, the first firing of Frost, stands far off and unbrought.

\textbf{The First Seam.} The deep survey shaft beneath Keld Keep, where the oldest repairs are recorded and a crossed-out entry of Y.H. 588 is kept.

\textbf{The first way.} The procedure of opening a channel in the forearm by cutting across a surface way and keeping it open while it scars.

\textbf{Five at the Teeth.} A proverb of Low Kiln said over the banked fire: \emph{The reed gives its last third to the water and keeps the count in the arm that carried it, and the arm does not know the figure. Hold a word five times at the teeth and it is a held word still; keep a tally where no thumb can read it and no Court will enter it.} A thing held five times is a thing kept and owed, not a thing paid; five likenesses in a row are five objects on a tray and must not be allowed to stand up and call themselves a doctrine, for a doctrine is an account that has found a payer. On Reed 17, Y.H. 813 the ear-sentence under the Vail roof was held at the teeth for the fifth time and did not become a loan called; on Reed 20 it came a sixth time and stopped at the word with no figure and no name, and the boy filed six stoppings on the interval tray as objects and not a rule. A thing held six times is a held thing still, owed and not paid; see \textbf{Six at the Teeth}. On Reed 23, Y.H. 813 it came a seventh time and stopped at the word with no figure and no name, and the boy filed seven stoppings as objects on the interval tray, refusing to let seven likenesses stand up and call themselves a doctrine; see \textbf{Seven at the Teeth}. On Reed 26, Y.H. 813 it came an eighth time and on Reed 29 a ninth, and nine likenesses must still be held apart by hand or they will stand up as an account with a payer; see \textbf{Eight at the Teeth} and \textbf{Nine at the Teeth}. See \textbf{Near-saying}, \textbf{A kept thing is owed} and \textbf{The tally under the shelf}.

\textbf{The Five (Five Cold Days).} The five days outside the months at the year’s end: Kindling, Weighing, the Long Night, the Remembering and the Last Day.

\textbf{Fish Blessing.} The rite held at the Weir one league upriver of Sill on Ilmen 15 (in Y.H. 813 it fell on Day 44), when the hearth-maids stand on the flat stone with its crossed mark and bless the weir and the eel traps. The traps have their mouths upriver so an eel goes in and cannot find the way out; the eels run whether anybody blesses them or not. A saying of the Weir: \emph{the brook takes what no slate will enter; the knot keeps what no clerk can spell; the eels run whether anybody blesses them or not.}

\textbf{Flat note.} The small dead sound a cracked vessel gives when it is set down or tapped --- the shadow of the full note, a sound that stops at the surface and will not go through. Dan hears it before anyone touches the vessel and has no Grathic word for it. By Stone 12, Y.H. 812 he has heard it five times from four sources --- a cup across a birth room, a pot in the Vail house, the district’s own reading slate twice, and a dying man at the Hearth Drawing, the fifth and the first from a person --- and nobody has tapped any of them for him. On Stone 13 a pot was turned toward before it was set down and gave nothing --- an interval with the shape of a sound, not a sixth hearing, which the boy kept as an object. On Stone 17 a second pot was turned toward under the Vail roof and gave nothing; the two intervals lie on a separate tray from the hearings, On Stone 22 a vessel carried past the Vail door gave it too far and too muffled to confirm, and on Stone 25 a pot cracked all the way through two paces from the basket and was called a pot gone wrong; both went on the separate tray of intervals, and through Stone 30 the count stands at five from four sources with no sixth. On Ilmen 6, Y.H. 813 a pot set down out of a woman’s shadow answered \emph{nearly full} --- a third sound, neither the flat answer nor a silence --- and was filed as the first earthly answer to the interval first kept on Stone 13; it is not a sixth hearing and there is no Grathic word for nearly. On Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813 the small flat knock came out of a woman lifted from the clay-heavy Slip Brook --- the sixth hearing, and the second that had ever come from a person --- and lay beside the five from four sources without being among them; no seventh came. Through Ilmen 16–18 the count stood at six, five from four sources and one from a person; the clerk’s open slate at the Fishstairs gave nothing and no seventh hearing came. On Ilmen 21, Y.H. 813 a vessel carried past the Vail yard door gave its note too far and too muffled to place and Tarn’s head did not turn, and on Ilmen 23 a second pot set down in the Clay Yard answered \emph{nearly full} with air under the note and a want in it; the boy filed the second answer beside the first as an answer to the interval kept since Stone 13, advanced and not paid. The count still stood at six with no seventh, no hand to tap either pot and no Grathic word for nearly.

Through Days 61–67 the count stood at six hearings --- five from four sources and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among, with no seventh; a third pot answered \emph{nearly full} on Silt 6 and was filed advanced and not paid beside the answers of Ilmen 6 and Ilmen 23, while three intervals stayed objects and water-over-water was a fifth low thing that was not a hearing at all. Through Silt 9–15 the count stood at six beside and never among, with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on the afternoon of Silt 15 and Tarn’s head did not turn, and the boy did not call it a hearing. In the flood the note of the whole district went on underneath the four low sounds as a fifth thing with no word in Grathic. Through Silt 16–18 the count still stood at six beside and never among, with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on Silt 16 and a whole vessel did so on Silt 18, and neither Tarn’s head nor the boy’s turned toward either. At the well a foundling turned his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy’s --- after the knuckle and after the note --- and the boy filed that turning with the intervals as a thing that came after the knock and was not a hearing. Through Silt 26–30 and Seed 1 the count held at six hearings --- five from vessels and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among with no seventh; a vessel gave its note past the door on Silt 27 and again on Seed 1 and neither Tarn nor the boy turned toward it or named the sound, and the foundling’s head turned a half-beat late at the market’s edge on Silt 30, which was not a hearing either. Through Seed 2–4 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among; a vessel gave its note past the yard door on Days 91 and 92, Tarn’s head did not turn and neither he nor the boy named the sound or called it a seventh hearing. Through Seed 5–11 they stayed six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh; vessels gave their notes past the door on Seed 7 and Seed 9 and neither head turned nor was the sound named. At the market’s edge on Seed 9 a foundling turned his head toward a pot half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, and stopped and rubbed the green sliver at his throat; the boy filed that delay as a thing that comes after the knock, not a hearing and not a seventh, and kept his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. Three near-full answers stood advanced and not paid, three intervals on another tray, and the river’s note of water going over water was a fifth low thing and not a hearing. Through Seed 2–4 and Seed 5–11 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh, while vessels gave their notes past the door and neither Tarn nor the boy turned toward them or named them. Through Seed 12–14, Y.H. 813 the count still stood at six beside and never among; no seventh came. A woman moving a pot on Seed 12 lifted it a hand’s breadth too high and something came up to the rim of a note and went back down, a near thing kept on the interval tray and added to no seventh, because a thing that comes up to the edge of a sound is not the sound. Through Seed 15–17 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers advanced and not paid, three intervals on another tray, four low things in four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut counting room joined to no kiln; no Grathic word for the flat note and no hand to tap any of them. Through Seed 18–20 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh, three near-full answers advanced and not paid, three intervals, the word forty unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart, four low things in four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room joined to no kiln; the heard bell stayed beside the told bell and no seventh hearing came. Through Seed 21–23 the count still stood at six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and Tarn’s broom checking half a beat behind Jorra’s bent finger standing in the damper on Seed 22 was filed on the interval tray as another place where a stroke should have gone on and did not --- not a hearing, not a seventh, and joined to no cause. The word forty stayed unspoken, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room stayed joined to no kiln. Through Seed 24–26 the six hearings stayed six beside and never among with no seventh; three near-full answers stood advanced and not paid, and the unchecking stroke of Seed 25 — Tarn’s broom going on over the flagstones without the half-check it had made the day before, the stones keeping the place where it had stopped — was filed beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray as another place where a stroke should have gone on and did not, held and not repeated, not a hearing, not a seventh and joined to no cause. The word forty stayed unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the two tellings of the shut room stayed joined to no kiln. Through Seed 27–30 the count stood at six beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with no seventh; the held unchecking stroke lay beside the earlier half-beat on the interval tray with no cause across them, three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and the word forty stayed unspoken and no sixth sighting of the neat dark hand came.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings --- five from four sources and the sixth out of a person --- beside and never among, with no seventh. Three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, three intervals stayed objects with the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat and no cause across them, the told bell stayed beside the heard bell, four low things kept their four places with the river’s note a fifth, and the word forty stayed unspoken with the readable double turn and the weight of a thumb apart. At the market’s edge on Reed 2 the foundling’s head went toward a pot half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, which was not a hearing and came after the sound; no seventh came in the three days. Through Reed 4–6, Y.H. 813 the six hearings stood beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, and the three older intervals lay on one tray with the near-saying stopped at the threshold of the word --- four objects and a stopped sentence, an interval and not a payment, not a rule and not a hearing. The told bell sat beside the heard bell in two places that do not touch, and the word forty stayed unspoken with its readable double turn kept without a name. Through Reed 7–9, Y.H. 813 the six hearings stood beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, three older intervals lay with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and the boy’s held breath, and the two stoppings of the near-saying lay on the same tray as objects and not a rule, an interval and not a payment. No sixth sighting of the neat dark hand came.

Through Reed 10–12, Y.H. 813 the count stood at six hearings beside and never among, five from four sources and the sixth out of a person, with \textbf{no seventh}; three near-full answers stayed advanced and not paid, the older intervals lay on their tray with the half-beat, the unchecking stroke and the boy’s held breath, and now \textbf{three} stoppings of the near-saying lay there as objects and not a rule, an interval and not a payment. The boy refused to let three stoppings stand up and call themselves a doctrine. The told bell stayed beside the heard bell, word forty stayed unspoken, and the charcoal under the shelf was a mark on wood and not a sound.
