Through Tallow 4–10, Y.H. 813 the clean dark line and the new finer grey beside it lay unswept and were called the thaw; the trough by the well stood bare and dark and the water within was called weather by those who did not taste it, and at the going of the light Sella told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it}. A man in Mud End taken quiet in his sleep was spoken of sideways and called merciful, and the boy read that danger as he read the kiln’s breath behind a screen, with no payer named to it. Through Tallow 11–13, Y.H. 813 the clean dark line and the new finer grey beside it lay unswept and were called the thaw; the trough by the well stood bare and dark with its skin of ice gone and the water within called weather, and at the going of the light Sella told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{The house will keep it} while the kiln breathed in fours behind the wall and the carried fire missed its fifth under the floor.

Through Tallow 1–3, Y.H. 813 the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the new finer grey beside it lay unswept and were still called the thaw; the trough by the well had lost the thin skin of ice that had lain on it like a skim of fat set aside in a dish, and the water stood bare and dark while a woman letting down a bucket called it weather. The kilns had been brought up for the year’s last working season and the yard went about the first firing with dust ground small as meal under the nails, the danger of the month carried carefully and without remarks. Sella told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and went on not sweeping the grey.

\textbf{Thin.} A vessel that leaks faster than it takes in; the common condition of the poor, the spent and the returned poor. Also the bottom rank of a vessel.

\textbf{Thin return.} A return in which many measures are pooled and divided among many infants; what comes back is a stranger with a faint interest in a life it cannot name.

\textbf{Thin-child.} \emph{See} The Hollow.

\textbf{Three askings do not make a witness.} A saying of the Clay Yard, told in the last tend of Grain: \emph{Three askings do not make a witness. The weather answers the first, the price of barley the second; the third goes up the terrace while the row stands where it stood. A witness stands somewhere and can be asked, and nobody stood.} It is said of the ownerless question that came over the boards of Low Kiln on Grain 21, again on Grain 23 and again on Grain 26 of Y.H. 813 (Days 230, 232 and 235), in a voice with no owner, no room, no hand at the kiln and no cause. Each asking went off up the terrace with the weather and the price of barley answering it and the row standing where it stood, and nobody leaned in to take the answer down. The boy kept the three tellings side by side on a seventh place with a finger between each pair and a finger between them and the sayings, the tellings, the hearings and the count; three askings are not one witness, not a fourth shaping of the pot saying, not a hearing, not a seventh, not a fifth telling of the burned slate, not a cause and not a name (T101 advanced and unpaid). A fourth asking came on Grain 29 and a fifth on Smoke 8, Y.H. 813 (Days 238 and 247); five askings are still not one witness, and the row still stands where it stood with no name and nobody standing to be asked (T101 advanced and unpaid). See \textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} and \textbf{Two tellings of one absence}.

\textbf{Tide-lore.} The Vhaleni discipline of reading the Sallow draw, taught by the dippers.

\textbf{Triage.} The old-life word for the surgeon’s act of sorting the wounded; Dan’s gift and his heresy in Sarn.

\textbf{Two tellings of one absence.} A neighbour’s saying at the loaf shelf of Low Kiln, from the morning of Seed 12, Y.H. 813: \emph{Two gaps named in one breath become one hunger. Keep your breath for the pot, and keep the bread where it was put.} It is spoken over the old space at the end of the loaf row and the empty place at a child’s ear, which the speaker takes for two things and never sees as one absence. The boy who hears it files the two sayings on two places and writes no cause across the space between them, having learned what likeness laid on likeness will do to a man who wants an answer; the witness is planted for a far-off day when a finger will lay the two places together and an account will want a name (T097). On Seed 18 a second neighbour named the old gap as a thing the planting brought in and went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; the two tellings were kept on two places with no finger laid across them, advanced and still unpaid. On Seed 21, Y.H. 813 a neighbour made a cause of two bare boards in one breath, calling the old space a thing the planting brought in and the new gap the price of a wet thing set down wrong, and went off with her pot without seeing that the two were one absence or seeing the empty place at the boy’s ear; this was a \textbf{third} shaping of the held thing, filed beside the two tellings and the watcher’s late turn, advanced and still not paid, with no joining, no name and no third gap. On Seed 24, Y.H. 813 a neighbour at the shelf again named the old space a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear a child’s appetite in one breath, laying two rooms under one cause without seeing they were one absence; a \textbf{fourth} shaping stood beside the two tellings, the watcher’s late turn and the Seed 21 cause, advanced and still \textbf{not paid}, with no joining, no name, no fourth likeness and no third gap. On Seed 27 and again on Seed 29, Y.H. 813 neighbours at this shelf named the old space at the row’s end as a thing the planting brought in and, respectively, the new palm’s breadth as the price of a wet thing set down wrong and the empty place at the child’s ear as a child’s appetite, each without seeing that two bare boards were one absence or that a room had been joined to a room; a \textbf{fifth} and a \textbf{sixth} shaping stood beside the two tellings, the watcher’s late turn and the earlier causes, advanced and still \textbf{not paid}, with no joining, no name and no third gap, and no finger in Low Kiln laid them together. See \textbf{The loaf shelf}.

\textbf{U}

\textbf{The Unbanked.} The Court’s name for a secret faction of persons of the sealed opinion, descended from the Ash Rising and dedicated to the Final Banking.

\textbf{Unclosed account.} The crime of refusing a lawful collection; the offender is clip-held by the wrist until consent.

\textbf{The Uncollected.} A dead vessel whose Warm has not been drawn and which walks until it leaks into the Waste.

\textbf{Under-seam.} The seam beneath the ground, below which lies the dark where nothing is kept.

\textbf{V}

\textbf{The Vail kiln-house.} The kiln-house in the Clay Yard held by the Vail family for four generations, where Corin is taken in as a foundling.

\textbf{Vhal.} The principal Vhaleni port on the Sallow shore, seat of the Council of Tides, with salt pans and glass furnaces.

\textbf{Vhalen.} The salt republic of port towns on the Sallow, governed by the Council of Tides.

\textbf{Vorr.} A people apart, tall, long-lived, who hold their measure in the bone, keep the Listening Stones and do not undergo the Return.

\textbf{W}

\textbf{Walking thin.} People with the measures of the returned poor who keep moving because stopping is the same as cooling.

\textbf{Warm.} The living, stored heat of which Sarn is made; the poor call it \emph{the warm} and the learned call it \emph{the kept heat}. It has pressure, currents, sources and sinks.

\textbf{Warm Court.} The institution that owns the Hearth, the banks and the Returns and calls itself the Keeping.

\textbf{Warm-stone.} A Keldish stone that holds heat longer than any other substance in Sarn. In Low Kiln a common river stone, warmed at a neighbour’s fire and wrapped in wool, does the same work for a newborn for a few hours; it is not a warm-stone and nobody calls it one. The stone Sella Vail gave Tarn in the winter Garl died is such a common stone, kept two years in an unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft above the wheel-shed, cold and not looked at in a year. On Ember 4, Y.H. 813 (Day 183) he took it out, held it, set it on the sill where the finger’s-width opening let in light, looked at it a long moment and put it back. No word, no figure, no payer, no slate; he did not reconcile the stone with the debt and did not forgive it, for not trying is not forgiving, and the debt stands exactly as it stood. From below the boy heard only the small dry scrape of a pot’s foot set down on stone from a room he cannot enter, and filed it on a place of its own (T006 advanced, T036/T076 advanced, not paid). Through Ember 7–15 (Days 186–194) the stone lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiving; on Ember 13–15 (Days 192–194) the boy kept only the remembering of that dry scrape on a place of its own, not joined to the three held changes and not made a cause (T006 held). Through Ember 16–18 (Days 195–197) the stone lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled by not trying, which is not forgiving; Tarn did not take it out again and the boy filed no new likeness across the scrape (T006 held, T036/T076 held).

Through Ember 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 186–188) the common stone lay back in its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, two years gone and cold, unreconciled with the debt by not trying, which is not forgiving; Tarn did not take it out again, and from below the boy filed the remembered holding as a remembering and not a holding made again, on a place of its own and not stood up beside the Day 161 damper fraction, the Day 166 held beat beneath the shelf or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T006 held, T061/T082).

\textbf{Warm-stone grub.} A beetle larva of the deep mines that eats warm-stone from within and is a sign that a sweating may follow.

\textbf{Warden of the Rim.} The hereditary ruler of Keld; Karric VII closed the Cold Pass in Y.H. 741.

\textbf{The Waste.} The cold country beyond the cracks at the edge of all things, where everything unheld goes.

\textbf{Wastelings.} The bands beyond the Rim who take what the world loses; they have no banks, no Returns and no word for a debt.

\textbf{Water over water (the river’s own note).} The low continual turning a stream makes when it has more of itself than its channel will carry; water going over its own rise. Heard behind the drying racks on Silt 2, Y.H. 813, it is not a vessel’s note and is not counted among the hearings; the district has no word for it and calls it the thaw. The boy files it on a place of its own beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap, and writes no cause across any of them. In the year’s flood of Silt 9–15, Y.H. 813 it became the note of a whole district under strain --- a low turning of many small failures inside one slow, certain one, a vessel of such capacity that no hand in it could have got around it, with a thin place nobody would name. The boy filed it beside the told bell, the heard bell, the early Sill note and the kiln’s gap and wrote no cause across any of them; no one in the district had a word for it or a hand to point at the thin place. At the going of the light on Day 100, Seed 11, Y.H. 813, the river’s low muttered note of water going over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open while the fire’s four, four and a gap came up through the floor, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred days; the boy’s hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water and came down. At the going of the light on Day 103, Seed 14, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note of water going over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming, while the fire’s four, four and a gap came up through the floor under blind ash, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and three days; the boards above kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, and the two counts did not meet. At the going of the light on Day 106, Seed 17, Y.H. 813 the two sounds came in the same two separate places as for a hundred and six days, under the Vail roof where one brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold and the fire’s payer was still unnamed; his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down, and the dark under the roof kept the count of one hundred and six without a figure. At the going of the light on Day 109, Seed 20, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the door standing a finger’s width open, nearer at the going of the water than at its coming, and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and nine days; the boards overhead kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and nine, unspent. At the going of the light on Day 112, Seed 23, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and twelve days; the boards overhead kept four nails, four, and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and twelve, unspent. At the going of the light on Day 119, Seed 30, Y.H. 813 the river’s low muttered note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the kiln’s four, four and a gap came through the floor under blind ash and the back of a broken pot, the two sounds in two separate places as for a hundred and nineteen days; the boards overhead kept four nails and four and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb, the two counts did not meet, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note of water over water and came down with the count standing at one hundred and nineteen, unspent. In the small hours of Day 137, Reed 18, Y.H. 813 the river’s note of water over water came through the door standing a finger’s width open while the carried fire gave four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been through the floor under blind ash, and the boards overhead kept four nails, four, and a fifth that was a knot the width of a thumb: three counts in three places that did not become one. The boy’s hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the note and came down with one hundred and thirty-seven exact, unspent and spoken by nobody.

\textbf{Weather.} The district’s one word for whatever a person can go home warm on. It does not name the thing it is said over; it grants permission to stop looking at it. On Silt 7, Y.H. 813 a washwoman said the water ran fast under the ice and then said weather and went home warm on the word, and a man come back from looking at the honeyed ice was answered with the same word and nodded as though it settled him. Through Frost 7–9, Y.H. 813 (Days 276–278) the word covered the white that would not go off the well lip, the stiffened rope, the skinned trough and the plate of ice Sella lifted and stood out of the path of feet: the yard called all of it weather, nobody gave a figure and no cause, lesson, mending or payer was made of it (T083/T085 advanced, not paid). See \textbf{Frost-bloom}.

\textbf{Weighing.} The second of the Five, when the year’s measures are read aloud and the rich learn how whole they are. In Sill the reading is given in a clean voice that wears a temple’s clothes and takes the speaker neatly out of his own sentences, in the same grammar heard at the Cross; a whole return may be announced for a person who is not in the room.

\textbf{Weighing Hall.} The hall in the Hearthseat where the measures are read at the Weighing and the Hearth-fire burns behind cold iron.

\textbf{The Weir.} The eel traps and plank walk one league upriver of Sill, where the Fish Blessing is held and Rusk walks at dusk.

\textbf{Welled.} The rank of a vessel that can draw on stores held in the world itself — wells, seams or another’s bank — without owning them.

\textbf{Well-draw.} The procedure by which a Welled practitioner draws on a store the world already holds; the level drops for everyone.

\textbf{What is kept in three places does not add up to an account.} A saying of the Clay Yard, spoken at the last tend of Tallow: \emph{The stone keeps the place where the broom stopped, and the iron keeps the finger that waits in it. The fire keeps its fifth where nobody has looked for a hundred days. What is kept in three places does not add up to an account.} It is the yard’s grammar for three kept things that must not be laid together to make a bill: the shallow bright patch on the flagstones where Tarn’s stroke stopped on Tallow 22, Jorra’s finger waiting in the cold damper until Sella’s sentence finished, and the carried fire’s fifth breath missing under the floor with no payer named for a hundred and seventy-two days. The boy kept all three on separate places and would not let them stand up as a rule, for a rule is an account that has found a payer. See \textbf{Half-beat}, \textbf{Damper}, \textbf{The carried fire} and \textbf{Loan that can hear}.

\textbf{What is kept is kept by being covered.} A saying of the Vail kiln-house kept over the dressing of the first grain: \emph{The bundle comes in on the arm and is covered. The flail comes down and the grain comes out smaller than it went in, and no slate is opened over it. Winnow it, cover it again, go around the empty place in the returning line: what is kept is kept by being covered, and the count of it stands nowhere. Ask the pot. The pot has no figures.} Through Grain 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 225–227) the year’s first grain was beaten out of the ear, winnowed on the river wind, dried on the flagstones and poured back under wool near the hearth --- dressed and stored, counted in glances and handfuls and by the carrying arm’s weight, entered on no slate and given no figure. The yard went around the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number, and the two keepings were not laid together or called an account, for a rule is an account that has found a payer and none stood to either. See \textbf{The first grain}, \textbf{The hand that does not come back} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}.

\textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid.} A saying of Low Kiln, spoken at the last market of Tallow: \emph{The slate reads one in twelve and the house keeps its count in loaves. The box goes up the road locked and the bell goes four, four and a gap; what is read aloud is not what is paid.} On Tallow 30, Y.H. 813 (Day 179), the third Account-day and last market of the firing month, Berr Clay read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the basket, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The printed figure stood unchallenged; the figure that went into the slate did not know the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come out. The boy kept the read figure and the paid figure on separate places and made no account of the difference, for a rule is an account that has found a payer. See \textbf{One in twelve}, \textbf{Account-day} and \textbf{The bell at the Cross}.

On Ember 10, Y.H. 813, the first Account-day of the kiln month, the saying held again over the basket at the Cross: Berr read one in twelve and denied the levy with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness; the bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, and a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid. The boy kept the told figure beside the paid figure and the told bell beside the heard bell, made no account of the difference and wrote no cause across them, for a rule is an account that has found a payer.

Through Grain 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 225–227) the saying waits offstage while the year’s first grain is dressed and stored under wool with no figure over it; the printed one in twelve stands unchallenged and the true subtraction stays locked in Berr’s box up the road, held toward the second reading of Grain on Day 229, where a figure will be read over grain that this house has kept, covered and refused to number. Nothing was read or paid under the Vail roof in these three days (T015/T041/T047, T077 held).

On Grain 20, Y.H. 813 (Day 229), the saying stood again over the second reading of Grain: Berr Clay read one in twelve twice over the basket with the dressed grain under wool near the Vail hearth, called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and went off with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done a kindness. The district’s arithmetic changed for the second time in Grain and cannot be changed back; the printed figure stood unchallenged, a figure read aloud was still not the figure paid, and the number read over the basket did not know what the covered grain had cost or answer for the hand that went in on Seed 15 and did not come back. The bell went four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, and nothing reached back under the roof to join the read figure to the dressed grain (T015/T041/T047, T077, T098 advanced and unpaid, T078). Ch 59.

\textbf{Which row did the pot go quiet on?} A question asked over the boards of the Clay Yard in Low Kiln on Grain 21, Y.H. 813 (Day 230), in a voice with no owner, no room, no hand at the kiln and no cause. The weather answered first and the price of barley after it, and the row stood where it stood; nobody leaned in to take the answer down. It is not one of the three shapings of the pot saying (\emph{sings itself out early}, \emph{not heard from since}, \emph{gone quiet on every row come the thaw}), for a proverb about pots and a question about a row are different instruments; it is not a hearing, not a seventh of the full note, not a cause, not a name and not a fifth telling of the burned slate. The boy filed it on a place of its own with a finger between it and the sayings, the slate, the two shut-room tellings, the hearings and the count. A row is a place; a place wants a witness; a witness wants a day when somebody stands somewhere and can be asked. No witness stands yet (T101 planted and unpaid). On Grain 23, Y.H. 813 (Day 232) the question came over the boards a \textbf{second} time in the same voice with no owner, no room, no hand at the kiln and no cause: the weather answered first and the price of barley after it, the voice went off up the terrace and the row stood where it stood. The boy set the second telling on the seventh place beside the first with a finger between the two, and fingers between them and the three sayings, the fourth burned-slate telling, the two shut-room tellings, the six hearings and the count. Two askings are not one witness, for a witness stands somewhere and can be asked and none does; the second asking is \textbf{not} a fourth shaping of the pot saying, a hearing, a seventh of the full note, a fifth telling of the slate, a cause, a name or a fifth witness, but a seed for the far-off day a witness stands somewhere and can be asked (T101 advanced and unpaid). On Grain 26, Y.H. 813 (Day 235) the question came over the boards a \textbf{third} time, low into the boards and not into the basket; the weather answered first and the price of barley after it, the voice went off up the terrace and the row stood where it stood, with nobody leaning in to take the answer down. The boy opened it as a surgeon opens a wound — what it asks, where it stands, what it would want before any man could answer it and who would stand under the answer to pay — and found no witness at the bottom; he set the third telling on the seventh place beside the first two with a finger between each pair and a finger between them and the sayings, the tellings, the hearings and the count. Three askings are not one witness, for a witness stands somewhere and can be asked and none does and none could; the third asking is \textbf{not} a fourth shaping of the pot saying, a hearing, a seventh, a fifth telling, a cause, a name or a fifth witness (T101 advanced and unpaid). On Grain 29, Y.H. 813 (Day 238) the question came over the boards a \textbf{fourth} time, low into the boards and not into the basket, the weather answering first and the price of barley after it, the voice going off up the terrace toward High Kiln while the row stood where it stood and nobody leaned in to take the answer down. Four askings are still not one witness, and no fifth asking came in Grain. On Smoke 8, Y.H. 813 (Day 247) the question came over the boards a \textbf{fifth} time in the same grammar: the weather answered first with a wrong wind off High Kiln carrying the sweet edge of lead glaze across the boards, touching the fold of dressed grain and going out on the wind that brought it, and the price of barley answered after it; the voice went up the terrace while the row stood where it stood. The boy opened the asking as a surgeon opens a wound and found no witness at the bottom. Five askings now stand on the seventh place with a finger between each pair: still not one witness, not a fourth shaping of the pot saying, not a hearing, not a seventh, not a fifth telling of the burned slate, not a cause, not a name and not a row named, held for the far-off day a witness stands somewhere and can be asked (T101 advanced and unpaid). Through Smoke 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 252–254) the question was \textbf{not asked a sixth time}. Five askings stand on the seventh place with a finger between each pair, no owner, room, hand at the kiln, cause, witness or row named; it was not made a hearing, a fourth shaping of the pot saying, a fifth telling of the burned slate, a third telling of the shut counting room, a cause or a name, and nobody stood somewhere to be asked. It is held for the far-off day a witness stands and can be asked (T101 held, unpaid). See \textbf{Three askings do not make a witness}, \textbf{The pot not heard from}, \textbf{Burned slate} and \textbf{Two tellings of one absence}.

\textbf{Whole.} A vessel that holds without leaking; also the rank of such a vessel.

\textbf{Whole return.} A return in which one person’s warmth is kept intact and the person comes back as themselves, with memory.

\textbf{Widow’s mark.} The Grathic institution by which a widow holds a kiln in her own right; the only Grathic institution nobody argues with. A thumb-length of lead-glazed clay with the kiln scratched into it, worn at the throat and touched only before the kiln is opened. The Court’s factor at Greybank confirms the mark; the confirmation is spoken of as a kindness, and kindness is entered. Through Reed 28–30 Sella Vail had gone around a hundred and forty-nine days of shelves, strips, racks, baskets and dusks without touching it, because none of them was an opening; on Tallow 1, Y.H. 813, before the first firing of the month, she put her hand to it, held it one breath and let go, tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot and did not touch it again at a shelf, a well, an afternoon or a dusk. The rule held exactly, with nobody to praise it and nobody to see it broken. Through Tallow 4–10, Y.H. 813 the mark hung where it hung, untouched at the loaf shelf, the yard well, the reed work at the Weir, the reading block at the Cross, the clay road and every dusk, because none of them was an opening; the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Tallow 11–13, Y.H. 813 the mark hung where it hung, untouched at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a bed and a dusk, because none was an opening; the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Tallow 24–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 173–179), the firing month’s last tend, the mark hung where it hung and was touched at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, market, post or dusk, because no hour among those seven days was an opening; on Day 179 Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off without explaining the turn to the basket. The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Ember 1–6, Y.H. 813 (Days 180–185) the mark was touched once — before the first firing of the kiln month on Ember 1, held one breath, with nobody praising the opening and nobody seeing what it mended — and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk on any of the six days; a morning and a shelf are not openings, and the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. See \textbf{The first opening} and \textbf{What is read aloud is not what is paid}. On Ember 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 180), before the first firing of the kiln month, Sella Vail put her hand to the mark again, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot; the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the fifth missing and no payer named, and nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended. Through Ember 2 and Ember 3 (Days 181–182) the mark hung where it hung, untouched at a loaf shelf, a yard well, a drying rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, because none was an opening; the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. Through Ember 4–6 (Days 183–185) it hung where it hung at every shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon and dusk; through Ember 7–9 (Days 186–188) it hung where it hung at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, and was touched at none of them, because a morning and a shelf and a dusk are not openings and the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1, nobody praising it and nobody seeing what it mended. On Day 188 Sella set the basket down at the yard’s edge, turned the boy’s face as she would turn a pot to the light and went wide around the place the carriers crossed, and did not touch the mark; the fire still answered four low pulls with its fifth missing and its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-eight days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 10–12, Y.H. 813 (Days 189–191) the mark hung where it hung at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, a yard, an afternoon and a dusk, and was touched at none of them, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour. On Day 189 Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off through the first reading of Ember and the bell, giving no instruction or reason to the basket; on Days 190 and 191 she went wide around the yard’s unswept places and the place the carriers crossed with a look and a wide step and no number. Nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended; the fire’s payer stayed unnamed for a hundred and eighty-nine, ninety and ninety-one days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 13–15, Y.H. 813 (Days 192–194) the mark hung where it hung at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, afternoon and dusk and was touched at none of them, because a quiet morning after a reading is not an opening and there has been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1. On the three days Sella gave every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, stood a half-pace from every open slate, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, and carried him home at the going of the light without looking at his face; nobody praised the opening and nobody saw what it mended, and the fire’s payer stayed unnamed for a hundred and ninety-two, ninety-three and ninety-four days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 16–18, Y.H. 813 (Days 195–197) the mark hung where it hung, untouched at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon and dusk, because a morning, a shelf and a dusk are not openings and there had been no opening since before the kiln on Ember 1; nobody praised what it mended and nobody saw it broken. Sella gave every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never the basket, said \emph{the house}, kept her half-pace from every open slate, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, and carried him home at each going of the light without looking at his face; the fire’s payer stayed unnamed for a hundred and ninety-five, ninety-six and ninety-seven days (T058/T079, T088). Through Ember 19–30 and Grain 1–30, Y.H. 813 (Days 198–239) the mark hung where it hung at every shelf, well, rack, road, basket, market, yard, afternoon and dusk, and was touched at none of them, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and no reading, harvest or tending is an opening; the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. On Smoke 1, Y.H. 813 (Day 240), after sixty days of going around, Sella put her hand to it before the first firing of Smoke, held it one breath, let go, lifted the clay lid with the back of a hand and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot; the fire took, still answering four low pulls with the fifth missing and its payer unnamed for two hundred and forty, forty-one and forty-two days, and nobody praised the opening or saw what it mended. Through Smoke 2 and 3 (Days 241–242) she did not touch the mark again at a shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk, because the hand goes to it before the kiln and at no other hour; the opening was put behind the household without a lesson, a figure, a slate, a bond or a payer, and the next real opening, the first firing of Frost, stands far off and unbrought (T058/T079, T088). See \textbf{The hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour}.
